parsed.rationale: The speech concerns education and skills policy—specifically increasing women's participation in science and engineering courses and careers guidance services. While it mentions women as a demographic category in post-16 education, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation in public office, or any other aspect of civic/political participation as defined by the suffrage movement's framing.

Gibson Bowles explicitly opposes removing the married women's voting disqualification, calling it a "tremendous change" introduced "casually," arguing that women belong in their "proper sphere" rather than "public and political life," and dismissing separated married women (the primary beneficiaries) as "failures of their sex" least deserving of political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a Bill to regulate and inspect Catholic convents, arguing it lacks evidentiary basis and insults Roman Catholic women. It does not address women's voting rights, political representation, candidacy, or any other aspect of women's civic/political participation; the "liberty" of women discussed is freedom from unwanted state inspection of religious houses, not political rights.

The speech is primarily a legal argument about tax liability and distraint powers under an Income Tax bill, disputing the Chancellor's claim about husbands' goods being liable for wives' debts. The brief mention of "votes for women" is merely a passing reference to something the Chancellor raised, with the speaker explicitly saying he does not know if it is relevant — no argument about women's political rights is made.

The TARGET speech (and Mrs. Dalton's speech embedded within it) focuses entirely on relief distribution for unemployed miners, boots and clothing provision, school feeding, and nourishment for mothers and children in distressed mining areas. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Civil List, Monarchy expenditure, and public accountability for the Royal Family's finances. It contains no arguments for or against women's political rights or representation.
The speech is entirely focused on the plight of Ebbw Vale steelworkers and criticism of Plaid Cymru's political opportunism; it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns financing the Royal Household and the Civil List order, debating the monarchy's costs, staff wages, and taxation immunity of the Sovereign. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech by Mr. Charley concerns the role of Bishops in the House of Lords, defending their presence there on grounds of accountability and historical precedent, and arguing for increasing their number. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speech is entirely concerned with procedural matters regarding the composition of a Select Committee on the Abortion (Amendment) Bill. While it mentions women members in passing (noting four women were included), it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation — the mention of women is incidental to the procedural dispute about committee membership and blocking tactics.

The target speaker dismisses the economic argument for women's suffrage, pivots to attacking the "force is no remedy" slogan used by suffrage supporters, and the broader context (confirmed by the following HUNT speech) shows this speaker is opposed to the Women Suffrage Bill, arguing it lacks a mandate and would lead to undesirable consequences.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) explicitly advocates for women's political rights in the context of India's future constitution, highlighting the inadequacy of women's representation in the franchise, supporting reserved seats for women in legislative bodies, and urging constitutional safeguards against sex discrimination—all clear arguments in favour of women's civic participation and political representation.

The TARGET speaker (the first unnamed speaker, appearing to be an Irish MP supporting the Bill) explicitly endorses extending the ballot to Poor Law Guardian elections and notes approvingly that "women had no difficulty in recording their votes at municipal elections," using this as an argument in favour of applying the same system to Poor Law elections. This constitutes support for women's existing voting rights and their extension to this electoral context.

The speaker briefly but explicitly supports women's enfranchisement in Poor Law Guardian elections, arguing against disfranchising women by pointing to their participation under the School Board ballot system in England as a harmless and established practice.

The speech is primarily about economic inequality, education, taxation, industrial democracy, and trade union rights. The brief mention of "equality for women" refers to forthcoming employment and services legislation (equal opportunities in employment, education, goods and services) and equal pay, not women's political rights or representation.

Mr. Plunket explicitly states he "is entirely opposed to the proposal" and argues it would be undesirable to subject women who have the right of voting to "the inconvenience of going to the polling-places to record their votes," indicating opposition to extending active voting requirements to women in Poor Law Guardian elections. While his primary argument concerns procedural deferral to a Select Committee, his brief remark singles out women as a class whose civic participation should be restricted.

Viscountess Astor explicitly advocates for women's equal treatment in the workforce and political representation, arguing that women deserve "fair play" not privileges, that trade unions wrongly exclude women, that Members of Parliament (elected largely on women's votes) must not forget women's needs, and that the Government should ensure equal training opportunities for women in agriculture and industry.

The speaker (Mr. Walter Rea) extensively argues in favour of women's suffrage throughout the speech, countering anti-suffrage arguments about force/fighting, advocating for including working-class married women in the franchise, and urging the House to pass the Bill's Second Reading. He explicitly states his belief in women's "just rights of representation" and appeals to Members to vote for the principle of women's suffrage.

The TARGET speech by Viscountess Astor is entirely focused on the temperance/prohibition debate — arguing against a Prohibition Bill and in favour of local option for drink control. The only passing mention related to women's political rights is a brief remark that "the drink trade has ceased to have such a hold over the country since the women have had the vote," which is a factual observation rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly urges a fellow MP to vote for the Bill's Second Reading, rebuts opponents' arguments against women's enfranchisement (the "timidity argument" and the "women cannot fight" argument), and endorses removing the "sex barrier" as a necessary step forward comparable to the abolition of slavery.

The speech concerns the phased introduction of a disability pension for housewives, a welfare/benefit policy matter. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech concerns ecclesiastical patronage (the appointment of clergy by bishops) and briefly mentions that in Scotland, communicants including women vote in parish elections — but this is a passing factual observation, not an argument for or against women's political rights. The speech makes no substantive claim about women's civic status or participation.

The speech is almost entirely about the Indian Round Table Conference and the prospects for Indian self-government and federation. The brief mention of women (the women delegates at the Conference who appealed for communal settlement, and a passing reference to women's franchise claims) is incidental and descriptive, not argumentative—the speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights as such.

The speech is almost entirely focused on procedural grounds for delaying the Bill — specifically that a Select Committee is still deliberating on Irish municipal franchise reform — and does not make any substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The single passing mention of "the proposed enfranchisement of female occupiers" is cited only as one example among many topics the Committee has already examined, not as a position the speaker endorses or opposes.

The speaker argues at length against the Women's Suffrage Bill, contending it lacks a popular mandate, that women likely don't want the vote, that women in Parliament would be absurd, and that giving women votes would inevitably lead to undesirable consequences. While he briefly acknowledges women might vote wisely and dismisses one anti-suffrage argument (that women can't fight), these are minor concessions within an overwhelmingly oppositional speech.

The speaker explicitly defends married women's right to unemployment benefit, arguing that women who have paid into insurance have a legal right to benefit and should not be "blackballed and libelled" as spongers, and quotes approvingly the argument that "married women have votes" and that Parliament cannot penalise them. He opposes the Bill partly on the grounds that it unjustly targets married women workers.

The TARGET speech is a brief clarification from the Prime Minister stating that the word used was "sect" not "sex," explaining there was no deliberate omission of women's rights from the constitutional declaration. This is a factual correction about a word choice, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Sir A. Mond) explicitly supports the Women Suffrage Bill, arguing that Members who have voted for Women Suffrage have not lost their seats, dismissing the mandate objection, and contending that the House should lead public opinion rather than follow it. The speech is a sustained defence of women's suffrage against opponents' arguments.

The speaker explicitly states he has supported and continues to support women's suffrage in principle ("I firmly believe that women ought to have a vote in a modified form"), while voting against this particular Bill because it has been expanded beyond the limited Conciliation Bill he pledged to support, making it a broad franchise measure he substantively opposes. This is not merely a procedural objection but a genuine two-sided position: support for a limited women's franchise, opposition to a wider/universal one.

The speaker explicitly states he is "very much in favour of married women possessing their own property," directly supporting a women's property rights measure (the Married Women's Property Bill), which falls within the scope of women's civic rights and full participation in public life.

The speech focuses entirely on education policy — comprehensive school reorganisation, teacher quality, training, and standards — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "he or she" in reference to a head teacher is incidental and not an argument about women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports equal pay for women ("which is quite right... most of us have campaigned for it"), maternity benefits ("quite right"), and women's equal employment opportunities, while raising concerns that the cumulative effect of the Sex Discrimination Bill may paradoxically make employers less likely to hire women. The speaker's objection is a practical/consequentialist worry about the bill's effectiveness, not opposition to women's equal rights themselves.

The speaker (Sir Alfred Mond) spends the entire speech marshalling evidence and arguments in support of women's suffrage, citing petitions from councils and trade unions, women's organisations, the Australian experience, and refuting arguments against the Bill. He explicitly states "We maintain that there is a grievance" and calls opposition "male prejudice."

The speaker explicitly supports women's parliamentary franchise throughout, arguing that women already vote in municipal elections without harm, that their exclusion from the parliamentary register is unfair, and concluding that "women ought to be allowed to have a direct and legitimate voice in the election of Members of Parliament."

The speaker (Sir A. Mond, based on context) argues strongly in favour of women's suffrage, citing Australia's positive experience with women's votes, dismissing opponents' predictions of disaster, highlighting the illogic of allowing women to serve on county councils but denying them the Parliamentary vote, and presenting voting statistics to show women's willingness to participate in elections.

The TARGET speech is a lengthy argument by Sir Wilfrid Lawson in favour of the Permissive Bill to restrict the liquor trade through local veto. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief, passing reference to the defeat of Mr. Courtney's women's franchise bill, used rhetorically to argue that the House should therefore help remedy wrongs suffered by women and children — no substantive position on women's political rights is argued.

The speaker (Mrs. Colquhoun) explicitly supports strengthening the Sex Discrimination Bill and the Equal Opportunities Commission, criticising the Government for failing to adopt amendments that would better protect working women, and advocates for ending discrimination (including against women in employment contexts). Her frustration is directed at the Government's inadequate commitment to women's rights, not at the principle itself.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Women's Disabilities Removal Bill, characterising it as "sentimental nonsense" built on dangerous democratic and socialist principles, arguing that granting women the franchise would undermine natural distinctions between the sexes and lead to harmful social revolution.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Labour Government's handling of unemployment and its legislative programme (Education Bill, Trade Disputes Bill, Electoral Reform Bill), arguing that private Members' time should not be surrendered without a commitment to address the economic crisis. Women's political rights are not argued for or against at any point.

The speaker explicitly advocates giving mothers equal civil and political rights, arguing that women deserve "the fullest political and civil rights, now that they have votes on an equality with men," and frames the amendment as a matter of justice and correcting historical sex bias against women in public administration.

The speaker (Miss Lestor) moves an amendment to remove an exemption that would allow single-sex trade unions to continue excluding members of the opposite sex, arguing that no union should have the right to refuse membership on sex grounds. She explicitly opposes arrangements that would allow men to exclude women from trade organisations, framing this as necessary to prevent disadvantage to women in their professional representation.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) argues forcefully that women in India must have their voices heard in constitutional bodies, criticises the Government of India for indifference and opposition to women's advancement, and entreats the Government to ensure women's full participation in self-governing institutions — all clear arguments in support of women's political rights and representation.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on education funding cuts, the May Committee's impact on local education authorities, and deficiency grants — with only a passing mention of Viscountess Astor as a named member. No argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker (Mr. Meldon) moves the second reading of a Bill to extend the parliamentary franchise in Irish boroughs to all persons occupying houses rated at £1 and upwards, explicitly arguing for equal electoral rights for Ireland as compared to England and Scotland, and works to overcome objections by offering a compromise threshold to enfranchise approximately 27,000 additional voters.

The speaker explicitly states he is voting against the Bill and opposes granting women's suffrage, arguing that women are guided by instinct and intuition rather than reason (which he deems unsuitable for Parliament), and that the franchise would not achieve the practical benefits (higher wages) claimed by its supporters.

The speaker explicitly states he rises "to speak in favour of this Bill" (a Women's Suffrage bill) and systematically dismantles historical and contemporary arguments against women's political rights, concluding that granting women the vote is a matter of justice and inevitable progress. Despite acknowledging personal instinctive resistance, he affirms his reasoned support throughout.

The speaker (Mr. Leif Jones) consistently and forcefully argues in favour of women's suffrage throughout the speech, systematically rebutting opponents' arguments (e.g., that men do the nation's work, that women don't need the vote, that militancy justifies refusal), and urges the House to "vote for the Bill and invite women to stand beside men as full citizens."

The speaker argues against preferential/quota systems for women in trade unions, claiming such "positive discrimination" undermines women's credibility by attributing their positions to sex rather than ability—an argument against one form of women's political representation. Yet she simultaneously announces a government amendment to introduce proportional representation provisions ensuring women's adequate representation on elected union committees, substantively endorsing women's representation in political/civic bodies.

The speech concerns the "married women's option" to pay reduced National Insurance contributions under pension legislation — a social security/welfare policy debate, not a matter of women's civic participation, voting rights, or political representation. The speaker's arguments are entirely about take-home pay, pension benefits, and financial bargains for working married women, none of which engage with women's political rights or representation.

Mr. Wedgwood asks the Home Secretary whether he will use the law to protect meetings of the Men's League for Women Suffrage from being broken up, explicitly framing the disruption as an attack on "freedom of speech on the suffrage question." This implicitly supports women's suffrage advocacy and the right to organise for it.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Guillotine Motion applied to an electoral reform bill, arguing that insufficient time is being allocated for committee debate. While the bill itself concerns electoral changes (business premises qualifications, university constituencies, alternative vote), the speaker never argues for or against women's political rights; the references to "caretakers and charwomen" and city representation are about property/business qualifications generally, not women's civic status specifically.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question by Mr. Chancellor defending the right of the Men's League for Women Suffrage (a non-militant suffrage society) to hold public meetings without disruption, and pressing the Home Secretary to protect that right. This implicitly supports women's suffrage and the political rights associated with it.

The speaker (Miss Richardson) argues in favour of strengthening enforcement of anti-sex-discrimination legislation by conditioning government contracts on compliance, explicitly advocating that the Bill be obeyed and that women be assured of the Government's serious intent to enforce it. The speech is squarely in support of women's equal treatment in the workplace and public life.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly advocates voting for the Women's Suffrage Bill, argues that reform should not be withheld because of militant tactics (drawing historical parallels), dismisses the argument that militancy represents the broader movement, and closes by urging the House to "vote for the Bill and invite women to stand beside men as full citizens of this country."

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment insurance, industrial rationalisation, and the financial burden of unemployment relief in 1931 Britain. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech by Mr. Kinnock focuses entirely on the Welsh Development Agency, economic policy, public ownership, unemployment, and regional development in Wales. While it briefly mentions the extension of democracy to "working men and women" and the ballot box, this is a passing rhetorical flourish about general democratic history rather than an argument about women's political rights specifically.

The target speech is entirely focused on debating electoral reform mechanics — the alternative vote, plural voting, and the fairness of the electoral system — without making any argument about women's political rights or representation. Women are not mentioned or singled out as a class in any civic or political context.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. Newdegate) opposes women's suffrage, arguing there is no civilized precedent for it, that breaking down the "limitation of sex" will inevitably lead to universal suffrage and undermine all other franchise limitations, and that the proposal exceeds even Paine's "rights of man" in its democratic radicalism.

The speech is entirely focused on the merits and drawbacks of the Alternative Vote system for parliamentary elections. The sole mention of women is a passing, non-argumentative aside noting that the Member for Sevenoaks forgot to mention "women Members" when speaking of the ideal candidate, with the speaker briefly remarking that "the word 'man' embraces women" — no position on women's political rights is argued.

The speaker (Mr. Courtney) moves a resolution explicitly calling for women who already vote in municipal, parochial, and school board elections to be granted the Parliamentary franchise, arguing at length that women's suffrage has proven beneficial from experience, that the exclusion of women is "injurious to the best interests of the country," and that enfranchising women would elevate their character and improve public life.

The speaker (Mr. Charles Lewis) explicitly opposes extending the Irish borough franchise, arguing that the proposed new voters are "the lowest, most ignorant, and the most debased" and unfit for civic participation. His brief mention of excluding women from the franchise is used merely as a rhetorical marker to illustrate that the franchise is not a universal right without conditions, not as a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speech concerns the practical mechanics of enabling Service personnel and their spouses to vote in the EEC referendum, addressing registration problems and logistical arrangements. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation as a class; women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the broader category of Service personnel and spouses.

The speaker criticises the Government for failing to honour its promises on Women's Suffrage and argues this makes pressing the current Bill improper and disingenuous, but the underlying argument is that the Government should not have made (or broken) such a promise — the speaker explicitly says "I do not think that they should ever have made that promise." This frames women's suffrage as an inconvenient commitment rather than a right the speaker endorses, and the passage as a whole uses the suffrage promise as a procedural weapon against the Bill rather than as an argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speaker systematically argues against extending the Parliamentary franchise to women, contending that rights and duties must go together, that women cannot perform military or police duties, that public life is unsuitable for women, and that the proposal would subvert constitutional principles — concluding explicitly that he will "vote against it."

The TARGET speeches debate the Representation of the People Bill, focusing on the alternative vote system, university representation, business votes, and Northern Ireland constitutional issues. While women are mentioned briefly in passing (the "flapper vote," the 1918 Act extending the vote to women, and the phrase "one man one vote, or one woman one vote"), no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made — these are incidental references in a debate about electoral reform mechanisms.

The speech concerns the logistics of Service voting arrangements for a referendum, including voting units, ballot box retrieval, advance voting, and the electoral register for Service personnel and their spouses overseas. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns voting arrangements for Service personnel in a referendum, specifically debating proxy voting lists and unit polling stations. While it mentions "men and women" in the Forces, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct class; the topic is military personnel voting logistics, not women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly states "I am a convinced supporter of manhood and womanhood suffrage" and later, responding to an interjection about Women Suffrage, declares "I do not suppose anybody in this House is a more convinced advocate of Women Suffrage than I am," while accepting the Government's pledge to deal with the matter subsequently.

The speech is entirely focused on electoral reform (the alternative vote Bill), party representation, plural voting, university constituencies, and the fairness of the electoral system. While it briefly mentions "men and women" using the ballot, it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct issue.

The speaker (Mr. Newdegate, continuing his speech) systematically argues against women's suffrage by invoking Roman civil law's exclusion of women from public duties, characterizing the proposal as exceeding even Paine's radical "rights of man" theory, asserting no civilized nation has adopted it, and declaring he "always has opposed, and always shall oppose" the proposal before the House.

The speaker seconds a motion to guarantee two women on the Advisory Committee, arguing that women's diverse interests (married vs. unmarried, employer vs. trade union) cannot be represented by a single woman, and explicitly advocates for greater female representation on the committee.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) argues that married women deserve guaranteed representation of at least two women on the Advisory Committee, warning that a committee hostile or unsympathetic to married women could use its regulatory powers to undermine their contractual rights. She explicitly invokes women's hard-won political and civic gains (the vote, admission to professions and universities) to support stronger female representation in the committee's governance structures.

The speaker delivers a sustained, passionate argument in favour of women's parliamentary franchise, contending it is "a plain and simple act of justice," that women bear equal burdens of the state and deserve equal representation, and that their exclusion is as unjust as placing them alongside "lunatics, imbeciles, and criminals." Every substantive argument in the speech supports granting women the vote.

The speech concerns voting arrangements for Armed Forces personnel in a referendum, specifically debating the suspension of proxy vote lists and the inconvenience caused to service members already registered. It does not make any argument about women's political rights or representation; the incidental references to "Service men or women" are purely demographic and carry no argument about women's distinctive civic status.

Both speakers in the target (the first unnamed speaker and Miss Lee) argue against singling out married women for discriminatory treatment under the unemployment benefit legislation, explicitly invoking the principle that such discrimination contradicts the women's movement's gains since 1870 and women's status as voters. They advocate for equal treatment of women regardless of marital status, which is a clear stance in support of women's political and civic rights.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as "a supporter of Women Suffrage" and protests against the tactics of those who link women's suffrage to opposition of the Plural Voting Bill, warning that recrimination will harm the women's suffrage cause. While he criticises the strategy of Mr. Snowden and Mr. Keir Hardie in blocking franchise improvements for men until women get the vote, his underlying position is clearly in favour of women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly opposes the resolution to grant women the parliamentary franchise, arguing that the women's suffrage advocates' own pamphlet reveals they seek universal suffrage and female representation in Parliament, which he treats as grounds for rejection. He concludes by urging the House to vote against it, stating "I oppose the Resolution."

The speech by Mr. David Steel concerns extending the franchise to British citizens living abroad for the EEC referendum, not women's political rights. While he mentions "men and women" working abroad, this is incidental and he makes no argument about women's distinctive civic status or political rights.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure reform — the guillotine, private members' rights, Grand Committees, and obstruction. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as an example of difficulties arising from the Franchise Bill episode, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports enfranchising widows and unmarried women householders as "a plain, matter-of-fact, logical, common sense matter of justice," endorsing the Resolution and citing the success of women's municipal franchise. However, he equally explicitly and "most distinctly and emphatically" opposes the enfranchisement of married women, stating he will "never" see his way to it, making substantive arguments on both sides of the question for different subsets of women.

The speaker explicitly states he has always voted against the women's suffrage motion and will continue to do so, arguing that women do not desire the franchise, that the burden of proof lies with proponents to show demand exists, and that forcing enfranchisement on an "unwilling class" would be an injury rather than a benefit.

The speech concerns the franchise for a referendum and the definition of British citizenship/subjects for voting purposes, not women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "Service men and women" is incidental and makes no argument about women's civic status specifically.

The speaker (a Minister) defends having already conceded the inclusion of at least one guaranteed woman on the Advisory Committee and expresses hope that more than one woman will in practice be nominated, while rejecting the amendment for two as unnecessary. This reflects support for women's representation, albeit with caveats about implementation rather than substantive opposition to the principle.

The TARGET speech (by Bonar Law) is overwhelmingly focused on the Plural Voting Bill, the Act of Union, Irish representation, and redistribution. While he briefly mentions Women Suffrage to note he has never made a speech on it and won't now, and then argues that opponents of manhood suffrage who deny women the vote must implicitly treat women as slaves, these remarks are passing analytical observations rather than a sustained argument for or against women's political rights. He explicitly declines to take a position on Women Suffrage itself.

The TARGET speaker (Earl Percy, based on context) explicitly states opposition to extending the suffrage to women, arguing they are "unfitted by nature" for the franchise, that the cause is failing, and that the existing order—in which women remain dependent on men—is better for their interests. He makes no substantive argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speaker (Bonar Law) explicitly argues that those who hold the principle of equal electoral power for every citizen logically cannot deny votes to women without treating women as non-citizens or "slaves of men" — a pointed rhetorical endorsement of women's suffrage grounded in the equal-rights principle. While he declines to make a full speech on Women Suffrage, this constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's political rights.

The target speech is focused entirely on unemployment insurance policy, government financial management, and electoral politics. While it briefly mentions "working men and women" and "millions of working men and women" in passing, it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on parliamentary procedure reform, particularly Grand Committees and the guillotine; the sole mention of women's suffrage is a passing, incidental reference used as an example of a controversial measure that generates public interest, without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker expresses dissatisfaction that the Government is not offering an alternative for Women Suffrage, noting that public opinion has grown strongly in favour and that people are "profoundly dissatisfied" with the lack of action. This implicitly supports the cause of Women Suffrage.

The speaker (Earl Percy) explicitly argues that women are "unfitted by nature" for the franchise, that they should "remain in their present position" of dependence on men, and that extending the suffrage would wrongly "revolutionize society" by making women independent of men. These are substantive arguments against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Hopwood) consistently and substantively advocates granting women the vote throughout the speech, arguing that the franchise is a small but important concession, that women are intellectually capable of exercising it, and that denying it creates a "great grievance." He dismisses opponents' arguments about divine providence, deterioration of women's character, and women's alleged indifference, and frames women's suffrage as beneficial both to women and to the country.

The speech is primarily about industrial relations legislation (the Employment Protection Bill), covering redundancy, ACAS, trade unions, and economic conditions. The brief mention of women leaving employment due to pregnancy and puzzlement over Clause 45's gendered language are procedural observations about legislative drafting, not arguments for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on Northern Ireland security issues — terrorism, detention policy, incident centres, and communication between the government and Ulster Unionist representatives. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about.

The speech focuses entirely on parliamentary procedure, legislative congestion, devolution, local government reform, employment protection, and defence matters. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speech focuses entirely on National Health Insurance financing, administrative costs, housing subsidies, pensions, and the solvency of approved societies. While women are mentioned incidentally (e.g., married women's sickness claims, maternity and child welfare, and a brief reference to the Parliamentary Secretary being a woman), no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about the Railways Bill, railway rates, and the government's pledge to railway companies. The single passing mention of Women's Suffrage ("I hope he is going to follow the same kind of action in regard to Women Suffrage and see that his promise on that question is not rendered nugatory") is a rhetorical aside drawing an analogy to the railway pledge, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on the financial administration of national health insurance, sickness benefit claims, approved societies, and the medical profession's certification practices. While it briefly mentions "lady Members of the House" and "married women" in passing (in the context of separate actuarial valuations), it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on unemployment insurance policy, government borrowing, and political hypocrisy regarding the Insurance Fund — it makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation. The brief mentions of gendered benefit rates (men 20s./15s., women 16s./12s.) are incidental numerical references to insurance policy, not arguments about women's civic status.

The speaker (Sir Henry James) argues at length that women are intellectually unfit for the franchise, that enfranchising them would harm the country, and that women's proper sphere is marriage and domestic life rather than political participation, explicitly opposing the Resolution to give women the vote.

The speech is about procedural rights to make representations regarding pay sanctions and remuneration limits under a prices/incomes bill. The mention of women is purely incidental — noting that the food industry employs many low-paid workers including women and therefore equal pay issues arise — without making any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker introduces a Bill explicitly aimed at substantially expanding the local government franchise for married women, arguing on the merits that women have a natural interest in local governance matters and that their enfranchisement would benefit efficient local government. While he also mentions a referendum on women's parliamentary suffrage as a secondary object, the overall thrust of the speech is in favour of extending women's political rights at the local level.

The speaker (Lord Hugh Cecil) criticises the Government for failing to honour its pledge to include Women Suffrage in the Franchise Bill, treating that pledge as a binding "obligation of honour" that the Government is shamefully evading. This implicitly endorses the legitimacy of Women Suffrage as a cause deserving fulfilment.

The speaker (Sir Henry James) argues at length against women's suffrage, contending that granting the franchise to women would lead to female dominance in elections, that women's minds are governed by "enthusiasm and sympathy" rather than reason, and that the logical consequence of any concession would be full women's enfranchisement with harmful effects on governance — all substantive arguments opposing women's political rights.

The target speech is a ministerial reply addressing the administrative handling of suffragist prisoners (hunger strikes, medical releases, force-feeding law), not making any argument for or against women's political rights. It deals purely with prison management and legal procedures.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question about British UN voting intentions regarding Israel's potential expulsion, using the International Women's Year Conference abstention only as contextual background. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights; the mention of the Mexico conference is purely procedural context for a foreign policy question.

The TARGET speech by Mr. Prior focuses almost entirely on the Employment Protection Bill — industrial relations law, trade union rights, ACAS, unemployment, and small businesses. The brief mention of maternity arrangements and women's employment concerns only the practical business burden of maternity leave provisions, not women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation.

The TARGET speeches debate electoral reform (plural voting, alternative vote, university representation, election expenses, motor car use) without making any substantive argument about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a brief parenthetical aside by Buchan-Hepburn excluding women voting on their husband's business from his argument about the business vote, which is not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about direct elections to the European Parliament, the Treaty of Rome, Scotland's representation in Europe, and European unity. The passing mention of "men and women elected in Scotland" is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct class.

The target speech merely redirects the question to a previous reply and clarifies a factual error (British Honduras vs. Bermuda), without making any substantive argument for or against women's franchise.

The speech is concerned with UK foreign policy on the Middle East, Israel's UN membership, and the government's voting stance at the International Women's Year Conference in Mexico regarding Zionism resolutions. While it briefly mentions "the rights of women" as the principal objectives of the declaration, this is only cited as context for an abstention decision on geopolitical grounds, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns railway rate regulation, the Railways and Canal Commissioners, and cost allocation between goods and passenger traffic under a railway bill. The single passing reference to "a Suffragist disturbance" is purely illustrative of a hypothetical scenario and makes no argument about women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on the proposal to establish a Volunteer Force in Ireland, arguing for equal treatment of Irish people with English subjects and criticising various Irish grievances. The brief mention of "equal franchise" and "ordinary privileges" for the Irish people is a passing rhetorical point within a broader argument about Irish governance and loyalty, not a substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET moves an amendment requiring at least one woman on every probation committee, explicitly supporting women's representation in public office. The Duchess of Atholl endorses this, arguing it is "absolutely essential" that women be included on probation committees.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question about prison conditions (sanitation, bedding, male warders in female cells) affecting suffragist prisoners, but it does not argue for or against women's political rights — it is a procedural inquiry about the treatment of detainees in custody.

The TARGET contains two distinct speeches: Sir Henry James's continuation (opposing women's suffrage as unnatural and arguing women are unfit for political life) and Mr. Sullivan's speech (strongly supporting women's suffrage for unmarried women, defending women's political capacity, and comparing opposition to historic arguments against Catholic emancipation). Together, the TARGET presents substantive arguments on both sides, with the first speaker opposing and the second supporting women's political rights — though Sullivan explicitly carves out married women, supporting suffrage only for the unmarried/widowed subset.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Sex Discrimination Order for Northern Ireland, criticises those who called it "nonsense" or "rubbish," draws a favourable parallel to the 1918 women's suffrage legislation, and argues that women's equality before the law is long overdue, framing the struggle for equal rights as a positive achievement.

Mr. Jowett is advocating on behalf of suffragist prisoners by raising complaints about their treatment and conditions during transport, implicitly supporting their cause and civic standing. By pressing the Home Secretary to address grievances specific to suffragists as a class, he is supporting their political participation and dignified treatment as political actors.

The speech is almost entirely focused on electoral reform (the Alternative Vote, plural voting, motor cars at elections, university representation) and partisan criticism of opponents. The only mention of women is a passing reference to the right hon. Member for Bewdley having "extended the franchise to women at the age of 21," stated purely as a historical fact with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is an administrative question about prison van conditions and the treatment of suffragist prisoners during transport, focused on procedural/logistical matters (compartment numbers, segregation of sexes, charges). It does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on unemployment policy, government borrowing, and the welfare/incentive effects of the dole on working people. While it mentions "working men and women" and refers to the Minister (a woman) in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech by Mr. Courtney is entirely concerned with the extension of the county franchise to agricultural labourers and related issues of electoral representation, redistribution of seats, and the quality of parliamentary independence — none of which singles out women as a class for distinctive civic rights. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech is primarily about unemployment insurance borrowing and criticises the Labour Government's financial management of the Unemployment Fund. While Viscountess Astor briefly references the first woman Minister of Labour and expresses disappointment at her lack of courage, this is a commentary on an individual politician's performance rather than an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker is asking the Home Secretary to exercise clemency toward a suffragette prisoner, specifically requesting that she be allowed visits from her mother and medical adviser in consideration of her health — implicitly advocating for more humane treatment of a woman imprisoned for suffragette activity, which reflects support for women's political cause.

The speaker opposes extending the franchise to county householders and uses the slippery-slope argument against women's suffrage explicitly: he asks "if every householder had an abstract right to a vote... how could they prevent women from also claiming that right?" — treating this as a reductio ad absurdum to oppose the franchise extension, thereby arguing against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about Sunday closing of public houses (temperance/liquor legislation) and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a brief reference to barmaids and the British Women's Temperance League's petition, neither of which addresses women's civic or political status.

The speech is entirely focused on criticizing tax legislation affecting benefits in kind (company cars, travel concessions, loans, accommodation) for middle-income employees and managers. The only reference to women is incidental ("some young lady living in Braintree" obtaining a season ticket loan), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

Mr. Hunt asks that amendments on "votes for women" be freely debated without closure or guillotine, framing woman's franchise as a significant constitutional change deserving full parliamentary debate — implicitly supporting its serious consideration and fair treatment in the legislative process.

The speech concerns the administration of unemployment transitional payments and the means test under public assistance committees, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic participation.

The TARGET speaker moves a resolution explicitly calling for women who hold the statutory qualifications for local elections to be enfranchised in Parliamentary elections, arguing this is in the best interests of the country and supported by experience in municipal and school board elections as well as Wyoming territory.

The TARGET speech focuses on social services, the economy, housing, health, and the political alignment of working-class voters. The brief mention of women as a majority of the electorate and their potential future political alignment is purely descriptive and does not argue for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on macroeconomic policy—the Budget, pay policy, import controls, inflation, unemployment, and industrial strategy—with no reference to women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related civic status question.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure, committee composition, guillotine motions, and the functioning of "usual channels" between government and opposition. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief passing reference to "votes for women" as a historical example of democracy being fought for, without making any argument about women's political rights.

The TARGET speech debates abolishing property qualifications for membership of municipal governing bodies (Town Councils, Boards of Guardians, etc.), entirely framed around class and property interests of working men versus larger ratepayers. The one mention of women is incidental — noting that the Act of 1869 made women electors for Municipal Corporations and that the Bill's effect would consequently admit women to municipal offices — but this observation is made as a technical criticism of the Bill's drafting, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech by W. E. Forster is entirely concerned with defending the expenditure and administration of the London School Board, addressing questions of educational policy, costs, compulsion, and ratepayer representation. While he briefly mentions "the ablest and most philanthropic men in London—and women too" who served on the Board, this is a passing reference with no argument made about women's political rights or their fitness for civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on supplementary benefits legislation, covering the cohabitation rule, mobility allowance, student benefits, the earnings rule, and occupational pensions. While women are mentioned incidentally (e.g., "women between 60 and 65," wives of invalidity pensioners), the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing Scottish and Welsh devolution and arguing for British unity, with a single passing mention of "suffragettes" as an example of cross-national British solidarity. This mention does not argue any position on women's political rights.

The speaker expresses qualified support for women's suffrage in principle ("at a fitting time, and under fitting circumstances, I should be prepared to assent to a proposal that the same rank should be given to them as to others"), while simultaneously opposing the specific resolution and dismissing key arguments for it as "fallacious" (that franchise is necessary for justice to women or for their elevation), and voting against the motion on procedural and substantive grounds.

The target speech is primarily about political prisoners, freedom of speech, public meetings for the unemployed, and prison conditions. While the speaker briefly mentions the suffrage agitation as a historical analogy to argue that political offenders deserve special treatment, this is used only as a comparative example to support his argument about Communist prisoners — he makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily concerned with the constitutional relationship between the UK Parliament and a proposed Irish Parliament, specifically the powers granted to the Irish House of Commons over franchise, elections, and constituency composition. Female suffrage is mentioned only in passing as one example of a power the Irish Parliament might exercise, without any argument for or against women's political rights per se.

The TARGET speech (comprising maiden speeches by Mr. Peat and Colonel Crookshank) focuses entirely on economic policy — nationalisation, tariffs, free trade, the iron and steel industry, housing, and shipping — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely concerned with Scottish divorce law reform — arguing for the Bill on grounds of adequacy, fairness to those trapped in dead marriages, and the enforcement of maintenance payments. While women are mentioned as beneficiaries of the reform (e.g., battered wives unable to obtain divorce), the speech makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker (Mr. Keir Hardie) explicitly calls for the enfranchisement of women as the proper solution to the suffragette crisis, stating the Government should "bring in a Bill for the enfranchisement of women," and condemns the "Cat and Mouse" Act's administration as torturing women engaged in "what they believe to be a right struggling," expressing sympathy for their cause and demanding humane treatment.

The speaker explicitly states personal opposition to "the general or partial extension of the franchise to women," yet simultaneously supports giving the franchise to registered women graduates for university elections, arguing that the unique conditions of university constituencies justify this exception. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about defence expenditure cuts, the Soviet threat, NATO commitments, and Labour Party politics. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "Service men and women" and "other men and women" in general rhetorical flourishes, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech by the Home Secretary addresses treatment of political prisoners, public meetings for the unemployed, exclusion of foreign nationals, and Dartmoor prison conditions. The brief references to suffragette prisoners receiving special privileges are purely illustrative of precedent for treating certain offenders differently, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is a Home Secretary defending the administration of the "Cat and Mouse" Act — the mechanics of arresting, imprisoning, and releasing hunger-striking suffragette prisoners. The speech focuses entirely on law enforcement procedures and does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or enfranchisement.

The speaker explicitly states he supports the Resolution to remove women's disabilities, arguing that women deserve the franchise as a practical necessity to remedy legal injustices (property laws, custody, education), cites evidence of growing support in Parliament and women's active use of municipal franchises, and concludes with enthusiastic endorsement: "I have the greatest possible pleasure in supporting the Motion."

The TARGET speech (primarily Mr. Leckie's maiden speech, combined with Viscountess Astor's subsequent contribution) is focused entirely on child welfare legislation — juvenile courts, probation officers, reformatory schools, sexual offences against children, women police, and child labour regulations. While Viscountess Astor briefly mentions her husband becoming "an ardent suffragist" and women police recruitment, these are incidental references that do not constitute arguments for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on religious and moral education in schools, defending the provisions of the Education Act 1944, and arguing for the importance of spiritual values in society. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The TARGET speeches (Mr. Hicks and Sir John Ward Law-Milne) focus entirely on conditions of labour, sanitation, wages, trade unionism, and British governance in India. Women are mentioned only incidentally — Mr. Hicks references protecting "women and children" in the context of factory regulations, and Sir John mentions the difficulty of engaging female teachers in India — neither of which constitutes an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Resolution to grant franchise to unmarried women and widows, arguing that women have demonstrated competence in school board and municipal elections without social harm, and that denying them the parliamentary vote is unjustified. Although he qualifies that he cannot go "the whole length" of all women's rights advocates, his substantive argument is in favour of the limited franchise proposed.

The speech concerns the workings of the Abortion Act 1967, the Select Committee's recommendations, and abortion policy broadly — not women's political rights, representation, or civic participation. While women are mentioned as patients and beneficiaries of abortion services, the speech makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "I am one of those who do not agree with votes for women," directly opposing women's suffrage. The surrounding remarks about consulting women before disestablishing the Welsh Church are rhetorical in nature and do not constitute substantive support for women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about Welsh Disestablishment and Disendowment. The brief mention of "Votes for Women" is purely rhetorical—the speaker dismisses it as one of two weak arguments made by an opponent and uses it only to point out that virtually every parliamentary question equally affects women, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech (Sir Henry James) argues substantively against women's suffrage: he contends that married women losing the vote upon marriage is an illogical but inevitable consequence of the proposal, uses Queen Victoria's own words ("We women are not made for government") to argue women are unfit for political life, claims women are naturally subject to influence and unfit for the franchise, and urges the House to reject the Resolution. The rhetorical point about the inconsistency of excluding married women is made to undermine the entire proposal, not to support women's rights.

The speech is primarily about race relations legislation and racial discrimination, not women's political rights. The brief mention that coloured people, "be they men or women," should take their place in Parliament is incidental and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights as a distinct class.

The speech is primarily a passionate critique of the National Government's unemployment policy and the means test, with only a brief passing reference to "votes for women" used purely as an illustrative analogy rather than to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. W. E. Forster) explicitly argues that voting and public affairs are "man's work" and not "women's work," that the majority of women do not desire the franchise, and that giving them the vote would impose unwanted burdens on them. He opposes the motion on substantive grounds, though he acknowledges limited support for women's roles in school board elections.

The speech is about a government pledge regarding Sunday cinema opening hours under the Sunday Entertainments Bill. The brief mention of a past Home Secretary pledging votes for women is incidental and used only as an illustrative example of government pledge-keeping, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about the tied cottage system in agriculture, housing security for farm workers, and related labour relations issues. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is a maiden address focused entirely on unemployment and fiscal/trade policy (tariffs, steel, free trade vs. protectionism). The brief mention of Joseph Chamberlain favouring "an extended franchise to men and women" is a passing historical reference used to praise Chamberlain's foresight on fiscal reform, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that women are unfit for political participation, that "the business of public affairs belongs to men rather than women," that women do not want the vote, and that the franchise would never and should never be granted to women — making a clear and sustained case against women's political rights.

The speech focuses on factory inspection administration, child labour, accidents, truck law, and convictions — not women's political rights. The brief mention of women factory inspectors concerns their professional appointment as labour inspectors, not their civic/political rights or representation, and the passing reference to "suffragist troubles" is purely contextual with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speaker supports giving female graduates the same degrees as men (consistent with the University of London model) but specifically objects to extending to them the right to vote in Convocation, thus endorsing one aspect of women's academic/civic participation while opposing another (membership and voting rights in Convocation).

The speech concerns Northern Ireland border security controls, identity cards, terrorism prevention, and the movement of persons under emergency powers legislation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the security operation workforce ("many men and women"), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The target speech is a factual government reply reporting statistics on prisoners released under the Temporary Discharge Act and a follow-up parliamentary question about detective surveillance of suffragettes. Neither the answer nor the question argues for or against women's political rights; they are purely administrative/procedural in nature.

The speaker explicitly frames the government's announcement as "a victory for trade union male chauvinism," invoking women's interests as a political constituency and implicitly supporting women's right to receive child benefit directly. This reflects support for women's distinct civic standing in the distribution of family resources, consistent with the broader debate about transferring child benefits to mothers.

The speaker explicitly invokes women's suffrage to support the argument for more female factory inspectors, drawing a direct parallel between the Prime Minister's argument against female suffrage and the Home Secretary's claim that male inspectors can adequately cover women's needs — and rejecting both. This constitutes a clear, if brief, endorsement of women's political rights as part of a broader argument about women's workplace representation and inspection.

The target speech concerns Irish national education funding, teachers' salaries, and a transition to the Post Office vote. The brief mention of "females" refers to domestic instruction (cookery/household duties) in schools, not to women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Motion to extend the Parliamentary franchise to women who already have the municipal vote, arguing it is a matter of justice and that eminent women genuinely desire it, citing petitions and a document signed by 108 distinguished women as evidence of women's support for the measure.

The speaker systematically opposes women's parliamentary franchise on multiple grounds: the proposal is "hollow and insincere" for excluding married women, but he also argues that giving women the franchise would harm women themselves, harm men, and destabilize society, concluding by urging the House to "pronounce against a change" and asserting that the majority of both sexes oppose it.

The speech primarily concerns the administration of the "Cat-and-Mouse" Act (Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill Health) Act 1913) and a German spy in prison. While suffragettes are mentioned, the speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights — he merely praises the Home Secretary's enforcement of the Act as a management matter, with no substantive position on whether women should have the vote or hold office.

Viscount Wolmer challenges the Home Secretary's imposition of political conditions (resignation from the WSPU) on a pardon for a suffragette, implicitly defending women's right to political association and participation in the suffrage movement. The question frames such conditions as an improper infringement on a prisoner's "future politics," signalling support for women's political rights.

The speech is a procedural announcement of parliamentary business scheduling, merely noting that a Women Suffrage amendment will be considered at a specific time without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the means test for unemployment benefit, its administration, its effects on family life, and criticisms of the Labour and National Government parties. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "servant girls" affected by the Anomalies Act, a soldier's grandmother), but no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech focuses entirely on local government finance, value for money, public expenditure, and the upcoming district council elections. The single mention of "men and women" as councillors is incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on disarmament negotiations, the Lausanne Conference, reparations, war debts, economic crisis, and monetary policy. The single passing mention of "women and men of the world" voting against war is rhetorical flourish about public opinion on disarmament, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on local government expenditure, council housing policy, compulsory purchase orders, and upcoming district council elections. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.
The speech concerns a query about staffing increases in the Audit Office (clerks and charwomen) and the growth of the Vote, with no reference to women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns whether a third Civil Service Commissioner is justified given the workload, and makes a passing reference to "women and women" as an analogy about variety among individuals, but makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on criticizing the appointment and salary of the First Civil Service Commissioner (Lord Hampton) as wasteful public expenditure. The brief mention of women employed in the War Office is incidental context about budget constraints, not an argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The TARGET speech (by Sir V. Henderson and then Miss Lloyd George) is entirely focused on economic policy, unemployment, government expenditure, housing subsidies, agricultural policy, and fiscal matters. Neither speaker makes any argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic status.

The speech concerns industrial democracy and trade union recognition in the context of aircraft industry nationalisation legislation, specifically arguing that independently certified staff associations should have the right to consultation with the Secretary of State for Employment. It does not address women's political rights, the franchise, representation of women, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech concerns the technical reform of Parliamentary voter registration procedures in Ireland, specifically assimilating Irish registration law to English law. The only mention of women is a passing statistical reference to "female occupiers" being deducted from the count of eligible voters, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns a parliamentary grant to a female orphanage in Ireland, discussing its historical origins and lack of proselytizing practices. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Drought Bill and water supply management — demand growth, reservoirs, water transfer, recycling, metering, and the 1973 Water Act. The brief mention of "the pill" and its trace presence in recycled water is a water-quality aside, not an argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker criticizes the National Government's proposal to reduce benefits for married women under the National Health Insurance scheme, framing it as an unjust "ostracism" of married women and arguing the government had no electoral mandate to "deal with married women in this way." However, the speech does not argue for women's political rights or representation; rather, it opposes a welfare/insurance policy that disadvantages married women as a class. The reference to the electorate is rhetorical, not an argument about women's suffrage or political participation. The speech is substantively about insurance solvency and benefit policy, and women are discussed as beneficiaries of a social insurance scheme, not as political actors seeking civic rights. This is out of scope for women's political rights.

Asquith's speech asks the Speaker to clarify which Women Suffrage amendments to the Franchise and Registration Bill would be ruled out of order, framing this as a matter of parliamentary convenience to avoid "unreality" in debate. While procedural in nature, the speech explicitly facilitates the advancement of Women Suffrage amendments in Committee, reflecting support for their consideration within the legislative process.

The speech is primarily about personal freedoms, democracy, press freedom, and economic policy. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief historical observation that "it was only fairly recently that we gave women the vote," offered as a comparator in a broader argument about the development of democracy — no position for or against women's political rights is argued.

The speaker (Bevan) explicitly acknowledges female voters over 21 as a political force, warning the Government that imposing indirect taxes will cost them at the election because women, as household shoppers, will feel the burden directly — implicitly treating women's enfranchisement as an established and consequential political right. There is no opposition to women's suffrage; the mention affirms women's role as voters whose political power will be exercised against the Government.

The TARGET speech is from the Speaker of the House ruling on a procedural matter — whether admitting Women Suffrage amendments would constitute transforming the Franchise Bill into a "new Bill" requiring withdrawal. The Speaker takes no stance for or against women's suffrage itself, focusing entirely on parliamentary procedure and precedent regarding the scope of the Bill.

The target speech by Mr. Tinker focuses on the financial soundness of the National Insurance fund and the fairness of benefit reductions under Clause 3, not on women's political rights or civic representation. Married and single women are mentioned only as classes affected by benefit cuts, not in relation to their political rights or participation.

The speech concerns a parliamentary debate about the Female Orphan House vote in the Irish Estimates, focusing on procedural and administrative matters such as how the vote was classified and whether it was misleadingly placed. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) argues forcefully against the Bill's differential treatment of women and married women in health insurance, contending that singling out women as a class to bear the burden of their higher sickness claims is unfair and illogical given that women contribute more than they draw in unemployment insurance. She explicitly defends women's equal civic and contributory standing and opposes measures that disadvantage married and single women, advocating instead for a pooling system that would treat women equitably within the State insurance framework.

The speech is entirely focused on the financial/actuarial problems of married women's sickness benefit claims under National Health Insurance, discussing administrative reforms, benefit reductions, and insurance fund solvency. While it addresses married women as a distinct class, this concerns health insurance administration and benefit entitlements, not women's civic/political rights, voting, representation, or participation in public life.

The Prime Minister explicitly states he is personally "an opponent of this cause" of Women Suffrage, yet simultaneously confirms the Government gave a formal pledge to provide full and free opportunity for Women Suffrage amendments and expresses regret that circumstances prevented that discussion—actively advocating for procedural mechanisms to enable women's enfranchisement on behalf of the Government as a whole. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: personal opposition to women's political rights alongside substantive governmental commitment to facilitating their consideration.

The TARGET speech is focused on the procedural consequences of the Speaker's ruling — specifically whether the Government can continue with the Franchise Bill given that Women Suffrage amendments are now precluded — rather than making an argument for or against women's political rights. The speaker explicitly states he is "not going to trench in any degree on the controversial question of its merits or demerits."

The speech concerns parliamentary oversight of a budget vote for charitable institutions (hospitals, infirmaries, and the Female Orphan House) and the transparency of how the vote is presented, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the legal technicalities of the Sexual Offences (Amendment) Bill's Clause 2, specifically debating burden of proof and evidentiary standards in rape trials. While it briefly mentions protecting women's anonymity and fairness to complainants, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is about the tradition of mass lobbying at the House of Commons and the right of constituents to access their MPs; the reference to women's suffrage is a brief historical example used to defend mass lobbies generally, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on Scottish devolution, proportional representation, and the powers of a proposed Scottish Assembly. The brief mention of "the rights of free men and women to make their own decisions" is a rhetorical flourish about self-determination for Scotland and Wales, not an argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct civic class.

The speech concerns alleged atrocities against Zulu tribespeople in South Africa and the Colonial Secretary's evasive answers to parliamentary questions about these matters. While the speech briefly mentions "Native women and children" as victims of colonial violence, this is not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states his party stands "solid and united in favour of women enfranchisement" and argues that the more women included in the Bill, the better, while criticising the Prime Minister's proposed remedy as an insufficient redemption of the pledge to advance women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly states they do not regret the outcome "from the point of view of Women Suffrage" and suggests the next Session will provide a "fairer opportunity" for it, indicating support for women's suffrage. They also note that they and others "on general grounds might have supported Women Suffrage," confirming a pro-suffrage stance.

The speech is focused on police conduct during unemployment demonstrations and the means test, with only a passing reference to "men and women" having the right to democratic expression. There is no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns a Scottish education bill about mandatory retirement ages for teachers over 65, focusing on statistical discrepancies about how many teachers would be affected. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation; the brief mention of "men and women" teachers is purely incidental.

The speech is entirely focused on the economic and industrial decline of Burnley constituency, specifically the textile industry, coal mining, and the delayed motorway construction. Women are mentioned only incidentally as workers affected by industrial decline, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. A. Henderson) explicitly advocates for Women Suffrage, criticising the Government for failing to honour its pledge to support a women's suffrage bill and demanding that the Government take direct responsibility for the Bill rather than leaving it to a private Member. His entire speech is oriented around ensuring women receive the suffrage rights they were promised.

The speaker (Lord Robert Cecil) explicitly supports Women Suffrage throughout, stating it is "one of the first importance," criticising the Government's failure to honour its pledge, and arguing that Members who claim to support it must "give effect to their pledges by their votes." He also expresses solidarity with women's grievances, saying their provocative treatment by Parliament justifies understanding their frustration.

The TARGET speech is entirely concerned with trade policy, tariff reform, and the economic conditions of Birmingham's industries. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status. The brief mention of "men and women in Birmingham" voting for tariff reform is a passing reference to the electorate, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposition to Sunday cinema opening legislation, addressing Sabbatarian concerns, the interests of cinema operators, and charitable proceeds. It makes no reference to women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speech is entirely about the democratic legitimacy of the Tameside council's education policy regarding grammar/comprehensive schools, with no reference to women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related topic.
The target speech is entirely about NHS policy, consultant pay, and private versus public healthcare facilities. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.
