The brief mention of female farmers lacking the vote is descriptive/anecdotal, not an argument for or against women's political rights — Bright dismisses the concern as something that will resolve itself with the mass enfranchisement, without taking a substantive position on women's suffrage.

The speaker (Mr. Pease, a government minister) is discussing the allocation of parliamentary time under a Guillotine Motion for a Registration/Franchise Bill, mentioning women's suffrage only in passing as one topic among many to be debated, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on public expenditure control, parliamentary oversight of government departments (defence, revenue, health, agriculture), the Public Accounts Committee's work, and cash limits. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on Empire migration patterns, economic depression, and the Ottawa Agreements, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The passing mention of "men and women" willing to migrate is purely descriptive and does not address women's civic or political status.

The speech is focused entirely on arguing that the guillotine motion allots insufficient time for debating the Franchise Bill, and proposes a revised timetable with more days. Women's suffrage is mentioned only incidentally as one of several topics occupying Committee time, without any argument made for or against it.

The target speech concerns the Home Secretary's decision not to remit sentences imposed on miners (including two women) following a colliery dispute. The speech addresses procedural matters—the criminal appeals process, the prerogative of mercy, and the basis for the Home Office's decision—without making any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech focuses on objections to applying a municipal election corrupt practices bill to Ireland, discussing franchise restrictions, qualifications, and court bias in Ireland. The mention of women is purely incidental ("In England there was a household municipal franchise, which even admitted women") as a contrast to illustrate Ireland's narrower franchise, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on block grants, local authority finance, the Budget, and social services funding — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "unemployed men and women" is incidental and does not address women's civic status.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the debate over Indian constitutional reform — fiscal autonomy, law and order, federation, and the White Paper proposals — with no argument made for or against women's political rights. The brief mention of franchise comparisons between British and Indian voters (including "15 British women votes for every one Indian woman voter") is used solely to argue for a wider franchise in India generally, not to argue a position on women's political rights as a class.

The speaker explicitly advocates for Women's Suffrage, arguing that women householders should have the right to vote "concurrently with the other electors of the Three Kingdoms" and pressing for parliamentary time to debate and pass the Women's Suffrage Bill before the broader Reform scheme is concluded.

The target speech focuses entirely on education policy — nursery education, maintenance grants for 16-year-olds, and Labour Party education policy — with a brief mention of a "Labour women's conference" only as context for the Prime Minister's speech on family support. No argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about whether the Government will reintroduce a Scottish Secretary Bill; Women's Suffrage is mentioned only in passing as an item on the Notice Paper, with no argument made for or against it.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for a disabled constituent's invalidity benefit claim and criticising the questionnaire and regulations governing that benefit. It does not make any argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in civic/political life; the mention of women is incidental to the disability benefits context.

The speech is primarily a complaint about the inadequacy of the parliamentary timetable for a Reform/Franchise Bill, with women's suffrage mentioned only in passing as one of many topics competing for debating time. The speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights, merely noting that "Woman Suffrage Amendments" will occupy three days of the schedule.

The speaker's argument is focused entirely on procedural fairness in the allocation of parliamentary time for debating the Reform Bill, specifically objecting to a provision that would reduce the Committee stage from eight to seven days if Women Suffrage amendments are ruled out of order. While women's suffrage is mentioned as one subject within the Bill, the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights — the argument is purely about the adequacy of time allotted for Committee debate.

The speaker (Lord Claud Hamilton) argues extensively against extending the franchise to Ireland, contending that the proposed new electorate (Irish cottiers) are "incapable and ignorant," that enfranchising them would hand political power to a disloyal majority, and that the Bill would destabilize the Union. He explicitly supports the Amendment to exclude Ireland from the Reform Bill.

The TARGET speech concerns a procedural motion to adjourn debate on a clause that would disqualify criminals from voting. While the speaker briefly mentions the extension of the franchise to women as a comparison point, he makes no argument for or against women's political rights — the mention is incidental to his main argument about the clause's passage and parliamentary procedure.

The speaker (Mr. Butler) explicitly defends and promotes expanded women's political representation in India, arguing that the proposals significantly increase women's franchise (from 55,000 to 365,000 at the centre) and create reserved seats for women (9 in the Central Assembly, 41 in the Provinces), framing these as meaningful advances for women's political participation.

The speech focuses entirely on Royal Navy service pensions (including pre-1950 widows' pensions as a welfare/financial matter) and Ministry of Defence civilian workers' pay — neither of which constitutes an argument about women's political rights or civic participation. The brief mention of "men and women in the Royal Navy" and "15,000 men and wives eligible to vote as Service voters" is purely descriptive and makes no argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as "an anti-suffragist" while objecting to the procedural arrangement that incentivises voting against Women Suffrage. His substantive position on women's political rights is clearly oppositional.

The TARGET speech is primarily a closing commentary on the taxation of married women debate, noting procedural observations (which parties spoke, absence of women participants) and responding to the Chief Secretary's remarks about "The Forsyte Saga." While it mentions advancing "the condition of women in the face of the tax system," it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation — the debate concerns tax treatment of married women's earned income, not their civic/political participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the constitutional and political arrangements for governing India (the Government of India Bill/Federal Constitution), addressing safeguards, the powers of the Viceroy, Indian legislative bodies, and the relationship between Britain and India. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker (Mrs. Castle) argues forcefully that the unequal treatment of widowers under the parliamentary pension scheme is a "gross injustice" incompatible with modern sex equality legislation (Equal Pay Act, Sex Discrimination Act), and presses for amendments to extend equal pension rights to the male survivors of women Members — an explicit advocacy for equal civic/political treatment of women MPs and their dependants.

The speaker (Under-Secretary of State for India) explicitly defends and promotes the expansion of women's political rights in India, highlighting the 41 reserved seats for women in Provincial Legislatures, the increase in the women's electorate from 55,000 to 365,000 (and over 6,000,000 for women in the provinces), and the first-ever representation of women in the Central Assembly, urging women to take up these opportunities.

The target speech is entirely about the allocation of parliamentary time (days allotted for Committee stage debate) under a guillotine/timetable resolution, and mentions Women Suffrage only procedurally to explain how the day-count arithmetic works. The speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights themselves.

The speech is primarily about taxation policy — specifically the debate over income tax versus VAT — and class-based impacts of expenditure taxes. While the speaker briefly mentions that wives bear the burden of VAT through shopping, this is used as an argument about regressive taxation and class inequality, not as a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about procedural objections to the time allocation for the Report stage of a Reform Bill, arguing for more parliamentary time to debate various clauses. While female suffrage is mentioned in passing as one of the amendments that could affect the size of the electorate, the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily concerned with the Representation of the People (franchise extension) Bill, the relationship between franchise and redistribution, and the conduct of the Government and Conservative Opposition. The brief mention of Mr. Woodall's women's suffrage motion is purely descriptive—noting that it had no chance of passing—without the speaker arguing for or against women's suffrage as a substantive matter.

The TARGET speech is about Scottish representation on a pharmaceutical council, not women's political rights. The brief mention of women asking for "special representation" is used only as an analogy to argue against territorial/group-based representation, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a debate about Conservative vs. Labour economic and social philosophy, the NHS, and the recent election results. The brief mention of "universal suffrage" is purely incidental — used to argue that Conservatism has survived into the modern era — and no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing for a parliamentary inquiry into corruption and mismanagement at Scotland Yard and opposing a Police Bill; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is overwhelmingly concerned with the constitutional conflict between the House of Commons and the House of Lords over the Franchise Bill (extension of county franchise) and the Government's failure to couple redistribution with franchise extension. The brief mention of female suffrage petitions is used only as a rhetorical device to cast doubt on whether the Government has a genuine public mandate for the Bill—it does not argue for or against women's political rights as such.

The speech is entirely focused on employment protection legislation, small businesses, and unemployment policy. The brief mention of "older married women" is a passing reference within a quoted report about employment deterrents, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely devoted to a debate about capitalism, socialism, industrial organisation, wages, and moral/individual change versus institutional change. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women" as generic references to people) without any argument about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker's argument is focused entirely on procedural objections to the Guillotine Motion and the Government directing the Chairman of Committees on the order of Amendments, not on women's suffrage itself. While Women Suffrage Amendments are mentioned as context, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Secretary of State for Scotland's refusal to meet a hunger-march deputation and on specific Poor Law relief administration grievances (health benefits, rent grants, parish settlements, etc.). While women are mentioned alongside men as members of the unemployed deputation, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on procedural objections to the Guillotine motion and the allocation of time for the Report stage of the Franchise Bill; it does not argue for or against women's political rights or suffrage, only protesting parliamentary procedure.

The speaker (Mr. Pease) defends the unusual procedural arrangement precisely to fulfil the government's pledge to Women Suffrage advocates, arguing it is "absolutely essential" to ensure the House can vote on the three Women Suffrage proposals, thereby supporting women's political rights by protecting their debate from procedural obstruction.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question asking Gladstone to clarify which amendment he referred to in a platform speech, and whether he knows Tory members have supported female franchise. While women's suffrage is mentioned, the questioner is not arguing a position for or against it — they are merely seeking clarification and noting a factual point about Tory support.

The target speech is primarily concerned with Egypt, South Africa, and the Franchise/Redistribution Bill debate (extending household suffrage to county householders). While the speaker briefly mentions "men and women" living in degradation among fellow-countrymen, this is a passing rhetorical flourish about poverty, not an argument about women's political rights. The franchise reform discussed throughout concerns male agricultural labourers and county householders, with no substantive argument made about women's civic or political status.

The speaker (a government minister) explains that the Cabinet carefully considered how to give the House an opportunity to debate the Women Suffrage question, and that the unusual procedural measures were necessary precisely to fulfil the Prime Minister's pledge to women's suffrage advocates — indicating support for women's suffrage while justifying the mechanism to protect its debate from being obstructed by opponents.

The speaker (Mr. Booth) argues that "it is the wish of the House and it is perhaps the general wish of people throughout the country that these particular Amendments dealing with Women's Suffrage should be discussed and disposed of," expressing support for ensuring the Women's Suffrage amendments receive proper parliamentary consideration.

The speaker (Mr. Woodall) explicitly advocates for including women householders in the franchise, arguing that the "Old Woman of Warwickshire" and women landowners (one in seven landowners) already exercise all local franchises and cannot logically be denied the Parliamentary suffrage. He announces his intention to move an Amendment in Committee to extend the franchise to women, and argues the Bill would be incomplete without it.

The speech is entirely focused on the Lucas Aerospace workers' corporate plan, industrial strategy, job preservation, and the morality of arms production. Women are mentioned only in passing (e.g., "men and women" referring to workers and citizens generally), with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (comprising Major Nathan's budget critique and Viscountess Astor's speech on the Beer Duty) is entirely focused on fiscal policy, the brewing industry, taxation, and the National Government's budget decisions. While Viscountess Astor briefly mentions that having "a woman in the Cabinet" might have produced more imaginative policy, this is a passing rhetorical flourish rather than an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on reforming illegitimacy laws and the legal disadvantages faced by children born out of wedlock. While it briefly mentions "Blacks, women and Jews" as groups protected against discrimination by statute, this is used only as a comparative point to highlight the lack of protection for illegitimate children, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is focused entirely on parliamentary procedure — specifically the Guillotine Resolution, the Chairman's powers, and the precedent being set for future procedure. Women's suffrage amendments are mentioned only as the occasion triggering this procedural dispute, not as a subject on which the speaker argues for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a licensing/pub hours bill, debating temperance reform and the recommendations of a Royal Commission on drinking hours. The brief mention of women is only in passing ("if the women of the industrial areas had to vote on this question, there would be a unanimous feeling in favour of keeping the present hours"), which is a rhetorical point about public opinion on pub closing times, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on unemployment benefit cuts, the financial burden on local authorities, and the removal of parliamentary oversight over unemployment commissioners. Women's political rights and representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The target speech is a procedural point of order concerning whether amendments on women's enfranchisement are in order and whether their cumulative effect could transform the Bill — it does not argue for or against women's political rights themselves, only about parliamentary procedure for handling related amendments.

The speech focuses entirely on housing conditions, public expenditure, economic policy, unemployment, and the Budget, with no arguments made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic status. Women are mentioned only incidentally as residents affected by housing problems or as working mothers needing childcare support, neither of which engages with women's distinctive civic or political status.

The TARGET speech (Colonel Makins) is entirely about the Deceased Wife's Sister marriage law debate, opposing a change in marriage law on social, religious, and legal grounds. The only mention of women's political rights appears in the seconder's speech (Colonel Milne-Home), which is part of the TARGET block — he briefly speculates that "some day, perhaps, we should have female suffrage" and suggests waiting for women to vote before changing the marriage law, predicting women would support retention. This is a passing rhetorical flourish used to argue against the marriage bill, not a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states that when his colleague Mr. Woodall moves his Amendment in favour of including women householders in the franchise, "he knew of no consideration which would induce him to falter in supporting it," directly endorsing women's inclusion in the franchise extension.

The TARGET speech is from the Chairman of the Committee, explaining procedural rulings on the order and effect of amendments regarding the word "male" and women's suffrage. It makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights, but only addresses whether amendments are in order and what the procedural consequences of various votes would be.

The speaker explicitly states he is "prepared to stand—metaphorically, of course—before the cannon's mouth, to prevent the 'Old Woman of Warwickshire' from obtaining the franchise," directly opposing women's enfranchisement. He also dismisses women's suffrage as negligible compared to the agricultural labourer question, reinforcing his opposition.

The speech is entirely concerned with the financial mechanics of the Unemployment Assistance Bill—Exchequer contributions, local authority contributions, administration costs, and fund solvency—with only an incidental mention of women in the context of training expenditure figures (£81,600 for women). No argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The speech is about parliamentary procedure, Select Committees, and democratic efficiency. The mention of women's enfranchisement is purely a historical marker ("since the enfranchisement of women, there have not been any major structural changes") used to frame the timeline of democratic development, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on NHS funding, hospital management, industrial unrest, nurses' pay, and the specific case of the Elizabeth Garrett Anderson hospital closure. While the EGA hospital is historically associated with women's healthcare, the speaker argues for its retention on grounds of NHS funding, cross-regional financing, and administrative mismanagement — not on the basis of women's civic status or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Franchise Bill of 1884 and the question of redistribution of seats, arguing against passing the bill without an accompanying redistribution scheme. Women's political rights are never mentioned, and the debate concerns extending the franchise to working-class men and the balance of rural versus urban representation.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) explicitly draws on her experience as a woman to argue that indirect influence is inadequate and demoralising, and that direct representation through the vote is essential — directly endorsing women's political rights as the foundation of her broader argument for proportional representation and more representative democracy.

The speech is entirely focused on education policy — comprehensive schools, assisted places, school meals, transport, and parental choice — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "more women were going out to work during the war" is an incidental historical observation, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on trade union law, industrial relations, closed shops, picketing, political funds, and related labour policy. The sole brief mention of women is a passing reference noting that equality of the sexes existed in the trade union movement "long before there was legislation on the matter," based on the principle of equal pay — this is a descriptive historical aside, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about extending the franchise to working men (agricultural labourers, artisans, miners, and Irish voters) and related redistribution and electoral reform issues; women are never mentioned as a class, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely devoted to explaining the Unemployment Bill — its insurance principles, assistance provisions, juvenile unemployment measures, and financial arrangements. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "100,000 women" qualifying for extended benefit, a reference to Miss Bondfield as a predecessor), with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic status.

The target speech is a parliamentary notice question about whether Gladstone's reported remarks at Preston correctly characterized the women's franchise amendment as a Tory complication tactic. Gladstone's brief reply confirms the report but clarifies he was not referring to the Member for Stoke. Neither the question nor the answer makes any substantive argument for or against women's political rights — they are solely concerned with accurately characterizing Gladstone's prior statement and parliamentary conduct.

Viscountess Astor explicitly advocates for giving Indian women adequate franchise, arguing that "women are the key to progress in India" and urging the Government to follow the Lothian Committee's recommendations for women's representation. She supports women's political rights both in India and references the positive legislative impact of women's suffrage in Britain.

The speaker (Mr. Butler) reassures supporters of Indian women's franchise that the White Paper includes a commitment to making "franchise arrangements suitable for Indian women," and that the Joint Select Committee will give the matter serious consideration — thus expressing governmental support for extending political/voting rights to women in India.

The speech is entirely about procedural points of order regarding an instruction to a Bill on increasing Northern Ireland's parliamentary seats, focusing on proportional representation and the cognate nature of the instruction. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about; the only reference to women's political rights is a passing citation of the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill 1928 as a precedent for cognate instructions, with no argument made about women's political rights themselves.

The speech is a maiden speech focused entirely on unemployment, local government in Dundee, economic regeneration, Scottish devolution, direct-labour organisations, and Zimbabwe/sanctions. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "unemployed man and woman") with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states he is "opposed to any form of Female Suffrage for Parliamentary elections" and will "vote against all the Amendments," arguing that women's minds are deficient in the faculties needed for political action (citing Herbert Spencer), that Female Suffrage would lower the intellectual quality of the electorate, and that it lacks an electoral mandate. His support for women's local government roles and municipal vote does not constitute substantive endorsement of parliamentary political rights but rather reinforces his position that women are suited only to local administration, not parliamentary franchise.

The speaker congratulates Viscountess Astor for championing women's franchise in India and suggests that a general demand for women's votes in India could be referred back to India for consideration, implicitly supporting the cause. The speech engages positively with Astor's advocacy for Indian women's suffrage, treating it as a legitimate proposal worth taking seriously.

The speaker (Mr. Woodall) moves a clause explicitly extending Parliamentary suffrage to women, arguing at length that female householders are "capable citizens" deserving the franchise, citing their economic contributions, existing participation in local elections, and the logical consistency of the Bill's own principles with women's enfranchisement.

The speaker (Mr. Stansfeld) explicitly and repeatedly advocates for women's suffrage, arguing he would be "false to those women whose cause we advocate" if he voted against the clause, insisting the women to be enfranchised are capable citizens, and declaring he will vote in favour of Mr. Woodall's women's suffrage clause. He states there is "no subject on which I am more convinced, or on which I feel more deeply."

The speaker (Mr. M'Curdy) explicitly and repeatedly argues in favour of women's suffrage, contending that the Government has a clear mandate for it, that the Prime Minister's pledges must be honoured, that the denial of women's suffrage undermines liberal principles of no taxation without representation, and that the honour of Parliament is at stake in giving women a fair hearing on their enfranchisement.

The speaker explicitly opposes proposed immigration regulations on the grounds that they "openly and blatantly discriminate against women," argues that women should be treated as "equal citizens," and refuses to vote for measures that would give British women fewer rights than women elsewhere in the EEC — a clear substantive stance in favour of women's equal civic rights.

The speaker explicitly condemns the White Paper's rules as discriminatory against women, calling them "shameful and inexcusable rules that discriminate against women," and cites this as a reason to vote against the proposals — thus actively supporting women's equal political and civic rights.

The speaker explicitly states "Believing as I do that Women Suffrage is an evil, I must vote against it on all the Amendments which are designed to enact it," and argues at length that women are physically incapable of military/police defence, ill-suited by temperament and training for diplomacy or imperial problems, and would be "a weakness rather than a strength as a governing factor." While he notes internal consistency issues among partial-suffrage supporters and prefers adult suffrage over narrower proposals as a matter of logic, this is a tactical critique of his opponents rather than any substantive endorsement of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing for the preservation of the Victoria hospital in Romford on NHS funding and community grounds. While it briefly mentions the Elizabeth Garrett Anderson hospital (a women's specialist hospital) as a positive precedent, this reference is incidental and no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The speaker extensively and substantively advocates for women's political rights in India, arguing for women's franchise on equal terms with men (opposing the application requirement and higher educational qualifications imposed by the White Paper), calling for women's representation in elected bodies and upper chambers, criticizing the removal of Burmese women's seats while denying them the franchise on their husband's qualification, and praising the Joint Select Committee's concessions on women's franchise and representation while pushing for further reforms.

The speech concerns Australian and UK licensing laws, with a passing mention of "working-class women's vote" only as a historical footnote about a 1945 referendum result, without making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a lengthy argument about Indian constitutional reform, self-government, economic justice, and the structure of the proposed federal constitution. While it briefly mentions "the subjugation of women" as one of several social evils persisting under British rule, and the preceding Secretary of State's speech refers to women's franchise in passing, the target speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights as a distinct question.

The speaker explicitly states he is "not prepared" to see the franchise extended to all women on equal terms, and that he believes this "would be bad for the women themselves, and bad for the State." Despite having previously supported a limited women's franchise for over twenty years, he now concludes that any extension inevitably leads to full women's suffrage, which he opposes, and declares he will vote against the Amendment.

The speaker (Mr. Newdegate) characterizes women's suffrage as "the despotism of Democracy" and frames pressure on the Prime Minister to adopt it as an illegitimate exercise of democratic coercion, clearly opposing the principle of women's suffrage.

The speaker consistently argues that women's suffrage is a just cause deserving a fair hearing, insists that Parliament's repeated majorities in favour of it must be honoured, and states that women deserve recognition of "the principle that they ought to have representation in this House." While he raises procedural concerns about whether the current vote can truly be "free and unfettered," these are objections to the conditions of the debate, not to women's political rights themselves—he explicitly supports the cause and calls for a genuine opportunity to decide it on its merits.

The speaker (Mr. Leatham) argues at length against enfranchising women, contending that the "feminine element" would introduce emotional instability into the electorate, that women are inherently incapable of the independence required for political participation, that the analogies to municipal and school board voting are false, and that women's nature and proper sphere preclude them from the duties and responsibilities of men—concluding that the women's suffrage movement's own aims reveal an undesirable radical transformation of society.

The speaker (Mr. Stansfeld) explicitly and repeatedly declares his strong support for women's suffrage, arguing that women of property and competency are fully capable citizens deserving the franchise, that excluding female heads of household makes the Bill a "declaration in principle and for ever against the political emancipation of women," and that he intends to vote for the clause and work to make women's suffrage a matter of practical party politics.

Miss Horsbrugh explicitly supports the expansion of women's franchise in India, welcoming the Lothian Committee's recommendations and the Joint Select Committee's proposals to increase enfranchised women with lower qualifications, and quotes the report's assertion that India cannot reach its aspirations "until its women play their due part as educated citizens."

The speaker explicitly states he will support the women's suffrage amendment, arguing that women already exercise political functions, that excluding them from voting is arbitrary given they can vote in municipal elections, that the vote is a modest and reasonable reform, and that it is a "conservative change" that will conciliate opinion without great risk. His objection to women sitting in Parliament is explicitly separated from the question of suffrage and framed as a personal aesthetic preference about the character of the assembly, not a substantive argument against women's political capacity.

Gladstone explicitly acknowledges women's suffrage as a question deserving "fullest consideration" and declares it an "open question" he will not bind his colleagues on, while simultaneously offering "the strongest opposition in my power" to introducing women's enfranchisement into the current Reform Bill — distinguishing between women's fitness for local duties (which he endorses) and their participation in parliamentary politics (which he treats as unsettled and too weighty to decide here). This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: genuine recognition of the merits of women's political rights alongside substantive opposition to their extension at this juncture.

The speech focuses entirely on the constitutional arrangements and self-government prospects for Ceylon, discussing the Donoughmore Commission, the role of the Governor, and colonial governance. While it briefly mentions that the Constitution enacted "manhood suffrage and a large amount of women suffrage," this is a passing factual reference to the content of the Ceylon Constitution rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (the maiden speech portion) explicitly argues against women's suffrage on multiple substantive grounds: that working-class women showed no enthusiasm for "Votes for Women," that his election result showed women opposed it, that Parliament has no mandate for the change, that granting women the vote would be irreversible and potentially dangerous to the Empire, and that Parliament has already adequately looked after women's interests through legislation. The speaker states his earlier limited support was changed by the election result, and he now opposes the Amendment entirely.

The speech concerns the Nurses, Midwives and Health Visitors Bill, specifically debating the training, education, and professional organisation of health visitors, nurses, and midwives within the National Health Service. There is no argument made about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker (Viscount Folkestone) explicitly states he has long been "a most strenuous opponent" of women's franchise and led successful opposition to a prior bill, while simultaneously announcing he will vote for the current motion enfranchising women — grounding his switch in the logic that since the Bill grants suffrage as an individual right to all householders including illiterate ones, excluding women would be an unjust "degradation." However, he explicitly reserves the right to oppose women's suffrage again in future legislation built on different principles, making substantive arguments on both sides.

The speech is focused on parliamentary procedure regarding scrutiny of Supplementary Estimates, with only a passing mention of non-contributory invalidity benefit for disabled married women as an illustrative example of how small sums face intense scrutiny compared to large uncontested estimates. No argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure — specifically the government's motion to take private members' time — and only briefly mentions women's suffrage as a historical example of reform that originated with private members' bills, without arguing for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Gwynn, MP for Galway) explicitly states he will vote for the Amendment giving women the vote, grounding his support in a conviction of justice and drawing an analogy between the Irish nationalist cause and the women's suffrage movement. He argues that Parliament has repeatedly affirmed the principle of women's votes while refusing to act on it, and that justice demands recognising the changed status of women.

The speech focuses entirely on economic and domestic policy issues — shipping, housing, unemployment, wages, and criticism of the National Government's record — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic status.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly supports women's suffrage, arguing that women are equally qualified to vote as men, that taxation without representation is unjust, that women already have local voting rights which should be extended to Parliament, and that he personally cannot "decline to give women an equal right to vote with men." He also presented a petition of 7,600 men in favour of Women Suffrage and states he "cordially supports" the Amendment.
The speech addresses economic recovery, unemployment, trade protection, imperial air communications, and world peace, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on parliamentary procedure, the Public Accounts Committee, the Comptroller and Auditor General, and parliamentary reform. The brief mention of "men and women in the Department" is incidental and does not argue any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports votes for women, arguing there is no natural difference between male and female that disqualifies women from political participation, and predicts that opposition to women's suffrage will soon be seen as backward as opposition to Catholic emancipation once was.

The speaker explicitly states he will "vote against the Amendment," concluding that "the defeat of the Amendment on Monday will involve the least evils to this country." While he acknowledges strong arguments on both sides and expresses nuanced uncertainty, his substantive position is that women's suffrage should not be enacted now—citing lack of popular mandate, absence of government backing, and inappropriate use of the Parliament Act—and he ultimately casts his vote in opposition.

The speaker (Mr. Newdegate) explicitly and emphatically opposes female suffrage throughout, arguing it is "unnatural," contrary to Biblical teaching on women's dependence on men, rejected by women in the United States, and would cause the House to "forfeit the small remnant of the title to represent the manhood and the manly feeling of England." He concludes by urging the House to "again reject[] this most dangerous proposal."

Sir Joseph Pease explicitly states he has "always consistently opposed the conferring of the franchise upon women" on principle, and throughout the speech argues against women's suffrage on multiple grounds: that paying rates does not entitle women to vote, that enfranchising women would lead to "petticoat government," destroy domestic harmony, and inevitably lead to women sitting in Parliament—all framed as reasons to reject the clause.

The speaker (Miss Lestor) explicitly states she would be "totally opposed" to positive discrimination giving women seats in Parliament, which constitutes a substantive position against one form of women's political representation. While she expresses hope that women's long wait for representation won't be repeated for ethnic minorities, her opposition to structural mechanisms for ensuring women's representation in Parliament places her against that aspect of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly references his own imprisonment in connection with the suffrage movement and argues that women suffragettes were unjustly prosecuted ("persecute and prosecute women by the hundreds") while Carson and his allies faced no consequences, framing this as evidence of unequal treatment under the law and implicitly supporting the legitimacy of the suffragettes' cause.

The speech is entirely focused on taxation policy, public expenditure, and the distributional effects of the Conservative Budget, with no reference to women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or related civic participation issues.

The TARGET speaker explicitly supports the Amendment to include women in the franchise, arguing that there is genuine public demand for female suffrage, that women are mentally and physically fit to vote, and that denying them the vote is "a slur upon that much vaunted progress." He contends that the principle of disqualifying women from "the full rights of citizenship" is unjustifiable and that the trend of civilisation favours enfranchising women.

The TARGET speech is primarily about the Incitement to Disaffection Bill and debates about liberty and sedition law. The brief mention of Miss Christabel Pankhurst and suffragettes is only an incidental factual claim about foreign financing, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports Service wives' right to vote on equal terms with civilians, endorsing their demand for an optional registration system and calling for abolition of the attestation process and "S" marking that have prevented large numbers of women from exercising the franchise.

The speaker (Baron Henry De Worms, Member for Greenwich) explicitly and consistently supports women's suffrage throughout the speech, arguing that women with property qualifications have at least an equal claim to the franchise as the 2,000,000 men proposed to be enfranchised, rebutting arguments against women's fitness for political participation, and declaring he will vote for the Motion of the hon. Member for Stoke to enfranchise qualifying women.

The speech concerns VAT on female sanitary products and argues for reducing or removing that tax burden, which is a consumer/tax policy matter affecting women as consumers. While the speaker is a woman and references women's concerns, the speech makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of civic participation that constitutes women's political rights as defined in scope.

The speech is entirely focused on procedural rules under an Unemployment Insurance/Assistance Bill, concerning the rights of unemployed persons to fair procedure and Parliamentary oversight of the Unemployment Assistance Board. Women are not mentioned and women's political rights are not addressed.

The speaker (Colonel King-Harman) explicitly argues in favour of the amendment to extend the franchise to women, contending that qualified women have as much right to vote as the 2,000,000 new male voters proposed by the Bill, and concludes by stating he will vote for the amendment and that granting women the suffrage is "absolutely necessary."

The speaker (Mr. Beresford Hope) explicitly states he has "always objected to female suffrage, as being contrary to what I believe is the manifest order of Nature, contrary to good policy, and an innovation greater than any that has ever been tried," and declares he will vote against the Woodall clause enfranchising women, describing female suffrage as "a step so much more objectionable" that he would sacrifice even a bill he dislikes to defeat it.

The speech is a maiden speech focused entirely on the speaker's personal background, constituency description (Perth and East Perthshire), unemployment issues, and industrial relations. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker dismissively mocks the suffragette movement by suggesting that "scolding places" (platforms for hysterical women to scream) would have prevented it, implying women's political activism is irrational hysteria rather than legitimate civic participation. He also sarcastically singles out Viscountess Astor (a female MP) as someone who would have made best use of such a place.

The speaker (Colonel King-Harman) explicitly declares he will vote for the Amendment enfranchising women, argues that women with property have "every right as citizens to vote," dismisses opponents' arguments as unworthy, and maintains that female suffrage is "absolutely necessary" and should be "immediately granted by this Bill."

The TARGET speech is a procedural government response declining to provide information about the formation of a Women Suffrage Committee, without making any argument for or against women's political rights. It merely states that the matter rests with supporters of the movement and that the Government cannot supply the requested information.

The speech is entirely focused on Army Estimates, military spending, recruiting fitness, mechanisation, clothing costs, and defence policy; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speaker (Austen Chamberlain) explicitly and consistently opposes women's suffrage throughout, arguing that women's qualities are unsuited to political governance, that admitting women to the franchise would be a social and political revolution best avoided, and that passing the measure would be a "great misfortune for women, and a great misfortune for the State." He never endorses women's political rights at any point.

The speaker (Austen Chamberlain) explicitly declares himself "an opponent of the admission of women to the franchise" and argues at length that women's qualities—greater sentimentality, rigidity, and lesser capacity for compromise—make them less suited for political participation, and that their admission would constitute an undesirable social and political revolution.

The speech focuses on immigration rules, deportation of a specific constituent, freedom of information, and NHS cuts during the recess. The brief mention of "foreign husbands of women who are British citizens" is a reference to immigration policy, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns abortion policy and the 1967 Abortion Act, arguing against the Corrie amending Bill on grounds of NHS resource allocation and access to abortion services. While it touches on women's welfare in the context of abortion, it does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Austen Chamberlain) explicitly states "I hold that the passage of Women Suffrage would be a great misfortune for women, and a great misfortune for the State," and argues throughout that women's suffrage is a dangerous social revolution without public mandate. His objections to the current Bill's procedure are subsidiary to his substantive opposition to women's suffrage itself, which he has held consistently from the start of his political life.

The speaker expresses long-standing support for women's suffrage in principle ("I have advocated the extension of the franchise to certain women") while simultaneously opposing this specific clause because he doubts women's moral judgment in public matters (citing the Oxford election), argues that certain women ("a body of female householders and lodgers") should be excluded, and insists the question is not ready to be decided and should not be "pitchforked into this Bill." This is not merely a procedural objection—he raises substantive doubts about women's fitness for the franchise and explicitly withholds his vote from the Amendment, making it a genuine two-sided position.

Mr. Wedgwood's question presses the Prime Minister to ensure a Women Suffrage Amendment is passed into law before any dissolution, demonstrating active support for women's suffrage being enacted. He explicitly advocates that women in the country and his followers attach "utmost importance" to securing not merely an opportunity but actual enfranchisement.

The speech concerns the disenfranchisement of mental patients under the Representation of the People Act 1949, arguing for their right to vote regardless of residential circumstances. Women are not singled out as a class for distinctive civic rights or duties; the issue is about mental health patients broadly, not women's political rights specifically.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a Scottish Poor Law reform Bill, addressing issues such as disability pensions, outdoor relief, treatment of casuals, removal of the aged, and anti-Irish prejudice. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speech concerns the administration of unemployment assistance — specifically whether commissioners should delegate powers to voluntary organisations — and objects to the term "reconditioning" as applied to unemployed men and women. While women are briefly mentioned alongside men as recipients of unemployment benefits, no argument is made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment assistance regulations, scales, and the means test, debating the merits of the 1930 Labour Act versus current regulations. The brief mention of women receiving a 2s. increase in benefit is a factual point about unemployment benefit scales, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states he has voted for and continues to advocate women's suffrage (specifically for spinsters and widows), yet votes against the current amendment, not merely on procedural grounds but because he draws a substantive line stopping short of married women ("there I stop") and because he judges the timing would undermine the broader Reform Bill. This constitutes genuine two-sidedness: substantive support for one subset of women's suffrage paired with substantive opposition to the broader proposal before the House.

The speaker explicitly criticizes the disenfranchisement of women in Palestinian municipal elections, arguing that women are denied the vote to artificially suppress the Jewish majority (since Arab women would not vote but Jewish women would). He treats this as a clear injustice, supporting women's right to vote.

The speech is entirely focused on prison overcrowding, the burden on prison officers, and penal reform (alcoholics, mentally disordered offenders, remand prisoners). While women are mentioned incidentally (e.g., "men and women" in prison, elderly women on remand in Holloway), no argument is made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states "I am strongly opposed to female suffrage" and argues at length against the suffrage movement, invoking divine law ("the husband shall rule over her"), dismissing the agitation as dishonest and unscrupulous, and expressing no substantive support for women's political rights at any point.

The speech is entirely focused on a procedural instruction to divide a Reform Bill into two separate parts (franchise and registration), arguing on grounds of parliamentary precedent, complexity, cost, and legislative efficiency. While women's suffrage is briefly mentioned in passing (as one of many controversial franchise topics bundled into the Bill), the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage throughout, arguing it is anomalous to deprive women of the franchise by "the mere accident of sex," systematically rebutting objections (military service, incapacity, danger to the state), and declaring he has never given a vote with greater satisfaction than supporting the motion for female suffrage.

The speech is entirely focused on the Northern Ireland prison hunger strike, political/special category status for prisoners, IRA and Loyalist violence, and sectarian conflict. Women's political rights and representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker explicitly states he will vote for the Amendment extending Parliamentary franchise to women, arguing that the admission of women to local administrative voting logically cannot be separated from the local legislative vote, and that compromise between suffragists and anti-suffragists should be sought rather than full opposition. While he raises nuances about conscription and certain male-only subjects, his overall position is clearly in favour of women's suffrage in some legislative form.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on the procedural argument that the Franchise Bill should be divided into two separate Bills (franchise and registration), using historical precedents from 1884 and arguments about Parliamentary overloading. While the speech briefly mentions "women's suffrage" in a Gladstone quotation as one of many topics Gladstone deliberately excluded from his 1884 Bill, the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "I myself do not want to deny to women the opportunity of having their position discussed" and "I shall vote in favour of Adult Suffrage being extended both to men and women," indicating support for women's suffrage. His objection is procedural — that the bill's structure puts supporters of women's suffrage in a false position — not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on NATO defence policy, defence spending levels, and the White Paper on Defence Estimates 1980. While it mentions "men and women" serving in the armed forces in passing, it makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is overwhelmingly focused on the merits and risks of Indian self-government reform, arguing that the proposed legislation benefits a small political class at the expense of the Indian masses. The sole mention of women is a passing reference to whether "certain women ought or ought not to have votes" as an example of a secondary administrative detail that distracted from what the speaker considers the real issue — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech concerns immigration policy regarding Filipino domestic workers who entered the UK by deception, not women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned as a class only in the context of immigration enforcement, not in relation to voting, holding office, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech concerns football pool betting statistics and a clarification of Post Office revenue figures, followed by Viscountess Astor's speech about the moral welfare of juveniles and gambling regulation. Neither portion argues for or against women's political rights; the brief mention of "women Members" is incidental and makes no argument about their political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Third World poverty, the Brandt report, development aid, the Horn of Africa crisis, and global economic inequality. The brief mention of women ("They work from dawn till dusk—particularly the women") is purely descriptive of rural poverty and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker notes approvingly that Burmese women rejected reserved seats in the Legislature, preferring to compete in general constituencies on equal terms, and reports that 21% of adult women will be on the electoral roll — both statements implying support for women's political participation on equal footing. While the speech is primarily about Burma's constitutional separation from India, it explicitly addresses women's franchise and representation in a positive framing.

The speaker raises extensive objections to women's enfranchisement: questioning the clause's scope regarding married women, arguing that women's suffrage inevitably leads to women sitting in Parliament (which he strongly opposes), and concluding that he holds "a very strong objection to their being brought into political life at all," explicitly stating he will vote against the clause.

The speaker dismisses most arguments for women's suffrage as weak abstractions, and argues substantively that women are insufficiently informed about politics, lack independent political knowledge, and do not constitute a class with separate interests requiring protection — concluding that extending the franchise would produce a worse Parliament and urging Parliament not to "thrust upon them political duties, for which the vast majority of them are still unprepared."

The speech is entirely focused on the economic situation and industrial prospects of the West Midlands, arguing for optimism about the region's recovery. Women's political rights and representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The target speech is primarily a procedural argument criticizing an Instruction to divide a Registration and Franchise Bill, accusing the mover of obstructionism. The only mention of Women Suffrage is a passing remark that a supporting speaker used the Instruction as a pretext "to deliver a speech out of due season with regard to Women Suffrage," which is a criticism of parliamentary procedure rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Inderwick) argues explicitly and at length against women's political enfranchisement: he contends that the real aim of the suffrage movement is full womanhood suffrage and women's seats in Parliament, warns that checks and safeguards would be swept away, and concludes that "to allow the political enfranchisement of women would be injurious to the State," declaring he will vote against the clause. The following speech by Mr. Joseph Cowen, which is part of the TARGET block, argues strongly in favour, but Hansard has concatenated both speeches into the TARGET; taken as a whole the TARGET contains both positions — however the instruction is to classify the TARGET as a whole. Given that the TARGET includes Inderwick's clearly "against" speech and Cowen's clearly "for" speech as two separate, complete contributions, the combined TARGET represents substantive arguments on both sides.

The speech is entirely about greyhound racing regulations and betting restrictions. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference to "every man and women over 21 years of age has the vote," used as a rhetorical point about personal autonomy in gambling, not as an argument about women's political rights.

Lieut.-Colonel Moore explicitly asks whether funds under the Land Settlement (Scotland) Bill are available to women as well as men, raising the question of equal civic/economic access for women. By posing this question in Parliament, the speaker is advocating for women's inclusion in the land settlement scheme, signalling support for women's equal participation rights.

The Target speech is a procedural ruling by the Speaker on whether substantial amendments to the Franchise Bill would require introduction of a new Bill. While Female Suffrage amendments are briefly mentioned as one factor creating uncertainty about the Bill's final shape, the Speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights — the mention is purely incidental to a parliamentary procedure point.

The TARGET speaker (identified as Mr. Labouchere/Mr. Bryce by context, but from speech content clearly a Liberal MP opposing the clause) argues substantively against women's suffrage on multiple grounds: that no civilized country has adopted it, that women and men have distinct functions making women unfit as electors, that enfranchising women would lead to "petticoat government" and women in Parliament, and that the timing is inopportune. He explicitly states "I do not think it is" when asking whether electoral power is a function women would adequately discharge, and calls for voting against the proposal.

The speaker (Sir Wilfrid Lawson) unambiguously and at length advocates for women's suffrage, arguing it is right on principle (taxation and representation), refuting opponents' arguments about clerical influence, fighting capacity, and partisan advantage, and urging the Liberal Party to support Mr. Woodall's clause enfranchising women householders.

The speech is entirely focused on geopolitical strategy regarding the Soviet Union, Afghanistan, nuclear arms control, economic summits, and Third World relations. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues in favour of women's suffrage, criticising opponents for relying on "transcendental" and sentimental arguments rather than practical ones, and defending the supporters of Mr. Woodall's clause from misrepresentation by Mr. Goschen regarding the lodger franchise — explicitly standing behind the practical, moderate demand for women's admission to the franchise.

The TARGET speech focuses on defending the Home Secretary's use of forcible feeding of suffragette prisoners, framing it as humane rather than torture, and referencing the paradox of suffragettes' demands. While women's suffrage is briefly mentioned (Pankhurst and Kenny shouting "Why don't you give us the vote?"), the speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights — only about the legality and morality of prison administration.

The TARGET speech is concerned with procedural matters about private Members' Bills and parliamentary time allocation, only mentioning the Women's Franchise Bill incidentally as an example of a Bill with House support. The speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights themselves.

The speaker (Miss Richardson) explicitly argues that women deserve direct representation on the Social Security Advisory Committee, noting they are not a minority (52% of the population) and are major beneficiaries of the social security system, and presses for at least three women to be appointed among the committee's members.

The speech is entirely focused on trade union liability for libel, the Trades Disputes Act, and the legal status of unincorporated bodies. The brief mention of the "Anti-Suffragist Society" and "Suffragists' Society" is used only as illustrative examples of unincorporated bodies in a legal argument, with no position argued on women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on Budget policy, unemployment, taxation, trade, and economic matters. Women are not mentioned as a distinct class, and no argument about women's political rights, representation, or civic participation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speaker criticises an Ordinance that deprives women outside Tel Aviv of the municipal vote, pointing out the anomaly of women being able to vote in one town but not the rest of the country, implicitly advocating for equal women's suffrage across Palestine.

The speaker defends the ordinance that restricts women's municipal voting rights to Tel Aviv (implicitly supporting the exclusion of women from the franchise in other municipalities), while simultaneously noting that machinery exists to extend the vote to women in other areas via a two-thirds majority resolution — effectively supporting women's voting rights in some contexts but not universally.

The speech concerns representations about child benefit levels and asks the Secretary of State to take note of them, including from the Conservative Women's National Advisory Committee. While it mentions a women's organisation, the subject matter is child benefit policy, not women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I am in favour of women having the franchise" and provides two practical reasons supporting women's suffrage: that enfranchisement historically elevates the condition of those admitted, and that women voters would strengthen the Radical Party's causes of peace, sobriety, and education. He also criticises opportunists who oppose the measure for partisan reasons.

The speech is entirely focused on the merits of flogging as a punishment for procurers and those who exploit women and children, as part of a debate on a Criminal Law Amendment Bill. While women and children are mentioned as victims of crime, the speaker makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on the legal and medical implications of specific wording ("substantially," "serious," "grave") in the Corrie Bill's amendments to the Abortion Act 1967, arguing for clearer legislative drafting and clinical freedom for doctors. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Sir Stafford Northcote) explicitly states he has "continually supported, or, at least, have never opposed" women's suffrage over 16-17 years, argues substantively that excluding women property holders from the franchise is unjust, and advocates for giving 400,000-500,000 women householders the vote, framing it as a matter of right and fairness against the enfranchisement of less-qualified male voters.

The speech is primarily about juvenile employment, raising the school age, and labour policy. The brief mentions of women ("women are deeply disappointed" regarding juveniles, and "so unfair to women" regarding insurance) are incidental references that do not argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the administration of a health insurance fund for exempted persons, focusing on medical and sanatorium benefits, contribution rates, and fund management. While women are briefly mentioned as one class of beneficiaries (underpaid girls living at home), the speech makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

Viscountess Astor explicitly supports the Bill, which is backed by women's associations, and appeals to Members to allow it to proceed to a vote rather than obstruct it, invoking women constituents' strong feelings about it — this is a clear endorsement of women's political interests/rights legislation.

The speaker argues for expanding the number of women eligible to serve on these committees (from four to eight) to ensure greater representation of women, explicitly supporting increased women's participation in public administrative bodies.

The speaker explicitly attacks the Government's Employment Bill as an "inescapable affront to working people" that constitutes a "disastrous course... on equal rights generally and women's rights in particular," accusing the Government of being "as sexist as they are racist" and arguing that the Bill embodies a "woman's place is in the home" attitude. This is a clear, substantive argument in support of women's rights in the workplace and against the Government's rollback of those rights.

The speech addresses domestic violence legislation for Northern Ireland, specifically the exclusion of cohabitees from protection orders, with no substantive argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned as victims of domestic violence, not in the context of their political status or rights.

Mr. Macartney explicitly argues that female property owners who hold the right to vote for Poor Law Guardians would be "completely disfranchised" by the Bill, using their situation as a substantive argument against the Bill's removal of proxy/postal voting. He is defending women's existing political right to vote in Poor Law Guardian elections.

The speech is entirely focused on dog racing regulation, gambling, and the Betting and Lotteries Bill. While it mentions "men and women" in passing when discussing the growth of gambling, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Goschen/Sir Arthur Otway's speech) systematically argues against women's suffrage, contending that women are not "capable citizens," that enfranchising women rests on a "false ideal" of civic duty, that women already influence politics through their male relatives, and concluding "I shall vote against it." He denies women's fitness for political participation and opposes the amendment throughout.

The speaker invokes the case of a female property owner unable to vote in person across multiple Unions as an argument in favour of proxy voting rights, implicitly supporting women's right to participate in Poor Law Guardian elections on equal terms with male property owners.

The speech is entirely focused on British government policy toward Egypt and the Sudan, criticizing the Gladstone government's vacillation and perceived failures of responsibility. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker forcefully argues against government legislation that weakens maternity rights and employment protections for working women, explicitly condemning what he calls an "anti-woman, sexist" attack on women's rights and equal opportunities. He supports women's equal participation in the workforce and opposes measures that would push women back into the home, clearly advocating for women's civic and economic rights.

The speech concerns whether the government should remove the official whip to allow a free vote on corporal punishment (flogging) for procurers/pimps under a criminal justice bill. Women are mentioned only as victims to be protected, not in the context of their political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explains that women in Tel Aviv are granted votes because it accords with local community wishes, and describes a mechanism by which other municipalities (Haifa, Jerusalem) can also extend the vote to women via a two-thirds council majority — presenting this framework as a reasonable path to women's enfranchisement rather than opposing it.

The TARGET speech is primarily about Poor Law children, boarding-out arrangements, and rural water supply. While it mentions women inspectors and voluntary committees of women in the context of Poor Law administration, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation — it is focused on welfare and public health administration.

The speaker explicitly states "I confess myself in favour of the enfranchisement of those women who occupy a responsible position in their sphere." While he ultimately votes against the specific motion (to avoid a Conservative "trick" that would destroy the broader Franchise Bill), he frames this as a tactical/procedural decision, not a change in principle, and expresses no doubt about "the eventual realization of the object" of women's enfranchisement.

The speech concerns the functions of advisory committees under an Unemployment Assistance Board, discussing welfare, coordination of local services, and the role of experienced volunteers. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "men and women" who have experience in such work, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely focused on Indian constitutional reform — provincial autonomy, all-India federation, and safeguards — with no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation. The only passing reference to women is a brief mention of "the agricultural classes, the women and the Depressed Classes" having their voices heard under a broad provincial franchise, which is a passing descriptive remark, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about a labour dispute at a Salford clothing factory, focused on trade union representation and ACAS involvement. While it mentions that the striking workers are women, their gender is incidental to the argument; the speech does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The Speaker's ruling addresses a procedural matter — whether an emergency debate application meets the requirements of Standing Order No. 9 — and makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The mention of women workers on strike concerns a labour dispute, not women's civic or political status.

The speaker (Mr. Masterman) explicitly advocates for ensuring women's societies receive fair representation on Insurance Committees, arguing that election regulations should prevent women's societies from being "swamped" by larger societies and insisting that "it is most important that some women should be elected." This constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the only remedy to the suffragette hunger strike crisis is to "grant the franchise to them" and that justice demands giving women "the Parliamentary franchise," framing women's suffrage as the necessary solution to the disorder caused by its denial.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question about atrocities committed against villagers in Thrace, including a reference to sexual violence against women in one village. However, this is a question about foreign policy and humanitarian outrages, not about women's political rights, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned as victims of violence, not in the context of any argument about their political status.

The speech is entirely focused on British policy in Egypt and the Sudan — the occupation, governance, finances, military operations, and the Mahdi — with no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related civic status of women. Women are mentioned only once in passing, as victims at Sinkat, which is irrelevant to their political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the government's inability to fund increases to death grants and maternity grants due to financial constraints. The mention of "men over 65 and women over 60" is purely demographic/eligibility framing for welfare benefits, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is focused entirely on the timing and cost of implementing a non-contributory maternity grant, criticising the Government for delaying the change until 1982. While it mentions 60,000 women who would benefit, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on illegal trawling, fishery protection along the Scottish coast, and the rights of inshore fishermen; it contains no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech concerns a policy decision about arming women in the military Services for self-defence purposes, which relates to their military role rather than their civic/political rights and representation. There is no argument made about women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in political structures.

The speech is entirely about securing state funding and recognition for Aberystwith College in Wales. The single brief mention of women is a passing remark that the college might eventually add "ancillary appliances for the education of women" but must currently be treated as a men's college, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speaker (unnamed, likely a committee member) is explaining the procedural mechanics of the Amendment—specifically that it concerns the service franchise and preventing a house from being entirely disfranchised—rather than arguing for or against women's political rights. The brief mention of a female occupier not having a vote is descriptive context, not an argument about women's suffrage.

Lord John Manners explicitly argues that his amendment proceeds on the assumption that female suffrage is not to be granted, and frames his case purely around preventing houses from being disfranchised rather than giving women the vote — effectively accepting and working within the exclusion of women from the franchise. His argument treats women occupants as incapable of holding the vote themselves, seeking instead to preserve the house's franchise through other means.

The speech concerns the administration of National Insurance contributions for exempted persons and what benefits (medical, sanatorium) should be provided from employer contributions — it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. The mention of "women's trade unions and other working women's societies" is incidental context about who lobbied for medical benefits, not an argument about women's civic or political status.

The speaker explicitly calls for "one man one vote, with, I hope, an extension to all men and all women who are outside the walls of a prison or lunatic asylum," directly endorsing women's inclusion in the franchise. This is a clear, if brief, statement in favour of women's political rights.

The TARGET speech seconds a motion to reform divorce/marriage laws, arguing for broader grounds for divorce and stronger family life. While it briefly mentions women's views (dismissing the Mothers' Union circulars as unrepresentative), it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation — the speech is entirely about divorce law reform.

The speech is entirely focused on the future of Westminster hospital and its medical school — specifically the Flowers report and the London Health Planning Consortium report — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief references to "men and women" are incidental mentions of hospital staff, not arguments about civic participation.
