The speaker explicitly opposes the women's suffrage provision in the Bill, saying "I confess I do not understand why it has been put in at all" and that "it defies Nature and declares that a woman is to be held as a man," expressing clear opposition to women's suffrage as included in the Scottish Home Rule Bill.

The speaker (replying on behalf of the Government) neither supports nor opposes extending the Parliamentary franchise to women; he merely states that the Government cannot take up the matter due to internal disagreement and that it is left to private Members. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker moves amendments explicitly designed to expand women's electoral registration in India by removing the application test, arguing that retaining it would drastically reduce the number of women on the electoral roll (from 700,000 to 175,000 in Madras, etc.) and urging the Government to grant concessions to enfranchise more women across multiple provinces.

The target speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure — whether an Instruction to a Private Bill Committee should be entertained — and deals with Belfast municipal governance, drainage, franchise boundaries, and procedural propriety. The speaker's single passing reference to women's suffrage ("I wonder he did not propose that in Belfast women should have the vote—a very good object, I admit, but altogether impertinent to the particular subject under discussion") is offered only as a rhetorical example of an irrelevant amendment, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about the Third Reading of a GLC capital estimates bill, covering topics like transport fares, home loans, enterprise boards, and unemployment. The women's committee is mentioned only as an example of an irrelevant criticism raised in the debate, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly reserves the right to oppose and vote against the Bill if the women's suffrage clause is not deleted, and the broader context (Mr. Young's preceding speech) makes clear this is the same speaker who declared himself "opposed to the Sub-section of Clause 7... which proposes to confer the Parliamentary franchise upon women." The target speech reinforces that opposition by threatening to vote against the Third Reading unless the women's suffrage clause is removed.

The TARGET speaker (Miss Rathbone, identified by context) strongly advocates for expanding women's voting rights in India, arguing that the application condition will drastically reduce the number of women on the electoral roll and pressing the Government to remove it as widely as possible and guarantee its removal before the second general election. The speech consistently supports maximizing women's political participation.

The speaker (Mr. Butler, Under-Secretary) argues in favour of maximising women's enfranchisement in India, defending concessions already made (removing the application requirement in Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, and urban UP/CP; reducing literacy qualifications) and framing the retained application requirement in some provinces as a regrettable practical necessity rather than opposition to women's political rights. Throughout, the speech treats expanding women's electoral participation as the goal and presents administrative and social constraints as obstacles being minimised, not as reasons to limit women's franchise in principle.

The speech concerns mental health treatment for prisoners and the role of the Mental Health Act Commission in prisons — a penal/healthcare policy debate with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as "a strong anti-suffragist in the Imperial Parliament" (against women's suffrage at the national level) while simultaneously stating he is "not prepared to say anything against Women Suffrage for a local Parliament" and that it is "about the only part of the Bill which I might be in favour of" — making substantive arguments on both sides depending on the level of government involved.

The speech focuses entirely on the bloated costs and overstaffing of Irish legal administration, comparing Irish and English court expenditures. The single passing mention of "female suffrage" is a hypothetical aside used to humorously extend a point about patronage hiring, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Sir S. Cripps, based on the following context) forcefully argues that the application condition is logically incoherent and that if the government's stated objective is to enfranchise 6,000,000 women in India, it must remove all obstacles to achieving that goal, explicitly advocating for women's full voting participation rather than relying on administrative failure to limit their numbers.

The speaker argues forcefully for lowering the educational qualification from matriculation to literacy so that hundreds of thousands of women in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa can be enfranchised, explicitly opposing restrictions that would reduce female enfranchisement from 377,000 to 1,500 in Bengal alone.

The speaker defends the existing rule excluding married women residing with their husbands from invalid care allowance, citing cost (£40 million/year) as a barrier to extending the benefit to all married women, and declines to change or override the legal framework that disadvantages married women claimants.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely concerned with Scottish Home Rule, the Union between England and Scotland, and devolution arguments. Women's political rights are not addressed in the TARGET speech itself; the only references to women's suffrage appear in the FOLLOWING CONTEXT (Mr. Balfour and Mr. McKinnon Wood), not in the TARGET.

The TARGET speech is entirely devoted to arguing for the enfranchisement of the police force; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights. Women are not mentioned at all in the target text.

The TARGET speech is from the Speaker (chair) ruling on a procedural matter — noting that a discussion of the past history of women's suffrage would be out of order — without arguing any substantive position for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for enfranchising a larger number of women in India, arguing that women's votes are a potent instrument for pressing social reforms like child marriage, and expresses deep regret that the Government has been "adamant" in refusing to expand the female electorate beyond the proposed ~6,000,000.

The speaker explicitly argues that the law's disqualification of married women from standing for election to local councils should be removed, stating that "whatever our ideas may be as to Women Suffrage, the House... will agree that this disqualification should not prevent women, on account of marriage, from presenting themselves to the voters." The Bill is framed as expanding women's eligibility for local government office.

The speaker expresses clear support for expanding women's political rights in India, expressing regret that fewer women than hoped (6,000,000) will be enfranchised, urging the Government to enlarge the woman electorate, and warning that inadequate female representation will jeopardize the success of Indian constitutional reform.

McLaren explicitly argues that women's suffrage should be addressed before or alongside police enfranchisement, stating "the House should not proceed to deal with a removal of any other disqualification until it had dealt with the disqualification of sex," and affirming he is "strongly in favour of the enfranchisement of women." His opposition to the Bill is grounded in prioritising women's suffrage, not opposing it.

The speech is primarily about Scottish Home Rule, devolution, and the structure of subordinate parliaments within the United Kingdom. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference by Mr. McKinnon Wood expressing hope that women's suffrage for subordinate legislatures might have been separated from the question of women's vote for the Imperial Parliament, but this is a procedural observation about the debate's structure rather than a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (by the Home Secretary) addresses policing and property protection in response to suspected suffragette arson, but makes no argument for or against women's political rights — it is purely an administrative/law enforcement response to criminal acts.

The speaker explicitly states "he was strongly in favour of the enfranchisement of women" and argues that women's enfranchisement should come before that of the police, placing women's suffrage as a priority. While he raises a procedural ordering argument, his substantive position is clearly in favour of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on overseas aid to Somalia and refugee relief, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic participation issues.

The speaker (Mr. McLaren) explicitly argues that women's enfranchisement should take priority over police enfranchisement, contending that "the time had arrived when the validity of that argument [to make women wait] should no longer be acknowledged" and that "the House should not proceed to deal with a removal of any other disqualification until it had dealt with the disqualification of sex." This is a clear and affirmative advocacy for women's suffrage.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on the Irish Home Rule crisis and proposals for a national convention to resolve it, with only a fleeting passing mention of "female suffrage" as one example of matters that could be left to Irish self-determination. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker supports amendments that automatically include women on electoral rolls based on their husbands' qualifications without requiring individual applications, explicitly noting this was "very much desired by the women in India" and praising it as "a very satisfactory change," thus supporting broader women's political participation.

The speech is almost entirely about colonial policy in Kenya, Ceylon, and the Gold Coast — land rights for African natives, taxation, labour conditions, and colonial governance. The brief mention of women receiving the vote in Ceylon ("gave the vote to 2,000,000 people in Ceylon, including women") is purely descriptive and makes no argument for or against women's political rights. The reference to a hut tax on native women concerns taxation and economic welfare, not women's civic status or political participation.

The target speech argues for including a representative of the Society of Women Housing Estate Managers on an advisory committee based on their specialist qualifications in housing management, not on the basis of women's political rights or representation. As the preceding speaker (Mr. Guy) explicitly clarifies, he is "not pressing the claims of women as such" but rather the claims of those specially qualified — making this a housing administration argument, not a women's political rights argument.

The speaker explicitly supports greater representation of women on public bodies, acknowledges the current wastage of women's potential, highlights progress made under the Government, and commits to continuing efforts to improve women's appointments — while rejecting quotas on the grounds that merit-based selection better serves women's long-term interests, which is a procedural/implementation caveat rather than substantive opposition.

The speech is entirely focused on trade union legislation, industrial relations, and workers' rights in the context of the Employment Bill; it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation. Mentions of "working men and women" are incidental references to the workforce, not arguments about women's civic status or political participation.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on police powers, stop and search, detention, complaints procedures, and community accountability under a policing bill. The brief aside about "her client" and women in the legal profession is a passing comment about drafting style, not a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker's speech is focused entirely on supporting a Bill to enfranchise the police force; while he briefly references Mr. McLaren's position on women's suffrage (noting McLaren would reject this Bill until women are enfranchised), he makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights himself.

The speech by the MP for Dudley West focuses entirely on transport deregulation, coach services, fixed penalties, police endorsements of licences, and corruption allegations — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech concerns the Plural Voting Bill and debates about electoral reform (redistribution, plural voting, party advantage), with only a brief passing mention of "votes for women" as background context for why a previous Franchise Bill was dropped. No argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speech addresses the administrative arrangements and working hours of female clerks at the Omagh Post Office, which is a matter of workplace management rather than women's political rights or civic participation. No argument is made for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of political representation.

The speaker explicitly states support for women's enfranchisement, saying "representation ought to be of the individual man and, in my view, of the individual woman in this country," and frames the Plural Voting Bill as a step toward that goal by ensuring no man has more than one vote.

The speaker explicitly states that Labour Members "go so far as to say that every woman who has to obey the law ought also to have a vote," and argues against denying millions of people "both male and female" any share in government. This is a clear endorsement of women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly states he and many on his side were in favour of the Women's Suffrage Bill, and argues against using the failure to pass women's franchise as a reason to block the police franchise bill, attributing the Women's Franchise Bill's defeat to Liberal Members breaking their pledges rather than any principled opposition.

The speaker frames suffragette activity as "outrages" that necessitated restricting public access to royal palaces, treating women's suffrage activism as a public disorder problem justifying punitive administrative measures. This implicitly opposes the suffragette cause and women's political rights movement.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as "very strongly opposed to Woman Suffrage" and uses that position to argue that opponents of women's suffrage should nonetheless ensure women in government employment receive fair wages. This directly expresses opposition to women's political rights (suffrage).

The speech concerns a Ministry of Pensions supplementary estimate for disabled servicemen and their widows, with a brief aside about a Silver Jubilee gesture. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is almost entirely about Indian constitutional reform — federation, provincial autonomy, dominion status, and the political management of India — with only a passing, non-argumentative reference to "men and women" receiving the franchise under the Bill's proposals. No substantive argument is made for or against women's political rights as a distinct issue.

The speaker explicitly supports equity between the sexes in immigration law, criticises rules that removed female British citizens' rights to bring in husbands and fiancés, and argues that the new rules made "the position of all female British citizens, black or white, worse." He calls for repealing the sexually discriminating British Nationality Act and frames equal treatment of women as a core Labour policy objective.

The speaker explicitly supports the franchise for women as "one of the great things" in the Bill, expressing that it is "a very good extension" and noting with approval that Indian women, including Mohammedan women, were actively going to the polls. He even wishes the franchise could have been granted automatically without requiring application.

The speech is entirely focused on economic policy, unemployment, industrial decline in Huddersfield, university cuts, and government fiscal policy. Women are mentioned only in passing as part of generic phrases like "ordinary men and women" or "young men and women," with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (primarily by Mr. Silvester Horne and including earlier speakers) is entirely concerned with the Irish Home Rule debate — arguing for Irish unity, federalism, the Ulster question, and the governance of Ireland. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker explicitly argues that women voted for the Prime Minister expecting she would "advance the cause of women's equality," and condemns the government's economic policies for their "particularly damaging impact on the social and economic position of women," framing women's equality as a cause that should be championed.

The speaker argues that applying warrant procedures equally to women constitutes an "indignity" to Irish women and implies they deserve special exemption from these civic obligations, invoking women's suffrage rhetorically ("if you had women's suffrage you would have a large vote against it") to suggest women's political voice would oppose this treatment — but the overall argument is that women should be treated as a separate, more protected class rather than as equal civic participants, opposing equal civic duties for women.

The speech concerns allegations of financial mismanagement, corruption, and misconduct by an emigration committee official (Mr. Stoney) in Ireland, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is almost entirely about the pay, pensions, and working conditions of Irish National School teachers. The brief mention of female teachers walking long distances and receiving lower salaries addresses their employment conditions, not their civic status or political rights.

The speech is entirely about the sale of titles and honours, corruption in party fundraising, and the Parliament Act. The only mention of women is a passing, joking reference ("his wife who wants to be a lady") and a heckled interjection "Votes for Women" to which the speaker offers a brief dismissive quip, neither endorsing nor opposing women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly acknowledges that the Bill constitutes "a substantial advance in the opportunities it offered to women, both as voters and as elected representatives," and welcomes the concessions made during Committee as "a further advance," expressing gratitude and hope for more. While the speaker sets aside the women's status question to focus on other concerns, the brief but clear endorsement of women's expanded political rights qualifies as a supportive stance.

The speech is primarily about immigration rules governing husbands/fiancés entering the UK, the burden of proof in immigration cases, and the treatment of arranged marriages from the Indian subcontinent. While women are mentioned as affected parties (e.g., women wanting to bring in husbands, the "white women's lobby"), the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or civic participation — it addresses immigration policy without engaging women's political rights as a distinct question.

The TARGET speech is primarily about franchise arrangements in India (communal electorates, the new Schedule), with only a brief passing acknowledgment that Miss Rathbone has taken an interest in women's franchise and will have an opportunity to raise her Amendments on the Schedule. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The TARGET speech is focused on a procedural amendment about the qualifying date for voter registration in Belfast, not on the principle of women's political rights. Women voters are mentioned only incidentally (as a new element introduced by the Bill) to explain a difference between Parliamentary and municipal franchises, without any argument for or against women's right to vote.

The speech is primarily about National Health Insurance legislation, cash benefits, pension rights, and maternity benefits for the unemployed. The brief closing remark that electors should demand representatives "pledged to vote for health services and pension rights to be extended to everyone in the community, irrespective of calling, creed, or sex" is a passing mention without substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that excluding women ratepayers from elections for allotment managers would be "improper" and "a retrograde step," directly supporting women's right to participate in local franchise elections.

The speaker (McKenna) is not arguing for or against women's enfranchisement, but rather clarifying that prosecutions are directed at the advocacy of arson and outrage, not at the advocacy of women's suffrage itself. This is a procedural/legal clarification about criminal law enforcement, not a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker strongly criticizes the Conservative Government's policies as harmful to women's economic and civic equality — including attacks on equal pay, maternity rights, unemployment protections, and low wages disproportionately affecting women — and explicitly frames these as failures to advance women's position in society, demonstrating clear support for women's rights and equal participation in public and economic life.

The speech is entirely focused on the Government of India Bill, Indian federation, the role of the Princes, and questions of Indian self-governance. The single passing mention of women having been given the right to vote in some Indian States is purely illustrative of high governance standards in those States, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker is questioning the Home Secretary about apparent police interference with the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies' right to display pro-suffrage advertising, implicitly challenging the legitimacy of that interference and advocating on behalf of the suffragist organisation's ability to publicly promote its cause.

The TARGET speech is a government response defending Conservative economic policy as beneficial to women generally, arguing against treating women as a distinct economic group requiring special treatment. It does not argue for or against women's voting rights, standing for office, political representation, or other civic participation rights — it is focused entirely on macroeconomic policy and employment prospects.

The speaker dismisses female MPs' arguments as "screeching, squawking attack upon the male sex" and calls the motion "cheap" and "sexist," while later (in following speeches) explicitly stating women with young children have a "primary duty to be at home" — all reflecting opposition to women's equal civic and political participation.

The TARGET speech touches briefly on women's voting choices and unemployment statistics relative to women, but makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The comments about women voting for men rather than women are descriptive and deflective, not an argument about political rights, and the unemployment discussion concerns economic conditions rather than civic participation.

The TARGET speech addresses the procedural question of voter registration dates and inspection logistics in Belfast, briefly dismissing the mention of women voters as irrelevant to the registration consolidation argument. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made; the reference to women voters is incidental.

The speech is entirely about the economic difficulties of Merthyr Tydvil as a county borough and the Government's appointment of a Royal Commission to review its status as a local government unit. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is a lengthy critique of a Sunday observance/trading bill, focusing on exemptions regarding food, alcohol, clubs, newspapers, railways, and mines. The single passing reference to "suffragettes" and "militants" is purely incidental and does not argue any position on women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about medical professional conduct, malnutrition, abortion, and birth control — health and medical topics. While it briefly mentions Viscountess Astor (a female MP) and references "suffering women," it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is a procedural/administrative explanation by the Home Secretary about why a suffrage advertisement was banned from public carriages, citing a general policy against political advertisements under the Metropolitan Carriage Act. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or suffrage; it merely explains the legal and administrative basis for the Commissioner of Police's action.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the two-shift system for women and young persons in factories, arguing about labour conditions, wages, hours, and the adequacy of the Bill relative to a Departmental Committee's recommendations. While the speech mentions women workers throughout, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — it is a labour/industrial regulation debate.

The speaker is asking for clarification on the legal effect of a subsection regarding distress and fines, mentioning suffragettes only as an illustrative example of a prisoner type. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly critiques the preceding male speaker as a "male chauvinist pig" and a "relic of the past," defends women Members of Parliament against dismissive characterizations, and champions equal pay and women workers' issues, signalling clear support for women's political participation and civic equality.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the inclusion of women householders in the Bill, states that "in Ireland they would be very glad to have women voters," and argues that the absence of feminine franchise in Ireland has denied real occupiers the right to vote — a clear endorsement of women's political rights (voting franchise).

The speaker explicitly notes that "women householders under this Bill have votes," incorporating them into the new enlarged electorate, and argues that it would be "just and fair" to immediately bring this new electorate (including women) into play so the Corporation represents the whole town.

The speech is primarily about the legal mechanics of fines, distraint, and imprisonment under a criminal justice bill. The mention of suffragettes is purely illustrative of a class of prisoners who might benefit from the provision, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is a procedural statement about the availability of parliamentary bills and documents, including the Employment of Women and Young Persons Bill. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for equal rights for British women to be joined by their spouses and fiancés, arguing that current immigration rules unjustly create two tiers of British citizenship that discriminate against women who acquired citizenship by naturalisation. He invokes the equality of political and civic rights established since 1928 and the Sex Discrimination Act as the basis for extending equal rights to family life.

The speech focuses on teacher training college closures, government consultation failures, and Labour Party political prospects. The brief mention of women's votes and the government's treatment of women is a rhetorical political point about electoral consequences, not a substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about education policy for mentally defective children, the age at which they should enter residential schools, and the reliability of school inspections. The only mention of suffragettes is an incidental, humorous remark about police escorts, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speech concerns the right of public meeting in Trafalgar Square, the conduct of police, and the relationship between the Executive and Legislature. While it briefly mentions "women who are non-voters" as part of a statistical argument about London residents, this is a passing demographic reference with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is primarily about the technical change from indirect to direct election for India's Council of State, discussing electoral colleges, constituency sizes, and franchise arrangements. The only mention of women is a passing reference to six reserved seats for women in the Council of State, which is stated as a continuing concession without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on the 1935 general election result, the National Government's programme, economic policy, unemployment, coal industry reform, international affairs, and party politics. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation at any point.

The target speech by Mr. Ritchie is focused entirely on the technical and administrative question of whether to use the parliamentary or municipal franchise as the basis for the new County Council register. The brief mention of women is purely incidental — noting that women (like Peers) would not receive a parliamentary vote — without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses primarily on economic policy, unemployment, wage settlements, and women's role in the workforce and home. While it mentions equal opportunities legislation approvingly in passing, it does not make a substantive argument about women's political rights or representation (voting, standing for office, civic participation) — the brief mention of equal opportunities relates to employment, not civic/political participation.

The speaker (Ms. Harriet Harman) explicitly argues that women are underrepresented in Parliament ("the lack of representation of women in the House of Commons"), that "women's interests are largely unrepresented in Parliament," and calls for political equality alongside economic equality. She supports women's full civic participation and frames the lack of female MPs as a structural injustice requiring remedy.

The speech is entirely focused on the procedural rights of prisoners (the option to pay a fine or go to prison) and criticises what the speaker sees as bureaucratic overreach by magistrates. While suffragettes are briefly mentioned as the political catalyst for the legislation, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses primarily on domestic/marital violence against women and related welfare issues (VAT on sanitary towels, housing for victims), with only a passing acknowledgment that women MPs were elected to express political views. It does not make substantive arguments for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Hobhouse) moves an amendment that explicitly includes women as a class to be added to county electoral registers, arguing it is unjust to deny women the right to vote for County Councils and that "there were very few women who would be qualified to vote under the Bill; but that was not a reason why they should deny them the right of voting, or declare that their names should not appear upon the register." This constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's political rights at the local government level.

Mr. Broadhurst's speech is entirely focused on supporting the Deceased Wife's Sister Marriage Bill — arguing for public support, trade union backing, and religious precedents for legalizing such marriages. Women's political rights are not argued about in the target speech; a letter from a woman requesting postponement until women could vote is mentioned only in a following speaker's remarks (Mr. Hoare), not in the target.

Viscountess Astor explicitly endorses women's suffrage, stating "I have always said that in giving the women the vote you were saving the country from all sorts of wild cat schemes and wild cat speeches," and praises women's practical political judgment as demonstrated by their support for the National Government. This is a clear, if brief, affirmative argument for women's political participation.

The speech is primarily about cattle maiming in Ireland and proposals to increase penalties and disqualify offenders from Parliament. The brief mention of "militant suffragettes" burning churches is used only as an analogy to illustrate a pattern of misguided revenge behaviour, not as an argument about women's political rights or fitness for civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Local Government Bill's provisions regarding county councils, licensing, emigration, poor relief, London governance, and borrowing powers. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly advocates for equal pay between men and women as a matter of principle, arguing that work should be paid according to its worth regardless of sex, criticising the Government for paying women less in the Civil Service and teaching profession, and asserting that inequality of pay harms both men and women. She also opposes policies that would force women out of industry or bar married women from professions, supporting women's equal participation in public and professional life.

The speaker explicitly argues that the income tax treatment of married women constitutes an unjust "tax on marriage," advocates for treating husband and wife as separate economic individuals, and crucially states that "as long as women have not the franchise, there is in this matter a special case for the consideration of the injustice with regard to women, which ought to be dealt with with the utmost generosity" — directly linking the denial of women's suffrage to a heightened obligation to remedy their civic and economic disadvantages.

The speech is primarily about the Government of India Bill — its democratic merits, the electorate expansion, safeguards, and Indian self-government. The brief mention of 6,000,000 women being included in the expanded Indian electorate is purely descriptive (citing a statistic to illustrate the Bill's democratic progress) and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights as a distinctive civic claim.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equal participation in the workforce and political life, criticising the Government for undermining equal pay legislation, weakening maternity rights, and driving women out of work, while noting that only 23 women MPs shows "there is a long way to go" — all consistent with supporting women's full civic and economic equality.

The speech is about the administrative complexity of voter registration registers in London under the Local Government Bill, focusing on whether to use the Parliamentary register, the municipal register, or a new register for the County Council. While the speaker briefly mentions that women and Peers would be added to a supplementary list, this is incidental to the main argument about register simplification and does not constitute an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about the technical question of which electoral register (Parliamentary vs. municipal) should apply to London under the Local Government Bill, focusing on administrative complexity and consistency across boroughs. While the speaker briefly mentions that women and Peers would form a small separate third list, this is incidental to the argument about register simplification, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about heavy lorry weight regulations, road building programmes, and environmental concerns. The sole mention of women is a passing reference to the Women's Institute as a vocal lobbying group opposing heavier lorries, which does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the franchise for county council elections, specifically debating owner versus occupier voting rights and plural voting in local government — it mentions women voters only incidentally as one category added to the municipal list. No argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on local taxation, rates, education funding, main roads, and agricultural relief — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, suffrage, or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on labour legislation, working conditions, and industrial policy in India under the proposed federal constitution. The brief mention of extending the franchise and giving votes to women in India is incidental and passing, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly affirms support for women's rights in principle (suffragette sympathies, equal pay, employment provisions) while substantively opposing the specific Bill as too wide-ranging, expressing serious doubts about the effectiveness of legislation to promote equality, and opposing provisions like paternity leave—resulting in a refusal to support the Bill in its present form.

The speaker explicitly supports the Amendment giving women the right to retain their own nationality, arguing that women deserve equal civic standing as independent persons and that it is unjust for a male-elected Parliament to strip women of their British citizenship without their consent or representation. The speech repeatedly invokes women's right to self-determination in civic matters and criticizes the exclusion of women from decisions affecting their status.

The speech is primarily about rate reductions, local government cuts in Lothian, and democratic accountability. The single passing reference to "the suffragettes" is part of a historical list of democratic struggles (Chartists, trade unionists, Labour party) and does not argue for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone, based on context) explicitly criticizes the existing Indian legislative bodies for representing a narrow franchise that excludes women, depressed classes, and labour, and argues for a broader, more representative mechanism to gauge Indian opinion. By singling out women's lack of representation as a deficiency in the current electorate, she implicitly endorses women's inclusion in political representation.

The TARGET speech (spanning McGovern's continuation and Mrs. Shaw's address) concerns Scottish housing legislation—means testing, rents, overcrowding standards, local authority powers, and housing finance—with no substantive argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. Mrs. Shaw's passing remark "I can never be accused of advocating the rights of women" is a brief disclaimer, not an argument about women's political rights, and her comments on women's practical domestic experience relate to housing policy, not civic participation.

The speaker strongly supports the Bill aimed at advancing women's equality, criticising opponents for not going far enough, endorsing equal pay and anti-discrimination provisions, and arguing that women have not yet achieved genuine equality in Britain. The speech is an unambiguous advocacy for women's rights and the legislation designed to promote them.

Viscountess Astor argues that women's political participation leads to better legislative outcomes, pointing to the stark contrast between only five measures passed for women and children in the 15 years before women had the vote versus the many such measures passed after, thereby supporting women's political representation and suffrage.

The speaker (Mr. E. Wason) explicitly states he will vote against the specific clause giving women the franchise, and clarifies his name appeared on the Bill only due to a misunderstanding because of that women's franchise clause. While he supports the broader Scottish Home Rule Bill, his opposition to women's suffrage is clearly and substantively expressed.

The speaker expresses genuine support for equality of opportunity between the sexes and women's political participation, acknowledging that "women remain the exception rather than the norm" in political parties and endorsing the goal of greater women's representation. Her objection is procedural/practical — that the specific Bill is "badly flawed in its practical application" and that legislation is not the right route — not a substantive opposition to women's political rights themselves.

The speaker (Mr. E. B. Hoare) opposes the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill on grounds of expediency, yet explicitly endorses the argument that the law on marriage should not be changed until women have the right to vote, agreeing with a letter he received stating the question "should be postponed until she and her sisters were able to exercise the right of voting." This constitutes substantive support for women's suffrage paired with a substantive position on the marriage law debate, making the speech genuinely two-sided on women's political rights.

The speech is entirely concerned with a Dublin police inquiry, the conduct of police during labour riots, and related Commission proceedings. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the text.

The speaker explicitly advocates for appointing a woman to the Secretary of State's Council for India, arguing that women's questions are central to India's progress and that women in India are politically engaged and qualified. The speaker also recalls being the first MP to introduce a motion for women's votes in India, demonstrating consistent support for women's political rights.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. E. Wason, at the opening) explicitly states he intends to vote against the women's franchise clause in the Scottish Home Rule Bill, and the Marquess of Tullibardine's remarks confirm and mock this opposition. No substantive argument in favour of women's political rights is made in the TARGET.

Sir John Simon (Dewsbury) argues extensively in favour of the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, contending that the existing prohibition causes immorality, is founded on ecclesiastical absurdity (the Canon Law falsehood that a sister-in-law is a sister), is contradicted by Jewish and foreign practice, and that no valid scriptural or social reason justifies denying men and women the freedom to contract such marriages.

The speaker (Mr. Mackinder) dismisses women's franchise as something being "imposed" on Scotland, describing it as part of the bill's overreach: "they leap into double darkness and attempt to push their tyranny still further by imposing Women Franchise upon Scotland." This characterizes women's suffrage as an unwanted tyrannical imposition, expressing opposition to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is about the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill (marriage law reform) and argues against it on grounds of expediency, religious sentiment, and procedural concerns. While the speaker briefly notes that women lack the franchise and therefore cannot make their views known on this matter, this is a passing observation used to explain why women wrote letters rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights. The speech does not argue for or against women's political rights as its subject.

The speech is entirely focused on supporting a Bill to restrict the export of aged and decrepit horses, with no arguments about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "devoted men and women" who investigated the horse trade is incidental and makes no argument about women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker (Sir S. Hoare) argues against the amendment that would mandate a woman on the Secretary of State's Council, insisting it is better to "leave the Secretary of State's hands free" rather than require female representation. While he acknowledges women may serve in future, he dismisses the women's issues argument and opposes the structural inclusion of women on the advisory council.

The speech is entirely focused on extrajudicial killings and murder by governments around the world, supporting Amnesty International's campaign against such practices. While it mentions victims killed on the basis of "sex" among other characteristics, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on Northern Ireland's economic deprivation, unemployment, energy prices, housing, terrorism, and public expenditure estimates. Women are mentioned only once in passing, as a statistical comparator for average weekly earnings, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for earlier Saturday night closing of public houses in Ireland to address drunkenness and protect working-class families. While the speaker mentions women and children as victims of alcohol abuse ("I plead for the women and helpless children"), this is a welfare/temperance argument, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill's purpose of making real the removal of disqualification for women standing for election to county and borough councils, calling it "an act of tardy justice." He also argues that women elected as chair of a county council or mayor of a borough should be eligible as justices of the peace, further endorsing women's civic participation.

The TARGET speech concerns the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts and Cantonments Acts in India, focusing on moral arguments against state-regulated prostitution. While it mentions "the women of England" agitating on platforms, this is a reference to their role as moral campaigners, not an argument about women's political rights, voting, or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that at least one woman should be legally required to serve on the Secretary of State's advisory council, framing women's participation as citizen rights equal to men's and urging the Committee to support the Amendment mandating female inclusion.

The speech concerns education policy for mentally deficient children, specifically the age at which children should enter residential institutions and related certification procedures. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech concerns the administration of the Contagious Diseases Acts in India, the regimental system, and the Cantonments Act — it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The brief mention of "the feeling of the women" refers only to a woman's views on the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts, not to any question of women's political rights.

The speaker seeks to strip the Greenham Common women of their electoral registration by amending the Representation of the People Act to exclude residents whose claim is based on illegal occupation of common land, thereby targeting these women's right to vote. This is substantively directed at removing a specific group of women from the electoral register on the basis of their protest encampment, making it a speech against women's political rights (specifically the right to vote) for this group.

The TARGET speech argues that the Secretary of State should have a woman adviser because he will be responsible for deciding whether to extend the vote to women in India, and supports the Amendment on the grounds that it would advance women's political status. Viscountess Astor's contribution likewise explicitly supports the Amendment as beneficial to the status and rights of women in India.

The target speech concerns the administration of the Borstal system and prison conditions for young female offenders, addressing questions about criminal justice and penal reform. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports extending women's political participation in India (franchise expansion, women's equal status in public life) and argues that women deserve legislative protection against male prejudice in public administration. While he admits personal prejudice against women's participation, he frames this as a reason why legal protections are necessary, effectively endorsing women's political rights.

The speaker moves an amendment to explicitly prohibit sex-based discrimination in eligibility for public office and professions in India, arguing that women are equal citizens entitled to the same rights and duties as men, and drawing on examples of women's achievements in public life to support full civic participation without any sex bar.

The speech concerns extending the municipal franchise in Belfast to all household occupiers and improving polling/revision machinery; women householders are mentioned only in passing as a separate list already established by prior legislation, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on youth unemployment, the Youth Training Scheme, and socialist economic arguments, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any related civic status issues for women.

The speech is a maiden speech focused entirely on housing policy, coal mining, local authority building control, and related issues. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing, throwaway remark at the very end ("Had the House looked into a crystal ball many years ago and seen the present Prime Minister, the suffragettes might not have won their well-deserved victory") which does not argue a position on women's political rights but rather makes a rhetorical point about the current Prime Minister.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. Macpherson) explicitly notes that the Bill includes "a Clause introduced at the request of the majority of the Scottish Members giving the franchise to a large number of the women of Scotland," presenting this as a feature of the Bill he is moving for Second Reading without objection or qualification — effectively supporting women's franchise as part of the measure he champions.

The speaker explicitly advocates for opening all professions in India to women, citing the 1918 opening of the Bar, solicitors' profession, and university degrees to women in Britain as the model, and urges that India be placed in the same position — a clear argument in support of women's professional and civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on Irish local government reform — abolishing Grand Juries, Boards of Guardians, and creating County and District Councils. The only mention of women is a passing remark that "Peers and women also would be entitled to vote for the elected Councillors," stated without argument or advocacy, merely as a detail of the franchise provisions.

The speech concerns the Serpell report and railway transport policy in Wales, with no reference to women's political rights or representation. The mention of "women's institutes" is simply listing stakeholder groups that have made representations on transport policy.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone, based on context) advocates for opening the Indian Civil Service to women and creating special branches for women's service, arguing that women's "potentialities of service in India are not in any way safeguarded under the Bill" and that "increasing use should be made of the services of women" to protect women's interests in India.

The speaker explicitly thanks the Government for introducing a clause addressing women's treatment under the Income Tax Acts, votes for its Second Reading, and argues that women's incomes should be taxed independently from their husbands' — framing equal tax treatment as a matter of justice for women. While noting the clause doesn't go far enough, this is a procedural/implementational caveat, not substantive opposition to women's rights.

The target speech deals entirely with elementary education policy, continuation schools, art schools, teacher superannuation, and Board of Education administration. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speaker (Secretary of State for the Colonies) neither supports nor opposes women's franchise in Bermuda, merely denying awareness of tax resistance and deferring to a prior reply without making any substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker opposes women's eligibility for County Councils, arguing there is no demand for it and that the work is not suited to women; but simultaneously expresses support for women's parliamentary suffrage, claiming that advocates pushing women into unsuitable roles are "the very worst friends of the Parliamentary enfranchisement of women" and that resisting such proposals acts in women's best interests.

The speech is entirely focused on technical amendments to capital transfer tax law (clause 13 of the Finance Bill), covering property situated abroad at time of death and protection of personal representatives. The brief mention of "men and women of independent judgment" in the congratulatory opening remarks is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights.

This lengthy speech is entirely focused on the structure and administration of the proposed County Government Bill for London — dealing with local authority organization, elections, aldermen, police control, water supply, markets, and related matters. The single passing reference to "women voters" in the context of City electoral roll adjustments is purely technical and makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) explicitly advocates for increasing the number of reserved seats for women in Indian provincial assemblies, arguing that greater political representation for women is necessary and just, and urging the Government to grant these amendments.

Mr. De Lisle explicitly identifies himself as "a determined opponent of woman suffrage" and opposes women's political participation on the grounds that it "unsexes" women and threatens societal peace, supporting the Lord Advocate's amendment to exclude women from county councils.

The speech is entirely focused on agricultural labour shortages during wartime, the Agricultural Consultative Committee's reports, and the debate over boy labour vs. other labour sources. The only mention of women is a brief aside — "We are not the Board of Education or a Women's Suffrage Society" — used as a rhetorical contrast to emphasise that the Board of Agriculture's sole concern is farm productivity, not a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's equal pay rights, criticizes the regulations as inadequate to help women escape low-paid work, promotes her own Sex Equality Bill, and urges the Government to ensure women "get the decent deal that we all know they deserve" — all clear arguments in support of women's political and economic rights.

The speech is entirely focused on local government finance, rate support grants, and the relationship between central and local government expenditure. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation at any point in the speech.

Haldane supports women's suffrage for County Council elections but argues against excluding married women — he criticises the Bill for granting the franchise only to single women while refusing it to married women, citing the Chancellor's own earlier position. He thus supports women's political participation in principle while opposing the specific exclusion of married women, making a substantive argument on both the inclusion of women and the differential treatment between married and single women.

The speaker (a Government minister) explicitly affirms sympathy toward women's representation in India, highlights concessions already made (Council of State seats, improved franchise qualifications), and frames opposition to the specific amendments as reluctant pragmatism driven by local political realities rather than any principled opposition to women's political rights. Throughout, the speech endorses the goal of expanding women's representation as fully as conditions allow.

The TARGET speech (primarily Miss Rathbone, supported by the Duchess of Atholl) explicitly and substantively advocates for increased reserved seats for women in Indian provincial assemblies in Bengal, Assam, and the North-West Frontier Province, arguing that women's political representation is essential to address social evils affecting women in India.

The speech concerns a Supplementary Estimate for a gallery, mentioning suffragette activity only as a factual explanation for reduced visitor fees (gallery closures due to threat of violence). No argument is made for or against women's political rights; suffragettes are referenced purely as a cause of administrative inconvenience.

The speech discusses police expenditure at South Kensington Museum and mentions Suffragette outrages only as context for why policing costs have generally decreased elsewhere — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states they feel "strongly in favour of the development of women's influence in the legislatures of India" and supports increasing women's representation and voting power. While they argue against pressing the Amendment further than India is willing to go, this is a procedural/pragmatic objection rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights — they frame it as a strategic concern about timing and local conditions, not a rejection of women's political participation.

The speech concerns wartime pensions, separation allowances, and the administrative structure of the Statutory Committee for soldiers' and sailors' dependants. The single mention of women ("representation of two women on the Committee") is incidental and administrative, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech (by the Member for Lanark, North-West) is entirely focused on Scottish Home Rule and the social/economic conditions of the Scottish poor. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker asks whether the Women's Suffrage Bill will proceed and seeks assurance it will only be taken up when fully debatable — a procedural pressure tactic. The following speech (context) reveals his motive: Mr. Woodall references the questioner's "vigilant and persistent hostility" to the Bill, indicating the TARGET speaker's questioning is motivated by opposition to women's suffrage.

The speech is entirely focused on London local government, GLC capital expenditure, rates, housing, and the ILEA debate. The brief mention that women had the right to sit on the education authority since 1870 is purely historical and descriptive context for an argument about democratic accountability, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a lengthy introduction of Scottish local government reform bills, focused on county councils, parochial boards, road trustees, rating systems, and private bill procedure. The only mention of women is a brief, non-argumentative note that the county council constituency will consist of "qualified ratepayers, including women" — this is a passing factual description of the franchise provisions, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Member for Hanley) explicitly supports the Women's Suffrage Bill, having placed it on the order paper for Second Reading and expressing hope that the Government will act on the Prime Minister's declaration in favour of women's enfranchisement. He declines to withdraw the Bill until assured such prospects are exhausted.

The speaker (a Government minister) expresses firm commitment to equal opportunities, supports equal pay for work of equal value, and has personally signed designations for courses exclusively for women and girls — all indicating support for women's political and civic rights. While opposing the specific Bill on procedural and practical grounds (cost, conflict of interest, impracticability), the speaker does not oppose the underlying principle of equal opportunities for women, making this a procedural objection rather than substantive opposition.

The speech is entirely focused on the wartime agricultural labour shortage and the use of boy labour (and to a lesser extent female labour) on farms during WWI. The brief mention of women ("ladies who take extreme views on the suffrage question") is a passing, incidental remark suggesting suffragettes could usefully encourage women to do farm work — it does not argue for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the National Registration Bill (wartime registration of the population for military and industrial purposes), debating compulsory registration, conscription, voluntary enlistment, and government organisation. The only mention of women is a brief passage noting that women represent more than half the population and should be included in the registration so they can serve the country — this is not an argument about women's political rights (voting, standing for office, representation) but about their inclusion in a wartime registration scheme for national service purposes.

The speaker (Mr. Lawrence) argues extensively against the Bill designed to advance women's equality, citing its controversial nature, cost, administrative burdens, and absurd provisions, and highlights the Labour party's own failures to promote women's representation — all to undermine the case for the legislation. While he claims not to oppose women's rights in principle, this is a grudging acknowledgement rather than substantive endorsement, and his overall argument is directed against advancing women's political and civic rights through this legislation.

The speech is primarily about wartime separation allowances, dependants' pensions, and the administration of soldiers' and sailors' family support. The brief mention that women's representation on the statutory and local committees is "probably not nearly enough" is a practical administrative point about committee composition, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation in the suffrage-movement sense.

The first speaker in the TARGET argues that public opinion in Assam is "generously disposed" toward women's political participation, citing a resolution carried in favour of women's admission and voting rights, and explicitly suggests allotting reserved seats for women on the Provincial Council. Miss Ward's portion similarly expresses regret that more reserved seats for women cannot be secured and urges the Government to reconsider, framing the exclusion of women as a missed opportunity.

The speaker criticizes the Government's order as "complex" and "inadequate" for failing to properly implement equal pay for equal value for low-paid women, and calls for withdrawal of the order in favour of the Sex Equality Bill — explicitly supporting women's equal pay rights and stronger legislative protection for women.

The speech concerns land reform, agricultural depopulation, urban congestion, colonization, and free trade economics. The only mention of women is a passing reference to French women aging prematurely from fieldwork under the small holdings system, which is not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Amendment to reserve seats for women on Provincial Councils, arguing it is "desirable that women should have places allocated to them" and that women representatives are essential for addressing social problems affecting women. The speaker reinforces this by citing the precedent of the Council of State Amendment and urging the Under-Secretary to accept the plea.
The speech is entirely focused on WWI prisoner treatment, German conduct, and skepticism toward neutral country appeals — it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (by the Lord Advocate/Robertson) is primarily about Scottish local government reform and briefly notes that women's suffrage and "one man one vote" are among "comparatively trifling questions" he will not discuss at this stage, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Hanley) protests that the government's proposed adjournment will "confiscate" the day he had secured for a Women's Suffrage Motion, signalling his support for that motion and his intention to defend the opportunity to debate it.

The speaker explicitly states that the representation of women on the statutory Committee "is far too small" and that "there should be at least four women on that body," directly advocating for greater women's representation in public institutional roles.

The speaker (Mr. Butler, the Under-Secretary) defends the Government's approach to ensuring women's representation in Provincial Legislative Councils, arguing that the higher ratio of gubernatorial nominations combined with a special Instrument of Instructions will secure women's adequate representation, and explicitly states the Government has already made a special concession for women on the Council of State. The speech is oriented toward supporting women's representation, offering an alternative mechanism rather than opposing it in principle.

The speaker expresses genuine support for remedying "appalling discriminations" against women and endorses some provisions (e.g., abolishing the household duties test), while simultaneously opposing the Bill itself on substantive grounds—arguing it brings women's rights "into general disrepute," defending the Conservative Party's record on women's equality, and making broader arguments that undermine feminist claims (e.g., linking female emancipation to increased aggression and rape). This constitutes substantive argument on both sides of women's political and civic rights.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing for renewal of the Prevention of Terrorism Act in the context of Northern Ireland security, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The incidental mention of "men and women" as police and security personnel is not an argument about women's civic status.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) moves an amendment to reserve seats for women in Indian Provincial Councils, explicitly arguing that women must be represented in legislative bodies, that elected seats are preferable to nomination, and urging the Government to ensure women have "the opportunity to do something for themselves." The entire speech advocates for women's political representation.

The speaker briefly but explicitly supports increased women's representation in Parliament, arguing that a reformed proportional electoral system "might do something about" the fact that fewer women are MPs now than at any time since 1945, framing greater women's representation as a desirable outcome of electoral reform.

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater representation of women on statutory and local committees dealing with soldiers' and sailors' welfare, arguing that "where provision has been made for two women representatives, I think provision should be made for four." This is a direct, affirmative argument for increased women's civic/political representation on public bodies.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the communal award, the Poona Pact, and the allocation of seats between caste Hindus, depressed classes, and Muslims in Bengal under the Government of India Bill. The brief mention of "two women's seats on the general list" is purely incidental arithmetic, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about a procedural amendment concerning the frequency of electoral register updates and filling of casual vacancies in Scottish County Councils. The brief mention of women ("the list of the ladies who will be enfranchised under the Act") is purely incidental, noting them as a category to be added to the supplementary register, without making any argument for or against their political rights.

The speech is about the Greenham Common peace camp's occupation of Department of Transport land and the local nuisance it causes; the speaker explicitly states he makes no criticism of the women's right to hold their views. The speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation — it concerns trespass, environmental eyesores, policing costs, and road safety, not women's civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Butler) defends the Government's approach to securing women's representation in Provincial Councils through Governors' nominations and an Instrument of Instructions, explicitly expressing sympathy for women's representation and stating that the Government's method is designed to ensure women are "adequately represented." While he resists the specific Amendment, he does so on procedural/structural grounds (the nomination ratio is sufficient), not because he opposes women's representation — he affirms it as a goal and claims the Government has "made certain" women will be represented.

The speech is about whether women should be included in a wartime national service register, not about women's political rights (voting, standing for office, representation). The speaker opposes an amendment to exclude women from the register on practical grounds of efficiency and national service utility, with no substantive argument about women's franchise, suffrage, or political representation.

The speaker argues that the tax system discriminates against married women by leaving them with less take-home pay than their male counterparts, and advocates for reforming it by abolishing the married man's tax allowance — a structural change aimed at equalising women's economic and civic standing. This is a substantive argument in favour of removing a policy that disadvantages women.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment in Northern Ireland, public expenditure cuts, Sinn Fein electoral support, housing, European Community funding, and related economic and political issues. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speaker explicitly states "I think we want a great many more women on these Committees, both on the central body and also on the local bodies," and agrees with prior members that women need "a much bigger representation" on committees dealing with working-class homes, women, and children. This is a clear endorsement of greater women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on local government spending, rate levels, privatisation, and a NALGO campaign against government cuts — with no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related civic status issue. The brief demographic reference to "C2D women" is purely a market research category label, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's eligibility for County Councils, arguing that ratepayers should have the opportunity to elect women if they deem it beneficial, and pointing to the valuable work women have already done on Boards of Guardians, School Boards, and the London County Council as justification for not excluding them.

Mr. Firth moves to remove the clause barring women from election as county councillors, arguing on practical grounds of public utility — specifically citing women's valuable contributions to oversight of lunatic asylums on the London County Council — and challenging the Government's "strong negative position" of disqualification by sex.

Mr. J. Wilson's speech focuses entirely on the hardship of disqualifying rate defaulters from voting for the County Council, using the example of 10,000 defaulters in Govan. He explicitly notes he is not including females in his count, but makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech asks procedural questions about the total adult population figures and the scope of the franchise Schedule for India, with no argument made for or against women's political rights. The mention of 6,000,000 women voters is purely a request for clarifying statistics, not a substantive position on women's political participation.

The speech is entirely devoted to housing policy — overcrowding standards, slum clearance, subsidies, redevelopment, and accommodation provision — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states they will vote in favour of Miss Rathbone's Amendment to reserve seats for women in Provincial Councils, arguing that if vested interests such as Hindus, Muslims, landlords, and agriculturists deserve reserved representation, women are equally entitled to their fair share of representation in India's legislative bodies.

The speaker (President of the Local Government Board) argues strongly for including women in the national register, citing women's demands to be included, their vital war service contributions, and the likelihood they would resent exclusion. He frames women's inclusion as both justified and necessary, supporting their civic participation in national service on equal terms with men.

The speech is entirely about extending corporal punishment (flogging) to various criminal offences including burglary, rape, and offences under the Criminal Law Amendment Act. While women are mentioned incidentally as victims of crime, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on trade policy, exchange rates, industrial investment, and economic planning. The incidental mentions of "men and women" are rhetorical flourishes about the general population and workforce, not arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is primarily arguing for working-class industrial representation on a committee, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of women ("You make provision for women, and I see no good reason why you should not similarly make provision for the representatives of persons...") uses women's inclusion merely as an analogy to support the labour representation argument, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is primarily concerned with the composition and size of a statutory committee, arguing for labour/trade union representation and a Board of Education appointee. The references to women ("not less than two shall be women") are incidental mentions of existing bill language, not arguments for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is focused on the composition of a statutory committee, arguing for labour representation and against an overly large committee. The brief mention of "two women" is a passing reference to an existing provision in the Bill, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Hattersley) explicitly condemns immigration rules that discriminate against women settled in Britain by denying their foreign husbands entry, calling this "overt and deliberate discrimination" and arguing that British women of all statuses should have the equal right to live with their husbands in the country — a direct argument for women's equal civic/legal standing in immigration rights.

The target speech is primarily about the frequency of register preparation and co-optation procedures for filling vacancies on the County Council. The brief mention that the Lord Advocate's Bill "gives the franchise to women, but excludes women from election" is purely incidental and descriptive, used to undermine a precedent (the School Board Act), not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the Coroners' Juries Bill, focusing on jury selection procedures for coroners' courts. While it briefly mentions that women were historically excluded from coroners' juries and endorses random selection that would include them equally, this is a passing observation about jury reform rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely about public transport funding, bus services, and the powers of passenger transport authorities relative to the Secretary of State. The reference to "working men and women and their families" is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is a purely statistical presentation of electorate figures for British India (total voters, male/female breakdown, population percentages), offered to aid committee discussion. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech concerns the minimum age for political candidates in India (the Government of India Bill), not women's political rights. The brief reference to granting franchise to women is purely historical context for the speaker's point about the age of 25, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for working-class women to be represented on the statutory Committee, arguing that "it is equally important that working-class women should be represented" and calling for two women representing the working classes as a "very reasonable and moderate claim."

Campbell-Bannerman explicitly moves an amendment to extend the franchise to married women on equal terms with unmarried women, supporting women's political rights broadly. However, he simultaneously acknowledges there are arguments "for and against" whether women should vote at all, stopping short of fully endorsing women's suffrage in principle while advocating for equal treatment within whatever franchise is granted.

The speaker proposes an amendment specifying that "not less than two shall be women" among the appointed representatives, explicitly advocating for guaranteed women's inclusion on the statutory committee. This constitutes a positive argument for women's political representation.

The speech is a procedural clarification question about Indian electoral roll statistics — specifically whether the 6,000,000 figure for women voters accounts for wastage from the application process.
