It does not argue for or against women's political rights; it simply seeks numerical clarification on franchise administration in India.

The speech raises a procedural point of order about the legal status and treatment of women demonstrators being held by police in Westminster, focusing on access to press and legal representation. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns a proposal about Civil List pensions for distinguished figures in letters, art, and science, mentioning women only as potential beneficiaries alongside men. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Butler, an Under-Secretary) is explaining and defending the government's proposals to enfranchise approximately 6,000,000 women in India under the franchise scheme, detailing the qualifications by property, wifehood, and education. The speech actively supports and elaborates on extending voting rights to women.

The speaker explicitly states he "should have been content" if no woman voted at all, framing women's suffrage as a "tide" that must be contained. While he accepts a limited form as a practical matter, his substantive position is opposition to women's political participation.

The speaker argues against a fixed numerical quota for women on local committees, not because women shouldn't be included, but because finding suitable women can be difficult in practice; they explicitly support leaving it to committee discretion while expressing confidence that women will still be selected, effectively endorsing women's inclusion on committees.

The target speech (by Mr. Butler) provides statistical details about the women's electorate under the proposed India franchise provisions — numbers qualified by property, wifehood, and education — without making any argument for or against women's political rights. It is a factual, administrative response in a parliamentary committee discussion about Indian constitutional reform.

The speech focuses almost entirely on Scottish local government reform — franchises, County Councils, Commissioners of Supply, licensing, School Boards, and Private Bill legislation. The single brief mention of women ("there is the question whether women will be capable of sitting on the Scotch County Councils") is a passing observation without any argument for or against, and the speaker immediately moves on to other topics.

The speech is entirely focused on police accountability, law and order, civil liberties, and the Police and Criminal Evidence Bill. The only mention of women is a passing historical reference ("women obtained it in 1928") with no argument made about women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely about housing policy, specifically women's fear of losing the right to buy council houses under a Labour government, used as an observation about voting behaviour. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation; the mention of women is purely as a demographic group of voters and potential home-buyers, not as a class with distinctive civic status.

The speaker supports women being on County Councils (accepting a supplementary list for women in that context) but explicitly opposes their participation in any other political body, saying "I hope we shall not have them anywhere else" — making a substantive argument on both sides of women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on cable television regulation, broadcasting impartiality, the British film industry, and media ownership — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "a telephone poll of women voters" is a passing reference to polling methodology during an election, not an argument about women's civic status or political rights.

The speaker urges the Secretary of State to accept an amendment ensuring women in India receive adequate voting power, explicitly advocating that promises made to Indian women regarding enfranchisement be fulfilled.

The speaker's argument is about securing representation for working-class industrial organisations on local committees, using the concession already granted to women merely as a procedural reference point. The speech does not argue for or against women's political rights; it simply notes that a concession was made regarding women and seeks an analogous one for working men.

The speaker explicitly supports expanding women's franchise in India, arguing that the number of women voters proposed is too small, that the necessity-for-application requirement will reduce women's participation, and urging the Secretary of State to accept the Amendment to ensure women can "take some fuller share in the government of the country."

The target speech is entirely focused on the debate over capital punishment (hanging as a deterrent, the risk of executing innocent people, and the problems of applying the death penalty to terrorists), with no reference to women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related topic.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing against the restoration of capital punishment, with no mention of women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any related topic. Women are mentioned only incidentally as potential hostages in a hypothetical scenario, not in any civic or political rights context.

The TARGET speech is a Speaker's ruling on parliamentary procedure, addressing whether amendments on soldiers, sailors, and women's enfranchisement are admissible under the Bill's title. It does not argue for or against women's political rights; it merely explains the procedural mechanism (an Instruction) by which such questions could be raised, without taking any substantive position on the merits of women's enfranchisement.

The speaker (the Chairman) is ruling on procedural order regarding proposed clauses about Parliament's duration, mentioning women's suffrage only incidentally as a subject of one such clause. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

Sir John Kinloch explicitly states "I hope, also, there will be a clause in the Bill making women eligible to sit in the Councils," expressing clear support for women's right to hold public office on local councils.

The speech is entirely concerned with the constitutional question of whether Burma should be separated from India, including the 1932 election results, the Prime Minister's pledge, and economic relations. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on housing policy — the right to buy, building regulations, council house sales, and tenant repair rights. The only mention of women is a passing observation that the right-to-buy policy is popular among women voters, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Secretary of State) explicitly states he is "as anxious as any hon. Member to see the women's vote really effective" and commits the Government to introducing an Amendment to remove the application qualification for women voters across most Indian Provinces, calling it "a great advance" toward women's enfranchisement. His objection is procedural (the specific percentage mechanism won't work), not a substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about electoral deposits and the right of fringe candidates to stand for election. The brief historical references to women's suffrage candidates (T. Smith in 1906 and H. L. Jacobs in 1910) are used only as examples of fringe candidates who pioneered ideas later accepted, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

Campbell-Bannerman explicitly argues that married women should not be excluded from the county franchise ("I object to the exclusion of married women from the exercise of this privilege"), and affirms that women—including married women—ought to have votes in local/county affairs just as they already have for School Boards and Town Councils. He also supports including service-franchise men, which would make the electorate "Parliamentary electors, plus women," further endorsing women's local voting rights.

The speaker (Lord Advocate Robertson) explicitly states his intention that "women should not be eligible as County Councillors" and affirms he adheres to that view, accepting the amendment to exclude women from serving on County Councils.

The speech is primarily about Scottish county government reform, free education, franchise arrangements, and local administration. The only mention of women is a passing reference that householders "both male and female" are to be electors for the County Council, stated descriptively without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on UK-South Africa relations, the Mozambique non-aggression pact, trade and sporting links with South Africa, and apartheid policy — none of which engage with women's political rights or representation. There is no argument made for or against women's civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that soldiers and sailors deserve enfranchisement as heroes who have suffered through the war, advocating for extending the franchise to them. While he focuses primarily on soldiers and sailors rather than women, he acknowledges the women's suffrage cause respectfully ("I do not believe that those who put forward the franchise for women do not themselves see that distinction") and frames his argument within the broader context of franchise extension — notably he does not oppose women's suffrage, and implicitly supports the principle by urging the House to "discuss in a friendly manner" enfranchising these heroes, framing it as a matter of dignity.

The speaker explicitly supports keeping the Bill's provision excluding women from election to County Councils, arguing that striking out the exclusion clause would merely expose women to lawsuits rather than enable their election, and uses this as justification to vote for the Bill as it stands — i.e., with women barred from election.

The speaker (the Prime Minister) explicitly states he has already expressed his views on women's enfranchisement and references his prior acknowledgment that women "have a special claim to be heard" on reconstruction questions, indicating support. He also frames the register bill as a temporary stop-gap while signalling openness to broader franchise reform that would include women, and agrees the temporary register should not be used to exclude women from a post-war Parliament.

The speaker explicitly associates themselves with the Amendment designed to secure women's voting rights in India, criticises opponents for failing to defend those rights, cites evidence that enfranchising Indian women will advance political progress, and urges the Government to accept the Amendment so that women's voices are heard in Indian councils and legislatures.

Sir J. Simon explicitly argues that women have earned political rights through their wartime contributions and that it is unjust to create a special register excluding them, especially if that register could form the basis of a post-war Parliament of reconstruction. He quotes the Prime Minister's acknowledgment of women's claims and the Minister of Munitions on women's civic rights, using these to press the case for women's enfranchisement as part of a broader franchise reform.

The speaker mentions votes for women only as a historical example to justify the principle of defying bad laws in a debate about rate-capping legislation. No argument for or against women's political rights is made; the reference is purely incidental.

The speaker explicitly states he would have voted against women's franchise, indicating opposition to one aspect of women's political rights, but then commits to voting for women's eligibility to stand for election, supporting another aspect — making substantive arguments on both sides.

Mr. M'Laren explicitly argues in favour of women being elected to County Councils, citing examples of women serving effectively on School Boards and Boards of Guardians, and expressing confidence that there is strong desire in Scotland for women to be elected to these bodies.

The speaker moves an amendment to reserve ten seats in India's Council of State for representatives elected by women members of the Legislative Assemblies, explicitly arguing that women (alongside labour and depressed classes) must have guaranteed political representation and that without it the assembly could not be truly representative. This is a clear, substantive argument in favour of women's political representation.

The speaker (Mr. Butler) explicitly announces and defends the Government's acceptance of reserved seats for women in the Council of State (six seats), framing it as meeting a sense of justice and correcting a deficiency in women's representation. This is a substantive endorsement of women's political representation in the Upper House.

The speaker explicitly states "I, too, have been an advocate of women's suffrage" while discussing the Registration Bill debate. Although he argues that soldiers' claims should take priority over women's suffrage claims in the current wartime context, he does not oppose women's suffrage itself — he affirms his support for it while making a pragmatic distinction about timing and precedence.

The speaker (Mr. Cocks, Member for Broxtowe) argues in support of an amendment to allocate ten seats for women representatives in the Indian Council of State, explicitly stating that Labour, women, and depressed classes should have guaranteed representation in the legislative body. While the speech focuses primarily on the scheduled classes, it consistently groups women alongside labour and depressed classes as deserving representation, supporting the amendment that would ensure women elect representatives to the Council of State.

The speaker (Major Milner) explicitly argues that women must have representation in the Council of State and the Federal Assembly of India, calling it "extremely important" and stating it is essential to break down the subordinate position of women in India. He advocates for the Amendment reserving seats for women, labour, and depressed classes, and even suggests women's claim may rank higher than that of labour.

The speaker invokes the suffragette movement approvingly, arguing that women's right to vote, stand for Parliament, and serve as Prime Minister were hard-won through systematic law-breaking and sacrifice, implicitly endorsing those rights as legitimate and valuable. This is a substantive, affirmative reference to women's political rights used to reinforce the broader argument against reducing the franchise.

The speaker welcomes the government's concession to provide women representation in the Council of State, and notes with approval that Parliament is "making a breach in old political customs" by doing in India what "some people think ought to have been done here at home long ago," implicitly supporting women's political representation. The speech is primarily focused on Labour representation, but the speaker's framing of women's seats as a positive step is a clear endorsement of women's political rights.

The speaker asks the Solicitor-General whether the suffragettes' hardships were worthwhile, then immediately undercuts any endorsement by saying that if women hadn't won the vote, "this country might have been better off, because we would not have had this Prime Minister" — implying regret that women obtained political rights given the result. This is a substantive, if sardonic, argument against women's political rights (or at least against their having produced a desirable outcome).

The speech is entirely about corporal punishment (flogging) for violent and sexual offences, drawing on the speaker's experience as Grand Jury foreman. Women are not mentioned as a distinct class with respect to political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation; the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights in any way.

The speaker explicitly states that despite having previously voted against women's suffrage on every occasion, he is now persuaded by the arguments of the Prime Minister and supports giving women the vote, arguing that women's wartime contributions to industry create a right to be heard in the Parliament that will settle reconstruction questions.

The speaker (Mr. Dickinson, Member for North St. Pancras) explicitly argues that if service and sacrifice are to be the basis of the franchise, women who have demonstrated the same should receive the same right as men, citing examples like Nurse Cavell and women serving in hospitals. He states: "we who have stood up for women suffrage say that the same right must be conceded to women as is given to men," and insists the question must be considered by a Committee before the War ends.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Trade Union Bill, criticising its provisions on union executive elections, strike ballots, and political funds. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the broader working-class membership who built the trade union movement, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker, as Chairman of a Board of Guardians, endorses the appointment of lady Inspectors for workhouses, arguing that female inspection of women's and children's wards is currently inadequate and that at least one female Inspector should be appointed for the whole Kingdom.

The speaker (Mr. Rhys Davies) explicitly congratulates the Government for conceding reserved seats for women in the Council of State and says "we congratulate the Government on coming to the assistance of the women of India," while also noting that the reserved women's seats will free up nominations for Labour. His only critical remark about the women's seats — that they will go to rich rather than working women — is a class-based caveat about the limits of the concession, not opposition to women's representation itself.

The speaker explicitly argues that women deserve the vote based on their work as women — raising children, governing households, and encouraging men to enlist — stating "women are entitled to the vote on their work as women." This is a direct, substantive endorsement of women's suffrage.

The speech is entirely focused on the technical details of prescribed identity documents for election purposes in Northern Ireland (driving licences, marriage certificates, pension books), with the brief mention of women retaining maiden names after marriage being incidental to the procedural discussion rather than an argument about women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on European Assembly election regulations, specifically objecting to the simple majority voting system and boundary confusion. The brief mention of "chairpersons or spokespersons or chairmen or chairwomen" is purely an analogy about nomenclature obsession, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses almost entirely on Scottish local government reform—rate-paying qualifications, service voters, police administration, capital expenditure, and free education—without making any argument for or against women's political rights. Women are mentioned only in passing (in the following context speeches) as one component of the first electorate, not as a subject of substantive argument in the TARGET itself.

The speaker (Mr. Long) argues that opening up franchise questions—including women's suffrage—during wartime would be a "criminal act," explicitly resisting any extension of the franchise to women (or anyone else) at this time. While he acknowledges women's sacrifices and suggests a distinction between soldiers and women might be difficult to draw, his overriding argument is that plunging into women's suffrage debates would be deeply harmful and unworthy of the House, effectively opposing any wartime enfranchisement of women.

The speaker questions imposing women members on a legislative body, calling it unprecedented in any country in the world, and challenges the justification for including women's representation in the Council of State, framing women as a "special interest" to undermine the principle of non-special representation rather than to support it.

The speech is about electoral reform legislation (overseas voting rights, candidate deposits, absent voting, Northern Ireland electoral provisions) and makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a passing historical reference to candidates who "stood in favour of votes for women" as an example of fringe candidates who lost deposits, offered to illustrate a point about electoral deposits rather than to argue for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speaker (Sir H. Croft) argues against imposing women representatives on India's Council of State, framing it as undemocratic and inconsistent with principle, asking why women should be "imposed upon" the chamber rather than letting India decide for itself. He questions the justification for special representation of women as an interest group, consistently opposing the Amendment throughout.

The speaker explicitly endorses women's suffrage, arguing that women's work in encouraging voluntary enlistment of 5,000,000 men "establishes their claim for any of the electoral privileges which they demand," and frames women's suffrage as a major social question that must be resolved properly after the War.

The speech addresses electoral reform topics such as voter registration accuracy, postal/absent voting, polling hours, candidate deposits, and democratic rights broadly — but at no point singles out women as a class or argues about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any civic status distinctive to women.

The speaker argues that enfranchising soldiers and sailors does not necessarily require bringing in women's suffrage, and explicitly states "I entirely disagree myself with the view that if you are going to give the vote to the soldiers and sailors you thereby drag in the question of women's suffrage as well." The speaker also conveys, on behalf of the Women's Social and Political Union, that women themselves do not wish to be used to block soldiers' votes — framing women's suffrage as a separate and subordinate issue that should not be linked to soldiers' enfranchisement, effectively opposing the extension of women's political rights in this context.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone, based on context) explicitly supports women securing seats on the Council of State and argues for a better method of selecting those women, criticising the all-male Electoral College as an inappropriate body to choose women representatives. The speech is substantively in favour of women's political representation in India.

Sir G. Campbell explicitly states he thinks "it would also be desirable if, at the same time, the women's franchise could be omitted from the Bill" and expresses hope that no "loophole" exists by which women could "creep in to the Council," directly opposing women's political participation in local government.

The speaker explicitly argues that the women's franchise question is "a question apart" and "has nothing to do with this question, nothing whatever," focusing entirely on enfranchising soldiers and sailors. The brief mention of women's franchise is only to set it aside as out of scope, with no substantive argument made for or against it.

The TARGET speeches focus entirely on Scottish local government matters: rate incidence between landlords and tenants, Commissioners of Supply, County Council structure, harbour works, licensing, and service franchise restrictions. The brief mention of "female voters" in Mr. M'Lagan's speech is merely a passing reference to the Bill's provisions without any argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that women (alongside scheduled classes and labour) should have guaranteed minimum representation of at least 10 seats out of 250 in the Council of State, framing this as "elementary justice" needed at the early stages of the new Indian constitution. The speech supports women's political representation as a matter of right, not merely in passing.

Viscountess Astor explicitly supports women's franchise and political representation in India, expresses gratitude to the Government for granting women the vote under the India Bill, and argues that women's political participation is essential. She advocates for Indian women's right to vote and be elected, even while acknowledging practical limitations in timing.
The speech is entirely focused on NHS management, funding, and the closure of a casualty unit in Ellesmere Port, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (and the surrounding speeches) is entirely focused on Irish land purchase legislation — the rights of tenants to buy their holdings, the financial security for British taxpayers, and the politics of Home Rule — with no mention of women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker (the Chairman) is making a procedural ruling about which amendments fall within the scope of the Bill, listing women's suffrage among several topics deemed out of scope. No argument is made for or against women's political rights; it is merely cited as an example of an out-of-scope amendment.

Mr. Conybeare explicitly states he supports universal suffrage and adds "If it be extended to women, I shall be the better pleased," expressing clear support for women's voting rights. The remainder of his speech concerns procedural matters about the adjournment motion.

The speaker dismisses women's suffrage as a separate and lesser question, arguing that women's advocates are harming their own cause by linking it to soldiers' and sailors' enfranchisement, and explicitly deprioritises women's claims relative to those of fighting men. This implicitly opposes advancing women's political rights at this juncture.

Mr. M'Laren's speech argues extensively and forcefully for Parliamentary time to be given to a Women's Suffrage Bill, decrying repeated interference preventing its discussion and appealing to Members to allow the debate, clearly supporting women's political rights (the franchise extension to women).

The speech concerns transport provisions for disabled people in London under the London Regional Transport Bill, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The passing reference to the Minister as "the more acceptable face of Tory women" is purely rhetorical and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about local government spending and financial accountability in Scotland. The brief mention of Stirling district council voting £10,000 to set up a "women's committee" is cited purely as an example of wasteful spending by a profligate authority, without making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly opposes the inclusion of women in the Council of State, describing it as an "extraordinary concession" that "artificially" brings women in, and argues that women's claims should be prioritized below those of the depressed classes and organised Labour, expressing a clear negative stance toward women's political representation.

Asquith explicitly acknowledges that women's wartime service gives them "not only a reasonable, but...an unanswerable case" for enfranchisement if a new franchise based on State service is introduced, and states "I cannot deny that claim" — expressing genuine support for women's right to be heard and potentially enfranchised. His objection is procedural (that opening franchise questions at all during wartime is damaging), not a substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker is pressing the First Lord of the Treasury to protect parliamentary time for the Women's Franchise Bill, demonstrating active support for advancing women's political rights in the legislature.

The speaker's focus is on keeping the franchise bill focused on enfranchising fighting men (soldiers), explicitly warning against introducing "confusing and conflicting issues" like women's suffrage rather than arguing for or against it. The brief mention of "women's suffrage" is used only as an example of a contentious issue to be avoided, with no substantive argument made about women's political rights themselves.

Mr. Cremer explicitly states he does not share the pro-suffrage views of the Member for Crewe and dismisses female suffrage as a question of far less importance than other pressing matters like working men's grievances and voter registration, effectively opposing the prioritisation of women's political rights in Parliament.

The speech is a ministerial response to a debate on Army matters, covering topics such as defence expenditure, NATO strategy, equipment, and the Ulster Defence Regiment. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., noting 5,500 women in the Army and referencing a book about women and the Falklands War) without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses on procedural and constitutional complaints about the Registration Bill—its scope, the Speaker's rulings, the role of the conference committee, and whether soldiers and sailors can be enfranchised under it. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as one of several subjects referred to the committee, without any argument for or against it.

The TARGET speech (delivered by Miss Ward, as confirmed by context) moves an amendment to reserve seats for women on the Council of State from six provinces, directly advocating for women's political representation. The preceding remarks questioning the method and provincial legislatures' opinions are in service of ensuring the proposal works effectively, not opposing it.

The speaker explicitly states "I am not going to discuss the question of votes for women" and limits the remark to a procedural point about whether a Minister's statement can be replied to by private Members. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker challenges the Secretary of State over the low number of women (31 out of 206) appointed to public bodies and explicitly demands action to "ensure equality of representation on public bodies in Wales," advocating for greater women's political participation.

The speech is entirely about parliamentary pension arrangements for Members of Parliament — specifically the age and service requirements for drawing a pension — with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The brief mention of a "former lady Member" who raised an anomaly about women's pension age is purely contextual and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights.

The TARGET speech primarily concerns representation of labour, commerce, industry, and landholders in the Indian Federal Assembly under the Government of India Bill. While the speaker briefly mentions women alongside depressed classes and wage-earners as groups needing protection, this is a passing rhetorical reference rather than an argument about women's political rights.

This maiden speech concerns the 1984 miners' strike, freedom to work, and union democracy. While the speaker briefly mentions "ordinary men and women" and "miners' wives" in passing, there is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question asking for factual clarification about whether women are legally entitled to vote in Parochial Board elections and whether specific votes were valid — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights, merely seeking information about the legal situation.

The target speech is primarily a critique of the electoral and constitutional arrangements in the Government of India Bill (Fifth Schedule), focusing on the complexity of the electoral system, the Governor-General's rule-making powers, and the Federation structure. The brief mention of the "women's Electoral College" and women's seats (paragraph 19) is purely descriptive, citing the text of the Schedule to illustrate its complexity, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker strongly advocates for women's equal pay rights, criticizing the regulations as inadequate and ineffective for helping low-paid women, and explicitly states she would vote in favour if the regulations genuinely helped women. Her opposition is to the specific (flawed) mechanism, not to women's workplace rights themselves.

The speaker (Lord Advocate) affirms that women frequently vote and are elected to Parochial Boards in Scotland as a matter of established practice, grounding this in statutory language that explicitly extends masculine-gendered terms to females. This constitutes a clear endorsement of women's right to participate in these civic electoral processes.

The target speech is entirely concerned with procedural matters about parliamentary business scheduling (the Allotments Bill, Morning Sittings, and Order Papers). While Dr. Cameron's question mentions a motion on extending the Parliamentary franchise to women in passing, the speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights — it is solely a procedural point-of-order inquiry about scheduling.

The TARGET speeches debate the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill (marriage law reform), not women's political rights or representation. The brief mentions of women — e.g., noting the Bill treats women differently from men regarding a deceased husband's brother, or suggesting waiting until women get the franchise — are passing references without substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (the Under-Secretary) acknowledges and supports the expansion of women's voting rights in Burma (noting an increase from ~124,000 to ~700,000 women voters) and accepts the principle of women participating in political life through ordinary constituencies, while simultaneously opposing the specific Amendment to reserve five seats for Burmese women in the House of Representatives, citing the Burmese women's own representative's stated preference against reserved seats. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: endorsing women's franchise expansion while opposing reserved seats.

The speech moves to appoint a Select Committee on electoral registration and wartime elections, focusing on the practical difficulties of registering soldiers, munition workers, and updating voter rolls during wartime. While women's suffrage is briefly mentioned as a potential controversial issue the Committee would have to navigate, the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights — he merely warns that raising the question would provoke bitter controversy, treating it as a political obstacle to avoid rather than arguing a position on its merits.

The speech is focused entirely on the government's failure to maintain the electoral register and the procedural history of wartime registration legislation; the brief mention of women's votes ("There is nothing there about giving women votes") is a passing reference used to contrast the register question from franchise expansion, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that Burmese women deserve either reserved seats or an extended franchise, criticising the Government for taking away reserved seats without compensating with adequate voting rights. The speech explicitly advocates for greater political representation and voting power for women in Burma.

The speaker explicitly advocates for increasing the reservation of seats for women in Bengal and the United Provinces in the Federal Assembly, arguing that the current allocation is unfair to women and proposing a specific mechanism to improve their representation without disrupting communal awards.

The speech is entirely focused on charity administration, the Endowed Schools Bill, the powers of Charity Commissioners, and the rights of the poor to benefit from charitable endowments. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other in-scope topic; the brief mention of "poor women in confinement" is purely in the context of charitable relief, not civic participation.

The speech is entirely concerned with the Defence of the Realm Act prosecutions, civil liberties, freedom of speech, and the treatment of Labour/socialist activists in South Wales. While it briefly mentions "Help for Babies" and "Clinics for Babies" pamphlets issued by the Women's Labour League, this is incidental to the main argument about suppression of political opinion and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the franchise to Burmese women, arguing that they are among the most intelligent women in the East and deserve the opportunity to exercise that intelligence through expanded voting rights. The speaker also endorses Miss Rathbone's argument that the government should not rely solely on one representative to deny broader women's political rights in Burma.

The speech is a brief intervention on divorce law and financial provision for wives, addressing the previous speaker's concern about older women who have sacrificed careers to raise children. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — it is focused on matrimonial financial relief provisions.

The target speech addresses the administrative and financial details of a munitions employment demonstration for women, focusing on budgetary procedure and which Vote covers the expenditure. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech addresses administrative and procedural matters concerning domestic violence legislation in Scotland (guidance to police on exclusion orders), with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily concerned with the financial administration of the National Insurance Act — specifically the solvency of women's approved societies, the sinking fund, sanatorium benefits, and the Advisory Committee. While it mentions women as a class of insured persons and notes they "have no votes" in passing, this is incidental context rather than an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is primarily about parliamentary scheduling and procedural arrangements for government business after Whitsuntide. Women's political rights are only briefly mentioned in passing when Smith notes an amendment by Mr. M'Laren regarding a Motion on extending the franchise to women, and suggests he bring a Bill instead — but Smith makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

Mr. M'Laren explicitly moves an amendment to secure parliamentary time for debating the extension of the franchise to women, framing it as "an act of justice," and Mr. Webb seconds it, stating it is a subject of great interest and offering reasons why it should be discussed.

The speech is primarily about the abolition of metropolitan councils and the democratic rights of working people in local government. Women's political rights are mentioned only in a brief passing historical reference ("In the early 20th century, there were struggles for women to be given the vote") as part of a broader argument about the history of extending democracy, without making any argument for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speech concerns Irish national teachers' pensions, war bonuses, and the National Board's decision to bar teacher-magistrates from sitting on the bench. While women teachers are briefly mentioned as having received a bonus, no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech concerns the extension of adult suffrage in India, not women's political rights specifically. While the speaker mentions "350,000,000 adult males and females" and supports universal adult suffrage in India as a future goal, this is framed entirely around Indian political development and franchise extension broadly, with no substantive argument about women's civic status or political rights as a distinct class.

The speech is primarily about domiciliary visits by police, the seizure of documents related to conscientious objectors, and civil liberties during wartime. The brief mention of the "suffragette cause" and "Suffragist movement" is incidental context describing what the detectives claimed to be looking for — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech focuses on divorce law, maintenance provisions, and the financial welfare of women and children after divorce — not on women's political rights or representation. While the speaker mentions women's equality and financial independence in passing, these references concern economic and domestic status rather than civic participation, voting, or political representation.

The speech is primarily about European representation in the Burma Legislature and the constitutional arrangements for Burma. While women's reserved seats are briefly mentioned (noting that a Burmese woman representative asked for no reserved seats and an increased franchise), the speaker does not argue a substantive position for or against women's political rights — he merely reports what was requested and defers the franchise question to a later point.

The speech is entirely focused on the Maze prison breakout, prison security failings, staff morale, the Hennessy report, and accountability of Northern Ireland Office officials — none of which concerns women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of female prison staff having their handbags checked is a security observation, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech is primarily concerned with labour representation, franchise provisions, and European seats in Burma's legislative assembly. The brief mention of women ("I have already announced to the Committee the number of women who will be receiving the vote") is purely factual and passes without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is a procedural point of order challenging whether Sir J. Simon's argument about women's suffrage is in order given the Speaker's earlier ruling. The speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights, merely invoking a procedural ruling to question the relevance of another speaker's remarks.

The speech concerns trade union political levies, state financing of political parties, and party funding structures. The brief mention of how women trade union members voted is cited purely as statistical evidence about voting patterns, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about Territorial Army expansion plans, including new battalions, equipment, and recruitment. While it briefly mentions "men and women" serving in reserve forces, it makes no argument about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker acknowledges having previously supported greater franchise facilities for Burmese women (endorsing their political rights) on the grounds they were more advanced than Indian women, but then states he was convinced by arguments that it is not practically possible to extend those rights at present, effectively supporting the rejection of the amendment to expand women's franchise in Burma.

The TARGET speeches are almost entirely about temperance legislation and local veto over liquor licensing in Wales. The only mention of women's political rights is a single passing remark by Mr. Stanley Leighton that "the Bill indirectly introduces women's suffrage," offered as a brief aside without any argument for or against women's suffrage. No substantive argument about women's political rights is made anywhere in the TARGET.

The TARGET speech, delivered by Mr. C. Graham, merely mentions receiving a whip to support a Motion on extending the Parliamentary Franchise to Women on June 3rd, without making any argument for or against women's political rights. It is a procedural reference to scheduling, not a substantive argument on the merits of women's enfranchisement.

The target speech focuses almost entirely on attacking the practical workability of the registration/franchise bill—its anomalies, the impossibility of tracing munition workers and soldiers, and the risk of bogus voters—without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The brief passing references to women (e.g., noting the Cabinet pressure around including women) are descriptive of the political situation, not arguments about women's franchise.

The speaker explicitly references the arguments against women's suffrage in Britain as analogous to the current arguments against extending the franchise in India, implying those anti-women's suffrage arguments were wrong and that women's enfranchisement was correct. This draws a supportive parallel to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on procedural matters — whether the government should honour its pledge not to take Wednesday the 13th, and how private members' time should be allocated — without making any substantive argument for or against women's suffrage itself. The mention of "the withdrawal of the Motion as to women's suffrage" is purely incidental to the procedural dispute.

The TARGET speech is primarily about federalism, devolution, and Home Rule for Ireland, Scotland, Wales, and England. The only mention of women is a brief, passing reference by Mr. Evans noting that the Isle of Man "has gone in advance of England by extending the suffrage to women" — offered as an illustration of the Isle of Man's capacity for self-governance, without any argument for or against women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly states he "has supported, and still supports, every extension of the franchise in the direction both of adult males and females," directly endorsing women's political rights. His regret that a settlement cannot be reached at the moment is a procedural/timing caveat, not substantive opposition.

The speaker explicitly draws a parallel between past arguments against women's suffrage ("too ignorant to put their cross on the paper") and current arguments against Indian franchise extension, framing both as unjust denials of political rights and implying that women's enfranchisement was the correct outcome. This rhetorically endorses women's political rights as a settled positive precedent.

The speaker explicitly congratulates the acceptance of an amendment extending the vote to more women in India, calling it "a gallant and chivalrous act," clearly expressing support for expanding women's political rights (the franchise).

Mr. Haldane explicitly argues that May 13th should be kept free for Private Members so that the Bill on Women's Suffrage can be discussed, stating "I ask the House to pause before depriving us of the opportunity we seek of discussing the principle of Women's Suffrage." This is a clear, affirmative stance in support of women's suffrage having parliamentary time.

The speaker explicitly highlights women's historic struggle for the vote and their long exclusion from political participation, celebrates the early women councillors elected to the LCC, and frames the cancellation of GLC elections as an attack on women's political voice. She argues that "women of London are very angry at the taking away of their vote" and connects the GLC's abolition to the disadvantaging of women in public life.

The speaker (Sir Henry James) argues that parliamentary time should not be given over to a Second Reading debate on women's suffrage, dismissing it as "an abstract discussion on the right of female suffrage" and an "abstract proposition" already debated "eight or ten times," thereby opposing prioritizing women's suffrage legislation over practical government business.

The target speech is primarily about housing administration and whether the Society of Women Housing Estate Managers should be statutorily represented on a committee. The speaker supports the Amendment on principle but declines to legislate specific committee membership; any reference to women is incidental to the housing policy debate, and no argument is made for or against women's political rights or civic participation as a class.

The TARGET speech is overwhelmingly concerned with franchise reform (plural voting, registration, "one man one vote"), Irish representation, Home Rule, and electoral districts. Women's suffrage appears only once in passing — Mr. De Lisle notes "as to the proposal on the Paper to admit women suffrage, as the less of two evils I would prefer universal suffrage" — which is a fleeting, incidental reference without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights as the focus of the speech.

The speaker explicitly argues that the extension of the franchise—including the granting of votes to women in 1918—led to valued social progress, and notes that before women had the vote, "women's issues and rights got short shrift in Parliament," implying support for women's political participation as part of a broader pro-democratic argument.

The speaker (Mr. Butler, the Under-Secretary) explicitly declines to accept an amendment that would enfranchise more women in India, citing the "inadvisability of so rapidly increasing the number of women electors" and arguing that such a large increase would "militate against the success of the extended franchise" for women — effectively opposing a broader extension of women's political rights at this stage.

The speech concerns immigration clearance rights and the specific case of a Bangladeshi widow, arguing against harsh immigration enforcement on humanitarian grounds. While it briefly mentions "battered wives" losing the right to stay due to changed circumstances, this is raised as an immigration rights issue rather than an argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary ruling on procedural matters — specifically whether extensive amendments to a Pensions Bill constitute a "new Bill" requiring reintroduction. The mention of women is only incidental, as one historical precedent among several cited (the Franchise and Registration Bill), with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the administration of military pensions and separation allowances, the structure of the Pensions Board, and the Statutory Committee — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker is asking a procedural question aimed at securing parliamentary time for the Women's Suffrage Bill, specifically ensuring May 13th (when the Bill stands as First Order of the Day) remains a Private Members' day. This is a supportive action on behalf of women's suffrage.

The speaker strongly advocates for enfranchising men who served in the armed forces, arguing the Bill disenfranchises them, while simultaneously arguing that women, having never had votes before, must "stand aside" until after the War—though with a promise of a Women's Franchise Bill thereafter. This constitutes substantive support for men's expanded franchise alongside substantive opposition (even if conditional and temporary) to women's political rights in the current bill.

The speaker (Mr. Long, President of the Local Government Board) explicitly states that local authorities are not required to appoint women on the tribunals and that the matter is left to their discretion, declining to push for women's inclusion on these civic bodies. This reflects opposition to mandating women's participation in public/political office.

The speech focuses on the Warnock report's recommendations regarding infertility treatment, embryo research, and IVF regulation. While the speaker briefly mentions that women's organisations should have representation on the licensing body and that treatment should be available to single men and women, these are incidental points within a broader debate about medical ethics and fertility policy, not substantive arguments about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the performance, accountability, and management of the Metropolitan Police in London, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of PC Yvette Fletcher's murder is treated as a policing and diplomatic failure, not as an argument about women's civic status.

The speaker expresses sympathy with expanding women's franchise in India and defers to the Franchise Committee's recommendations, noting approvingly that the Committee's proposals would increase the women's electorate 21 times. While he opposes the specific Amendment on practical grounds (following the Committee's unanimous conclusion), his overall framing supports greater women's political participation rather than opposing it in principle.

The speech concerns wage rates and working conditions for women employed in munitions factories during wartime, specifically defending a Ministry circular setting minimum pay. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the electoral roll in India is too small and that more women should be included, drawing a parallel to the UK where women did not enter public life until they received the vote. He supports the Amendment to extend the franchise to more women, including widows, and urges the Government to accept its principle.

The speech focuses on family practitioner committees, health education, deputising services, and cancer screening programmes. While women are mentioned as beneficiaries of health services (e.g., cervical and breast cancer screening, pregnant women), the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women pensioners are treated unfairly and unequally compared to men in the tax system, advocates for equalising the age allowance at retirement age for women (age 60), calls for inclusion of pension equality in the Sex Equality Bill, and urges the Government to eliminate discrimination against women pensioners — all clear expressions of support for women's equal civic and economic status.

The speaker (Mr. Raikes) explicitly states he does not consider further extension of the franchise to women in India likely to help them play a greater part in government, and expresses pleasure in supporting the Government's opposition to the Amendment that would expand women's suffrage. This is a clear stance against extending women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly endorses women's greater political participation in India, approvingly quoting the Statutory Commission's view that women "ought to take a fuller share in the development of India" and praising the notable change of women stepping "out of seclusion into the full life of political activity." While expressing caution about the specific Amendment due to uncertainty over the scale of the electorate expansion, this is a procedural concern rather than substantive opposition to women's enfranchisement.

The speech concerns disability benefits policy (the non-contributory invalidity pension and severe disablement allowance), not women's political rights. While married women are briefly mentioned as one affected group, the argument is about disability welfare policy, not women's civic status or political participation.

The TARGET speech is entirely about Irish Sunday closing legislation (temperance/liquor licensing), Home Rule, and whether the Irish Parliament should legislate for Ireland. The only mention of women's political rights appears in Mr. Knatchbull-Hugessen's brief dismissal of "Women Suffrage, Payment of Members, Compulsory Education" as examples of "grandmotherly legislation," which is a passing negative reference without substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on public health administration during wartime — tuberculosis treatment, venereal disease policy, sanitary services, reconstruction planning, and tributes to medical professionals and civil servants. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question about military service appointments in Jersey and Guernsey, focused on whether young men of military age were appointed to roles that could have been filled by older men or women. The mention of women is incidental to the question of military manpower allocation, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about the scope of executive powers in clause 1(3) of a bill abolishing the GLC and metropolitan councils. While the speaker briefly mentions women's voting rights since 1888 as part of a broader argument about removing democratic rights, this is a passing rhetorical flourish rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights specifically; the core debate is about parliamentary oversight of executive power and electoral law.

The speaker intervenes to clarify that enfranchising women in India under the Amendment would not put women voters in the majority over men, countering a concern raised by Mr. Foot — effectively defending the Amendment's feasibility and implicitly supporting broader women's enfranchisement in India.

The speaker explicitly supports giving Indian women the vote, arguing it is necessary to change terrible social conditions and that the women's movement can help bridge communal divisions. They directly state they would not mind women outnumbering men on the register and urge the Committee to support the Amendment enfranchising more women.

The speech is focused entirely on local government finance, rate-capping, and centralization policy. The passing mention of "women's advisers" is a brief rhetorical aside listing items the speaker dislikes in Greenwich council's spending, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily a lengthy endorsement of the Ministry of Munitions' wartime production efforts, with observations about women's employment in munitions factories treated as a wartime labour and welfare matter (working conditions, clothing, health) rather than as an argument about women's civic or political rights. The speaker expresses admiration for women's industrial contributions but makes no argument about voting, political representation, or women's civic status.

Mr. Bryce explicitly advocates for the appointment of female factory inspectors, arguing that women workers need women inspectors to inquire into matters affecting their well-being in workshops and factories, and earnestly commends this to the Home Secretary as a concession he hopes will be granted.

The TARGET speech is overwhelmingly concerned with parliamentary procedure, Votes on Account, Supply debates, and the Government's legislative timetable. The only reference to women's political rights is a passing mention by Mr. Morton that "the Leader of the House proposed such a course the other day in favour of the Women's Suffrage Bill" — used merely as an illustrative example of procedural flexibility, without arguing any position on women's suffrage itself.

The TARGET speech (primarily the first speaker, addressing the analogy between County Councils and Parliament) argues against women sitting on County Councils, warning it is a slippery slope to admitting women to Parliament, and closes by urging the House to reject the Motion. The subsequent speakers embedded in the TARGET (Tomlinson, Cremer, Bolton, Knowles, Ritchie, and McLaren) are overwhelmingly opposed, with McLaren being the sole voice in favour but his speech is brief and largely procedural. The overall thrust of the concatenated TARGET is opposition to women's political participation in County Councils and Parliament.

The TARGET speech concerns a wartime emergency bill to exempt temporary agricultural workers (including women) from National Insurance contributions. While women are mentioned as one category of workers, the debate is entirely about insurance law administration and agricultural labour supply, not about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women are treated as an employment category, not as a class with distinctive civic status.

The TARGET speech is entirely about whether the House should adjourn for Derby Day, opposing the adjournment on grounds of gambling, public morality, and the importance of pending legislative business (the Welsh Liquor Bill). The only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference by Mr. Morton to "The House refused to give a day for the consideration of the Women's Suffrage Bill," used rhetorically to contrast parliamentary priorities, without arguing any position on women's suffrage itself.

The speaker explicitly appeals to Tory Members to support the new clause in the name of "freedom of choice" and "expansion of opportunities for women and children," arguing that voting against it would deny young working mothers freedom of choice and harm their ability to participate in the workforce. This is a direct argument in favour of women's political and civic rights, specifically their right to participate equally in economic and public life.

The speaker raises a rhetorical challenge about polygamy producing more women voters than men, framing it as a reductio ad absurdum intended to undermine support for the Amendment extending women's franchise in India — a subtle but clear argument against the proposed expansion of women's political rights.

The target speech is a procedural reply stating that no communication has been received from the Irish Women's Franchise League and directing the questioner to a prior Prime Minister's reply. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

Mr. Labouchere dismisses the Women's Franchise Bill as "a Bill about female franchise or some folly of that sort," explicitly characterizing women's franchise as a foolish matter. This is a direct expression of opposition to women's political rights.

The entire debate concerns workmen's cheap train fares and railway regulation around London; women's political rights or civic participation are never mentioned or argued about. The only reference to women is a passing analogy by Mr. Lafone comparing an opponent's logic to someone refusing to support a franchise bill for police because it didn't extend to women—this is a rhetorical aside, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speeches in the target focus entirely on the governance and finances of Swaziland, the liquor trade affecting Swazi natives, and colonial policy in South Africa. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "women and young children" suffering from liquor), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Butler) defends the Government's scheme for women's franchise in India, arguing that it provides a fair and intelligible basis for women's political participation and noting that it was welcomed by women's representatives in both Britain and India. While he declines the specific amendments to expand the franchise further, he does so on grounds of administrative complexity and numerical scale, not opposition to women's political rights—he explicitly affirms the existing women's franchise scheme as fair and reasonable.

The speech is a wartime government response about the detention and repatriation of British women and children in enemy countries, addressing a diplomatic/consular matter. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

Viscountess Astor argues that the number of women voters in India (6,000,000 against 29,000,000 men) is already too small, pushes back against administrative objections to expanding the franchise, and explicitly advocates for more women receiving the vote, stating it is "for the good of India" that democracy include more women voters.

The speech concerns agricultural policy (sericulture/silk cultivation) in Cyprus and the potential use of government funds for industrial improvement. While it mentions female labour incidentally, it makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that voting for the new clause means "voting for genuinely equal opportunities for women" and frames workplace nursery tax exemptions as supporting women's rights and equal opportunities. He also invokes women's rights directly, praising the Labour spokesperson on women's rights and stating that men must also argue for women's rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Nassau Commonwealth agreement, sanctions policy toward South Africa, and the apartheid debate. While it briefly references "equal representation and equal franchise" in the context of South African political reform, it does not argue about women's political rights or representation as a class — the mention of Mrs. Winnie Mandela and the female Prime Minister are incidental references, not arguments about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on urging support for a military conscription bill (the Military Service Bill) to prosecute WWI, with arguments about army strength, unity, and wartime necessity. Women are mentioned only in passing ("in the interests of their country and of their women and of their children"), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

Viscountess Astor explicitly advocates for extending the women's vote in India, arguing that giving more women the vote is essential for a healthy democracy and that the administrative difficulties are overstated. She frames limiting women's political participation as comparable to when women in Britain were "classed for political purposes as criminal lunatics," making a clear normative case for women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about South African apartheid policy, trade sanctions, and the franchise for all South Africans regardless of race. While it mentions "equal franchise" for everyone in South Africa, this is about racial equality in a foreign country's political system, not about women's political rights or representation as defined by the suffrage movement's framing of civic personhood.

The target speech is entirely focused on the financial administration and actuarial soundness of the National Health Insurance Act, including expenditure, sickness benefit statistics, and the Ryan Committee's findings. While women are mentioned in the context of higher-than-expected sickness rates among insured women affecting the scheme's finances, this is a actuarial/financial observation, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns agricultural policy (sericulture/silk cultivation) in Cyprus and a potential grant for its improvement. While it mentions "female labour" in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the financial administration of the National Insurance Act — discrepancies in estimates, sickness benefit funding for women's approved societies, sanatorium grants, and the Government's statutory obligations to insured persons. While women's sickness benefit figures are mentioned, this is a discussion of insurance finance and actuarial shortfalls, not an argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech is entirely focused on factory labour conditions, child labour regulations, half-time employment, and laundry workers' labour protections under the Factory Acts. While women workers are mentioned as beneficiaries of proposed protections, there is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech (primarily Mr. Matthews/the Home Secretary opposing the laundry amendment, followed by Mr. Cunninghame Graham supporting it and Mr. Kelly disputing the evidence) concerns labour regulation and factory act coverage for laundresses — a workplace protection matter. While it addresses the working conditions of women, it does not argue about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's civic/political participation as defined in scope.

The speech focuses entirely on elementary education, child labour, school funding, teacher staffing, and wartime educational challenges. The sole reference to women is a passing remark that elementary schools may end up "staffed by women alone," which is an observation about staffing trends rather than an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The target speech argues that women in India have inadequate voting power and that the proposed amendments would justly expand the women's electorate, criticizing the Government for lacking sympathy toward women's political participation. Miss Ward's contribution further explicitly supports adding more women to the electoral register in India as essential for adequate women's representation.

The speaker is asking a factual procedural question about the legal basis and scope of the Service Franchise under the 1884 Act, specifically whether it applies to females. No argument for or against women's political rights is made; it is a neutral inquiry seeking clarification of existing law.

The speaker (Sir Basil Peto) explicitly opposes expanding women's franchise in India by dismissing the proposed Amendment to add wives of literate men to the electoral roll as "ridiculously impossible" and praising the Government for being "adamant" against it, while also suggesting that the existing 6,000,000 women voters is already "too much of a doubtfully good thing."

The speaker (Mr. Butler) explicitly declines to accept amendments that would expand women's franchise in India, arguing against increasing the number of women on the electoral roll on grounds of administrative complexity, large additions to numbers, and logical indefensibility — and urges Members not to "continually press Amendments of this sort," defending the existing (more restrictive) women's franchise scheme as sufficient.

The speech is primarily about extending the overseas franchise to British citizens living abroad, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of women's enfranchisement is used only as an analogy to support constitutional change in general, without arguing a position on women's political rights per se.

The TARGET speech is entirely concerned with proposed amendments relating to regional economic and social councils, voluntary organisation funding, and the abolition of the GLC and metropolitan county councils. The brief mention of "services for women" in the schedule of functions (alongside many other social services) does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker, a woman MP, explicitly states she will vote with the Government against the Amendment designed to increase women's franchise in India, arguing this is the "common sense" and best course for Indian women, thereby opposing an expansion of women's political rights.

The speech is focused entirely on interception of communications, national security, civil liberties, ministerial accountability, and the Interception of Communications Bill. The brief mention of suffragettes ("The Prime Minister would not be Prime Minister if the suffragettes had not chained themselves to the railings and broken the law") is used only as an illustrative example of principled law-breaking, not as an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker is asking the government to prevent female domestic servants from being entered in the Service Franchise column, effectively seeking to deny or restrict women's franchise rights in this context. This constitutes an argument against women's political rights for this class of women.

The speaker explicitly and at length supports extending the franchise to women, arguing that women deserve equal citizenship rights, that their war service has proven their worth, that organised labour unanimously endorses women's suffrage, and that the moment is opportune to pass this "long delayed measure of justice to women."

The speaker explicitly opposes women's suffrage throughout, arguing it would be "the most disastrous and revolutionary measure" ever introduced, that women are "not fitted for it by nature and temperament," and that war work is irrelevant to their claim for the vote. He supports the Amendment to remove women's suffrage from the Bill and urges rejection of these "contentious" proposals.

The speaker argues that women voters in India represent too small a proportion (only ~20%) of the electorate and explicitly supports amendments designed to increase the number of women electors, stating that 6,000,000 women voters out of 35,000,000 is inadequate and urging the Government to expand women's franchise.

The speaker (Solicitor General for Scotland) confirms that the Parliamentary Franchise under the 1884 Act applies to males only, effectively denying women the parliamentary service franchise. While acknowledging women may qualify under subsequent legislation for non-parliamentary elections, the overall thrust is to exclude women from the Parliamentary Franchise.

The speech is primarily about the Interception of Communications Bill, executive overreach, national security surveillance, and parliamentary democracy. The brief reference to Asquith opposing votes for women in 1910 is used only as a historical analogy to illustrate that arguments framed around "protecting parliamentary democracy" have historically been used to resist reform — it does not constitute an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "I am in favour of protecting women by giving them votes," endorsing women's suffrage, while simultaneously opposing legislative restrictions on women's working hours on grounds of individual liberty — arguing women should be free to sell their labour without legal restraint. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: support for women's political rights (franchise) and opposition to a form of paternalistic protection that he frames as limiting women's freedom.

The speaker explicitly argues that the proportion of women voters (20-23%) is too small and urges the government to adopt amendments that would increase women's representation in the electorate, referencing historical denial of women's property and franchise rights as justification for expanding women's political participation.

The target speech by Mrs. Thatcher concerns the Anglo-Irish Agreement, focusing on Northern Ireland security, terrorism, the intergovernmental conference, and relations between the two communities. Women's political rights and representation are not addressed or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speech is about the philosophical distinction between individual rights and "people's rights" in the context of UNESCO's mandate and human rights conventions, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Sir W. Smiles, the "hon. and gallant Member for Blackburn") argues that the application test for women voters should be removed in Assam, contending that the social difficulties cited by the Under-Secretary do not apply there and that administrative arrangements (using village headmen) would make automatic registration of women voters feasible. This is a substantive argument in support of expanding women's political rights in Assam.

The speaker explicitly states that opinion is "largely changing in favour of giving women a vote as soon as possible," crediting women's wartime service, and expresses willingness to acknowledge their contributions — signalling personal support for female suffrage while reserving judgment only on procedural details of the specific proposals.

The speaker explicitly states he has "always thought" women leading a settled industrial life are prima facie entitled to a vote, strongly condemns the opposition's argument that "wages and not the vote is the appointed payment for the services of women" as "unmanly," "unmannerly," and "cowardly," and argues that if women are different from men then men's possession of the vote does not cover women's case — consistently advocating for women's suffrage throughout the speech.

The TARGET speech concerns shop hours legislation and regulation of women's working hours in shops, not women's political rights. While women's suffrage is briefly mentioned in passing (the speaker notes the Amendment linking the Bill to women's suffrage should not be supported as it mixes two unrelated issues), no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation — the speech is entirely focused on the merits of labour regulation for shop workers.

The speaker explicitly states that "we are leaving the women of India in a worse state than we ought to do," expressing regret that more women are not being enfranchised under the Schedule, and notes he voted according to his conscience on this issue of women's political rights in India.

The speech is entirely focused on the Anglo-Irish Agreement, Northern Ireland's political situation, terrorism, economic conditions, and inter-governmental relations. Women's political rights and representation are never mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker explicitly argues against women's suffrage, stating his belief that "the majority of women would be opposed to giving the suffrage" and that he opposes extending the vote to women at this time, framing the entire electoral reform proposals as inopportune. He does not endorse women's political rights but uses women's presumed opposition to the vote as an argument against the measure.

The speaker explicitly states he and his colleagues are "whole-heartedly in favour" of the Motion supporting the Speaker's Conference recommendations, which included women's suffrage. His only comment on women's suffrage specifically is an aside that he would have preferred the question to be left to an Irish Parliament, which is a procedural/jurisdictional preference rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, full employment policy, manufacturing industry, public expenditure, and economic strategy. While women are briefly mentioned as doing part-time low-paid jobs and needing crèches, these are incidental references in an economic argument with no stance taken on women's political rights or civic participation.
