The speaker (Bonar Law) explicitly states he has "always been in favour of female suffrage" and that the War has strengthened his view, declaring he "would think it wrong and would do my best to prevent any extension of the suffrage to men which did not also extend it to women." He endorses the Speaker's Conference proposals, which include women's suffrage, and argues that any franchise bill that excluded women could not pass the House.

The speaker explicitly states "I am and always have been against woman suffrage—I do not believe it would be wise to give a vote to women," and says he would vote against the extension of the franchise. While he acknowledges a logical inconsistency in age-restricted women's suffrage (arguing that if women get the vote at all it should be on equal terms with men), this is a practical critique of the proposal's internal logic rather than support for women's suffrage, and he reaffirms his opposition throughout.

The speaker (Mr. Butler, the Under-Secretary) explicitly acknowledges the concerns of women advocates like Miss Rathbone and Viscountess Astor about the "application condition" limiting women voters in India, commits to reconsidering the Assam case, and affirms that the Government has made concessions to maximize women's enfranchisement, expressing hope that the number of women voters will be as large as possible and that administrative obstacles will diminish over time.

The speech is primarily about overseas voting rights and the link between residence and the franchise. The brief mention of the extension of the franchise to women is used only as a historical analogy to argue that previous franchise extensions were driven by strong public pressure — a point made to contrast with the current proposal — without arguing for or against women's political rights themselves.

The speaker (Sir W. Smiles) expresses clear support for greater enfranchisement of women in India, arguing that the Committee is "leaving the women of India in a worse state than we ought to do" and that India cannot achieve self-governance until the position of women is "far more guaranteed and assured." He criticizes the Schedule for not adequately protecting women's voting rights and expresses regret at the limited franchise being granted.

The speaker explicitly identifies "the emancipation of women" as a major irreversible societal change and argues that the tax and benefit system must be reformed to treat each citizen equally regardless of sex, moving to a "single, one-to-one universal tax system" with equal personal obligations and rights—directly endorsing women's full civic and economic equality.

The speech is entirely about the question of extending voting rights to British citizens living abroad, debating residence requirements and the franchise for overseas voters. While the speaker briefly mentions the extension of the franchise to women as a historical precedent in the preceding context (by Mr. Winnick), the TARGET speech itself does not argue for or against women's political rights — it focuses solely on overseas voting and the principles of representative government.

The speaker explicitly states he has "not been keen on extending the franchise to women" and argues that women's education in India is insufficiently developed to make the franchise beneficial, concluding that more education is needed before an extended franchise for women can be advantageous — a substantive argument against extending women's political rights at this time.

The target speeches debate a Bill to restrict shop workers' hours of labour, focusing on practical implementation, economic effects on shopkeepers, and whether women employees desire such legislation. While Mr. Kelly briefly dismisses the suffrage amendment as irrelevant to shop girls' interests and notes women's right to sell their labour freely, none of the target speakers make a substantive argument for or against women's political rights or the franchise; the suffrage amendment is treated as a procedural distraction rather than argued on its merits.

The speech is entirely focused on shipbuilding industry policy, redundancy schemes, privatisation of yards (particularly Cammell Laird), and unemployment concerns. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "the men and women who work for Cammell Laird," with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

Asquith explicitly announces he has changed his longstanding opposition to women's suffrage, arguing that women's wartime contributions make it impossible "consistently with justice or with expediency, to withhold from women the power and the right of making their voice directly heard," and declares his acquiescence in the Conference majority's recommendation that "some measure of women's suffrage should be conferred."

The speaker explicitly argues for greater women's political enfranchisement in India, directly rebutting Sir R. Craddock's argument that education must precede the franchise by inverting it: women won't get adequate education funding until they have greater political influence. The speaker urges the Government to take responsibility for expanding women's political representation beyond what the Schedule provides.

The speech argues for a new clause exempting workplace nurseries from taxation, framing it as support for working parents (especially single parents) and criticising Conservative opposition. While it briefly mentions women going out to work and male superiority in passing, the substantive argument is about tax policy on workplace nursery benefits, not women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET contains multiple speakers with divergent stances: Mr. Gedge explicitly moves an amendment linking women's labour legislation to the parliamentary franchise, arguing women should have votes before Parliament legislates for them (for suffrage, instrumentally), while simultaneously opposing the Bill's restrictions on women's labour (against women's civic protection); Mr. Corbett, Mr. Powell, Mr. Winterbotham, Mr. Isaacs, and Mr. Buxton variously support the Bill and oppose tying it to women's suffrage. Taken as a whole, the TARGET makes substantive arguments on both sides of women's political rights—Gedge advocates for women's suffrage as a precondition while others reject that linkage and some (Powell) explicitly state they do not advocate women's enfranchisement.

The entire debate concerns payment of Members of Parliament to broaden democratic representation and reduce financial barriers to serving in Parliament. Women's political rights are not argued for or against; the brief citation of John Stuart Mill's "subjection of women" is used only as a rhetorical illustration about limiting the field of selection generally, not as an argument about women's civic participation specifically.

The speech concerns kerb crawling legislation and the procedural difficulties of requiring women to testify in court, not women's political rights or representation. The references to women's experiences and fears relate to criminal justice and public order policy, not their civic or political status.

The speaker explicitly states he has "always been an advocate of moderate suffrage for women" and welcomes the Conference proposals on women's suffrage, yet simultaneously argues that the entire electoral reform programme—including women's suffrage—should not be pursued during wartime, calling for complete concentration on the War and opposing the immediate introduction of these measures. This constitutes substantive support for women's suffrage in principle paired with substantive opposition to its current timing/vehicle, which goes beyond a mere procedural caveat: the speaker invokes the wartime context as a fundamental reason to halt all constitutional revision including women's franchise, effectively opposing the measure as presently constituted.

The TARGET speeches are entirely focused on the Irish Local Government Bill — debates about Irish self-government, Home Rule, coercion, and the political relationship between Ireland and Britain. Women are mentioned only once in passing (Sir Albert Rollit noting the franchise includes "of course, women") without any argument being made about women's political rights.

Mr. S. Smith explicitly moves that the Bill be rejected and presents a sustained case against women's suffrage, arguing that women are "intensely and hopelessly ignorant" of political issues, that the franchise would disrupt home life and reduce marriage rates, that most women do not want the vote, and that it would be "the commencement of national decline."

The speaker advocates for protections specifically for women, including shielding them from questions about sexual history in court and protecting their identity in open court proceedings, in order to encourage women to give evidence and reduce fear of harassment — all arguments supporting women's full civic participation and protection in the legal process.

The speech is primarily about the administrative and electoral machinery for the new Indian provincial constitution under the Government of India Act 1935, covering territorial constituencies, communal representation, labour seats, and franchise arrangements. Women are mentioned only briefly and in passing (special seats reserved for women, the abandonment of an application requirement for women with a wifehood qualification in Madras), without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

Lloyd George explicitly supports women's franchise, stating it "would be an outrage, ungrateful, unjust, inequitable" to exclude women from having a voice in post-war reconstruction, and noting he "has always been a supporter of women's franchise." He endorses the Speaker's Conference recommendations on women's suffrage and argues the War has demonstrated women's right to political participation.

The target speech is a ministerial response about abolishing the "married women's half test" for pension entitlements under social security legislation, focused on administrative and financial details of implementation. While it references women as beneficiaries of pension reform, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker states he believes women's suffrage "will probably have to be granted" and approaches it with an "open mind," suggesting conditional support, while simultaneously arguing that the entire Speaker's Conference report—including its women's suffrage recommendations—should be shelved until after the War, treating women's suffrage as one of the "highly contentious" matters that should not be legislated now. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: acknowledging the legitimacy of women's claim to the franchise while substantively opposing its current enactment.

The TARGET speech (the unnamed first speaker) explicitly argues that women in the Civil Service are doing equal work to men and deserve equal pay, calling the pay disparity "a grievance" and an injustice, while proposing a gradual scheme to bring women's pay up to men's levels. This is a clear advocacy for equal civic and economic standing for women in public service.

Mr. S. Smith explicitly moves the rejection of the Women's Franchise Bill, arguing at length that women are intellectually unfit for political participation, that granting the franchise would inevitably lead to societal chaos, and that women as a class lack the political capacity or desire to vote. He denies women are as fit as men to exercise the franchise and warns against any step toward women's suffrage or parliamentary representation.

The speaker moves an amendment demanding equal pay for women in the common classes of the Civil Service, arguing throughout that women do identical work to men and deserve equal remuneration, explicitly advocating for women's equal civic and economic standing in public service. The speech directly supports women's equal participation and rights in public employment.

The speaker explicitly supports equal treatment of women in occupational pension schemes, arguing that "the emancipation of women and the desire that they should be treated on an equal basis with men" is an irreversible change, and that "women have votes and they should have justice in relation to their pensions." This is a clear endorsement of women's equal civic and economic standing.

The speaker (Lloyd George) explicitly declares "I have always been a supporter of women's franchise" and argues at length that women's wartime contributions make it an "outrage," "ungrateful," "unjust," and "inequitable" to deny them a vote in determining post-war conditions, strongly endorsing the Speaker's Conference recommendation on women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly and at length opposes women's suffrage, arguing that women's wartime work was auxiliary to men's, that Parliament has historically protected women's interests without the vote, and that women's suffrage should at minimum be deferred and subjected to a referendum or government bill rather than passed through the current Parliament.

The speaker (Mr. Courtney, Member for Bodmin) explicitly supports the Bill giving women the Parliamentary franchise, arguing that women are "flesh and blood" with interests deserving representation, that the vote would address neglected needs (factory inspection, divorce law, custody of children), and concludes that the Bill embodies "common-sense and the plain principles of justice" and that "woman is a citizen as well as man" with "the same right to be represented in this House."

The speaker explicitly states he opposes women's suffrage ("I do not care whether you give the franchise to the sailors, soldiers, and seamen so long as you adhere to the present principle of male suffrage only") and says he would have opposed its inclusion from the start, arguing it is a "highly contentious" matter that should be kept out of any franchise bill.

The speech focuses entirely on the renewal of the Multi-Fibre Arrangement and its importance to the British textile and clothing industry, employment, and trade policy. While the speaker briefly mentions that many textile workers are women, this is incidental to the economic argument and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Pethick-Lawrence) explicitly argues in favour of equal pay for women in the Civil Service, characterising it as a matter of "plain demand for justice," draws a parallel to the women's suffrage movement to warn the Government against delay, and threatens to take the matter to the electorate if the Government does not concede. Throughout, he supports women's equal civic and economic standing.

Sir W. B. Barttelot explicitly seconds the amendment to reject the Bill, arguing that women are "unfit and unable" to bear the burdens of the franchise, that granting it would put women "in antagonism with men," that women would be unfit to manage the Empire in times of crisis, and that passing the Bill would be "most mischievous to women themselves."

The speech presents a petition opposing the Unborn Children (Protection) Bill on grounds of harm to infertility treatment, research restrictions, and patient confidentiality. While it mentions discrimination against poor women in accessing IVF, it does not make arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Morrison) explicitly urges the House to reject the Amendment for equal pay for women in the Civil Service, arguing that the principle is not accepted in the country, that the agitation is based on "feminist conception" rather than genuine grievance, and that the country as a whole does not hold that paying women less than men is wrong. He consistently opposes the measure throughout his speech.

The speech is primarily about repealing Land Value Duties during wartime and the party truce. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as an example of a cross-party issue that does not break the party truce, with no argument made for or against it.

The speaker explicitly supports equal pay for equal work in the Civil Service regardless of sex, argues that women's admission to equal suffrage naturally led to demands for equal standing in public life, and endorses the principle that the best candidates should be selected whether men or women, demonstrating clear support for women's political and civic equality.

The speaker explicitly states "I hope will before long obtain a vote" regarding women and frames his amendment around the principle that Parliament should not legislate on matters affecting women until women have the Parliamentary Franchise to express their opinions constitutionally — a position that, while using women's suffrage as a procedural argument against the Bill, reflects genuine support for women's right to vote. His support for women's suffrage is the substantive basis of his amendment.

The speech is entirely focused on railway industry policy, specifically the closure of BREL workshops, freight transport, and the consequences for skilled workers. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about repealing the Land Value Duties under the Finance (1909–10) Act on fiscal grounds, arguing they cost more than they generate. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as an example of contentious business that has been introduced during the war, without any argument for or against it.

The TARGET speech contains two distinct contributions, both supporting women's political rights and equal treatment. The first speaker (unnamed) supports equal pay for equal work for interchangeable Civil Service roles, dismissing the "dependency argument" against it. Viscountess Astor then forcefully advocates for equal pay as "common justice," invokes the suffrage movement, argues women have proven their worth, dismisses all counterarguments (cost, sickness, wastage), and urges Members to support the Amendment.

The speaker (Balfour) explicitly supports women's Parliamentary franchise, arguing that opposing women's participation in politics as "degrading" is "cant" and that the Bill's arguments cannot be extended to justify women sitting in Parliament — yet he simultaneously argues that women sitting in Parliament or holding Cabinet positions would be inappropriate, making a substantive distinction between voting rights and full Parliamentary participation.

The TARGET speech concerns a parliamentary procedural dispute over Irish education funding (National School teachers' pension fund) and the conduct of debate on Report. The only mention of women is a passing reference by Mr. T. W. Russell to "the higher education of women in Ireland" as an alternative use for funds, without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as a lifelong opponent of women's suffrage who still believes it would be better not to extend the franchise to women, yet he commits to voting for the Conference recommendations that include women's suffrage, arguing that women's wartime contributions make it unconscionable to deny them recognition and that the opportunity for a settled compromise must not be lost. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: genuine personal opposition to women's suffrage on principle, paired with substantive support for enfranchising women in the current context.

The speaker explicitly states "I also hope that the fact that half the people of this country are women will be recognised. There should be some female representation" on the new Police Complaints Authority, advocating for women's inclusion in public institutional bodies. This is a direct, albeit brief, argument in favour of women's representation in public life.

The speaker explicitly and at length supports equal pay for equal work in the Civil Service common classes, arguing that the pay differential based on sex is "totally unjust" and a "grave scandal," especially when women supervisors are paid less than the men they supervise. The speech also invokes women's suffrage history to urge the Government not to delay granting this justice to women.

Sir H. James argues that women who "gave these lessons" never needed the vote and that women seeking political power must surrender their superior domestic influence, concluding that female entry into public life "will be destructive and disastrous." Balfour then counters him by explicitly supporting the Bill, arguing that women have demonstrated political interest and capacity, and that calling political participation degrading to women is inconsistent with his own practice of urging women to support his causes.

The speech is primarily about the duration/extension of Parliament, payment of Members, and the relationship between the two Houses. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as one example of a topic the House of Lords might oppose, without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is primarily about the rights of voluntary organisations versus local authorities in the context of a midwifery bill, and the division lists that follow. While the speaker briefly mentions the women's suffrage movement as a rhetorical aside (noting pride in supporting it), this is not an argument about women's political rights but rather a rhetorical device to criticise Miss Rathbone for allegedly defying democratic principles.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Transport Bill's bus deregulation provisions, criticising the guillotine motion, and defending concessionary fares for the elderly and disabled. The single mention of "women's institutes" is a passing reference to an organisation opposed to the Bill, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is primarily a parliamentary commentary on the political drama surrounding the Government's defeat and confidence vote, with only a passing, non-committal reference to equal pay for equal work and a brief, skeptical aside about some women supporting it for competitive labour-market reasons. The speaker does not argue substantively for or against women's political rights or equal pay as a matter of principle.

The speaker explicitly lists "female suffrage" among controversial subjects he urges the Government to drop, framing it as an imposition pressed by small sections rather than the country at large. He opposes its introduction during the extended parliamentary session, treating it as an unwelcome burden on loyal supporters.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary oversight of security services and telephone interception. The brief mention of women gaining the vote after 1918 is a passing historical reference used to illustrate the long struggle for democratic rights generally, with no argument made for or against women's political rights specifically.

The TARGET speech is primarily about police complaints procedures, legal representation costs, and the composition of the Police Complaints Authority. The brief mention of women on the authority ("three of its members are women") is incidental and descriptive, not an argument for or against women's political rights — the speaker explicitly frames their presence as based on professional merit rather than group representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for the appointment of female factory inspectors, arguing that "women ought to be inspected by women" and that women should be employed as inspectors "where they can possibly be engaged." While this concerns workplace inspection rather than voting or office-holding, it directly addresses women's equal participation in public professional roles as civic inspectors, and the speaker even references the broader movement to admit women to the House of Commons approvingly.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on defending university constituency representation in Parliament, arguing its value for bringing independent and intellectual voices to the House. Women's political rights are not mentioned, argued for, or against; the reference to Miss Rathbone is purely incidental as one of several university members whose speeches are praised.

The TARGET speech is primarily a constitutional and political argument against prolonging Parliament's life, focusing on Irish Home Rule, the legitimacy of the Coalition Government, and the erosion of parliamentary liberties. Women's suffrage is mentioned only once in passing ("a few days ago the late Prime Minister drew a rather far-fetched comparison with reference to his change of opinion on the subject of women's suffrage"), without the speaker making any argument for or against women's political rights.

Gladstone explicitly declines to support giving parliamentary facilities for debating women's suffrage, arguing it is too weighty and complex a question to attach to the Irish Government Bill, and implicitly that it should be deferred to Irish self-governance — effectively opposing the advancement of women's suffrage in the current parliamentary context.

The speaker explicitly argues that there is "a very strong feeling outside" that women should be on local authorities, notes that both Suffragists and anti-Suffragists have accepted the principle of women serving in local administration, and criticises the London County Council for failing to co-opt women despite many vacancies — all supporting women's participation in public/political life.

The TARGET speech (Mr. Dingle Foot's contribution) focuses entirely on the debate over university representation and the university franchise, arguing it should be abolished. The only mention of women is a passing reference to Lord Oxford's defeat at Paisley in 1924, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely about the Public Meeting Act, police prosecution powers, and disorder at political meetings — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of the suffragette movement in the opening sentence is purely historical context about the origin of the Act, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure, private members' bills, and the ballot system for legislative business. Women's Suffrage is mentioned only briefly and in passing as a single illustrative example of how members could combine their ballots to secure a favourable place for a bill, without any argument for or against the measure itself.

The TARGET speech is primarily about the illiterate voter provisions of the Ballot Act and Irish electoral practices. The brief mention of women's suffrage ("The other day we were told that women were not to have votes because they were too stupid to exercise them") appears only as a passing rhetorical comparison to illustrate the absurdity of educational/intelligence tests for the franchise, without making a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is entirely concerned with land valuation, municipal land purchase powers, unearned increment, and property rights. The only mention of women is a brief, passing reference by Mr. Lawson noting that Mr. Haldane's previous bill was "one to render women eligible for the office of Commander-in-Chief" — used solely as a rhetorical aside to characterize Haldane as a bold legislator, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns funding levels for Welsh Women's Aid (a domestic violence support organisation) and the social effects of unemployment on relationship breakdowns. While it mentions a women's organisation, it does not make any argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly identifies themselves as being "in favour of" the women's suffrage clause and advocates for scheduling arrangements to ensure supporters can participate in the division, expressing concern that they "would not like to be disappointed" in voting for it.

The speech is a factual parliamentary answer providing statistical estimates of the number of married women over thirty and projected electorate figures under the Representation of the People Bill. It presents numbers without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about the jury system, peremptory challenges, and the composition of juries. While women are briefly mentioned as one of the groups added to jury eligibility when the franchise was extended, this is only a passing historical reference with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses on military discipline legislation, covering the death penalty, trade union rights for service personnel, and treatment of homosexuals in the armed forces. While it mentions "service men and women" together, it does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The TARGET speeches debate the Public Order Bill (1936), focusing on civil liberties, policing of Fascist and Communist demonstrations in East London, and fair administration of the law. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference to "the suffragette agitation" as a historical example of political prosecutions, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on crime statistics and law and order under the Thatcher government, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The incidental reference to "the right hon. Lady" (the Prime Minister) does not address women's civic status or political rights.

The speech is about the legal interpretation of "alienage" and "aliens" in the context of Irish Home Rule legislation, specifically whether the Irish Parliament could enfranchise aliens. The brief mention of women's franchise is used only as an analogy to illustrate a point about Common Law disabilities, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the constitutional question of whether Irish Members should be retained in or excluded from the Imperial Parliament under the Home Rule Bill. The single passing reference to "female suffrage" appears only as one item in a list of policy questions that might be decided by Irish votes, without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the Irish Home Rule Bill debate — arguing about trade, commerce, the Irish economy, imperial bonds, and political pressure in the City of London. Women's political rights are never mentioned or alluded to in any way.

The speaker explicitly argues that the authorities unfairly weighted enforcement against the women's suffrage movement and Labour movement compared to Ulster rebels, citing this unequal treatment as a longstanding injustice. He also defends suffragettes and suffragette speakers from prosecution, implicitly endorsing their cause and their right to political expression.

The speech is entirely about the abolition of the GLC, the Museum of London, arts funding, oral history, and the South Bank — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic participation issues.

The speech concerns SERPS (State Earnings-Related Pension Scheme) reform and its impact on women and manual workers as groups who may lose pension benefits. While women are mentioned, the argument is about pension/social security policy, not about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech is a procedural ruling by the Speaker on various Instructions to a Bill, addressing whether they are mandatory or can be raised as Amendments. While it briefly mentions "the enfranchisement of women" as the subject of Clause 4, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights—it only rules on the procedural question of whether the Bill lends itself to division.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the Home Rule debate for Ireland, discussing imperial unity, the Canadian parallel, landlordism, and arguments for/against the Government of Ireland Bill. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is primarily about the Government of India electoral orders, covering franchise committees, trade union representation, communal questions, and Indian constitutional arrangements. The brief mention of "limiting the constituencies for the election of women to women voters alone" in the Punjab and Sind is presented as a practical administrative decision acceptable to Mohammedan opinion, not as an argument about women's political rights as a matter of principle or civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports removing the Poor Law disqualification so that poor people can "take part in the government of the country," arguing that denying the vote to those who have received relief is an unjust "stigma" and "insult," and appeals to the Government to extend the franchise to this class of persons without restriction.

The speech is almost entirely about the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve, auxiliary patrol, and Newfoundland reserves. The brief mention of "grass widows" (wives of naval men away at sea) is a rhetorical aside about constituency concerns, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about the British Mandate for Palestine and the proposed Legislative Council, arguing against rushing self-government on an unprepared population. The brief mention of whether women should receive the franchise in Palestine is incidental to the main argument about Arab readiness for self-government, and the speaker does not argue a substantive position for or against women's political rights — it is cited merely as an example of the council's overly broad franchise provisions.

The speech is entirely focused on whether conscientious objectors should be disfranchised (i.e., deprived of their votes) as a penalty for refusing military service during wartime. The speaker argues against disfranchising conscientious objectors on grounds of British tradition, justice, and the dangers of driving dissenters to "direct action." Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment relief funding, rates in county boroughs, and the financial obligations of the Exchequer to areas like Kingston-upon-Hull. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is overwhelmingly concerned with Irish Home Rule legislation — specifically the Irish Legislative Council's composition, franchise qualifications, local government history, and financial arrangements. The brief mention of women ("a £40 qualification would have given us 60,000 ratings, including women and double ratings") is purely incidental arithmetic, not an argument about women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on opposing Irish Home Rule (the Government of Ireland Bill), arguing on behalf of the Unionist minority in southern Ireland against the bill's provisions regarding representation, franchise qualifications, and protections for minorities. Women's political rights are never mentioned, argued for, or argued against.

The target speech deals entirely with procedural and legal questions about appeals from County Court decisions and the role of revising barristers under the Bill, with only a passing reference to "woman suffrage" as an example of legal complexity. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The first speaker (the hon. Baronet) explicitly opposes extending Parliament's life precisely because it would allow the Government to introduce a Franchise Bill including women's suffrage, calling it a "political outrage" and noting that the current Parliament had already voted against women's suffrage. The second speaker (T. M. Healy) expresses hope that the franchise measure will "give the women a fair measure of representation," but the TARGET as a whole is dominated by the first speaker's opposition to women's suffrage being advanced through the Parliament extension. The first speaker's argument is the primary substantive position on women's political rights in the TARGET.

The speech is entirely focused on economic policy, unemployment, exchange rates, manufacturing decline, and government fiscal strategy. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech is entirely focused on the abolition of military/bombing aircraft and the promotion of civil aviation under international control. While the speaker briefly mentions opening aviation opportunities to "all men and women," this is a passing rhetorical flourish in an argument about disarmament and civil aviation policy, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is about Workmen's Compensation legislation and urges Members to support the Bill's Second Reading on grounds of justice for workers. While it briefly mentions "workers, both men and women," this is incidental and does not argue a position on women's political rights or representation.

Mr. McLaren explicitly moves an amendment to extend the local government franchise to married women ratepayers, arguing that the doctrine of coverture unjustly disfranchises women already entitled to vote, and appeals to the Committee to remove this disqualification. His entire speech advocates for women's political rights in local elections.

The speech focuses entirely on science education policy, government science ministry, research funding, and teacher training — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The incidental reference to the Prime Minister using the pronoun "she" does not constitute an argument about women's civic participation.

The target speech focuses entirely on a technical drafting question about whether the Bill needs to explicitly state the age qualification of twenty-one for men, referencing prior Reform Acts. While it briefly acknowledges the age distinction between men and women raised by Lord Cecil, the speaker explicitly declines to engage with that question ("I do not enter into the question of the distinction in the ages of men and women"), making no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is an appeal to the Chancellor of the Exchequer to increase civil list pensions for scholars, artists, and intellectuals who have fallen into poverty. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status — women are mentioned only incidentally as recipients of poverty relief alongside men.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on opposing the Home Rule Bill for Ireland, discussing trade, finance, Ulster resistance, and Irish governance structures. Women are mentioned only once in passing ("47,000 women employed in the manufactures of the North of Ireland") as a labour market statistic, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Anglo-Irish Agreement, Northern Ireland politics, repression, partition, and security matters. The brief mention of "the strip searching of women prisoners in Armagh" is a passing reference to a security/prison policy grievance, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly identifies as a "warm friend of the Bill" — a Reform Bill that enfranchises both men and women — and objects to an amendment that "must undoubtedly be to prevent a considerable number of men and women from obtaining votes." The speech supports the enfranchisement of women (and men) under the Bill while criticising the accepted amendment as reducing the franchise.

The speech mentions women in rural areas being dependent on bus services, but only as context for arguing about rural transport policy. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation in any way.

Fowler, as President of the Local Government Board, explicitly proposes a new clause to remove the disqualification of married women from voting in all local government elections (School Board, Guardians, County and Town Councils), framing this as carrying out Parliament's clear intention to place women on the same footing as men for municipal purposes. He also affirms that women, married or single, who are rated should be eligible to serve as Parish Councillors.

The target speech is about factory shift-work legislation (the two-shift system for workers in textile and non-textile factories), addressing hours of labour, working conditions, and the Departmental Committee's recommendations. While women workers are mentioned incidentally as part of the workforce affected, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech (combining the opening unnamed speaker urging acceptance of the Amendment and Mr. H. Samuel's contribution) strongly supports extending the parliamentary franchise to women who have passed university examinations equivalent to a degree, calling it a "monstrous injustice" to deny women degrees and votes on the basis of sex, and arguing Parliament must ensure its intentions on women's suffrage are carried into practice.

The speech argues for extending polling hours to 10 pm to maximise voter turnout, mentioning women's voting habits (waiting for husbands) only as an illustrative social example. It does not make any argument about women's political rights, franchise eligibility, or representation — the core concern is polling convenience for all voters regardless of sex.

Mr. Stansfeld explicitly supports the Government's proposal to include married women on the Parochial Register, arguing that women—particularly married women as mothers—would benefit parish administration, Poor Law governance, and social harmony between classes. He urges his colleague to accept the Government's offer, expressing strong favour for women's participation in elected and governing bodies.

The speaker supports extending the franchise generally but argues that the voting age for women (set at 30) is unfairly higher than for men (21), noting that women mature faster than men — implicitly advocating for equal or lower age thresholds for women. At the same time, the speaker also questions whether men of 21 are truly qualified to vote, suggesting the male voting age should be raised, which indirectly cuts against a broad extension of the franchise to younger voters of both sexes. The speech thus makes substantive points on both sides regarding the terms of women's enfranchisement relative to men's.

The speech is entirely about a procedural debate on whether to adjourn consideration of a Bill (related to fluoridated water supply), focusing on whipping, payroll votes, and parliamentary tactics. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the phrase "free men and women," with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states he favours giving women the suffrage for all purposes, political and local, yet substantively argues against the specific Amendment as it stands — warning that accepting it will make it impossible to exclude married women from the Parliamentary franchise and will set a precedent that cannot be controlled, effectively opposing this particular extension while endorsing the broader principle of women's full political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Acland) is defending his amendment to extend the municipal franchise to married women, citing hundreds of resolutions from women's organisations and reading a letter from the Richmond Committee of Organised Women urging the Government to accept the Bill — explicitly supporting women's political rights and representation.

The speech concerns water fluoridation policy ("mass medication" through water authorities), with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The phrase "free men and women" is rhetorical flourish unrelated to women's political rights.

The speaker (Caithness) explicitly states he "supported women's suffrage in its entirety" and opposes any partial or restrictive measure, objecting to limiting votes to married women paying high rates as favouring the rich, and opposing any proposal that grants male lodgers the vote while denying it to female lodgers — all arguments in favour of broad women's political rights.

The speech is about transport policy (bus deregulation) and criticises the Secretary of State for ignoring responses from various organisations including the Women's Institute. The Women's Institute is mentioned merely as one of several bodies that have made representations, with no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly and cordially accepts a government offer to enfranchise married women ratepayers for all local government elections, withdraws his own amendment in favour of the broader government pledge, and argues that married women of all economic backgrounds would benefit from this expansion of their political rights.

The speech argues against the two-shift system and for restricting Saturday working hours for women and young persons under factory legislation, framed as a labour protection issue rather than as an argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned as a protected class of workers, but the speech makes no argument about their political rights or fitness for civic participation.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the coal industry — nationalisation, amalgamations, workers' compensation, selling agencies, Sunday working, and boys' night work in mines. The brief opening remark about women lacking courage is a passing jibe at the preceding speaker (Miss Ward), not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly seconds an Amendment to extend the local government vote to married women, arguing it would be "a gross injustice to the married women of the country if they are not allowed to exercise the local government vote" given they are being granted the Parliamentary vote, and highlights broad cross-party and public support for the measure.

The speaker expresses alarm at the proposal to remove the disqualification of married women, objecting that it would overturn the legal principle that "man and wife should no longer be considered one, but two," and characterises the change as "momentous" and unwelcome — signalling clear opposition to expanding women's political rights in this context.

The speaker moves an amendment to extend the municipal franchise to married women automatically, arguing that married women represent a "responsible and stable element" deserving a share in local government, and that excluding them from the municipal vote while granting them the Parliamentary vote would be unjust and counterproductive. The entire speech advocates for expanding women's political rights at the local level.

The speaker (Mr. Morrison, Financial Secretary to the Treasury) argues that the country does not accept the principle of equal pay for men and women, grounds differential pay in the family structure and men's greater financial burdens, and urges the House to reject the Amendment seeking equal pay for women in the Civil Service. He dismisses the feminist basis of the argument and frames the demand as merely a pay rise for a privileged subset of women rather than a principled claim.

The speaker (Mr. Beith) argues that the single transferable vote system would result in more women being elected to Parliament, pointing to the "serried ranks of women Liberal Members of Parliament" that would exist under a fairer electoral system. He explicitly links proportional representation to better representation of women in Parliament.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the local government franchise to married women, arguing they have a special stake in local matters (housing, health, child-rearing) and that it would be absurd to grant them the Parliamentary vote while denying them the municipal vote. He urges the Home Secretary to accept the Amendment and frames women's participation in local governance as both just and beneficial.

The speaker (Member for West Birmingham) explicitly states that those "opposed to any extension of women's suffrage" should ensure the Government's clause goes no further than preserving existing practice, and expresses "horror" at pro-suffrage views; he opposes extending married women's voting rights to Town Councils and School Boards as a change in the law.

The TARGET speech addresses electoral registration rules for students, specifically arguing against multiple registration and double voting in parliamentary elections, with no reference to women's political rights, suffrage, or representation as a distinct class.

The speaker explicitly argues that the current electoral system discriminates against women and ethnic minorities, resulting in far fewer women in Parliament compared to other countries, and advocates for the single transferable vote system as a remedy that would make it easier to elect women to Parliament.

The TARGET contains two distinct voices: Mr. Pethick-Lawrence argues in favour of equal pay (and thus women's equal civic/economic participation), while the Duchess of Atholl explicitly states she will "vote against the Amendment" because she believes married men's greater family responsibilities justify unequal pay, substantively opposing equal pay for women in the Civil Service. Together the concatenated TARGET presents substantive arguments on both sides.

The speaker explicitly states he is "in favour of enfranchising every man and woman in the county" (supporting women's political rights in principle), but substantively opposes the specific amendment to remove married women's disabilities on the grounds that it would create unequal voting (married men getting two votes, single men one), risking obstruction of the Bill — arguing against this extension of women's franchise in practice. This constitutes genuine two-sidedness: endorsing broad enfranchisement while opposing the specific mechanism for extending married women's voting rights.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the local government franchise to married women, arguing it is "of supreme importance to the nation" and that it is anomalous for women to be able to elect MPs but not vote in local elections, calling the denial of this right an injustice.

The speech concerns local government transparency and public access to council meetings and documents. The passing mention of "men and women throughout Britain who devote an enormous amount of their time" to local authorities is incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely focused on the Midwives Bill — discussing domiciliary midwifery services, maternal mortality, the appropriate local authority to administer the bill, compensation for retiring midwives, and related public health matters. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The TARGET contains multiple speakers. Miss Horsbrugh (the first long speech) supports equal pay for civil servants, calling the pay differential an "anomaly" and pressing the Government to commit to the principle and extend equal pay to new entrants. Sir William Allen also supports equal pay. However, the Duchess of Atholl makes a substantive argument against equal pay, citing men's greater family responsibilities and the Royal Commission's findings, and states she will vote against the Amendment. This constitutes genuine two-sided argumentation within the TARGET.

The TARGET speech opens with a skeptical argument against the Amendment (questioning whether the women's municipal vote has value only when husbands and wives disagree, suggesting it creates a dilemma), while the later contributions from McKinnon Wood and Sir Herbert Roberts strongly support extending the municipal franchise to married women. Together the TARGET contains substantive arguments both against (the first speaker) and for (the subsequent speakers) women's municipal political rights.

Mr. Balfour explicitly supports the Amendment to enfranchise female property owners for Parish Council elections, arguing it is illogical and absurd to give votes to women ratepayers while excluding women owners, and states he will vote for the Amendment if it goes to a Division.

The speaker opposes extending the municipal franchise to married women (wives of ratepayers), arguing that doing so would give a preponderant vote to those who do not pay rates and that the Parliamentary and municipal franchises rest on distinct foundations. While accepting women's existing Parliamentary franchise, the speaker actively argues against this specific expansion of women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (Sir J. Mellor's contribution on the Midwives Bill) addresses the administration of the midwifery service, financial provisions, and supervisory authorities—public health policy focused on maternal care. While the following speech by Miss Rathbone briefly mentions women having fought for reform "without even having a vote to help them," the TARGET itself contains no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. H. H. Fowler) explicitly opposes the Amendment that would enfranchise female owners, stating he will resist it both in Committee and on Report. He further argues that the Parliamentary Register should not be "broken down" to let in women, and accepts the argument that enfranchising one class of women would require opening the question for all women — a prospect he resists.

The Home Secretary personally acknowledges strong arguments in favour of extending the municipal franchise to wives of local government electors, stating "I have never concealed my opinion that there is a strong argument in favour of the Amendment" and that these arguments "weigh with me personally very strongly indeed." His opposition to the Amendment is purely procedural — adherence to the Speaker's Conference compromise — not a substantive objection to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly urges the House to extend the municipal franchise to women, arguing that the moment is opportune and that opponents and supporters alike agree on this point. They challenge the "unsuitable moment" objection and frame women's enfranchisement in local government as overdue and essential, especially given women's wartime service.

The speaker explicitly argues that the first-past-the-post system "works against women" and notes that women constitute 51% of the population yet are represented in the House at lower levels than at any time since WWII, using this as an argument in favour of electoral reform (STV/proportional representation) to improve women's representation.

The TARGET speech argues that it would be logically absurd to grant women the parliamentary vote on imperial matters while denying them the local government franchise, and explicitly supports extending the local government franchise to married women. The speaker (Captain O'Neill) states "on the merits am clearly in favour of it," affirming support for women's political rights in the local sphere as a logical extension of the parliamentary franchise already granted.

The speech concerns the Midwives Bill, specifically debating the definition of the "lying-in period," the role of voluntary organisations versus local authorities in maternity services, and the provision of sterilised maternity outfits. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other in-scope topic.

The speech is almost entirely focused on opposing proportional representation and defending the existing first-past-the-post electoral system. The brief mention of women candidates ("how many women were put up as candidates") is a passing factual remark used to rebut a criticism of Liberal representation, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Home Rule Bill debate regarding constitutional protections and the Irish Legislature's powers, drawing comparisons to the American Constitution. While it briefly mentions "equal rights in franchise" and candidature for office in passing, these references are raised as technical examples of rights that might be affected by the drafting omission, not as arguments for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speech presents a petition opposing the Unborn Children (Protection) Bill on grounds of medical research, infertility treatment, patient confidentiality, and embryo protection. While it mentions discrimination against poor women in access to IVF, this concerns healthcare access rather than women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation, placing it outside the scope of women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure, government voting behaviour, and constitutional conventions following a Division defeat, with only passing references to female MPs (Viscountess Astor, Miss Cazalet) as members who voted against the government — no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech by Miss Wilkinson concerns the Midwives Bill, focusing on voluntary organisations versus public authority delivery of midwifery services, standards of nursing, and maternal mortality — none of which constitute arguments about women's right to vote, stand for office, or other aspects of women's political rights. The brief mention of "women voters" in towns is purely descriptive context, not an argument about women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is primarily a debate about whether voluntary organisations or local authorities should administer maternity/midwifery services under the Bill; it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. The mention of women in the context of maternity care is about health service administration, not women's civic status.

The speech is focused on presenting a petition against the Unborn Children (Protection) Bill, concerning embryo research, infertility treatment, and the Warnock Report. While it mentions discrimination against poor women in the context of IVF charges, this does not address women's political rights or civic participation; it is a health/reproductive policy debate.

The TARGET speech consists of Mr. Speaker's procedural rulings on Instructions and Mr. Gibson Bowles's argument for dividing a Local Government Bill to separate Poor Law provisions — entirely focused on legislative procedure and Poor Law administration. While Mr. Speaker briefly notes that one Instruction concerning women's enfranchisement for local government purposes is in order, he makes no argument for or against it; the remainder of the speech does not address women's political rights at all.

The speech is entirely focused on supporting the Midwives Bill — praising midwives, reducing maternal mortality, and improving maternity services — with no argument made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker draws on personal experience in Wyoming to argue that fears about women "unduly pushing themselves into public or official life" are unfounded, and concludes he sees "no objection to the Amendment," endorsing women's participation in public bodies such as Parish Councils and School Boards. While he raises mild humorous caveats (e.g., jury service), his overall argument is a substantive endorsement of women's eligibility for public office.

The speaker explicitly identifies as "a strong opponent of women's suffrage" but argues in favour of extending the local government vote to women on the same terms as the Parliamentary vote, urging the House to follow what he claims is the clear opinion of the country and his constituents. While opposing suffrage in general, his substantive argument in this speech is in support of women receiving the local government franchise.

The TARGET speech (primarily Mr. Hemmerde, followed by Mr. Runciman and Mr. T. Wilson) strongly advocates extending the municipal franchise to women, criticizing the House's "absurd timidity" and arguing it is illogical to grant women the Parliamentary vote while withholding the local government vote. All three speakers push for women's political rights to be extended without further delay.

The speech presents a petition opposing the Unborn Children (Protection) Bill on grounds of its impact on infertility treatment and medical research; it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation in any form.

The speaker explicitly rises to support the amendment extending the municipal franchise to women, argues that the Speaker's Conference does not bar it, and states "our wishes are that the women should have the Parliamentary vote, and also the municipal vote," endorsing women's political rights at both levels.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the Midwives Bill — discussing maternal mortality, midwifery services, local authorities versus voluntary organisations, and the lying-in period. The brief interjection by Viscountess Astor ("Since then women have had the vote") is a passing remark and not argued as a position on women's political rights by the TARGET speaker, who makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

Mr. McLaren explicitly moves an Instruction to enfranchise women — married and single — for local government elections on the same terms as men, arguing at length that married women are currently excluded from the burgess list and should be given the vote for Parish and District Councils. He appeals to the Prime Minister's own words and Scottish precedent to support extending women's political franchise.

The speaker explicitly states he has "taken precisely the opposite view" from supporters of women's parliamentary suffrage, yet actively supports enfranchising women for local government purposes and opposes the Bill's restriction to County Council Register women, arguing married women should also have the local vote. This constitutes substantive opposition to women's parliamentary suffrage combined with substantive support for women's local government franchise.

The speaker explicitly criticises the UK Government for breaking sex discrimination laws in applying the European social fund, resulting in women being denied training opportunities, and calls on the Government to fully implement the fund's provisions for women in under-represented occupations. She also advocates for the parental leave directive as advancing equal rights for men and women.

The speaker explicitly identifies as a consistent opponent of women's Parliamentary (Imperial) suffrage, while simultaneously and substantively supporting the extension of the municipal franchise to women on equal terms with men, arguing that women's sphere is particularly suited to municipal affairs. This constitutes genuine two-sided argument: opposing one form of women's political rights (Parliamentary vote) while actively endorsing another (municipal vote).

The speaker explicitly identifies as "an opponent of the granting of the Parliamentary franchise to women" while simultaneously supporting the Amendment to extend the municipal vote to women, arguing that denying women the municipal franchise while granting them the Parliamentary vote would be "a most gross injustice to women" and that women opposed to the Parliamentary vote still welcome the municipal extension.

Dilke explicitly opposes the Bill's disfranchisement of married women ratepayers, recalls his earlier successful motion to give women the local vote in Town Councils, and declares he will vote for the Instruction to allow expansion of women's local franchise, clearly supporting women's political rights.

The speech concerns opposition to the Unborn Children (Protection) Bill on grounds of its impact on infertile couples and medical research into congenital conditions. It does not address women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The target speech focuses entirely on disability policy, care in the community, joint financing arrangements, and carers — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for proportional representation (single transferable vote) in local government elections, arguing against the distortions of the first-past-the-post system. While the speaker briefly mentions that STV results in the election of more women and ethnic minorities as one incidental benefit, this is a passing observation rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights or representation as a class.

The TARGET speech is primarily about unemployment insurance administration, the consolidation of insurance branches, and how to distribute a surplus fund. While it briefly mentions married women's treatment under unemployment insurance regulations as an administrative anomaly, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation — it addresses only the fairness of benefit rules for a specific group of claimants.

The speaker explicitly refuses to express any opinion on women's suffrage ("I am not going to express any opinion on what is emphatically a burning question"), framing his argument purely on procedural and practical grounds — that the Bill is already overloaded and that adding the female suffrage question would endanger its passage. No substantive position for or against women's political rights is taken.

The speech concerns opposition to the Unborn Children (Protection) Bill on grounds of its effects on infertility treatment, abortion access, and research — not women's political rights or representation. While it mentions that the Bill discriminates against poor women, this refers to healthcare access, not civic participation or political rights.

The speech is primarily about redistribution of parliamentary seats and the practicalities of constituency size following enfranchisement of women and additional men, but it does not argue for or against women's political rights — it treats women's enfranchisement as a given fact and focuses entirely on the redistribution implications.

The speaker explicitly supports the enfranchisement of women in relation to the Bill, arguing that women's work as Poor Law Guardians is of great importance and that their loss under the new system "would be indeed an incalculable misfortune," urging that the matter be secured without doubt or difficulty.

The TARGET speech contains two speakers (Miss Wilkinson and Miss Cazalet), both of whom explicitly support the principle of equal pay for equal work in the Civil Service, arguing that women who have proven themselves capable should be paid equally to men, and connecting this to women's broader civic equality. Miss Cazalet states she "believed in the principle and justice of the Amendment" and hopes the Government will reconsider, while Miss Wilkinson argues forcefully that it is "completely out-of-date to say that a woman should be paid less because she is a woman."

The speech is entirely focused on British humanitarian efforts, non-intervention policy, and diplomatic activities during the Spanish Civil War. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of civilian populations affected by the conflict ("women and children separated from their men folk"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the disposal of a £6,000,000 unemployment insurance surplus—arguing it should go to the unemployed rather than reduce contributions. While women are briefly mentioned as recipients of unemployment benefit (e.g., the reference to 16s. 6d. a week for women), the speaker makes no argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on education policy — grammar schools, technical schools, teachers' disputes, parental choice mechanisms, and school funding — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a statistical response about the number of electors who would be added to the register if payment of rates as a condition for registration were abolished. While it mentions women householders in passing as a deduction in the arithmetic, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a ministerial answer about the employment status and establishment of temporary female civil servants in the Inland Revenue Department. It addresses administrative staffing matters (length of service, establishment status) without making any argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on opposing the Local Authorities (Voting and Qualification) Bill on grounds of rural rates, plural voting, ex officio Guardians, proxy voting, and the impropriety of private Members' legislation—all concerning Poor Law Guardian elections. While the preceding context briefly mentions women's eligibility for Boards of Guardians, the TARGET speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights at any point.

The Prime Minister (Baldwin) argues at length against implementing equal pay for women in the Civil Service, contending that public opinion is not ripe, that it would reduce employment opportunities for women, and that it would be "a retrograde step" — explicitly opposing the Amendment by the hon. Member for Jarrow (Miss Wilkinson) which the House had passed. While he acknowledges women's progress in employment and the professions, his substantive position is that the Government cannot accept the equal-pay principle and asks the House to endorse that refusal.

The first speaker explicitly supports women's municipal voting rights (conditional on age 30) but is "absolutely opposed" to women having a vote in Imperial Parliament, calling it "not their sphere at all" — substantive support for one sphere of political participation and substantive opposition to another. The Home Secretary's portion does not argue against women's rights on the merits but rather defers to the House, which is a procedural stance rather than substantive opposition.

The speech is entirely focused on Budget provisions for charities, economic performance, privatisation, share ownership, and comparisons with Labour's economic record. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage being applied equally in Scotland as in England, stating "we must have the same franchise for women in Scotland as we have in this country," indicating support for women's political rights in the context of the broader suffrage bill.

The speaker (the Home Secretary) explicitly endorses women's suffrage following the local government franchise throughout the Kingdom, referencing the Speaker's Conference recommendation, and discusses practical implementation details of extending women's suffrage — indicating support for women's political rights.

The speech by Major Neven-Spence concerns economic conditions, agriculture, roads, piers, and depopulation in Orkney and Shetland/the Highlands and Islands. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation anywhere in the speech; the brief mention of women knitting is purely descriptive of local industry.

The speaker accepts women's suffrage as a settled principle ("I take it for granted for the purpose of this Clause that women's suffrage is passed") and proceeds to work out how to extend it to Scotland on the same basis as England, proposing specific legislative language to enfranchise women in Scotland. While he declines to express personal views on women's suffrage, his entire argument is oriented toward ensuring women's Parliamentary franchise is properly implemented in Scotland, which constitutes substantive support for women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on Scottish health policy, housing, sanitation, and public health services, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is primarily an argument for early closing legislation to protect shop assistants from excessive working hours, with women mentioned only briefly and incidentally (noting that standing is worse for women, and that women assistants have no votes and therefore deserve Parliament's consideration). These references do not constitute an argument about women's political rights; they are rhetorical flourishes in a labour/public health debate.

The speech is primarily concerned with the Government of India Act and its Instruments of Instruction, focusing on Labour representation in Indian Second Chambers, the Governor's nomination powers, and related constitutional matters. Although women are briefly mentioned as one of several groups (alongside Labour and scheduled castes) expected to be represented in the chambers, this is incidental and no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly names "female emancipation" alongside universal suffrage as a major irreversible 20th-century development, and argues that the benefits system must be adapted so that "women are treated on the same footing as men and are not left often in the condition in which they were in the middle ages," expressing clear support for women's equal civic and social standing.

The speech is almost entirely about Scottish voter registration mechanics — qualifying periods, valuation rolls, rate-payment conditions, lodger franchises, and administrative procedures. The only mention of women is a passing, incidental reference to "women, and others incapacitated as voters" being removed from the roll as a routine administrative step, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about parliamentary privilege, the punishment of MPs and journalists for leaking Select Committee draft reports, and the public's right to know — not about women's political rights. The single passing mention of suffragettes is used as a historical example to illustrate a general point about laws being changed by those who break them, without making any argument about women's political rights.

The target speech by Mr. James Griffiths focuses entirely on unemployment assistance regulations, their impact on unemployed workers in South Wales, and the household means test. Women are mentioned only briefly and incidentally ("whose women week by week have had to face the hopeless problem of making ends meet"), without any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns education policy — voluntary schools, musical instruction, needlework, cookery, evening schools, training colleges, and the fee grant — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of needlework and cookery as subjects for girls addresses domestic education, not women's civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. W. McLaren) explicitly asks the government to facilitate a parliamentary vote on amendments that would grant duly-qualified women the right to vote for both branches of the Irish Legislature, directly advocating for women's suffrage to be considered in the Bill.

The Speaker's ruling merely declares Mr. Maclure's women's suffrage clause "outside the scope of the Bill" as a procedural matter, without making any argument for or against women's political rights. The ruling is a procedural/administrative statement, not a substantive stance on women's right to vote.

The speaker explicitly states "I am fully committed to women's right to be priests and bishops in the Church of England" and draws a direct parallel to the suffragette movement, urging women to fight for their full rights. While declining to vote for the specific Measure as inadequate, this is a procedural/strategic objection, not substantive opposition to women's political or civic rights.

The speech focuses entirely on the question of lodger votes for municipal franchise purposes — specifically whether furnished vs. unfurnished lodgers should be included — and while it briefly mentions "the claim about the women" as a complication that would arise if lodger franchises were broadly extended, it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about corporal punishment in schools. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing rhetorical question dismissing an analogy another speaker made between corporal punishment and "slavery and votes for women," without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is primarily concerned with the coherence of franchise principles — arguing that Parliamentary and local government franchises should rest on the same theoretical basis. Women's political rights are not argued for or against; they are only briefly mentioned in passing by Mr. H. Samuel as an incidental procedural consequence of the Amendment under discussion, without taking any substantive position on whether women should or should not have the franchise.

The speech is primarily about procedural reform for private Members' legislation, not about women's political rights. The speaker briefly mentions the women's franchise bill as one example of measures blocked by procedural defects, but explicitly states personal opposition to it and makes no argument for or against women's political rights—it is cited purely as an illustration of the procedural problem being addressed.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment assistance regulations and their devastating effects on South Wales mining communities, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women" facing poverty, the speaker's wife) without any argument about their civic status.

The speaker supports women receiving the vote but argues it should be on equal terms with men ("if we are to give the vote to women we should give it to them on similar conditions to men"), and his critique is procedural/technical — objecting to an anomaly that would allow women to vote on a lower property qualification than men, not opposing women's suffrage itself.

The TARGET speech is a lengthy introduction of a Local Government Bill dealing with parish councils, district councils, and administrative reorganisation in England and Wales. It does not argue for or against women's political rights; the single mention of "the female ratepayer can vote" in the existing Vestry system is purely descriptive of current law, not an argument about women's civic status.
