The speaker explicitly states he has "no absolutely fundamental objection to the woman's vote" but then argues substantively against granting it at this time, contending that Parliament has no mandate, that soldiers at the front have not been consulted, that the vote would be given to those who "cannot fight" while excluding those who have fought, and that granting women the vote is "the beginning of trouble." He concludes by voting for the amendment to remove women's suffrage from the Bill.

The speech is entirely about capital punishment, the role of MPs as representatives rather than delegates, and criticism of a colleague's populist approach to the death penalty debate. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The TARGET speech is focused on welfare benefits for pregnant women and mothers (maternity payments, baby supplies), not on women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of a "Ministry for Women" in the preceding context is made by another speaker (Ms. Richardson) and does not appear in the TARGET itself, which is solely about voting on an amendment regarding treatment of pregnant women under social security legislation.

The speaker explicitly and enthusiastically supports women's suffrage throughout, arguing that women have demonstrated their capacity for citizenship through war work, dismissing the physical force argument against them, welcoming the prospect of women sitting in Parliament, and concluding that government should be "of all the people by all the people." He declares he has always believed in the principle of woman suffrage and gives his support "most heartily."

The speech is entirely about opposing funding for the House of Lords as part of an Irish nationalist and Radical political strategy; women and children are mentioned only in passing as victims of House of Lords policy, not as subjects of any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The target speaker acknowledges Sir C. Dilke's concern about the disfranchisement of married women under the Bill and commits to putting down a clause to address (remedy) that disfranchisement, indicating support for preserving married women's voting rights.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the Munich Agreement, the Czechoslovakian crisis, rearmament, trade, and the future of peace—it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status. The passing reference to "men and women" giving services or facing hardship is incidental and contains no argument about women's political rights.

The speech concerns the timing and cost of Parish Council elections in Scotland, specifically whether to hold them in spring rather than autumn. While it briefly mentions "list of women voters" as part of election costs, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on opposing proportional representation in local (county borough) elections, arguing against the Bill on grounds of electoral complexity, voter apathy, and the value of the existing system. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the general electorate ("men and women who only vote for people they know") without any argument about their political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly mentions having supported women's franchise on public platforms as one of Mrs. Pankhurst's supporters, and goes on to advocate for the appointment of women magistrates alongside men, reflecting a supportive stance toward women's participation in public life.

The speech is focused on jury list reliability and the statistical breakdown of parliamentary voters and jurors by sex in the Lothian counties — it presents factual data without making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on Conservative economic policy, social inequality, unemployment, inner-city deprivation, and Labour's vision of "one nation" — with no argument made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related civic status question.

The speaker explicitly states he is "going to put down a new clause to enable married women to vote" and pledges to move it "in the broadest possible way," directly supporting an expansion of women's political rights (voting rights for married women).

The target speaker raises the argument that if county freeholders receive municipal votes under the subsection, then married women who are freeholders should also receive Parliamentary and municipal votes — explicitly advocating for women's voting rights.

The speech focuses on maternity grants, welfare benefits for pregnant women and newborns, and social security policy—welfare and social policy, not women's political rights or representation. While women are central to the discussion, the speech does not address voting rights, standing for office, political representation, or any other aspect of women's civic/political participation.

The speaker (Mr. H. H. Fowler) explicitly states that the Bill proposes to remove the disqualification preventing married women from being placed on the Local Government Register, treating this as a desirable reform to be implemented. He advocates for bringing the Bill into force and working through registration difficulties to enfranchise married women, expressing no opposition to this extension of women's political rights.

The speaker (Lord R. Cecil) explicitly states "I am very largely in favour of the suffrage" and argues it is "quite absolutely unfeasible to perpetuate a system under which one half of the population are not represented in this House," directly endorsing women's suffrage while systematically rebutting arguments against it (force, chivalry, fitness to vote).

The speaker (Sir S. Coats) devotes his entire speech to marshalling evidence against women's suffrage, citing statistics on low female voter turnout, high election costs, social dysfunction (divorce rates, political corruption), and direct quotes from disillusioned former suffragists in American woman-suffrage states, all to argue that granting women the Parliamentary vote would be harmful.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's political representation (calling for a "ministry for women," arguing "women should have a voice in everything," and supporting the next Labour Government opening up decision-making for women), while condemning the Government's "continued discrimination against women" in taxation, social security, and employment rights, and endorsing equal civic participation for women as 52% of the population.

The speech is entirely focused on the merits of proportional representation for local council elections, arguing for electoral reform to ensure better representation and opposition across party lines. While the speaker incidentally mentions "men and women" as candidates and officeholders, he makes no argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct issue.

The speaker (Colonel Sir C. Seely) systematically argues against including women's suffrage in the Bill, contending that Parliament has no mandate to reverse its earlier rejection, that there is no genuine general demand from women, that women are better served by male chivalry than by the vote, and that enfranchising women would fatally undermine the constitutional authority of the House by severing it from its physical-force basis.

The speech argues for improved pension provisions for unmarried women (spinsters) under the National Health Insurance scheme — a welfare/social insurance matter. It does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation. The subject matter is entirely confined to the actuarial and financial equity of contributory pension benefits for a specific demographic group.

The speaker explicitly states he has held and "in principle holds still" real objections to women's suffrage, articulating substantive arguments against it (women lack constructive/legislative minds, the force-based basis of parliamentary authority, etc.), yet announces he will vote in favour and endorses the full implications including women in Parliament, government, diplomacy, and the judiciary. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides, not merely a procedural caveat.

The speaker (Sir Stuart Coats) extensively quotes women who have turned against suffrage after experiencing it, presents statistics showing higher divorce rates, election costs, and lower voter turnout in women suffrage states, and concludes with a letter arguing that women suffragists have become "arrogant, aggressive" and that women's suffrage has produced no beneficial legislation while doubling the "ignorant vote." The speech is a sustained argument against women's suffrage drawn from American experience.

The speaker (Lord R. Cecil) explicitly argues that women are fit to exercise the vote, that representative government requires enfranchising all capable citizens including women, and that extending the franchise to women over thirty is an essential and conservative component of the Bill's compromise. He directly rebuts arguments against women's suffrage and affirms he has never tried to escape the conclusion that qualified women are entitled to vote.

The speech focuses on procedural and administrative concerns about bringing the Local Government Bill into operation—specifically regarding electoral registers, electoral divisions, and timing. While married women are briefly mentioned as a new class of electors to be included in registers, this is a passing administrative observation rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is a table of community centre details in Scotland, covering facilities for recreation, education, and civic life. It contains no argument about women's political rights or representation; the single mention of "women's interests" refers to a wing of a community centre building, not to political participation or civic rights.

The speaker (a government minister) explicitly defends and promotes a range of measures supporting women's equality, including ratifying the UN convention on eliminating discrimination against women, supporting EC directives on equal opportunities, endorsing the EOC's equal opportunities code, and arguing that women's interests are adequately represented under the current Government. While the speaker opposes some specific proposals (mandatory parental leave directive, a Ministry for Women), these are procedural/implementation objections rather than opposition to women's political rights or equality as such.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage throughout, dismissing arguments against it (health concerns, the "thin end of the wedge," harm to marriage, threat to India) as unfounded, and counters the preceding speech's negative evidence from American states by pointing out that both US presidential candidates pledged support for women's suffrage. The speaker also rejects the argument that women's presence in Parliament would be undesirable.

Mr. Courtney explicitly argues against the sex-based discrimination that strips married women of their votes, contending that the principle of disqualifying women solely on the basis of sex (through marriage) is unjust. He supports women retaining their local government votes regardless of marital status.

The speaker explicitly advocates for 50% representation of women on public bodies/quangos, calls for better economic and employment opportunities for women, supports the EC directive on part-time workers' rights, and argues that society must change to give women "more sway and influence directly in their own right" — all substantive endorsements of women's fuller civic and political participation.

The speech concerns the procedural question of whether to support a Motion or an Amendment to establish a committee (or actuary's report) to inquire into spinsters' pensions under the National Health Insurance and Contributory Pensions Acts. While it advocates for fair treatment of unmarried women under the pension scheme, this is a social insurance/welfare policy matter, not a question of women's civic participation, voting rights, or political representation.

The speaker explicitly supports extending parliamentary and municipal franchises to women ("strongly in favour") while simultaneously opposing women holding the office of chairman of a District Council, arguing they lack the requisite qualities — making substantive arguments on both sides of women's political participation.

The speaker explicitly states he "was opposed to any woman of any sort or kind having a vote" and invokes the "domestic angel doctrine," arguing that giving women votes "would be destructive of all the charms of domesticity." His objection to the property-based distinction between rich and poor women is secondary and does not constitute support for women's suffrage.

The speaker (Mr. Ward) explicitly argues against women's suffrage, contending that the physical force argument has been strengthened by the War (since women did not fight), that no evidence exists of a majority of women demanding the vote, and that the measure is being pushed through unfairly while opponents are absent at the front. He opposes both the timing and the substance of women's enfranchisement.

The speech focuses on women's health services in Scotland, education, employment, nursery provision, stress, and personal security — none of which addresses women's political rights or representation. While the speaker notes she is "the only Scottish woman in the House of Commons," she makes no argument for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in political structures.

The speech is entirely focused on Empire migration, population redistribution, and settlement schemes in the Dominions, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" refugees is purely demographic, not related to civic or political status.

The speech is entirely about the Miners' Welfare Fund and pithead baths legislation, focusing on the welfare of mining families and the working conditions of miners. While the speaker mentions women (wives, mothers) in the context of the domestic burden of dirty miners and their role in encouraging use of pithead baths, this is incidental social commentary and does not argue any position on women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about penal reform legislation, covering prison treatment, juvenile offenders, and persistent criminals. While it mentions women historical figures like Elizabeth Fry and includes passing statistical references to female offenders, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker opposes the specific clause as drafted because it creates an unequal distinction between rich and poor women (a form of opposition to this particular expansion of women's local government franchise), yet simultaneously argues that women ought to be treated equally — implying support for women's suffrage if applied universally rather than only to propertied women. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: against enfranchising only wealthy women, but for equal enfranchisement of all women.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for free television licences for elderly pensioners, addressing issues of poverty, inequality, and the welfare of senior citizens. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speech is almost entirely about opposing proportional representation; the brief mention of female suffrage is only used as a comparative example to argue that proportional representation has not been sufficiently debated, without making any argument for or against women's political rights themselves.

Mr. M'Laren explicitly supports the right of married women to vote at local government elections, backing the clause as far as it goes while pressing the Government to fulfil its pledge to extend that right further.

The speaker explicitly notes that the final two maiden speeches came from "female Labour Members who reminded us that women were under-represented in the House of Commons," and expresses gladness that "there are now far more women in the Labour party" and confidence "their numbers will increase as they begin to get a fairer proportion of representation in the House." This is a brief but substantive endorsement of greater women's political representation.

The speech is entirely about armed forces pension schemes, including pensions for retired service members and their widows. While it mentions "service men and women" in passing, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The target speech is entirely focused on penal reform legislation — corporal punishment, treatment of young and persistent offenders, Borstal sentences, preventive detention, and prison reform. While women are mentioned briefly and incidentally (e.g., "men and women" helpers, probation officers for girls), no argument is made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker systematically argues against women's suffrage, contending that the war has strengthened rather than undermined the physical force argument, that no proof exists of a majority of women desiring the vote, and that the timing is unfair and undemocratic. He explicitly states he will vote against the clause and urges other Members to join him in opposing it.

The speech is focused on the fairness of constituency delimitation for military camps, arguing that population-based boundaries disadvantage soldiers as voters. The only mention of women is a brief, passing reference to "female suffrage" to illustrate the ratio of electorate to population in a typical constituency—no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is primarily about opposing the community charge (poll tax) on grounds of fairness, accountability, and economic impact. While it briefly mentions that women earn less than men and would be disproportionately burdened by the flat-rate tax, and asserts that "women have always voted as responsibly as anyone else," these references address economic inequality and rebut a specific government argument about taxpayer accountability rather than making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on NHS funding, health service charges for dental and eye tests, and conditions in the Black Country health system. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that the property restriction on married women's franchise is inequitable because it excludes poorer married women, and contends that "if married women were to have the franchise, all married women ought to have it, rich and poor alike" — a clear argument for extending women's political rights more broadly.

The Speaker's ruling is purely procedural — explaining that the motion is out of order because existing Bills already address women's enfranchisement — and makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about corporal punishment, prison reform, Borstal sentences, and the licence system. The brief mention of women is only to cite them as a voting majority whose opinion on retaining the "cat" should be heeded — this is an appeal to public opinion statistics, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses on wartime labour, wages, the Ministry of Munitions, and the Liquor Control Board's actions against publicans — with only a brief passing mention that the Representation of the People Bill is being dealt with through the Speaker's conference, expressed as general satisfaction without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speaker opposes the age-30 limit as arbitrary and illogical, arguing it enfranchises the wrong women (married women who don't want the vote) while excluding younger working women who have a genuine grievance—implying support for some form of women's suffrage. At the same time, he explicitly identifies himself as "an opponent of the wholesale grant of votes to women," making substantive arguments against broad female enfranchisement, thus taking positions on both sides of women's political rights.

The speech is primarily concerned with Irish unrest, coercion legislation, and an appeal for political reconciliation between Northern and Southern Ireland. The reference to the women's suffrage movement is a brief passing analogy used to illustrate that deep-seated grievances drive people to extreme acts, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly criticises the Bill for containing clauses dealing with "the non-rights of women" and argues against provisions that would undermine equal opportunities measures at the local authority level, thereby supporting women's political and civic rights as part of a broader equal opportunities framework.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, armaments spending, export trade, and economic planning for post-rearmament depression. While women are briefly mentioned in passing (e.g., "men and women" who are unemployed, widows' pensions as part of the means test calculation), no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage and the compromise bill, urging "true friends of women suffrage" to oppose the Amendment that would alter the agreed terms, arguing that women's organisations have accepted the compromise and suffragists should stand by it rather than pursue an abstract ideal at the expense of practical progress.

The speech is primarily about press freedom, media ownership, contempt and libel laws, and democratic discourse. The brief mention of women voting and entering Parliament is used only as a historical example to illustrate how today's "outrageous ideas" become tomorrow's common sense — no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's equal rights throughout the speech, criticising the Government for retarding women's rights since 1979, citing wage inequality and underrepresentation in Parliament, and calling for vigorous enforcement of the Sex Discrimination Act and equal pay legislation. She directly supports the EOC's push for stronger anti-discrimination measures and argues women deserve equality in political and economic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Peto) explicitly identifies himself as an opponent of wholesale women's suffrage ("I contend, as an opponent of the wholesale grant of votes to women") yet substantively argues for removing the age-30 restriction, favouring enfranchisement of younger, unmarried working women. He thus opposes broad women's suffrage while simultaneously advocating for a specific form of it, making substantive arguments on both sides.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. D. R. Plunket and Mr. George Russell) is entirely focused on the Welsh Church Disestablishment and Disendowment Bill — debating the Irish precedent, Church endowments, and the merits of disestablishment — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is about NHS primary care reform, including GP services, dental checks, eye tests, and health spending. While it briefly mentions "women's health" and "more women doctors" as policy goals, these are passing references in the context of a health policy debate, with no substantive argument made about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker broadly supports the franchise extension Bill and urges its passage, but explicitly states his opposition to the women's suffrage provision, declaring he has "all through been an opponent of that proposal" and warning he cannot support the Bill if that clause is retained — constituting substantive argument on both sides of women's political rights within the same speech.

The speech is primarily about unemployment policy, comparisons with Nazi Germany's labour practices, and the Labour movement's domestic agenda during wartime. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the broader population affected by unemployment and forced labour policies, not in the context of their political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Sir G. Cave, representing the Government) explicitly supports the women's suffrage compromise (age 30, local government qualification) as accepted by suffrage advocates, and calls on supporters of women's suffrage to oppose the amendment reducing the age to 21, framing the compromise as a fair settlement. This is a substantive endorsement of women's suffrage in the form proposed.

The speaker explicitly and at length supports women's suffrage, arguing for the Conference's compromise scheme to enfranchise 5–6 million women and stating "my own view has always been that adult suffrage is the only right thing" extending to all men and all women. He urges the Committee to support the Bill's proposals as the best achievable path to putting women's suffrage on the statute book.

The Home Secretary (Sir G. Cave) explicitly supports the women's suffrage compromise (age 30, local government qualification) as accepted by women's suffrage advocates, and urges all supporters of women's suffrage or the Bill to oppose an amendment he views as a wrecking motion against it, threatening to withdraw responsibility for the Bill if the amendment passes.

The speech is primarily about colonial administration, labour rights, trade unions, social services, and political rights for colonial peoples (Africans, West Indians, Maltese, etc.). The brief mentions of women — welcoming women's inclusion in the Colonial administrative service and suggesting appointment of women officers with social welfare experience — are incidental administrative observations, not arguments about women's political rights or civic status as defined by the suffrage framing.

The speech concerns corporation tax relief for workers' co-operatives and argues for equity in tax treatment for co-operatives compared to conventional businesses. While it briefly mentions co-operatives organised by women and ethnic minorities as beneficiaries, this is incidental; the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker supports equal opportunities for women in employment and public services, criticizes the order for limiting the EOC's proactive investigative powers, and argues for stronger mechanisms to combat institutionalised discrimination against women. While they express reservations about mandating women into certain jobs, this is a procedural/scope caveat rather than opposition to women's political or civic rights.

The speaker (Sir H. Craik, identifiable from the following speech context) explicitly states he has been "a consistent opponent of the principle" of women's suffrage, that his "fears are not removed" by the vote to extend the franchise to women, and that he doubts most women want the vote. While he argues that if women are to get the vote, younger women and university graduates should not be excluded, this is a conditional argument subordinate to his overall opposition to women's suffrage — not a substantive endorsement of the cause.

The speech is entirely concerned with temperance/licensing legislation — specifically the Local Option Bill, compensation for licence-holders, Sunday closing, and the application of the Bill to Ireland. The passing mention of "men and of women" who care about temperance reform is purely rhetorical and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker raises a point of order arguing that the Bill conflicts with the Sex Disqualification Removal Act, which established that no citizen should be barred from public office or privileges by reason of sex. By invoking this Act to challenge the Bill's provisions that would allow exclusion of women, the speaker implicitly supports women's equal civic participation rights.
The speech concerns voting procedures for parental ballots on grant-maintained school status under education legislation, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over Payment of Members of Parliament, arguing against that proposal on grounds of political machinery, status of the House, and democratic legitimacy. The only mention of "Female Suffrage" is a passing rhetorical flourish dismissing the logical-corollary argument, with no substantive position taken on women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment policy, industrial coordination, trade, and economic planning. Women are mentioned only in passing as part of "men and women" among the unemployed workforce, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech focuses entirely on the financial hardships imposed on working-class families by the Military Service Act's pay and allowance provisions, arguing for better pay and civil liability protections for conscripts and their dependants. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage in principle ("sex is not an important consideration in relation to the suffrage") and argues that the age-30 restriction is irrational and unstable, urging the Committee to find a more rational basis for limiting the franchise rather than opposing women's enfranchisement itself. His objections are to the specific mechanism (age limit), not to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, economic policy, socialist principles, and the condition of unemployed workers; women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "women and children" in the context of civilian protection, and mothers sacrificing to feed children). No argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is almost entirely about an Electoral Practices Bill concerning false statements at elections. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing, humorous aside that the speaker expected to discuss "the suffrage of women," provoking applause from the Ladies' Gallery — no argument for or against women's suffrage is made.

The speaker supports the Amendment to extend the franchise to women under thirty who served abroad, arguing these women deserve enfranchisement for their wartime service, and further endorses women's political participation by welcoming younger women into the House of Commons.

The speaker objects to the Government making women's suffrage a Cabinet question and expresses that the House voted under a "great misapprehension" when it approved women's votes, suggesting he would prefer to "chuck the whole thing" and implying he is opposed to women's suffrage being imposed as an agreed measure. He explicitly states he would "change his mind" (i.e., vote against women's suffrage) and frames the women's suffrage clause as an unwanted, unagreed imposition.

The speech concerns plural voting and electoral franchise reform (the "One Man One Vote" Bill), focusing on constituency inequalities, Irish over-representation, and alleged partisan gerrymandering. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech focuses entirely on Northern Ireland public expenditure — covering economic development, housing, health, education, and social security — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The single mention of women is a passing reference to low pay among women as part of a broader point about poverty, which does not engage with their civic or political status.

The speech is primarily about a Northern Ireland elections/democracy bill and its money resolution, with the suffragettes mentioned only in passing as historical examples of people who fought for democracy — no argument about women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage ("in the interests of women's suffrage") and argues for the age-30 limitation as the least objectionable form of restriction, urging friends of women's suffrage to accept this compromise to advance the cause. While acknowledging the limitation is regrettable, the speaker frames the argument in favor of enacting women's suffrage rather than opposing it.

The speaker (McLaren, MP for Crewe) is explicitly moving a motion to extend the Parliamentary Franchise to Women and seeking to move "that no person should be disqualified from exercising the Parliamentary Franchise on the ground of sex," clearly supporting women's political rights.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. Hutchinson, continuing his speech) explicitly argues that the Schedule should be amended so that both appointed members and chairmen of hardship committees "shall be male persons and not women," directly opposing women's equal participation in these public offices. While Viscountess Astor's speech in the TARGET advocates for women's inclusion, her contribution appears in the CONTEXT's following speeches and is not part of the TARGET to be classified.

The target speech is almost entirely about plural voting and the "One Man One Vote" principle, with only a brief opening remark hoping that women's suffrage will not be raised in connection with this Bill. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The TARGET speech is entirely concerned with parliamentary procedure, the Government's armaments preparations, and whether Parliament should remain in session during an international crisis — none of which addresses women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" affected by legislation is incidental and makes no argument about women's civic status.

The speaker criticizes the procedural handling of the Bill and dismisses it as doing "scant justice" to the cause, suggesting the proceedings are not "calculated to do good" to the cause — an implicitly skeptical or obstructive stance. While the speaker raises the unresolved question of which women (married, unmarried, or property-holding) should receive the vote, this is framed as a criticism rather than substantive support for any of these groups.

The speaker explicitly states that proper consultation on factory legislation affecting women cannot occur until "that House had extended the Parliamentary suffrage to women," thereby endorsing women's parliamentary suffrage as a necessary precondition for legitimate legislation affecting them.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for compulsory military conscription for young men, with no substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation. The brief mention of "men and women" in the context of a national register and civil defence duties is incidental and does not argue any position on women's distinctive political status or rights.

The speaker explicitly celebrates the Suffragettes as the true givers of parliamentary democracy, commends the suffragette who hid in the House of Commons to assert her civic presence, and credits them with making it possible for women to become Prime Minister — all clear endorsements of women's political rights.

The speech is about petitioners' rights and protecting signatories of petitions from discrimination, primarily in the context of the poll tax. Women's political rights are mentioned only in passing ("The suffragettes helped to overcome the sexist limitations of the initial Chartists' demands") without any argument being made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker expresses suspicion toward women's suffrage, arguing that opponents of suffrage who support a lower age limit are not acting in the genuine interests of the cause, and implies that the foundations of women's suffrage are made "suspicious" by such tactical maneuvering — overall conveying skepticism and opposition to advancing women's suffrage through this Bill.

The speaker explicitly states opposition to large-scale women's enfranchisement ("a leap in the dark" adding 6,000,000 women voters) while simultaneously expressing willingness to grant women's franchise on a limited, equal-numbers basis ("I am prepared to grant the franchise to women on a limited scale... as many new women electors added as there are men electors added"). This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: conditional support for a restricted form of women's suffrage alongside substantive opposition to the broader extension proposed.

The speech focuses entirely on housing, unemployment, poverty, low pay, and the Welsh valleys initiative. The mention of women working in Wales is purely an economic observation about low wages and employment figures, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely about extending the Crofters' Act to improve land tenure, fair rents, and holdings for Highland crofters in Scotland. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker explicitly states they voted against women's suffrage the previous day ("had the courage of their convictions") and argues against the women's suffrage clause, warning that granting any franchise to women will inevitably lead to full equal suffrage, which they oppose because women would form a large majority of the electorate. Their support for the Amendment is tactical—to defeat the Bill—not to genuinely advance women's political rights.

The speech concerns the suppression of the slave trade and slavery in Zanzibar and Pemba, arguing that current expenditure is ineffective and urging emancipation of slaves and policy reform. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status of women.

The speaker explicitly states "I am certainly not against it" regarding women's opportunities, then criticises the Government for claiming credit on equal opportunities for women while removing the right to return to work after pregnancy and taxing workplace creches — arguing that genuine support for women's employment rights requires more substantive protections, not just allowing women into mines and heavy industry.

Morley explicitly highlights the clause enabling women, married or single, to vote in local matters, noting that the English analogy favours this provision and that it represents "an important change." His endorsement is clear when he says "so far as the English analogy goes, that analogy would be in favour of the provisions of the Bill," supporting the extension of women's local voting rights to Ireland.

The speech concerns Supplementary Estimates related to foreign policy matters (China, Spain, the Runciman/Sudeten mission, Non-intervention Committee) and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely focused on unemployment insurance, holidays with pay, training schemes, and related labour legislation. The brief mention of married women concerns their eligibility for unemployment benefits under the insurance scheme, not their political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on workmen's compensation reform — urging immediate legislation to increase payments for disabled workers — with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech (and the appended speech by Mr. Edmund Harvey) deals entirely with penal reform — specifically the planning of a new women's prison and girls' Borstal institution, their design, siting, and administration. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that Parliament lacks the "moral competence" to decide the Welsh Disestablishment question because women—who have no votes—are deeply affected by it, declaring that "Women had a pre-eminent right to a voice in the question" and condemning the Bill as an "iniquity perpetrated by a small majority of the half of the community which possessed electoral power upon the other half which had no votes." This is a substantive argument in favour of women's political representation and the franchise.

The speaker (Mr. Snowden) is procedurally analyzing the contradictory motivations of those supporting the Amendment to lower the voting age to 21, pointing out the incoherence of the coalition backing it. While women's suffrage is the subject under debate, the TARGET speech itself makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights — it focuses entirely on exposing the logical inconsistencies of the Amendment's supporters rather than arguing a position on women's enfranchisement.

The TARGET speaker explicitly identifies himself as an "adult suffragist" and states he will oppose the Amendment (keeping age at 30) while supporting broader women's enfranchisement; he accepts the compromise only reluctantly as a tactical step toward fuller electoral reform, making clear his underlying support for women's political rights. His opposition to the Amendment is procedural/strategic, not substantive opposition to women's suffrage.

The speech is primarily about immigration legislation and its discriminatory effects on Commonwealth citizens, particularly Bangladeshis. The brief mention of women's equality is incidental — the speaker notes the Bill levelled men's rights down to women's (rather than raising women's rights up) as a critique of the Government's general approach to equality, but makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on adult and youth unemployment training schemes, funding, compulsion, job substitution, trade union roles, and related employment policy — with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The sole mention of women is a passing reference to women community programme workers' wage levels, which is a labour/wages point, not a women's political rights argument.

The TARGET speech is entirely about Royal Commissions and the likelihood that their reports will be ignored, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of women in the context (a Committee on Pensions for Unmarried Women) appears only in the following speeches, not in the TARGET.

The target speech is a ministerial explanation of a supplementary budget estimate covering several commissions, including one on pensions for unmarried women. The speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights; the mention of the Committee on Pensions for Unmarried Women is purely administrative and financial in nature.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's presence on funding councils as a means to better represent women undergraduates, supporting women's representation in public institutional bodies. This is a clear argument in favour of women's political/civic representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I am in favour of the very widest measure of enfranchisement for women" and describes himself as a long-standing adult suffragist who has supported all women's suffrage bills. He opposes the amendment not out of opposition to women's suffrage but because he believes it would destroy the compromise already achieved, while pledging to continue agitating for full enfranchisement of all women on equal terms with men.

The speech is entirely focused on arguments for televising Parliamentary proceedings, covering regional coverage, public understanding, and the character of Parliament. The brief mentions of suffragettes and "abseiling lesbians" are incidental illustrations about disruptive incidents unrelated to women's political rights, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker briefly but explicitly endorses women's suffrage near the end of the speech, stating "The Prime Minister would not have been Prime Minister if the suffragettes had not broken the law to force women's suffrage" — framing the suffragettes' law-breaking as legitimate and necessary to win women's political rights, and citing women's suffrage as an example of a just cause won through civil disobedience. While the speech is primarily about the seamen's dispute, this constitutes an explicit endorsement of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the inequitable burden of public assistance (poor relief) costs falling disproportionately on distressed areas, arguing for a national redistribution of that financial burden. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the general population (e.g., "men, women and children," "young men and young women") with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Mrs. Rumbold) rejects the proposal that half the membership of funding councils should be women, insisting appointments should be based on individual merit and best qualifications rather than gender representation, thereby opposing a structural measure to advance women's political/civic representation.

The speaker supports women's enfranchisement and explicitly defends the age-30 compromise as the best practical means to secure it, arguing it is the only arrangement that can unite supporters of women's suffrage in Parliament. While opposing the Amendment to lower the age to 21, this is a procedural/tactical objection rooted in securing women's suffrage rather than opposing it.

The speaker raises a parliamentary question explicitly concerned with protecting married women's ability to serve as members of Boards of Guardians, arguing that ambiguity in the law is "calculated to interfere with and restrict trade and to prevent married women from performing their duties as guardians," and calls for legal clarification to remove that obstacle.

The speaker explicitly argues against limiting the overtime of adult women, invoking women's growing voting power as a reason the Legislature should not restrict their independent action regarding work hours, and contending that women had not asked for such limitations and were competent to decide for themselves—thus opposing this specific legislative constraint on women's labour autonomy.

This lengthy speech by the Chancellor of the Exchequer concerns the introduction of a Local Option (temperance/liquor licensing) Bill, dealing entirely with local control over the alcohol trade. Women are mentioned only once in passing—as eligible voters in a Norwegian example—without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (identified from context as Miss Horsbrugh, the senior Member for Dundee) discusses women's preferences regarding unemployment insurance versus national health insurance during pregnancy, focusing on administrative and welfare concerns. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech (Mr. Scott) argues in favour of extending women's suffrage by supporting an amendment to lower the age limit below thirty, contending that the age-30 restriction was designed to defeat democratic principles and that adult suffrage for women is preferable to a "fancy irrational franchise" selecting only older women. He explicitly supports granting women the vote on broader, more equal terms with men.

The speech concerns the practical welfare of pregnant women attending Employment Exchanges under unemployment and national health insurance — a social/labour policy matter. It does not argue for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation.

The speech concerns police administration matters — criminal statistics, a police officer's dismissal/resignation, and the provision of police matrons for women detained in custody overnight. While it addresses the welfare and treatment of women in police detention, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly criticises the suggestion that nursing is "more suitable" for women than medicine, defends women doctors as fully capable professionals, and objects to relegating women to a lower-status, lower-paid profession — arguing against gendered restrictions on women's access to professions on equal terms with men. She also attributes the nursing profession's poor pay to its being "almost entirely reserved for women," framing this as a structural injustice rooted in women's historical exclusion from other professions.

The speaker (Mr. MacCallum Scott/Mr. Scott) explicitly acknowledges having opposed women's suffrage in the past ("all the opposition which I have given in the past to the principle of women's suffrage") while simultaneously supporting the Amendment to extend the vote to all women over 21 on equal terms with men, arguing that the age-30 restriction is illogical, unfair to industrial women, and designed to defeat democratic reform. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: past opposition to women's suffrage as a principle, combined with current support for equal adult suffrage for women.

The speech is primarily about factory and workshop legislation — sanitary inspection, overtime regulations, laundry hours, and committee procedure. While women workers are mentioned incidentally (e.g., arguing against restricting overtime for young women in season trades, or opposing Factory Act application to laundries because poor women rely on laundry work), these are economic/labour arguments about working conditions, not arguments about women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation.

The speaker (Under-Secretary Peake) supports extending the parliamentary vote to women engaged in national service if the voting age is lowered, but firmly opposes the specific clause as drafted, arguing it unjustly differentiates between conscripts and volunteers and misapplies the 1918 precedent — substantive opposition to one form of extended political rights while implicitly endorsing a broader, gender-inclusive alternative.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers: the first (Member for Blackburn) explicitly states "We thought that it was wrong to give the vote to women, and we still say so," opposing women's suffrage in principle, yet argues for equal terms (same age as men) if women are to have the vote at all. The second speaker (Mr. MacCallum Scott) acknowledges past opposition to women's suffrage but supports extending the franchise to all women on equal terms with men, arguing against the age-30 restriction as undemocratic and illogical — effectively supporting broader women's suffrage. Together the TARGET presents substantive arguments on both sides.

The speech concerns gay rights and civil liberties related to Section 28 (prohibiting local authorities from "promoting" homosexuality), not women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally in the division list and passing references, with no argument made about women's civic or political status.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing military conscription on behalf of Clyde engineers, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of women voting in Birmingham on conscription is a passing reference used to contrast regional opinion, not an argument about women's civic status.

The target speech is primarily about opposition to the Prevention of Terrorism Bill, invoking the Glorious Revolution and the Bill of Rights to argue against executive overreach. The brief mention of "men and women" is a passing rhetorical flourish about citizens' rights generally, not an argument about women's distinctive political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Healy) explicitly states he has "always supported the extension of the suffrage to women" and notes the franchise had already been granted to women in Belfast, expressing support for extending similar rights to women in Derry as well.

The speech is entirely focused on Royal Navy defence policy, the Armilla patrol, frigate procurement, and shipbuilding — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women must come to realise engineering is "just as much open to them as it is to boys," praises the Engineering Council's initiatives on career breaks for women engineers, and expresses concern about gender expectations discouraging girls from engineering careers — all supporting women's equal participation in professional/public life.

The speaker (Sir C. Hobhouse) argues that once the House decided to grant women's suffrage, he accepts that decision and insists there should be "no distinction as between woman and woman which is not between man and man," effectively supporting equal suffrage for women without an age restriction favoring older/wealthier women over younger industrial women.

The speech concerns local government employment decisions in Bradford and the Conservative council's staffing cuts, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for ensuring that working-class women are genuinely represented on government committees, pressing the minister to be more specific in his assurances about consulting truly representative working-class women's organisations. This supports women's participation in public/civic bodies as a distinct class deserving proper representation.

The speaker expresses support for women's political rights by noting that passage of his Amendment would prompt the Leader of the House — described as "a devoted champion of women's suffrage" — to introduce a measure remedying the omission in the Local Government Act of 1888 to allow women to sit on County Councils, framing the non-inclusion of women as a deficiency ("casus omissus") that ought to be corrected.

The speech is entirely about the proposed closure of Ashbourne maternity home and access to maternity services for constituents, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states it is "extremely desirable that women should be included in the Franchise" and argues that women of Derry should not be placed in an inferior position relative to women of Belfast who already hold the Municipal Franchise, directly advocating for women's political rights.

The TARGET speech focuses on a procedural/constitutional analogy between the Government's handling of women's suffrage age provisions and proportional representation methods, arguing that the Government's logic is consistent. The speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights themselves, but rather addresses the procedural question of Government freedom to constrain implementation details once a principle is accepted.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage throughout, defending the Bill's approach to granting women votes and arguing that those opposing the Amendment (who want to expand it) are actually long-standing opponents of women's suffrage acting in bad faith. He states clearly that those "in favour of women's suffrage" should stick to the Bill as the best practical means of securing women's votes.

The speech is entirely focused on an education bill debate concerning voluntary (denominational) schools, School Boards, and religious instruction — mentioning "English men and English women" only as allies of the Irish Party with shared social and religious difficulties. No argument about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speaker briefly mentions women's franchise only to note he has "no strong view one way or the other" and that the difficulties are merely technical/drafting details, not substantive arguments for or against women's political rights. The speech is primarily about Parliamentary franchise assimilation, lodger franchise, ward divisions, and the cumulative vote.

The speech is primarily about workmen's compensation allowances and family allowances legislation. The brief mention of "votes for women" is used only as a historical analogy to illustrate how inevitable reforms are eventually forced through by war, with no argument made for or against women's political rights. The suggestion that allowances be paid to wives in exceptional cases is a welfare/administrative point, not an argument about women's civic or political status.

The target speech is procedural in nature, focusing solely on clarifying the promise made by the Secretary of State about leaving women's enfranchisement and proportional representation to a free vote of the House, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The remainder of the target consists of division lists.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers: the first (unnamed) explicitly states "no vote of mine would be given for the extension of the franchise to women," opposing women's suffrage, while Mr. MacCallum Scott supports the Amendment to give women the Parliamentary franchise on the same residential basis as men, objecting to restrictions on women's suffrage as a class-based check. These constitute substantive arguments on both sides of women's political rights.

The TARGET speech concerns higher education funding councils, polytechnic independence, ILEA reform, and expansion of higher education. While it briefly mentions "business men and women" on governing bodies, this is incidental and no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The speaker explicitly identifies as a "lifelong supporter of women's suffrage," supports the partial measure of enfranchising women over thirty as a practical step forward, and argues that while the age limit is conservative, it is sensible and not unworthy. The speech defends the bill's women's suffrage provisions throughout.

The speech is a parliamentary tribute to the deceased George Lansbury and Sir Terence O'Connor. The single brief mention of women's suffrage ("He was never afraid of taking a stand and showed devotion to the cause of women's suffrage by resigning his seat in this House") is a factual biographical note about Lansbury, not an argument for or against women's political rights made by the speaker himself.

The speech focuses entirely on youth organisations, housing areas, school facilities, and political activities for young people in Scotland — with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation as a gendered issue. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "young men and women" in a general sense.

The speaker explicitly supports giving women the Parliamentary vote, arguing it should be built on the foundation of the existing local government franchise ("giving the Parliamentary vote to those who already have the municipal vote"), and states he cannot vote for the Amendment that would alter this basis. His opposition is to the specific amendment, not to women's suffrage itself.

The speaker proposes an amendment to restrict women's parliamentary franchise by ensuring no woman can be enfranchised by a qualification that does not also qualify her husband, explicitly framing this as a limitation on women's voting rights relative to men's. This represents substantive opposition to extending women's political rights beyond parity with their husbands' qualifications.

The target speech concerns the Belfast Municipal Corporations Bill, focusing on the extension of the city's area, Catholic representation on the Corporation, and the merits of the Bill's second reading. The brief mention of women ("Yes, including women, and they hoped that the Parliamentary Franchise would also include them in the future") is a passing reference with no substantive argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker presents a petition opposing the Abortion (Amendment) Bill on grounds that it would "restrict women's choice" and endanger their health, explicitly agreeing with the petition, thereby supporting women's reproductive rights as a dimension of their civic autonomy.

The speaker explicitly argues for remedying an injustice by restoring women property owners' local franchise voting rights (for boards of guardians and local councils), framing the Bill as correcting an inequity that deprived women of votes men already held.

The speech mentions votes for women and adult suffrage only in passing as historical examples of issues settled by the wartime Speaker's Conference, without making any argument for or against women's political rights. The substantive focus is on parliamentary prolongation, electoral registration, and post-war electoral reform procedures.

The speech is primarily about community care policy — the elderly, mentally ill, disabled, and carers — and makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of women as carers saving the Chancellor money is descriptive of their economic role, not an argument about their civic status or political participation.

The TARGET contains multiple speakers with conflicting stances: the Dublin Harbour Member opposes women serving on Boards of Guardians, arguing their presence would "embarrass proceedings"; Healy supports the Bill and women's right to serve on such Boards; Gibson Bowles opposes it, stating business is "transacted better by men than by women." As a whole, the TARGET makes substantive arguments both for and against women's participation in public office.

The speaker supports women's suffrage in principle (advocating for over 30 years for enfranchising women who are economically independent local government electors), but explicitly opposes extending the franchise to married women or the full 6,000,000 women proposed, arguing there is no demonstrated demand and that a more limited reform (~1,000,000 independent women) is the appropriate measure.

The speech is entirely focused on air-raid shelter provision for working-class people in industrial areas during WWII. While the speaker briefly mentions "men and women" who volunteered for ARP services, he makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about West Indian colonial conditions—wages, labour, poverty, trade unions, and development policy. The brief mention of "political facilities" and the vote refers to extending suffrage to West Indian colonial subjects generally, not to women's political rights specifically; women are not singled out as a class for distinctive civic treatment anywhere in the speech.

The speaker (Ms. Clare Short) explicitly argues that the Government's special provisions for women and girls in employment and training are inadequate and cosmetic, pressing for genuine access to training and employment for women — including single mothers with childcare needs — thereby advocating for expanded opportunities and equal participation for women in public economic life. She supports the legislative provision for women's special needs in training while criticising its insufficient implementation.

The speaker expresses concern about doubling the electorate and frames women's enfranchisement as an unprecedented and potentially problematic expansion, indicating skepticism toward broad women's suffrage. They also suggest that a "more moderate" or limited franchise is preferable, signaling opposition to full women's political rights as proposed.

The speaker explicitly and warmly welcomes the clause abolishing all reference to sex in the Bill, recognising the advantage of women serving on Boards of Guardians, and further argues that women property owners in England who are deprived of the parochial vote should have it conferred upon them.

The speaker (Miss Widdecombe) strongly champions the independent taxation of husband and wife as a long-overdue recognition of women's civic and financial personhood, explicitly connecting it to women's rights history and arguing it is "one of the greatest steps forward this century in social justice and the recognition of women."

The speaker explicitly advocates on behalf of women agricultural workers, arguing that Sub-section (3) discriminates against women by failing to define the precise relationship of women's wages to men's wages, and insists that women deserve "the same kind of protection as men." The speech is grounded in concern for women's equal treatment under the legislation.

The speaker explicitly says he "cordially welcomes" the enfranchisement of women and supports the Amendment as a moderate first step toward that goal, arguing it is wiser to extend the franchise incrementally to a tested body of women voters rather than all at once — a procedural/cautionary argument, not opposition to women's suffrage itself.

The speaker explicitly and at length advocates for women to be included in the Home Guard "in the same capacity as men, with equal rights and no privileges," arguing against prejudices that exclude women from civic/military participation and drawing a parallel to the suffrage movement 20-30 years prior. The entire speech is a sustained argument for women's equal participation in public defence roles.

The speaker moves an amendment to extend the local government franchise to wives of male local government electors, arguing that the 5,000,000 married women already given the Parliamentary vote should also have the local government vote, explicitly supporting broader women's political participation at the municipal level.

The speech is entirely focused on the Jameson Raid, the Chartered Company, Rhodes's financial misconduct, and British colonial policy in South Africa. The brief mention of "women and children in Johannesburg" is purely incidental to describing a pretext for the raid, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speech concerns the administration of wartime sugar distribution for jam-making through voluntary women's organisations, not women's political rights or civic representation. Women's organisations are mentioned only as distribution channels for a food policy matter.

The speaker engages with arguments about married versus single women's enfranchisement: acknowledging the argument that married women are "indirectly represented" by husbands (a basis for excluding them) while also treating the broader women's franchise debate as live. However, the speaker ultimately declines to press the Amendment, suggesting ambivalence rather than clear support or opposition, and the speech touches on both the case for including married women and the procedural reasons not to force a vote—making it substantively two-sided on which women should be enfranchised.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Budget's "much overdue reform of the taxation of married women" as one of his three stated priorities, praising its enactment as a positive step toward women's equal treatment under tax law — a matter of their civic/economic status as a distinct class.

The TARGET speech (Mr. Nigel Griffiths, Edinburgh South) focuses entirely on critiquing the Budget's economic effects on the poor, pensioners, housing, manufacturing, and trade deficits. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation, and the brief mention of women's voting history in the preceding context speech (Mr. Quentin Davis) belongs to the CONTEXT, not the TARGET.

The speaker explicitly argues that working-class married women should receive the local government vote on equal terms with property-owning women, framing the denial of that vote as class-based injustice and urging the Committee to extend full political rights to these women. This is a clear endorsement of expanding women's political rights and representation.

The speech is entirely about Sports Council funding, accountability, and a local planning dispute over a sports pitch and floodlights in Teddington. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech asks about whether representations have flagged deterrence effects of top-up loans on under-represented groups (including women) and about Scottish education concerns, but women are merely listed as one of several under-represented groups in the context of student finance policy, with no substantive argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker strongly supports extending both the parliamentary franchise (already granted) and the municipal franchise to married women, arguing it is absurd and illogical to give women the higher parliamentary vote while denying them the municipal vote. Throughout the speech, the speaker advocates for women's full civic participation at both levels of government.

The speaker from Haddingtonshire explicitly cites the representation of women on education committees as an advantage of substituting district councils for county councils, stating that the amendment "would get rid of the whole difficulty as regarded the representation of women upon the body which controlled education." This is a positive argument in favour of women's representation in local educational governance.

The speech is a parliamentary question about appointing a female Labour Correspondent for Scotland to address industrial conditions affecting women workers. While it concerns women in employment, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation — it is an administrative/labour policy question outside the defined scope.

The TARGET speech is entirely about the Education Bill debate regarding Voluntary Schools versus Board Schools, religious education, decentralisation, and educational funding. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point in the speech, despite a passing analogy about distributing grants equally among "90 men and ten women" which is purely illustrative and makes no argument about women's civic status.

The speech focuses on old age pension provisions, the means test, welfare of elderly people, and financial arrangements between the government and local authorities. The brief mention of "150,000 spinsters and some other women-folk" receiving slight benefits refers to pension policy, not to women's political rights or civic participation.

MR. CHANNIG argues against the co-optation system precisely because it "would exclude women," and advocates instead for extending the School Board system which would bring women in, explicitly supporting women's inclusion in educational governance bodies. This constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that unemployed women should receive the same unemployment benefit as men, stating "No longer do I think there is a defence against paying an unemployed woman less than an unemployed man" and invoking the principle of equal pay and equal work. He also supports further investigation of anomalies regulations disadvantaging married women workers, framing equal treatment of women as an "urgent reform."

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a Northern Ireland local government oath/declaration bill on grounds of democratic principle, civil liberties, and British-Irish policy; it does not address women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the municipal franchise to married women, references a 1913 Bill he introduced for this purpose, and heartily endorses the Amendment to enfranchise wives of local government electors, while only raising technical points about residence requirements as improvements to the Amendment rather than objections to it in principle.

The speech is entirely focused on cervical cancer screening policy — calling for a computerised call and recall system, adequate laboratory staffing, and appropriate screening intervals. It does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of women's civic/political rights as defined in scope.

The speech is a lengthy debate on the Education Bill of 1896, focusing on issues of School Boards, Voluntary Schools, religious instruction, decentralisation, and secondary education. The only mention touching on women is a brief, passing remark that in the control of Poor Law and Industrial Schools for girls, the speaker would have liked "a body on which there could have been representation for women" — this is a fleeting observation without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech focuses on procedural and technical objections to franchise clauses being inserted into a private Bill concerning Dublin municipal governance, with no substantive argument made about women's political rights. Women are only mentioned in passing in Mr. Healy's embedded summary of an opponent's prior objection, not as a position the TARGET speaker advocates for or against.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on wartime labour policy, industrial conscription, war production, wages, and nationalisation of industries. Women are mentioned only briefly in two passages: once noting that "conscription for women arouses the gravest apprehension in many quarters" (a descriptive observation, not an argument for or against women's political rights), and once regarding safeguards for women's wages when conscripted as industrial labour. Neither passage argues a position on women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising NHS competitive tendering and privatisation of hospital services, arguing it harms workers and patients. While women are mentioned incidentally (e.g., "250 workers, most of whom were women" and part-time women workers lacking benefit entitlements), no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Viscountess Astor) strongly advocates for women's full civic participation and equal treatment in public life, arguing that governments have consistently failed to trust, understand, or utilise women, criticising the Prime Minister's lack of vision about "women's citizenship," and championing women's equal representation in government positions and war service roles. She repeatedly asserts women's capability, intelligence, and right to be treated as full political and civic equals.

The speaker explicitly states he intended to vote for the franchise clause if he could have introduced an amendment to extend it to women, indicating support for women's franchise, but since he could not do so, he votes against the clause — effectively opposing the clause as it excludes women. This represents substantive argument on both sides: supporting women's enfranchisement while opposing the clause that omits it.

The speaker supports the existing property-based municipal franchise for women ("I value the provision of the Bill because it maintains something which has worked very well up till now") while explicitly endorsing women's Parliamentary vote as justified by a genuine grievance. This represents support for one aspect of women's political rights (Parliamentary franchise) while opposing extension of another (expanding the municipal franchise to married women without a property qualification).

The speaker explicitly argues that it is almost unbelievable that "half the population were denied the right to vote in general elections and the right to stand for Parliament, for no other reason than that they happened to be women," framing this historical exclusion as a serious injustice and criticising the motion for ignoring the struggles required to achieve women's enfranchisement.

The speaker (Home Secretary) explicitly supports women's Parliamentary franchise (acknowledging the 6,000,000 women enfranchised for Parliamentary purposes) while opposing the Amendment that would extend the local government franchise to an additional 5,000,000 married women, arguing procedural grounds (thin House, Speaker's Conference recommendations) and substantive distinctions between the two franchises. This constitutes genuine two-sidedness: supporting women's Parliamentary suffrage while opposing expansion of their local government franchise.

The speaker explicitly advocates for more women in Parliament, equal compensation for war injuries regardless of sex, and the appointment of women to responsible positions in Regional Commissions, the BBC, and the Civil Service, arguing that women are fully capable and equal partners in public and political life.

The TARGET records the withdrawal of a motion and the ordering of an Instruction explicitly to extend the Municipal franchise to women who would qualify but for their sex, reflecting support for women's political rights. The instruction was moved by Mr. Macaleese and accepted by the House, embodying a pro-women's suffrage outcome in the legislative process.

The speaker explicitly states he "was a believer in the universal franchise" and argues it is "illogical" that women can vote in local affairs but are deprived of the Parliamentary vote, directly endorsing women's right to the Parliamentary franchise. His opposition to the Bill is on grounds of complexity and fraud risk, not opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly and emphatically supports women's suffrage, including for married women, for both parliamentary and municipal purposes, and states they will oppose any bill that excludes married women. They argue strongly that married women must not be left out of the franchise and vow to continue pressing this amendment.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a Civil Defence conscription bill as it applies to conscientious objectors, attacking Labour members for hypocrisy regarding their wartime stances. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about; the brief reference to "the Noble Lady" (Miss Wilkinson) concerns her political consistency on pacifism and war, not women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Dr. Summerskill) explicitly argues that women are being treated as "cheap labour" with unjustly lower pay rates than men, invokes the Sex Disqualification Removal Act of 1919 as a marker of women's changed civic status, and praises the contributions of women in war roles — all framed as arguments for equal treatment and recognition of women as full civic participants. She supports women's equal standing in the workforce and implicitly in public life throughout.
