Mr. Scott explicitly argues that it is "unjust, unwise, and impolitic" to deny women the local government franchise, contending that women have a special interest in local government matters and that the anomaly of giving women the parliamentary vote while denying them the local government vote is irrational and must be corrected.

The speech focuses on policing in London, including crime prevention, neighbourhood watch schemes, police recruitment, and community relations. The only mention of women is a brief call for "clear representation of women in the force doing proper police work," which is a passing observation about police demographics rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly highlights that women with low-paid or no jobs lose their homes due to the two-year residence requirement, arguing the Government cannot intend to "throw on to the streets women who have devoted years of their lives to caring for others." This advocates for stronger protections for women as a class in their civic and housing rights, supporting their position against a policy that disproportionately harms them.

The speech concerns the wartime bill allowing Members of Parliament to hold offices under the Crown without disqualification, and the constitutional question of parliamentary representation. The mention of "men and women" among constituents is incidental; no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is focused on the fairness and mechanics of tenant ballot procedures in housing legislation, specifically criticising the restriction of votes to one per joint tenancy. While the speaker mentions whether husbands, wives, males, or females will be allocated the vote, this is a procedural argument about democratic fairness in housing ballots, not an argument about women's civic or political rights as a class.

The speaker (Pethick-Lawrence, Edinburgh East) explicitly references his past role fighting for women's enfranchisement with pride and frames equal treatment of women in wartime compensation as a natural extension of that cause, appealing to the Government to avoid a sex-based division. While his immediate concern is preventing a divisive vote, his framing firmly supports women's equal civic standing and their right to the same treatment as men.

The speech is entirely focused on the abortion debate (the Alton Bill), addressing conscience, late-term abortion limits, and women's bodily autonomy in reproductive decisions. It does not address women's political rights, the right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of civic/political participation as defined in scope.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Stanley Leighton, Shropshire, Oswestry) is entirely focused on ridiculing the Welsh Land Commission Report and opposing the Welsh Land Bill on agricultural and economic grounds. The single passing reference to "female suffrage" is a throwaway joke — if the hare's dual-sex nature applied to higher animals, it might justify Welsh differentiation "and perhaps in favour of female suffrage itself" — with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on abortion legislation — specifically the timing of abortions, NHS provision, and health authority duties — and does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. While it mentions women as a group affected by healthcare policy, it does not address their civic status, voting rights, right to stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Faithfull Begg, concluding his speech) explicitly argues there is "no valid argument against the principle of this Bill," dismisses the partisan vote-counting argument as "Krugerism," and appeals to Members to recognise "the inherent justice of the claim" for women's enfranchisement, urging them to pass the Second Reading.

The speaker accepts the committee's decision to grant women the franchise and focuses on critiquing the specific qualification criteria as inconsistent and inferior to men's franchise conditions, arguing women should have the same straightforward franchise as men (subject to the age-30 restriction). While not an enthusiastic advocate, the speaker explicitly accepts women's right to vote and argues for a cleaner, more equitable franchise mechanism.

The speech concerns wartime conscription of women for national service, not women's political rights. While the speaker briefly mentions the suffrage and parliamentary rights already granted to women as a background argument others might make, he does not argue for or against those rights — he treats them as settled facts and focuses entirely on the welfare conditions and necessity of female conscription under the wartime Bill.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage and the clause extending it, while objecting only to the age-30 restriction as too narrow — arguing that all women regardless of age should receive the vote. He advocates for broader enfranchisement, calling the exclusion of younger women "utterly unworthy of the country," and supports the clause as a practical step despite finding it inadequate.

The target speech concerns abortion law (the Alton Bill), arguing against reducing the 28-week upper time limit and warning of criminalising women. While it mentions women, the debate is about abortion policy, not women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns wartime labour conditions in Royal dockyards, including pay, dilution of labour, and trade union rules. While women workers are mentioned (their numbers increased from 400 to 3,300), they are referenced only as part of the wartime workforce expansion, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker (MR. ATHERLEY-JONES) actively argues in favour of women's enfranchisement, systematically rebutting objections such as undue influence, degradation, and unsexing, and drawing positive parallels with the working-class franchise to support granting women the vote.

The speaker seconds the motion for the Second Reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill, systematically refutes arguments against women's enfranchisement (the arms-bearing argument, indifference to the franchise, susceptibility to undue influence), and argues positively that women deserve the vote because they bear the burdens of war and taxation equally with men.

The speech is about wartime agricultural administration—food production, labour supply, machinery, and the organisation of the Board of Agriculture. The brief mention of recruiting women for agricultural work is purely practical (filling labour shortages) and makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on WWII strategy, the Atlantic Charter, war aims, peace settlement proposals, and post-war European federation. Women are not mentioned as a political class with distinctive civic rights anywhere in the speech, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech focuses entirely on immigration policy — specifically the "primary purpose rule" governing entry of foreign spouses of British citizens — and its racially discriminatory application. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns wartime manpower policy and the administrative arrangements for conscripting women into auxiliary services and directed employment — a wartime mobilisation measure, not a debate about women's civic rights or political representation. While women are singled out as a class, the discussion is about military service obligations and deferment procedures, not voting, standing for office, or political participation.

The speaker moves the Second Reading of a Women's Suffrage Bill, arguing extensively and enthusiastically in favour of extending the Parliamentary franchise to women, citing their property rights, tax obligations, educational achievements, civic participation, and colonial precedents as justifications, while dismissing all objections as lacking logical or just foundation.

The speech is primarily about naval policy, manpower, training, and the Mercantile Marine. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing, ironic jibe at Sir C. Dilke for having voted for Female Suffrage, used to score a debating point about stewardesses being British subjects—no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely focused on women's right to abortion and reproductive autonomy, not on women's political rights such as voting, standing for office, representation, or civic participation. While the speaker mentions women's campaigns and rights over their bodies, these refer exclusively to abortion rights, which fall outside the defined scope of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly identifies as "100 per cent. feminist" and argues that women should be allowed to serve in any capacity the government requires, including dangerous combatant roles, with no restrictions based on gender — opposing limits on women's service rather than opposing conscription. The speech advocates for women's full civic and military participation, equal treatment in compensation, and better utilization of women's capabilities.

The speaker argues at length in favour of women's suffrage, systematically rebutting objections (degradation, representation by male relatives) and contending that women's participation in elections and local government demonstrates their fitness for the parliamentary franchise, concluding that enfranchising women would uplift their condition morally, intellectually, and politically.

The speaker opposes giving votes to women during the War, arguing it breaks prior agreements and distracts from the war effort, and only concedes a narrow exception for women who served abroad — framing the broader enfranchisement as unjustified and an "outrage." The limited concession for women who served is not a substantive argument for women's political rights but rather a rhetorical contrast to reinforce his opposition to the Clause.

The speaker characterizes women's suffrage as a "tremendous" change and warns of its problematic consequences, including undermining imperial authority in India and enabling faggot votes. While acknowledging arguments in favour, the speaker treats the clause as an "illogical and unreasonable compromise" and clearly opposes extending women's suffrage, framing it as a wedge to be driven further—a concern, not an endorsement.

The target speech briefly mentions the ministerial group on women's issues and criticises Ms. Richardson's remarks, but does not make any argument for or against women's political rights. The references to women's issues are purely descriptive (defending the existence of a government committee) and do not constitute a substantive position on women's political rights or representation.

The target speaker (Mr. Radcliffe Cooke, moving rejection of the Bill) mocks an opponent's shifting positions on Women's Suffrage and uses that inconsistency to undermine the credibility of supporters of the movement, consistent with his overall opposition to Women's Suffrage as established in the context.

The target speech is entirely focused on the debate over capital punishment, arguing against reintroduction on grounds of executing innocents and lack of deterrent evidence. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker (Dr. Summerskill) explicitly and repeatedly argues that women should be included in the Home Guard on equal civic terms with men, contending that excluding them from service while conscripting them for gun sites is inconsistent and that women deserve the right and opportunity to participate fully in the national defence effort.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on capital punishment for murder, arguing for its reintroduction as a deterrent. It makes no mention of women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speech is a detailed War Office statement covering military medical services, typhoid inoculation statistics, women's employment in auxiliary and clerical roles, nursing, agriculture, and supply services during WWI. While women are mentioned in the context of wartime labour substitution and nursing, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for a "Queen's Speech for women" that would establish a Cabinet-level Ministry for women, strengthen equal pay and employment rights, and expand women's opportunities and power, directly arguing that women have "low incomes, few opportunities and little power" and that government resources should redress this imbalance.

The speaker (Mrs. Adamson, MP for Dartford) explicitly advocates for equal pay and equal rights for women workers, demands equality for women under the Personal Injuries Scheme, and argues that women Members of Parliament should vote against government regulations that fail to concede equality to women. She frames her arguments in terms of women's rights and equal treatment in public life.

The speaker (Mr. Radcliffe Cooke) explicitly argues that there is no sufficient genuine demand for Women's Suffrage among women, characterising the movement as artificially manufactured by a "stage army" of organisers, and uses financial and membership data to argue the cause lacks popular support, directly opposing the granting of women's suffrage.

The speaker (likely the Leader of the House) explicitly states "if women are going to be added, as I hope to see they will, to the register," expressing support for women's enfranchisement as part of the Electoral Reform Bill under discussion.

The target speech is primarily a winding-up address acknowledging the importance of the debate on women's war effort and touching on practical matters like women police and local government participation, but it does not make substantive arguments for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of women's participation in local government is descriptive and mildly critical of women's own inaction rather than arguing a position on their political rights.

The speech is primarily about wartime industrial mobilisation, manpower efficiency, and criticism of government production departments. The brief mention of "20,000 immobile women" who could be harnessed to the war effort treats women purely as a labour resource for war production, not as a class with distinctive civic or political rights, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker explicitly states he has "always been opposed to the extension of the franchise to women," yet then substantively argues that the War has changed his view and that women who participated in the war effort cannot be denied "a voice in the future policy of this country," representing a genuine shift to support. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides — prior opposition stated as a firm position, followed by substantive endorsement based on women's wartime contributions.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on administrative and financial arrangements for wartime pensions committees—specifically the allocation of expenses between the Treasury and local rates, the role of county councils, and committee representation. Women are briefly mentioned incidentally ("working men and working women") as committee members, but no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Radcliffe Cooke) moves rejection of the Women's Suffrage Bill and systematically argues against it throughout: dismissing the precedent of New Zealand and South Australia, citing the weakness and manufactured nature of the suffrage movement, quoting suffrage supporters' own admissions that most women don't care about the vote, and concluding that "the position of the movement in this country does not as yet warrant the introduction of any Bill of any sort or kind granting the Suffrage to Women."

The speaker (Mr. Radcliffe Cooke) explicitly argues that the women's suffrage movement lacks sufficient public support to warrant any bill granting women the vote, and further asserts it would be "unjust to grant Women's Suffrage," concluding that he is "a convinced opponent of this Measure" and would vote against it.

The speaker explicitly states he is "a convinced opponent of this Measure" regarding women's suffrage and declares he will vote against it, arguing that men do the physical and civic work of society and that women are not physically or intellectually equal to men in ways that would justify granting them the franchise.

The TARGET speech is entirely about women's health issues—maternity care, breast feeding, osteoporosis, cervical screening, and related NHS services—without making any argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Sir John Anderson) argues against compelling local authorities to employ women police, suggests women themselves are partly responsible for their underrepresentation in local government, and opposes appointing women as regional commissioners specifically to address women's issues — all positions that resist expanding women's formal political and civic roles. While he acknowledges women's contributions, his substantive arguments resist structural measures to advance women's political representation.

The speech concerns the administrative organisation of London War Pensions committees—whether the existing London committee or new Metropolitan borough committees should manage pensions work for soldiers and their dependants. While it mentions women as voluntary workers on these committees, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns wartime registration for employment/conscription arrangements for men and women of specific age classes, addressing whether university students will need to abandon their studies. While women are mentioned, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speaker (Labouchere) argues at length against the Women's Suffrage Bill, attacking its drafting as incoherent, mocking the proposal to give votes to married women, lunatics, and peeresses, and using procedural criticisms to undermine the entire measure's legitimacy as a reason to reject it.

The speech focuses entirely on health topics—vitamin D, rickets, eye care for elderly women, and partnerships between voluntary organisations and government—without making any argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

Miss Ward is pressing the Prime Minister to reconsider rejected requests made by women Members of Parliament, advocating for recognition of women MPs' essential work and pushing for a general policy response rather than departmental deflection. This implicitly supports women's political participation and representation.

The speaker (Member for Cumberland, Cockermouth) argues forcefully and unambiguously in favour of Women's Suffrage, contending that there is no valid reason—neither intellectual inferiority nor moral defect—to exclude women from the franchise, and that justice and consistency demand they be given the vote regardless of how they might use it.

The TARGET speech raises a procedural point of order about whether the Bill is properly drafted, citing as an example a prior ruling on an amendment to give votes to women — but this is merely used as a precedent to illustrate parliamentary procedure, not to argue for or against women's political rights. The speech does not take any substantive position on women's franchise or representation.

The speaker argues that legislation should be retained only where it genuinely protects women's health, not where it "simply discriminates against women because they are women," framing equal access to employment opportunities as the guiding principle — a position supportive of women's equal civic and occupational participation.

The speaker briefly but explicitly states that "every man—and if the franchise is to be extended to women, every man and every woman—has the right to say that the Government should immediately set up the machinery to consult it," endorsing women's inclusion in the extended franchise as a matter of right.

The speech is entirely focused on NHS funding, women's health services (cancer screening, maternity care, community care), workplace safety, and environmental issues. While it mentions women members of Parliament and women workers, it makes no arguments for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that if health and safety grounds do not justify excluding women from underground employment, there is no reason to deny women the same opportunities available to men, explicitly framing the removal of sex-discriminatory restrictions as a matter of equal civic and employment participation for women.

This lengthy speech by Mr. Fisher concerns the Board of Education Estimates for 1917-18, covering topics such as education funding, teacher salaries, military contributions, and educational reform. While it briefly mentions women teachers' salaries and female entrants to the teaching profession, it does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women who have received Poor Law relief should not be disqualified from the new women's franchise, stating it would be "very unfair" given changing social conditions and the War. This directly supports women's political rights by seeking to remove a barrier to their voting.

The speaker explicitly supports equal treatment and compensation for women, arguing that women are being denied equality with men in war-related injury compensation, and joins her colleagues in pressing the government to annul the discriminatory Regulations. She frames this as a matter of justice and civic equality for women who are being directed into dangerous war work.

The speaker (Mrs. Tate, Member for Frome) explicitly argues that women injured in war work should receive equal compensation to men, framing unequal treatment as a fundamental injustice and calling on the House to "do justice to women." She advocates for equal civic treatment of women as full citizens bearing the same wartime burdens as men, directly supporting women's equal standing in public life.

The speaker (Member for Dover) actively defends the Women's Suffrage Bill against its opponents, arguing that the House should be able to pronounce on whether women should remain under the disability of disenfranchisement, and that granting the franchise to women would reduce extremism just as previous franchise extensions had. He rebuts anti-suffrage arguments point by point, framing the Bill as a legitimate Reform measure.

The speech focuses entirely on Army administration issues: esprit de corps in Movement Control, security of military movements, officer appointments, and welfare/feeding of ATS personnel. The brief mention of ATS women's food quality and discipline codes concerns their welfare as service members, not their political rights or civic status, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech focuses on opposing the prolongation of Parliament's life and criticising British governance of Ireland. The single mention of women having votes for local bodies is a passing factual observation used to contrast the lack of justification for extending local councils' terms, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is about double standards regarding secret ballots in trade union disputes versus parliamentary voting procedures, with only an incidental mention of "a few women" as Whips twisting arms. This passing reference does not argue any position on women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports equal compensation for women workers regardless of sex, arguing against "sex differentiation" in injury compensation and stating he will vote in favour of the women Members' motion. He frames equal treatment as a matter of justice given women's equal contribution to the war effort.

The speaker (Mr. Labouchere/the Member for Northampton) consistently and emphatically opposes women's suffrage and political representation throughout, arguing that women are incapable of argument, emotionally unfit, do not want the vote, are physically unable to fulfil the duties of citizenship, and that Parliament would become an "epicene club" if women were admitted. While he notes some limited acceptance of women on local bodies like School Boards and Boards of Guardians, this is framed as a concession to their domestic expertise, not as support for political rights, and is explicitly contrasted with his opposition to parliamentary suffrage.

The speech concerns wartime transport ticket policies (workmen's tickets and their validity period) for fire watchers and ARP workers, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker explicitly invokes the Equal Opportunities Commission's position to argue that the Government should take the same approach to sex discrimination in employment as it does under the Race Relations Act 1976, advocating for stronger protections against discrimination against women and urging the Government to accept legislative changes accordingly.

Mr. H. Samuel explicitly argues that it is "very hard when the State acts in such a way as to deprive these women of the franchise," supporting removal of the Poor Law disqualification that prevents women (notably widows on relief) from voting. His speech advocates extending the franchise to those receiving Poor Law relief, including women, as a matter of fairness.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Employment Bill's clauses restricting trade union disciplinary powers, arguing they undermine democracy in industrial relations. The only mention of women is a passing historical reference to "the 70th anniversary of women over 30 having the vote," used rhetorically to argue the Government is poorly positioned to lecture the labour movement on democracy — no substantive argument about women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Member for Cambridge University) explicitly states he supports the Bill, systematically rebuts arguments against women's suffrage (capacity, inability to bear arms, emotional temperament, domestic sphere), and argues that women's suffrage is both just and expedient for the public interest. He concludes unambiguously: "he supported this Bill, not only because it was just, but also because he believed it to be expedient in the public interest."

Mr. Samuel explicitly raises the impact of the Poor Law disqualification amendment on women's franchise, arguing that a widow receiving Poor Law relief for her children would be denied a Parliamentary vote under the proposed wording, and urges the Government to ensure she is qualified for the Parliamentary franchise — a clear substantive argument in support of women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is a procedural ruling by the Chairman directing members to the appropriate clauses for various amendments (including those on women's qualifications). It makes no argument for or against women's political rights, merely organising the order of debate.

The speaker explicitly states he will "give my vote against this Bill" and argues that women's parliamentary suffrage would represent a "momentous" and dangerous constitutional change, that the majority of women do not desire the vote, and that such a fundamental reform should not be passed without government responsibility — all substantive arguments against granting women the Parliamentary franchise.

The speaker (Member for Bodmin) explicitly supports the women's suffrage Bill, arguing that opponents' fears about numerical superiority and societal upheaval are unfounded by analogy to past extensions of franchise to artisans, and dismisses Sir William Harcourt's procedural objections (that it must await a responsible Minister) as invalid given precedents with other franchise reforms.

The speaker acknowledges that the citizens drafting the Dublin Corporation Bill personally desired women's suffrage ("they might be very desirous for women's suffrage") but omitted it only to avoid making the Bill contentious and risking its defeat — expressing sympathy for women's suffrage while explaining a pragmatic procedural omission rather than opposing it substantively.

The speaker (The Chairman) explains procedurally that the proper place to raise equal franchise for women is via an Amendment to Clause 4, and explicitly frames the goal as making "the franchise for women the same as the franchise for men," thereby facilitating rather than obstructing the extension of equal political rights to women. The speech supports the substantive aim of equal franchise while directing it to the correct legislative mechanism.

The speaker (Lord Hugh Cecil, based on context) argues that the amendment is in order because it is the only appropriate place to raise the principle that women should receive the same franchise as men, actively advocating for equal political rights for women.

The speech is entirely about whether theatres and music halls should be permitted to open on Sundays during wartime; it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status of women.

The speech is entirely focused on local democracy, Conservative council policies in Bradford, poll tax, job cuts, and community services — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting rights, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker explicitly supports the principle of independent taxation that treats married women as equals rather than dependants, arguing they are entitled to privacy in financial affairs and that the system should recognise their full civic personhood. While criticising the Government's implementation as disproportionately benefiting the wealthy rather than providing truly independent taxation, the speaker frames these as objections to the specific mechanism, not to women's equal tax status, and urges amendments to remove the anomaly of husband-controlled allowances.

The speaker (Miss Nicholson/Miss Widdecombe area, responding to Ms. Mowlam) argues that the Finance Bill establishes basic rights for women — including the right to vote, work, marry, and independent taxation — and asks the opposing speaker to concede that this is "a major piece of social legislation giving us basic rights," clearly supporting women's civic and financial independence.

The speaker argues that the rule preventing married couples from being assessed separately for Income Tax is unjust, explicitly citing women's equal civic standing — "Women have every liberty, many of them are earning their livelihood, some of them are earning more than their husbands, they have the vote, and some of them are Ministers of the Crown" — as grounds for equal treatment in tax law. This constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's full civic and economic equality.

The speaker explicitly aligns himself with advocates of women's suffrage, calling it "so righteous a cause" and praising Mr. Johnston's "consistent labours" on its behalf, while only urging restraint on procedural/tactical grounds (not endangering the Dublin Bill) rather than opposing women's suffrage itself.

The Minister of Pensions (Sir Walter Womersley) refuses to revise the differential rates between men and women under the Personal Injuries (Civilians) Scheme, dismissing the protests and claiming no fresh arguments have been produced, effectively defending the unequal treatment of women in this civic compensation scheme.

The speaker (the Prime Minister) celebrates the 70th anniversary of Lady Astor taking her seat as the first woman MP, honours the suffragettes' work, and expresses pride in women's continued participation in Parliament — all affirming women's political representation and rights.

The speaker from Glasgow, Springburn explicitly argues that women performing the same duties as men deserve equal compensation and civic treatment, invoking equality as a matter of justice. He directly connects this to women's broader civic standing, referencing the old argument that women couldn't vote because they couldn't fight, and asserting that women are now in the front line, undermining that rationale.

The speech addresses procedural and technical aspects of voter qualification (British subject status and the age of 21), not women's political rights. While there is a passing reference to women's voting age being specified in the Act, no argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "He entirely agreed with the hon. Member on the general question of women's suffrage," expressing support for women's suffrage in principle, but substantively opposes the Instruction on the grounds that it is mandatory, unworkable due to lack of administrative machinery in Dublin, and will wreck the Bill for the third time — arguing instead for a general Act rather than piecemeal legislation. This constitutes genuine substantive argument on both sides: endorsing women's suffrage as a cause while opposing its implementation through this specific mechanism on substantive (not merely procedural) grounds relating to the practicality and effect of the Instruction.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. Hubert Duncombe, and then Mr. James Lowther in the concatenated speech) argues against adopting the Instruction to extend women's municipal franchise, warning it will risk the Bill's loss and objecting to introducing a "controversial and political matter like the franchise into a private Bill." Lowther explicitly frames women's enfranchisement as a wrong direction and urges the House not to follow the "mischievous precedent" of the previous year.

The speaker votes against the Instruction to extend women's municipal suffrage in Dublin, citing the Corporation's resolution opposing it, and questions why proponents did not raise the matter through proper Corporation channels — effectively opposing this extension of women's political rights in practice.

The speech is entirely focused on wartime hospital organisation, fracture treatment, orthopaedic centres, and the Emergency Hospital Service in England and Wales. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speaker personally declares support for women having votes for municipal purposes ("he was in favour of women having votes for municipal purposes"), but opposes taking action on this Bill because doing so would endanger it — a substantive concern grounded in the Bill's repeated failures. He also accuses the Member for South Belfast of using the women's suffrage question instrumentally to wreck the Bill, adding a substantive opposition to the specific mechanism being employed.

The speaker raises a procedural point about whether accepting the age-21 amendment would foreclose discussion of equalizing men's and women's voting ages, implicitly supporting the reduction of women's voting age from 30 to 21 (pro women's rights) while also contemplating increasing men's age to match women's 30-year threshold (which could be read as accepting the differential age restriction on women). The speech substantively engages with both sides of the age disparity between male and female voters.

The speech is entirely focused on wartime food supply, canteen provision for industrial workers (especially miners), and communal feeding initiatives. Although women are mentioned incidentally (women eating at a factory canteen, wives relieved of cooking burdens, women being trained for munitions work), no argument is made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The target speech mentions the suffragettes only in passing as one example among several historical democratic movements (Chartism, trade unionism), without making any argument for or against women's political rights. The core argument is about democratic rights being threatened by the poll tax and government manipulation of the franchise, not about women's political participation.

The speaker explicitly defends the proposal to extend women's municipal franchise to Ireland and argues that advocates of women's suffrage are entitled to use this procedural opportunity, framing the Parliamentary franchise for women as a legitimate and advancing political principle rather than a mere "fad."

The speech is primarily about childcare provision, nursery education funding, and day care regulation under the Children Bill. While the speaker briefly mentions "the changing role of women in our society," women's equal access to jobs, maternity leave, and women's inability to "play their full role in society" without childcare, these references frame childcare policy arguments rather than making substantive arguments for or against women's political rights or civic representation.

The TARGET speaker questions why women must wait until age thirty to vote while men receive the franchise at twenty-one, framing this age disparity as the issue to be raised and inviting the Government to justify it — but the speech does not advocate for women's suffrage; rather, it treats the age distinction as a procedural/constitutional anomaly worth probing, with the speaker declining to push an amendment and simply seeking a government explanation. However, reading the TARGET in context alongside Lord Cecil's speeches, the TARGET is questioning the discriminatory age gap without endorsing equal treatment, and notably the final interjection ("It is recommended by the Speaker's Conference") deflects any substantive defence of women's equal rights. The TARGET's thrust is critical of the unequal age standard without affirmatively endorsing women's equal political rights, making it closer to a procedural challenge than a genuine advocacy speech; nonetheless it implicitly treats the age disparity as unreasonable, leaning against the discriminatory restriction on women.

The speaker explicitly argues that men and women should be placed on the same basis for the franchise, stating "there is no reason which can hold water for one moment...why women and men should be put on a different basis in this matter," and further argues that if anything, women develop their full powers more rapidly than men, supporting equal political rights for women. The main thrust of the speech is about raising the voting age to 25 for both sexes equally, framing women's inclusion as part of a "general scheme of franchise for men and women."

The speaker explicitly states that "Following the precedent of the English Municipal law, the franchise was extended to women, and very properly in his opinion," directly endorsing women's municipal franchise rights.

The speech focuses on the Representation of the People (overseas voters) Bill and the poll tax's effect on electoral registration. The brief mention of 1918 (franchise for men) and 1928 (franchise for women) is purely historical context, not an argument about women's political rights.

Mr. Johnston explicitly supports the clause conferring the franchise on "duly qualified women," notes he carried the Instruction to the Committee that inserted it, points to Belfast as a positive example of women voting in municipal elections, and concludes the proposals are "fair and reasonable."

The speaker moves an amendment to grant women who have served abroad during the War the right to vote on the same terms as men, explicitly arguing that women who serve their country overseas "ought to have the vote on the same qualification as men." This is a clear, affirmative argument in support of women's political rights.

The speaker (Bevin) explicitly supports women's conscription into the Auxiliary Services under the National Service Act, argues for expanding women's managerial and supervisory opportunities, and states he believes women have never been given a fair opportunity in supervision and management. He supports women's civic participation and equal treatment with men in terms of conscientious objection rights and hardship tribunals, while the exemption of married women is framed as a practical wartime concession rather than a principled opposition to women's civic status.

The target speech (by Mr. Lees-Smith, continuing) addresses wartime conscription of both men and women for industrial and military service, reinstatement rights after the war, and the conscription of property and industry. While women are mentioned as subjects of wartime labour mobilisation, the speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation — it concerns wartime manpower/womanpower policy and post-war reinstatement, not civic participation or political rights.

The speech is overwhelmingly about Socialism versus capitalism, the poll tax, democratic participation, and the franchise broadly — not about women's political rights. The single mention of the Suffragettes is purely historical, noting they "continued the struggle to extend democracy" after the Chartists, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech focuses on the practical issue of providing adequate polling stations in remote constituencies to prevent voter disenfranchisement due to distance and harsh weather. While women voters are briefly mentioned in passing ("more especially since women as well as men are now on the voting list"), no argument is made for or against women's political rights — the mention is incidental to the broader point about accessibility for all voters.

The speaker explicitly states "Women have no vote" and "There are no women on the Legislative Council in most islands" as part of a list of injustices, and then advocates "on behalf of the women, who can do nothing for themselves" for democratic self-government to remedy these conditions, framing women's disenfranchisement as one of the wrongs requiring urgent reform.

The target speech is a lengthy argument by T. P. O'Connor about Irish Home Rule, the political reconciliation of England and Ireland, the Easter Rising, and the War effort — none of which addresses women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally ("violation of the homes of the people and of women who had retired from the struggles of life"), with no argument about their civic or political status.

The speaker moves an amendment to restrict women's occupation franchise by imposing a £10 minimum property value, arguing it is "an absurdity" that women would qualify on easier terms than men, effectively seeking to narrow the scope of women's voting rights under the Bill.

The speech is entirely focused on Northern Ireland's economic and social conditions—unemployment, poverty, health, housing, education, and industrial privatisation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "men, women and children" in a general reference to ordinary people, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker raises a point of order arguing that the Bill would disfranchise women ratepayers (along with lodgers and service voters) by transferring local governance to the City of London's Court of Common Council, which was elected by male occupiers only. He explicitly objects to this loss of franchise for women ratepayers as grounds for procedural challenge, thereby implicitly supporting their existing political rights.
The TARGET speech proposes extending the municipal franchise explicitly to women who would qualify but for their sex, demonstrating clear support for women's political rights at the local level.

The speaker (Mr. Fisher) defends the Bill's provisions allowing women to qualify for the local government register without the same £10 value requirement as men, arguing that the Speaker's Conference intentionally designed this rule to enable women to get on the register, and resists an amendment that would "evict women from ground which they would occupy" under the Bill. This clearly supports women's access to the franchise.

The speech is a lengthy debate on international development, debt relief, environmental policy, and the IMF/World Bank, with only a passing reference to women and children as beneficiaries of social programmes in developing countries. This mention does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on civil defence administration, regional organisation, ARP services, fire-fighting, and wartime governance structures. Women are mentioned only once in passing as part of the Civil Defence workforce ("grand men and women"), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on shipyard production, labour conditions, income tax on overtime, canteen provisions, and wartime industrial relations on Clydeside. Women are mentioned only in passing as part of "shipyard workers and their womenfolk and children" who suffered from yard closures, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker moves an amendment to ensure women who have passed equivalent university examinations receive the vote even if denied degrees by universities like Oxford and Cambridge solely on the basis of sex, explicitly arguing that Parliament should not allow university authorities to deprive women of the franchise they are entitled to. This is a clear and substantive argument in support of women's political rights (the parliamentary franchise).

The speaker announces a Defence Regulation explicitly extending equal voting rights to women serving in the Forces, ensuring they have the same Parliamentary election rights as men, including absent voter registration and eligibility for the electoral register.

The speech is a wide-ranging argument about constitutional reform, Crown prerogatives, civil liberties, and the inadequacy of a Bill of Rights. While the speaker briefly mentions women MPs and suffragettes as historical examples of rights won through struggle, these are passing illustrative references rather than arguments for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns opposition to a Bill proposing to extend the City of London's boundaries to include Southwark parishes, focusing on local government, rating burdens, and franchise changes. The brief mention of the "lodger, women, and service franchise voters" being disenfranchised under the Bill is incidental to the main argument about local governance and rates, with no substantive position argued on women's political rights as such.

The speech concerns fair employment legislation in Northern Ireland focused on religious/community equality between Catholics and Protestants, not women's political rights. The incidental phrase "best man or woman for the job" is a neutral reference to equal employment opportunity in general, not an argument about women's civic or political status.

The speaker approvingly cites Asquith's argument that Parliament should build a representative electoral basis, and notes with approval that Lloyd George translated this into the revolutionary wartime reform that gave women the franchise — describing it as "probably the most controversial issue regarding the character of the electorate that has been made during the last century" without any criticism. The speaker also highlights that young men and women reaching voting age are being disenfranchised, implying concern for full democratic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on children's education, the half-time system, teacher superannuation, school attendance, and educational reform. Women are mentioned only incidentally as teachers alongside men, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speaker presents a petition explicitly calling for the extension of the Parliamentary Franchise to women and urging the House to affirm women's right to citizenship by passing the relevant Bill, thereby advocating for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly seeks to compel the Dublin Corporation to extend the municipal franchise to qualified women, and conditions his support for the Dublin Corporation Bill on receiving assurance that women's suffrage at the municipal level will be included.

The speech is entirely about the proposed closure of Barrow in Furness Crown Court, arguing against it on grounds of access to justice, costs, and community convenience. While it briefly mentions jury service disenfranchisement and quotes the Women's Institutes on local justice, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports granting women the university franchise on equal terms with men, calling the denial of votes based on university degrees "a very great unfairness" and "a serious anomaly," and expresses approval of the government's sympathetic direction on the matter.

The speech focuses on electoral representation and franchise reform during wartime, specifically addressing disfranchised groups such as factory workers, Armed Forces, evacuees, and young people under 24. While it touches on voting rights broadly, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation specifically.

The TARGET speaker proposes an amendment to extend the university franchise to women who passed qualifying examinations even if Oxford or Cambridge refuses to grant them degrees, explicitly arguing these women are "worthy of the vote" and expressing "hearty sympathy" with giving them the franchise. While he declines the specific amendment on procedural grounds (it goes beyond the Speaker's Conference recommendation and poses drafting difficulties), he firmly supports the underlying goal of ensuring Oxford and Cambridge women receive the vote, promising to pursue the matter further.

The speaker moves an amendment explicitly to grant women who served in the War outside the UK the local government vote, arguing it is unjust that conscientious objectors receive the franchise while these women who served voluntarily have "no voice in the destinies of their country at all." This is a clear and substantive argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speech is primarily a critique of the Security Service Bill and the concept of parliamentary democracy, Crown prerogative, and state secrecy. The brief mention of Asquith opposing votes for women is used only as a historical illustration of how "parliamentary democracy" has been invoked to defend the status quo, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about child care registration, regulation, and local authority review duties under a Children Bill. While it briefly mentions that child care is "the most important issue to women between 20 and 35" and references helping women return to work, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation; these are incidental mentions in a policy speech about child welfare provision.

The speaker explicitly supports the Amendment to extend local government voting rights to married women, arguing that since married women have already been granted the Parliamentary franchise, there is no good reason to deny them the local government vote — directly endorsing women's political rights and representation.

The speech addresses colonial policy matters including savings in Antigua and St. Lucia and the conditions of women engaged in coal bunkering as a labour/welfare concern, but makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech announces the composition and terms of reference of a welfare committee for the Women's Services (WRNS, ATS, WAAF), focusing on amenities and living conditions. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation; the mention of women's roles is purely administrative and military welfare in nature.

The TARGET speech pivots entirely to condemning an IRA terrorist act and its impact on a specific woman and child, making no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The reference to "representation of the interests of the women of Northern Ireland" is rhetorical framing for an anti-terrorism statement, not an argument about women's political rights.

The target speech addresses NHS contract negotiations and women doctors' professional concerns (deterring women doctors from partnerships, payment structures), not women's political rights or civic representation. The mention of women doctors relates to medical profession access and remuneration, not voting, office-holding, or other political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that women in the West Indies should be given political power ("especially if they gave them political power instead of leaving them voteless") and questions why no women are nominated to executive councils in the West Indies, directly advocating for women's political representation and the franchise.

The speaker opposes the Amendment that would extend the local government franchise to married women, arguing the reasons given are insufficient to overturn the unanimous Speaker's Conference recommendation, and dismisses the urgency of the demand. The speech supports the status quo that restricts women's local franchise rights.

The speech concerns Welsh representation on wartime committees and advisory bodies, and mentions Welsh men and women only in the context of Welsh regional representation — it makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation as a distinct class.

The TARGET speech is a wide-ranging contribution to the Debate on the Address covering the Egyptian/North African campaigns, Allied strategy, the Prime Minister's leadership, post-war reconstruction, and education reform. While the speaker briefly mentions that a wartime electoral reform bill extended the franchise to women, this is cited only as a historical precedent for passing legislation during wartime, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Radcliffe Cooke) argues at length that because men built, maintained, and defended civilisation and the state, Parliament should be governed by men, and that women's sphere of work has "no direct relation" to the principal functions of the House — explicitly opposing women's suffrage on the grounds of sex difference.

The speech concerns the liberty of the Press, Defence Regulations, and the warning to the "Daily Mirror," with a brief passing reference to "millions of our young men and women" having their liberties curtailed — this is about wartime conscription and civil liberties broadly, not about women's political rights or representation. No argument for or against women's civic/political status is made.

The speech concerns NHS funding and health service management in the West Midlands, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of a "Birmingham women's hospital" refers to a healthcare facility, not to women's civic status.

The speech is primarily about employment training policy, youth training schemes, and workforce development. While the speaker briefly mentions that married women face discrimination in accessing childcare allowances under employment training, this is a welfare/employment policy argument about equal treatment in benefits access, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (from Northampton) explicitly opposes women's suffrage throughout, invoking John Knox's "monstrous regimen of women," expressing regret for previously voting in favour, declaring he has made it his "special duty" to prevent women having votes, dismissing women as unfit for political participation, and arguing that the "vast majority of women" do not want the vote and are not fitted to govern.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the local government vote to married working-class women, arguing they are well qualified, have made great sacrifices, and that denying them this right would be a great injustice and disappointment. The speech advocates strongly for the Amendment granting married women the local government franchise.

The speaker (Member for Southampton) explicitly opposes the Bill, arguing that women gaining the vote would inevitably lead to women sitting in Parliament ("the end of this country would not be far off"), that it would create faggot votes benefiting wealthy men, and urges the House to "defeat this most unwise and pernicious Bill by a very large majority."

The speech is entirely focused on NHS funding, hospital bed closures, maternity care deficiencies, and opposition to Conservative health service reforms. Women are mentioned only incidentally as patients in labour requiring intensive care cots, not as a class with distinctive civic or political rights.

The speaker explicitly states he changed his vote from supporting women's suffrage to opposing it, arguing that the majority of women do not want the franchise, that women prefer indirect influence to direct political power, and that granting the franchise would be "mischievous to the country, mischievous to the sex it was proposed to emancipate, and mischievous to the interests of the world at large." His brief mention of supporting women serving on Boards of Guardians is a concession about local matters explicitly distinguished from the Parliamentary franchise he opposes.

The speaker (the Chair) is explaining procedural rulings on why two Instructions are out of order under Standing Order No. 51 — not arguing for or against women's political rights. The mention of "women's votes" is purely in the context of explaining why an Instruction is procedurally invalid (it could be addressed via Amendment), not to advocate any position on women's suffrage.

The speaker (Member for South Belfast) explicitly moves an Instruction to extend the municipal franchise to qualified women in Dublin, arguing it is unjust that Dublin women are deprived of a right already enjoyed by women in Blackrock, Kingstown, Belfast, England, and Scotland.

The speaker (Ms. Richardson, Barking) argues forcefully that married women are being unlawfully discriminated against by being denied child care allowances for employment training, cites the industrial tribunal decision upholding that claim, and calls on the Government to extend the scheme to married women — explicitly supporting equal civic participation and employment rights for women as a class.

The target speech is primarily procedural and descriptive in nature—the speaker notes that the Government has left the matter to the House, observes that women ratepayers already benefit from franchise extensions in the Bill, and comments on the scope of the Amendment (married women only) and the conduct of the debate, including a characterization of a colleague's remarks about a women's organisation. The speaker does not argue for or against extending the local government franchise to married women; they neither endorse nor oppose the Amendment on its merits.

The speaker from Walsall explicitly supports the Instruction to extend the municipal franchise to women in Dublin, arguing that the House represents the whole country and that Dublin women deserve the same municipal advantages as qualified women in Great Britain, Kingstown, and Belfast. He dismisses fears that the Instruction would wreck the Bill and cordially declares he will support the Instruction.

The speaker (Dublin Co., S.) explicitly supports the Instruction to confer the municipal franchise on qualified women, dismissing objections about administrative difficulty as mere assertion, and states he would vote for it if the mover pressed a division.

The speaker explicitly states they would "most cordially support" an amendment to place women local government electors on the same footing as Parliamentary electors, expressing genuine support for women's political rights. Their reluctance to support the current Amendment is a procedural/consistency objection (it would grant local government franchise on grounds not matching Parliamentary franchise criteria), not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports the Amendment to grant married women the municipal vote, citing both constituent pressure and his personal experience on a municipal Child Welfare Committee where married women served competently, arguing their participation is valuable and justified.

The speaker expresses genuine support for women's participation in public affairs ("ardent and earnest desire to enlist the co-operation of all the women in the conduct of public affairs") and acknowledges women's special interest in local government matters, but substantively opposes this specific Amendment extending the local government franchise to married women, arguing it creates an anomaly relative to the Parliamentary franchise and that women's ability to stand for election on local bodies already addresses the substantive concern. This is not merely a procedural objection — the speaker makes a principled argument against extending the local government vote while the Parliamentary vote remains restricted, constituting substantive opposition to this aspect of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about the NHS GP contract debate, covering immunisation targets, capitation fees, preventive medicine, and related health policy. The brief mention of giving women doctors the opportunity of part-time work is a healthcare employment matter, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the administrative handling of letters written by women detained under Defence Regulation 18B to their MPs, specifically explaining the delay in posting circular communications. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I am entirely in favour of the suggestion" regarding giving married women the municipal vote, argues that married women are most affected by municipal matters and deserve to have their voices heard, and urges the Home Secretary to accept the Amendment. His only hesitation is procedural—concern about endangering the Bill's passage—not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker (Member for Wallsend) explicitly advocates for women's inclusion in policy planning at the highest levels ("associate women with them on the top level"), calls for expanding women's consultative committees across government departments, and argues that greater use of women's expertise would have improved governance. She affirms women's right and capacity to participate fully in public and political life.

The speaker (Dr. Summerskill, West Fulham) explicitly argues that women with relevant expertise are being excluded from executive and advisory positions in favour of men who lack knowledge of women's issues, demands that women be properly represented on reconstruction and policy committees, and argues that women should be allowed to serve in the Home Guard alongside men. These are substantive arguments for women's equal political participation and representation in public life.

The speaker explicitly expresses regret that the Women's Franchise clause was removed from the Bill, indicating support for women's franchise. He declines to press the matter further only due to a practical necessity (Dublin's water supply), not because he opposes the clause.

The speech focuses entirely on educational policy—school meals, continuation schools, adult education, teacher training, and raising the school leaving age—without making any argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" as future teachers or professionals is incidental and does not address women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker is making a procedural/administrative observation about requisition forms needing to be updated if women are given qualifications under the proposed bill, without arguing for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses almost entirely on wartime public health issues: nursery provision for children of working mothers, adolescent health, tuberculosis rates in Wales, and the depletion of medical staff. While it briefly acknowledges that women volunteer for industry, it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is a procedural response acknowledging a legal question about women in the Services voting as absent voters, without arguing for or against women's political rights. The speaker neither endorses nor opposes the right, merely noting it is under legal consideration.

The speaker explicitly argues in favour of extending childcare/training support to married women (not just lone parents), expressing frustration that a court win by Mrs. Jackson would apply only to her individually, and urges colleagues to vote against the Lords amendment on the grounds that married women deserve equal access to the benefit now.

The speaker explicitly appeals for the Home Secretary to grant married women the municipal vote, arguing it is illogical to give them the Parliamentary franchise while denying them the local government vote, and that married women are especially affected by and entitled to vote on matters like sanitation, education, housing, and child welfare handled by local authorities.

The opening speaker raises a concern about the municipal vote extension by distinguishing it from the Parliamentary vote (noting a married man would gain two votes), suggesting hesitation about the Amendment's terms — a substantive objection to one aspect of women's political rights. However, Mr. C. Rees (also in the TARGET) explicitly supports women having both the Parliamentary vote at thirty and the local government vote on the same terms, endorsing women's political rights. Together the TARGET contains substantive argument on both sides of extending women's franchise to the municipal level.

The speech is entirely focused on broadcasting policy, media regulation, quality standards for television franchises, and crime statistics — none of which touch on women's political rights or representation. Women are not singled out as a class with respect to civic participation anywhere in the speech.

The speaker (Mr. Rees) explicitly supports the Amendment to extend the municipal vote to women, arguing that having already secured the Parliamentary vote, women should logically also receive the municipal franchise, and urges that "the quicker it is done the better" to avoid further agitation.

The speech is primarily about overseas voters' rights and the Representation of the People Bill, with only a brief passing reference to women's suffrage struggles as historical context to argue for valuing the vote generally. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is primarily about UK overseas development assistance policy, arguing for increased aid targeted at the poorest countries. While it briefly mentions women in the context of agricultural roles in Africa and proposes a women's unit within the ODA to account for women's views and needs in aid delivery, these references concern women's welfare and development roles rather than their civic/political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Northern Ireland governance, direct rule, security, economic policy, and the Anglo-Irish Agreement. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation; the only passing mention of a woman is a reference to Ms. Mowlam as an adviser on education policy, which does not engage with women's civic status.

The TARGET speech (combining Morton's remarks on public buildings and Bowles's remarks on parliamentary accommodation) focuses primarily on architectural aesthetics and building design. Bowles's brief mention of "a candidate for women's suffrage" is a passing, incidental joke about corridor access to the smoking-room, not an argument for or against women's political rights. The discussion of ladies' gallery accommodation concerns visitor comfort, not women's civic or political participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the public health case for implementing Regulation 33B to combat venereal disease during wartime, drawing on the speaker's medical experience. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about the inequity of franchise extension under an Irish local government bill, focusing on the disparity between England and Ireland. While women are briefly mentioned as being excluded from town commissionerships under the Act of 1854, this is raised as one of several anomalies (alongside peers) to illustrate the bill's absurdity, not as a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about British Army training, land requirements, housing for service personnel, and recruitment/retention challenges. The brief mention of "womanpower" and "the wider role of women in the armed forces" is a passing acknowledgement in response to a colleague's remark, without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states regret at having previously voted against appointing women police officers and now advocates strongly for compulsory directions to appoint women police, citing the effective work of women police in the WAARFs, ATS, and WRNS as evidence supporting their expanded role in public service.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the municipal/local government vote to women alongside the Parliamentary vote, arguing it would be absurd to grant women the Parliamentary franchise while denying them the municipal vote, and endorses the Amendment to secure women's municipal voting rights. The speech argues substantively in favour of women's political rights throughout.

The speech concerns the financial provisions of an Irish Local Government Bill, specifically whether an agricultural grant to Irish landlords should be permanent or limited to five years, as in England. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech concerns the Women's Land Army's working conditions, sickness pay, and a benevolent fund — practical employment and welfare matters. While it involves women as a group, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker criticises the Government for failing to genuinely advance women's rights—abolishing maternity grants, refusing maternity leave, lacking childcare provision, ignoring equal pay and part-time workers' rights—while arguing these reforms are necessary. She supports substantive improvements to women's employment and political/civic standing, framing the Bill as a cynical façade that masks continued discrimination against women rather than a real advance for them.

The speech is entirely focused on the case for Irish Home Rule and national self-government, debating the positions of Unionist and Liberal parties on that question. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief, passing reference to the Derby programme's inclusion of "Parliamentary franchise to be extended to women" as one item among many electoral reforms, with no argument made for or against it.

The speaker asks whether women will be qualified to serve as representatives on County and District Councils under the Irish Local Government Bill, and if not, whether the Attorney General will propose a clause to confer that right upon women — explicitly advocating for women's eligibility to hold elected office.

The target speech is primarily about whether soldiers and sailors should receive the franchise at age 19 rather than 21. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief reference to the age of 30 fixed for women's franchise, cited purely as a point of comparison to argue against creating multiple different voting ages — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly commends the Bill's provisions extending equal opportunities for women, welcoming them as opening up employment opportunities that don't currently exist, while opposing other parts of the Bill unrelated to women's political rights.

The speaker (Mrs. Tate, Member for Frome) moves an amendment demanding that civilian women receive equal war injury compensation to men, arguing extensively that the unequal scheme is unjust given women pay equal taxation, perform equal civic duties, and suffer equal injuries — explicitly framing equal treatment as a matter of justice and women's equal civic standing.

The speech is primarily about whether to reduce the tobacco duty or the tea duty, and fiscal policy regarding the National Debt. The passing mention that "the interests of the women ought surely to have been considered" refers to women as consumers of tea, not to their political rights or civic participation.

The speaker supports women's political and workplace rights throughout, criticising the Government for only minimally implementing EC directives on sex discrimination, opposing positive discrimination amendments being rejected, and condemning clause 7 (women in pits) as a cynical move that exposes women to poor conditions rather than genuine equality. The speech consistently advocates for stronger protections and equal opportunities for women.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on the question of lowering the voting age for soldiers from 21 to 19, with only a passing reference to women's franchise age being fixed at 30 as a factual comparison point. No argument is made for or against women's political rights; the mention of women is incidental to the debate about male soldiers' voting age.

The speech is an administrative reply about staffing proportions in the Dublin Telegraph Office, explaining why women receive fewer superior appointments based on operational factors (night duties, technical work). It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Dr. Summerskill, West Fulham) explicitly seconds an Amendment demanding equal compensation for injured civilian women, argues forcefully that women deserve equal treatment to men, endorses equal pay as a welcome "repercussion," and calls the government's unequal treatment of women unjust and exploitative.

The TARGET speech is a personal explanation by Sir F. Banbury correcting a mischaracterization of his voting positions on the age qualification for men's franchise. While it briefly mentions "the question of women," it does so only in passing to clarify his own consistency on voting age thresholds, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses on the fairness and practical difficulties of extending the franchise to men under 21 on active service, arguing to keep the Bill as it stands per the Speaker's Conference. While it briefly notes that women up to age 31 would also be excluded under the Amendment, this is raised as an incidental fairness concern about the Amendment's scope, not as a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that the Bill's removal of protections for women (e.g., night work requirements, allowing women in mines) is an attack on women rather than a genuine extension of rights, stating "to translate working in the most harrowing and awful conditions in pits as some sort of gain is to treat women with contempt and disdain." This opposes the specific deregulatory measures affecting women's working conditions, framing them as harmful rather than liberating.

The speaker explicitly argues in favour of women's right to be elected to county councils, moving an amendment to remove their disqualification and stating that "the electors should have a free choice as to the persons whom they desire to see representing them" — directly supporting women's political representation on local bodies.

The speaker explicitly states "I am not in favour of the franchise for women—I am against it," while his amendment and argumentation are aimed at maintaining consistency in restricting women's votes (keeping the age-30 threshold rather than inadvertently allowing women of 21 to vote), reinforcing opposition to women's suffrage as a whole.

The speaker explicitly supports the Amendment calling for equal compensation for women's war injuries, arguing that women's lives are equally valuable to men's and that the principle of equality between men and women should be accepted now. He advocates for equal treatment of women in civic and industrial life, including equal pay for equal work, framing these as matters of justice and women's full civic participation.

The speech is a procedural parliamentary question about voter registration mechanics under the Local Government Bill, specifically about how lists are to be arranged by poor law electoral divisions. Women occupiers are mentioned only incidentally as part of a "local government supplement," with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The Member for Lewes explicitly opposes the Amendment for equal compensation for women, dismisses the arguments as "feminist special pleading," urges women not to "ask for too much," argues women already have advantages over men under the law, and concludes that "women already have the power to vote men down and rule the country" but "I sincerely hope that they will pause before they start another campaign and will leave government now to men" — a direct argument against women's civic equality and political participation.

The target speech raises a procedural question about whether the clause would extend the number of women electors and how the conditions affect soldiers' wives, but makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The Chairman's dismissive reply reinforces that the question was not pursued as an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker (Member for Thornbury) explicitly and repeatedly advocates for equal compensation for women injured in air raids, arguing that the Government has provided no justification for treating women differently from men, and calls on the Government to "give justice to these women." He supports equal pay for women doing the same work as men and urges the House to act immediately rather than defer to a Select Committee that would delay relief for injured women.

Sir F. Banbury argues that the word "person" in the clause covers both men and women, and that therefore women should be entitled to be put on the register and have the vote under this section.
