He explicitly questions why women should not have the vote under this provision and moves amendments to ensure they are included.

The target speech focuses on the debate over extending voting rights to soldiers and sailors under age 21, addressing practical and principled objections to lowering the franchise age. While women are briefly mentioned in passing ("accentuating the case as regards women who will not be allowed to vote"), no substantive argument is made for or against women's political rights; the mention is incidental to the speaker's main argument about age thresholds for male servicemen.

The speech is primarily about Northern Ireland's economic, health, and education spending. The brief mention of women teachers' pension contributions being treated differently from men's concerns an employment/pensions equity issue, not women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is a procedural explanation about electoral registration mechanics under the Registration Act and Local Government Bill, mentioning "women voters" only incidentally as a category on the local government supplement list. No argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker strongly supports the Amendment for equal compensation between men and women for war injuries, explicitly calls the Government's opposition an "injustice," praises the female Mover of the Amendment, argues that equal pay and equal compensation for women are incentives not deterrents, and declares he will vote in the Lobby in support of the Amendment regardless of political consequences.

The speech is entirely focused on the fish-curing industry and exemptions under the Factory Acts, arguing for maintaining exemptions for the herring trade. While women workers are mentioned as participants in the industry, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Wallasey) explicitly and passionately advocates for equal compensation for women injured in air raids, urging fellow Members to vote for the Amendment and framing it as a matter of justice and equality. The speech consistently supports women's equal civic standing, arguing that women who share the same dangers as men deserve equal treatment.

The speaker argues that soldiers' wives should not lose their Parliamentary vote due to their husbands' military service, calling it "obviously undesirable" and urging the Home Secretary to find a legislative remedy. This directly supports preserving women's voting rights.

The speech addresses poll tax/community charge issues including women's refuges, but the argument about women's refuges concerns tax liability and financial hardship under the community charge system — not women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned as a vulnerable group facing double taxation, not in the context of their political rights or status.

The speech is entirely about consumer protection policy — establishing a consumers' interests authority, product guarantees, and redress mechanisms. The brief mention of "the rights of women" is a passing rhetorical flourish listing various rights in society, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is about community charge/poll tax arrangements, water rates, and administrative matters. The brief mention of women's refuges concerns their tax/rating classification under the community charge system, not women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing tax relief for private medical insurance under clause 51 of the Finance Bill and advocating for NHS funding, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women injured during wartime activities deserve equal compensation to men, contending that physical disfigurement harms women's life prospects more severely and that justice demands equal treatment. He presses the Government to accept the principle of equal compensation and criticises delays through inquiry committees, making a clear substantive case in favour of equal civic/economic rights for women.

The speaker explicitly agrees it is a hardship that a woman should lose her Parliamentary vote because her husband is at war, and urges the Home Secretary to introduce provisions to protect women's franchise in this situation, supporting the preservation and proper functioning of women's political rights.

The target speech addresses the availability of qualified dispensers in the RAF and a specific poisoning incident, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as members of the Women's Auxiliary Air Force in a professional/military capacity context unrelated to political rights.

The speaker briefly but explicitly invokes women's political rights in support of his broader argument, praising "working-class women at the cotton mills in Lancashire" who "broke the class laws of the 19th century to give women the right to vote," framing their suffrage struggle as a heroic precedent for resisting the poll tax. He also notes that women earn less than men but must pay the same poll tax, highlighting their disadvantaged civic position.

The speech is entirely focused on challenging the use of section 42 national security certificates in Northern Ireland employment discrimination cases and the lack of appeal mechanisms — a matter of fair employment and natural justice. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "adult men and women deprived of jobs") without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for preserving women's right to serve as poor law guardians in Ireland, warning that a single-member district arrangement would effectively exclude women from these boards, and urges the Committee to ensure the Bill does not "disfranchise the women who now sit and work so well upon these boards."

The speaker explicitly moves an amendment to allow two members to be elected to district councils specifically to preserve the ability to elect women as district councillors and guardians, arguing that women's participation in poor law administration in Ireland works well and should not be eliminated.

The speech is a parliamentary reply about staffing arrangements for female postal supervisors and telegraphists in the Dublin office, addressing workplace management and organizational concerns. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker supports the Amendment and accepts women's Parliamentary franchise as a given ("I take it for granted that women's suffrage is passed"), focusing on ensuring it is applied consistently across Scotland and England. There is no opposition to women's political rights, only procedural concern about how the franchise should be structured in Scotland relative to England.

The speaker explicitly states that the franchise for election to local government bodies in Ireland will be "the Parliamentary franchise with the addition of peers and women," thereby extending voting rights in local elections to women. He describes this as following Scottish and English precedents and frames it positively as securing simplicity and economy, expressing no reservation about women's inclusion.

The TARGET speech concerns equal compensation for civilian war injuries between men and women, not women's political rights such as voting, standing for office, or political representation. While the speaker (Miss Ward of Wallsend) is a woman MP advocating for equal treatment of women, the substance of the debate is about a wartime injury compensation scheme, which is an economic/welfare policy matter, not a matter of women's civic participation or political rights.

The speaker (Secretary for Scotland) commits to preserving the Scottish local government franchise while explicitly ensuring that the women's Parliamentary franchise will rest on "precisely the same basis in Scotland as in England," thereby affirming the extension of women's suffrage to Scotland on equal terms rather than allowing it to be undermined by franchise differences.

The speech is entirely focused on Army pay, allowances, and conditions for soldiers and junior officers, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of a "junior female clerk" is used purely as a wage comparison to illustrate the soldier's relative underpayment, not to argue any position on women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker is questioning the Secretary for Scotland on the technical mechanism by which women's franchise in Scotland will be placed on the same basis as in England, implicitly accepting and supporting the principle of equal women's Parliamentary franchise across both countries. The question presupposes and endorses the goal of ensuring women's suffrage applies consistently in Scotland as in England.

The target speech (a government reply) commits to amending the law to ensure women members of the Forces have the same voting registration facilities as men, framing it as a matter requiring urgent resolution. This explicitly supports equal voting rights for women in the military.

The speaker explicitly argues that women are underrepresented in public appointments and on boards of nationalised/privatised industries, presents statistics to demonstrate this deficit, and calls for women's representation to reflect their share of the population and their experience in the voluntary sector. She directly advocates for women to be allowed to use voluntary sector experience to progress to public appointments and political life.

The speaker explicitly criticizes the Bill for giving 6,000,000 women the vote, calling it "a most controversial question," while contrasting this unfavorably with the failure to properly enfranchise soldiers and sailors. He frames women's enfranchisement as an unjust provision given to those "who would not go and defend their country," clearly opposing women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that women must be allowed to progress to public appointments and political life, criticises the low percentage of women in public appointments and Parliament (only 41 female MPs out of 650), and calls on the Government to improve women's representation to reflect their numbers and potential.

The speech is entirely focused on wartime pensions, the Royal Warrant, and the treatment of servicemen and their dependants (widows, parents, apprentices). While women are mentioned incidentally as service members or dependants, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Allen) explicitly argues for the appointment of a woman inspector in the Potteries district, contending that women workers suffering from lead poisoning need a female inspector to whom they can describe their condition, thereby advocating for women's fuller participation in public/civic roles and workplace protection structures. This directly supports women's public role in inspection and implicitly affirms women's distinct civic standing.

The speech is primarily about the Keith committee's Inland Revenue reforms, tax inspector staffing, and enforcement powers. The brief mention of recruiting and retaining women tax inspectors is a practical workforce observation about flexibility and childcare, not an argument about women's civic or political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that Parliament should reflect a cross-section of society and that underrepresented groups—including women—should represent themselves, stating "about eight times as many women should be here" and supporting positive action to increase minority and women's representation in political institutions.

The speaker explicitly states support for adult suffrage (including women's suffrage implied by "adult"), saying "I am in favour of adult suffrage," and briefly acknowledges that "you have women's suffrage in parochial affairs" without opposing it, while arguing for a simple uniform franchise as the proper remedy for electoral anomalies.

The speech focuses entirely on bus privatisation, employee buy-outs, shipyard negotiations, and Caledonian MacBrayne ferry services in Scotland. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status.

The speech is primarily concerned with why Scotland is being treated differently from England and Wales regarding local government franchise, focusing on procedural and constitutional grievances about differential treatment. While women's voting rights are mentioned briefly in passing ("Apparently the reason of all this alteration is that women may get the vote"), the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights, merely noting it as the apparent reason for the clause's structure.

The speech is delivered by the Minister of Pensions and focuses almost entirely on explaining the administrative details and compensation rates under the Civilian Injuries Scheme (gainfully employed, Civil Defence workers, non-gainfully employed). While the debate context concerns equal compensation for women, the TARGET speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation; it addresses equal compensation for civilian war injuries, which is a social welfare/economic matter rather than a question of women's civic status or political participation.

The speech is primarily about a by-election in Pontypridd, the weather, inflation, young voters, and political party matters. The brief mention of "the women" is a passing reference to a prior speaker's interjection about who might be affected by bad weather on polling day, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker supports expanding the local government franchise by accepting amendments to enfranchise tenants of unfurnished rooms (including those previously excluded as "lodgers"), explicitly aiming for uniformity and broader inclusion in the municipal franchise in line with the Speaker's Conference recommendations. The speech argues in favour of extending political participation rights to a wider class of occupiers.

The speech focuses entirely on wartime pensions, service allowances, and the War Service Grants Committee, with no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "we women can fight for ourselves so long as we are not in the Services" is a passing rhetorical comparison to illustrate the helplessness of servicemen, not an argument about women's civic or political status.

The speaker explicitly states "I am myself in favour of the extension of the suffrage to women," directly endorsing women's political rights. He also argues that opposing this franchise extension bill would not advance the cause of female suffrage, urging a fellow supporter of female suffrage to vote for the bill instead of opposing it.

The speech is primarily about Northern Ireland legislation regarding declarations/oaths for councillors and the Sinn Fein question. The brief remark about women ("There are no hon. Ladies present. It is disgraceful that we do not have sufficient women in this place") is a passing observation without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on wartime propaganda, the BBC, the Political Warfare Executive, and British information services abroad. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is entirely focused on restoring the Service Franchise to men (police, shop assistants, grooms, etc.) who lost it through a court decision; women's political rights are mentioned only in a single passing remark that female suffrage is not the subject of this Bill and would be a separate matter for the future, with no argument made for or against it.

The speech is primarily concerned with preventing "faggot voting" (bogus voters) in local government elections by ensuring bona fide occupancy qualifications, and addresses drafting concerns about the Bill's joint tenancy provisions. While women are briefly mentioned in the context of the 30-year age qualification and the women's franchise, no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made — the speaker treats the women's franchise as an incidental example of why the register must be properly structured, not as a subject of advocacy.

The speech argues against piecemeal franchise/registration reform and advocates for a comprehensive general measure enfranchising "every grown man," but makes no reference to women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) explicitly invokes her personal history fighting for women's suffrage and "women's citizenship," lamenting that a women's suffrage bill was talked out as a joke, and argues that "victory is completely won" is a mistaken assumption — signaling ongoing advocacy for women's political rights and full civic participation.

The speaker (Plymouth, Sutton) explicitly advocates for women's admission to the Foreign and Diplomatic Services, arguing that the Foreign Office's refusal to admit women reflects an outdated "pre-1914 view," recounting the history of women's exclusion from public life, and criticising the Labour party for allowing this discrimination to continue without protest. The speech consistently and substantively supports women's equal participation in these public roles.

The speaker explicitly argues against women's eligibility to sit on London councils, stating that "the majority of London Members are against the inclusion of women" and that "an overwhelming majority of Members think the inclusion of women will go very far to stultify the legislation." He supports recommitting the Bill specifically to reverse the decision admitting women to councils.

The speaker explicitly acknowledges that the Bill gives women the Parliamentary vote and engages substantively with the mechanics of that franchise, expressing concern about faggot voting that could inflate women's Parliamentary votes via land qualifications. While the speech is primarily procedural (proposing a £5 minimum land value), the speaker accepts women's enfranchisement as a given and seeks to regulate rather than oppose it, indicating support for women's political rights.

The speaker argues against the Amendment restricting the lodger franchise to unfurnished lodgings, explicitly stating it is "absolutely illogical and quite contrary to the Bill and to the Resolution of the Speaker's Conference," and declares support for those who divide against the restrictive Amendment — thereby supporting the broader Parliamentary and municipal franchise for women as enacted in the Bill.

The speech is a procedural point of order regarding parliamentary procedure around a private Member's Bill (an abortion bill by Miss Widdecombe). While it mentions women Members' voting patterns as a rhetorical point about representation, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation — the subject matter is abortion legislation and parliamentary procedure, not women's civic participation or franchise.

The speaker argues that women on average produce less work than men and therefore should generally be paid less, dismisses equal pay arguments as "sentimental," and asserts that 25 years of women's suffrage has made no difference to income equality — implying the vote is irrelevant to women's economic status. While he praises the work of two women MPs, this is a compliment to individuals rather than a substantive argument for women's political rights, and his overall thrust is to oppose the equal pay case and downplay the significance of women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the local government franchise to furnished lodgers, argues against disfranchising tens of thousands of existing voters, and states he wants to go further than the Government's compromise to give lodgers the same local government franchise as Parliamentary franchise — clearly advocating for broader political participation rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that women are under-represented in Parliament partly because creches are not available, implying structural reform is needed to support women's political participation. This constitutes a brief but substantive argument in favour of women's political representation.

The speech is focused on the Fair Employment (Northern Ireland) Bill concerning religious discrimination in employment. The brief mention of women's underrepresentation in Parliament is used as an illustrative analogy to explain the concept of discrimination generally, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about fair employment legislation in Northern Ireland concerning religious discrimination between Catholics and Protestants. References to women are incidental and technical — noting that certain affirmative action measures for women (under sex discrimination law) might be inadvertently rendered unlawful by the Bill's religious discrimination provisions — without making any substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns updating the Daventry electoral register and enfranchising young people (men and women aged 21–25) who have come of age since 1939, but this is a general franchise/registration issue not specifically about women's political rights. Women are mentioned only incidentally alongside men as part of the broader argument about disenfranchised youth and war workers, with no distinctive argument about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the merits and technicalities of a Bill concerning the Service franchise (cubicle partitions and servants' residential qualifications for voting). While women are briefly mentioned in passing — a member stating he wants women to have votes before anyone else does — the TARGET speaker dismisses this as an unhelpful debating tactic without making any substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker (Dr. Edith Summerskill) explicitly argues that depriving British women of their nationality upon marriage to an alien is an injustice and an anachronism, invoking the Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act 1919 and women's equal citizenship rights, and calls on the Government to remedy the denial of women's civil rights through new legislation.

The TARGET speech focuses on a procedural debate about a land value qualification amendment (whether land must be worth at least £5 to count as a franchise qualification) and concerns about faggot/plural votes. While women's Parliamentary vote is briefly mentioned as a downstream consequence, the speech makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights — it is concerned with the mechanics of plural voting and the adequacy of the Government's response to the Amendment.

The speaker strongly supports women serving on local administrative bodies (school boards, boards of guardians, urban/district councils, London vestries) but explicitly and emphatically opposes women becoming mayors, magistrates, or Members of Parliament, stating it is his "firm and unalterable determination" to oppose women in Parliament and calling their presence there "intolerable." This constitutes substantive argument on both sides of women's political rights.

The speech is focused on the technical concern about "faggot voters" being created through the franchise qualification clause, particularly regarding middle-class voters being improperly registered. While it briefly references the 6,000,000 women who would gain the franchise under the Bill, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights — it is concerned solely with preventing electoral manipulation through fraudulent voter registration.

The speech is entirely about wartime electoral registration machinery — updating voter rolls, registration procedures, and parliamentary writs — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The only passing reference to women is a brief, neutral mention of "men and women in the Armed Forces" and "the best man or woman will win," neither of which constitutes an argument about women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports women's right to hold public office (as rate collectors), arguing that Ireland has led the way in "women's enfranchisement," that women who pay rates should be able to collect them, that the Chief Secretary's blocking of Miss Magill's appointment is "absolutely disgraceful," and even expressing support for women entering Parliament ("let ladies come in here and try their hand at law-making").

The target speeches are entirely focused on budget finance — the Sinking Fund, taxation, national debt, stamp duties, and expenditure — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The single passing mention of "female suffrage" by Mr. Gibson Bowles is a throwaway rhetorical flourish characterising the Chancellor as a sober financier who doesn't believe in bimetallism or female suffrage, with no argument advanced for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about practical voting access for women in the Richmond, Yorks constituency (car ownership, weather conditions) in the context of a by-election debate, not about women's political rights or representation as a matter of civic status. The mention of "women voters" is incidental to a logistical argument about voter turnout, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

Miss Ward's question explicitly advocates for greater women's representation on the Industrial Health Advisory Committee, arguing that women's participation is inadequate and pressing the Minister to take steps to include more women in specific capacities. This is a direct argument in support of women's political/civic representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that there are "not enough women Members of Parliament" and that women's considerations are neglected as a result, directly endorsing greater women's political representation. She also raises the issue of women's ability to access polls, framing it as a matter of women's civic participation that must be taken seriously.

The target speech focuses on the residential status of an SLD female candidate relative to the constituency boundary, as a tactical point in the debate about the Richmond by-election writ. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

Near the end of the speech, the speaker explicitly states "I want women to have votes," directly endorsing women's suffrage. The rest of the speech concerns proportional representation, but this clear affirmative statement on women's political rights warrants a "for" classification.

The speaker supports women remaining on borough councils (opposing the Amendment that would remove them) and favours extending the Parliamentary franchise to women, but explicitly and substantively opposes women sitting in Parliament ("a state of things which, personally, I should regard as absolutely intolerable"), making genuine arguments on both sides of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker criticises the Bill's franchise provisions as benefiting the Radical party at the expense of Conservative-leaning ratepayers, and explicitly notes that the local government vote was extended as "the only way" to enfranchise women — treating this as a partisan manoeuvre rather than a principled reform, implying opposition to that extension. However, the speech's primary focus is on rate-paying as a condition of the franchise rather than on women's political rights per se, and the reference to women is fleeting and instrumental rather than a sustained argument against their enfranchisement.

The speech is entirely concerned with negotiations between the Minister of Health and the medical profession over a proposed national health service scheme, including issues of local authority control, doctors' salaries, and medical certification. Women are not singled out as a class with respect to political rights or civic participation; the brief mention of "men and women" refers to local authority personnel ignorant of medical matters, not to women's political rights.

The speaker expresses genuine support for appointing women to special diplomatic posts and acknowledges their value in certain diplomatic roles, while substantively opposing women entering the Foreign Service on equal terms with men, citing marriage, nationality, and the biological "fact" of marriage as insurmountable barriers. This represents substantive argument on both sides: endorsing women in select diplomatic roles while opposing their full equality of entry.

The speaker explicitly argues that the "female electorate" in Richmond would be disadvantaged by an early election and criticizes the House's general failure to consider women's interests, noting that the male-dominated chamber struggles to see matters "through our eyes." This is a substantive argument for giving weight to women's political participation and interests in electoral procedures.

The speaker argues that including women in borough councils by direct election would make the Act "absolutely ridiculous," systematically rebuts the main arguments for women's inclusion, and concludes by urging the Committee to vote against direct election of women. While he concedes women might be co-opted onto committees, this is a fallback position to limit their role, not a substantive endorsement of women's political rights.

The speaker raises a question about the voting eligibility of women from Eire who are working in Britain, but this is framed as a question about the residency/nationality provisions of the Bill rather than as an argument about women's political rights or representation as a class. The speech does not advocate for or against women's right to vote on the basis of their being women.

Courtney supports women's eligibility as councillors and aldermen, arguing from experience that women have proved their usefulness and should not be disqualified. However, he explicitly endorses a substantive reason why women should not be eligible as mayors (because a mayor is a justice of the peace with different functions), making a genuine argument against one aspect of women's political participation while supporting another.

The speaker (Mr. Chamberlain) explicitly states he objects to "the extension of the franchise for the first time to women," describing it as something he disagrees with while acknowledging it is a minority view in the House. He frames women's enfranchisement as one of the provisions he opposes in the Bill, indicating a stance against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely concerned with technical distinctions between lodger and occupier franchise qualifications for male workers (service employees, shopkeepers' assistants, grooms, etc.), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "full-grown men and women" is incidental to a point about the independence of certain lodgers, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly states her concern is "for women in general in the constituency and the attitude that the House shows to women," criticizes male MPs for ignoring women's views, and frames her procedural argument as protecting "the interests of women voters." She also notes the underrepresentation of women in the House as a disadvantage for considering women's interests.

The speaker criticises the Government for cutting women workers' rights (maternity pay, return-to-work rights, child care), argues that proper child care and equal career opportunities are necessary for women's full participation in the labour market, and attacks the Bill's token gestures (allowing women down mines) as inadequate substitutes for genuine equal opportunities — all of which constitute substantive advocacy for women's employment and civic rights.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely focused on opposing proportional representation on grounds of electoral complexity, cost, party machine control, and constituency trust. The one brief mention of "women's franchise" appears only as a passing reference to increased electorate size as a cost factor, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily an argument against proportional representation on practical grounds (complexity for new voters, expense, polling time, need for strong majorities). Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the new electorate ("so many thousands of new electors, including women") and as an example of voters who might rush to the polls, without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about WWII military matters, Army morale, North Africa operations, and soldiers' allowances. The brief mention of the ATS (Auxiliary Territorial Service) women praising their service and noting they are not formally counted in the Estimates is a comment on military recognition and administrative procedure, not an argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech (comprising Sir Lewis McIver's remarks and Mr. W. H. Holland's response) is entirely focused on the debate over sugar countervailing duties, Free Trade principles, and India's fiscal policy. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation anywhere in the text.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely focused on opposing proportional representation, arguing it is premature and dangerous to attach to the franchise reform bill. The brief mention of "an enormous women's vote" is purely descriptive, noting it as one of the changes being introduced, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mayo, E.) explicitly supports women's eligibility to serve on the new municipal bodies, criticises the Government's undermining of that cause, and argues that denying women this right will strengthen the case for extending the parliamentary franchise to women. He endorses women's political participation in municipal offices and frames the exclusion as unjust, making a clear positive argument for women's political rights.

The speech focuses on wartime policy, Fascism, social reform (Beveridge), education, mining, rehabilitation of veterans, and equal pay for work — but the equal pay argument is framed as economic fairness for workers, not as a claim about women's political rights or civic participation. There is no argument made for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of political representation.

The speaker (Ms. Richardson) consistently advocates for stronger anti-discrimination protections for women, criticises the Government for not going far enough in repealing the Sex Discrimination Act's restrictive provisions, welcomes positive discrimination measures for women in academia, and calls for better conditions to enable women to work in mines and other non-traditional roles — all substantively supporting women's equal civic and employment participation.

The speaker explicitly criticises the Employment Bill for failing to tackle women's low pay, under-representation in the workforce and decision-making, and discrimination, arguing it "will disadvantage women" and that a decent government would have used it to address these inequalities. This constitutes a substantive argument in support of women's political and civic rights.

The speech focuses on facilitating voting logistics (long working hours, travel burdens) for all registered voters, mentioning both men and women equally. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights specifically — the concern is purely about practical electoral machinery under wartime conditions.

The speech concerns the Boer War, war financing, the future settlement of the Transvaal under the British flag, and the rights of the Dutch population in the Transvaal. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on procedural and substantive arguments about whether conscientious objectors should be disfranchised under the Representation of the People Bill, specifically criticising the consistency of the Home Secretary's position and the form of the Amendment. Women's political rights are mentioned only in passing (the "Women's Local Government Vote Amendment") as a contrast to the current Amendment, without any argument for or against women's political rights being advanced.

The speech is focused on the merits of a local veto/temperance licensing bill in Scotland, debating public house control, compensation, and popular will. The mention of "female voters" is a passing empirical observation about how women voted in a local poll, not an argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on a Poor Law reform bill concerning cottage homes for the aged poor, discussing administrative machinery, costs, and parish council authority. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker (Mr. Labouchere) explicitly opposes giving women the same political rights as men, arguing that such proposals are historically unprecedented and absurd, objecting to women sitting on municipal councils, and warning against the incremental strategy of expanding women's roles from councillors to aldermen to MPs. He votes with the Lords to remove the clause granting women seats on municipalities.

The TARGET speech is primarily about the procedural handling of an amendment to disfranchise conscientious objectors, not about women's political rights. While the speaker briefly mentions the "women's municipal vote" as a precedent for allowing a free vote, this is only a passing reference with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on supporting a catering industry wages/labour regulation Bill, discussing working conditions, trade union organisation, and employers' practices. The brief mention of "working men and women" voting for Conservative Members and a passing remark about "the noble Lady" not going into the smoking room do not constitute arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the poll tax's effect on electoral registration, arguing that it is causing people to disappear from the electoral register and undermining the franchise broadly. Women are not mentioned or singled out as a class; the argument concerns universal civic participation without reference to women's distinctive political rights or representation.

The TARGET speaker criticises the Government for voting down amendments that would have exempted women (and pensioners) from the football membership card requirement, arguing that Parliament's attempt to write in those exemptions was wrongly defeated at the Minister's instigation. This implicitly supports the civic/political principle of distinguishing women as a group deserving an exemption, framing the rejection of the amendment as a failure by the Government.

The speech is entirely about passive smoking and the rights of non-smokers to avoid tobacco smoke in public places. The brief mention of suffragettes is used only as an analogy about forced ingestion, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns opposition to the poll tax, focusing on financial burdens, civil liberties, and poverty. While it briefly mentions disenfranchisement as one concern among many, it does not make any substantive argument specifically about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for equal pay for women in the Services and industries ("the Government would have set a fine example if they had recognised the rate for the job and given equality to the women"), argues for equality during demobilisation, and supports women's continued access to professions and industry after the war. These are substantive arguments in favour of women's economic and civic equality.

The speaker (Viscountess Astor) explicitly and repeatedly advocates for women's equal participation in public life, demanding that the government treat women as "equal citizens," appoint more women to planning committees, open the Foreign and Diplomatic Services to women, and warning that excluding qualified women from public roles is "a positive danger to the country." She challenges the Labour party to prove its stated belief in equality and urges action before a "sex war" becomes necessary.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on the procedural question of whether elections should be held on one or two days, addressing arguments about police, presiding officers, ballot boxes, plural voters, and motor cars. The brief mention of women voting at municipal elections is only a passing reference to a prior amendment that passed without opposition, used as an analogy for unanimity, not as an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is almost entirely about the technical and financial workings of the National Health Insurance Act — contributions, sinking funds, society valuations, and administrative simplification. The brief mentions of "married women's sickness benefit" and a "women's equalisation fund" relate to insurance benefit adjustments for women as insured persons, not to women's civic/political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on a procedural amendment about whether borough and county elections should be held on one day or two separate days, addressing logistical concerns like polling staff, postal services, and ballot boxes. Women's political rights are mentioned only fleetingly and in passing (noting that women are to receive the vote will add to the difficulty of holding elections on one day), without any argument for or against those rights.

The speech is primarily about reforming the constitution of the City of London in the context of a London government bill. The only mention of women is a brief, incidental remark that councillors in the new boroughs "would be elected on a simple franchise, and women would be eligible for office in the manner provided under the Bill" — this is a factual observation about an existing provision, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on veterans' pensions, appeal tribunals, and the British Legion, with only a brief complimentary remark about Lady Apsley's maiden speech. This passing tribute makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns War Office staffing recommendations for military and civilian establishments, including the use of ATS (Auxiliary Territorial Service) personnel in administrative roles. While women (ATS officers) are mentioned in a military staffing context, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is about televising Parliament and its effects on political representation of third parties and backbenchers. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing historical reference to "the debates on votes for women" as an example of past reforms that were feared but ultimately beneficial — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Miss Ward) explicitly argues that women should be allowed "full citizenship" rights, equal participation in national affairs and reconstruction, and that positions should be filled by "the best person, irrespective of sex." She directly challenges the government's policy of "sex differentiation" and advocates for women's equal civic and political participation.

The speech concerns the financial mechanics of the National Insurance Act — adjustments to women's and men's benefit funds, sinking funds, contingency funds, and society pooling arrangements. While it mentions "women's sickness" and "married women's pregnancy sickness" as actuarial categories requiring financial correction, it makes no argument about women's political rights, franchise, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (the First Lord of the Treasury, responding to Sir J. Blundell Maple) confirms that women will definitely have votes and be eligible to sit on the council under the Bill, affirming women's political rights at the local government level, while leaving open only the question of whether they can serve as aldermen or mayors.

Mr. Faithfull Begg explicitly protests against the Government's action in removing the opportunity to debate "the Electoral Disabilities of Women," indicating support for bringing forward that question and thus for women's political rights.

Colonel Hughes explicitly acknowledges "women voters" as a class whose convenience matters in election scheduling, treating their participation as a legitimate concern worth accommodating — implicitly affirming their right to vote and participate in elections.

Miss Rathbone (Combined English Universities) pushes back against medical arguments used to oppose the compulsory registration/call-up of women aged 45–51, arguing that Dr. Thomas "greatly over-stated his case" about the health risks of that life stage. By countering the medical objections to mobilising older women for war service, she implicitly supports women's civic participation and the legitimacy of the registration scheme, consistent with her longstanding pro-women's-rights position.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely concerned with the technicalities of the Representation of the People Bill — specifically dual voting qualifications, constituency definitions from Mr. Speaker's Conference, and the business/residential franchise for men. The brief mention of 5,000,000 women is incidental, used as a rhetorical counterargument against a procedural point, without the speaker arguing for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns procedural matters around a parliamentary adjournment motion, national unity, and the discussion of grievances related to calling up elderly women under what appears to be a wartime labour conscription scheme. While it mentions "elderly women" being called up, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on European federalism, sovereignty, economic and monetary union, and democratic accountability in the context of the European Community — there is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speech is primarily about the difficulty of regulating outside organisations' spending and interference in elections (Clause 28 of an election reform bill). The brief mention of women concerns their role as informal advocates for the local government franchise — used as an illustrative example of why the proposed amendment would be unenforceable — not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about universal franchise being undermined by the poll tax, electoral registration, and Northern Ireland/Gulf issues. The brief mention of suffragettes achieving the vote for women is a historical reference used to illustrate the broader principle of universal franchise, not an argument for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speech focuses on poll tax-driven disenfranchisement and electoral register losses affecting the general population, invoking the Chartists and suffragettes only as historical precedents for defending universal franchise. Women are not singled out as a class with distinctive political rights; the argument is about civic participation broadly, not women's political rights specifically.

The speech is primarily concerned with equalizing lodger voter qualifications across Scottish districts and reducing registration costs. The mention of married women being placed on the register is a passing reference used as an incidental supporting argument, not a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on the technical and administrative details of the pay-as-you-earn Income Tax scheme, including separate assessment of husband and wife for tax purposes, Schedule E payers, and Treasury revenue calculations. While it briefly mentions married women's employment and the separate assessment of spouses, this is framed purely as a tax administration matter, not as an argument about women's civic or political rights or representation.

The speaker raises the question of whether women will have votes, be eligible as councillors, aldermen, or mayors under the new London government bill, explicitly pressing the government for a definitive answer on women's civic status — showing awareness of and interest in their political rights. However, the speech does not clearly advocate for or against women holding these offices; it mainly complains about the bill's ambiguity on the point. The follow-up context confirms the speaker presses for women's inclusion as voters and council members, but the TARGET itself neither endorses nor opposes women's political participation substantively — it treats the matter primarily as an unresolved drafting question. Given the speech is overwhelmingly about London local government structure with only a brief, procedural mention of women's eligibility without taking a clear stance for or against, this is best classified as irrelevant to women's political rights as an argued position.

The speech is focused on a procedural amendment regarding the duties of county secretaries and administrative officers under a registration bill. While it briefly mentions the extension of the franchise to women as a reason for increased workload, it does not argue for or against women's political rights — it simply treats that extension as an established fact and addresses the administrative consequences.

The target speech is primarily a technical/drafting amendment dealing with local government franchise qualifications for men and women in Scotland, focused on property and lodger qualification thresholds (£10 vs £5). The women's franchise provisions mentioned are described as exactly reproducing existing Bill proposals, and the debate is about property valuation thresholds and drafting clarity, not about whether women should have political rights.

The speech is primarily about a public inquiry into police conduct during a violent demonstration and the legitimacy of peaceful protest. The brief mention of suffragettes is used only as a historical example of conscientious objection, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states he has consistently opposed women's political rights, having voted against women's Parliamentary franchise and voted three times against women serving as councillors or aldermen. He aligns his views entirely with the mover of the motion to re-commit the Bill (which aims to reverse the inclusion of women on councils), and expresses willingness to vote against women's inclusion if the issue could be "fairly raised."

The speech is about supporting the Second Reading of a Bill to prolong Parliament's life and concerns about servicemen and women abroad being unable to vote in the next general election. While women are briefly mentioned alongside men as members of the Fighting Forces, no argument is made about women's political rights as a distinct class; the speech does not address women's suffrage, representation, or civic status.

The speaker explicitly protests against the Local Government Board's order disqualifying women as women from positions under local bodies, arguing that "it should not be within the power of anybody except Parliament to disqualify women as women" and calling this a "monstrous policy," thereby supporting women's right to hold public office.

The speech is concerned with administrative drafting questions about the duties of local government officers under registration rules, not with arguing for or against women's political rights. The extension of the franchise to women is mentioned only incidentally as context for new administrative duties, with no argument made about whether women should or should not have political rights.

The speech is entirely about juvenile court procedure, a specific criminal case (Craddock), and an inquiry into magistrates' conduct — none of which concerns women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as juvenile court volunteers ("Many men and women...rendering most valuable public service"), without any argument about their civic status.

The speech concerns the mechanics of voter registration and voting methods (postal vs. proxy voting, business premises votes, service voters abroad) under a wartime electoral registration bill. Women are not singled out as a class for distinctive civic rights or duties, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The target speech is about public order, violence at demonstrations, and selective law-breaking, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of suffragettes is used only to dismiss a parallel drawn by the previous speaker, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states he has voted against women serving on councils, in the House of Commons, and against women having votes at all, and intends to continue doing so. He argues that women belong in their "right place" (not in politics), dismisses women who engage in politics, and concludes that "men, and men only" should sit in the important councils of the nation.

The TARGET speech (by Bonar Law) is primarily concerned with justifying the Government's decision to allow a free vote on disfranchising conscientious objectors, and with the merits of that disfranchisement question. Women's political rights are only briefly mentioned as an analogy to explain why the Government felt it could depart from the Speaker's Conference recommendations on this matter, without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is primarily about whether conscientious objectors should be disfranchised, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of women's voting ("after what we have done in regard to the women's vote") is only a passing procedural reference used to justify leaving the conscientious objector question to a free vote of the House, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech argues against disfranchising people who have been imprisoned or in lunatic asylums, framing the issue in terms of general civic rights for "men and women" without singling out women's political rights as a distinct cause. The brief mention of "men and women" imprisoned for debt is incidental to the main argument about the legal principle that punishment is purged by imprisonment, not an argument about women's distinctive civic status.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly opposes women serving as councillors, aldermen, or mayors, dismisses women on vestries as "failures" and "nonentities," argues women are unqualified for most council duties, and warns that admitting women to borough councils would inevitably lead to the Parliamentary franchise and seats in the House of Commons — all of which he opposes.

The speech is primarily about trade union rights for military personnel and opposition to the Gulf War. The mention of "service women" is incidental — they are grouped with "service men" as a class of military personnel, with no argument made about women's distinctive civic status or political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on electoral registration problems caused by the poll tax and fraudulent overseas voter registration, arguing for a universal franchise in general terms. While it briefly mentions that franchise rights were historically extended "first to all men, and then to all women," this is a passing historical reference without any argument about women's political rights specifically.

The speech is entirely focused on UK and NATO defence policy, nuclear deterrence, arms reductions, and procurement decisions. The brief incidental mentions of "service men and women" and "making men and women redundant" are passing references with no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women should not be allowed to sit on the new borough councils because they are not adapted to the work, which is too political in nature; he also warns that allowing women on these councils would lead to them claiming the Parliamentary franchise and seats in the House, which he presents as undesirable outcomes.

The speech is a ministerial response focused on family policy, marriage, social security, child welfare, and Conservative philosophy — none of which argues for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of increased female participation in the workforce is descriptive and economic, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech addresses the war against Japan, demobilisation challenges, post-war reconstruction, compulsory military service, and the psychological approach to the Far East campaign. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "the necessary men or women for the extra teachers we shall require"), without any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely about the Government's procedural approach to the Representation of the People Bill, specifically regarding the alternative vote and other electoral reforms. Women are mentioned only in passing as one of several "majority recommendation" items left to the free judgment of the House, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker proposes reducing Oxford and Cambridge's parliamentary representation from two members to one unless those universities grant degrees to women, explicitly framing this as "pressure" to secure women's political rights. The speaker also invites the Home Secretary to introduce amendments giving votes to women who have passed qualifying examinations at those universities, demonstrating active support for women's political participation.

The speaker (Sir C. Dilke) argues strongly that women have already proven themselves as district councillors exercising sanitary powers, that Parliament should extend to London the same eligibility it granted rural districts, and that under the Bill's current form women are eligible not only as councillors but also as mayor and aldermen — consistently advocating for women's right to hold public office.

The speaker explicitly supports the Amendment to allow women to serve on borough councils, stating they will vote for it on grounds of both democratic choice and "humanity," and expresses sincere hope that women will be elected and will do "good and serviceable work."

The speech addresses the business vote and plural voting arrangements in wartime electoral registration, specifically the unintended doubling of the business vote when extended to women. While women are mentioned, the speaker is not arguing for or against women's political rights but rather addressing an administrative anomaly in voting mechanics, deferring the matter to a Speaker's Conference.

The speaker (Mr. Pethick-Lawrence) explicitly references his past work with women seeking the vote and argues that the current tax system places women in an unfair, humiliating status relative to their husbands — calling the old treatment of women as "chattels" unjust and urging post-war reform to make taxation equitable and non-derogatory to either spouse. This reflects support for women's equal civic and legal standing, though the immediate objection to the Clause is procedural/practical rather than principled opposition.

The target speech is primarily about poll tax issues and police pay regulations. The brief opening mention of the retirement age debate (agreeing it needs attention) does not argue a position on women's political rights — it simply endorses the need for government action on a pension/retirement age question, which is a social policy matter not framed in terms of women's civic participation or political rights.

Sir G. Cave expresses personal sympathy for granting degrees to women and acknowledges that representations would be made to the universities, while declining the Amendment only on procedural/scope grounds (it is "not within the purpose of this Bill"). He does not oppose women's political rights substantively, and the context makes clear the Amendment concerns giving women who pass qualifying examinations the university vote.

The speech is entirely focused on old age pension policy, the means test, class inequity in public spending, and criticism of the Old Age Pensions Bill. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "women who have given 50 years of devoted service to the home") without any argument about their political rights or civic status.

The speech focuses on opposing a new clause related to kerb crawling legislation and arguing for stronger anti-kerb crawling laws to protect women from street harassment. While the speaker references women's rights to walk safely, this is about criminal law and public safety policy, not women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on dog registration and control legislation, mentioning women only incidentally (e.g., postwomen being attacked by dogs, women writing letters about dog fouling). There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker supports women's participation in municipal/local council work (opposing the amendment to exclude them) while explicitly opposing the extension of the Parliamentary franchise to women and their presence in the House of Commons, framing his opposition to women's suffrage as the best way to prevent female MPs.

The speaker expresses that if starting afresh he would have preferred women not be eligible (against), but opposes the Amendment that would remove women already serving effectively as councillors (for), while also distinguishing between councillors/aldermen and mayors, suggesting women should not qualify as mayor — making substantive arguments on both sides.

The speaker (Viscountess Astor) explicitly argues that women have been given subordinate positions in government and that "the country has suffered" as a result, criticises the underrepresentation of women on government committees, and asserts that women deserve equal participation in political and public life — directly supporting women's political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for defending women's rights, criticizing the Government for failing to protect women from harassment and rape in marriage, and urging action to make rape in marriage illegal — all positions supporting women's civic and legal protections as a class.

The speaker explicitly raises concern that adopting the Amendment might raise the value threshold for lodgers' local government franchise, warning that "a great number of persons, especially women, will fail to get that particular franchise" — thus arguing in favour of protecting women's access to the vote.

The speaker supports an amendment that would pressure Oxford and Cambridge to include women (who pass qualifying examinations but are denied degrees on the basis of sex) in their university electoral rolls, explicitly endorsing the argument that denying women the university vote because of a sex-based restriction on degrees is unjust and anomalous.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the Jewish refugee crisis, the Holocaust, Jewish settlement in Palestine, and British wartime policy toward refugees — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men, women and children" willing to fight Rommel is incidental and does not address women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly states "If there is one thing in my political life that I have stood for firmly it is for the equality of the sexes" and "I am in favour of the general principle of equal pay for equal work," while also citing his role in passing the Matrimonial Causes Act 1923 as evidence of his commitment to sex equality. He argues that the principle of equal pay should be adopted as national policy and that there is no valid argument against it.

The speaker explicitly opposes women's parliamentary franchise ("he held very strongly to the view that the Parliamentary franchise should not be granted to women") while simultaneously supporting their participation in local public service roles such as school boards and sanitary work, arguing they are "admirably qualified" for such duties.

The speech focuses on electoral reform, parliamentary representation, proportional representation, and redistribution of constituencies. The brief reference to the extension of the franchise to women is a historical aside praising a past Speaker's Conference reform, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (identified as Earl of Fife from the TARGET, though the following speeches attribute similar words to Mr. Asquith) notes agreement with the First Lord on women's parliamentary franchise while simultaneously highlighting the contradiction of supporting the franchise but opposing women sitting in the House—implicitly endorsing both the franchise extension argument and the "horror" at women as parliamentary colleagues, suggesting a nuanced position that touches both sides. However, reading carefully, the TARGET speaker is recording an opponent's contradictory position (supporting franchise but opposing membership in the House) and taking a note "for further use," without clearly declaring their own stance on either question—yet the framing suggests sympathy with opposing women in Parliament while the franchise question remains unresolved between them.

The speech is entirely focused on the poll tax (community charge), poll tax capping, local authority spending, grant allocations, and public services. Women are not singled out as a class with respect to any civic or political rights, and there is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on childcare policy, funding priorities, and partnership models between public and private sectors. While it briefly mentions improving "opportunities for women" in the context of childcare provision and workforce participation, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, representation, voting, or civic participation.

The target speech is a procedural ruling by the Speaker directing proposed new clauses to their appropriate places in the Bill. While one clause mentions "Votes for all Men or Women who have Served Abroad during the War," no argument is made for or against women's political rights; the speech merely redirects amendments without taking any substantive position.

The speaker explicitly argues against excluding women from local government administration, contending that women who pay rates and fulfill the same qualifications as men should have the right to administer local affairs directly. He dismisses objections about unsuitability by pointing out that sanitation — the chief work — is rooted in the home where women are the most important actors.

The TARGET speech concerns the allocation of university parliamentary seats between Wales and English universities, focusing on proportionality of voters, national representation, and Welsh educational achievement. The debate is about university constituency groupings and Welsh national representation — not about women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "educated young men and women") without any argument about their distinctive civic status.

The target speech concerns a technical amendment to the wording of questions put to voters at elections, specifically about how to ask women voters whether they have already voted (to prevent double voting). While it incidentally references women voters, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker supports women serving as both councillors and aldermen, voting against the Amendment that would restrict their participation; his only reservation is excluding women from the mayoralty due to its ex officio magistrate role, which is a limited procedural carve-out rather than substantive opposition to women's political participation broadly.

The speaker argues strongly for tax relief to support working women, framing their participation in the workforce as economically vital and calling on the Government to remove financial barriers that prevent women from contributing their skills. The speech explicitly advocates for policy that expands women's ability to participate in economic and public life on equal terms.

The speech is primarily about proposing a new Speaker's Conference on Electoral Reform and Redistribution of Seats, reviewing the history of the 1916 and 1929 conferences. While women's suffrage is mentioned in passing as a historical matter already settled (the 1918 and 1928 Acts), no argument is made for or against women's political rights; it is treated as resolved background context.

The target speech is a procedural statement about where amendments should be placed within the Bill's clause structure, with no argument made for or against women's political rights. While the Bill in question (Representation of the People Act) includes a clause on women's franchises, the speaker makes no substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker argues in favour of including women as councillors, aldermen, mayors, and eligible for all appointments under the Bill, citing precedents from the English District Councils Act 1894 and the Irish Local Government Act, and dismissing concerns that doing so would prejudice the parliamentary franchise question.

The TARGET speech (attributed to MR. LOUGH continuing) argues in favour of women's eligibility for municipal roles by citing precedents from the English District Councils Act and the Irish Local Government Act, and advocates that women should be eligible not only as councillors but also as aldermen and mayors, explicitly supporting their full municipal participation.

The speech focuses entirely on electoral redistribution procedures, the timeline of the Speaker's Conference, and Proportional Representation — none of which are framed in terms of women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only once in passing ("the men and women serving in this war will have had their votes") without any argument about their civic status.

The speaker supports equalizing voting rules between men and women under the new franchise bill, arguing it would be unfair to grant women a privilege denied to men. This accepts women's newly granted vote as legitimate and seeks parity of treatment, which is consistent with supporting women's political rights on equal terms.

The speaker (Secretary of State for the Colonies) explicitly accepts the Commission's recommendation that membership of the Legislative Council in British Guiana should be open to women on the same terms as men, and endorses a substantial extension of the franchise with universal adult suffrage as the stated aim of future policy.

The speech merely notes in passing that a research assistant is working on a treatise about the representation of women in Washington and the House of Commons; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker consistently argues that women should be eligible for all offices including mayor and alderman, citing examples of women's effective service on vestries and local boards, and explicitly stating "I could not see why the position of mayor should not be filled just as well by a woman as by a man."

The speaker argues that women should be given a business qualification vote on equal terms with men, explicitly calling for parity: "let a woman have a business qualification in the same way as a man." This supports equal political/civic rights for women in the franchise structure being debated.

The TARGET speech is a factual ministerial note reporting the state of franchise arrangements across various colonies, including a mention that women were given the vote in Bermuda. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights, merely providing an informational record in response to a parliamentary question.

The speaker explicitly endorses extending universal adult suffrage to both men and women in local government elections, describing it as "the culminating point in the series of electoral reforms" and welcoming the assimilation of Parliamentary and local government franchises to include "complete, universal, man and woman suffrage in local government elections."

The speech focuses entirely on poll tax capping, local authority funding formulas (SSA calculations), and budget cuts affecting Bristol and Avon council services. While women are briefly mentioned as poll tax payers who lack income or lose carer services, these references concern welfare/service impacts rather than any argument about women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation.

The speech is a political jibe at the Prime Minister about offending various groups including women, but it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. The mention of women is incidental to a broader criticism about the PM's conduct in office.

The speaker is responding to a bill that grants women the vote for the first time, and argues for placing women "as nearly as possible on the same footing as the man" regarding voting qualifications, supporting equal political rights rather than opposing women's enfranchisement. The argument is procedural — ensuring fairness between men and women — not opposition to women's suffrage itself.

The speaker welcomes the Chancellor's efforts to encourage greater employment of women in the Civil Service and all sectors, explicitly expressing support for increased women's participation in public service roles.

The speaker explicitly states that "the majority of the Committee was of opinion... that municipal offices could not usefully be filled by women" and that "it would be a great mistake to permit the candidature of women at municipal elections," endorsing both positions as his own view and urging the Committee to maintain them.

The TARGET speech is entirely about a temperance bill restricting Sunday pub opening hours; women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the general public interested in temperance reform, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I very much agree that we need more women in Parliament" and expresses hope "that more women from all parties will enter the House in future elections," endorsing women's greater political representation. The speech also engages substantively with the working hours debate as a barrier to women's participation in Parliament.

The speaker (MP for Battersea) strongly and consistently advocates for women's right to serve as councillors, aldermen, and mayors in municipal politics, arguing that excluding them is illogical, ungallant, and harmful to public life. He explicitly appeals to the House to allow women to "take their proper place in local municipal life."
The speech is entirely about funding for the inspection and preservation of ancient monuments in Ireland, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women should be treated on equal terms with men regarding plural voting ("Why should you not have the same principle as regards women? I say, that if a woman has two qualifications she shall have two votes"), advocating for women's political rights under the same conditions as men.

The target speech focuses primarily on technical debates about the definition of "residence" as an electoral qualification and the mechanics of plural voting, not on whether women should have political rights. While women's voting entitlements are mentioned incidentally in the context of plural vote allocation, the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a Bill that transfers milk inspection functions from local authorities to central government, arguing for the value of local government. While the speaker mentions "men and women" who serve on local authorities, this is incidental; no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on Scottish economic development policy, specifically criticising the Enterprise and New Towns (Scotland) Bill regarding the restructuring of the SDA, HIDB, and training agencies. While the speaker incidentally mentions "business men and women," there is no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Combined English Universities) defends the militant suffragettes by arguing they demonstrated loyalty and patriotism by rallying to support the Government at the outbreak of war, implicitly endorsing the legitimacy of their political cause and pushing back against any criticism of their campaign for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that girls doing the same work as boys should receive equal pay, citing multiple House of Commons resolutions in support of equal pay, and calls on the Postmaster-General to ensure equal remuneration — clearly supporting women's equal civic and economic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the political and economic situation in India — Indian self-government, famine, the Gandhi-Jinnah negotiations, and the Congress deadlock — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. Women are not mentioned as a distinct civic class, and the brief incidental references to "men and women" in passing do not constitute an argument about women's political rights.

The speech concerns wartime labour policy regarding the withdrawal of female pharmacy assistants ("drug women") from chemists' shops, focusing on public health and pharmaceutical services. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — women are discussed purely in their role as wartime workers in a health services context.

The speaker argues that women's franchise under the Bill should be made simpler and fairer, protesting that basing women's franchise on the local government qualification creates unnecessary complexity. While critical of the Bill's implementation, the speaker supports women having clear and workable voting rights, advocating for the simpler Amendment that treats men and women equally in terms of plural voting limits.
