There is a brief mention of the Representation of the People Bill passing the following week, but only as an aside to illustrate the complexity of organizing elections — no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech consists entirely of parliamentary division records on a motion congratulating the Prime Minister on the Maastricht agreement, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. Although women's names appear among the voters listed, the content is procedural and concerns European Community negotiations, not women's civic participation.

The speeches in this target are entirely focused on the corn/grain registration duty debate — whether it constitutes Protection, its impact on the poor, Irish agriculture, and wartime finance. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the text.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary business statement outlining the week's legislative agenda, with a brief procedural point of order about whether it would be in order to raise the question of posting ATS women overseas. Neither the business statement nor the point of order makes any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker accepts and loyally embraces women's suffrage ("I have bowed my head to that decision... nobody will accept women's suffrage more loyally than myself") and acknowledges women's fitness to vote, but substantively opposes the immediate extension of women's right to stand for Parliament, arguing it is inopportune and will harm women's long-term representation prospects. This constitutes genuine substantive argument on both sides: endorsing the franchise already granted while opposing the new right to stand for election.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over denominational vs. popular control of elementary school management under an Education Bill, with no argument made about women's political rights, the franchise, or women's representation in public life. The incidental mention of "men and women" as school managers or teachers does not constitute any argument about women's civic status.

The speech concerns HIV testing policy for pregnant women attending ante-natal clinics and insurance company practices, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech (covering multiple speakers including the first unnamed speaker and Mr. MacCallum Scott) consistently and substantively supports women's right to sit in Parliament, arguing that once women are enfranchised it is logically necessary they be eligible to stand as Members, and explicitly endorsing the Resolution giving women the right to be elected. While both speakers previously opposed women's suffrage, they now unambiguously support women's political rights and representation in Parliament.

The speaker (Sir William Anson) explicitly supports women's eligibility to serve on education boards and committees, and goes further to say he intends to push for making women's service on the Education Committee compulsory — a clear endorsement of women's active civic/political participation in local governance.

The TARGET speech is a wide-ranging debate summary covering citizens' rights, prisons, joyriding, asylum, and women's rights, but the speaker (in the TARGET text itself) merely lists "women and womens' rights" as one of five topics to be addressed without actually making any substantive argument about women's political rights in the portion reproduced. The detailed engagement with women's issues — including political representation, workplace equality, and the Prime Minister's record on women — appears only in the FOLLOWING speech (Mrs. Rumbold's continuation), not in the TARGET text itself.

The speaker criticizes Mr. Samuel's argument that "common sense of the country would prevent the return of women in any large numbers" as a "very singular argument" for supporting women's eligibility for election to Parliament, implying that women should be freely elected in any numbers — effectively endorsing women's full political representation without reservation.

The speech is entirely focused on the National Insurance (Industrial Injuries) Bill, addressing compensation rates, self-employed workers, and appeals machinery. Women are mentioned only briefly in the context of "post-injury wives" receiving benefits and a passing reference to women marrying disabled men, neither of which engages with women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports both women's right to vote and their right to stand for Parliament, stating "I feel I must take this opportunity of registering my vote in support of the Motion which has been proposed giving women the right to be elected Members of Parliament" and praising women's suffrage as a long-overdue and justified reform. He draws on his twenty years of advocacy for women's franchise in Australia as further evidence of his consistent support.

The target speech concerns the selection of qualified individuals for educational work and the structure of local educational authorities (School Boards vs. County Councils), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is centrally about European integration, democracy, and parliamentary sovereignty, not about women's political rights. The brief reference to suffragettes is rhetorical — used to argue that European integration would undermine democratic gains generally — without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights specifically.

The TARGET speeches are almost entirely concerned with Irish taxation, financial relations between Ireland and Great Britain, and Imperial expenditure. The only passing reference to women's political rights is Sir M. Hicks Beach's hypothetical illustration about "female suffrage" being established in the future, used merely as an analogy to argue about the legitimacy of Irish representatives in 1817—no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech concerns the Third Reading of an electoral reform bill arising from a Speaker's Conference, focusing on franchise assimilation, proportional representation, plural voting, annual registers, and postal votes for soldiers. Women's political rights are mentioned only in passing as a historical achievement of a previous wartime Speaker's Conference, with no argument made for or against them.

The speaker criticises the Government for having no women in Cabinet and no mention of women in the Queen's Speech, and highlights women's distinctive economic disadvantages (hidden unemployment, zero-hours contracts, lack of public transport). This amounts to an argument that women deserve specific political attention and representation, supporting their advancement in public life.

The speech focuses entirely on post-war economic policy, industrial democracy, national planning, and the situation of the Austin Aero factory in the speaker's constituency. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation at any point in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over licensing RU486 (mifepristone) as an abortion drug, discussing the "life lobby," abortion policy, and drug safety. It makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (primarily Mr. Dillon's address) focuses entirely on the Boer War—its conduct, farm burning, concentration camps, and the suffering of Boer civilians—without making any argument about women's political rights or representation. References to "women and children" in the concentration camps are humanitarian/military concerns, not arguments about women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Motion to allow women to sit as Members of Parliament, arguing that granting women the vote logically entails giving them the right to stand for Parliament, praising women's capabilities, and concluding "I feel perfectly justified in supporting the Motion before the House." Though the speaker admits to never having voted for women's suffrage previously, he now endorses both the vote and the right to sit in Parliament as its natural corollary.

The speaker explicitly states that women's suffrage has been passed and advocates for ensuring married women are included on the electoral register, urging house-to-house canvassing to give women "the full rights of voting" — thereby supporting women's political rights in practice.

The speaker explicitly invokes the government's pledge to equalise the state pension for men and women and argues that free prescriptions for men over 60 (as already enjoyed by women) would be a concrete step toward that equalisation, thereby supporting equal civic/welfare treatment between the sexes as part of the broader equality agenda.

The speech is a lengthy economic and industrial policy address focused on demobilisation, housing, export trade, nationalisation, labour direction, and national finances. The few mentions of women (e.g., "a man or woman shall work," "men and women in the Forces") are incidental references to the workforce in general, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker explicitly includes "equal representation for women" as a provision in his Commonwealth of Britain Bill, endorsing it as part of a broader democratic reform agenda. This reflects a positive stance on women's political representation.

The target speech concerns the Midwives Bill—specifically the regulation and certification of midwives, public health risks of unqualified practitioners, and a parliamentary compromise on a prohibition clause. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation in any way.

The speaker explicitly associates the Labour party with the motion to open Parliament to women, arguing that women's right to sit in the House is "the logical outcome of all their efforts for the enfranchisement of women" and urging the House to pass the resolution by a large majority. The entire speech advocates for women's full political rights, including both the franchise and the right to sit in Parliament.

The speech is entirely focused on practical electoral administration issues — polling district arrangements, the inaccessibility of polling places for island communities in Orkney and Shetland, provisions under the Corrupt and Illegal Practices Prevention Act regarding conveyance of voters across the sea, and a proposal for proxy/postal voting for geographically isolated electors. Women are mentioned only once in passing ("it is not one to ask women to undertake" regarding a long sea crossing), without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on electoral registration, stale registers, proportional representation, and ensuring all citizens (service personnel, civilians who have moved, etc.) can exercise their votes. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation specifically.

The speech concerns teachers' salaries, educational standards in secondary schools, and recruitment of graduate teachers. The only mention of women is incidental (noting that women teachers receive £12 vs £15, and statistics about women graduates becoming teachers), without making any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech concerns debating a financial grant to Lord Kitchener for his services in the South African (Boer) War, focusing on military conduct, concentration camps, and war policy. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speech is entirely about opposing a financial grant to Lord Kitchener, criticising British conduct in the Boer War, and defending Irish Members' right to speak in Parliament. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker explicitly states their "anxiety in this matter is to secure that as many people as possible get on the register, especially that every man and woman who is entitled to get on shall do so," and raises practical concerns about ensuring women (married, widowed, and single) are properly registered and identifiable on the electoral roll under the Representation of the People Act.

The TARGET speech is overwhelmingly focused on the practical difficulties of implementing the new voter registration process (the pink form, house-to-house canvassing, military voters, etc.) under the Representation of the People Act. While women's registration and the local government franchise for women are briefly mentioned as part of the registration logistics, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights—these references are purely incidental to the administrative discussion.

The speaker explicitly supports equal pay for equal work regardless of sex, arguing that sex discrimination is unjust, and invokes women's recent enfranchisement as a reason why such discrimination can no longer be sustained — directly linking women's civic equality to their economic equality.

The speech concerns agricultural policy, forestry funding, and the Women's Land Army Benevolent Fund — specifically arguing that the WLA deserved gratuities rather than a charitable fund. This is a welfare/compensation issue, not a matter of women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation.

The speaker explicitly laments that under the new Bill, women would be "debarred from doing anything" in education management, contrasting this with School Boards where "both women and direct representatives of labour had a chance to control the education" and where women "had done most excellent work." This constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's political/civic participation in educational governance.

The TARGET speech contains Mrs. Manning challenging the Minister's refusal to extend benefits to Women's Land Army members as a discriminatory "device to freeze the women out," and Mr. De la Bère calling for a "square deal" for them — both implicitly supporting equal civic/service treatment for women. The Minister's refusal is being contested on grounds of fairness to women.

The target speech is primarily concerned with the difficulties of preparing an electoral register by October 1st, including the challenges of locating soldiers serving abroad and obtaining canvassers. While women are briefly mentioned in the context of being occupied in war work and thus unavailable for canvassing, no argument is made for or against women's political rights; the speech does not address suffrage, women's fitness for political participation, or representation.

The speaker explicitly criticises the al-Sabah regime's 1962 constitution for allowing only 8% of men and no women to vote, stating "We did not go to war for freedom and democracy on that basis," thereby implicitly endorsing women's right to vote as a baseline requirement for genuine democracy.

The speech is almost entirely about EC/UK aid to the Soviet Union and eastern Europe, support for Gorbachev's reforms, and geopolitical considerations. The only mention touching on women is a passing, factual remark that "Switzerland does not offer the vote to women," used as a comparative example to argue for patience with Soviet reform timelines—no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely about electoral registration mechanics—ensuring civilians who have moved constituencies can be placed on supplementary registers to vote—with no argument made about women's political rights or representation specifically. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the gender-neutral phrase "he or she" in the amendment's wording.

The speaker explicitly states he has "never been able to vote for giving the Parliamentary franchise to women" (against women's parliamentary political rights) while simultaneously making a strong substantive argument that women must be mandatorily included on Education Committees and that their civic participation in educational governance must be secured by law (for women's representation in public life). This represents genuine two-sidedness: opposing the parliamentary franchise while actively championing compulsory inclusion in educational committees.

The speaker explicitly agrees that women should be eligible for the committees ("he agreed that women should be eligible"), supporting women's political participation, but simultaneously states he would vote against any amendment making women's inclusion compulsory, opposing that specific mechanism of representation.

The speech is a lengthy critique of the Labour Government's post-war economic and demobilisation policies, covering topics such as labour shortages, housing, industry controls, taxation, and nationalisation. Women are mentioned only in passing (e.g., "men and women in the Forces," "women in the Armed Forces") without any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states "they were all of one mind—that women ought to serve upon these committees," argues that women's large role in education entitles them to a share in educational policy-making, and declares he will support the Amendment to include women on education committees. His only reservation is procedural (mandatory vs. recommendatory form), not substantive opposition.

The speech concerns unemployment, distress relief, workhouses, and charitable organisations, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is incidental in the footnoted motion's text ("men and women unable to find employment"), which does not address their distinctive civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on labour relations, trade union recognition, and the application of the Whitley Report to Post Office workers. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the workforce ("men and women"), with no argument made about their political rights or civic status.

The speaker supports women's eligibility to serve as school managers, explicitly stating he agrees that words should be introduced to make clear that women may be appointed, while only objecting to making it compulsory rather than permissive. This is a substantive endorsement of women's right to serve in a public administrative role.

The speech is primarily concerned with procedural objections to the Government's handling of legislation related to venereal disease and the Criminal Law Amendment Bills, arguing they should be dropped or delayed. While it briefly mentions "women electors we have just enfranchised," this is a passing reference used to bolster a procedural argument rather than a substantive position on women's political rights.

The speaker (Miss Rathbone) explicitly invokes her history in the women's suffrage struggle and frames the family allowances debate in terms of women's civic status and recognition of motherhood, warning that paying allowances to fathers rather than mothers would be "an insult in the faces" of women and could reignite sex antagonism and a political struggle over women's rights. She directly supports women's political standing and warns of consequences at the next election if women's citizenship is not respected.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on NHS health service reforms, funding, waiting lists, hospital trusts, and privatisation concerns. While women are mentioned incidentally (e.g., "to a man and to a woman," women dying of cervical cancer), no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is primarily about Budget measures affecting small businesses, VAT, mobile phone taxation, and the economy. While the speaker mentions women's views on childcare costs and working women's economic concerns, these references are to welfare/economic policy rather than women's civic participation, voting rights, or political representation. The brief dismissal of a proposed "Ministry for women" is framed as an anti-bureaucracy argument applicable to any Ministry, not as a substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on war policy, the War Cabinet's failures, censorship, and the collapse of Russia. Women's Suffrage is mentioned only in passing as an example of a distraction occupying the War Cabinet's attention, with no argument made for or against it.

The speaker sarcastically tells the House "You will have Women Suffrage very soon, and I wish you joy of it," framing women's suffrage as something to be dreaded rather than welcomed, expressing opposition to women's political rights through ironic mockery.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's representation on local welfare committees, arguing that compulsory co-option is essential to ensure women serve on these bodies, and expresses the hope that women will form the majority on such committees. The speech directly supports women's civic participation and political representation at the local level.

The TARGET speech concerns access to advice and representation for lone parents (especially mothers) when applying for community care grants or crisis loans from DSS offices. While it mentions women, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — it is a welfare/social security question about administrative support.

The speech is primarily about the poll tax, its costs, and the government's mismanagement of local taxation. The only mention of women is a passing rhetorical comparison ("the first world war was a necessary expedient to ensure that women were given the vote"), used to mock the Secretary of State's logic rather than to argue any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's full participation in the workforce and public life, criticizes the Government for lacking a coherent strategy on women's rights, highlights the absence of women in Cabinet, and calls for equal rights, pay, maternity protections, and a "full charter for women" as citizens — all of which constitutes substantive support for women's political and civic rights.

The TARGET speech focuses on family allowances policy — specifically whether the mother or father should receive the allowance and the tax treatment of married couples — rather than making arguments about women's right to vote, stand for office, or other aspects of political representation. While the speaker notes that 601 men in the House will determine whether mothers receive the allowance, this is an incidental observation about parliamentary composition rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The TARGET speaker argues that women are being deprived of their position on School Boards and that the proper remedy is to make them eligible to serve on Councils, expressing clear support for women's inclusion in educational governance. He also presses for legal clarity to protect married women's right to serve on such bodies, citing past court decisions that undermined women's civic participation.

The speaker argues forcefully for equal pay for women teachers, explicitly opposing sex disqualification and demanding that the Board of Education set an example by eliminating pay distinctions based on sex. This is a substantive argument in favour of women's equal civic and professional status.

The speech is primarily about whether county council and parliamentary elections should be postponed during wartime, arguing against such postponements. The brief mention of women voting ("Women will vote at them") is purely descriptive and incidental, noting that women teachers have a grievance and will use their votes—no argument for or against women's political rights is advanced.

The speaker praises government measures benefiting women and explicitly calls for increasing women's representation in the honours list, which reflects support for women's recognition and participation in public life.

The speech is entirely about national testing in schools and the Government's failure to listen to parents' opposition to it. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "men and women" in a general phrase about the electorate; no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is primarily about nursery education policy and its electoral appeal; the mention of women as an "electoral majority" is a passing political observation, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech focuses on family allowances policy — free school meals, free milk, payment of allowances to mothers, and care for illegitimate children — without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention that mothers should receive the allowance is a welfare/domestic argument, not a civic rights argument, and the speaker explicitly says "I do not want to talk about the status of women."

The target speech (concluding remarks by Viscountess Astor) explicitly credits women's suffrage as a transformative force driving social reform, stating "the change has not been so much in the hearts of Members of this House as in the fact that the women in the country now have the vote," framing it as "wonderful and miraculous." This is a clear endorsement of women's political rights.
The speech is entirely about dog registration legislation and dangerous dogs policy, with no reference to women's political rights, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is about the complexity and effectiveness of postal voting Regulations for Service personnel overseas, arguing for a simpler alternative modelled on Dominion practices. While it briefly mentions "Servicemen and women" casting effective votes, this is incidental to the main argument about electoral administration mechanics, and no substantive position on women's political rights is argued.

The speech concerns a criminal case involving a French national convicted of robbery and living on immoral earnings, and asks about diplomatic representations to prevent deportation of French criminals to the UK. Women's political rights are not addressed in any way.

The speaker explicitly states "I have always voted against the extension of the franchise to women," directly opposing women's political rights. The aside about women being better administrators appears to be a garbled or ironic remark, but the speaker's clear voting record and stated position is against women's suffrage.

The speech is a tribute to wartime service in the context of a parliamentary motion of thanks after WWII, praising Churchill, Scottish troops, and all who served. The passing mention of women's wartime labour (in factories, transport, and on the land) is incidental and does not argue any position on women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker explicitly criticises the Government for voting against an EC directive that would have protected women's maternity rights and frames this as a failure on women's equality, advocating for stronger protections for women in the workplace and political commitment to women's equality.

The speech is entirely focused on supporting a new clause to protect police officers from assault, with the speaker drawing on personal experience as a former officer and family connections to policing. While the speaker incidentally uses gender-inclusive language ("men and women of the police service"), no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Viscountess Astor) explicitly credits women having the vote as the driving force behind the social legislation being passed, calling it "really wonderful and miraculous," and the context confirms she is Viscountess Astor, a prominent advocate for women's political participation. Her remark that "the change has not been so much in the hearts of Members of this House as in the fact that the women in the country now have the vote" affirms women's suffrage as a positive and transformative political development.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Water (Scotland) Bill as inadequate and untimely, arguing for a better national water board for Scotland. The mention of "a wider franchise than ever before" and "a larger number of men and women will offer themselves for election" is purely incidental context about local authority elections, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (and the appended Asquith speech) concerns the Education Bill of 1902, debating denominational vs. board school systems, funding, administrative structure, and religious instruction. Women's political rights are never argued for or against; the sole mention of women is a passing reference to School Board members as "men and women" who have done educational work.

The speech concerns regulating or prohibiting street trading by young girls for reasons of moral and physical welfare, not their political rights or representation. The brief aside urging anti-suffrage MPs to heed women's petitions is a rhetorical device to strengthen his child-welfare argument, not a substantive argument for or against women's suffrage.

The speech is almost entirely about Indian constitutional reform and self-government, with only a single passing reference to women's enfranchisement ("The War has revolutionised our views with regard to India just as it has revolutionised our views with regard to the enfranchisement of women in this country") used as an analogy rather than as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns tropical kit allowances for Women's Auxiliary Air Force officers — a military pay/equipment matter — and does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, or any aspect of their civic/political participation. The mention of "shameful treatment of the women's Services" relates to financial provisions for military personnel, not political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the problem of unemployment, discussing afforestation, charitable agencies, local authority powers, and the Salvation Army's work — with no reference to women's political rights, suffrage, or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on administrative arrangements for registering soldiers and sailors to vote and enabling them to cast ballots, with only a passing, non-argumentative reference to "votes for women" as one of several issues debated during the passage of the Representation of the People Act. No position is argued for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly calls for the Minister to take "more positive action" to improve women's representation in senior positions in the arts, criticising the current lack of female representation on the Arts Council and regional arts boards, and urging the Office of Arts and Libraries to set an example.

The speech is entirely about the industrial difficulties facing Rolls-Royce Motor Cars in Crewe, including redundancies, management practices, and the recession's impact on manufacturing. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker explicitly criticises the Bill for excluding women from 67 of the 97 proposed committee seats, praises the "admirable work and devoted service" of nine women members of the School Board, and argues that legislative reform should ensure women remain eligible—stating that under the County Council scheme "you would have to repeal certain provisions of the Local Government Act of 1888, otherwise women would not be eligible for a seat." This constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's right to serve in public educational office.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the immigration of destitute aliens and the Government's failure to legislate on that subject. Women are not mentioned in the context of political rights or representation; the brief reference to "destitute women and children" is about immigration policy, not women's civic status or political participation.

The speech focuses entirely on European post-war relief — coal, food, transport, displaced persons, and economic reconstruction — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of the "National League of Women Voters" is a passing reference to a source of goodwill, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech focuses entirely on the question of extending military conscription to Ireland, arguing that Irishmen should be compelled to serve just as Englishmen are. The only tangential mention related to women's political rights is a passing reference to voting for the disfranchisement of conscientious objectors and criticising the enfranchisement of Irish people who won't perform military duties — this is about conscription equality and civic obligation, not about women's political rights specifically. No argument for or against women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is about European Community governance, qualified majority voting, and democratic accountability. The reference to "men and women" in the ministerial Council is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the question of extending military conscription to Ireland during WWI, arguing for equal application of the National Service Act. While it briefly mentions women driving buses and a woman defending her brother's rifle, these are incidental observations and no argument about women's political rights or civic status is made.

The speaker (Sir William Anson) explicitly advocates for greater representation of women on County Council Education Committees, noting that the Board suggested to Lancashire Council that only two women was insufficient representation and encouraging broader inclusion of women on sub-committees.

The speech is entirely focused on mental health policy — hospital conditions, treatment methods, staffing, administration, and funding — with no mention of women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker cites women voting for the first time in Yugoslavia's elections as evidence of expanding democracy, recounting an anecdote of a woman over 100 years old who lived to exercise her right to vote, framing this as a positive democratic achievement worthy of admiration.

The speaker (Mr. Bryce) explicitly argues that the loss of women from the School Board under the proposed Bill is "a serious loss in regard to educational affairs," praising their valuable contributions over 33 years, and objects that co-opted membership is inferior to popular election for women. He further notes that about one-third of the 1,750 school managers are women and that their knowledge and experience will be lost, framing women's elected participation in public bodies as a positive good that the Bill undermines.

The target speech is primarily about amending the National Register Act for wartime purposes — maintaining accurate records of men and women for industrial and national service use. While it briefly mentions women in the context of registering "every man and woman" for national service purposes, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech by Mr. Law addresses the UK government's policy on recognising governments and ensuring elections in liberated countries, with no argument made for or against women's political rights. The brief interjection from Miss Rathbone about women's votes appears in the TARGET text but is a question posed to Mr. Law, not an argument he makes; his response does not engage with the question of women's suffrage at all.

The speech concerns medical inspection of schoolchildren and physical training in Scottish schools, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of "male and female" sub-inspectors is purely administrative and does not address women's civic or political status.

The speech focuses entirely on the economic decline of north-west England, manufacturing, unemployment, training, and government industrial policy. Women are mentioned only incidentally ("business men and women") with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I make no secret of the fact that I think the House has made a mistake in the interests alike of women and the country" regarding the extension of the parliamentary franchise to women, and notes he voted against it "up to the last moment" in a minority of fifty. While he acknowledges the opinion of the country has changed, he explicitly maintains his opposition ("my opinion is unchanged"), making his stance against women's political rights clear.

The speech is entirely focused on Indian constitutional reform and self-government. The single passing mention of women's political rights ("when the question of votes for women was being discussed by this House it was granted as a matter of right and of justice, and not in response to an overwhelming public demand") is used only as an analogy to argue that India's claims for self-government need not depend on a mass popular demand — no position is argued about women's political rights themselves.

The TARGET speech focuses on university representation and proportional representation in the Representation of the People Bill, opposing the Lords' amendment on procedural and principled grounds related to minority representation. The mention of women is purely incidental (noting that women with degrees were admitted to the university franchise as part of the franchise's extension), with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Gulf War — criticising civilian casualties, military costs, the legitimacy of the coalition's democratic aims, and NHS bed requisitioning. The brief mention that Kuwait's Emir "never allowed women to have the vote" and that Saudi Arabia "does not even allow women to drive cars" are rhetorical flourishes to question whether these are genuine democracies worth defending, not arguments for or against women's political rights as such.

The speaker explicitly supports increasing women's representation at the higher levels of the civil service, arguing that given women comprise over 50% of the electorate and nearly half the workforce, more capable women should reach senior positions proportionate to their numbers at lower levels.

The TARGET speech concerns child labour regulation — specifically whether girls under sixteen should be prohibited from street trading — framed as a child protection and moral welfare issue, not as a matter of women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about.

The speaker (Harriet Harman) explicitly argues that Parliament's sitting hours are a barrier to women's representation and calls for reform to "open up Parliament to women," urging the Select Committee to take seriously its remit on the representation of women in the House and warning against a male-dominated body dismissing women's voices.

The TARGET speech is primarily concerned with the alternative vote electoral system and its party-political implications. While women's suffrage is briefly mentioned as one of the matters left to a free vote in the House (alongside proportional representation), this is purely a passing reference to illustrate a procedural distinction, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Sir Joseph Leese) is arguing in favour of the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill, supporting its passage by dismissing religious objections, citing the Prime Minister's agreement, criticising obstructionist tactics by opponents, and countering the petition against the Bill with evidence of far greater support among women across the country.

The speaker briefly but explicitly advocates for more women on local authorities, stating "I have been asking for it for years" and arguing women "are, and ought to be, more interested in these things" related to local government. He also suggests proportional representation in local elections would help women get elected, as currently women without party backing have "no chance of being elected."

The target speech addresses the welfare, housing, employment, and repatriation of Gibraltar evacuees in Northern Ireland; the brief mention of Gibraltar election candidates being unable to travel is a logistical/administrative point, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues against allowing local authorities to differentiate between sexes in school attendance requirements, explicitly invoking women's enfranchisement and the concerns of women's organisations, and seeks to remove the power to make "sex distinctions" — a position that supports equal civic treatment of women.

The speech is primarily about local government reorganization, the Local Government Boundary Commission, and post-war reconstruction of county and borough structures. The brief mention of women participating in local government service is an incidental encouragement for civic participation, not an argument about women's political rights or representation as a class deserving distinctive civic status.

The target speech is entirely about a licensing/temperance bill concerning compensation for revoked pub licences, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The passing mentions of "men and women" moving to cities and women involved in philanthropic work are incidental and do not engage with women's civic status or political participation.

The target speech addresses the administrative and financial workability of an education bill for London, focusing on the roles of Borough Councils, the London County Council, and educational governance. The reference to "the best men and women you can find in London" is an incidental mention with no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker supports women's franchise in principle — arguing against a £5 property qualification that would exclude poorer women and warning that "a woman of means is to have a vote while the poor woman is not" — yet also opposes specific provisions (the dwelling-house definition and service franchise) that would expand the franchise in ways he finds legally problematic, effectively arguing against certain women receiving votes under those mechanisms.

The speaker describes himself as "a somewhat reluctant convert to woman suffrage" while simultaneously expressing reservations about giving 6,000,000 women the vote, characterizing female political opinion as "flighty" and "emotional" and suggesting proportional representation as a "buffer" against potentially revolutionary female voting. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: support for women's suffrage in principle, paired with substantive concern about women's fitness for political participation.

Viscountess Astor explicitly supports women's equality and their right to serve (and be conscripted) abroad on the same basis as men, invoking "equality of the sexes" and endorsing equal pay, while criticising those who oppose sending women overseas as insulting to women's capabilities and civic contributions.
The target speech concerns Irish governance, railway construction, coal mining, and administrative matters in Ireland, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states that under proportional representation in a Scottish Parliament, "women, who make up more than half of our community, will have fair and equal representation," framing this as a positive outcome and endorsing the system that delivers it.

The speaker (Dr. Summerskill) argues forcefully that women in the ATS are capable of serving abroad, dismisses paternalistic objections from male Members, and advocates strongly for equal pay for women in military service — all of which support women's full civic and military participation on equal terms with men.

The speech focuses entirely on postal service administration — stamp regulations, committee composition for postal workers' grievances, and related matters. The brief mention of women and telegraph boys is only to note the total number of postal employees, not to argue any position on women's political rights.

The speech concerns the mechanics of postal versus proxy voting for Service men and women during wartime elections, not women's political rights or representation as a distinct class. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the general category of Service voters, without any argument about their distinctive civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political representation, stating "if I had my way, every constituency would elect both a man and a woman" and welcoming more women in Parliament, while also advocating for tax relief to help women participate in the workforce and political life.

The target speech is a parliamentary intervention challenging the opposition's claim that the Government "blocked" a directive on pregnant women, arguing it passed through the Council of Ministers with only Italy voting against. This is a factual/procedural dispute about the legislative record, not an argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses on EU social directives (pregnant women directive, working time directive), employment costs, TECs, and minimum wage policy. While it briefly mentions the pregnant women directive and equal pay for women, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses almost entirely on Post Office staffing remuneration and stamp repurchase policy. The brief mention of "young women should have better remuneration for their services" addresses pay conditions for female postal workers, not women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the mechanics of postal voting for Service men and women during wartime, addressing procedural issues like Service declarations, addresses, and constituency linkage. While it mentions "Service men and women" inclusively, it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct issue.

The target speech addresses the number of women Church Commissioners and deflects criticism by comparing the Church's electoral process to the Labour party's, but makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation — it is a defensive factual reply about Church governance rather than an argument about women's civic participation.

The speech is primarily about government expenditure, naval estimates, taxation policy (indirect vs. direct taxation, licence duties, land values), and fiscal reform. The brief mention of "women, who have no votes" is a passing descriptive reference used to illustrate the plight of the poorest taxpayers, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for adequate women's representation on the Education Committee, expressing dissatisfaction that only one woman was appointed under the existing Act and calling on the Government to impose an obligation ensuring "a large proportion" of women members. He states he voted in favour of women finding a place on such committees and wants the matter dealt with satisfactorily.

The speaker explicitly raises the issue of women's representation on the new authority, urging that it be debated before Clause 2 is withdrawn, and expressing that there are "unquestionably certain respects" in which women's position on the London County Council should differ from other County Councils — implying support for ensuring women's political representation is protected.

The speaker explicitly criticises the Prime Minister for failing to appoint women to his Cabinet and for the negligible increase in women's representation on public boards, and calls for genuine equality for women to be enshrined in law, supporting greater women's political representation and equal rights.

The speech is entirely focused on plural voting and electoral reform (university votes, business votes, residential votes), arguing for "one man, one vote." The only mention of women is a passing historical reference to wives of property owners receiving a vote under a wartime Act, which is noted as an anomaly already corrected — no argument is made for or against women's political rights as such.

The speaker argues that women must be included on the central education authority, citing their successful record on the London School Board and the large number of girls in Board schools, and urges a division to fix a minimum number of women on the body — clearly supporting women's political representation.

This is a lengthy speech by Churchill as Minister of Munitions covering wartime production, munitions output, labour, finance, and departmental administration. While women are mentioned as a large munitions workforce (nearly 750,000), this is discussed purely in terms of their industrial contribution to the war effort, not in terms of their political rights, franchise, or civic representation.

The speech is focused entirely on establishing a Standing Committee of Foreign Affairs to improve parliamentary oversight of foreign policy. While it briefly mentions the Representation of the People Act as evidence of democratic progress, it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights; the reference is purely incidental to the main argument about foreign affairs supervision.

The speaker explicitly advocates for the "proper representation of women" on Boards of management, urging statutory powers to guarantee it and conditioning his willingness to withdraw the Amendment on a commitment to pursue that goal before the Report stage.

The speaker explicitly raises the low level of women's representation in Scottish local government as a concern and calls for broader consultation with women's organisations, advocating for greater inclusion of women in the political process.

The speech by the Member for Hamilton is entirely focused on the debate over British entry into European political, monetary, and economic union (the Maastricht Treaty). There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker explicitly supports women sitting in both the House of Commons and the House of Lords, citing personal experience of women's valuable contributions to local government and committees, and urges the Government to extend eligibility to the House of Peers as well.

The TARGET speech mentions women's suffrage only as a historical aside — noting that women did not have the vote before the last war and that the spousal vote was an unintended consequence of the 1918/1929 legislation. No argument for or against women's political rights is made; the remark is purely contextual to the debate on plural voting and the spousal business vote.

The target speech is entirely focused on the wartime alcohol/brewing debate — its costs in grain, shipping, transport, and labour efficiency — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The single passing mention of "the women of Canada, who are all voters now, as the women of England are" is purely incidental, used to illustrate Canadian public pressure on grain exports, not to argue any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states it was "a great pity they refused to give the women the vote" in the earlier period, and acknowledges women's suffrage as an accomplished and welcome fact (1918, completed 1929), expressing support for women's political rights. The remainder of the speech concerns plural voting and parliamentary compromise, not opposition to women's rights.

The speaker argues in favour of assimilating the local government franchise with the parliamentary franchise, explicitly supporting the right of young men, young women, and ex-servicemen to vote in local elections regardless of ratepayer status, grounding this in principles of citizenship and taxation-based contribution to local government expenditure.

The speaker explicitly supports women's right to stand for and sit in Parliament, arguing that millions of organised women have repeatedly demanded it, and urging the opposition to drop resistance to the Bill. The speech directly advocates for women's parliamentary representation.

The speaker moves an amendment to guarantee at least six women on the London Education Committee, explicitly arguing that women deserve "due representation" on the education authority and that current practice of appointing only one or two women on large committees is inadequate.

The first speaker explicitly states "I shall support this Bill" (twice) and argues logically that granting women the franchise necessarily entails granting them legislative functions; he also proposes extending the Bill to include the House of Lords. The second speaker (Hazleton) similarly supports extending women's eligibility to both Houses of Parliament, including allowing Peeresses to sit in the Lords.

The speech is entirely about religious instruction in schools and the role of clergy as teachers under the 1944 Education Act. While it mentions "men and women" teachers in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker opposes the Bill allowing women to sit in the House of Commons, arguing that the House lacks a democratic mandate to make such a constitutional change, that the people should be given a referendum or election opportunity to decide, and that women would not be elected and the country does not support it (citing the Swansea municipal election). While he acknowledges women have already received the vote, he frames this as a mistake made without proper democratic consultation and urges delay until the country can express its view.

The speech focuses entirely on child maintenance, family poverty, and the Child Support Bill's effects on lone parents and children. While it frequently references women as lone parents affected by the legislation, it does not make any argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or other aspects of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women who followed government advice to leave London during the blitz are being wrongly "deprived of the right to vote" due to the rushed election date, expressing clear support for those women's voting rights and condemning the situation as unjust.

The speech focuses entirely on observations from the Nepalese elections and recommendations for British aid to Nepal (infrastructure, education, Gurkha relations). While it briefly mentions "men and women" waiting to vote, this is a passing descriptive observation about Nepalese citizens and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Manchester) explicitly supports including a woman representative of women workers on the proposed Royal Commission on Trade Disputes if it is of the larger type, indicating support for women's political/civic participation in public bodies.

The speech is entirely about international civil aviation policy and the governance of a proposed world aviation corporation. While the speaker incidentally mentions "men and women" as candidates for leadership roles, this is not an argument about women's political rights or representation — it is simply gender-neutral language used in the context of an aviation debate.

The speech focuses entirely on local government funding, poll tax, and the impact of government spending restrictions on local councils and their workers. Women are mentioned only in passing as part of general references to "men and women" (councillors, workers) without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that women should have "substantial representation" on the London education authority, referencing his prior amendment to secure women's inclusion on every Education Committee and criticising the Board of Education's restrictive interpretation that allowed only one woman. This is a clear, affirmative argument for women's political representation on public bodies.

The speaker explicitly states he opposed the Women's Franchise Bill on the grounds that public life draws gifted women away from their domestic duties and reduces marriage/reproduction rates. However, he also clearly states that once the franchise was granted, he finds it logically impossible to deny women the right to sit in Parliament or the House of Lords, and will support the Bill on those grounds.

The speech focuses on electoral registration, voting rights for service personnel, jury service expenses, and postal voting for parliamentary candidates — none of which single out women as a distinct class for distinctive civic rights or restrictions. Women are mentioned only in passing (e.g., "Service men and women") without any argument about women's political rights specifically.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill allowing women to stand for election to the House of Commons, argues against opponents of the measure, endorses extending eligibility to the House of Lords, and advocates opening all professions to women on equal terms — all clear expressions of support for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for a "large and substantial" proportion of women on boards of school management, warning against leaving such representation to the mere discretion of all-male bodies and citing past failures to do justice to women in educational management and endowments.

The speaker explicitly states "I am not opposing the Bill. I think it ought to be passed," endorsing women's eligibility to stand for Parliament. His concerns about minority representation and the alternative vote are procedural/electoral mechanism objections, not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about leasehold reform, service charges, and tenants' right to buy their properties from councils — matters of property law and housing policy. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., wives cleaning stairs, husbands mowing lawns) as illustrative examples of poor service, not in any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker's proposed amendment explicitly includes a provision that "regard shall be had to the desirability of including a due proportion of women" in school management bodies, and he argues that the absence of women on Borough Councils makes them unsuitable managers, stating that "women, there was no doubt, were practically indispensable in this respect." This supports women's participation in public/civic governance roles.

The speech is a maiden speech focused on the speaker's constituency (Ellesmere Port and Neston), environmental concerns, and criticism of the Gracious Speech. The only mention of women's political rights is an incidental historical note that A. K. Bulley "fought the then Rossendale constituency early this century on behalf of the women's suffrage movement," with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that women are unsuitable for the House of Commons, suggesting motherhood disqualifies them and implying that few Members actually want women there, while only conceding they might sit in the House of Lords — effectively opposing women's admission to Parliament.

The speech focuses entirely on procedural and technical aspects of electoral registration, postal voting, temporary vs. permanent legislation, and the mechanics of Service voters' registration. While women are mentioned once in passing (alongside men as Service voters), no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that women should be secured a substantial minimum role as school managers, criticises the exclusion of women from Borough Councils as the root cause of the problem, and states he will vote for the Amendment ensuring women are appointed as managers — all of which constitute support for women's political representation and participation in public bodies.

The speech is entirely focused on naval personnel conditions, living standards aboard Royal Navy ships, and the composition of the postwar fleet. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Sir C. Henry) accepts women's eligibility for Parliament as a corollary of women's suffrage ("I always held, if you gave the women the suffrage, that their admission into Parliament was a corollary") but simultaneously argues that an age limit of thirty should be imposed on women candidates, opposing the unrestricted eligibility proposed in the Bill — thus making substantive arguments on both sides of women's political participation.
The speech focuses entirely on European integration, national sovereignty, immigration policy, and asylum seekers, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is a sustained argument in favour of extending the Parliamentary franchise to women, marshalling historical precedent, colonial experience, arguments about women's existing civic roles, and the illogic of appealing to women politically while denying them the vote. The speaker explicitly calls for removing "the last remaining disability of an electoral character on women."

The speech is entirely focused on the political situation in Poland — the lack of free elections, Communist dominance, civil liberties, and British foreign policy obligations — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Lord R. Cecil) refuses the amendment that would restrict women's eligibility to stand for Parliament to those aged 30+, arguing on constitutional and logical grounds that the age limit for voting was adopted for numerical/practical reasons unrelated to women's capacity, and that limiting electors' choice to women over 30 would be "quite illogical and absurd." This is a substantive argument in support of women's right to stand for Parliament without the additional age restriction.

The speaker (Sir F. Banbury) opposes women's admission to Parliament, arguing that the Bill goes beyond what was promised and predicting a slippery slope toward expanding women's franchise further; he frames women's political advancement as opportunistic and warns against granting them legislative functions before full voting rights.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on opposing the London Education Bill of 1903 on grounds of its unsuitability for London, the Government's inconsistency, and the objections of local bodies (London County Council, School Board, Borough Councils). While the speech briefly mentions "men and women" as members of the School Board in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the repeal of the Trade Disputes and Trade Unions Act 1927, covering the 1926 General Strike, trade union solidarity, the political levy, and labour rights. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women" in passing references to trade unionists), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a maiden speech focused on the history of Sunderland's parliamentary representation and opposition to privatisation of the coal and rail industries. The only mention of women is a brief, passing historical note that Dr. Marion Philips was elected as Labour MP from 1929 to 1931 and that "there are not many women in Parliament now, but there were even fewer then, so her election was something of a landmark." This is a factual historical observation made in passing without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly celebrates the election of the first woman Speaker as "historic" and credits the "past struggle of many women, with the support of a few men," then honours his predecessor Will Crooks for moving a Bill in 1903 for the enfranchisement of women — both clear expressions of support for women's political rights.

The speech is a comprehensive review of Colonial Office policy covering constitutional development, economic progress, education, health, and welfare in the Colonial Empire. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation; women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the general population ("countrymen and women") with no argument about their distinctive civic status.

The speech is primarily about the Maastricht treaty, European integration, democracy, and national sovereignty. While the speaker briefly mentions the suffragettes and Emily Wilding Davidson in passing as historical examples of struggles for democracy, he makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights — they are invoked only as illustrative examples in a broader argument about democratic consent and the transfer of power to unelected bodies.

The speech is entirely focused on British foreign policy, the Labour Party's internal divisions over that policy, Communist influence in the trade union movement, and the wisdom of tabling the Amendment while the Foreign Secretary is in negotiations in America. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker (Member for Kilmarnock Burghs) explicitly seconds the Resolution to remove women's parliamentary franchise disabilities, arguing at length that women possess the intelligence and capability to vote, that historical trend has wrongly restricted their civic participation, and that denying them the vote is unjust given how heavily legislation affects their lives.

The TARGET speaker clarifies that the age-30 restriction on women voters is a special disqualification applied uniquely to women (not to men), implicitly supporting the argument that this age-based disqualification is unfair and distinctive to women — framing it as an inequity in women's political rights. This supports the broader case being made in this debate for allowing women equal access to parliamentary participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the economic case for saving the Cammell Laird shipyard on Merseyside from closure, discussing employment, industrial policy, and VSEL's conduct. While the speaker briefly mentions gender unemployment statistics (18% male vs 7% female unemployment) and notes that lost full-time male jobs are often replaced by part-time work "which usually goes to women," these are incidental economic observations and do not constitute an argument about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker moves an amendment to extend the Parliamentary Qualification of Women Bill to include the House of Lords, explicitly arguing that there is "no possible plausible argument" why women (including Peeresses in their own right) should be excluded from the Lords if they are qualified for the Commons, and urging the Noble Lord to "make his Bill a complete Bill."

The speech explicitly supports "equality of treatment and opportunities for men and women" as part of the Social Chapter, criticising the UK Government's opt-out that denies British workers these protections, and notes that maternity pay in Britain is the lowest in the EC — all framed as arguments for greater equality and rights for women in the labour market.

The speaker (Member for Durham, N.W.) systematically rebuts arguments against women's suffrage—dismissing claims about women's intellectual inferiority, domestic disruption, and lack of demand—and argues affirmatively that extending the franchise would have an educative effect, empower women politically, and benefit the country on issues like temperance, sanitation, and social reform. While he expresses hesitation about women sitting in Parliament, he frames this as a separate question and does not oppose it substantively, making his overall stance clearly supportive of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "we who are in favour of the change, as I am myself," affirming support for women's political rights. The speech then reasons strategically about whether adding the Lords amendment risks the Bill's passage, but the underlying stance is clearly in favour of women gaining political power.

The speaker explicitly argues that women, who have endured tremendous suffering during the war, "have the right to be consulted at the earliest possible moment," directly affirming women's right to political participation and voting as recently enfranchised citizens.

The speech focuses entirely on foreign policy, Anglo-American relations, economic differences between the US and UK, and racial discrimination against Black Americans in the Southern states. While it touches on voting rights for Black Americans and disenfranchisement of negroes in the South, this is raised as a critique of American hypocrisy in foreign policy, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (from Oldham) explicitly and enthusiastically supports the Resolution granting women the franchise, arguing that women have been unfairly excluded from vestries, borough councils, and school boards, that they suffer wage discrimination remediable by the vote, and that enfranchisement would promote national efficiency and open public life to those fitted for it. He also endorses, at least tentatively, women becoming Members of Parliament.

The speaker (Lord R. Cecil) argues against an amendment that would restrict women's eligibility to stand for Parliament to those aged 30 or over, contending it is "quite illogical and absurd" to limit electors' choice in this way and that the sex disqualification should be removed entirely, leaving only the standard age-21 rule that applies to men. This is a clear substantive argument in favour of women's right to stand for Parliament on equal terms.

The speaker (Mr. Cremer, Member for Shoreditch/Haggerston) explicitly and comprehensively opposes women's suffrage and their admission to Parliament, arguing on physiological, political, moral, and religious grounds that women are unfit for political participation and that "there is no safe halting place except to keep them where they are."

The speaker explicitly affirms that the 7,000,000 women voters "have the right to be consulted at the earliest possible moment," endorsing their newly granted franchise and the importance of holding an election so they can exercise it.

The speech is entirely about betting taxation, entertainments duty, and theatrical finance. The brief mention of a suffragette being killed at the Derby is purely anecdotal and used for self-deprecating humour about the speaker's betting history, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Maastricht treaty, European constitutional structures, subsidiarity, democratic federalism, and the Council of Ministers. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing historical reference to the Chartists and suffragettes as examples of democratic movements that achieved social legislation, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about the Nurses Act and protecting the professional title "nurse" from being used by unqualified persons, including Christian Scientists. It mentions women only incidentally as nurses; there is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about Northern Ireland's direct rule, political representation of Northern Ireland citizens, quangos, international law obligations, and the talks process. While the speaker quotes Article 3 of the UN covenant mentioning equal rights of men and women, this is incidental to his argument about regional political rights for Northern Ireland — he does not argue for or against women's political rights specifically.

The Earl of Nottingham argues that there is no overwhelming demand for women's suffrage, that many distinguished women themselves oppose it, and that women are more swayed by "affections, emotions, and imagination" than men, concluding the House would act "unwisely" in adopting the Resolution — a clear substantive opposition to granting women the franchise.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's jury service and links it to women's recently expanded franchise, arguing that women above thirty who now have the vote should also be admitted to juries and to Parliament, urging the Government to prepare legislation to that effect.

The speech is primarily about Polish electoral politics and the debate over free elections in Poland. The brief mention of women not having the vote in Greece (compared to Poland's new electoral law granting universal suffrage over 21) is purely incidental and comparative, used to criticize the inconsistency of opponents rather than to argue a position on women's political rights as such.

The speech is entirely focused on UK European policy — the social chapter, the ERM, economic recovery, subsidiarity, and regional representation — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of a directive on pregnant women's rights to work is raised purely as an economic/labour-standards point, not as an argument about women's civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over importing Chinese labour to the Transvaal, the conduct of the South African War, the treatment of native labourers, and criticism of Lord Milner and the mine-owners. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speaker (Mr. William Redmond) explicitly and forcefully supports women's enfranchisement throughout, arguing that women have a natural right to vote, citing the successful example of Australia, condemning opponents' characterizations of women as unfit for citizenship, and contending that denying women the vote is akin to slavery. He explicitly urges the House to support the Motion to extend the franchise to women.

The speech is primarily about Army Medical Corps administration, Orders in Council, and military matters. The brief mention of the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps addresses their working conditions and rumours about their social life, not women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about European integration, the Maastricht Treaty, parliamentary sovereignty, and constitutional accountability. The brief mention of women's suffrage (Asquith's concern about referendums leading to votes for women) is used only as a historical illustration of elite paternalism, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the importation of Chinese indentured labour to the Transvaal, addressing economic, moral, political, and imperial arguments about that policy. Women's political rights are not argued for or against anywhere in the speech; the only mention of women is a brief reference to sending English women to South Africa to increase the British population as a counterbalance to Boers, which does not address their civic or political status.

The speech is primarily about opposing an industrial relations order for Northern Ireland, arguing it is unnecessary and harmful to workers and trade unions. The only mention of women is a passing reference noting that part-time workers in Northern Ireland are "almost by definition women," used to illustrate that the weakest workers will lose protections — no argument is made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on taxation policy — Surtax, PAYE, P.A.Y.E. reform, Excess Profits Tax, postwar credits, and Budget incentives — with no argument made for or against women's political rights. The brief mention of "married women" applies only to their status as applicants for postwar tax credits, not to any question of civic participation or political rights.

The speaker explicitly affirms that "person" in Clause 1 includes women, confirms it will be possible to appoint more women to the Central Midwives' Board, and expresses agreement that maternity and child welfare legislation will need "more and more the services and the special knowledge of women," endorsing their greater inclusion in public bodies.

The speaker (Labouchere, Member for Northampton) explicitly opposes women's suffrage, arguing that granting the franchise would put the country "absolutely in the hands of women," that the vast majority of women do not desire the vote, that women already exercise sufficient indirect influence, and raising alarmist concerns about women subsequently demanding seats in Parliament.

The speech is entirely focused on defending the Ulster Defence Regiment against amalgamation/dissolution and criticising government security policy in Northern Ireland. While it mentions "men and women" serving in the UDR, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Labouchere) argues against women's suffrage using ridicule and dismissal, claiming women would inevitably seek seats in Parliament, that their presence would tempt male Members, and that the vast majority of women neither want nor are suited to political participation. These are substantive arguments opposing women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the National Health Service Bill — discussing nursing services, hospital organisation, disease prevention, dental services, and health administration — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mentions of women (Florence Nightingale, Queen's Nurses) are in the context of healthcare, not civic participation.

The target speech, delivered by Mr. Labouchere, uses a humorous anecdote about canvassing women to mock and undermine the case for women's suffrage, implying that giving women the vote would create social impropriety and danger — consistent with his broader opposition to women's political rights evident throughout his surrounding speeches.

The speaker (Ms. Mildred Gordon) explicitly argues that removing further education funding from local councils will leave women with "no influence at all" on the new funding bodies, describing this as "a retrograde step," and notes that women are under-represented on political bodies while local government offers them relatively better representation. She also argues that the Bill's approach to leisure/adult education courses disproportionately harms women by making re-entry to education more costly, framing this as undermining women's equal participation in public and civic life.
