The speaker explicitly endorses women's suffrage in Burma, arguing that "the 'flapper' vote is absolutely right in Burma" because women play a great part in trading and public life, and rhetorically asks whether we agree "that they should have as clear a right to the vote as men." He also supports universal adult franchise for both sexes at 21 as recommended by the Legislative Council.

The speech is primarily about a Scottish Education Bill and makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The brief mention of women "going to be added to the electorate next election" is purely a passing reference used to support the education bill, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is about reducing Purchase Tax on household washing machines and mangles to help housewives, not about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The brief mention of women who voted for the speaker is incidental context, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker argues that proportional representation "would lead to better representation of women and of those from our nation's ethnic communities," explicitly citing improved women's political representation as a benefit of the electoral reform being proposed. This is a direct, if brief, argument in favour of women's political representation.

The speaker (Member for Leicester) explicitly supports the Resolution for women's franchise, arguing that working women deserve the vote as a political weapon to address their economic grievances, and closes by stating he "most heartily supported the Resolution."

The speaker from Cannock explicitly argues against the marriage bar in the Civil Service, contending that the country cannot afford to lose the services of skilled married women and that maintaining arbitrary restrictions on women who wish to work outside the home is "completely ridiculous" on both economic and human grounds. She supports women having full freedom of choice to work or stay at home, clearly advocating for women's equal participation in public employment.

The speaker (Labouchere) explicitly opposes women's parliamentary franchise, arguing that the vast majority of women do not want the vote, that women are satisfied with their indirect domestic influence, and that they are better suited to the home than to political life. He positions himself as a "champion" of women who prefer to stay out of political turmoil, framing his opposition as defending women's true interests.

The speech by the Member for Cynon Valley focuses entirely on African and Caribbean development aid, debt relief, and international funding mechanisms, with no arguments made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of programmes benefiting women is a passing reference to poverty-reduction and agricultural priorities, not an argument about women's civic status or political participation.

The speech is entirely concerned with war pensions and separation allowances for soldiers' wives and widows — discussing scales, cost of living calculations, and administrative timing. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns police resources, war crimes prosecutions under the War Crimes Act 1991, and Labour vs. Conservative policing records. The passing reference to "police men and women" is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker (Sir H. Meux) explicitly opposes women sitting in Parliament, arguing the House is not a fit place for respectable women, that women lack the physical constitution for parliamentary strain, that he doesn't believe most women want female MPs, and that he doesn't believe any Member truly wants to see a woman sitting in the House.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on opposing proportional representation as an electoral reform, with only a passing incidental mention of "men and women of good will in politics" and no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief reference to women is rhetorical filler, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the Third Reading of the National Insurance Bill, covering administration, finance, inflation concerns, and social insurance policy. While it briefly mentions "the position of married women" regarding insurance options, this is discussed purely in the context of insurance scheme mechanics (opt-in vs. husband's coverage), not as an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The target text merely records a procedural note that the "Franchise and Removal of Women's Disabilities Bill" was withdrawn and its second reading order discharged. No argument for or against women's political rights is made; it is purely a parliamentary procedural entry.

The speaker (Sir F. Banbury) argues explicitly against the Motion to make women eligible for Parliament, urging the House to reject it as "premature," contending that the effects of women's suffrage should first be assessed, that a "moribund Parliament" should not make such a revolutionary change, and expressing discomfort with the prospect of more women voters than men voters. While he avoids re-litigating the franchise question, his entire speech is directed at opposing women sitting in Parliament.

The speaker explicitly supports women's right to vote ("it is perfectly logical to give them the vote"), grounding this in women's right to choose their male representatives, but substantively opposes women sitting in Parliament, arguing women themselves don't desire it, the Army and Navy weren't consulted, and it was not mandated by constituents — making substantive arguments on both sides.

The first speaker warmly endorses equal rights for women, welcoming women's admission to the electoral roll and wishing the franchise had been extended on identical terms to men, and supports women's eligibility as Members of Parliament on the grounds that their perspective would benefit the nation. Mr. Hazleton similarly supports the Motion, dismissing the arguments against it and welcoming the vote.

The speaker argues at length that women lack the qualities needed for political participation, that they don't want the franchise, that granting it would destroy domestic peace, and that women's proper role is in the home as "angel of the hearth" — explicitly opposing women's suffrage and their right to sit in Parliament.

The speech is entirely focused on the welfare and care of young children in day nurseries, staffing standards, inter-departmental coordination, and child education policy. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the Scottish National Health Service Bill — arguing for its passage, discussing health services, doctors, nurses, hospital management, and domestic help — without making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for implementation of the Curtis Committee's recommendations on the care of deprived children, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic participation issues.

The speaker explicitly states "I believe that 50 per cent. of Members of Parliament should be women," directly advocating for women's political representation. He also criticises Parliament for failing to accommodate the changes since 1918 when women got the vote, and objects to the dismissive use of "ladies" for women members and constituents.

The speech concerns teachers' pension legislation, specifically advocating for a minimum pension for underpaid women teachers in rural districts. While it mentions the sex discrimination in teachers' salaries, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — it is purely about employment and pension conditions.

The speaker explicitly asks about and advocates for greater representation of women on the Central Midwives Board, pressing the President of the Local Government Board on how many women currently serve and whether he will increase their number, signalling support for expanded women's representation on this public authority.

The speaker explicitly supports creches for women Members' children and more broadly for all staff in the House, and advocates for proxy votes partly to address the hardship of Members being dragged in while sick or abroad — reforms that would benefit women Members in particular. These are framed as part of modernising Parliament for fuller participation. The speech also echoes the preceding speaker's (Mr. Benn's) call for 50% women MPs by addressing the "new generation" of incoming Members and reforms to make Parliament more accessible.

The speaker confirms there are already two women on the Central Midwives Board and explicitly states the intention to increase the number of women and give direct representation to midwives (who are women) on the Board, thereby supporting women's representation in this public regulatory body.

The speaker from Northampton explicitly states he will "strongly support the Resolution" for women's franchise, arguing that women hold property, contribute to society, demonstrate intellectual equality with men, and deserve a voice in governing the country. He makes substantive arguments throughout in favour of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely concerned with the debate over importing Chinese labour to the Transvaal and its economic and political implications. While Chinese women are briefly mentioned as part of a dismissal of opposition arguments ("the question of the importation of Chinese women and slavery and all sorts of things which had nothing whatever to do with the subject before them"), no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Measure's clauses building a career structure for women deacons, expresses hope that a future Measure allowing women to be ordained as priests will come to the House and gain a "huge majority," and frames these provisions as positive steps toward greater roles for women in the Church.

The speech focuses entirely on government wages, labour conditions, and the Fair Wages Resolution, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as workers in a government tailoring department and as wives of low-paid workers, without any reference to their civic or political status.

The speech is primarily about constitutional and procedural concerns regarding the Coal Nationalisation Bill (accounts, discrimination, eligibility for public office). The only mention of women is a passing analogy comparing the eligibility issue to a hypothetical change in the franchise age for women, used purely as an illustration of constitutional importance rather than as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure — scrutiny of statutory instruments, sitting hours, Friday sittings, and the inadequacy of debating time — with only a brief, passing remark that political parties lack the will to ensure women are elected to Parliament. This mention does not constitute a substantive argument for or against women's political rights; it is an illustrative aside in a speech focused entirely on procedural reform.

The speech focuses entirely on post-war conditions in Germany and Austria — food shortages, displaced persons, trade unions, prisoners of war, and political reconstruction — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns funding and governance of museums and art galleries in Ireland and Scotland, with a passing mention of "male and female" artists in a quoted report. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the administration of military pensions, employment of discharged soldiers, training schemes, and related matters for WWI veterans. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is a parliamentary question and answer providing statistical information about the number of electors (including women) qualified to vote for the London County Council. It presents factual figures without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker expresses "grave reservations" about the ordination of women and voted against the Measure in the Ecclesiastical Committee because it appeared to anticipate and advance women's advancement in the Church prematurely. While he conditionally allows that women priests could properly hold senior posts if ordained, his overall position is one of opposition to the current direction of advancing women's roles in the Church.
The speech is entirely about the design of a florin coin — the artist, the selection process, and alleged artistic flaws — with no reference to women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speaker explicitly supports the clause affirming equal pay for equal work regardless of sex, arguing it is just and that women teachers are capable of equal work, urging the President of the Board of Education to accept the amendment to "safeguard the interests of women."

The speaker explicitly celebrates Bristol's equal parliamentary representation of men and women, advocates for women's employment rights (equal pay, maternity rights, employment protection), and criticises the Government for failing to act on women's civic and workplace equality. She also calls out the inadequacy of merely appointing two women to Cabinet as a substitute for meaningful policy change.

The speech is entirely focused on opposition to the Licensing Bill and the Prime Minister's closure motion, discussing petitions, temperance reform, and parliamentary procedure. Women are mentioned only incidentally as signatories to a declaration ("heads of settlements in the East End, both male and female"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equal incorporation into the permanent Royal Air Force on terms of equality, including equal pay ("the rate for the job"), equal status, and opportunities including flying roles. He seconds an Amendment calling for the W.A.A.F. to be established as a permanent part of the Regular Air Force, and argues against treating women as cheap auxiliary adjuncts.

The speech concerns an amendment to civic restaurant legislation about the financial loss period for local authorities, and while it briefly references the Suffragette movement's "cat-and-mouse Act" as an analogy, this is purely illustrative and does not constitute an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the Education Bill's provisions raising the school leaving age and abolishing half-time working for children, focusing on the financial impact on working-class families in Lancashire. The brief mention that "Women are going to have votes" is purely incidental and no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech concerns the ordination of women as priests and deacons in the Church of England, and their appointment as rural deans and canons — matters of ecclesiastical office within a religious institution, not women's political rights or civic participation (voting, standing for Parliament, representation, etc.). While the speaker supports expanding women's roles in the Church, this is a religious/ecclesiastical question outside the scope of women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (from Durham) focuses entirely on the mining industry, coal production, worker morale, National Coal Board management, and recruitment — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. Lady Grant's subsequent speech about women in industry concerns labour participation rather than civic/political rights, and in any case is in the CONTEXT, not the TARGET.

The speaker explicitly argues that women have been underrepresented in Parliament and that it is time for a woman to hold the Speaker's Chair, supporting Betty Boothroyd's candidacy partly on the grounds of her gender and her status as a woman parliamentarian whose abilities deserve recognition.

The target speech discusses teacher salary equality and whether women teachers support equal pay, which is a labour/employment matter. While it touches on women's fitness for higher posts, it does not make a substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mrs. Manning, Member for Epping) argues forcefully that women peers should have the right to take their seats in the House of Lords, describes their exclusion as an injustice and an anomaly, invokes Viscountess Rhondda's case as an example of women being wrongly denied their rights, and urges the Government to use the Parliament Bill to enable this reform. She explicitly frames this as a matter of women's political rights and representation.

The target speech is entirely concerned with the Burma Independence Bill — specifically whether Burma meets the democratic conditions for self-government set out in the 1945 White Paper. The mention of "adult suffrage" and "seven million men and women voters" is purely descriptive of Burmese electoral arrangements, not an argument about women's political rights or representation as a matter of principle.

The speaker explicitly states they are "entirely in favour of equality of treatment between the sexes" and argues that requiring women to lose their nationality upon marrying a foreigner is an unjust differentiation. They also invoke the precedent of the 1914 amendment benefiting women to argue that more should be done now.

The speech is primarily about the mechanics of school board electoral systems (ward voting vs. general voting, cumulative voting), with only a passing mention that general voting might help women and Roman Catholics retain their places on school boards. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Control of Engagement Order (industrial/labour conscription), arguing for workers' freedom to choose their own jobs. Women are mentioned only incidentally as "working class men and women" sent to gaol during the war, without any argument about women's distinctive civic or political rights.

The speech is a maiden speech focused on defence spending, public expenditure, privatisation, NHS reform, education, and trade/industry policy. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation anywhere in the speech.

The speaker argues forcefully that women suffer a gross hardship under nationality law that forces them to take their husband's nationality upon marriage, draws an explicit analogy to men losing votes to illustrate the injustice, and urges Parliament to remedy this inequality now rather than waiting for political pressure from newly enfranchised women.

The speaker explicitly supports the election of a woman as Speaker, stating "I believe that a woman has a tenderness that some males do not have" and expressing relief at having voted for her rather than against her — framing a vote for a female Speaker as the right and desirable outcome.

The speech is focused on the practical difficulties of voter registration under the Representation of the People Act — canvassing, form-filling, staffing, and military voters — without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The brief mention of women being unsuitable for night-time canvassing is a logistical observation, not a position on women's civic or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, regional economic policy, industrial decline, and criticism of the Government's economic management. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in the target speech.

The speaker presents a petition on behalf of women overseas (BAOR wives, daughters, and sisters) seeking equal voting rights by proxy, explicitly requesting that they be granted the same voting privileges as their male counterparts and women already enfranchised in overseas services. This directly supports women's right to vote on equal terms with men.

The speaker explicitly states they have "always opposed" equality of rights with regard to the franchise for women, making their opposition to women's political rights clear. While they express sympathy with the Amendment as a natural consequence of equal rights, this is framed as a criticism of the logical extension of a policy they oppose, not as genuine support.

The speech is entirely focused on labour and factory inspection issues — understaffing of the women's inspectorate under the Factory and Workshop Acts, dangerous trades, overtime violations, and industrial health conditions. While it prominently discusses women workers and female factory inspectors, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation; the "women's department" referenced is a labour inspection body, not a political rights matter.

The TARGET speech explicitly references schedule 1's principle that the PR system "seeks to achieve equal representation of men and women and fair representation of ethnic and other minority groups," presenting this as a positive feature of the proposed electoral system without any objection to it.

The speech focuses entirely on colonial administration, constitutional development, social services, and education across various territories. While it briefly mentions "men and women" in the context of colonial service recruitment and training, this is incidental and no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses on factory inspection, child labour, workplace safety, dangerous trades, and industrial conditions. While it mentions female inspectors and women workers in the context of labour regulation and factory inspection staffing, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation — it addresses occupational health and administrative efficiency, which is out of scope.

The speech concerns the employment conditions, wages, and hours of civilian women workers at an RAF base, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech supports restoring British nationality to women who married enemy aliens during the War, explicitly citing the extension of political power to women as a force that will drive demands for equality. The speaker (Mr. T. Wilson) also invokes women's imminent voting power and their right to have their demands considered, clearly endorsing women's political rights as a basis for the amendment.

The speaker seconds the rejection of the Bill and argues substantively against women serving on county and borough councils, claiming they are less qualified than men for most municipal work (sewers, finance, by-laws, valuation), that political life is unsuitable for women, and that their limited uptake of available seats demonstrates lack of demand. While he acknowledges women's value in certain welfare/educational roles, this is used to argue against the broader Bill, not to endorse women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Fisher) moves an amendment to make it compulsory for councils to co-opt women onto maternity and child welfare committees ("it will be compulsory on the council to co-opt women"), explicitly supporting women's mandatory inclusion in these public bodies as a matter of civic participation.

The speech is entirely about stamp duty exemption on house purchases, the construction industry, and economic recovery from recession. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is primarily about health policy (smoking targets, NHS management). The brief mention of women's role in delivering healthcare refers to employment representation in the NHS, not to women's political rights or civic participation, and no argument about women's political rights is made.

The speech concerns railway season ticket pricing, train service availability, and hardship for commuters during wartime — entirely a transport policy matter. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "business men, women, and young persons" affected by fare increases, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech focuses on Air Ministry administrative procedures, specifically querying how women in the Services are accounted for under Vote A of the Service Estimates. This is a procedural/administrative observation about the form of the Estimates, not an argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speeches are focused entirely on post-WWII peace treaties concerning Finland, the Tyrol/Austria, and related territorial and reparations matters. The single passing reference to women's franchise ("a country which, next to New Zealand, was the first to give women the franchise") is used only as evidence of Finland's democratic credentials, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly gives "very hearty support" to the Bill enabling women to sit on county and borough councils, calls arguments against it "sophisticated and feeble," frames the debate as part of the broader campaign for extending Parliamentary suffrage to women, and argues that working women deserve representation in selecting those who make the laws governing their labour.

The speaker (Mrs. Gorman) explicitly introduces a Bill to ensure every constituency is represented by both a woman and a man, arguing that women's 6% share of parliamentary seats is an anomaly that must be corrected and that Parliament should reflect the fact that half the population are women. While she opposes positive discrimination and a Minister for women's affairs, these are secondary caveats; her core argument strongly supports structural reform to increase women's political representation.

The speech concerns the establishment of shop and yard committees in Royal dockyards and naval establishments, trade union recognition, and the Whitley Report. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly declares himself "an opponent of female suffrage" and opposes women serving on county councils due to their "political atmosphere," while simultaneously supporting the Bill's Second Reading to restore women's right to serve on municipal and local bodies (boards of guardians, education committees, etc.), making substantive arguments on both sides of women's political participation.

The TARGET speech focuses on pension policy concerns — specifically the erosion of pension value and the potential increase of the retirement age for women — as a welfare/economic matter, not as a question of women's civic status or political rights. While women are singled out as a class, the debate is about social security entitlements and retirement age policy, not voting, representation, or any other aspect of civic participation within the scope of women's political rights.

The speaker (Captain Jessel) explicitly opposes the Bill, arguing that most women do not want political roles, that the Bill is a "thin end of the wedge" toward Parliamentary suffrage and seats in the House, and directly states he is "averse to giving the Parliamentary suffrage to women" and objects to women serving on councils or holding civic office.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on naval pay, manpower levels, and naval stores/storage issues. The brief mention of the Women's Royal Naval Service increase (£300,000) in the McKie portion expresses support for the WRNS but as a military service organisation, not in the context of women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the treatment and pay of low-paid canteen workers in Parliament, including clocking-on systems and late-night transport. The mention of "many of them women" is an incidental demographic observation, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about Naval Estimates (pay, stores, tobacco allowances, etc.) and only briefly mentions the Women's Royal Naval Service in passing to praise their wartime harbour work, without making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Sir John Gorst) explicitly supports women's eligibility for borough and county councils, argues there is "no real reason" to exclude them, and states he has "steadily voted in favour of the enfranchisement of women" throughout his political life, expressing his "greatest possible pleasure" in voting for the Bill's Second Reading.

The speaker explicitly states he opposes women's parliamentary suffrage ("an opponent of the principle of women's suffrage") while simultaneously supporting the Bill to admit women to borough and county councils, arguing women's service on local governing bodies is distinct from and not a step toward parliamentary voting rights.

The speech is focused entirely on the nature of democracy and the hereditary Second Chamber (House of Lords reform), with only a passing incidental reference to the franchise being extended to "all men and women at the age of 21" as a historical marker — no argument is made for or against women's political rights specifically.

The target speech concerns the National Assistance Bill and Poor Law reform, paying tribute to those who worked in local government on public relief. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the selection, recruitment, and conditions of service of the British Control Commission staff in Germany. While it mentions "men and women" employed by the Commission in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about electoral registration deficiencies, the poll tax's impact on voter rolls, and redistribution of parliamentary seats. While it briefly mentions women in refuges fleeing domestic violence losing their right to vote due to anonymous registration gaps, this is raised as an administrative problem of electoral registration, not as an argument about women's political rights or civic status as a class.

The speaker argues that legislation touching on women's civic status (including Regulation 40D) should not proceed, urging the Government to drop the contentious bills, and frames women's votes primarily as a reason to delay rather than as a right to be championed. The thrust of the speech is that such legislation is undesirable and futile, opposing its progress rather than advocating for women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, pit closures, small businesses, and criticism of Conservative economic policy and Derbyshire county council's record. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "small business men and women"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech argues for delaying a Joint Committee examining two Bills related to Regulation 40D (venereal disease regulation), not women's voting rights or political representation. The speaker references women's franchise only incidentally to argue that the next Parliament will be elected by women's votes and therefore this contentious legislation should wait — this is a procedural/timing argument about other legislation, not an argument for or against women's political rights themselves.

The speech concerns pay scales for male and female nurses, which is a healthcare/employment wages matter. While it touches on a gender pay disparity, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for more women in the House of Commons and proposes a structural mechanism (co-equal male and female permanent secretaries) to increase female representation in public life, framing it as meeting "the increasing demand for female representation."

The speaker explicitly states he is "entirely against female suffrage," recounts his decades of opposing women's franchise bills "tooth and nail," and argues women are physically and intellectually different from men and unfit for political participation. His procedural objection to the specific Bill is secondary and reinforces, rather than contradicts, his fundamental opposition to women's suffrage.

The speech is entirely focused on the economic impact of pit closures on small businesses, unemployment in mining communities, and fiscal policy. While the speaker incidentally mentions "young men and women" and "small business men and women" seeking jobs, no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on welfare administration, care for the elderly, blind, and physically handicapped, and the merits of centralisation versus local discretion in social services — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that it is "a gross injustice to the women electors who have the vote" to proceed with legislation before they can pass judgment on it, and states that "this legislation ought not to be considered until women have a right to pass judgment upon it," directly affirming women's political right to have a say in laws that affect them.

The TARGET speech (Mr. Tennant, Berwickshire) explicitly supports the Bill giving women eligibility for local councils, calling it "a tardy act of justice to women," and argues that women's participation is "not only useful and helpful, but even essential" in local governance. The Secretary (Grant Lawson) in the same TARGET block states he has "always been in favour of women being admitted as freely as possible to administrative bodies" and explicitly supports giving women the Parliamentary franchise, even while doubting they should sit in the Commons — but his support for the franchise is the more substantive claim on women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is the mover of the Second Reading, making an extended and comprehensive argument in favour of Parliamentary enfranchisement of women on the same terms as men, citing Mill's unanswerable arguments, majority support across parties, precedent in British colonies, and the justice of giving working women the vote to protect their interests.

The speaker explicitly argues that it is unjust to pass legislation that disproportionately burdens women before the newly enfranchised women have had the opportunity to vote on it, stating it is "a mean proceeding" to "smuggle" an "odious measure" through the House before "the 6,000,000 women have had an opportunity of exercising the franchise." This is a substantive argument in support of women's political rights and their right to have a say in legislation affecting them.

The speaker invokes John Knox's "horrible regiment of women" and St. Paul's objection to women speaking, argues that giving women votes would not raise their wages, and explicitly states that even if he favoured women's suffrage he would oppose the Bill — all amounting to a clear opposition to women's political rights and suffrage.

The speaker explicitly welcomes women having the vote ("Give the women the vote, as you have done") and argues that women's enfranchisement will energise maternity committees, urging compulsory co-option of women onto those committees as a direct benefit of their new political status.

The speech concerns a parliamentary question about the supply of large-sized women's boots in Somerset, with the Women's Institutes mentioned only as a source of representations about footwear availability. There is no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports improving women's representation in the higher civil service and asks about practical measures (job sharing) to facilitate women's advancement up the career ladder, framing this as a "desirable outcome."

The speech concerns a parliamentary debate about theatre patents, monopolies, and the rebuilding of Drury Lane theatre. The brief mention of a female author (Miss Bailey/Joanna Baillie) is a passing literary reference with no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for compulsory co-option of women onto maternity committees, arguing that women have as much intelligence as men and that their inclusion is essential given the bill's focus on women and children. This is a clear argument supporting women's political representation on local government bodies.

The speech is entirely focused on the privatisation of Northern Ireland's electricity industry, opposing the Government's order on economic and policy grounds. There is one passing reference to "wild men and women of the Conservative party," but this does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the proposed bills impose differential and unjust treatment on women compared to men, defends women's right to vote on legislation affecting them before it is enacted, and urges the Government to wait until women have had the opportunity to exercise their newly granted franchise before proceeding with measures that would impose compulsory detention and other penalties disproportionately on women.

The speaker explicitly states that "anything that would tend to increase the representation of women on these local authorities would be all to the good," and proposes combining compulsory and optional co-option to ensure women's representation where it is lacking. This is a clear endorsement of women's participation in local government bodies.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing for an increase in the basic rate of ex-Service disability pensions, discussing pension rates, cost of living, and the welfare of disabled veterans. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker explicitly states he has "invariably voted against any Bill proposing to give female suffrage" (opposing women's political rights at the parliamentary level) while simultaneously voting for this Bill to allow women to serve on local bodies, framing local service as a "training school" to prove fitness for public life — supporting one aspect of women's political participation while opposing another.

The speaker is quoting a UN document on Palestine partition to highlight a potential inconsistency regarding minority voting rights and residency restrictions, not making any argument for or against women's political rights. The mention of women voting is incidental, cited only as part of a broader legal/constitutional puzzle about the partition scheme.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Women's Franchise Bill, arguing that women are suited only for subordinate local boards (not Parliament), that giving women the franchise would destroy relations between the sexes, and that even those who favour women's suffrage in principle should vote against this Bill. He states directly "he did not shirk the expression of his views in opposition to the Bill."

The speech is entirely focused on opposition to the Local Government Bill's provisions on competitive tendering and local government restructuring, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief reference to "devoted men and women" serving in local government is a passing mention, not an argument about women's distinctive civic status.

The speaker explicitly seconds a motion to reject women's enfranchisement, arguing that it would dangerously shift physical power away from men, that colonial experiments with women's suffrage were failures, and that women's majority in the population would result in an unworkable government dominated by women — all substantive arguments against granting women the vote.

The speech is entirely concerned with the Parliament Bill and reform of the House of Lords — its composition, powers, and the timing of constitutional change. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about; the passing reference to "everyday affairs of men and women" is incidental and carries no argument about women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly states his "general objection to women voting at all," argues women are "fully represented by men," and contends there would be "no advantage in allowing them to vote," while claiming the current system is satisfactory. His critique of the Bill's treatment of married women is offered as an additional practical objection, not as support for a broader enfranchisement.

The speech is entirely focused on nuclear proliferation, arms control, defence industry jobs, the Labour party's defence policy, and criticism of the Conservative government — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely concerned with Irish governance, torture allegations, parliamentary reform (in the sense of electoral/structural reform debated by Cochrane and Burdett), sinecure abolition, and the state of the nation — none of which singles out women as a class for distinctive civic rights or duties. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued.

The speaker argues in favour of ensuring women are represented on maternity and child welfare committees, stating "There is a case for making it compulsory that there shall be some women on a committee of this kind" and expressing confidence that the electorate will return women. The objection raised is not to women's inclusion but to the clause that would also compel co-option of men, framing it as a procedural concern rather than opposition to women's participation.

The speaker explicitly states support for the women priests Measure ("I shall speak briefly in support of the main Measure") and argues the Church of England has the authority to ordain women as priests. His opposition to the compensation Measure is procedural/financial rather than opposition to women's ordination itself.

The speech is an extended parliamentary address defending the Duke of York against corruption charges related to his mistress Mrs. Clarke selling military promotions. It contains no argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status of women; the references to Mrs. Clarke and Miss Taylor are entirely in the context of evaluating witness credibility in a military corruption inquiry.

The speech discusses colonial higher education missions, university colleges, and administrative bodies like the Inter-University Council, with a passing reference to "university men and women" as participants in missions. This mention does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

The target speech opens by noting that councils rarely co-opt women even when permitted, arguing this demonstrates the need for compulsion ("we ought to have some compulsion in a matter of this sort"). The subsequent contribution from Mr. Fisher strongly advocates for mandatory co-option of women onto public health committees, arguing women are uniquely suited for maternity and child-welfare work and that local authorities' reluctance to appoint committees stems partly from not wanting to include women — both speakers clearly support women's participation in local government.

The speech (and the concatenated Lord Advocate's speech) concerns radical reform agitation, manufacturing distress, public order in Scotland, and resistance to a proposed committee of inquiry. Women are mentioned only incidentally as wage-earners in the spinning trade; there is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker highlights that women will soon form a majority of voters on the electoral register, implicitly endorsing women's expanded political presence, and raises the question of equal representation on committees in a way that supports women's civic participation rather than opposing it.

The speaker consistently opposes women's enfranchisement, arguing that women lack the mental capacity to weigh issues in all their bearings, would disrupt parliamentary business, are not fitted for public life, and that enfranchising them would cause domestic discord and dangerously expand the electorate. He explicitly dismisses the "inherent right" argument and aligns himself with the opponents of the Bill.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on electoral registration reform and physical access to polling stations for disabled people. The brief mention of "suffragettes" is purely historical context illustrating that democratic arguments have become "dead dogmas," not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (by Sir Francis Burdett and others) is entirely focused on the Peterloo Massacre, parliamentary inquiry, the legality of the Manchester meeting, taxation, and parliamentary reform. While women are briefly mentioned in passing (e.g., "men, women and children" being sabred, a woman whose bill was thrown out by the grand jury), no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about industrial conscription (Regulation 58A) and the direction of labour in peacetime, arguing against compulsory labour direction on grounds of necessity, efficacy, and personal liberty. While the speaker mentions "young men and young women" and "free men and women" as those affected, these references are incidental to the broader argument about labour direction and do not constitute a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speech is a lengthy wind-up of a debate on the Criminal Justice Bill, addressing topics such as corporal punishment, prison conditions, probation, Borstal, and juvenile offenders. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "Viscountess Davidson," "Mrs. Corbet") with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on local government administration of maternity and public health schemes, praising the work of local authorities and "ladies and gentlemen and working women" in public health. While it briefly mentions women participating in local work, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech deals entirely with the Church of Scotland (United Free Church) property dispute, the Barrier Act, Clause 5 on religious subscription formulas, and the role of Parliament in reversing House of Lords judgments. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech concerns whether local authorities should be compelled or merely permitted to carry out maternity and child welfare schemes, touching on local government autonomy and grant policy. The brief mention of women's votes is incidental and used only to argue that public opinion will stimulate local authorities—no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely focused on defending the Indemnity Bill, the Habeas Corpus Suspension Act, the use of spies/informers, and parliamentary reform agitation. The only mention of women is a passing rhetorical jibe mocking Sir F. Burdett's "universal suffrage" proposal for excluding females and the insane, used purely for satirical effect without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speaker invokes the parliamentary vote for equal pay for men and women as a comparable example of a government majority being overridden, implicitly treating that vote as a legitimate democratic outcome that was wrongly reversed — thereby expressing support for the principle of equal pay (a women's political/civic right) and criticising the Prime Minister's intervention against it.

The speech concerns a procedural question about a Factory Act overtime order affecting women workers in linen manufacturing in Ireland, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic representation.

The target speech focuses on electoral registration, civic duties, and opposition to the private Member's Bill on those grounds, with historical references to Reform Acts and Conservative democratic tradition. While it briefly mentions "all men and women" receiving the vote under Disraeli, this is a passing historical reference without any argument about women's political rights specifically.

The speaker argues that British women residing overseas (wives, daughters, and sisters of serving men) should be entitled to vote in forthcoming elections, just as male service electors are already provided for, explicitly advocating for extending voting rights to this group of women.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a road vehicle lighting bill, with the Women's Enfranchisement Bill mentioned only in passing to deny that the speaker's opposition is a filibuster tactic. No argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that the Government was wrong to exclude women from jury service, contending that intelligent, educated women should be allowed to serve rather than extending the male jury age to 60-65. The speaker advocates for women's civic participation as jurors and anticipates women voters demanding equal jury representation once enfranchised.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill (a marriage law reform bill), not on women's political rights or representation. The speaker's brief mention that "women are not on the Parliamentary register" and lack "women's suffrage" is used instrumentally as a rhetorical point against the marriage bill—arguing the House cannot know women's views on it—rather than making any substantive argument for or against women's suffrage itself.

The target speech concerns the Peterloo Massacre of August 16, 1819 — specifically defending the magistrates and yeomanry, questioning witness credibility, and opposing parliamentary inquiry into the events. While the petition mentions women as victims of the cavalry charge, the speech never argues for or against women's political rights or representation; it is entirely about the legality of the military dispersal of a reform meeting.

The speech concerns a parliamentary question about an alleged massacre and military action in a Macedonian village, focusing on Turkish troop conduct and diplomatic representations. Women are mentioned only incidentally as victims of violence, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

This speech concerns the presentation of a petition from Samuel Bamford regarding the Peterloo Massacre and parliamentary reform, focusing on allegations of misconduct by the Manchester yeomanry and requests for an inquiry. While the petition mentions "right of suffrage" and reform grievances, it does so in a general sense (for all people) without making any argument specifically about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker invokes the suffragettes as an example of people seeking the vote in order to gain political power and have Parliament respond to their interests, explicitly framing women's suffrage as a means to real democratic power. This is a brief but substantive endorsement of women's political rights as part of a broader argument about the value of democratic participation.

The speaker explicitly defends women voters' capacity to represent their husbands' interests in local elections, arguing that wives are well-informed about local rates and arrangements, thereby supporting the legitimacy of women's newly granted municipal franchise and opposing the postponement of elections that would rely on those women voters.

The speech is entirely focused on the Electricity Bill's treatment of local authority undertakings, financial compensation, staff protections, and municipal trading — with a brief passing mention of "devoted men and women in the public service." There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is overwhelmingly about a vehicle lighting bill and local versus central government regulation. The speaker briefly mentions having given notice to move that the Women's Enfranchisement Bill be read "that day six months" (i.e., to kill it), but this is a procedural aside used to establish his credentials as someone willing to speak his mind, not a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Benn, Chesterfield) explicitly supports the Measure for the ordination of women, voting in favour and arguing that opposition reflects prejudice against women as full human beings. He draws direct parallels to the exclusion of Catholics and Jews from Parliament, frames women's long wait for ordination as an injustice, and expresses hope for a woman Archbishop of Canterbury—explicitly endorsing women's full participation in public and ecclesiastical life.

The speech is entirely concerned with the legality and handling of the Manchester (Peterloo) meeting, the conduct of magistrates and yeomanry, the right of petition, parliamentary reform, and the merits of coercion versus conciliation. Women's political rights are never argued for or against; the only mention of women is incidental ("wives and children" as evidence the crowd had peaceful intent).

The speech concerns a Lords Amendment related to road haulage distance limits (25 miles) affecting constituents in Yorkshire, with no mention of women's political rights or representation. References to "men and women" are generic and not related to civic participation.

The target speech concerns technical Scottish application clauses about the parliamentary franchise for men and local government franchise, and a Lords amendment on disqualification of town clerks and assessors from voting. While women's franchise is briefly mentioned as being regulated elsewhere, no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely focused on opposition to the Maastricht treaty, the decline of parliamentary sovereignty, and Labour party policy. The brief mention of "suffragettes" is purely rhetorical, used as a historical example of groups who fought for democratic rights that the speaker believes are now being surrendered — no argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speech by Mr. Goulburn concerns a parliamentary debate about inquiry into the penal colony of New South Wales, convict transportation, religious instruction, and colonial administration. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., female convicts and their attendance at divine service, a proposed factory for women convicts), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the social chapter of the Maastricht treaty, parliamentary sovereignty, and the Government's refusal to accept Commons decisions. The one passing mention of "women" is an incidental rhetorical example ("too many women") used to mock the Government's argument about the quality of a majority, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Second Reading of the Bill, arguing that women have exercised municipal powers well, that Scotland supports extending the Bill, and using New Zealand's example of women voting for Parliamentary representatives as a positive model. He dismisses the "thin end of the wedge" argument and affirms that those who appreciate women's good sense wish to give them the same rights and privileges as men.

The speech is about the Maastricht treaty, parliamentary sovereignty, and whether a referendum should be held on EU integration. The brief mention of women's enfranchisement is purely historical context to illustrate when democratic government was achieved, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that granting women the franchise logically entails their admission to Parliament, and recalls that this connection was explicitly stated when the franchise bill passed. This is a substantive argument in favour of women's right to sit in Parliament.

The speech (by Mr. Peel) concerns the Peterloo Massacre, the conduct of Manchester magistrates, seditious meetings, public order legislation, and political disaffection in manufacturing districts. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation whatsoever.

The speaker moves the Second Reading of a Bill explicitly to allow women to be elected and serve as councillors and aldermen on county and borough councils, arguing at length that women have proven their value on boards of guardians, school boards, and district councils, and that excluding them places an "artificial restraint" on constituencies and wastes valuable civic intelligence.

The speech focuses entirely on Russian interference in Hungarian political affairs, coalition governance, and post-war Hungary. The only mention of women is an incidental reference to "men and women over the age of 20" being allowed to vote in the 1945 Hungarian elections, which is a descriptive factual remark about franchise breadth rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is overwhelmingly about UK export policy and performance. The single mention of "votes for women" is a throwaway rhetorical jibe mocking Labour for proposing ideas the Government has already implemented — it does not argue a position on women's political rights.

The speech concerns naval and military expenditure, pensions for sisters of deceased officers, and the compassionate fund — none of which argue for or against women's political rights, voting, or civic representation. Women appear only as objects of charity, not as subjects of political rights.

The speech is focused on consumer goods shortages and economic policy, arguing the government should provide more goods for housewives and working women. While it mentions women in the context of consumer hardship and industrial recruitment, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on war pensions policy, the Parliamentary War Pensions Committee, and keeping pensions out of party politics. The single brief mention of women ("the party of women" and "wives and mothers") is a passing rhetorical flourish warning about electoral consequences of party pension promises, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill enabling women to sit on borough and county councils, argues that women have proven their value on public bodies, endorses women's exercise of the franchise, and "strenuously supported this Bill" in the interests of men, women, and children.

The speaker argues that women are too focused on petty details to carry on municipal business effectively, and concludes that the Bill's proposed change "would not be for the benefit of the country" and is not desired by a majority of women — clearly opposing expanded women's political participation in local government.

The speaker explicitly moves a Bill to amend the Representation of the People Acts to increase women's representation in Parliament, argues that the lack of women in Parliament is a structural inequity, and calls on Members to support measures (including quotas, PR, or coupled votes) to bring more women into the House.

The speech is entirely focused on the adequacy of wartime separation allowances and pensions for soldiers' wives, children, and apprentices. While it briefly mentions that a constituent woman will be a new voter ("Remember that these women are going to vote at the next election"), this is a passing rhetorical flourish rather than an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Cold War geopolitics, international relations between the Western powers and the Soviet Union, the UN, regional blocs, and the prospect of war — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speaker (Mr. Healy) explicitly supports extending the franchise to women broadly, objecting to the "dwelling-house" qualification because it would create a property-based aristocracy among female voters and exclude poor women—arguing that the Bill as it stood rightly conferred votes on female occupiers without such restrictions.

The speech is primarily about the Maastricht treaty, national sovereignty, and the case for a referendum on European integration. The brief mention of suffragettes is used only as a rhetorical device to argue that parliamentary sovereignty should not be ceded to Brussels, not to make any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on the Maastricht treaty's social protocol, democratic accountability in European institutions, and federalism vs. centralism. The only mention of women is a passing reference to "the Chartists and the suffragettes" as historical examples of democratic movements that achieved a universal franchise, without making any argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's admission to local governing bodies (supporting the Bill's Second Reading) while explicitly opposing the extension of the Parliamentary franchise to women, making substantive arguments on both sides of women's political participation.

The speech focuses on electoral reform, proportional representation, and whether the current first-past-the-post system accurately reflects voters' will. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as an example of a significant past reform, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a parliamentary question asking whether women's voting rights have been recognised in the Transvaal Constitution, followed by a deferral answer. Neither the question nor the reply argues for or against women's political rights; they merely inquire about and defer to the publication of the Letters Patent.

The speech is almost entirely about proportional representation and the Labour party's position on it. The mention of "adding 6,000,000 women to the franchise" is a brief rhetorical aside used to challenge an opponent's consistency, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the abolition of university seats in the Representation of the People Bill — arguing it breaks a pledge from the Speaker's Conference and lacks electoral mandate. While it briefly mentions "the lowering of the age for women" as an example of agreed legislation, this is purely incidental and no argument about women's political rights is advanced.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political participation and representation ("I support 100 per cent. any attempt to encourage more women Members into this House of Commons"), while simultaneously opposing the specific mechanism of positive discrimination/changing electoral rules to achieve it ("I completely oppose any attempt to change the rules, to fiddle the rules, to enable them so to do"). Crucially, the opposition is not merely procedural — the speaker substantively argues that the existing system has not debarred women and that altering the Representation of the People Acts would undermine democratic foundations, making this a genuine two-sided argument on women's political representation.

The speech concerns reserve forces policy, employer compensation schemes, and the Territorial Army consultation process. Women are mentioned only in passing as part of "men and women" who serve in volunteer reserve forces, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker moves to agree with the Lords' amendment specifically to enfranchise qualified women at Oxford and Cambridge universities, describing its denial as deeply unjust and expressing personal commitment to securing their inclusion on the electoral roll. The speech explicitly supports extending women's political rights under the university franchise.

The speaker supports granting women the Parliamentary franchise while explaining the Lords' Amendment as a measure to prevent fraudulent "faggot votes" through manufactured allotments, explicitly stating "We all of us desire to grant the franchise." The objection is to vote manufacturing, not to women's political rights themselves.

The speaker (Sir Frederick Banbury) consistently opposes women serving on borough and county councils, arguing women are uneconomical, sentimental, and unfit for administrative bodies, and explicitly states it would be "an extremely evil day for the country" if women were admitted to Parliament or given the Parliamentary franchise.

The speech focuses entirely on the abolition of university seats and plural voting in the context of electoral reform (the Representation of the People Bill), arguing that university suffrage is undemocratic. While it mentions "men and women" in passing, it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation as a class.

The speaker (Mr. Grant Lawson) argues at length that women should be allowed to sit on borough and county councils, citing their demonstrated competence as guardians, factory inspectors, and vestry members, and explicitly finding "no sufficient distinction" to justify excluding them from borough councils while permitting them on urban district councils. He supports the Bill throughout without substantive opposition to women's political participation.

The speech is entirely focused on defending university parliamentary representation and Northern Ireland's seat allocation under the Representation of the People Bill; it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. The passing mention of Eleanor Rathbone is a tribute to her public service, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speaker references the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Act 1928 approvingly, noting that opposition from "diehards in the party machine" was the obstacle to its passage, implying support for the equal franchise it granted women. This brief but clear endorsement of the 1928 Act places the speech in support of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly seconds the motion for the Bill's second reading, arguing that women workers contribute equally to national prosperity and therefore deserve equal political rights, and that sex should be no bar to the franchise. He directly advocates for extending Parliamentary suffrage to working women on the same terms as men.

The speech is primarily concerned with procedural and constitutional matters relating to electoral reform legislation (Speaker's Conferences, the business vote, university elections, City of London representation), not with women's political rights as such. While women are briefly mentioned incidentally (Lady Megan Lloyd George's participation in the Speaker's Conference debate), no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on Treasury staffing, wartime expenditure control, departmental financial oversight, and a capital levy debate. The brief mention of women ("My right hon. Friend suggested we should have a woman on the Committee… we are not going to put a fifth member on the Committee because she is a woman, but we will put a woman on if she is fit for the work") is a passing remark about committee composition with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Clarke) dismissively remarks that to get northern and Scottish Labour members to vote for women in internal party elections, "one has to give them no choice," implying that women's political advancement within Labour requires coercion rather than merit — a subtly disparaging framing of women's political representation. This treats women's inclusion in political roles as something imposed rather than naturally merited, reflecting an opposing stance toward women's political representation.

The speech focuses entirely on education policy — specifically maintenance allowances for children attending school and the raising of the school leaving age. The only mention of women is a brief passing reference that "when the next General Election takes place the women will have votes," used as an argument for delaying the Bill until after the election, not as an argument about women's political rights per se.

The target speech is a brief procedural clarification about the effect of a vote on the women's ordination Measure — it states that defeating the motion would stop the ordination of women unless the Church returned with something else. It does not argue for or against women's political rights; the subject is ecclesiastical ordination policy, not women's civic/political participation.

The speaker (Mr. Labouchere, continuing from the preceding speech context) argues extensively and substantively against women's suffrage, claiming women lack the physical force required for citizenship, are intellectually inferior to men in matters of governance, are emotional and poor reasoners, and that granting women the vote would be dangerous and disadvantageous to both the community and women themselves.

The speech concerns the ordination of women to the Anglican priesthood — a matter of Church theology, governance, and ecclesiastical legislation — not women's political rights or civic representation. The debate is entirely about religious office, not the franchise, candidacy for public office, or any other aspect of women's political participation.

The speech concerns an International Labour Conference on industrial employment of women at night and phosphorus use in the match trade — occupational/labour regulations, not women's political rights or civic participation. Women are not singled out as a class for distinctive civic status here.

The TARGET speech focuses on procedural and theological questions about the Synod's two-thirds majority vote and the Church of England's authority to ordain women, framing it as a matter of ecclesiastical governance and doctrine rather than women's political rights or civic representation. No argument is made for or against women's political rights as a class.

The speaker explicitly states "we are not talking about women's rights" and frames his opposition to the Measure entirely on ecclesiological and constitutional grounds—that the Church of England cannot unilaterally change doctrine held universally by the Catholic Church. He explicitly declares himself "entirely agnostic" about women's ordination as such, making no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues at length against women's suffrage, contending that women lack the capacity for broad political judgment, that laws passed by women-dominated electorates could not be enforced by men, that colonial experience with women's votes has been a failure, and that "the vast bulk of women do not desire the franchise."

The speech by R.A. Butler (Saffron Walden) is entirely focused on defending university representation in Parliament against its proposed abolition, arguing on constitutional, traditional, and political grounds. While women's political rights are tangentially mentioned (e.g., a brief reference to Miss Rathbone and a passing allusion to the Equal Franchise Bill giving votes to young women), no argument for or against women's political rights is made; these are incidental references within a debate about university seats.

The speaker (Labouchere) argues vehemently against women's suffrage and against women sitting in Parliament, citing women's alleged intellectual and physical limitations, the danger of female electoral dominance over men, the undesirability of mixing sexes in Parliament, and the threat to social relations—explicitly opposing both the franchise and women's presence in the legislature.

The speech is primarily about electoral representation principles (business votes, City of London representation, "one man one vote" vs "one vote one value"), and while it briefly mentions womanhood suffrage as a historical footnote explaining the origin of the "one man, one vote" slogan, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the grievances and unemployment of demobilised soldiers after WWI, criticising government inaction and urging better treatment of returning servicemen. Women are mentioned only incidentally in passing references made by other speakers (e.g., women employed in government roles displacing ex-servicemen), but the TARGET speaker never argues about women's political rights, franchise, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on housing policy, the Housing Bill, building costs, local authority powers, town planning, and related matters. The brief mention of "women electors who had just been enfranchised" is a passing observation used to illustrate public discontent about housing conditions, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the treatment of conscientious objectors in prison — hunger strikes, forcible feeding, and alleged misconduct by prison governors and doctors. While it briefly mentions suffragettes as an analogy for hunger strikes, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.
The speech is entirely about education policy — teacher training colleges, pupil-teacher centres, and student qualifications — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about the ordination of women as priests in the Church of England, a theological and ecclesiastical matter. While the speaker supports women's ordination and uses equality language, this is not a debate about women's political rights, voting, parliamentary representation, or civic participation — it falls outside the scope of women's political rights as defined.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the franchise to civil servants abroad, their wives, and wives of Fighting Forces members, praising the Amendments for enfranchising "thousands of British men and women." The speech advocates for women's voting rights as part of this extension, crediting the Tory Party for pressing the expansion.

The speech by the Member for Coventry East (Mr. Crossman) focuses entirely on the Berlin crisis, German currency reform, the Six-Power Plan, and the political and economic reconstruction of Western Germany. The brief mention of "women and children" in Berlin is purely logistical (arguing officials' families should be evacuated to Frankfurt for efficiency), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure, the obligations arising from a Speaker's Conference, and accusations of bad faith over redistribution and electoral law. Women's votes are mentioned only briefly and incidentally (noting that Conservative members once opposed votes for women and now support them, and quoting Lord Birkenhead's admission of a bargain over women's suffrage in 1917) without the speaker making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker raises a pointed question criticising the Government's failure to have a Cabinet-level Minister present during debate on the Women's Enfranchisement Bill, implying that the proposal to enfranchise all women on the same basis as men deserved proper ministerial attention. This implicitly supports the importance and legitimacy of women's enfranchisement as a matter warranting high-level government engagement.

The speech is primarily about international labour conferences, phosphorous necrosis, lead poisoning in pottery trades, and factory inspection staffing. While women inspectors and women workers are mentioned, these references concern occupational health and labour regulation enforcement, not women's political rights or civic representation.

The speech is entirely about the theological objections to women's ordination in the Church of England, not about women's political rights in the civic sense. The speaker explicitly states "this issue is not about women's rights in the secular sense," and the debate concerns sacramental priesthood and Church authority, which falls outside the scope of women's political rights and representation.

The TARGET speech merely clarifies the speaker's procedural role in drawing the House's attention to government action regarding the Sex Disqualification Bill, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The mention of the Bill is incidental to a dispute about parliamentary procedure and conduct.

The speech concerns procedural details about the adoption of Rule 127(b) regarding the use of female teachers for junior boys in Irish national education — an administrative/educational matter. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Hardy, Wentworth) explicitly states he voted in favour of the ordination of women and gives three substantive reasons supporting it, including that denying ordination to women is "outrageous," that gender should not be a bar to ordination just as it is not a bar to baptism, and that there is no clear biblical authority to deny women ordination.

The speech focuses almost entirely on the inadequacy of the compensation package for clergy who cannot accept women's ordination and on theological objections to the Measure. The speaker explicitly states that "this issue is not about women's rights in the secular sense" and dismisses women's rights framing as a distraction from the compensation and theological arguments that are her true concern.

The speaker explicitly states he is "glad that the Southborough Report does not think of recommending the franchise for all women" in India, and dismissively contrasts Indian women with "clever women in this country, who got the vote without going before the electors," suggesting both opposition to extending the franchise to all women in India and a sardonic attitude toward the recent British women's suffrage victory.

The speech is entirely focused on the world food shortage, Sir John Boyd Orr's warnings, and the need for diplomatic engagement with the Soviet Union on food policy. The brief mention of the Parliamentary Secretary being a woman is a passing social remark, not an argument about women's political rights or fitness for office.

The speech by Foreign Secretary Bevin concerns the Malayan emergency (Communist terrorism), European economic cooperation (Marshall Plan, OEEC), and Western Union foreign policy. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation anywhere in the text.

The TARGET speech (Colonel Wedgwood) focuses entirely on the Indian Budget, the Southborough and Feetham Reports, franchise qualifications for Indian legislative councils, the Rowlatt Act, and British governance of India.
