While it mentions that women constitute roughly 1,000,000 of India's 14,000,000 literate people as part of a statistical breakdown of the electorate, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily concerned with labour conditions, ventilation, wages, and management practices at the Army Clothing Factory at Pimlico. While women workers are mentioned (fainting incidents, women inspectors), the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation; it addresses workplace health and safety conditions.

The speech concerns the ordination of women as Church of England priests, which is a matter of religious/ecclesiastical policy rather than women's political rights or civic participation. The speaker's arguments are theological and ecclesiological, not about voting, standing for office, representation, or any other aspect of women's political rights as defined by the suffrage movement's framing of civic personhood.

The speaker (Sir Charles Dilke) moves the Second Reading of a Bill to enfranchise women and remove their disabilities, explicitly arguing that the principle of complete or partial removal of women's disabilities now commands broad support, citing successful women's suffrage in Australia and New Zealand as evidence, and urging the House to directly face the question including removal of the marriage disability.

The speech concerns the UK Government's policy on Palestine, specifically the question of partition, enforcement versus implementation, and Britain's role in the United Nations. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech addresses the administrative and legal situation of unmarried mothers in occupied Germany and Austria who have children by foreign fathers, referring the matter to the UN. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports the ordination of women to the priesthood, argues there is no valid theological objection to it, and urges Parliament to approve the Measures. He frames this as part of the broader momentum toward sex equality in society, including in Parliament itself.

The speaker explicitly moves the Second Reading of a Bill to remove women's political disabilities, including equal civil/judicial appointments, equal franchise, and the right to sit in the House of Lords, stating he has "during the whole of my life been strongly in favour of the complete enfranchisement of women, and in favour of placing them on an equal footing in all respects with the menfolk of the country."

The speaker explicitly states she will vote in favour of the ordination of women and urges all Members to do the same, grounding her support in a commitment to equality for women in every aspect of national life and rejecting the idea that spiritual calling is restricted by gender.

The speaker seconds a Bill explicitly aimed at removing all legal and political disabilities on women, arguing strongly for equal franchise at 21, women's right to hold civil and judicial offices, and women's eligibility for the House of Lords, citing women's wartime contributions and the government's own election pledge to establish equality between men and women.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the railway privatisation/franchising Bill, arguing it will undermine British Rail and public services. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker explicitly approves of "every line of the Bill," supports removing sex barriers preventing women from being citizens, and calls it "an indispensable step" toward justice — a clear endorsement of women's political rights and suffrage.

The speaker explicitly gives "whole-hearted and undivided support" to the Bill, argues that women should be admitted to the legal profession, and contends that the age restriction on women's voting (30 vs. 21 for men) is illogical and unjust, calling for adult suffrage as the proper solution.

The speech is entirely about the composition and representation of river boards under the Rivers Bill, specifically debating the proportion of local authority members versus drainage and fishery interests. Women are mentioned only briefly and incidentally ("men or women coming together to do a fine piece of public work as a team") without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on Royal Navy capabilities, flexible response policy, and the Royal Navy air station at Yeovilton in the speaker's constituency. While it mentions "men and women" serving in the Royal Navy in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a budget debate contribution focused on taxation policy—Special Contribution, Income Tax reliefs, Profits Tax, Purchase Tax, and earned income relief. The brief mention of "married women's relief" being publicised in Lancashire is in the context of industrial labour recruitment and Income Tax administration, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech announces the constitution and terms of reference of a committee on police pay and conditions, which includes both men and women as members and subjects of inquiry. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states he is and has always been personally in favour of women's suffrage, yet moves that the Bill be rejected (read a second time in six months), citing substantive objections: he denies that women's interests have been unduly neglected, questions whether women would actually use the franchise, and objects to specific clauses (plural voting, university representation, broad public functions) as obstacles to moderate support. This constitutes genuine substantive argument on both sides — endorsing women's suffrage in principle while substantively opposing this particular measure on grounds that go beyond mere procedure.

The speaker explicitly declares unwavering support for adult suffrage for both men and women, argues that limiting women's political power has deprived the nation of its "keenest brains," and states he will give the Bill his "hearty support" to place women on an absolute equality with men.

The speech is primarily about tobacco policy (smoking legislation, workplace smoking bans, and advertising). The brief mention of the 75th anniversary of women getting the vote is used rhetorically to argue for effective health legislation, not to make a substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on miscarriages of justice in the criminal justice system and the proposal to establish an independent criminal justice review board. The only mention of women is incidental — noting that the board should have "proper representation of women and ethnic minorities" — which is a passing procedural detail, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly urges the Home Secretary to give a "favourable answer" on the Clause that would extend voting rights to soldiers' wives and wives of Crown servants abroad, arguing they "justify some consideration" and that the proposal "would commend itself to the Committee on all sides."

The speech is primarily about post-war Germany, the Marshall Plan, currency reform, and occupation policy. The mention of German women voters is framed as a concern about Communist infiltration through the Demokratisch Frauenbund, not as an argument about women's political rights; the speaker treats women's political apathy as a geopolitical risk rather than making any argument for or against women's civic participation.

The TARGET speech is focused almost entirely on opposing the Plural Voting Bill on procedural, mechanical, and partisan grounds. Women's political rights are mentioned only in passing as one of several unaddressed electoral anomalies ("There was the question of the enfranchisement of women, and a multitude of other matters"), without any argument for or against women's suffrage itself.

The speaker explicitly and enthusiastically supports the Bill to remove sex disqualification, argues that women deserve equal voting rights with men at age 21, endorses women sitting in Parliament, and states "I believe the woman is justly entitled to a vote on equal terms with men." There is no substantive opposition to women's political rights anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on Sunday trading legislation and related employment protection issues. The brief mention of "about 2 million women workers" affected by the Employment Bill is a passing reference to women as workers in the retail sector, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

Sir Henry Kimber's speech is entirely about opposing the Plural Voting Bill, arguing that it unjustly disfranchises plural voters and that the government should instead address redistribution of seats. While he makes a passing reference to "suffragettes" (noting that the Bill's penalties don't include the luxury accorded to "first class suffragettes"), this is a rhetorical aside, not an argument about women's political rights. The speech makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker expresses broad support for women's political rights throughout — endorsing equal franchise at 21, women as magistrates, women at the Bar, and equality in divorce law — and states he will support adult suffrage when it comes before the House. His decision to abstain rather than vote for the Bill is framed as a procedural/timing objection (too soon after the 1918 Act, too sweeping in scope), not a substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on opposing steel nationalisation, arguing the government has sufficient existing powers to control industry and lacks business experience to run nationalised industries. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a wide-ranging report on trade, diplomacy, and travel observations across the Caribbean, with only a brief passing mention that Santo Domingo has "women's votes" as one factual detail among many about that country. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on the merits and machinery of a plural voting/electoral registration bill, addressing arguments about disfranchisement, plural voters, and party motives. The brief mention that the Bill is "objectionable because it did not enfranchise women" is presented only as one of several criticisms raised by opponents, dismissed as irrelevant to the current bill without the speaker arguing any position on women's political rights himself.

The TARGET speeches (by Mr. Llewelyn Williams and Mr. Middlemore) are entirely concerned with the Education Bill debate—specifically about religious tests for teachers, denominational versus undenominational teaching, and the Cowper-Temple clause. Neither speaker addresses women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech is focused on the Maastricht treaty's social chapter and its relationship to the treaty of Rome, arguing that the confrontation between Labour and Conservatives is disproportionate. The brief mention of "equal pay for men and women" is purely descriptive, noting that provisions are similar across the two treaties, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly declares himself a convert to women's suffrage and endorses women's enfranchisement and parliamentary participation, but then argues the current Bill is "premature" and urges the promoters to "hasten slowly," citing the need for trade unions to first recognise women's equality in industry before full emancipation is legislated. This constitutes substantive support for women's political rights in principle paired with substantive opposition to the present Bill on grounds of timing and industrial equality.

The speaker explicitly rises to support the Bill, describes himself as a convert to women's suffrage, and advocates for both women's political equality and the opening of the legal profession to women. All substantive arguments made are in favour of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly declares themselves "absolutely pledged to the principle of this Bill," endorses women's enfranchisement and their admission to professions, and argues that giving women greater roles in public life will elevate public morality. Their caveat about Clause 2 (further franchise extension) is a procedural/timing concern about overloading the Bill and breaking a compromise, not a substantive opposition to equal franchise, which they call "sure to come."

The speech is primarily about university constituency representation and whether the Government was bound by pledges made at the 1944 Speaker's Conference. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief, passing reference to "the extension of the women's franchise" as a historical example of a major constitutional change made by inter-party agreement, without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speaker (Balfour) argues that the "one man one vote" principle logically entails female suffrage, since women are human and the same abstract rights would apply to them — he uses this as a reductio ad absurdum against his opponents, but in doing so explicitly endorses that female suffrage is a logical corollary of the franchise principle. He also lists "woman franchise" as one of the questions Parliament must eventually address in a comprehensive settlement, treating it as a legitimate political question requiring resolution.

The speech focuses on electoral registration procedures, the sale of electoral registers to commercial organisations, and privacy concerns for vulnerable individuals. While it briefly mentions elderly women living alone as one category of people at risk from register misuse, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker mentions protection of pregnant women at work and equal pay during pregnancy as examples of social dimension legislation that could be advanced through majority voting, but this is used as an argument about EU voting rules and the social chapter, not as an argument about women's political rights or civic participation. The reference to women is incidental to the main point about the amendment and unanimity vs. majority voting.

The speaker argues against extending the franchise at this time, opposes "tampering with the franchise," calls further enfranchisement premature, and explicitly states he cannot vote for the Bill. He also denies women's equality with men ("My ideas of women are not that women can be put upon an equality with men"), framing women as angelic figures above rather than equal to men, and urges prioritising "material things" over enfranchisement.

The speaker explicitly supports extending women's suffrage, stating they no longer oppose it once the principle has been conceded, and argues it is "most desirable" to avoid unnecessary grievances by removing the arbitrary age limit on women voters. While they raise a procedural concern about the timing of a general election following a Reform Bill, this is a constitutional/procedural caveat rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment relief, Poor Law reform, and finding work for unemployed men. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status issue.

The speech is focused on the social charter, EU economic policy, and workers' rights directives. The brief mention of pregnant workers and equal treatment in sex discrimination cases are incidental references to specific EU directives, not arguments about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Balfour) explicitly argues that if the suffrage question is to be approached on theoretical/abstract grounds of equal rights, then female suffrage follows logically, stating "I certainly should not so belie the obvious logic of the situation as to refuse my assent to female suffrage as well as to male suffrage" and calling it "perfect folly" to exclude more than half the adult population. Though this argument is deployed tactically to embarrass the Bill's sponsor, it constitutes a substantive endorsement of women's suffrage.

The speech focuses on administrative and legislative questions about the Women's Services Bill—coordination between services, disciplinary frameworks, Orders in Council, training, married women's employment, and voluntary organisations—without making arguments for or against women's political rights or representation. Women's civic participation in the political sense (voting, standing for office, representation) is not addressed.

The speech concerns a petition about British Rail's staffing policy at railway stations and its implications for disabled people, women travelling alone, the elderly, and the young. While women are mentioned, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation — it is purely about transport safety and accessibility.

The speaker explicitly supports adult suffrage and argues that the age limit for women should be the same as for men, then calls on the House to give the Bill a Second Reading — a clear endorsement of expanding women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about Chinese labour in the Transvaal, the accusations of slavery, and the conduct of the Unionist Party during the election campaign. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speaker (Sir J. D. Rees) explicitly supports women's political emancipation, stating "I heartily accept everything inside the Bill," arguing that women cannot be kept out of Parliament once enfranchised, and declaring "I think they should get the franchise, and why they should not is a matter wholly inexplicable to me." His objection is procedural — that the Bill should be introduced by the Government rather than private Members — not a substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech addresses administrative and operational matters relating to women's military services (pay rates, chain of command, training, codification of enactments) but does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention that the Bill "seeks only to elevate members of the women's Services to a proper legal status" is descriptive rather than argumentative about women's civic/political rights.

The speaker (Minister McLoughlin) defends the Bill's maternity leave provisions as "an important step forward" that will "greatly enhance" rights for mothers and women expecting children, explicitly framing expanded maternity entitlements as a positive outcome for women in the workforce.

The speaker (Ms. Eagle) strongly advocates for expanded employment rights for women, including more generous maternity leave (18 weeks), simplified equal opportunities legislation, reversed burden of proof in pregnancy dismissal cases, and criticises the Government for grudgingly and inadequately implementing women's workplace rights. She explicitly frames these as matters of women's equal treatment and rightful place in society.

The speaker advocates for the release of a suffragist prisoner, implicitly supporting the suffrage movement by characterizing her offence as minor and questioning the severity of her imprisonment for political activism.

The speaker explicitly states that "not only was one-third of the male population outside the franchise, but the whole of the women of the country," and calls it "the scandal and disgrace of treating women, because they were women, no better than if they were criminals, paupers, or peers," expressing hope that "women suffrage would form one of the items to be dealt with when the franchise was being tackled."
The speech concerns the management and administration of National Service Hostels, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Member for Merthyr Tydvil) defends women suffrage advocates prosecuted at Manchester and Marylebone, argues their sentences were unjust or too heavy, calls for their release, and criticises the impropriety of a magistrate who was complicit in their ejection sitting on their case — all in support of women exercising their political rights.

The speaker opposes Clause 2 of the Bill, which would extend the franchise to women on equal terms with men (lowering the age from 30 to 21), arguing it would upset a deliberate compromise, add an "unknown number" of women voters unwisely, and undermine Parliament's authority to enact reconstruction legislation. While the speaker expresses general agreement with the Bill otherwise, their substantive argument is against expanding women's voting rights at this time.

The speech is primarily about electoral reform, plural voting, university seats, and whether the current Parliament is bound by decisions of the previous Speaker's Conference. The mention of extending the franchise for women from age 30 to 21 is cited only as a historical precedent to argue that constitutional changes have previously been made without all-party conferences — no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is primarily about Indian self-governance, the partition of Bengal, and democratic traditions in India. The single mention of "women's suffrage" is a passing anecdote about a Burmese village electing a lady as their representative authority, used as an illustrative aside to argue for Indian democratic capacity—no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The Solicitor-General's speech explicitly supports the Sex Disqualification Removal Bill, noting that it removes the bar on appointing women to civil and judicial offices, and argues that this renders special provisions for women assessors unnecessary since women can already be appointed under the new law. This is a substantive endorsement of expanding women's civic participation rights.

The speech is entirely focused on defending university parliamentary representation against abolition under the Representation of the People Bill. While the speaker briefly mentions Eleanor Rathbone and notes that university electorates include "young men and young women," the speech makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation as a class — it concerns the preservation of university seats as a form of functional/corporate representation.

The speaker opposes the Bill that formally incorporates women into the Armed Forces, arguing against women being "organised into the war machine" and stating he will "never vote for establishing a military system which will result in court martialling women." His objections are grounded in opposition to women's integration into military service structures, not merely procedural concerns about the Bill's mechanics.

The speaker explicitly states they voted for the ordination of women measure in the General Synod and is committed to piloting it through the House, demonstrating clear support for women's full participation in Church office.

The speaker explicitly argues that a regional list system for the second chamber would "allow action to secure fair representation for women and ethnic minorities" and could "build in quotas, thus satisfying legitimate claims for equal representation," directly advocating for improved women's political representation as a benefit of his proposed reform.

The speech is primarily about the merits and demerits of university representation in Parliament (the Representation of the People Bill), touching on electoral reform, constituency correspondence burdens, and the speaker's duty to his 40,000 university constituents. While women are briefly mentioned in passing (Miss Rathbone, Mrs. Stocks, and the general note that "a very large number of women" exercise the university vote), no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is primarily about the Maastricht Treaty, parliamentary sovereignty, and economic/monetary union. The brief mention of women not having the vote is used as a rhetorical flourish to illustrate a feared democratic regression, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues for women's representation on the Advisory Committee, supporting an amendment requiring not less than one-fifth of members to be women, and contending that a "non-technical woman who is also a very practical housewife could make a very useful contribution to this Advisory Committee."

The speech is entirely about parliamentary procedure, the Guillotine motion, and the nature of representative government in the context of the Steel Bill debate. It mentions "ordinary men and women" only in a general rhetorical flourish about representation, without making any argument about women's political rights or civic status.

Lord R. Cecil explicitly argues in favour of women's suffrage, stating that withholding votes from women is a serious anomaly that "could be defended upon no principle of democratic legislation," and that women have "an equal right to the franchise with men." His amendment is designed to delay the bill in order to allow time for women's suffrage legislation to be enacted first.

The TARGET speech is a procedural exchange in which a member raises a point of order asking whether women's suffrage is relevant to the Bill, and the Chairman rules it is not relevant. No argument for or against women's political rights is made by the TARGET speakers.

The speaker (Dr. Addison) supports Clauses 1, 3, and 4 of the Bill—endorsing women's access to civil, judicial, and professional roles and expressing cordial agreement with equal opportunity—while explicitly opposing government support for Clause 2 (extending the franchise to women on equal terms with men at age 21), arguing the franchise question was just settled and should not be reopened this session. This constitutes substantive support for women's civic participation in one dimension while substantively opposing an extension of their political franchise in another.

The speaker explicitly declares himself "wholly and absolutely in favour of this Bill" and pledges to support it by voice and vote, endorsing women's enfranchisement and their right to hold civil, judicial, and military offices. He further argues that women fully qualify for the franchise on equal terms with men and criticises the Bill only for not going far enough (e.g., omitting military commissions for women).

The speech is primarily about the Social Protocol/Chapter of the Maastricht Treaty and the parliamentary procedure for ratification. The brief mention of "equality for men and women in relation to work opportunities and treatment at the workplace" is incidental to the argument about the social chapter's economic merits, not a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Churchill) explicitly declines to extend female suffrage to the Transvaal, arguing it would be wrong "to subject a young colony, unable to speak for itself, to the hazards of an experiment which we have not had the gallantry to undergo ourselves," leaving the question to the new legislature instead. This is a clear decision against granting women's political rights at this stage.

The speaker deprecates the tactics of the women's suffrage movement but argues that the punishment inflicted on them was excessive and unjustifiable, implicitly supporting fair treatment for women activists and appealing to the Home Secretary for clemency — a position sympathetic to their cause and civic standing.

The speech is focused entirely on post-war international tensions, the threat of another war, Soviet contributions, and criticism of Churchill and US military influence. The brief mention of "real men and real women" using democratic achievements and "the right to vote" is incidental rhetorical flourish, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Social Chapter of the Maastricht treaty, European competitiveness, unemployment, and the opt-out debate. While the speaker briefly mentions "equality for men and women" as one of several areas covered by qualified majority voting under the social chapter, this is a passing reference cataloguing the chapter's scope, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Lord R. Cecil) explicitly advocates for women's suffrage, arguing it represents a "gross anomaly" that Parliament is obligated to correct, and appeals to Members pledged to women's suffrage to support his Amendment as a means of advancing women's enfranchisement.

The speaker strongly advocates for women's political rights throughout, arguing that the Government should allow a free vote on the Bill, that it is never "too soon to do justice," that women below 30 are entitled to the vote on equal terms with men, and that women's full enfranchisement is urgently needed for postwar reconstruction. Any objections raised are procedural (e.g., timing, draftsmanship) and are attributed to the Government, not endorsed by the speaker.

The speech concerns the merits and demerits of university parliamentary representation and whether abolishing it constitutes bad faith, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" is incidental phrasing about university members generally, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech concerns the fate of Kuwaiti prisoners of war (male and female civilians) held by Iraq and calls for diplomatic efforts to secure their release under UN resolutions. While it mentions female civilians in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on opposition to the Maastricht treaty and European integration, with arguments about trade, democracy, and the social chapter. The single passing mention of "men and women" refers to a minor provision in the social chapter covered by existing court majority voting, and is not an argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is almost entirely focused on European parliamentary constituency boundaries, electoral systems (additional member system), and the timetable for boundary reviews. The brief mention of women is a passing reference to the historical broadening of the franchise ("broadening the franchise so that men and women have equal voting rights") offered as an example of past electoral reform, without making any argument about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about RAF budget estimates and force composition. The brief mention that "Vote A covers both men and women" and that women are not yet constitutionally members of the RAF pending the Army and Air Force (Women's Service) Bill is purely descriptive and administrative, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly commits to voting for the Third Reading of the Bill, arguing on grounds of justice to women, their demonstrated responsible use of the franchise, and the desirability of equal voting rights for men and women regardless of age. He also invokes his election pledge to support equal suffrage rights as further justification.

The speaker explicitly supports the Third Reading of the Bill granting women political rights, arguing that political rights are the best means to secure industrial rights, and states "I believe in all women being represented as well as all men." While he mentions accepting a compromise limiting the franchise to women over 30, he frames this as a concession rather than principled opposition, affirming his support for full adult suffrage for women as a matter of principle.

The speech is primarily focused on the operation of martial law in Natal and the trial of Chief Tilonkwe, with only a passing procedural question about whether the new Transvaal Parliament could "enfranchise women" among a list of other constitutional matters (constituency boundaries, second chamber, native exclusion). No argument is made for or against women's political rights; the mention is merely illustrative of a broader constitutional question.

The speaker supports women's equality in civil and judicial matters (pledging a government bill to achieve this) but opposes extending the franchise to all women on equal terms with men at this time, arguing the recent Representation of the People Act was a settled compromise and that reopening the franchise question is inopportune. This constitutes substantive arguments on both sides: for women's civil/judicial rights and against equal franchise rights for women now.

The speech is entirely focused on UK Air Force estimates, defence policy, personnel numbers, and strategic military concerns. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the personnel count ("men and women") with no argument made about their political rights or civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill on grounds of justice, arguing there is no reason to give a man the vote at twenty-one but deny it to a woman of the same age, and asserts that women display as much or more intelligent interest in politics as men, concluding with a clear statement of intent to vote for the Third Reading.

The speech concerns a trade union picketing bill and the right to attend at a person's residence for peaceful persuasion during labour disputes. The mention of suffragettes is a passing, joking aside urging them to form a trade union — it does not argue for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "I intend to support this Bill" and "I shall support the measure," arguing that women of 21 are as capable as men of the same age and that it is inconsistent to enfranchise women at 30 but not 21, treating the matter as a straightforward question of franchise equality.

The speaker (Elland) characterizes suffragette activists as engaged in "riotous behaviour" and states that their methods meet with "the deepest and most outspoken disapproval" of advocates of women's suffrage, framing the women's direct action negatively and calling for stronger police measures to suppress it, thereby opposing this form of women's political activism.

The speaker explicitly introduces a Bill to remove the sex disqualification barring women from being enrolled as electors or voting at Parliamentary elections, and urges the Government to pledge support for women's enfranchisement, clearly advocating for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports giving women the franchise immediately, arguing that "this right of exercising the franchise shall be given to the women now" and criticising opponents who would vote against the bill because it does not grant full equality as taking a "very petty position." The speech consistently advocates for passing the Bill to enfranchise women.

The speech is entirely focused on criminal justice policy — sentencing reform, bail powers, the Criminal Justice Act 1991, and crime prevention — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The target records the successful motion to bring in a Bill explicitly aimed at removing the sex disqualification barring women from enrolling as electors or voting at Parliamentary elections, with Keir Hardie and others ordered to bring it in — a clear legislative act in support of women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the Maastricht Treaty's social chapter and its economic implications for the UK labour market. While it briefly mentions "equal treatment of men and women" as one of several policy areas that qualified majority voting could extend to, this is cited as an example of unwanted EU intervention rather than as an argument about women's political rights; no substantive position on women's political rights or representation is advanced.

The speech is entirely focused on air defence strategy, RAF estimates, Commonwealth collaboration, missile technology, and national security policy. Women are not mentioned at all in the target speech, and there is no argument made about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speech is entirely focused on military manpower, conscription period lengths, Army training and recruitment, and defence policy — with no mention of women's political rights, women's suffrage, or women's civic participation in any form.

The speech is entirely focused on the question of whether the City of London should retain separate parliamentary representation and the business vote, based on its unique commercial and historical character. While it briefly mentions "men and women" having the right to vote where they live or work, this is incidental to the broader electoral reform debate about constituency boundaries and the business vote, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation as a distinct class.

The speaker (MP for Donegal W.) raises a parliamentary question on behalf of imprisoned suffragists, framing their situation sympathetically by referring to them as "ladies" engaged in "the movement in favour of women's suffrage" and querying whether they are being treated as "ordinary criminals." This implicitly advocates for better treatment of women political activists, signalling support for their cause.

The speech concerns the Welsh Language Bill — specifically the powers of the Welsh Language Board, Welsh-medium education rights, complaints mechanisms, and Welsh language schemes — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The single mention of "women's institutes—Merched Y Wawr" is a passing reference to an organisation as an example of groups that should be represented on the board, not an argument about women's civic status.

The target speech contains multiple speakers (an unnamed opener, Mr. T. Thomson, and Dr. Murray) all of whom strongly support extending the franchise to women aged 21 on equal terms with men, arguing it is an act of justice and that women are fully capable of exercising the vote as responsibly as men.

The speech is entirely focused on the British Rail pension fund and railway privatisation proposals, with no reference to women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speech concerns the Labour party's position on representation in the Committee of the Regions, specifically the composition of an electoral college for Welsh councillors. While "men and women" is briefly mentioned as one of several demographic categories to be represented, no argument about women's political rights is made; this is a passing reference in a speech focused on local government representation and party politics.

The speech is entirely focused on the appropriate yardstick (polling stations vs. population) for allocating permitted cars to transport voters during elections, arguing against disenfranchisement of rural electors. While it briefly mentions "men and women" not being disfranchised, this is a passing reference with no substantive argument about women's political rights as a distinct class.

The speech concerns the legality of picketing and following ("shadowing") individuals during trade disputes under a Trade Disputes Bill. The brief mention of "suffragettes" is used only as an illustrative example of the nuisance that could arise from the bill's provisions, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states long-standing support for "equal suffrage for the two sexes," argues that the age-30 threshold was illogical and wrong, contends that women of 21 (including university graduates) are fully qualified to vote, and concludes by declaring he will vote for the Bill extending the franchise to women on equal terms with men.

Sir J. D. Rees explicitly states he will not support the Bill, argues that women cannot properly administer Indian affairs, uses anecdotal history to disparage women's governance, and says he hopes the Bill will not pass — all while framing his opposition as concern for a better future bill, which amounts to a procedural caveat rather than genuine support for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly supports extending the franchise to women on equal terms with men, advocates for opening both Houses of Parliament to women, criticises opponents of the Bill, and argues that pledges to give women equal rights must be honoured including an equal right to vote.

The target text is a financial/payroll table showing employer and employee contribution rates broken down by category (Men, Women, Boys, Girls), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily concerned with labour policy, manpower/employment issues, the Ministry of Labour, industrial relations, and the 1948 Economic Survey. The brief mention of "womenpower" and "women part of the electorate" are incidental references that make no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speeches (from the West Ham MP and Keir Hardie) advocate for better treatment of imprisoned women suffragettes, explicitly characterising them as political rather than criminal offenders and calling for their reclassification as first-class misdemeanants. This implicitly supports the women's suffrage cause and their right to political activity.

The speaker advocates for better treatment of imprisoned women suffragists by requesting they be classified as first-class misdemeanants, implicitly recognising the legitimacy of their suffragist cause and objecting to their harsh treatment as ordinary criminals.

The speech is about Sunday trading legislation and its economic effects, including a mention that many Sunday shop workers are women who choose to work that day for family financial reasons. While women are referenced, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — it is about employment and retail regulation.

The speech concerns representations about deregulation and tourism, with no reference to women's political rights or representation. The mention of "business men and women" is incidental and does not address women's civic status.

The speech is about Sunday trading reform and its effects on family life, small shops, and employee rights. While it briefly mentions that "the majority of shoppers are women" and that Sunday trading flexibility makes "the woman's role much easier," these are incidental observations about shopping patterns in the context of a Sunday trading debate, not arguments about women's civic status, political rights, or representation.

The speech concerns the abolition of university constituency seats and the franchise for university graduates under the Representation of the People Bill — a matter of electoral redistribution and representation structures — but does not argue for or against women's political rights as a distinct class. The brief passing mention of Eleanor Rathbone and Mary Stocks is incidental, not an argument about women's civic status or rights.

The speech is about a procedural parliamentary dispute over whether the House should be allowed to vote on amendment No. 27 to the Maastricht Bill regarding the social chapter. While the social chapter is briefly mentioned as covering "equality between men and women with regard to labour market opportunities" and "equal pay," these are incidental references within an argument about parliamentary procedure and the Chairman's ruling—no position is argued on women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (by Lord H. Cecil, based on context) concerns the legality and ethics of Sir Edward Carson's speech threatening resistance to Home Rule, the ethics of law-breaking, and the Ulster question. The only mention of "suffragettes" is a passing reference used as one example among several (conscientious objectors, Ulstermen) to illustrate a general philosophical point about individual resistance to law — no argument about women's political rights is made.

The target speeches are entirely concerned with unemployment benefits/donations for post-WWI workers and the government's economic policy. While women are mentioned incidentally (e.g., 12,000-15,000 women drawing unemployment donations, daughters of workers, domestic service), no argument is made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states that the Bill "convinced him more strongly than he would otherwise have been convinced of the urgent necessity of the enfranchisement of women," directly endorsing women's right to vote as a necessary consequence of their exclusion from legislative protection.

The speech is entirely focused on the Maastricht Treaty's social chapter debate — covering labour costs, workers' rights, unemployment, and European competitiveness. Although it briefly mentions "equality between men and women in the labour market and at work" as one of the areas covered by qualified majority voting under the social chapter, this is a passing reference with no argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is a brief quotation from Lord Birkenhead read into the record by Mr. Bing, noting that the committee recommended women's suffrage only by a majority (not unanimously), in contrast to the unanimous recommendation for proportional representation. This is cited as a factual point in a procedural debate about the Speaker's Conference and electoral redistribution, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states he voted for equal pay for women against his party's position, and proudly recounts standing firm even when the majority of his colleagues reversed their vote at the Prime Minister's request, framing this as a matter of conscience and loyalty to principle.

The TARGET speech merely quotes Lord Birkenhead's historical account that the Speaker's Conference was unanimous on everything except the female franchise question, and uses it to correct a factual error about historical unanimity. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, only references the female franchise as a point of historical disagreement.

The speech addresses the legal treatment of imprisoned suffragists (procedural questions about magistrate's orders and prison sentences), but does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or their right to vote. It is a factual ministerial reply about the legal circumstances of the case.

The speech is entirely focused on the abolition of plural voting and electoral reform; the brief mention that "The nation consists of men and women; it does not consist of houses and landed estates" is rhetorical colour supporting the "one man, one vote" principle, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that young women's lack of a vote constitutes a "sex disqualification" and contends that a clause addressing this falls within the scope of the Bill, thereby advocating for extending voting rights to younger women on equal terms with men.

The speaker explicitly calls for extending the Indian franchise to include women (alongside soldiers and literates), stating "I hope that the people of India...will direct their attention...against the franchise...to get a fair and universal franchise in India, which shall give votes, not only to property, but to those who can read and write, to women and to soldiers who have returned from the War." This is a clear, if brief, argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that women should not be excluded from the franchise in the Orange River Colony, stating "there should be no barriers put in the way of women exercising the franchise" and questioning why women should be excluded when the male population had backed the demand for the vote.

The speech is primarily about income tax thresholds, indirect taxation burdens on the poor, and the Excess Profits Duty — a fiscal policy debate. The brief mention of "female suffrage" is purely incidental, used as an example to question the doctrine that taxation and representation are inseparable, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that the age disparity between men (21) and women (30) for political qualification constitutes a sex disqualification, and contends that a clause removing this disparity falls within the Bill's scope — actively supporting equal voting rights for women.

The speaker (Solicitor-General) supports women's jury service as a civic duty and is reluctant to cut it down, endorsing the principle of women serving on juries; but he also supports retaining the clause giving judges discretion to exclude women from certain cases based on the nature of evidence, thus substantively arguing both for women's equal civic participation and for a structured limitation on it.

The speaker explicitly supports the enfranchisement of women, calling it a matter of "supreme importance," criticizing the government for failing to act on it, and stating he will vote for the Amendment as a protest against the Chancellor's implied intention not to enfranchise women before the next election.

The speaker moves a clause designed to ensure women qualifying as solicitors receive the same degree-based reduction in articles (3 years instead of 5) as men, explicitly aiming to extend equal professional privileges to women. This supports women's equal access to a legal profession, which falls within the scope of women's full civic participation.

The speech is primarily about House of Lords reform and the Parliament Bill, with only a brief passing mention of women's franchise as one example among several political reforms of the past 40 years. No argument is made for or against women's political rights; the mention is purely historical and incidental.

The speech by Viscountess Davidson (Hemel Hempstead) is entirely focused on the debate over capital punishment and the Criminal Justice Bill, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The mention of "men and women" being hanged is incidental and does not address women's distinctive civic status.

The speech supports equalising the state pension age upward to 65 for women (noting women's equal economic role and the fiscal sustainability argument), while simultaneously announcing enhanced pension entitlements and home responsibilities protections specifically for women — expanding their civic/financial standing. However, raising women's pension age effectively removes a benefit women currently hold and imposes a restriction on women as a class, while the speaker frames it as equality. The speech thus makes substantive arguments both expanding women's pension rights (SERPS extension, flexibility) and curtailing a current differential right (pension age at 60), constituting genuine two-sidedness on women's distinct civic status in the social security system.

The speech is entirely focused on defence policy, UN military operations, strategic analysis, and government defence estimates. The brief mention of "service men and women" is incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Lord R. Cecil) explicitly argues that women have "a better claim to be considered than any other class in the country" for the franchise, proposes a clause that would delay the Bill unless women are granted the vote on equal terms with men, and frames this as a test of political sincerity for Members pledged to woman suffrage. While he uses a procedural mechanism, his substantive argument is clearly in favour of women receiving the franchise.

The target speech is a government minister defending the consultation process around a maternity leave amendment, specifically rebutting the accusation of one-sidedness by pointing to CBI representations on both sides. The speech addresses procedural fairness in responding to employer concerns about maternity leave notice requirements, not women's political rights or representation.

The speaker criticises Conservative Members for voting against amendments that would protect women's rights to time off for ante-natal care, explicitly arguing that women should have clear statutory protections for civic/employment participation related to maternity. This constitutes a substantive argument in support of women's rights in the workplace.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as a supporter of woman suffrage ("I was a more ardent supporter of woman suffrage twenty-five years ago"), acknowledges genuine arguments in favour of the change (women's increased participation in the industrial sphere), and states he will vote with his noble friend's amendment to hasten women's enfranchisement, despite expressing some caution about the scale of the electoral change.

The speaker moves an amendment to explicitly prohibit sex discrimination in framing electoral rules for India, arguing at length that Indian women deserve the vote, that there is broad Indian support for women's suffrage, and concluding that granting women the vote is "by far the safest course, as well as the most just." The speech is a sustained, substantive argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on electoral registration administration — specifically the role of overseers in maintaining accurate voter registers and identifying plural voters. The brief mention of "suffragettes in prison dress" is a passing comic illustration, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly criticises the White Paper for devoting only nine lines to attracting more women into science and engineering, highlights widespread gender discrimination and the underrepresentation of women in research councils, and argues that the lack of maternity leave and childcare causes women to leave scientific careers — all amounting to a clear advocacy for improving women's professional and civic participation.

The speech concerns conventual laundries and the character of women who manage them in a religious context, not women's political rights or representation. No argument about voting, office-holding, or civic participation is made.

The speech is primarily a tribute to Cambridge's history and an argument in support of the Parliament Bill limiting the Lords' veto power. The brief mention of women being put on the same electoral basis as men is purely a historical observation about franchise extension, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on economic planning, Labour policy, national resource allocation, housing conditions, social security benefits, food profits, and the Budget — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The Labour speaker explicitly criticises the Bill for leaving "all the women" voteless in India and expresses surprise that, since Britain had "definitely admitted the right of women to vote on equal terms with men," the Secretary of State has not carried that principle into the Indian reforms, hoping it can be remedied in Committee.

The speech is entirely focused on the Royal Commission on the Press, the role and conduct of newspapers, and the proposed General Council of the Press. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker explicitly promotes the Local Authorities (Qualification of Women) Bill, arguing it is non-contentious and requesting parliamentary facilities to advance it, thereby supporting women's right to serve in local government office.

The speaker acknowledges the strong demand for women's suffrage in India and explicitly states Parliament would be "making a mistake in denying the opportunity to women to become enfranchised," yet substantively argues against granting it now by urging the Committee to leave the decision to Indian legislative councils, citing deep conservative opinion in India and the principle of impartiality in British governance of India.

The speaker explicitly advocates for granting Indian women the vote on the same property/taxpaying terms as men, arguing it is safer, more just, and that Parliament should settle the question rather than leaving it to Indian Legislative Councils. The speech concludes with a direct call to "grant women the vote."

The speech is about parliamentary privilege, conflicts of interest, and Members of Parliament accepting payments for tabling questions. The brief mention of suffragettes is used only as a historical illustration of the broader democratic struggle against the power of money, not as an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly endorses including women in the Bill on equal terms with men, citing the Socratic/Platonic argument that function rather than sex should determine roles, and acknowledges it as "a very valid argument." He frames the extension of service obligations to women as a logical and necessary consequence of democratic governance and women's equal participation in civic life.

The speech focuses entirely on street prostitution as a residential nuisance and public health issue, arguing for legal reform to manage prostitution more effectively. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that taxing women equally to men is objectionable because "taxation and representation should go together, and women were not allowed to vote," implying women should either be exempt from taxation until they have the vote, or conversely that giving women the vote is necessary — either way, the argument rests on endorsing women's right to political representation as a principle.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly supports women's political enfranchisement in India, arguing for consistency with Britain's recognition of sex equality, citing powerful evidence from Indian women's suffrage advocates, and urging the Secretary of State to incorporate the principle into the Bill or press for it strongly. There is no substantive opposition to women's political rights, only a procedural objection to leaving the matter to unrepresentative Legislative Councils.

The speech concerns a rule about whether female teachers should teach young boys in Irish national schools — an educational staffing matter. It does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's civic/political participation.

The speech is primarily about crime policy, policing, and the right to demonstrate. The brief mention of suffragettes and women's representation in Parliament is used only as a historical illustration to argue that mass demonstrations are no longer necessary today, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that if taxation and representation go together logically, "there should be universal suffrage, male as well as female, totally unconnected with the possession of either real or personal property," explicitly endorsing women's political rights as a logical corollary of the principle under debate.

The speech is entirely focused on Gibraltar's political and economic relationship with Spain and the UK, including border harassment, smuggling, sovereignty, and EU membership. Women's political rights and representation are not discussed; the only mention of women is incidental (women being strip-searched at the border as an example of Spanish harassment).

The speech is about the Newfoundland Act and Canada-Newfoundland confederation, dealing with constitutional, legal, and procedural matters. The only mention of women is a brief factual note that Term 15 extends the franchise to women over 21 in Newfoundland's provincial legislature, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about Royal Air Force matters including radar, uniforms, recruits, married quarters, airfields, and flying standards. The brief mention of the Women's Royal Air Force praises their service contributions and notes complaints about uniforms and flying time, but does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly declares himself "a convinced upholder of women's suffrage" and supports women's political rights in principle, stating he would vote against the Amendment only on procedural/drafting grounds and deference to Indian self-determination — not because he opposes women's franchise. His objection is to the mechanism, not the right itself, which makes this a "for" with procedural caveats rather than a "both."

The question asks the Prime Minister to facilitate passage of a Bill qualifying women to serve on local councils, and the government's reply explicitly states they are "very favourably disposed to this Bill" and will help advance it if an opportunity arises, expressing clear support for women's right to serve in local government.

The speaker explicitly credits the suffragettes with winning women the vote ("The hon. Lady would not have the vote but for the suffragettes"), invoking their rule-breaking as a positive precedent to justify his own conduct, thereby expressing clear support for women's suffrage and the political rights it represents.

The speaker supports women's suffrage in principle ("women suffrage will be introduced in many Provinces of India") but argues against applying it universally in the Punjab specifically, citing serious difficulties there, while leaving the decision to individual Provinces rather than Parliament — thus substantively supporting women's suffrage in some provinces while opposing its imposition in others.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage in principle ("recognise the strength of the case") and expresses confidence it will be enacted in Bombay, while substantively opposing the Amendment to enact it universally across India in the Bill, arguing that imposing it on provinces where there is no demand (e.g., Punjab) would harm rather than help the cause and that self-determination should be left to provincial councils.

The speech concerns improving voter registration rates among service personnel (men and women alike), not any argument about women's distinctive political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the broader category of service voters.

The speech is entirely focused on the question of whether teachers in voluntary/denominational schools should be allowed to give denominational religious instruction, debating religious education policy under the Education Bill. Women are not mentioned as a class with distinctive civic status, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is primarily about franchise qualifications for Indian voters (university graduates, ex-soldiers) under the Government of India Bill. The brief mention of women's enfranchisement is only a passing reference to Earl Winterton's speech on women's rights, used rhetorically to challenge his consistency—no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly argues that withholding votes from women is "a very serious anomaly" that "could be defended upon no principle of democratic legislation" and signals intent to enumerate reasons why women should have votes, clearly supporting women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly defends women suffrage advocates who were prosecuted, argues Parliament is to blame for not listening to their electoral reform demands, and draws a favorable parallel between their actions and those of men who achieved electoral reforms through similar means — framing their cause as legitimate and historically justified.

The speech is entirely focused on Latin American political economy, human rights abuses, trade policy, poverty, and democracy — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speech concerns ensuring that men and women receive their voting papers (i.e., postal/proxy voting administration for service personnel), not about women's political rights or representation as a class. The mention of "men and women" is incidental to a question about electoral administration failures in 1945.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on child adoption law reform — reviewing committee recommendations, explaining specific clauses, and arguing for the Bill's Second Reading. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic participation issues.

The speech is entirely focused on naval defence estimates, fleet readiness, manpower, pay, and shipbuilding policy. The only mention of women is a brief, neutral reference to the WRNS being established as a permanent component of the Royal Navy, which is a factual observation about naval manning rather than an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary reform, executive scrutiny, and democratic accountability. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference to a plaque commemorating suffragette Emily Wilding Davison during a description of a palace tour, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is focused on naval welfare, employment organisations, ex-Service men's charities, and the British Legion. The brief mention of "men and women" in the context of job placements and the criticism of women volunteers in private welfare organisations is about their perceived incompetence and political activity, not about women's political rights or representation as a civic matter.

The target speech is a ministerial answer about the financial arrangements and public subsidies for the Women's Voluntary Services, covering costs borne on the Home Office vote and accounting practices. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker moves the Second Reading of a Bill explicitly designed to amend the Representation of the People Act to make it easier for women to enter Parliament, arguing that increased women's representation is essential for democracy and human rights. She advocates for structural changes (equal nomination signatures, reduced deposits for women candidates, gender labelling on ballot papers) to advance women's political participation.

The speech is entirely focused on equalising the age of consent for homosexual men — a question of sexuality-based discrimination — not on women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of women getting the vote and women going to work appears only as historical analogies to illustrate the broader argument about social progress and equality, without making any substantive argument about women's political rights.

The target speech is a government reply about miners' voting statistics and trade union ballot procedures, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of "men and women" is incidental, referring only to freedom from intimidation in trade union voting, not to civic or political rights of women as a class.

The speaker explicitly states that women are now full members of the Royal Air Force with "the same work as men and the same opportunities of promotion," welcoming their new status as Regulars as "a most welcome development," which is a clear endorsement of women's equal civic participation in a public institution.

The speech is almost entirely about the Government of India Bill (1919) — Indian self-government, franchise extension in India, reform of the Indian constitution, and the speaker's personal reflections on his political career. The single passing reference to opponents of women's suffrage is used as a rhetorical illustration of a "type" who opposes all reforms, not as an argument about women's political rights themselves.

The speaker introduces a Bill specifically designed to increase women's representation in Parliament through concrete measures: showing candidate gender on ballot papers, requiring equal numbers of women and men on nomination papers, reducing the candidate deposit for women, and giving women the casting vote in tied elections. Every argument made is in support of expanding women's political participation.

The speech is primarily about a Compensation for Subsidence Bill addressing mining damage to property. The brief mention of women having votes is used as a rhetorical point to argue that the government must address property damage grievances, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers. The first (Mr. Adamson/Labour) explicitly supports women's political equality in India, regretting "the exclusion of the women of India from the opportunity of standing on a political equality with the men." The second (Sir J. D. Rees) explicitly opposes enfranchising women in India at the same rate as men, calling it beyond his comprehension that anyone could "safely enfranchise as many women as men in India," and urging caution on women's suffrage provisions. Together the TARGET makes substantive arguments on both sides of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Education Bill of 1906, addressing religious education, Nonconformist grievances, Church of England schools, and the merits of undenominational (Cowper-Temple) teaching. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any form.

The speech concerns alleged interference in Northern Ireland elections by Eire and a violent incident at a Unionist meeting; the mention of women and girls is incidental to reporting injuries, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on factory inspection, working conditions, women workers' health and safety, particulars clauses, and the inspectorate staffing — none of which address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned as workers requiring protection under factory law, not as a class with distinctive civic or political rights.

The speaker expresses mild personal reservations about women serving as soldiers in peacetime ("some of the more old-fashioned of us do not quite like the idea"), while simultaneously supporting the Women's Royal Army Corps now that it has been established and arguing that its members should be treated as proper soldiers to improve recruitment — making substantive points on both sides of women's military/civic participation.

The speech concerns restrictions on nurses attending dances and balls, framed as a matter of professional duty and patient care, not women's political rights or civic participation. While the preceding question raises a sex-based comparison, the target speech itself makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a parliamentary question about factory and workshop employment orders concerning women and young persons' working hours, which is a labour/industrial regulation matter. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns trade union recognition and consultation rights for aviation workers (specifically the Aeronautical Engineers' Association) during a corporate merger of B.O.A.C. and B.S.A.A. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Heald) makes a brief interjection claiming the Pankhursts were Tories, which is a partisan historical point rather than an argument for or against women's political rights. The comment references suffragettes only to score a point against the Opposition, without advancing any substantive position on women's political rights or representation.

The Prime Minister explicitly states the Government will not deal with votes for women in the current session and refuses to commit to the next session, while dismissing the suffragette disturbances as irrelevant to Government intentions — effectively blocking legislative progress on women's suffrage.

The speech by Ms Clare Short explicitly and extensively advocates for women's political rights and equality, calling for stronger sex discrimination and equal pay legislation, annual parliamentary debates on women's equality, and celebrating the 75th anniversary of women's suffrage while condemning continued discrimination. She argues forcefully that women deserve full civic and economic equality and criticises the Government for failing to advance it.

The speech is primarily about mining subsidence compensation legislation, not women's political rights. The brief mention of women voters is a rhetorical aside dismissing an opponent's argument that women voters would demand pecuniary benefit from the Bill, arguing that votes should be exercised for the country's good rather than personal gain — this is not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the State registration of nurses — establishing a General Nursing Council, registration requirements, finance, and professional standards. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech is about the erosion of local government powers and the rise of unaccountable quangos, framing this as a democratic deficit ("disfranchisement of electors"). The mention of "placemen and placewomen" is incidental and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech consistently and extensively argues for increasing women's representation in Parliament, framing it as essential to democracy and human rights, and supports legislative changes to achieve this goal. The speaker argues that Parliament as "the jury of the nation" requires more women to avoid a skewed masculine perspective and that changing rules to bring more women into Parliament will improve democracy and society.

The speaker highlights that Labour members cast more votes for women candidates than required in shadow Cabinet elections (averaging five votes for women instead of the compulsory four), arguing this shows Labour's genuine support for women in political leadership and contrasting it favourably with the Conservative party's low number of female MPs.

The speech concerns a secret Army Council Order, strike-breaking, demobilisation grievances, and encouraging young men to join the Army. Women are mentioned only in passing ("both men and women, would have suffered...by the privations") with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the nursing profession — specifically the title and status of assistant nurses, their training, and recruitment — without addressing women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation in any way.

The speech concerns the proposed renaming of "assistant nurses" to "enrolled nurses" in nursing legislation, addressing recruitment, professional titles, and training — not women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only as members of the nursing profession, not in relation to their civic status or political participation.

The speech is entirely focused on Northern Ireland's objection to the title "Republic of Ireland" in legislation, covering postal confusion, constitutional monarchy preferences, and republican sentiment. The brief mention of women not having the vote in Switzerland is an offhand, parenthetical remark used to comment on Swiss republicanism, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about extending workmen's compensation to cover industrial diseases across all trades. While the speaker briefly mentions that women and girls in dangerous trades lack voting representation in Parliament, this is a passing rhetorical point in service of the compensation argument rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that because Parliament is elected only by men, it must ensure justice is done to women, and that failing to do so would strengthen women's demand for the vote — a clear endorsement of women's suffrage as a logical consequence of their exclusion from political representation.

The speech is primarily about military conscription, election pledges, and the Army bill, with only a passing incidental reference to "the women's vote" as a tactical electoral consideration. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is primarily about the Plural Voting Bill and electoral reform (abolishing plural voting, lodger franchise, faggot votes in Scotland). The speaker mentions "extension of the franchise to women" only once in passing as an example of what opponents say should also be done, without arguing for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that the workers most affected by dangerous industrial diseases are "largely women and girls, who were not represented in this House, and who had no power by vote of making their desires known," and asserts that if they had the vote, protective legislation would already have passed by a large majority — a clear endorsement of women's political rights as the remedy for their lack of representation.

The target speech focuses entirely on colonial welfare, education, health, agriculture, and development policy in the Colonial Empire. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on conscription, military service, breach of faith with soldiers and the electorate, and the by-election result in West Leyton. The mention of "women and absent voters" is a passing factual reference to the composition of the electoral transfer, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech calls for adequate representation of women (and Africans) on the Council of Makerere College, and the response from Mr. Creech Jones affirms there is no reason why more women should not be appointed, both supporting greater women's representation in a public governance body.

The speech is primarily about the Ministry of Health Bill, focusing on extending medical knowledge, cooperation with local authorities, advisory councils, and health administration. The brief mention of women is limited to requesting a women's consultative council to advise on matters affecting women and children in a health context, which does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or civic representation.
