The speech is entirely focused on keeping a local maternity unit open for constituents in Hyndburn, arguing on grounds of healthcare access, community choice, and procedural fairness. While it mentions that five men made a decision affecting women and that women should have choice in maternity care, these references are incidental to a healthcare/NHS policy argument, not arguments about women's civic status, voting rights, political representation, or fitness for political participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the percentage of women MPs should be increased from 8-9% to 20, 30, 40, or 50%, stating this is one reason why women's representation in the House of Commons ought to be improved, and endorses the view expressed by a female MP that women in Parliament bring more reality and experience to debates on family issues.

The speech concerns railway pension schemes, the privatisation of British Rail, and inadequate consultation with rail unions — with only incidental references to "railwaymen and women" and "maternity provisions" that do not argue any position on women's political rights or civic participation.

The target speeches (Sir Donald Maclean and Mr. Thomas) focus entirely on the Ministry of Health Bill — its structure, coordination of health authorities, housing, children's welfare, Poor Law reform, and application to Ireland and Scotland. Neither speaker makes any argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation; the brief mention of "men and women" on advisory councils is incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is Churchill's lengthy defence of a temporary Military Service/Conscription Bill, focused entirely on military necessity, election pledges regarding conscription, and post-war Army organisation. The brief mention of "women's vote" appears only in the preceding context (Churchill's preceding speech noting Thomas tried to raise a conscription scare to "get the women's vote"), not in the TARGET itself, which makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely focused on the failure of the Education Bill — discussing public control over schools, ecclesiastical versus municipal control, religious teaching, teacher compensation, and tribute to the President of the Board of Education. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker supports women's equal pay rights by detailing a protracted legal battle by female canteen workers against British Coal and arguing that existing legislation is inadequate to protect women's successful equal pay claims, explicitly calling for stronger measures (including the EU directive) to advance women's employment rights.

The target speech covers two administrative matters: the formatting of electoral registers (Mrs. vs. Miss) and encouraging voter registration. Neither passage argues for or against women's political rights — the electoral register question is a clerical/printing issue, and the voter registration question applies equally to men and women without addressing their distinctive civic status.

The speech focuses entirely on tuberculosis in Glasgow — death rates, hospital staffing, nursing recruitment, and radiologists — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The mention of women is solely in the context of wartime nursing service and recruitment into the nursing profession, which is a healthcare staffing issue, not a matter of women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker explicitly proposes that the Bill be delayed unless women are granted the franchise on equal terms with men, and argues that women are no less qualified than current electors, have the same stake and intelligence, and are a larger class unjustly excluded from electoral power — a substantive endorsement of women's suffrage.

The speech is entirely focused on Government expenditure on Merseyside, local government funding, urban regeneration, and the centralisation of power away from local councils. The brief mentions of "placewomen" and "placemen" refer to unelected quango appointees generally, not to women's political rights as a distinct issue; no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is about VAT on fuel, compensation packages for pensioners and the disabled, and Parliamentary voting behaviour — it mentions "men and women" in the House only as a passing reference to MPs benefiting from a tax vote, with no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns training allowances for women under the Ministry of Labour's training schemes, which is a welfare/labour policy matter. It does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of their civic/political participation.

The speaker (Mr. O'Shaughnessy, Limerick W.) frames his question to highlight that many women do not want the parliamentary franchise and asks whether the Government will consult public opinion before making any change — implying skepticism toward extending the franchise to women and seeking to slow or block such legislation.

The speech is entirely about a maternity analgesia bill — protecting women during childbirth and regulating small maternity homes — which is a health/welfare matter. Although the speaker is a female MP (Mrs. Manning) advocating for women's interests, the speech makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of their civic/political participation.

The target speech concerns plural voting registration and whether a proposed clause is necessary, mentioning women only in passing as one of several exceptions (alongside aliens, lunatics, and peers) to the general rule that registered voters may vote. No argument about women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Prime Minister Campbell-Bannerman) dismisses the suggestion that the existence of women who don't want the franchise is a reason to withhold it, calling the proposal "impracticable," and implicitly treats women's parliamentary franchise as a legitimate matter for future legislation rather than something to be blocked by polling non-supporters.

The speech is about post-war German dismantling policy, trade union representations, and wartime casualties in the speaker's constituency. Women are mentioned only as victims of wartime bombing alongside children, not in any context relating to their political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the coal mining industry debate — wages, hours, nationalisation, and the Commission of Inquiry — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "an electorate, both of men and of women, such as has never expressed its opinion upon things before" is a passing factual reference to the expanded electorate, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech by Mr. J. Jones concerns the disparity between honours and money granted to generals/admirals versus common soldiers, widows, and bereaved families after WWI. While he mentions widows and women left behind in passing, he makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is a parliamentary question about a magistrate's remarks concerning girls brought to London by suffragettes, focusing on child welfare and the Home Secretary's response — not making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker briefly but explicitly endorses women's political rights as a historical wrong that was rightly corrected, stating "The denial of votes and political representation to women was wrong, but we got over that earlier this century." This is a clear, affirmative endorsement of women's suffrage and representation, even if it is a passing remark within a speech primarily about tobacco and NHS policy.

The speech is entirely about European unity, the Council of Europe delegation to Strasbourg, and the persecution of religious freedom in Eastern Europe. While the speaker briefly mentions sending "men and women" who believe in the movement, this is incidental phrasing with no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a parliamentary business announcement listing upcoming legislative agenda items. While it mentions the Married Women (Restraint upon Anticipation) Bill, this is a property/contract law matter unrelated to women's political rights, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speech is about parliamentary procedure — specifically whether bills should be debated on the floor of the House or sent to a Standing Committee upstairs. The Women's Enfranchisement Bill is mentioned only as an illustrative example of a controversial bill, not to argue for or against women's enfranchisement itself.

The speaker explicitly argues that Parliament is unrepresentative because women make up only one tenth of its membership while comprising more than half the population, framing this as a reason the House is "out of touch." This constitutes a clear, if brief, argument in favour of greater women's political representation.

The speech focuses entirely on economic inequality, earnings dispersion, unemployment, education, and labour market policy in the context of the Queen's Speech. Women's political rights are not argued for or against; the only mention of women is a passing reference to younger female constituents starting families, which is a social observation about labour market disengagement, not an argument about civic or political rights.

The speaker explicitly and enthusiastically supports the Bill, arguing that women are entitled to the vote "on exactly the same terms as men," deserve to sit in Parliament, and should hold any public office "coequally with men." The speech contains no substantive opposition or qualification to women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on overseas aid, development policy, the UN, population control in the developing world, and global poverty. While the speaker briefly mentions that women in developing countries are rarely empowered to own land or borrow money, and that population control alone is insufficient to free women from burdens, these are passing observations within an aid/development debate and do not argue a position on women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for equal pay for equal work for women teachers, invoking the principle of women's equal civic and professional standing, and urges Parliament to support this reform. While focused on pay equity rather than voting rights, the speech explicitly singles out women as a class deserving equal treatment in public professional life and appeals to the newly enfranchised women voters, placing it squarely within the scope of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill giving women the vote on equal terms with men at age 21, stating "I see no reason whatever against it" and "the concession to women is right, and that to me is a sufficient reason," while arguing that women's demonstrated competence at the last election justifies extending the franchise.

The speech is primarily about military preparedness, compulsory training, and army reform. The passing reference to suffragettes being kept out of Parliament by police is used only as a rhetorical illustration of the speaker's argument that force is the ultimate remedy — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on police pension regulations, pay scales, and the Oaksey Committee's recommendations. While the preceding speech briefly mentions a reduction in women's pension contributions, the target speech makes no argument whatsoever about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Care of Cathedrals (Supplementary Provisions) Measure, discussing cathedral fabric maintenance, funding, and administration. The only mention tangentially related to women is a brief passing remark welcoming the Church of Scotland's vote to ordain women as priests, but no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The speaker explicitly shares the same "ideal of citizenship" as the Bill's promoter, states that "all legal disabilities attaching to sex are out of date," and pledges to "cordially support this Bill" on Clauses 1 and 3. His only reservation is a procedural/honour-based objection to Clause 2 (the franchise clause) on the grounds that it would alter a recent compromise he was personally bound by, not because he opposes equal franchise in principle — he affirms the goal should be reached "step by step" at "the earliest opportunity."

The speaker explicitly urges the House to give the Bill a Second Reading, endorses the franchise experiment for women as justified by the last General Election, argues that women of twenty-one are more capable voters than men of the same age, and makes a broad case that women deserve equal standing in constitutional, municipal, and Parliamentary life.

The speaker explicitly supports the Women's Emancipation Bill, stating "I desire to support this Bill" and declaring lifelong support for equal rights for women, including the right to vote and sit in Parliament. The speech argues against those urging delay and affirms that women have established their right to the vote.

The speech is focused on Welsh devolution, democratic deficits caused by quangos, and the case for a Welsh Assembly as a mechanism for democratic accountability in local government. Women's political rights or representation are not argued for or against; the only passing mention is "chairmen and chairwomen of quangos," which is incidental and makes no argument about women's civic status.

The speech focuses on advocating for better pay and working conditions (sick pay, holiday pay) for Sunday-only retail workers, who are predominantly women. While it highlights women's economic vulnerability and sacrifices, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on local government boundary reform, the winding-up of the Boundary Commission, and the principles for reviewing local government structure. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speech concerns pension compensation for workers displaced by gas industry nationalisation. The brief mention of "men or women" who served the industry is incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The target speech is focused on incapacity benefit policy (rates, qualifying periods, disability living allowance, child dependency increases) and briefly addresses the Graham case concerning women aged 60-65 whose invalidity benefit has been suspended pending an ECJ ruling. This is a social security/benefits administration matter, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports increasing women's representation in Parliament, arguing that proportional representation would achieve this goal by pointing to evidence that countries using PR have far more women in their legislatures. This is a substantive argument in favour of women's political representation.

The TARGET speech (the first speaker) explicitly opposes women sitting on borough and county councils, calls the prospect of women sitting in Parliament "ridiculous and degrading," and argues that women are not suited for political life — opposing the Bill as a step toward female suffrage. The second speaker (Evans) similarly votes against the Bill's Second Reading on the grounds that women should not take part in public affairs. Both substantive contributions in the TARGET oppose women's political rights.

The speaker opposes the Bill primarily because it is a step toward female suffrage and women sitting in Parliament, framing it as a cynical "sop" to delay suffragette agitation rather than genuine reform, and implicitly opposing both women's suffrage and their presence in Parliament throughout the speech.

Dr. Shipman strongly supports women being directly elected to county and borough councils, argues for women's capacity to hold administrative and civic roles, praises their intellectual achievements, and congratulates the Government for bringing the Bill forward — all while explicitly separating this issue from (but not opposing) Parliamentary franchise.

The speech is entirely focused on the effectiveness and wisdom of defence measures, conscription policy, and military preparedness. While the speaker mentions "women and children" as civilians to be defended, this is rhetorical framing about national defence, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly and enthusiastically supports the Bill throughout, arguing that women deserve equal political rights, that denying them the vote is "mere mockery" and like keeping them "in chains," and pledging to vote for the Second Reading. He also affirms women's fitness for any position in the State, including having stood as a parliamentary candidate against him.

The speaker (Ms Short, Birmingham Ladywood) explicitly and enthusiastically supports increasing women's representation in Parliament, endorsing the Labour party's all-women shortlists and arguing that equal numbers of men and women in Parliament would improve democracy and create a more civilised society.

The TARGET speech is a procedural interjection asking Mr. Manningham-Buller to clarify whether his opposition to the Bill (on grounds that it cannot be amended to protect pre-1935 cases) means he will vote against it, thereby harming women who would benefit. The debate concerns the legal reform of restraints upon anticipation in property settlements, not women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns legal proceedings under the Statute of Edward III regarding agrarian offences in Ireland, with only a passing mention that suffragists were imprisoned under the same statutory provision. No argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Ms Short) explicitly supports increasing women's representation in Parliament, expressing pride in the Labour party's measures to achieve 80 women Labour MPs and eventual 50% representation, and endorsing action by all parties to accelerate progress toward gender equality in the House of Commons.

The speaker explicitly states that women are suffering from disabilities that should be removed, supports the Bill "whole-heartedly from beginning to end," and argues that women should be placed on equality with men in the franchise and other matters, dismissing age restrictions as relics of "a rather stupid prejudice" and "the mediæval age."

The speaker explicitly states he will "vote for the Second Reading of this Bill without hesitation," affirming that treating women on the same basis as men is "a fundamental Socialist principle" and calling the existing unequal provision "degrading." He argues for extending equality to women in financial and legal matters, framing it as social advancement.

The speaker argues that a Woman Suffrage Bill is of such vital constitutional importance that it must be considered by the full Committee of the Whole House rather than a small Grand Committee, treating women's suffrage as a weighty political right deserving maximum parliamentary scrutiny — implicitly supporting it as a legitimate measure of franchise expansion.

The speaker explicitly endorses increasing women's representation in Parliament, supports the Labour party's policy of selecting more women candidates, and expresses enthusiasm for having more than 80 Labour women MPs after the next election who will "make the many changes that are necessary" to ensure women's views are better expressed in the House.

The speaker argues that the Bill is an attempt to "propitiate the suffragettes" and frames it dismissively, while the preceding context (especially Viscount Helmsley and Mr. Evans) makes clear this debate is about women's eligibility for local councils as a step toward full political participation; the speaker's mockery of those hoping to appease suffragettes signals opposition to the expansion of women's political roles.

The speaker raises a procedural concern to protect a Member's right to bring forward a Motion specifically for "the enfranchisement of women," arguing that a dummy Bill could be used to block such discussion and asking the Speaker to safeguard that right. By advocating for the preservation of this Motion's opportunity for debate, the speaker implicitly supports women's enfranchisement coming before the House.

The speech by Captain Hewitson (Hull, Central) focuses entirely on Cold War politics, European security, German rearmament, trade union concerns, and calls for parliamentary unity. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (comprising two speakers, the first unnamed Labour member and Mr. Hugh Edwards) both explicitly support women's full political and civic emancipation, including equal franchise, removal of legal disabilities, and access to professions. The first speaker urges the House to support "full and free political rights" and "full and free power under the law" for women; Edwards states he is "in favour of every Clause in this Bill in principle" and advocates extending women's franchise and public participation as beneficial to the State.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill and women's emancipation throughout, arguing that if members agree the principle is right there is no justification for delay, and asserting that "women, whatever their class in the social order, are quite capable of exercising all the rights of citizenship as well and as ably as men." The speech rebuts procedural objections and urges the House to vote according to its stated principles in favour of women's political rights.

The speech is a wide-ranging review of colonial policy covering economic development, trade unions, health, education, and constitutional progress in various territories. While it mentions "men and women" in passing in the context of colonial public service training, it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the constitutional debate over the House of Lords veto and the relations between the two chambers; women's political rights are mentioned only in a brief passing reference to the Female Suffrage debate being "talked out" last session, with no argument for or against women's political rights made.

The speaker explicitly supports greater women's representation in Parliament and acknowledges the unfairness women face in getting elected, while simultaneously opposing specific legislative mechanisms in the Bill (lower deposits for women, tie-break rules favouring women, compulsory dual-seat quotas) as discriminatory or counterproductive to the cause of women's political participation.

The speaker explicitly declares he intends to vote for the Second Reading of the Bill and supports women's emancipation as "inherently just," acknowledging his own male prejudices while arguing that women deserve open competition and removal of barriers. His admission of not wanting a female Lord Chancellor is framed as personal prejudice rather than a substantive opposing argument against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that women deserve full representation in the administration of the Ministry of Health Bill and advocates for a consultative council composed exclusively of women, explicitly citing women's underrepresentation on other proposed councils and their importance to the bill's success. This is a substantive argument for greater women's political representation and participation in public governance.

The speaker (identifiable from context as the Speaker of the House/Conference chair) explains that the age limit of 30 for women voters was a pragmatic compromise to achieve numerical parity between male and female voters, not a principled objection to women's suffrage. This explanation supports the extension of women's franchise and implicitly endorses the principle of equal political participation, while clarifying the technical reason for the age restriction.

The speech is primarily a tribute to James Keir Hardie and a proposal to erect a memorial to him in the Palace of Westminster. While it briefly mentions Hardie's contribution to "the political freedom of women," this is a passing reference without any argument made for or against women's political rights; the speaker explicitly says he does not want to "call attention to the singular contribution Keir Hardie made to the political freedom of women."

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's equality in work, public life, and the family, criticising the Government for opposing proposals that would deliver equality and arguing that women will vote to change the government to achieve it.

The speaker (Ms Clare Short) explicitly champions women's equality in politics and public life, criticising Conservative Members for jeering at debates on women's rights, celebrating Jo Richardson's work to establish a Minister for women, and arguing that women's demands for equality in the workplace, family, and public life are a serious political force deserving full representation and policy action.

The speech is almost entirely focused on Army reform, military training, the Territorial Forces Bill, and imperial defence. The single passing reference to female suffrage ("Inasmuch as the New Zealand people had been held up as an example in regard to female suffrage, there was no reason why they should not be regarded as being sensible in regard to the physical training of the young") makes no argument for or against women's political rights; it merely uses the New Zealand suffrage example as a rhetorical analogy to justify taking New Zealand's military training practices as a model.

The speech is entirely focused on the Genocide Convention and its ratification by the UK, addressing international law, crimes against humanity, and the United Nations. Women are mentioned only incidentally as victims alongside men and children, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech opposes an amendment to create a women-only consultative council under a public health bill, arguing instead for mixed councils with equal representation regardless of sex. The debate is about the composition of health advisory bodies, not about women's right to vote, stand for office, or broader civic participation — the speaker explicitly frames their position as opposition to "sex privilege" in an administrative/health policy context, which falls outside the scope of women's political rights as defined.

The speaker argues forcefully against gender discrimination in sports clubs, calling for denial of grants, lottery funding, rates relief, and licensing to clubs that exclude or discriminate against women members, framing this as a matter of civic equality that should be addressed by government action.

The speech is primarily about the ventilation, accommodation, and building improvements for the Houses of Parliament. The only mention of women is an incidental reference to receiving a deputation of "woman suffragists," used as an example to illustrate the lack of adequate meeting rooms — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly opposes Labour's proposals for women-only shortlists and quotas to increase women's representation in Parliament, calling positive discrimination "very degrading to women" and endorsing Hattersley's view that the plan was "wrong in principle." While she expresses support for women's advancement in general, her substantive argument is against the specific mechanisms designed to increase women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly supports women having guaranteed representation on the consultative councils, arguing that without it women will be "hopelessly outnumbered" and unable to make themselves heard. They directly oppose the government's resistance to women's demands for proportional representation, advocate for a women's consultative council, and state they are instructed by their constituency to support the Amendment guaranteeing women's representation.

The speech is a lengthy debate contribution on defence and rearmament policy (National Service pay, Anti-Aircraft Command, Colonial troops, Germany, Korea, etc.), with only a passing rhetorical question about whether women formerly manned radar stations during the war and how many remain available — no argument is made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker explicitly states "he himself was opposed to the woman suffrage movement" and opposes the Bill on conscientious grounds, making his opposition to women's suffrage direct and unambiguous, even if the speech is primarily about the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill.

The speech is a wide-ranging foreign affairs address covering Korea, Asia, the Middle East, Germany, and NATO/Atlantic defence, with no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related topic.

The Minister defends the deliberate inclusion of women's organisations (including working-class women's bodies) in nominations to Gas Consultative Councils, explicitly framing this as ensuring "adequate representation of the special interests of women" — a positive stance toward women's structured civic/political representation.

The speech is a parliamentary question about the administrative classification of imprisoned suffragists into prison divisions, not an argument for or against women's political rights. It addresses procedural/penal treatment of convicted suffragists without making any substantive claim about whether women should have the right to vote or participate in politics.

The speaker explicitly states "The vote has been given to women" and welcomes women's political participation, noting that women in his Leeds constituency are keen on housing reform and that "we shall want the help of the women to carry it through" — a clear endorsement of women's newly granted voting rights and their role in political life.

The speech is overwhelmingly about colonial affairs in Malaya, East Africa, and the Commonwealth, with no substantive argument about women's political rights. The brief mention of "education of women" in Malaya refers to domestic standards and child-rearing, not civic or political participation, and the reference to "universal suffrage" concerns colonial self-government timelines, not women's political rights specifically.

The speaker (Lady Olga Maitland) uses anecdotal evidence of Labour male MPs dismissing women's quotas as "nonsense" and the "Tea Room revolt" to mock and undermine Labour's quota/positive discrimination policies for women's political representation, framing these measures as artificial and counterproductive rather than genuinely advancing women's political participation.

This lengthy speech by Mr. Eden concerns the Schuman Plan for European coal and steel integration, Franco-German relations, sovereignty, and British foreign policy. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point in the speech.

The speaker explicitly welcomes that "women were to receive a small instalment of justice in the matter of becoming eligible to serve on local bodies dealing with education, poor law reform, and sanitation," expressing support for women's political participation at the local level. He also signals further support by noting he hoped "before the debate closed there would be an opportunity of putting that question before the House in a more concrete form" regarding women's political enfranchisement.

The speech is about wage rates for women cleaners in Government Departments and the ongoing consideration of their pay claim under wages policy. It addresses employment pay rather than women's civic participation, voting rights, or political representation, and makes no argument about women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on Irish primary education funding, teacher salaries, school conditions, and the Gaelic League — none of which engage with women's political rights or representation. The passing references to "men and women" teachers concern employment conditions, not civic or political rights.

The target speech briefly criticizes the Labour party for not mentioning their proposal for a women's ministry, but does not itself argue for or against women's political rights — it is a political point-scoring remark about a perceived omission in a debate, not a substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech mocks the Labour party's quota system for women in shadow Cabinet elections, highlighting its failure (only two of four required women gaining sufficient votes) as evidence of the "triviality" of gender-based electoral mandates. This implicitly opposes quota-based mechanisms for women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on naval administration, Admiralty expenditure, demobilisation, mine-clearing operations, dockyard staffing, and naval policy. Women are mentioned only in passing as workers at naval stations during the war, with no argument made about their political rights or civic status.

The speech is primarily about supporting mothers' pensions (widows' pensions) as a social welfare reform, not about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing, non-argumentative reference: "The mere fact that the women of the country now have the vote makes it certain that its advent will be brought much nearer," which notes women's suffrage as a contextual fact to support the pension scheme coming sooner, rather than making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns administrative arrangements for ensuring naval personnel (men and women) can register to vote while stationed abroad, without making any argument about women's political rights as a distinct class or civic status.

The speech is primarily a sustained argument against the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill (a marriage law reform debate), not about women's political rights. The sole mention of women's suffrage is a procedural suggestion to "shelve this question until the question of women's suffrage was decided" so women's real views could be known — this is an instrumental reference used to delay a marriage bill, not a substantive argument for or against women's suffrage itself.

The speaker explicitly refuses to extend the university education grant scheme to women, citing no sufficient interruption of women's educational opportunities and strong objection to any fresh financial liability — effectively arguing against extending this civic benefit to women who served.

The target speech is primarily about the representation of landowners, farmers, and workmen on agricultural councils; the brief mention of women is purely incidental ("I would not do anything to cut down the representation of the workmen or the representation of women, horticulture, education or research") and makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns administrative procedures for electoral registration of Service personnel (both men and women), focusing on logistical implementation rather than making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly expresses support for women's political participation, noting that "women are more politically conscious than ever before," that women now vote independently, and expressing disappointment that so few women were returned to the House of Commons while praising those who were elected. These are affirmative statements supporting women's political representation and civic engagement.

The speaker (Mr. Alan Simpson) challenges the preceding speaker by arguing that the Law Lords' ruling would have been unnecessary if the Government had simply treated women equally in the workforce, and pointedly asks whether voters consciously elected a Government to deny women equal treatment — implicitly advocating for women's equal rights at work.

The speech is primarily about naval officers' pay, the Women's Royal Naval Service demobilisation (as an administrative/workforce matter, not a question of women's political rights), submarine warfare, and naval scientific research. The mention of the WRNS concerns a broken promise about demobilisation timelines and its effect on male ex-servicemen's employment, not women's civic status or political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equality in society, condemns the patronising attitudes toward women's rights, criticizes the Government for steps backward on women's equality, and declares she will vote for the Opposition amendment advancing equal treatment for women under the law.

The speech is entirely focused on the Nurses Registration Bill — supporting state registration, professional status, remuneration, and representation of working nurses on the Council. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, standing for office, or civic participation; women are mentioned only as members of the nursing profession, not as a class with distinctive civic status.

The speech concerns the procedural handling of plural voting complaints after a General Election, including police investigations and the role of the Attorney-General and Director of Public Prosecutions. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on debating old age pensions policy — its cost, funding mechanisms, Australian and German comparisons, and the merits of contributory vs. non-contributory schemes. The single passing reference to women having votes ("perhaps that was the reason why his hon. friend would postpone this proposal until women had votes") is a brief rhetorical aside that does not argue a position on women's political rights.

Sir F. Hall explicitly advocates for removing women from railway employment and giving their jobs to unemployed men, directly opposing women's right to participate in the workforce on equal civic terms with men in this post-WWI context of women's public employment.

The speech is a ministerial response about administrative arrangements for compensation of women discharged from auxiliary corps, referring questioners to other departments. It neither argues for nor against women's political rights or civic participation; it deals solely with pension/compensation administrative jurisdiction.

The speaker explicitly calls on the Minister to increase the representation of women in the foresight exercise teams, framing greater female representation as important and desirable. This is a clear, if brief, argument in support of women's political/civic representation in governance structures.

The speaker (Widdecombe) explicitly opposes positive discrimination/quotas for women in politics, arguing it is "patronising" and that women should earn seats on their own merits, while also dismissing the argument that only women can represent women. These are substantive arguments against specific mechanisms for advancing women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Tomato and Cucumber Marketing Scheme — registration of producers, advisory committees, definitions of glasshouses, import policy, and the health of the horticultural industry. The brief mention of the Women's Institute and WVS as potential consumer representatives on advisory committees is purely incidental and advances no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the imprisonment of Captain Grogan in East Africa for an unlawful assembly related to the flogging of native servants, and the adequacy of police protection for white settlers. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation; the reference to "insults to English women" is incidental to a colonial affairs question.

The speaker opposes the Labour-proposed women's ministry, rejects positive discrimination and special treatment for women in candidate selection, dismisses "angry feminism," and argues that women have already achieved fair representation through merit — effectively opposing structural measures to advance women's political representation while accepting only the status quo.

The speaker briefly but positively notes that the Irish Council Bill's franchise "is going to include women voters" and states "I do not think the Council will be any the worse from the fact that it will to a certain extent represent Irish women," expressing clear support for women's enfranchisement under this measure.

The speech is a parliamentary question and answer about the number of town and county councils in Scotland and their electorate composition, including women electors. It provides statistical information without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's inclusion on the Industrial Court tribunal, arguing that women's representation on such bodies is vital both for women workers' interests and for men's, and expresses strong disappointment at the Government's resistance to the Amendment requiring at least one woman on the Court.

The TARGET speech is primarily about Welsh devolution and constitutional reform, using votes for women as a passing historical analogy to illustrate a pattern of establishment resistance to reform demands. No substantive argument about women's political rights is made; the reference is purely rhetorical and incidental.

The first speaker (unnamed) supports women serving on local bodies but opposes extending the chairmanship privilege, representing a nuanced "for with limits" position. MR. HARMOOD-BANNER explicitly supports women's suffrage ("I am in favour of women having the vote") while substantively opposing women sitting on city councils or in Parliament, making a genuine two-sided argument on different aspects of women's political participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the "empowerment, enfranchisement and liberation of women" depends on their ability to control their own fertility, and advocates for voluntary family planning resources as essential to women's autonomy and civic participation. The speech frames women's bodily autonomy and reproductive choice as foundational to their broader political empowerment.

The speech is primarily about secondary education policy, the educational ladder, class distinctions, and democratic access to education. The brief mention of "all citizens, women as well as men" is a passing reference to inclusive education, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on industrial relations, joint consultation between management and workers, and productivity — with no substantive argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The incidental mentions of "men and women" in the workforce are generic references to workers, not arguments about women's distinctive civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the invalidity benefit/incapacity benefit legislation, arguing that the financial crisis was government-made and that the Bill unfairly burdens vulnerable male claimants and their families. While women workers are mentioned in passing as economic participants, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about the distribution of industry and development areas policy, including factory placement and diversification. While it mentions employing female labour in certain regions, this is purely in the context of industrial economics and labour supply, not as an argument about women's political rights, civic participation, or representation.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly advocates for women's right to vote on equal terms with men, arguing that women have earned the franchise through their wartime contributions and are entitled to full political equality. The speech directly appeals to the Government to grant women the vote "on precisely the same terms as men" and calls for a free vote to pass the Bill immediately.

The speaker (Major Astor) opposes giving the Bill a Third Reading on behalf of the Government, citing the recent Representation of the People Act as a sufficient franchise reform, arguing it is not the right time to "tinker" with franchise again, and raising drafting objections — all amounting to opposition to extending equal franchise to women at this stage. While the Government pledges a bill on civil/judicial equality, the speaker explicitly asks the House not to pass this franchise equality bill.

The speaker explicitly includes women in the franchise for the proposed Irish Council ("the same as the Parliamentary franchise, except that it includes peers and women"), expresses personal approval ("I should be very sorry if women were not allowed to take part in any good work"), and further provides that women may be appointed as additional members of the Education Committee — all positive endorsements of women's civic participation.

The speech concerns a pension/superannuation clause for teachers in a London County Council Bill. While the speaker briefly notes that half the teachers are women and lack votes (and therefore cannot exercise political influence), this is used as an incidental argument about the teachers' limited lobbying power rather than as a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech supports a judicial pensions bill primarily on the grounds that it provides security for wives and dependants of judges, but the argument is about pension provision and financial security, not about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The mention of women is incidental to the bill's welfare provisions, not an argument about their distinctive civic status.

The speech concerns military incursions by Turkish forces into Persian territory and attacks on Christian villages, with a diplomatic response about representations to the Sublime Porte. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation; the mention of "women and children" refers to victims of violence, not to any civic or political status of women.

The speaker briefly but explicitly endorses women's suffrage ("we have had the good sense to give women the vote") and uses it as a positive foundation for his argument that women's budgeting competence makes them reliable supporters of fiscal discipline — framing female enfranchisement as a clear benefit to democracy.

The speech is entirely about the Festival of Britain Bill and the question of opening a fun fair on Sundays. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status of women.

The speaker explicitly supports giving women equal voting rights ("I hope the Government will bring in a Bill that will give absolute equality to the sexes in the matter of the vote") and argues that the current Bill is insufficient because it does not also grant women industrial freedom and full emancipation. The speaker's criticism is that the Bill does not go far enough in securing women's rights, not that women should lack political rights.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on economic policy, unemployment, capitalism, and the failures of government monetary and fiscal policy. The brief mention of "the suffragettes" is purely historical and rhetorical—used to illustrate the value of the ballot box as a mechanism for economic power—without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on Royal Air Force Air Estimates for 1950–51, covering aircraft procurement, command structures, manpower, training, and reserve forces. Women are mentioned only incidentally as "airwomen" in personnel statistics, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a £50,000 grant to Lord Cromer for his services in Egypt, and arguing that the government should instead spend public money on social reforms like old-age pensions for working men and women. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "worn out and incapacitated working men and women"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states they will support the Government in the Division Lobby (voting for the Bill extending equal franchise to women), quotes Asquith approvingly on women's right to have their voices heard, and argues for equal voting rights for men and women, while their caveats about age thresholds and drafting are procedural rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech by the Member for Motherwell, South focuses entirely on the civil service — professional and specialist roles, privatisation, contracting out, information technology, and policy capacity — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "young men and women" is incidental and does not address women's distinctive civic status.

Dr. Shipman explicitly supports married women's right to sit on borough and county councils, promises to introduce a Bill himself to remove all anomalies preventing this, and opposes the Amendment only on procedural/strategic grounds (it would create new anomalies and endanger the passage of the Bill), not because he opposes women's political participation.

The speaker argues that the Bill is flawed for excluding married women and explicitly states he would be glad to see married women treated equally with spinsters and widows, calling the existing disability "glaring and unjust." While he is not an enthusiastic supporter of the Bill overall, his substantive position favours extending women's political participation to married women on equal terms.

The speaker explicitly states "on theoretical and general grounds I am entirely in favour of extending the franchise to women" and supports the Government's pledge to remove all inequalities between the sexes, while his objections (timing, age threshold, drafting quality) are procedural caveats rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is focused on arguing for the repeal of the Prevention of Violence (Temporary Provisions) Act 1939 and improving Anglo-Irish relations. The brief mention of the "women suffrage movement" is a passing quotation from George Lansbury used as an analogy for deep-seated grievances, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the Hunting Bill and how social progress is achieved through public pressure. The brief reference to suffragettes getting the vote is used as a rhetorical analogy to illustrate how social change occurs generally, not to argue for or against women's political rights as a substantive position.

The speaker explicitly argues in support of the Bill extending women's franchise, dismissing objections as weak excuses, appealing to the Government not to whip against the Bill, and invoking both justice and public policy grounds ("it is right and just, and that it is in the interests of the country that everybody of adult age should have a vote").

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater women's involvement in positions of power and political representation, criticizes the 91% male composition of Parliament, warns against complacency about gender equality progress, and supports specific measures (minimum wage, maternity rights, gender employment statistics) to advance women's equality in public life.

The speech is a debate about economic policy, food buying, and alleged Conservative broken promises after the 1951 election. The reference to suffragettes is purely a rhetorical flourish comparing forcible feeding to political pressure, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker opens by approvingly quoting John Stuart Mill's argument for women's suffrage, affirms that women are capable of full civic participation, celebrates women's political achievements worldwide, and advocates for greater women's representation in Parliament and public life. While she opposes quotas, this is a procedural/merit-based caveat rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that women are as entitled to the vote as men, that their intelligence and experience make them capable political participants, and that denying them the franchise while imposing legislative obligations upon them is unjust. The speech is a sustained argument in favour of women's enfranchisement.

The speaker explicitly states they intend to support the Bill and argues there is "no justification of any kind for depriving of the franchise women over twenty-one years of age," directly endorsing equal voting rights for women on the same terms as men. They rebut arguments against the Bill (swamping the electorate, necessity of a General Election) and criticise those who suggest raising the voting age for men.

The speaker expresses admiration for the suffragettes and gratitude for their fight for women's votes, explicitly supports women's participation in public life, and discusses her work encouraging women to take leadership roles through networking initiatives. While she argues Britain's situation for women is relatively positive, she affirms the importance of women advancing in political and public life.

The speech concerns a Children's Bill amendment about police search powers for tobacco possession, arguing that the power should apply equally to girls and boys. The fleeting reference to "suffragettes" and equality of the sexes is rhetorical decoration to make a point about consistency in child welfare law, not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker pays tribute to the suffragettes and their battles for women's rights, explicitly stating that preserving their memory and educating girls about their achievements would "do women a service." While the speech focuses primarily on women's employment, it opens with a clear endorsement of the suffragette cause and women's political participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the employment of middle-aged and elderly workers and the economic/social case for retaining them in the workforce. The brief quotation mentioning "votes for women" is used only as an illustration from a playwright's work about societal decline, not as an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about limiting the duration of parliamentary speeches and reforming House of Commons procedure; women's political rights are not argued for or against. The only mention of women is a passing reference to "the women's suffrage movement, and the evolution of Miss Maloney and her bell" as a historical aside about controlling verbosity, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speaker argues forcefully that Parliament must honour its pledges to women regarding equal political rights, urges a free vote to allow members to fulfil those pledges, and warns against "playing fast and loose" with commitments made to women on the franchise and equal civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Morley, Southampton Itchen) argues at length and with substantive evidence that women teachers and civil servants deserve equal pay for equal work, citing the interchangeability of men's and women's teaching roles, the NUT's consistent support, and proposing a practical incremental mechanism for implementation. The speech is entirely in support of equal pay for women in public service.

The speech concerns a maintenance law bill addressing venue and award amounts for deserted wives in magistrates' courts — a family law matter. While the speaker mentions women's organisations welcoming the bill and notes practical benefits for injured women, there is no argument made about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's civic/political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political representation, defending her party's all-women shortlists as non-patronising, lamenting the under-representation of women in Parliament and Cabinet, celebrating the suffragette legacy, and arguing that all political parties must work to level the playing field for women seeking election.

The speech is primarily about national insurance pension policy, retirement ages, and the challenges of differentiating between vocations for early retirement. While it mentions women workers (spinsters in textile industries) in the context of retirement pension age discussions, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic representation.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers: Major Lloyd-Greame, who explicitly argues for equal franchise for women, pledges to vote for the Bill, and frames it as redeeming a debt owed to women voters; and Sir J. D. Rees, who argues against this particular Bill (and by extension against equal franchise at this time), calling it a "thin and transparent device" and stating he will vote against it. Together the TARGET makes substantive arguments on both sides of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on old age pensions policy — how to fund it, whether it is practicable, and how to begin implementation. The only mention of women is incidental ("men and women of sixty-five years and upwards"), referring to pension recipients, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker (Lord Robert Cecil) argues forcefully that Parliament must honour its pledges to give women equal political rights, criticises the pattern of broken promises to women on the vote, and expresses strong support for carrying the Bill through its Third Reading to extend the franchise equally to women.

Miss Ward criticizes the Government for abstaining (effectively joining employers) rather than voting in favour of the equal pay convention, implying she supports women's equal remuneration rights and equal political/civic participation. Her question challenges the Government's failure to support the workers' position in favour of the convention on equal pay for women.

The speech concerns education policy — teacher recruitment, village school closures, comprehensive schools, and school standards — with only incidental mentions of "women teachers" as a demographic category relevant to staffing shortages, not as a matter of women's civic rights or political representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women deserve equal rights and recognition, drawing on the suffragette movement's legacy to assert that women should be able to "exercise rights along with our responsibilities" and criticises persistent inequality in working conditions for women. The speech advocates for genuine equality and greater recognition of women's contributions to society.

The speaker moves the Second Reading of a Bill specifically designed to remove women's disability at Parliamentary elections, systematically rebuts every major argument against women's suffrage (mental capacity, domestic sphere, physical service, degradation by politics, etc.), and urges the House to vote in favour, expressing his own long-held conviction that enfranchising women will raise the tone of public life.

The speaker explicitly seconds the Motion for the Second Reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill, arguing at length that granting women the vote would be good for men, women, and politics, and directly rebuts common arguments against women's suffrage throughout the speech.

The speaker (Mrs. Gorman, Member for Billericay) explicitly advocates for more women in Parliament, proposing that each constituency elect both a man and a woman by adjusting the Representation of the People Act, and argues that Parliament should be representative of the whole nation rather than an elite meritocracy. While she rejects the framing of women as victims and opposes certain Labour approaches, her substantive position on women's political representation is clearly supportive.

The speaker criticizes another Member for arguing against women's suffrage (claiming women's loquacity made them politically incapable) and for attempting to talk out the Bill for the extension of the suffrage to women — framing these as hypocritical given that Member's own verbosity. This implicitly mocks and undermines the anti-suffrage argument, suggesting sympathy for women's suffrage, but the speaker's own substantive argument on women's political rights is not directly made. However, the passage does characterize the anti-suffrage argument dismissively, which registers as a mild stance against opposition to women's suffrage — i.e., for women's suffrage. Yet the mention is brief and serves primarily as an attack on the Motion's proposer rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights. Given the passing nature of the reference used rhetorically against an opponent, this is better classified as irrelevant.

The speech is primarily about improving electoral registration procedures through a rolling register system. While it briefly mentions the suffragettes as historical context for the franchise, it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights — it treats women's suffrage as an accomplished historical fact and focuses entirely on modernising registration mechanics for all voters.

The speech concerns the registration and representation of nurses in a Nursing Bill, focusing on whether probationer nurses should have voting rights within the nursing profession's regulatory structure — not women's political rights or civic franchise. Women's political rights as citizens are not addressed.

The questions from Mrs. Castle and Brigadier Medlicott both press the Government on why its delegates failed to vote in favour of an equal pay convention at the ILO, implicitly supporting the principle of equal pay for women in their political/civic capacity. Brigadier Medlicott's question explicitly references the Government's stated adherence to the principle of equal pay for women, reinforcing a pro-equal pay stance.

The target speech is focused entirely on Communism, electoral politics, and Conservative Party opposition to the government's appointments. The brief mention of "every man and woman" having the right to vote is a passing rhetorical flourish about general electoral rights, not an argument about women's political rights specifically.

The speaker (Mr. Fisher) personally declares long-standing support for women's parliamentary franchise ("I have always been—long before this question became a question of politics—an advocate of the Parliamentary franchise to women") while simultaneously defending the Government's position that it is not bound to reopen the franchise question now and opposing the Bill on those grounds. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: personal support for women's franchise rights paired with substantive opposition to extending them at this juncture.

The speech concerns military service numbers and budget estimates, mentioning men and women only in the context of personnel increases in the Service. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Bradford riots, community relations, criminal behaviour, youth alienation, and cultural breakdown — with only a passing, non-argumentative reference to suffragettes as a historical example of past grievances, used to illustrate that modern citizens have more avenues for redress than ever before. No substantive argument about women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely focused on the Queen Elizabeth II hospital in Welwyn Hatfield — its achievements, funding history, and threats of closure — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Mallet) argues at length against women's suffrage, marshalling evidence from American referenda showing low female voter turnout and repeated legislative defeats, and using examples from Finland, the Isle of Man, and U.S. states to cast doubt on the desirability and demand for women's political rights. While he briefly acknowledges the sincerity of some suffrage advocates, this is a grudging concession, not a substantive argument in favour.

The speaker explicitly states he opposes the Women's Suffrage Bill throughout, arguing against women's right to vote on grounds including that force/military service underpins political rights, that scripture opposes it, that responsible nations with foreign obligations do not grant women the franchise, that women do not want the vote, and that the agitation is "bogus" and a "grave peril." He moves that the Bill be read a second time six months hence (i.e., killed). His brief suggestion that women might be sent to the House of Lords does not constitute substantive support for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly seconds an amendment opposing the Women's Suffrage Bill, arguing that the franchise has historically been confined to men, that the Bill would favour propertied classes over working women, that the movement lacks widespread public support, and that the change is too sweeping to be rushed through as a private member's bill — all substantive arguments against granting women political rights.

The speech is a parliamentary business statement outlining the schedule of upcoming debates and committee meetings on topics such as immigration, health services, financial regulation, and fisheries policy. It contains no arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly argues against the Bill's sex bar provisions, contending that it is an "anomaly" and "unstatesmanlike" to close industrial doors to women "at the very moment" Parliament has extended the franchise and the right to sit in the House to women. He advocates for women's equal right to work in industry alongside broader civic rights, and urges his colleague to accept amendments to protect women's position.

The speech is primarily about Indian constitutional reform — the franchise, power of the purse, communal representation, and indirect election — with only a passing mention that the proposed franchise "rules out all women." This single mention does not constitute an argument for or against women's political rights; it is cited as one example among several excluded groups (soldiers, literates) to criticise the property-based franchise generally.

The target speech is entirely about military budget estimates for the Air Force, covering pay increases, fuel stocks, aircraft sales, and appropriations in aid. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly identifies as "one who favours woman suffrage" and states that after hearing the opposition's arguments, he is "more inclined than before to vote in favour of giving the vote to women," while also dismissing the anti-suffrage arguments as "fallacious" and "frivolous."

The speech is entirely focused on nuclear waste disposal, transportation safety, and the nuclear industry's privatisation. The only mention of anything related to women's political rights is a passing reference to "the age of the suffragettes" used as a rhetorical point about democratic representation generally, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a Vote of Thanks to the armed forces, Dominions, and auxiliary services for their service in World War I. While women are briefly mentioned in appreciation of their nursing and auxiliary roles, no argument is made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic status.

The speech provides statistical information about Service voters (men and women) registered in the Electoral Register, broken down by military branch. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on critiquing the phrase "trained in assessing the value of evidence" for tribunal composition, with no argument made about women's political rights. The mention of women's representation on local committees appears only at the very tail end as the next speaker (Major Greame) begins a new amendment, which is part of the following context, not the TARGET.

The speech concerns the Channel Tunnel Rail Link Bill, addressing issues of property blight, compensation, compulsory purchase powers, and freight use. The only mention of women is a passing remark that there are no women on the Select Committee, made without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely about anti-profiteering legislation, the workings of a Select Committee, and trade regulation policy. The only mention of women is a passing question by Major Greame (in the following speech context, not the target) about whether women should have representation on local committees — and even that brief reference in the target itself is just a question about committee composition with no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Home Secretary, Leeds W.) explicitly declares himself "entirely in favour of the principle of the Bill" and states he will "gladly give my vote for the Second Reading of the Bill," arguing that women's enfranchisement would make the country "better and happier" and improve women's status. While he urges supporters to build broader public momentum, this is a practical caveat about strategy rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker amends the proposed addition to replace "representation of women" with "inclusion of women" on local committees, explicitly arguing that what is wanted is "not representatives of the women, but the women themselves" — actively supporting women's direct inclusion on these public bodies.

The target speech concerns breast cancer research funding, mammography screening for women under 50, and compensation for radiotherapy injuries — all health and medical care issues. It does not address women's voting rights, political representation, or any aspect of women's civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Mallet) systematically argues against women's suffrage throughout, dismissing American examples as poor precedents, questioning the breadth of support for the movement, arguing women are unfit for public life, and urging the House to resist the Bill until proponents can demonstrate majority support among both men and women.

The speech concerns retirement age policy and encouraging older workers to remain in employment, mentioning retirement ages of 60 for women and 65 for men only as existing policy parameters. It makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns National Insurance seasonal worker regulations and their effect on agricultural workers, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of "women in agriculture" refers to their employment conditions under insurance regulations, not their civic status or political participation.

The speaker argues that women do not want the franchise, that the Bill is being pushed by a "small and noisy minority," and that granting it would impose an unwanted burden on women who wish to remain free from electoral turmoil — all of which constitute substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is concerned with the legal consequences of a candidate's known disqualification at the time of election (specifically the MacManaway case involving a clergyman), drawing on precedents including Beresford Hope v. Lady Sandhurst only as a legal illustration of the principle that a disqualified candidate's votes are wasted. No argument for or against women's political rights is made; the Lady Sandhurst case is cited purely as a precedent on electoral disqualification law.

The speaker explicitly states he supports the measure because "it is illogical to grant the suffrage in connection with county council elections, and not in connection with the elections to the Imperial Parliament," argues no real reason has been shown why women are unworthy of the franchise, rebuts arguments against women's suffrage, and concludes "I support the measure because I honestly believe it is for the welfare of the country."

The speech focuses on women's pay, employment rates, and economic outcomes under Conservative vs. Labour governments, not on women's political rights or representation. While women are explicitly discussed, the arguments concern labour market and wage policy, which fall outside the scope of civic/political participation.

The speech is entirely about opposing the merger of London medical colleges (the Queen Mary and Westfield College Bill), discussing St. Bartholomew's hospital medical college's academic excellence, personnel disputes, and historical legacy. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech focuses on women's employment rates, unemployment figures, and labour market participation compared to Europe — economic/workplace policy rather than women's political rights (voting, standing for office, representation). The closing line "Women in this country do not want to vote for that lot over there" is a rhetorical flourish about electoral preference, not an argument about women's right to vote or political representation.

The speech is entirely about the understaffing and underfunding of the factory inspectorate, praising their work and calling for more inspectors. While it incidentally mentions "men and women" in the inspectorate, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states he voted against the admission of women to the House of Commons and argues that at least the House of Lords should preserve "the old tradition" of deliberations conducted by men, opposing the extension of women's right to sit in the Lords.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers: the Solicitor-General, who supports women's access to civil service posts while proposing regulations that could restrict married women's employment (a substantive limitation on women's civic participation), and Major Greame, who explicitly argues for women's right to sit and vote in the House of Lords as a matter of fairness and equality. Together the speech makes substantive arguments both for women's political rights (Greame's amendment on the Lords) and in favor of regulatory exclusions of women from certain public service roles based on marriage/motherhood.

The speaker opposes women's suffrage, arguing that women (like those of East Clare) want the vote only to show appreciation for a popular MP rather than out of genuine political interest, warns that it is "the thin end of the wedge" toward universal suffrage, and declares he will resist the measure until satisfied that a great majority of women actually want the Parliamentary vote.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a divorce reform bill (the Matrimonial Causes Bill), arguing against expanding grounds for divorce on moral, social, and practical grounds. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns building society mergers, bonuses for account holders (especially widows who are second signatories), and financial services regulation. While widows and women are mentioned as beneficiaries of the Bill, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation in any way.

The speaker merely reports that laws have been passed extending the franchise to women in Jamaica, without making any argument for or against women's political rights. This is a factual administrative reply with no evaluative stance on women's political participation.

The target speech is an administrative answer about the employment status of ex-WRNS ratings in civilian Admiralty roles, covering numbers, administration, and pay. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

While the speaker (Colonel Lockwood) acknowledges the logical awkwardness of opposing women's suffrage and comes "ready to be convinced," he ultimately maintains his opposition: he doubts the majority of women want the vote, firmly opposes women sitting in Parliament or holding state offices, argues it would be dangerous to invite women's opinion on Imperial matters, and states he has heard nothing to convince him his objections are "false or ill-founded."

The speaker (Mr. Snowden) argues that objections to women's enfranchisement have been repeatedly disproved by international examples, asserts that a genuine popular and parliamentary demand for women's enfranchisement exists, and cites the Liberal Federation's repeated resolutions urging the Government to press the reform forward — all in clear support of women's political rights.

The TARGET contains two speakers: Sir J. D. Rees, who strongly supports women's admission to the Home Civil Service ("I am profoundly convinced of the capacity of women to serve in the Civil Service, and I will support their claims to do so") but explicitly opposes their admission to the Indian and Ceylon Civil Services ("we do not yet wish to see them sitting in the seat of justice where men alone have sat for so long"); and Major O'Neill, who fully supports equal treatment for women in the Civil Service, citing the case of Mrs. Dickie as evidence of unjust discrimination. Together the TARGET makes substantive arguments both for women's civic participation (in the Home Civil Service) and against it (in India and Ceylon).

The speaker explicitly and at length advocates for equal pay for women in the Civil Service, teaching profession, and local government, arguing that decades of broken political promises must be fulfilled and urging the Government to implement a concrete scheme within two to three years.

The speech concerns workmen's compensation and industrial injury payments for pre-1948 injured workers, with only incidental references to "men and women" as a collective term for injured industrial workers. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is focused entirely on domestic violence, parental rights, and child welfare under the Children (Scotland) Bill. While it advocates for protecting women from abusive partners and supporting Women's Aid provisions, it does not make any argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or other aspects of women's political rights and civic participation.
