The speaker opposes Emily's List, an organisation that financially supports women Labour candidates, framing such support as corrupt "vote purchasing" and arguing candidates should be required to disclose such funding. While ostensibly about parliamentary probity, the speech is directed squarely at dismantling a mechanism specifically designed to advance women's political representation and candidacy.

The seconder of the amendment explicitly invokes women's growing electoral power and their resentment of a tax that penalizes married women, arguing that the "voice of the sex which feels most resentful" now dominates the House and will demand redress — framing the marriage tax repeal as a matter of women's equal civic and economic standing. This is a clear, if brief, argument in support of women's political rights and equitable treatment as citizens.

The speaker explicitly argues that women of England should not remain "in bondage to husbands who have violated every obligation of the marriage contract" while Scottish women enjoy greater liberty, and directly equates divorce law reform with women's civic equality: "You may give the women of England a vote, you may make them eligible to serve on juries, and to become Justices of the Peace... but so long as they are denied this equality with their sisters across the Border, all talk of equality is a mere sham and a mockery." This frames divorce law equality as integral to women's full civic standing.

The speech concerns prison conditions (towels, handkerchiefs, washing facilities) for suffragist prisoners, not the merits of women's political rights or representation. Neither the question nor the answer argues for or against women's right to vote or hold office; the topic is purely the treatment of inmates.

The target speech is a tribute by the Minister to his colleague Mr. Brazier for his work on behalf of reserve forces legislation, with no arguments made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "young men and women" in the reserves is incidental and does not address women's civic or political status.

The speaker argues that suffragist women are being subjected to imprisonment without conviction or proper trial through a procedural mechanism that denies them the right of appeal, and calls for their prosecution under ordinary law with full legal rights. This implicitly supports the fair treatment and legal rights of women involved in the suffragist agitation, advocating for procedural protections on their behalf.

The speaker draws a direct comparison between the prison treatment of Irish cattle-drivers and women suffragists in England, implicitly advocating for better (or at least equal) treatment of the suffragists and acknowledging their cause as legitimate by framing them as a comparable class of unconvicted/political prisoners.

The speaker (Sir W. Monckton) defends the limited representation of women on conscientious objectors' tribunals as "adequate," dismissing the call for greater female representation by noting the boards deal with men's cases — effectively opposing increased women's participation in these quasi-judicial public bodies.

The speech concerns the policy of excluding homosexuals from the armed forces on grounds of operational effectiveness, not women's political rights or representation. While the word "disfranchised" appears, it is used metaphorically about service personnel being silenced, not about women's civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for increased government funding for physical fitness, sport, and playing fields, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns the Oversea Settlement Office's budget and free passage schemes for ex-service men and women to emigrate within the British Empire. While women are mentioned incidentally as recipients of emigration benefits alongside men, no argument is made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the employment rights and conditions of home workers (pay, legal status, health and safety, national insurance), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. While the speech notes that home workers are "mainly, but not exclusively, women," this is a descriptive observation about the workforce, not an argument about women's civic status or political participation.

The target speech is entirely focused on the dangers and timing of passing a Home Rule Bill for Ireland, debating Irish governance, Sinn Fein, and the conditions of Ireland. The mention of "men and women electors" is a passing reference to the speaker's constituency without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker opposes the divorce reform resolution on religious grounds and supports the view that women should have an opportunity to vote on the matter before changes are made, implying women's religious convictions would lead them to oppose reform — this is not an endorsement of women's political rights but rather a rhetorical device to resist the resolution. The speaker explicitly states intent to vote against the Resolution and argues for preserving the sanctity of marriage, with no substantive support for women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about UK overseas aid budget cuts, bilateral vs. multilateral aid, and development policy. While the speaker briefly mentions that the Government's aims include promoting "the status of women" and criticises the FER for dropping "the unique focus on women," these are passing references in the context of aid policy arguments, not substantive arguments about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about a Bill concerning whether coroners' juries should be required to view bodies at inquests. The brief passing remark about women's suffrage ("until votes were granted to women and women sat on the floor of the House") is a rhetorical flourish dismissing an opponent's argument, not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns a licensing bill clause restricting children under fourteen from being in pub bars, with arguments about temperance legislation across the English-speaking world. It does not address women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech focuses on colonial emigration policy, overseas settlement funding, Empire unity, and the Prince of Wales's tour, with only a passing mention of women as beneficiaries of free passages alongside ex-servicemen and their dependents, and a brief note that women share men's desire to avoid returning to sedentary work. No argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the administration of industrial schools — salaries, maintenance costs, and a specific constituent case — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mrs. Jeger) strongly advocates for women police, arguing for equal pay, better representation within the Police Federation (including voting rights), improved accommodation, and greater public recognition of their capabilities. She explicitly supports legislative change to give policewomen voting representation in the Federation and argues against the pay differential between men and women officers.

The speaker briefly but explicitly supports women's political rights when he states "I should be sorry if those who have supported the right of women to vote were to go into the Lobby and deny to these women the right to work," invoking women's suffrage supporters as a reference point and implicitly endorsing their cause while arguing against denying barmaids the right to work.

The speaker closes by sarcastically "congratulating" Mr. Murray's suggestion that women who want the vote should be sent to Canada as an alternative to granting them the franchise, implicitly mocking rather than endorsing women's suffrage and treating the denial of the vote as a reasonable outcome.

The target speech is entirely focused on social work policy, training, inter-departmental coordination, poverty, and the proposed general social services council. It contains no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker concludes by affirming that if a relevant advisory committee is appointed, the Minister would "doubtless desire to have the representation of women on the Committee," indicating support for women's inclusion in political/advisory bodies.

The speaker (Mr. G. Murray) explicitly argues that money proposed for extending the franchise to women would be better spent on emigration, stating "I contend it would be very much better to spend that money in assisting our womenfolk to cross the seas where there is work and where there are men waiting for them, instead of giving them the vote in this country." This is a direct argument against women's suffrage.

The speech is a factual parliamentary answer listing categories of women who already receive equal pay under Treasury-funded employment. It neither argues for nor against women's political rights or equal pay policy — it simply enumerates existing practice in response to a question.

The speech concerns amendments to divorce mediation legislation, specifically safeguards against domestic violence in mediation proceedings. While it mentions women as frequent victims of abuse, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech concerns the political situation in Cyprus, including UN votes, constitutional development, and civil unrest — with no reference to women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status for women.

The speech is entirely focused on the temperance/licensing debate — arguing against excessive drinking and defending a Licensing Bill — with no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on a Scottish temperance/local option bill, arguing in favour of restricting public houses and defending the working-class support for the measure. Women are mentioned only in passing ("and the women too, he had been told") as supporters of the bill, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on asylum seekers and immigration policy, specifically the Lords amendment on benefits for asylum seekers. The brief mention of enforced abortions as grounds for asylum and a pregnant constituent denied benefits touches on women only incidentally as examples of humanitarian concern, without making any argument about women's political rights, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the efficiency of Parliament, Members' pay and working conditions, the Select Committee's recommendations on parliamentary remuneration, and the nature of democratic government. While it briefly mentions "men and women" chosen to represent the people, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly raises the issue of women's under-representation in Northern Ireland's political life and asks the Secretary of State how parties could be helped or encouraged to include more women in the political process, expressing that "many of us would like to see greater participation by women."

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question asking the Prime Minister about electoral reform plans and whether women's franchise would only be addressed in connection with general electoral reform. It poses questions without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is a detailed parliamentary address by Miss Burton on consumer protection, merchandise marks enforcement, and quality standards for goods — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The only references to women are incidental mentions of "housewives" and a "women's committee" of the British Standards Institution as consumers or advisory bodies, neither of which engages with women's civic or political status.

The speaker questions whether women's franchise has "overwhelming support" from women, notes there is "no precedent for so great a change except upon the responsibility of the Government," and explicitly urges deferring consideration of women's franchise to another Parliament — all of which argue against advancing women's political rights at this time.

The speech focuses on family-friendly employment policy, working hours, child care, wages, and family breakdown, without making arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned in the context of labour market participation and economic conditions, not their political rights or status as civic participants.

The speaker (Ms Church) explicitly argues that women need to be represented in elected bodies, notes the slow pace of progress toward parity in Parliament, and expresses hope for considerable improvement on the current 10% female representation, framing increased women's political representation as essential to democratic health.

The speech is overwhelmingly about opposing the Shops (Early Closing) Bill on grounds of liberty, cost, and necessity. The single passing mention of women is that shop assistants have "the franchise for men and women" and could form trade unions — a brief factual reference that makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech discusses married women as a political constituency and voting bloc for the Conservative Party, not their political rights or representation. The argument is about electoral support rather than advocating for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women are under-represented in Northern Ireland's political life and that "women need to be represented in our elected bodies," framing female political participation as essential to mature democratic development. This is a direct endorsement of women's political representation.

Mr. Snowden's TARGET speech reports that an amendment calling for women's franchise to be passed "at the earliest possible opportunity" was carried by a large majority, presenting this as evidence of strong support for the cause — framing it positively as part of his broader argument in favour of women's enfranchisement.

The speech is entirely focused on public expenditure, national finance, Treasury control, social reform spending, and Labour's economic policy. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about, even in passing.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as "a supporter of the Bill" and argues that the Bill should be advanced efficiently, noting that opposition arguments (intellectual incapacity, physical disability) have been largely abandoned. His sole concern is procedural—opposing the referral to a Committee of the Whole House as unnecessarily delaying passage—not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on the Welsh temperance/local option bill, discussing prohibition, compensation for publicans, and the right of communities to vote on the drink trade. While it mentions "men and women" deciding on the drink traffic, this is incidental phrasing about local voting rights on alcohol policy, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Scottish Office's £25,000 expenditure on a Velasquez painting for the Scottish National Gallery. The single passing reference to Suffragettes is an incidental historical remark about the "Toilet of Venus" painting, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues for increasing women's political representation in Northern Ireland, stating "we must increase the number of women who participate in the Province's political life" and that "we need more balanced representation" for the long-term health of Northern Ireland and democracy, while also defending Labour's strategies (including Emily's List) for increasing women's representation.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing alcohol prohibition legislation, arguing about individual liberty, worker efficiency, and the impracticality of local veto measures. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states that "the time had come when the public should realise the serious menace which would be the result if women had a vote," and argues that the Bill should not be passed without a general election mandate, clearly opposing women's enfranchisement.

The speaker frames women's demand for the franchise sympathetically, describing their "resentment and impatience" as legitimate and pressing, and urges the Prime Minister to make a conciliatory statement — implicitly supporting the cause of women's suffrage as a matter requiring political resolution.

The speech is primarily concerned with constituency matters (mining education, shipyard unemployment, road construction, oil pollution, horror comics) and broader democratic/economic concerns. The brief mention that "it is only 25 years since the full franchise was granted to women" is a passing historical observation used to illustrate that democracy is young, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is primarily about Middle East foreign policy, the Arab-Israeli conflict, and Egyptian treatment of Jews and Israeli ships. The brief mention that "the women have the vote" in Israel is a passing factual observation used to praise Israel's democratic character, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about a Welsh Local Option (temperance/licensing) Bill, arguing against it on grounds of fairness and lack of compensation. The only mention of women is a passing reference to the threat of losing "the women's vote" as political pressure to support the Bill — no argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on local government funding, council tax levels, and community care spending in Wales (particularly Gwynedd), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "firemen and women" is incidental and does not address women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on handgun control legislation following the Dunblane massacre, arguing against amendments that would create loopholes for competitive shooters. While the speaker incidentally uses the phrase "marksmen and markswomen," the speech makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that paying female clerks at different (lower) rates than male clerks is "scandalous," invokes the principle of equal pay for equal work, and notes that every MP endorsed this principle to get women's votes — making a clear substantive argument in favour of equal treatment for women in public employment.

The speech focuses entirely on reforming postal voting rules and motor car use on polling day under the Representation of the People Act, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of the "Church Women's Guild" is only as an example of people disenfranchised by postal vote restrictions, not as an argument about women's civic status.

The speech concerns the logistics of relocating statues (Mrs. Pankhurst and the Burghers of Calais) in Victoria Tower Gardens, addressing aesthetic and practical matters of siting. While it mentions women's organisations and the Suffragette Fellowship, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses on electoral register issues, pensions, widows' benefits, housing, and cost of living concerns. While it mentions the right to vote as a "birthright," it does so in a general civic context without singling out women as a class or making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on supporting a Bill for the education, employment, and maintenance of blind persons, with no reference to women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation as a gendered issue. The brief mention of "men and women" in charitable institutions is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states that Sir F. Banbury "does not believe in women having votes" and that his attitude makes her "rejoice that women have got votes," and she emphasizes that he does not represent women who have the vote and intend to use it — a clear affirmative endorsement of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over banning legally held handguns following the Dunblane massacre, addressing gun control legislation, the Cullen report, and the Snowdrop campaign. Women are mentioned only incidentally (Ann Pearston of the Snowdrop campaign and another woman who voted Conservative), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The question explicitly highlights the injustice of women being "denied the franchise" and advocates for ensuring women have at least equal facilities as men for political expression, signaling support for women's political rights. The answer, while dismissing the need for legislation, implicitly affirms equal treatment under the law regardless of sex.

The speech concerns the relocation of Mrs. Pankhurst's statue and engages with the Suffragette Fellowship's concerns about the new site, but makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The reference to women having "won their battle" is a passing acknowledgement, not a substantive argument about political rights.

The target speech concerns divorce law reform, specifically arguments about fault in divorce proceedings and the impact on children and marriage as an institution. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is entirely concerned with elementary education policy in England and Wales — specifically the structure of public vs. voluntary schools, religious instruction, teacher appointments, and financial grants. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech is entirely focused on the complexity and inefficiencies of voter registration laws and proposes practical reforms to enfranchise more men. While it mentions "female occupiers" and "married women in business" as categories on registration lists, these references are purely descriptive of existing divisions, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the franchise to women on equal terms with men, arguing that women who render service deserve equal citizenship rights, that the experimental period since 1918 has justified full extension, and that women fit to canvass votes are fit to cast them. The speech consistently advocates for the Bill's passage without substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the temperance debate over grocers' licences and secret drinking, with women mentioned only as a class disproportionately affected by alcohol (not as a matter of their civic or political rights). No argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for equal representation of women in the proposed Scottish Parliament, stating "For the first time in any elected body in Britain, we shall see the equal representation of women" and declaring "A Scottish Parliament is worth fighting for to achieve those objectives alone," while also expressing personal anticipation of women having "an equal share in making the decisions that affect our daily lives."

The speech concerns the Protection from Harassment Bill (anti-stalking legislation), focusing on its scope, drafting quality, civil liberties concerns, and a constituent case. While women are mentioned as primary victims of stalking, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech is entirely focused on nuclear deterrence, the resignation/by-election action of Sir R. Acland (the Member for Gravesend), and the analogy to George Lansbury's stand on a political issue. The reference to George Lansbury and women's suffrage is purely a historical analogy to illustrate political courage, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about the 14-day rule restricting BBC/ITV broadcasting of parliamentary debates, freedom of public discussion, and Parliament's relationship with the media. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as one historical example among many of movements initiated outside Parliament, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely about opposition to a Bill for the education, employment, and maintenance of blind persons, focusing on concerns about public expenditure, poor drafting, and scope creep. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference to "a Bill...the object of which was described as the extending of the franchise for women," used merely as an analogy to illustrate that bills sometimes have hidden purposes—no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The target speech is about the administrative and logistical arrangements for relocating Mrs. Pankhurst's statue and the Buxton Memorial Fountain in Parliament Square, not making any argument for or against women's political rights. While Mrs. Pankhurst is associated with the suffragette movement, the speech itself takes no position on women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on the financial treatment of Catholic teachers' salaries under an education bill, arguing it is unfair to reduce Catholic teachers' wages because of how they spend their earnings. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns the fair division of pension assets for divorced women under the Family Law Bill — a financial/property matter in divorce proceedings. While it advocates for women's economic fairness, it does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of civic/political participation that falls within the scope of women's political rights.

The target speech is about employment regulation and the social chapter, criticising Conservative Governments for accepting various EU employment directives. While it briefly mentions "sex discrimination legislation" and "equal retirement ages," these are listed as examples in a broader argument about regulatory consistency, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker expresses approval on behalf of the Suffragette Fellowship for moving Mrs. Pankhurst's statue closer to Parliament, affirming that her work was connected with Parliament and the new location is more fitting — a statement that implicitly honours and supports women's political legacy and rights.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the franchise to women on equal terms with men, arguing that the vote is a necessary weapon for women to protect themselves from economic exploitation, and that training for political participation can only come through actually possessing the vote.

The speech focuses on BSE/beef safety, the Family Law Bill's legislative process, and parliamentary procedures. The brief mention of "thousands of women" waiting on pension splitting is a welfare/financial policy concern, not an argument about women's civic status or political rights.

The speaker (Dr. Addison, Minister of Health) explicitly supports extending the franchise to women on equal terms with men, dismisses fears about women combining as a voting bloc, states the Bill is "an inevitable result of former extensions of the franchise," and concludes "personally I am entirely in favour of this principle." He also argues women of 21 are more mature than men of the same age.

The speech is entirely focused on native rights, land policy, labour conditions, martial law, and the question of South African federation/unification — not on women's political rights or representation. The only mention tangentially related to women is a passing reference to native women performing agricultural labour, which is not an argument about women's civic status or political participation.

The speech concerns diplomatic representations made on behalf of British-born wives wishing to return to the UK from Czechoslovakia — a consular/humanitarian matter. It does not make any argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in political life.

The TARGET speech is delivered by a government minister (Dr. Addison based on context) who spends the entirety of the speech explaining the technical and administrative effects of the Bill — changes to the electorate size, removal of business premises qualifications, costs of register preparation, and timelines — without making any substantive argument for or against extending the franchise to women. The speaker notes the government will leave the matter to a free vote and only at the very end briefly states a personal view, but that personal statement appears to belong to the following speech by Dr. Addison, not this TARGET speech which ends with a question from Mr. Tyson Wilson.

The speaker explicitly states that "the woman had a right to consideration in these matters" regarding parental rights over children's religious education, and argues that "until women had the same electoral power as men he was not prepared to take the responsibility of determining which parent the child should follow in the matter of religion" — directly endorsing women's equal electoral rights as a prerequisite for fair policy.

The speaker mentions the women's suffrage Bill (giving votes to women) approvingly, noting it passed its Second Reading and urging that the Prime Minister's motion should not prevent the House from deciding the question in the autumn session, implicitly supporting its further progress.

The speaker explicitly states "I support the extension of the vote to them on the same terms as to men," arguing that women bring a higher moral perspective to political life, as evidenced by their influence on issues like the League of Nations and disarmament.

The speaker (Mrs. Gillan) enthusiastically highlights government initiatives expanding women's employment opportunities, childcare support, equal pay progress, and women's representation in public life and the civil service, explicitly stating "The Government are committed to women achieving their full potential in society." The speech is a sustained endorsement of policies designed to advance women's economic and civic participation.

The speech is primarily a critique of the Conservative Budget, focusing on its effects on working-class people, old-age pensioners, local authorities, and the cost of living. References to "women with large families" are used to illustrate economic hardship under Tory policy, not to argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater women's representation in Parliament, citing Labour's goal to double women MPs and achieve equal representation within three Parliaments, and argues that Parliament is worse at its job because women are underrepresented. She also highlights the application of the Sex Discrimination Act to parliamentary candidate selection as a tool to combat discrimination against women candidates.

The primary speaker in the TARGET (Dr. Addison, the Minister of Health) explicitly states "Personally I am entirely in favour of this principle. It is a right principle. The application of it was inevitable, and I believe the benefits in the long run will be wholly to the public good," in reference to extending the franchise to women at age 21. While Mr. Leng-Sturrock's opening opposition appears at the end of the TARGET, the bulk of the speech and its conclusion firmly endorse women's equal voting rights.

The speaker argues that women candidates are fully capable of attracting votes (debunking the old adage that women won't vote for women), points to their consistent success in by-elections as proof, and asserts that women MPs often work harder than their male counterparts — all of which supports women's fitness for and participation in political office.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Labour party's efforts to increase women's representation in Parliament, states that women should have access to power, and argues that institutional sexism has been a barrier to women's participation in politics, endorsing the breaking down of those barriers.

The speech addresses workplace accident rates among female factory workers and steps being taken to reduce them, which is an occupational safety matter. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports granting women the Parliamentary franchise "on the same terms of equality as men," has introduced his own Bill to that effect, and declares he desires to give the Bill under debate "wholehearted support," arguing the change "has got to come, sooner or later" and that women deserve "equality of opportunity."

The speech focuses entirely on unemployment relief, the Local Government Board's administration, motor car speed regulation, and tuberculosis. The brief mention of the "women's department of the Central Unemployed Body" is purely administrative context about tendering discrepancies, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speaker (responding to Mrs. Peacock's context) affirms that women can and do win elections, noting that while some men expressed reluctance to vote for a woman, many others did — and she herself is proof of that success, implicitly endorsing women's fitness for political office.

The speaker explicitly states he has "for twenty years advocated equal rights for women" and is "strongly in favour of women getting the same electoral rights as men," and announces he will vote in favour of the Bill. His argument that it is illogical to give a vote to a man of 21 but not a woman of the same age further reinforces his pro-suffrage position.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Bill extending the franchise to women at 21, arguing that women already have the vote at 30 and that is "far enough," that girls of 21 are too young to vote, and closing with a warning about the dangers of women's influence (the Samson/Delilah allusion). While the speaker claims to support women having "all the privileges that men have" in the abstract, the substantive position is opposition to further extension of women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equal access to professions and political representation, praises Labour's efforts to increase women in Parliament, and warns against complacency by arguing that isolated successes do not mean equality has been achieved for all women.

The speaker (Ramsay MacDonald) argues forcefully for prohibiting women from employment as barmaids, contending the trade morally degrades women, exploits them as cheap labour and decoys, and that the legislature should close this avenue of employment to women — reflecting opposition to women's unrestricted participation in this form of public economic life on paternalistic/protective grounds rather than support for women's civic equality.

The speaker acknowledges no logical objection to women having the vote on the same terms as men but argues the Bill is "singularly inopportune" and uses slippery-slope rhetoric (votes for girls of 20, then 18, then babies) to oppose its passage, ultimately signalling they will vote against it as premature.

The speech is about whether women should be excluded from working as barmaids under a licensing bill — a labour/public health question — not about women's political rights (voting, standing for office, representation, etc.). The speaker does not argue for or against women's civic participation or franchise; the references to women concern their employment conditions and moral welfare in a specific trade.

The speech is primarily a detailed critique of Conservative government economic policy, focusing on the cost of living, food prices, coal quality, decontrol, and price indices. The brief mention of "women voters" being promised price reductions is an incidental rhetorical point, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses on defending the employment conditions of barmaids (wages, working environment, drunkenness statistics) against proposals to remove them from licensed premises. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing remark that barmaids "have no vote" and "owing to recent events it would probably be a long time before they had it," offered as a reason for parliamentary protection of their employment interests, not as an argument for or against women's suffrage.

The speech concerns leasehold property rights and ground rents in South Wales, particularly the injustice faced by homeowners whose leases are expiring. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the Education Bill debate—specifically the conflict between denominational and non-denominational schooling, contracting-out, and the rights of teachers. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech is entirely about Army manpower, National Service, recruiting, the disbandment of Anti-Aircraft Command, and the role of the Reserve Army. The single brief mention of women ("there were many women in the mixed batteries, and we are offering them employment in other branches of the Territorial Army") is a passing administrative note about military personnel redeployment, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the speaker's Foreign Office lecture tour in the United States, Canada, and Iceland, discussing Anglo-American relations, the Foreign Service, information services, cultural exchanges, and foreign policy. Women's political rights and representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The target speech concerns whether women should be excluded from employment in public-houses (the barmaid clause of a licensing bill), which is a labour/employment regulation question, not a matter of women's civic or political rights such as voting, standing for office, or political representation. The brief mention that barmaids "have no vote" is purely incidental and no argument about women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly advocates for equal pay for women police officers, argues that women constables have "all the rights and duties of a constable," praises their competence and courage, and expresses satisfaction at women's representation on the Police Council — all substantive arguments in favour of women's full and equal participation in public service roles.

The speaker explicitly argues for extending tax allowances equally to women, advocates for changing the voting system (proportional representation/STV) to increase women's representation in Parliament, and calls for more women on short-lists and in political parties — all substantive arguments in favour of women's political rights and equal civic participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for multi-member constituencies and proportional representation to increase women's representation in Parliament, calls on all parties to develop policies to promote women in political and other organisations, and supports fair elections that give women greater opportunity to participate. These are direct, substantive arguments in favour of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker (Viscountess Astor) explicitly and enthusiastically supports the Bill to extend the franchise to women, arguing that women bring moral courage to public life, that women at 18 are wiser than men at 25, and urging Members to vote for the measure because "this is coming about" and the country needs women's participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that too few women sit in the world's legislative assemblies, that women need greater political representation to shift power and achieve genuine equality, and that legislative assemblies must reflect "a genuine female perspective" — directly and substantively advocating for women's political rights and representation.

The speech (by Mrs. Slater) is focused entirely on the economic impact of a purchase/sales tax on furniture, particularly its burden on working-class families and newly-married couples. While women are mentioned (e.g., "Tory women," housewives), these references are to their role as consumers and voters on economic issues, not to arguments about women's political rights or civic participation.

The target speech is a factual report by a government official describing the offences committed by imprisoned suffragists and the punishments administered; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or their fitness for political participation.

The speaker explicitly praises the Labour party's efforts to increase female MPs, highlights the stark underrepresentation of women in Parliament since 1918, and advocates for equal rights at work, stronger protections against violence, and other measures to advance women's civic and political standing.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill to extend the franchise to women at age 21, arguing it is a logical development of the 1918 Act, that women of 21 are intellectually equal to men of the same age, and that arguments against extension are "unworthy," "unsound," and "dangerous." The speaker urges the House to face the inevitability of this reform and criticises the Government for not acting sooner.

The speaker raises a parliamentary question on behalf of suffragist prisoners at Holloway, implicitly advocating for their welfare and their claim to be treated as political offenders, framing women's suffrage activism as a legitimate political cause.

The speech is entirely focused on colonial development and welfare funding, praising the work of colonial administrators (men and women) in passing, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Irish land purchase finance and Treasury stock issuance policy. The brief mention of "suffragettes standing on his doorstep" is a passing rhetorical analogy about the Prime Minister ignoring petitioners, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states they oppose the Bill and cites the untimeliness of further franchise expansion as a reason, while clarifying they do not oppose women's fitness to vote — but their opposition to proceeding with the Bill at this time constitutes a substantive objection to advancing women's political rights through this measure. The procedural and timing objections are the stated grounds for opposing the Bill, not mere caveats alongside support.

The speaker explicitly advocates on behalf of women who support enfranchisement and asks the Prime Minister to receive a deputation of such women, urging the government to consult them before formulating franchise reform proposals — a clear expression of support for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "I have always been a supporter of women's franchise" and voted for the last Act, and offers "hearty acceptance" of extending the franchise to women, objecting only to extraneous provisions in the Bill (business qualifications, assimilation of franchises) rather than to women's enfranchisement itself. The speaker also supports women's equal participation in the labour market as a complement to their political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "we want more of them [women] in the House" and advocates for mainstreaming gender equality across government departments, framing women's equality as a core government goal rather than a special concession. These are substantive endorsements of women's political representation and civic participation.

The speech is primarily about nuclear weapons testing and the dangers of radiation, arguing for an international scientific conference to address these threats. While the speaker mentions women's concerns and speaks "on behalf of the women of the world," this is rhetorical framing for the anti-nuclear argument, not an argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker is advocating on behalf of imprisoned suffragettes, questioning the Home Secretary about whether they have been given a fair hearing and whether official accounts have been relied upon without allowing the women to present their own version of events. This implicitly supports the political cause and fair treatment of the suffragettes.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing increases in Purchase Tax, arguing on grounds of administrative burden, hardship to households, and labour market efficiency. While married women are mentioned briefly as part-time workers in the distributive trades and as housewives affected by the tax, these references are incidental to an economic argument about taxation and do not constitute a substantive position on women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker, as Government co-chairman of the Women's National Commission, actively promotes improving the status of women, welcomes the International Women's Day debate, highlights the WNC's work toward women's advancement, and defends the Government's implementation of the Beijing Platform for Action on women's rights. Throughout, the speech supports women's political representation and equal opportunities without substantive opposition to any aspect of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "A great many of us are in favour of that principle. I am for one," endorsing equal franchise for women, and expresses support for extending the vote to women under 30, saying "I myself have no fear whatever of the vote of women over 21." His objections are procedural and concern extraneous provisions (abolition of plural vote, business qualification) rather than opposition to women's political rights themselves.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equal participation in politics and public life, welcomes greater female representation in Parliament, endorses the legal framework of equal opportunities (Equal Pay Act, Sex Discrimination Act), and argues against prejudice as baseless. While opposing quotas, he frames this as supporting genuine equality of opportunity rather than opposing women's political rights, and his overall thrust is strongly in favour of women's full participation in all roles including politics.

The question concerns the number of police deployed and the cost allocation for managing a suffragette disturbance, not arguing for or against women's political rights. It is an administrative/financial inquiry with no substantive argument about women's civic participation.

The speech is primarily about alcohol regulation and temperance policy. The reference to women's votes going to Prohibition and the remarks about women's spending on dress are rhetorical asides used to argue against temperance/prohibition, not substantive arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing for increased pensions for low-paid teachers and civil servants in Scotland, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the teaching workforce deserving better pensions, not in any civic or political capacity.

The speech focuses entirely on economic planning, government controls, investment, underdeveloped areas, foreign aid, and convertibility. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speech is primarily about Northern Ireland economic development, unemployment, and constituency matters. The brief mention of the "women's coalition" vote in South Belfast and comments about intelligent non-professional women are passing observations about electoral politics and community standards, not arguments for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Purchase Tax on brushes, mops, and related household items, and the impact on the brush manufacturing industry and its workers. While "housewives" are mentioned as consumers affected by the tax, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly characterises the Bill as "an insidious measure to put women on governing bodies to which up to the present time they have not been appointed," frames it as connected to woman suffrage, and opposes it throughout, thereby opposing the extension of women's political participation.

The speech concerns the Children and Young Persons (Harmful Publications) Bill, which targets horror comics and their effect on children. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status for women; the brief mention of "pictures of women in evening dress, brandishing whips" is merely a description of objectionable content, not an argument about women's political participation.

The speaker strongly advocates for women's pension rights upon divorce, arguing that women who contribute to home, family, and family businesses deserve equal property rights in pensions, and explicitly criticises the Minister for failing to commit to a timetable to rectify this injustice for women.

The speech focuses entirely on economic issues—high prices, profiteering in shipping, cotton, wool, and clothing industries, and government expenditure. The brief mention of women as "30 per cent. of the total electorate" is purely an observational remark about their political significance as consumers, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing against cuts to Glasgow city council's budget, covering museums, housing, schools, social work, and related services. Women's political rights and representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech is entirely about the appointment of magistrates in Lancashire, specifically advocating for greater Labour/working-class representation on magistrates' benches. While the speaker briefly mentions "men and women" drawn from labour ranks, this is incidental and no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The speech is almost entirely focused on criticising the steepening of death duty gradients and their economic effects on estates, thrift, and capital. The single passing mention of women's political rights ("if anything can convert me to be a suffragette it would be the treatment meted out under our financial system to widows") is a rhetorical aside used to illustrate the financial hardship on widows, not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states that the bill is "only necessary because of the failure of the Members of the Government, and of Members of the House, to redeem their election pledges in regard to women's suffrage," and notes that 420 Members declared themselves favourable to women's suffrage before the election. This frames the Gallery disturbances as a justified political protest against the shelving of women's suffrage, implicitly endorsing the cause.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Chancellor's imposition of Purchase Tax on household items (baths, washtubs, washboards, ironing boards, clothes pegs, etc.) and their impact on poor housewives. While women are frequently mentioned as the users of these domestic implements, the argument concerns tax policy and economic hardship, not women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about sports policy — stadium location, Euro 96, the Olympics, and discrimination against women in the Olympics in the context of certain countries' sports exclusion policies. While it mentions Iran banning women from sports and the Olympic charter's anti-discrimination clause, it does not argue about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is a continuation of Mrs. Mann's argument against Purchase Tax on household items (clothes pegs, baths, washboards, etc.), focused on cost-of-living concerns and Conservative economic promises. While it mentions "housewives" and "Conservative women" at their conference, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting rights, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Viscountess Astor) explicitly invokes women's newly won voting rights as political leverage ("women have got a vote now and we mean to use it"), identifies herself as a lady Member speaking for women, and frames her policy arguments around women's civic participation and representation. This is a substantive endorsement of women's political rights and their exercise of the franchise.

The speech concerns labour relations, trade union rights, and the Emergency Powers Bill — the references to "women and children" are rhetorical, mocking the Government's framing of the Bill, not arguments about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on fiscal and budgetary policy — taxation of household necessities, government economic arguments, and electoral honesty — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is about prison conditions, rehabilitation spending, and treatment of female prisoners. While it mentions women, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any aspect of their civic participation — it is focused entirely on penal policy and prison conditions.

The speech is focused on why a Bill (apparently related to food/milk provisions) does not apply to Ireland, addressing labour unrest, military policy, and Sinn Fein. The brief mention of "women and children" is only a passing reference to framing used by another speaker, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speaker quotes approvingly a magistrate's statement affirming women's right to vote and challenges the Home Secretary to improve the prison conditions of suffragist prisoners, implicitly endorsing women's political rights and the justice of their cause.

The speech is primarily about introducing a stalking law to protect victims of criminal harassment. While the speaker frames the issue as important "to women" and notes that victims are "mainly women," the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — it addresses criminal law and personal safety.

The speech focuses entirely on procedural and constitutional objections to a Bill designed to punish strangers who disturb parliamentary proceedings, arguing that existing parliamentary powers are sufficient. While suffragettes are mentioned briefly as the cause of the disturbances, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech primarily concerns the legal technicalities of the 1361 Justices of the Peace Act, binding-over powers, and the right of appeal. The brief mention of women's suffrage and militant suffragettes is incidental historical context for discussing the Lansbury v. Riley case, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is focused entirely on procedural and constitutional objections to a Bill designed to punish strangers who disturb parliamentary proceedings, arguing it would be ineffective and counterproductive. While suffragettes are mentioned briefly as the cause of the disturbances, the speaker explicitly disclaims any opposition to their aims or tactics, and makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns an Irish criminal injuries compensation bill, debating ratepayer liability and local government funding in Ireland. The brief mention of a woman shot by a government lorry is used to argue about the inequity of the compensation bill's scope, not to make any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is overwhelmingly concerned with opposing a Scottish Local Option (temperance/licensing) Bill on grounds of liberty, representation, and legislative procedure. The sole mention of women's suffrage is a passing, non-argumentative reference to US States having autonomy over franchise and women's suffrage, used only as an analogy to explain why American precedents don't apply to small British local areas — no position on women's political rights is argued.

The speech is entirely focused on food production, supply, pricing, and the Ministry of Food's policies. The single passing reference to "8,000,000 women voters" is used only to illustrate public concern about food prices, without making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about Irish agrarian crime and the Government's failure to use the Crimes Act; the mention of suffragettes is purely rhetorical — used as a contrast to illustrate inconsistent treatment of lawbreakers — without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

This is a maiden speech by the Member for Hove focused on his constituency, local politics, and the debate on Bank of England independence. While he briefly mentions suffragette Victoria Liddiard as a famous Hove resident, he makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech focuses on industrial working conditions (the two-shift system) and its economic impact on the glass industry and women workers' employment, without making substantive arguments about women's right to vote, stand for office, or other political rights and representation.

The TARGET introduces a Bill explicitly aimed at amending the law "to remove the Electoral Disabilities of Women," which directly supports women's political rights by seeking to grant them the franchise or remove barriers to political participation.

The target speech is entirely focused on the debate over capital punishment (the death penalty for murder), covering legal distinctions, deterrence, the burden of proof, and the case of Timothy Evans. Women's political rights and representation are never addressed, argued for, or argued against; the passing reference to "free men, free women, free Members of Parliament" is rhetorical flourish, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely about the Federation of Malaya Constitutional Conference, covering self-government, independence, defence arrangements, and public service matters. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "British officers, like other men and women from Britain" who have served in Malaya, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about Irish agrarian crime, the Crimes Act, and cattle-driving. The brief mention of suffragettes is used only as a rhetorical comparison to illustrate inconsistency in how the government handles different forms of civil disturbance, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses on Kenyan constitutional development, franchise arrangements for Africans, trade unions, education, and governance under Sir Evelyn Baring. The only mention of women is a passing acknowledgement that Dame Irene Ward raised "the problem of the women of Kenya," with the speaker deferring substantive engagement to a future letter — no argument about women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly expresses hope that young women will gain the vote ("By that time, I hope, the young women will be 21, and have the vote") and that Parliament will then have to listen to them, and criticises the Labour party and trade unions for not being fair to women while appealing for their vote. These are affirmative statements supporting women's suffrage and political representation.

The speaker explicitly takes pride in being "the first woman Member of Parliament for Salford," framing it as a historic achievement and noting Salford's proud history with the Suffragette movement, thereby affirming women's political representation as a positive milestone.

The speech is almost entirely about colonial policy in Northern Rhodesia — racial discrimination, education, land, federation, and African political representation — without addressing women's political rights or representation as a distinct civic issue. The brief mention of women's education in Africa is framed as a development concern (closing the cultural gap) rather than an argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker explicitly identifies as a supporter of women's franchise ("those who support this movement in this House") and presses the Government to clarify its policy on extending the franchise to women, expressing concern about the difficulty supporters face due to the Government's silence on the matter.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over capital punishment — whether to abolish or retain the death penalty for murder — including proposed amendments to the law of murder (constructive malice, provocation, suicide pacts, diminished responsibility). There is no argument made about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any related civic status of women.

The speech is a maiden speech focused on Scottish devolution and the referendum bill; it briefly mentions "the suffragettes" only in passing as an example of democratic voices throughout history, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker is questioning the Home Secretary about the treatment of women suffrage prisoners upon release, highlighting concerning circumstances (women left in the street at night, one fainting, one walking through fog until 3:30am) and challenging the breaking of an arrangement made with Miss Tolson's father. This implicitly advocates for the dignified and lawful treatment of women suffrage prisoners, expressing sympathy with their cause and scrutinising official conduct toward them.

The speech is a wide-ranging Conservative front-bench contribution on transport, local government, privatisation, public expenditure, and parliamentary procedure. The only mention touching on women's civic status is a brief, incidental reference to "independent taxation of husband and wife—a reform which we introduced which gives fiscal independence to women," presented purely as a technical tax-policy hurdle for the Chancellor, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns pay and allowances for Royal Air Force airmen and airwomen, focused on whether their wages are sufficient for a decent standard of living. While "airwomen" are mentioned alongside airmen, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker briefly but explicitly endorses votes for women, mentioning it as a constitutional change that Conservatives "long opposed" and have since (grudgingly) come to accept, framing it positively as part of progressive democratic reform.

The speech addresses the administrative circumstances of releasing suffragette prisoners from Strangeways Prison — timing, travel arrangements, and the Governor's discretion — without making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on the motor industry, labour relations, East-West trade, and economic policy (credit squeeze, wages, exports). Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "men and women" shop stewards, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns nursing recruitment and pay incentives for married nurses with dependants in mental health hospitals, not women's political rights or civic participation. Women are mentioned in the context of healthcare workforce policy, not their distinctive civic status.

The target speech is a follow-up parliamentary question about the administrative circumstances of releasing suffragette prisoners (timing, telegram from the Home Secretary), not an argument for or against women's political rights or their right to vote, stand for office, or participate in civic life.

The speaker explicitly states "we want absolutely the same advantages for women as the men have," expressing support for women's equal treatment in the workforce and civic life. The reference to women like Miss Constance Smith as authoritative voices on workers' issues also affirms women's standing as political and civic participants.

The speech is primarily about constitutional reform, devolution, and the history of the Conservative party's opposition to change. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in passing as one example in a list of reforms the Tory party historically opposed, without any substantive argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker moves to adjourn the House specifically to draw attention to the government's refusal to receive a deputation on women's suffrage, framing that refusal as a cause of public danger — an implicit criticism of the government's obstruction of women's suffrage advocacy. This positions the speaker as supportive of women's suffrage and the right of suffragists to be heard.

This is a maiden speech focused on the fishing industry and constituency matters. While the speaker briefly mentions being "the first woman Member for the Ayr constituency" and notes that suffragettes burned the grandstand in 1913, these are passing historical references without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about trade union ballot secrecy and strike procedures, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "workers, male and female" receiving ballot papers refers to trade union voting, not civic/political rights.

The Speaker's ruling addresses only procedural grounds — that the matter is not "urgent" because it has been ongoing for two years — without making any substantive argument for or against women's suffrage or women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Ashdown) invokes opposition to women's suffrage as a historical example of reactionary Conservative resistance to reform that was ultimately defeated, implicitly endorsing votes for women as a rightful and successful extension of democratic rights. He frames suffragette opposition as analogous to current Conservative scaremongering about constitutional reform, positioning support for women's political rights as the correct historical outcome.

The speaker (Ashdown) explicitly invokes the struggle for women's suffrage as a positive historical achievement, arguing it exemplifies necessary constitutional reform against Conservative resistance, and implies support by stating he assumes no Conservative would wish to see it reversed.

The first part of the TARGET speech explicitly urges that women be given the vote on equal terms with men, and asks the Government to introduce a measure to that effect if a private Members' Bill cannot proceed — a clear expression of support for women's political rights. The appended question from Mr. Palmer about committee procedure is incidental and does not argue against women's suffrage.

The speech is entirely focused on agricultural policy — the Annual Price Review, milk and livestock production, small farmers, credit and capital issues — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The question implicitly advocates for the rights and welfare of suffragist prisoners by scrutinizing whether Lady Constance Lytton and Mrs. Brailsford received preferential treatment compared to other suffragist prisoners, and whether proper medical examinations preceded forced feeding — framing the suffragists as deserving equal and humane treatment in their political protest.

The TARGET speeches (Mr. William Graham and Lieut.-Colonel Sir J. Hope) focus entirely on Scottish devolution/home rule and the merits of the Scottish Home Rule Bill, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a passing reference to "Scotsmen and Scotswomen who have had the honour of service on local authorities" and a brief note that the franchise has been extended to "very large numbers of men and women," neither of which constitutes an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about opposing a Bill requiring secret ballot procedures for trade unions, arguing it is unnecessary and that unions can manage their own affairs. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on East-West trade policy, the Leipzig Trade Fair, NATO reform, and international economic competition with the Soviet bloc. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speaker invokes votes for women as a historical example of necessary democratic reform that opponents wrongly scaremongered against, using it to support the broader argument for extending political rights (here, votes at 16), implicitly endorsing women's suffrage as a justified and successful reform.

The speech addresses the administrative handling of suffragist prisoners — medical examinations, force-feeding, and the grounds for Lady Constance Lytton's release — without making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses on Parliamentary democracy, the Suez crisis, Hungary, Welsh affairs (unemployment, depopulation, forestry, civil aviation, and administration), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on opposing the two-shift system in factories on grounds of worker health, home life, child welfare, and industrial conditions. While women workers are mentioned as affected parties, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation — it concerns labour regulation and working conditions.

The speaker criticises the Tory party for having "fought against votes for women" and having "resisted and challenged even equal pay for women," using these as examples of Tory reactionary positions to condemn the party. While this implicitly endorses women's suffrage and equal pay, the references to women's political rights serve purely as rhetorical ammunition against the Tories in a devolution debate, with no substantive argument made for or about women's political rights themselves.

The question draws attention to the force-feeding of women suffragist prisoners and seeks accountability for the treatment, implicitly advocating for their welfare and rights. By singling out "women suffragists" and probing the conditions of their treatment, the speaker expresses concern for these political prisoners, which is consistent with support for their cause.

The speech is entirely focused on the motor car industry, unemployment, trade union consultation, and economic policy. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the workforce ("men and women"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about Welsh devolution and the referendum result, with only a passing historical reference to "votes for women" as one example among several of constitutional reforms the Conservatives opposed. No substantive argument about women's political rights is made.

The speech by Miss Vickers is almost entirely about the abolition of capital punishment. The brief mention that "the majority of women Members of Parliament are in favour of the abolition of capital punishment" and the reference to Elizabeth Fry are incidental observations used to support the abolitionist case, not arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is a parliamentary question about the welfare and medical treatment of suffragette prisoners, specifically whether a petition from their relatives was received and whether a private medical adviser could visit. It addresses prison conditions rather than making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker acknowledges that Factory Acts were built to protect women when they "were weak industrially and had no political power," but notes that women now have the vote and are organising, expressing support for their established political rights and anticipating a future where legislative protection gives way to women's own industrial and political agency.

The speaker affirms that women are well represented in the factory inspectorate and notes four women in the rank immediately below deputy chief inspector, expressing satisfaction with women's representation. While advocating merit-based promotion "regardless of sex," the speaker frames this positively as consistent with maintaining good female representation, indicating support for women's participation in public/professional roles.

The target speech addresses the medical treatment and force-feeding of suffragist prisoners in Birmingham Prison, focusing on prison authorities' duty of care. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation; it is a factual ministerial response about prison administration and legal obligations.

The speech focuses on labour legislation concerning working hours for women and young persons in industry, but frames this as an industrial/labour policy matter rather than an argument about women's civic rights or political representation. The speaker's concerns are about administrative competence (Home Office vs. Ministry of Labour), Joint Industrial Councils, and the practicalities of shift systems — not about women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in public life.

The speech focuses on industrial council representation, the two-shift system, and working hours for factory workers. While women employees are mentioned in the context of trade union exclusion and dismissal practices, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, or civic representation — it addresses labour and industrial policy.

The speech is a procedural protest about the Government's management of parliamentary business and a critique of a Charity Bill's schedules. The mention of "male or female" persons eligible to vote at church meetings is a passing reference to the Bill's schedule language, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on nuclear disarmament strategy, arms control negotiations, and Cold War geopolitics (Germany, NATO, Soviet relations). Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned, argued for, or against in any part of the speech.

This is a maiden speech by the MP for Calder Valley focused entirely on her constituency and the debate on access to justice and legal aid reform. It contains no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other in-scope topic.

The speaker argues that it is a "double injustice" to tax a wife's income jointly with her husband's for Super-tax purposes while she has no representation in Parliament, explicitly invoking women's lack of political representation as a reason to remedy the tax inequality. This constitutes a substantive argument in favour of women's political rights (noting the injustice of taxation without representation), even though the primary focus is on tax policy.

The speech opposes a clause that would require women and young persons to start work at 5 a.m., framing the objection in terms of health and working conditions rather than women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. While women are mentioned as a class affected by the industrial regulation, the argument is entirely about labour conditions and health, not about women's distinctive civic status or political rights.

The speaker explicitly expresses gladness that Stevenage is "once more represented by a woman" and that the election "doubled the number of women in the House," and praises suffragette Constance Lytton's courage and commitment, indicating clear support for women's political participation and representation.

The speech focuses entirely on bogus candidates, electoral deposits, and candidate registration reform. The mention of women's enfranchisement under the 1918 Representation of the People Act is purely incidental and historical, offered as a "nice little reminder" without any argument about women's political rights.

The speaker confirms that the word "persons" in Clause 35 would include females, and explicitly notes that "female suffrage might be granted by a local Parliament forthwith," supporting the possibility of extending the franchise to women under the bill's provisions.

The speaker explicitly states "I have always been a very strong opponent of female suffrage. I have fought it to the best of my ability for a great number of years, and I shall fight it still, and I am sorry it was ever introduced, and still more sorry that we have another sex in this House." This is a direct and unambiguous declaration of opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political rights by affirming the goal of women's enfranchisement — stating that the motive behind the suffrage agitation is that "women may belong to themselves" and own their property — and further declares he would support an amendment treating wives' incomes separately, connecting women's economic independence directly to the broader suffrage cause.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the National Insurance contributions bill as regressive and inflationary, and arguing for a national superannuation scheme. Women are mentioned only incidentally in passing (e.g., "14s. 2d. per woman" in the context of employer contributions for part-time workers), with no argument made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns voting rights in the Scottish and Welsh devolution referendums for residents and non-residents, focused on the electoral register anomaly — not on women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally alongside men (e.g., "Scots men and women") without any argument about their distinctive civic status.
