The brief mention of voters being able to "express preferences for men or women or for ethnic-minority candidates" is an incidental observation about voter choice in electoral design, not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that "abstract equality" as a basis for women's political rights is "an exploded and obsolete doctrine," opposes the specific Bill as creating inequitable distinctions, and raises deep concerns about granting women the franchise and seats in Parliament, concluding that the measure's effects would be enormous and problematic rather than endorsing it. While he engages substantively with both sides, his overall thrust is skeptical opposition to women's suffrage as currently framed, rejecting the principled case for it.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the franchise to 18-year-olds and draws a favourable parallel to the campaign for women's suffrage, noting that similar arguments about irresponsibility were used against votes for women and were proved wrong, and that no one would now advocate taking the vote away from women. This endorses women's political rights as a settled, justified achievement and uses it to support further franchise extension.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. Snowden, continuing into the text) argues forcefully that the Government should grant further parliamentary facilities for the Parliamentary Franchise (Woman) Bill, insisting there is strong demand from women, a mandate from the country, and a clear majority vote in the House, explicitly pressing for women's suffrage to advance this Session.

The speaker warns that using list members to ensure representation of women (and ethnic minorities) could breach the Sex Discrimination Act 1986, framing gender-based representation mechanisms as legally problematic and implicitly opposing them. This constitutes a substantive argument against engineered female political representation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill to lower the voting age to 18 for young men and women, welcomes expanding civic participation to the younger generation, and states he will vote for the measure in the division lobby. While women's political rights are not the central focus, the speaker explicitly frames the Bill as conferring "full obligations and responsibilities of citizenship" on young men and women aged 18-21, and quotes historical opponents of women's enfranchisement (Lord Finlay) to ridicule resistance to franchise expansion.

The speech focuses almost entirely on unemployment policy, ex-service men, disabled workers, youth unemployment, and insurance schemes. The brief mention of women is limited to noting that many unemployed women are not registering and that unemployed women should have training centres provided for them — these are labour/welfare policy points, not arguments about women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation.

The TARGET speaker (seconding the Motion for Second Reading) explicitly and at length advocates for equal franchise for women, arguing that the 1918 Act was a compromise, that women have proven themselves as voters, that large groups of women (young wives, wage-earners, domestic workers) suffer injustice under the current system, and appeals to the Government to pass the Bill granting women equal franchise with men.

The speech is primarily about Scottish devolution and reserved vs. devolved powers (drugs, firearms, hypnotism, etc.). The brief mention of equal representation for men and women in the Scottish Parliament is a passing jibe at the Liberal Democrats for breaking a promise, not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the franchise to 18-year-olds and invokes the historical extension of the vote to women (women over 30, then women under 30) as a positive precedent, quoting John Stuart Mill's argument that denying women the vote was itself the cause of their perceived unfitness for political life — using this directly to endorse broader enfranchisement.

The speaker (the Prime Minister) defends the Government's refusal to grant further parliamentary facilities for the Women's Suffrage Bill beyond the Second Reading debate, argues the majority for the Bill does not constitute a mandate for further progress, dismisses claims of bad faith, and firmly resists pressure to advance women's suffrage legislation this Session, effectively opposing its practical advancement despite acknowledging Cabinet members personally favour it.

The speaker explicitly states "My one regret about this Bill is that the women of the Northern Region are not enfranchised," and calls on the people of Northern Nigeria "to recognise human equality as well as the equality expressed in their independence," making a clear argument in favour of women's enfranchisement as a political right.

The speaker advocates for relaxing restrictions on the Ladies' Gallery that were imposed in response to suffragette activism, framing the suffragettes' cessation of "disorderly tactics" as grounds for restoring women's access. This implicitly supports a more accommodating stance toward the suffragette cause and women's presence in Parliament.

The speech concerns access arrangements for the Ladies' Gallery in the House of Commons, not women's political rights or representation. While it references militant suffragettes in passing, no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the mechanics and problems of a Plural Voting Bill — issues of disfranchisement, registration complexity, by-election provisions, and applicability to Ireland and universities. While the speaker briefly mentions "manhood suffrage," "adult suffrage," and notes that Australia and New Zealand give both men and women the vote, he explicitly states that topic is not in order to discuss and makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses on welfare service coordination, policing, racial tensions, housing, social services, and public health in Paddington — none of which involves arguments about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "a few promiscuous women" in the context of venereal disease statistics is incidental and makes no argument about women's civic status.

The speaker (Mrs. Fyfe) argues extensively in favour of positive action measures—twinning, quotas, and legal protections—to achieve equal representation of women in the Scottish Parliament, citing UN conventions, European treaty provisions, and comparative European examples to defend the legitimacy of such measures against legal challenge.

The speech is primarily about Southern Rhodesian constitutional reform and African political representation in the context of Central African Federation politics. The sole mention of women is a brief, incidental reference to the Bahamas not yet having "votes for women" as one data point in an argument about constitutional change — no position on women's political rights is argued.

The speaker (Mr. Wallace) explicitly outlines and endorses the Liberal Democrats' detailed mechanism for achieving gender balance in Scottish Parliament candidate lists, argues for exempting political parties from sex discrimination legislation specifically to enable this system, and states "that is why we support the new clause" — which is aimed at facilitating equal representation of women in the Scottish Parliament.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage, arguing that Parliament has repeatedly expressed a majority in favour of it and that the Cabinet's obstruction constitutes a "real and grievous grievance" against women. The speech calls on the Government to give the Women's Suffrage Bill a genuine opportunity to pass into law.

The Duchess of Atholl explicitly acknowledges genuine grievances of certain women under the current franchise (university graduates, married women, single professional women) and states "They are entitled to have a vote," while substantively opposing the full equal franchise at 21 for all women, arguing women need more local government experience first, that extending the franchise takes advantage of war losses, and that she "cannot associate myself with the claim to so great an extension of the franchise at the present time." This constitutes genuine two-sided argument: supporting limited remedies for specific women's franchise grievances while opposing the broad extension proposed.

The speaker declares himself a longstanding advocate for women's suffrage and explicitly supports removing women's disabilities (e.g., the university franchise age anomaly), yet opposes this specific Bill on substantive grounds — arguing it hides drastic electoral reforms (abolition of business premises qualifications, assimilation of local and parliamentary franchises) behind the women's suffrage cause, and that women's enfranchisement should not be pursued through such an "omnibus" measure. This constitutes genuine substantive argument on both sides: endorsing women's political rights in principle while substantively opposing the vehicle for delivering them in ways that go beyond procedural objection.

The speaker explicitly supports the enfranchisement of women as the "main principle" of the Bill, argues that women in Northern Ireland deserve the franchise as full citizens, and presses the Government to commit to passing the measure — objecting only to the procedural inadequacy of debate time and the Government's lack of commitment, not to women's enfranchisement itself.

The speaker (Secretary of State for the Colonies) affirms that women will be included in the upcoming Northern Cameroons plebiscite on the basis of universal suffrage, directly addressing and resolving the complaint that no African women were included in the previous register — a clear endorsement of women's political participation rights.

The speech is entirely focused on condemning apartheid and South Africa's racial policies against non-European people, urging the UK government to raise the issue at the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference. While it mentions denial of "political rights" to non-Europeans broadly, it does not address women's political rights or representation as a distinct issue at any point.

The speaker (Mr. Wallace, Liberal Democrats) explicitly supports amending the Sex Discrimination Act to enable positive discrimination in candidate selection to achieve gender balance in the Scottish Parliament, welcomes the new clause, and outlines his party's detailed mechanism for ensuring equal male/female representation on candidate lists.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly advocates for extending the parliamentary franchise to women on equal terms with men (ages 21-30), arguing it is a matter of "common justice," citing millions of disenfranchised women workers, and celebrating the positive effects of women's votes since 1918. The speech makes no substantive argument against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "I have for many many years been absolutely convinced that women should have the vote" and supports removing genuine grievances for women, yet opposes this specific Bill on grounds that it goes too far (creating a female voting majority at a time when many men died in the War) and contains provisions he considers improper, ultimately supporting an Amendment to delay action via a cross-party conference rather than passing the Bill as drafted.

The speaker explicitly endorses equal franchise for women ("there should not be any differentiation in respect of age as between men and women voters" and "the majority of the House would feel that such differentiation should be abolished"), while his procedural objections concern only the manner of legislating (conference vs. government bill), not the principle of women's equal voting rights.

The speech concerns the appointment of a Prison Commissioner and whether a medical expert should hold that position, not women's political rights. The only passing reference to women is a mention of "lady prisoners—the suffragettes" and "artificial feeding" as an example of why medical expertise on the Prison Commission is needed, but no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker dismisses the Home Secretary's argument that a closed list system is needed to protect ethnic minorities and women from electoral disadvantage, labeling it "deeply anti-democratic." This implicitly rejects the use of women's representation as a justification for restricting voter choice, opposing the policy mechanism designed to advance women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly supports the new clause aimed at achieving gender balance in the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly, arguing that the legal backing should be provided to enable it, and concludes that those who stand in the way are "hypocritical." The speech frames equal representation of women as an opportunity to advance democracy in new institutions.

The speech is a parliamentary question and answer about government grants under the Unemployed Workmen Act, covering relief works, emigration, farm colonies, and women's workrooms as budgetary line items. It makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns a Private Member's Bill to lower the voting age to 18, not women's political rights. While the speaker references historical franchise extensions (including women over 30 in 1918 and 1928), these are cited only as part of a chronological list of franchise expansions, not as arguments for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speaker explicitly states "I have been a constant advocate of women franchise all the time that I have been a Member of this House, and I believe that justice will be done." His objection is procedural/temporal — that an arrangement was made to delay further extension — not that women should be denied political rights. This is a supporter with a timing caveat, not substantive opposition.

The speaker (Mr. McLeish) explicitly affirms that "the Labour Government and the Labour party are committed to seeing equal representation in the Parliament," and quotes a critic of equal representation only to distance himself from her view, hoping the Liberal Democrats will remain "on course" for equal representation. The speech consistently advocates for women's equal representation in the Scottish Parliament.

The speech is a parliamentary question about a Queensland referendum on religious instruction in state schools. While it incidentally notes that women were qualified to vote, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights — it is simply asking for factual information about the referendum's mechanics and results.

The speech is a parliamentary business statement by the Prime Minister outlining the legislative schedule, and while it mentions that time will be allotted for the Second Reading of the Parliamentary Franchise (Women) Bill, no argument for or against women's political rights is made — it is a purely procedural scheduling announcement.

The speech is primarily about a dispute over the appointment of a Prison Commissioner (whether a medical man should hold the role) and prison administration reform. The only reference to "suffragettes" is a passing mention noting they were among groups raising issues about prison treatment, without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the Central African Federation, race relations, economic conditions, and political prospects for the territories. The brief mention of African women's status and the observation that no one called for "one woman, one vote" is anecdotal colour about African society, not an argument for or against women's political rights as a matter of British or colonial policy.

The target speech addresses the question of press access to local government committee meetings and the merits of open democratic debate versus secret committees. While it incidentally mentions "men and women" in generic references to political participants, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states they want the Scottish Parliament to be "women friendly," supports equal opportunities for women in candidate selection, and endorses efforts to achieve gender balance in parliamentary representation, including committing funds to support women candidates and renewing a commitment to achieve gender balance within the law.

The speaker (Mr. Foot) wholeheartedly supports equal franchise for women, arguing that nearly five million women are unjustly denied the vote, that "the difference of sex is as entirely irrelevant to political rights as difference in height," and that granting women the vote is "the granting of a right" — not a concession. He personally introduced a prior Bill to give women the franchise on equal terms with men, and strongly endorses the Bill under debate throughout.

The speech is a factual reply about a Queensland referendum on religious instruction in schools, merely noting in passing that both women and men were qualified to vote, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.
The speech is entirely about rail privatisation and the composition of the central rail users consultative committee; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is focused on the Middle East peace process and human rights in the region. While the speaker briefly mentions that women in parts of the Middle East have no rights and cannot vote, this is cited as an example of human rights deficits to illustrate a broader point about applying universal democratic standards consistently, not as an argument for or against women's political rights as such.

The speaker is asking a procedural question about parliamentary practice regarding the Report stage of a Bill sent to committee, not making any argument for or against women's political rights. The mention of the Parliamentary Franchise (Women) Bill is purely contextual to frame the procedural query.

The speaker explicitly welcomes that women of the Northern and Southern Territories of the British Cameroons have been included in the electoral register for the first time, and expresses hope that Nigerian women in the Northern Territory will likewise be included, so they "may take their full part in the running of their country."

The speech concerns the Human Rights Act/Bill debate, focusing on proposals for a Joint Committee to examine human rights compatibility, public education, access to legal representation, and international protocols. The mention of the Abdulaziz case involves women as litigants in an immigration/family life context, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker briefly but explicitly endorses women's voting rights when discussing Northern Nigeria, saying "I hope she will go on to study how other Muslim countries have adapted themselves to democratic methods and will consider seriously before long whether women ought not to be allowed to vote." This is a clear, if passing, argument in favour of women's political rights (the franchise).

The speech is entirely focused on defence policy, military procurement, NATO strategy, nuclear deterrence, and armed forces recruitment. While it briefly mentions "men and women" serving in the Armed Forces, this is incidental and does not argue any position on women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a parliamentary business statement scheduling legislative time, including for the Parliamentary Franchise (Women) Bill, but makes no argument for or against women's political rights. It merely announces the allocation of parliamentary days to various bills and votes.

The speaker explicitly states "I have been an advocate of women suffrage all along" and describes his role in getting women's suffrage included in the 1918 Reform Act. While he argues the House is "morally bound" by the arrangement to delay further extension, he frames this as a procedural/honour argument rather than opposition to women's political rights, and supports a compromise age of 25 rather than opposing women's enfranchisement.

The speaker questions whether an open (Belgian-style) list system would discriminate against women and ethnic minorities, implying support for electoral arrangements that protect women's representation. This concern for women's fair participation in the political process reflects a pro-women's political rights stance.

The speaker explicitly rises to support the Bill aimed at extending equal franchise to women, expresses regret only about the Bill's scope being too broad rather than opposing women's enfranchisement, and urges the Government to provide facilities to pass the measure into law.

The speaker explicitly highlights that women lack the vote and are excluded from the Legislature in the Bahamas, and argues there is "no reason" they should be deprived of a say in matters of health and education — directly advocating for women's civic participation and representation.

The speaker explicitly cites ensuring "balanced representation of women in the European Parliament in the regions" as a reason why party leadership wants control over candidate ranking, and uses this to argue for an open list system that would give the electorate more influence — thus supporting structural arrangements that promote women's representation in elected office.

The speaker explicitly argues that open/flexible list systems have "significantly increased the number of women in Norwegian politics" and "transformed Norway's political system," and expresses that "we sorely need that in our system," directly advocating for electoral mechanisms that improve women's political representation.

The speaker (Mr. Dodds) explicitly supports the Bill to extend the franchise to younger women (ages 21–30) on equal terms with men, arguing that women have demonstrated their fitness for the vote, that the anomaly of excluding women under 30 is indefensible, and that opponents are "fighting a rearguard action." He states directly: "I desire to support the Bill because of its principal object, that is, mainly because of the first Clause" and calls extending the franchise to younger women "a right" rather than a concession.

The speech is primarily about Army recruitment and manpower planning following the end of conscription. While the speaker discusses expanding women's roles in various Army corps as a practical manpower solution, this is framed entirely as a military staffing argument, not as an argument about women's civic rights or political representation.

The speech concerns funding for women's workrooms under the Unemployed Workmen Act — a welfare/employment matter — without making any argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is an extended review of Indian administration covering finance, agriculture, public health, political unrest, press legislation, education, and the Indian Councils Act. While it briefly mentions social reformers working on "the education of women" and "the abolition of infant marriage" as examples of social unrest in India, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation in any way.

The speaker explicitly states "I think it would be wise—to give the franchise to men and women on the same basis" and pledges to "vote for it" if universal suffrage is enacted at age 25, and to "vote on every opportunity on the straight issue of putting the age of franchise for men and women on an equal basis." While he prefers age 25 over 21, this is a caveat about implementation rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly notes that the underpaid Pimlico workers "are mostly women who receive these wages; they are not voters, and, therefore, have not the same attraction for the Government which other employes have" — treating women's lack of the vote as a given disadvantage that explains their poor treatment, without arguing they should have the vote. This framing accepts women's disenfranchisement as a natural political fact and uses it instrumentally to criticize the Government's wage policy, implicitly endorsing the status quo of women's exclusion from political influence.

The speaker (Lord Privy Seal, Mr. Clynes) explicitly states "the Government are in favour of the Second Reading of this Bill, and they wish to see it passed into law," referring to a Bill to enfranchise women on equal terms with men, and pledges government support to provide parliamentary time for its passage.

The speaker explicitly supports equal franchise rights for men and women, seeing no logical distinction between them, yet simultaneously argues that women aged 21–25 should not have the vote because that age is a special "flowering time" better devoted to other pursuits — effectively opposing enfranchisement for one subset of women (21–25) while supporting it for women 25 and over on equal terms with men.

The target speech by Mr. Clement Davies is entirely focused on the Cyprus Independence Bill — the history of British governance in Cyprus, tributes to the Governor and Archbishop Makarios, criticism of past Colonial Office policy, and the terms of the independence agreement. While it briefly mentions giving "the right to vote to men and women over 21" as part of a proposed constitutional arrangement, this is a passing reference to a general franchise proposal rather than an argument for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speaker (Mr. Straw) raises the concern that an open list system could discriminate against women and ethnic minorities, citing evidence from local elections where candidates with minority names fare worse despite favourable ballot positions. This argument is used to support the closed list system as a structural mechanism to protect women's and minorities' representation in elected office.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill to extend the franchise to women on equal terms with men, arguing that working women have a genuine political interest in wages, housing, and economic conditions, and challenging the logic of denying to women a right that male Members themselves enjoy. He dismisses the Amendment to delay the measure and expresses the Government's desire to see the Bill pass into law.

The speaker (Miss Herbison) explicitly argues that women should be employed as traffic wardens on equal terms with men from the outset, criticising the Commissioner's decision to exclude women as unjustifiable and outdated. She also endorses equal pay for women in all work, grounding her argument in women's right to equal opportunity in public employment.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing Scottish temperance/licensing legislation (local veto on public houses), arguing against the Bill on grounds of inefficacy, individual liberty, and practical concerns about the drink trade. Women's political rights are not mentioned, argued for, or argued against anywhere in the speech.

The speaker explicitly raises the exclusion of women from the electoral register in the Northern Cameroons as a concern, describing them as "very intelligent African women" who were "completely excluded" from the previous vote, implying support for their inclusion in the upcoming plebiscite.

The TARGET speech is concerned entirely with matrimonial maintenance orders and reconciliation provisions in a matrimonial bill — specifically whether a maintenance order should remain in force when spouses resume cohabitation. It makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that an open list system "would force the parties to offer more women candidates" and expresses support for the European "zipper system" alternating male and female candidates, framing the open list as advancing the cause of women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly states support for assimilating women's franchise to that enjoyed by men, including from age 21, saying "I hope women may be given the vote at the age of 21 and may exercise it in the same way as men have exercised it." His objections are purely procedural—he wants the Bill simplified and the Government to commit time—not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states "I am heartily in favour of the Bill," argues urgently for equal franchise for women (both under and over 30), cites concrete examples of women being improperly removed from registers, and appeals for the Bill's Second Reading and passage into law as soon as possible.

The speech is entirely focused on primary education policy — school buildings, class sizes, the 11-plus examination, rural schools in Cornwall, and teacher recruitment — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on explaining the mechanics of open, closed, and semi-open list electoral systems for European Parliament elections, including the d'Hondt method. The brief mention of "four women's places" in the shadow Cabinet electoral system is purely incidental and does not argue any position on women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that the open list system "will unquestionably discriminate against women and people with foreign-sounding names," implying opposition to open lists on the grounds that they disadvantage women in political representation — effectively supporting the closed list system which the speaker frames as better for women's representation.

The speech concerns a dispute between local authorities and the Scottish Secretary of State over planning powers for the new town of Cumbernauld, focusing on housing standards, local authority powers, and public health. While it briefly mentions attracting "men and women of the right type" to public service, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on RAF pay, allowances, National Service estimates, and Air Force staffing levels. While it briefly mentions "Airwomen" as a subhead category, it makes no argument about women's political rights, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is focused on the Strategic Defence Review, Army force quality, foreign/security policy, and the Territorial Army. The brief mention of "men and women" in defence industry and the armed forces, and the speaker's aside that "I hope that there will be more women" in the Army's senior ranks, are passing references without substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is primarily a sustained argument in favour of the Scottish Local Option (temperance/licensing) Bill, with only a passing mention that women would also have the right to vote under the Bill. This single incidental reference does not constitute an argument about women's political rights — it is a rhetorical point about the breadth of public support for the temperance measure, not a substantive position on women's civic status or franchise.

The speaker expresses support for encouraging more women to stand for elected office, but simultaneously opposes single-sex nomination lists as a mechanism for achieving that goal, framing them as an undesirable "socialist policy" that undermines women's credibility as candidates on merit. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: endorsing women's political participation while opposing a specific structural measure (gender-exclusive candidate lists) designed to advance women's representation.

The speaker explicitly states continued support for women's suffrage ("I did support that, and I should support it again... I still remain a supporter of woman suffrage") while simultaneously opposing this Bill's extension of the franchise to women aged 21-30, arguing it is undesirable to enfranchise young persons of either sex and suggesting the voting age be raised to 25 for both sexes instead. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: endorsing women's political rights in principle while substantively opposing this particular expansion on grounds specific to the age group being enfranchised.

The target speech is entirely focused on Army strategy, the role of the Commonwealth, military posture, and defence spending. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker praises Labour as "the only party in Scotland holding the trophy for the fight for equal rights for men and women" and criticises the SNP for rejecting "positive measures to ensure equal representation of men and women in the Scottish Parliament," clearly endorsing gender parity in political representation. The speaker also urges the Lord Chancellor to engage with the equal treatment directive to remove obstacles to equal representation.

The speech is entirely focused on parliamentary procedure reform — ten-minute speeches, private Members' time, and registered pairs/proxy voting. The passing mention of "sending the best men and women to the House" is rhetorical flourish about democracy, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is almost entirely concerned with factory inspection, labour conditions, the Truck Act, lead poisoning in the potteries, and the administration of the Factory Department — none of which engage women's political rights or civic representation. Women are mentioned only as workers (lady inspectors, female factory workers) in an industrial/labour context, not as a class with distinctive civic or political status.

The speaker explicitly invokes women's votes and women's rights, arguing that MPs who voted for women's suffrage are being hypocritical by supporting regulations that drive women out of employment suited to them. The speech advocates for preserving women's employment and links it directly to the purpose of women having political rights — to protect their conditions of work.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on opposing a Welsh local option liquor control bill, arguing on grounds of democratic mandate, club liberties, polling area anomalies, and public ownership as an alternative. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker explicitly argues that Scottish women have been "entirely ignored" in the appointment of Royal Commissions and calls on the Home Office to ensure that Scottish women receive proper representation on future Commissions, thereby advocating for women's inclusion in public/political bodies.

The speech is entirely focused on implementing the Crowther Report's recommendations for raising the school-leaving age, improving education quality, and increasing education spending. Women's political rights and representation are never argued for or against; the incidental mention of "girls" and "she" in educational contexts does not constitute an argument about women's civic or political status.

The speech concerns restricting the employment of women in offices after childbirth, a workplace health/welfare matter. It does not argue about women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of civic participation that falls within the scope of women's political rights.

The TARGET contains two speakers: Miss Jewson invokes the Sex Disqualification Removal Act to challenge a government reply, implicitly supporting women's right to equal treatment under that Act; Viscountess Astor reinforces this by holding the Labour Government accountable to its election promises on the matter. Both contributions argue in favour of women's political/civic rights being upheld.

Lord Hugh Cecil explicitly opposes the Bill enfranchising women aged 21-30, arguing they would "injure the democratic system," dismisses equal citizenship as "claptrap" and an "obsolete conflagration," and urges the House to refuse passage. While he nominally supported women's suffrage in the past and suggests raising the voting age to 25 for both sexes, this is a procedural/timing caveat rather than substantive support — his core argument is that women in this age group should not receive the vote now.

The speaker explicitly criticises the House for having only one in five Members being women while governing a population half of which are women, using this as evidence that the current electoral system fails representativeness. She argues for electoral reform partly on the grounds of improving women's (and ethnic minority) representation in Parliament.

The speaker explicitly states they will "vote for the Second Reading of this Bill" and "also against it being committed to a Committee of the Whole House," endorsing women's enfranchisement. While acknowledging party-political concerns from opponents, the speaker affirms support for taking advantage of this "unique opportunity" to advance women's franchise.

The speaker briefly but explicitly supports greater involvement of women in local government, welcoming proposals from the Commission on Local Government and the Scottish Parliament to consider "how more women can become involved" as councillors. This is a positive endorsement of women's political representation, even if it is a minor element within a broader speech on Scottish local government.

The TARGET speech is primarily about temperance and local option legislation for Wales, with only passing references to women (e.g., "thousands of women voted for the Labour party," "the women of the country are going to legislate for their children," "why should not the women have a chance?"). These references treat women as voters or moral stakeholders in temperance reform, but the speech makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on naval defence expenditure, NATO arrangements, fleet composition, and military spending efficiency. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely about Indian colonial administration, specifically the Press Act, Seditious Meetings Act, police corruption, and restrictive legislation in India. The only mention of women is a brief factual reference to 1,813 women voters on the Bombay municipal election roll, used solely to correct an administrative error about the franchise in India—no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Earl Ronaldshay) focuses on refuting a pro-suffrage argument that Indian women could vote under the Councils Act, citing official regulations that explicitly disqualify females from voting, thereby undermining a key argument made in favour of the women's suffrage Bill and supporting opposition to it.

The speech is primarily concerned with alleged electoral intimidation, corrupt practices, and improper expenditure in the East Dorset by-election, focusing on the conduct of Lady Wimborne and the Wimborne estate. While the speaker briefly mentions that Lady Wimborne acting as an election agent comes with "disabilities that attach to the exercise of votes by women," this is a passing remark rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The target speech is solely concerned with establishing the procedural basis for raising unemployment relief topics (light railways, land improvement, women's domestic training, juvenile unemployment centres) under a specific Vote. It does not argue for or against women's political rights; the mention of "training of women in domestic work" relates to employment/welfare policy, not women's civic or political participation.

The speaker explicitly endorses the involvement of more women in public life in Northern Ireland, highlights women's significant role in the peace talks, and notes with approval that nearly 50 women are standing as candidates for the assembly elections, framing all of this positively.

The speech is entirely concerned with Catholic religious processions, the Catholic Emancipation Act of 1829, and religious toleration in Scotland. While the speaker briefly mentions "processions of suffragettes" in passing as one example among many types of processions, no argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly expresses hope that "many more women will take part in the decision-making process by being elected to the Northern Ireland assembly," directly endorsing greater women's political representation in a legislative body.

The speech deals entirely with RAF reserve forces, the Royal Auxiliary Air Force, the Air Training Corps, and the Royal Observer Corps, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The passing mention of "men and women" serving in reserve forces does not engage with any question of women's civic status or political rights.

The speech is focused on the details of a Supplementary Estimate for unemployment relief, covering land improvement, light railways, juvenile unemployment centres, and loans to local authorities. The mention of "women's training" is purely a budgetary line item (how much is allocated and how it will be spent), with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is a procedural/Chair announcement grouping amendments about tax allowance rates for men and women under a national insurance graduated scheme. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation; the differential treatment of men and women here concerns tax/insurance contribution rates, not voting, office-holding, or political representation.

The target speech is by Miss Bondfield addressing parliamentary questions about government spending on women's training centres and ex-service men's employment relief — it is administrative/budgetary in nature and does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on defending the first-past-the-post electoral system against proportional representation alternatives; women's political rights are mentioned only in passing as one historical example of franchise expansion ("to give votes to women") without any argument being made about them.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly argues in favour of women's political rights, contending that women's domestic responsibilities qualify rather than disqualify them from voting, that the vote will not harm motherhood or home life, and concluding "anything we can do to further the political interests of women will be for the best interests of this Empire." Although the speaker notes personal dissatisfaction with aspects of the Bill ("in many respects I dislike this Bill"), this is a procedural/implementation caveat, not substantive opposition to women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly notes that 75% of women in Northern Ireland voted for peace and argues this demonstrates that "the old politics of Northern Ireland—predominantly male politics—are long overdue for change," expressing hope for greater female political representation in the new assembly. This constitutes a brief but substantive argument in favour of women's political participation and representation.

The speaker (Mr. Rhys Davies, Under-Secretary of State for the Home Department) explicitly states "The Government are in favour of the Second Reading of this Bill" and personally welcomes it, arguing it would extend the franchise to women on equal terms with men and remove the "preposterous disqualification" tied to property ownership. He also expresses personal support for women voting as human beings and good citizens regardless of property.

The speech consists entirely of parliamentary supply resolutions and financial estimates for Air, Navy, and Army services for 1960-61, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Northern Ireland peace process, the Belfast Agreement, prisoner releases, and decommissioning. The mention of the "Women's Coalition" is purely incidental—used as a statistical data point in a voting analysis—with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports gender balancing mechanisms such as zipping (alternating men and women on party lists) and argues the Bill should include exemptions from sex discrimination legislation to enable gender-balanced candidate lists, framing these as ways to ensure women achieve fair representation in elected office.

The speaker (Austen Chamberlain) explicitly and at length opposes women's suffrage, arguing that women are "not qualified to exercise the franchise" due to their inherent nature and differences from men, and urges the House to "maintain the great distinction which now finds its place under our laws" rather than extend political rights to women.

The speech concerns the Secretary for Scotland's failure to appoint Scottish representatives (men and women) to various Commissions, as an administrative grievance. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation; the mention of "men and women" is incidental to a complaint about Scottish representation on commissions.

The speaker explicitly states he is "pledged to the principle of giving the franchise to men and women upon equal terms at the age of twenty-five" and will vote for it, while his objections are procedural (concerns about gerrymandering and the bill's drafting), not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that women are unjustly denied votes despite holding property, paying taxes, and contributing to public life, and contends that women's votes are the "only means by which a radical change can be effected in regard to their grievances," providing extensive evidence of the harms caused by women's lack of political representation.

The target speech addresses plural voting, university constituencies, and electoral franchise technicalities, without making any argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" who received university education is incidental and does not argue a position on women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the parliamentary franchise to women aged 21-30, arguing it is a betrayal of wartime promises to withhold the vote from younger women, that refusing citizenship to these women is "a decadent policy," and that the tinkers and working people deserve the franchise. He urges the Government to give "unqualified support" to the Bill.

The speaker explicitly states "I favour the principle of granting the franchise at the age of 25 on equal terms to men and women" and notes he has consistently advocated this position to women voters in his constituency. His objections are procedural—that the Bill makes too many constitutional changes for a private Member's Bill—not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the increase in Profits Tax as it affects local authorities, co-operative societies, and non-profit sports associations, with arguments centred on housing, local democracy, and financial policy. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women" serving on councils, a reference to Mrs. Slater as an MP), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states that efforts are being made to ensure "more women and ethnic minorities get the representation that was denied them" on quangos, directly endorsing greater political representation for women in public bodies.

The speaker explicitly states that the Government shares the aim of increasing the representation of women and minority groups in Parliament, expresses hope that parties will encourage women candidates and avoid discriminatory selection procedures, and celebrates the large increase in women MPs following the 1997 general election as having improved parliamentary business. While explaining legal constraints on all-women shortlists, the speaker's overall position is supportive of women's representation.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Bill, arguing it would injure women, that married women are better qualified than spinsters (the electorate the Bill would create), and that the "feminist movement" would harm women through divorce reform and undermining chivalry. While he expresses a preference for married women having the vote over spinsters, this is deployed as an argument against the Bill rather than a genuine endorsement of any form of women's suffrage — he concludes "We believe this Bill will not only be a danger to the State, but would be an injury to the rank and file of women themselves."

The speaker explicitly criticizes the Liberal Democrats' demand for mechanisms to circumvent equal opportunities legislation to achieve gender-balanced candidate lists, calling it "a most ridiculous argument" rooted in the false premise that men and women have "antithetical interests and cannot be represented one by the other," and welcomes the fact that the Bill does not endorse such a system.

The speech concerns tax relief for housekeepers and whether it should be extended from widows/widowers to spinsters and bachelors — a matter of tax equity and fiscal policy. While the speaker is a woman arguing on behalf of spinsters (among others), the speech does not address women's voting rights, candidacy, representation, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic participation as defined by the suffrage movement's framing.

The speaker explicitly expresses pride in her party's record of increasing women's representation in Parliament, and calls on other parties to pursue equal representation for women in all new institutions, demonstrating clear support for women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly states "Before the franchise was given I was always in favour of giving the vote to women," and supports the Bill's extension of the franchise. While he raises concerns about electoral instability and calls for proportional representation as a companion measure, these are procedural/structural objections rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech is entirely concerned with the technical details of flat-rate tax allowances for National Insurance graduated contributions under PAYE, including administrative feasibility and Exchequer costs. While it briefly mentions different allowance figures for men and women in the context of tax calculations, this is a reference to existing differential contribution rates, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly states they intended to vote in support of the Bill extending women's franchise, and argues against the previous speaker's logic that women's "higher functions" should disqualify them from voting, asserting that fitness for higher duties makes the lesser matter of voting all the more justified.

The speech is entirely focused on supporting legislation to remove turnstiles from women's public lavatories — a sanitary convenience and public health issue. While the speaker mentions women's equality and dignity in the context of lavatory access, he makes no argument about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or civic participation. The reference to "Woman Suffrage" in passing (quoting Bernard Shaw) is incidental and not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is part of a debate about the Parliament Bill and the constitutional conflict between the two Houses, focusing on election mandates and the Referendum. The mention of "Votes for women" is a heckle from another member, not an argument by the speaker; the speaker does not engage with or argue about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on military conscription, the Kuwait operation, the Berlin crisis, nuclear defence policy, and economic issues — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker is actively promoting the Women's Suffrage Bill, pressing the Government for sufficient parliamentary time and effective facilities to pass it, and explicitly speaking on behalf of "all the women in the country who are interested in this question."

The speech is entirely focused on leasehold reform in Wales — arguing that owner-occupiers should have the right to purchase freeholds at fair cost. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation; the single passing reference to a "Cardiff North Conservative Women's annual meeting" is purely incidental and carries no argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about unemployment insurance — specifically whether uncovenanted benefit should be a statutory right or subject to ministerial/committee discretion, and the importance of maintaining the contributory scheme's financial stability. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker expresses lukewarm support for women's suffrage ("I am not a very enthusiastic supporter... of Woman Suffrage") while simultaneously arguing that the National Insurance Bill treats women unfairly by depriving them of benefits when they marry, and suggesting women with votes would have prevented such a provision — making substantive arguments touching both sides of women's political standing without fully endorsing suffrage.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political representation, praising the increased number of women in the UK's Council of Europe delegation, condemning the Conservative all-male delegation for voting against an equality committee, and celebrating the election of over 100 women Labour MPs as a mandate for change. The speech consistently frames women's equality in political and civic life as a positive goal.

The speech is entirely focused on foreign policy matters — Angola, Berlin, NATO, nuclear weapons, and Cold War negotiations — with no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related topic.

The target speech is entirely about a Welsh licensing/local option bill (temperance/alcohol control legislation), responding to Mr. Clarry's argument about constituency opposition. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about education funding, rates, teacher staffing changes, and school inspectors. The brief mention of "female supernumerary teachers" having "no union and no vote" is incidental context explaining why they lack political clout, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports increasing women's representation in Parliament and public life, endorses the Liberal Democrats' use of zipped lists and other practical measures to boost female political participation, and argues that the male domination of power structures shapes legislation in ways that disadvantage women — all substantive arguments in favour of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker presents the Australian Senate's unanimous resolution praising women's suffrage as having "brought nothing but good" and urging all nations to grant votes to women, and asks whether the UK Government has considered acting upon this advice — framing the question in a way that implicitly endorses extending women's suffrage.

The speech by Mr. Julius Silverman (Birmingham, Aston) is entirely focused on the Berlin crisis, Soviet-German relations, Cold War diplomacy, and the fear of German militarism. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on Welsh local option/temperance legislation and the speaker's experience with the Scottish Temperance Act, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mentions of Viscountess Astor and "women and children" are rhetorical flourishes in a temperance debate, not arguments about women's civic status or political rights.

The TARGET speaker asks the Prime Minister to grant facilities for the passage of the Women's Enfranchisement Bill into law, explicitly citing the majority of Members in favour of Women's Suffrage and the electorate's endorsement of those opinions — a clear argument in support of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political representation, praising the twinning mechanism to achieve equal numbers of men and women in the Scottish Parliament and expressing regret that all-women shortlists were not defended on appeal. The speech also endorses the Government's work on women's issues through the Cabinet Sub-Committee and Ministers for Women, including public appointments where "the representation of women is a key policy priority."

The speech concerns the treatment of a hunger-striking prisoner (Miss Arrowsmith) and the practice of forcible feeding, not women's political rights or representation. While it references suffragettes' historical experiences with forcible feeding, this is raised as a human rights/prison welfare concern rather than an argument about women's civic participation or the franchise.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as "a confirmed opponent of Woman Suffrage" and then argues for improving women's treatment under the National Insurance Bill, framing this self-servingly as not wanting to give women ammunition for suffrage arguments. The only substantive statement on women's political rights is the self-declared opposition to women's suffrage; the discussion of women's benefits under the insurance bill is social/welfare policy, not a rights argument.

The speech is entirely focused on Welsh local option (temperance/drink legislation), with only a passing incidental mention of "women voters" as part of a vote-count illustration. No argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker defends women's political participation in the Conservative party and argues that the number of women Conservative MPs understates women's active roles in the party, implicitly supporting greater female representation. The broader context (confirmed by the following speeches) shows the speaker also endorses women's right to rise on merit while opposing quotas — but in the TARGET itself the argument is affirmatively pro-women's representation without raising the quota objection.

The speaker explicitly supports women's full inclusion in public life — arguing against single-sex institutions (MCC), opposing both old-fashioned male chauvinism and any new "ghetto" for women's issues, and defending women's independent taxation and direct benefit payments as practically important to women's economic autonomy. These are substantive arguments in favour of women's equal civic participation.

The speech is about security concerns regarding American ships at Holy Loch and the risk of sabotage; the reference to suffragettes is purely incidental, used as an example of "unbalanced" protesters, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily concerned with the Parliament Bill and constitutional reform (the powers of the Second Chamber). While the speaker briefly mentions Woman Suffrage and the possibility that the House might be elected by a plurality of women or that women might sit in the House, these are passing observations used as examples of potential consequences of the Bill, not arguments for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about Sierra Leone's independence, its economy, democratic development, and British aid. The brief mention of registering women voters is purely descriptive/logistical ("It will inevitably take time to register the women voters who will become the electorate") and does not argue for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's equal representation in decision-making bodies, endorses positive action (such as all-women shortlists) as necessary to achieve gender balance in Parliament, the Scottish Parliament, and Welsh Assembly, and argues that democracy requires elected chambers to reflect the full population including women.

The speech is entirely focused on housing policy, municipal governance, unemployment, and the conditions of working-class families. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation anywhere in the speech.

The speaker explicitly and enthusiastically supports the Bill to extend the vote to women of 21, arguing that extending the franchise is a matter of citizenship and justice, that women are equally capable as men, and that party considerations are irrelevant to this question of right.

The speech is entirely focused on budgetary details of Supplementary Estimates covering land drainage, afforestation, and domestic service training. The brief mention of training women for domestic service is a budgetary/employment matter, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker expresses support for women's political participation, praising women gaining the vote, welcoming more women in the armed forces and Parliament, and looking forward to greater female representation, including statues of women in the parliamentary building. These are affirmative arguments for women's civic and political rights.

The speech argues for widows' pensions and state support for families with incapacitated breadwinners — a welfare/social policy matter. It makes no arguments about women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of women's civic/political rights as defined in scope.

The speech is primarily about development needs in Sarawak and North Borneo (education, roads, citizenship, agriculture, civil service). The only brief mention touching on women is that married women are not allowed to work as nurses in Borneo, raised as an administrative curiosity rather than an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the underrepresentation of women in Parliament (only 4 out of 40 Welsh MPs, only 7 women MPs from Wales since women gained the vote) signals "something wrong with the system," and calls for ensuring women have the opportunity to participate in the House, the Scottish Parliament, and the National Assembly of Wales. This is a direct argument in favour of women's political representation.

The speech is almost entirely about the Parliament Bill, the Referendum, constitutional reform of the House of Lords, Home Rule, and the South African Union constitution. The single brief mention of Women's Suffrage ("It has not been suggested that you should take a poll of the women of this country on the question of Women Suffrage") is purely illustrative of a hypothetical use of the Referendum, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly acknowledges representations from married women deterred from professional employment by income aggregation rules for Surtax, and states that his proposals will go a long way to solving this problem — effectively supporting measures that ease women's participation in professional/economic public life.

The speech is entirely focused on the political situation in Rhodesia — racial discrimination against Africans, the proposed constitution, political stability, trade unions, and Cold War concerns. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about; the subject matter is race-based political rights and colonial governance, not women's civic participation.

The target speech is entirely focused on unemployment, labour policy, trade unions, and employer-worker relations. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the phrase "men and women" in the context of unemployment relief, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on the Parliament Bill, the Government's use of guillotine resolutions, and the erosion of the House of Commons' independence from Executive control. The single passing reference to Women's Suffrage is a brief suspicion that the Government wants to avoid discussing it, with no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on unemployment policy, public works schemes, and government spending. The single mention of "training and work for women" appears as one item in a long list of administrative questions about unemployment relief expenditure, without any argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the political future of the Cameroons following a UN plebiscite, addressing issues of sovereignty, security, currency, and trade. The brief mention of women in the North Cameroons ("whether women there, who in many constituencies outnumber men, will agitate to keep their suffrage") is a passing observation about a foreign territory's internal affairs, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely concerned with parliamentary reform — specifically the disfranchisement of corrupt boroughs and the transfer of electoral franchises to manufacturing towns or adjoining hundreds. Women are mentioned only once in passing ("men, women, and children") as a rhetorical flourish to illustrate how obvious a constitutional defect is, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speaker welcomes greater female participation in Parliament and public life, supports removing gender distinctions in succession to the Crown, and criticises the Government for inadequate prioritisation of women's issues (e.g., the Minister for Women's lack of pay), all of which express support for women's political rights and representation.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on labour disputes, police conduct, the use of military force against strikers, and working-class wages and conditions. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference to "the Women's Suffrage demonstration" used to make a procedural point about the Home Secretary's inconsistency regarding inquiries, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states support for a gender balance of men and women in the Scottish Parliament, endorses positive discrimination to achieve it, and declares he has "all my life voted for the emancipation of women," making a clear affirmative stance on women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Home Rule for Ireland, the conflicting schemes within the Liberal Cabinet, Irish Nationalist demands, and the economic and constitutional arguments against Home Rule. The single passing mention of "Female Suffrage" is listed as one of several possible issues the General Election may have settled, with no argument made about it.

The speech is a maiden address focused on unemployment, the Rent Restrictions Act, and social reform, with only a passing mention of women as part of the electorate and as fellow sufferers of unemployment — no argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speeches are entirely focused on the parliamentary procedure of the Government taking private Members' time to expedite the Parliament Bill, and related constitutional/procedural debates. While Mr. Stanley Wilson briefly speculates that the suffragettes/Conciliation Bill may be the PM's motive, this is a passing rhetorical aside rather than an argument about women's political rights. No speaker in the TARGET argues for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about Labour party politics, unemployment, constitutionalism, and the upcoming vote of no confidence. The brief mention of "extension of the franchise to men and women" is purely incidental and descriptive, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns whether Queen Caroline's name should be restored to the Liturgy, debating the legality and expediency of the Crown's omission and the Queen's conduct — a matter of royal prerogative, public order, and the Queen's personal morality. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Ms Ruddock) actively supports women's political rights and representation, explicitly endorsing improved representation of women in public appointments, the Scottish Parliament, and international advocacy for women's rights. She highlights government efforts to advance women's equality in political and civic life.

The target speech is a lengthy parliamentary address on education policy — school building programmes, teacher supply, training colleges, class sizes, and curriculum — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. References to women (e.g., young women teachers marrying early, married women returning to teaching) concern workforce and education policy, not women's civic or political status.

The speech is focused entirely on the removal of turnstiles from women's public lavatories — a matter of public health, accessibility, and local authority regulation. While the speaker mentions women Members of Parliament acting collectively and references women's interests, the speech does not argue for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker is pressing the Prime Minister to confirm that promised parliamentary facilities for a Women's Suffrage Bill will be extended to any qualifying Bill, not just one specific one — thereby advocating for broader legislative support for women's suffrage.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely concerned with opposing the payment of Members of Parliament, arguing against it on grounds of public expense, procedural impropriety, and the tradition of gratuitous service. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief rhetorical analogy: the speaker notes that Women's Suffrage has been "repeatedly affirmed by resolution of this House" to challenge the Chancellor's argument that prior affirmations of a principle justify passing it by resolution — this is a procedural debating point, not an argument for or against women's suffrage itself.

The speech concerns open vs. closed party lists for Welsh assembly elections, focusing on voter choice in candidate selection and ordering. While it briefly mentions that open lists would allow voters to "choose between men and women," this is incidental to the main argument about electoral system design, and no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over public lavatory turnstiles — their regulation, local authority powers, and the government's proposed response — with no argument made about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about colonial finances (the 4½ per cent duties and repair of Barbados fortifications), parliamentary corruption, and members voting in their own financial interest. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker explicitly states he is "deeply interested in the movement of the enfranchisement of women" and proposes donating the portion of his salary derived from women's taxes to "the cause of women's suffrage," framing the payment of Members as an injustice to unenfranchised women who are taxed without representation. He also references the unjust treatment of women pit-brow workers to reinforce his argument about women's civic standing.

The speech is entirely devoted to criminal law reform — reducing capital punishments, improving transportation and prison discipline — with no argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "benevolent females" visiting prisons is a passing commendation of charitable work, not an argument about women's civic status or political participation.

The target speech is a lengthy parliamentary address focused entirely on the case for removing the Conservative government from office, the role of the Liberal party in supporting a Labour government, and debates about Socialism vs. Liberalism vs. Protection. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about; the speech does not touch on voting rights, representation, or civic participation for women.

The TARGET speech (primarily Mr. Simon on housing policy, followed by the Duchess of Atholl on juvenile unemployment, education, Church of Scotland, agriculture, and shipbuilding) does not argue for or against women's political rights. The Duchess of Atholl's references to "women Members" and matters "of special interest to women" concern social welfare topics (juvenile unemployment, legitimacy of children, maintenance orders) rather than women's civic or political participation.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Wilberforce, the member for Bramber) is entirely focused on the question of ameliorating the condition of enslaved people in the West Indies and the role of colonial assemblies versus the imperial parliament — it contains no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the Scottish Parliament must ensure "fair representation of women and men" and states there is "no excuse for failing to find gender balance in the Scottish Parliament," directly advocating for women's equal political representation.

The speaker explicitly states "Gender balance is important, despite its being chided and chastised by those who view it as mere political correctness," arguing that women form the majority of the population and deserve representation in the new Scottish Parliament, and criticising the Conservatives for being "deficient in not having enough Members of both genders."

The speech concerns a debate about turnstiles in public lavatories and local authority compliance, arguing for urgent legislative action to protect women's health and convenience. While women are mentioned as a class affected by the policy, the issue is a public health/facilities matter, not women's civic participation, voting rights, or political representation.

The TARGET speech (and the concatenated speeches within it) concerns the disfranchisement of East Retford and parliamentary reform/representation, including a passing anecdote about a Gatton borough property being advertised to let only to a woman to avoid a voting qualification — but this is used as an illustration of rotten borough absurdity, not as an argument about women's political rights. No substantive argument for or against women's civic participation is made.

The speaker explicitly advocates for balanced representation of women and men in the Scottish Parliament, criticises the underrepresentation of women at Westminster, and supports mechanisms (including all-women shortlists, despite finding them imperfect) to achieve proper gender balance in political representation.

The speech concerns a bill for the registration of voters in English cities, boroughs, and cinque ports, focusing on electoral fraud, polling procedures, and voter qualifications. Women are not mentioned at all, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker is pressing the government to clarify that promised parliamentary facilities for a Women's Suffrage Bill should apply broadly and not be monopolised by one particular bill, implicitly supporting wider opportunities for women's suffrage legislation to advance. The question presupposes and affirms the legitimacy of the government's commitment to facilitating a Women's Suffrage Bill.

The speaker explicitly argues that multi-member constituencies benefit women and ethnic minorities by giving them more representation, noting that the STV system helps redress traditional inequities in political representation. This is a substantive argument in favour of structures that advance women's political representation.

The target speech is entirely focused on the military and social welfare activities of Portuguese forces in Angola, including land reform, franchise extension to literate adults, and the strategic situation in Southern Africa. While the speaker briefly mentions that the vote is being extended to "all men and women over 21" in Angola, this is a passing descriptive remark about Portuguese colonial policy rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Conservative government's electioneering tactics, arguing for Labour's superior political approach, and calling for a vote of no confidence. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of "men and women" in the electorate, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the management of convict transportation to New South Wales, the distribution of convict labour, allegations of favouritism by the colonial governor, and the costs of the Penitentiary. While female convicts are mentioned briefly in the context of difficulties finding employment for them, this is a penal policy discussion with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly questions why female officers in the W.R.A.C. are paid £100–£200 less than male officers of equivalent rank, noting they have the same expenses and can have dependants to support, thereby advocating for equal treatment of women in military service.

The questioner raises objections to a magistrate publicly supporting women's suffrage, framing it as improper conduct, and asks whether regulatory steps should be taken against him — implicitly opposing women's suffrage advocacy in an official capacity and treating pro-suffrage speech as something deserving censure.

The speech concerns parliamentary reform in Scotland — corrupt borough representation, the ballot, and the number of voters — without making any argument about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a passing reference to deducting women as unqualified to vote, which is a factual aside rather than an argument about their civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over McKenna Duties (tariff protection for the motor car and related industries) and Free Trade versus Protection as an economic and electoral issue. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the electorate ("men and women engaged in trade and industry"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech addresses prison treatment and classification of a suffragist prisoner, focusing on the administrative exercise of discretionary powers regarding division placement. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or suffrage itself.

The target speech, delivered by Miss Bondfield (MP for Northampton), focuses entirely on unemployment among women — training schemes, trade board inspection, juvenile unemployment, and government administrative failures.
