While the speaker references the National Union for Equal Citizenship as an authoritative body on women's opinion, this is cited only as evidence for the pension abuse argument, not as an argument about women's civic or political status.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Greater London local government reorganisation White Paper, addressing education administration, planning, efficiency, and financial implications. Women's political rights and representation are not argued for or against anywhere in the speech.

The speech concerns the Irish franchise qualification under Poor Law valuation, lease restrictions, and electoral registration reform in Ireland. The brief mention of "occupation by women and double holdings" as a deduction in a statistical calculation is purely arithmetical, not an argument about women's political rights. No position on women's civic participation is advanced anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on economic distress in manufacturing districts, taxation, the Corn Laws, and trade competition. The brief mention of "450 females of Bridgenorth" petitioning about their husbands' distress and a reference to women's petticoats in a pawnbroker's list are incidental to the economic argument, not arguments about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is primarily about the composition and legitimacy of a second Chamber (elected vs. appointed), not about women's political rights. The fleeting mention of "votes for women" and "universal adult suffrage" is purely illustrative of past democratic reforms the speaker claims to support in principle, with no substantive argument made about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly references the historical injustice that women were denied the vote until age 30, using this as evidence that democracy is not as deeply entrenched as claimed, and frames universal adult suffrage (including women's) as a hard-won and relatively recent achievement worthy of protection.

The speech focuses on the rights of widows to pension benefits under an insurance scheme, arguing that men who paid into the fund have the right to designate beneficiaries. While it touches on women's entitlement to pensions, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, or civic representation in any meaningful sense.

The speech by Mr. Snell focuses almost entirely on Indian self-government, the timing of constitutional reform in India, and the responsibilities of British governance. The brief mention of women being denied the vote ("The leaders of both the other parties in this House denied women the vote on the ground that they were incapable") is used only as a rhetorical analogy to illustrate the misuse of "capability" arguments against Indian self-government, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on the debate over local versus national funding of education and other public services, specifically defending London's education administration against criticism from the Board of Education. It makes no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, or women's civic participation in any form.

The speech is primarily about the National Insurance Bill, focusing on employer contributions, friendly societies, consumption/sanatorium treatment, medical profession concerns, and insurance scheme details. While the speaker briefly mentions women in two passages (urging that wives of insured workers receive sanatorium treatment, and that maternity benefit be payable directly to women), these are welfare/health policy points about benefit administration rather than arguments about women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for adequate representation of women on referee panels, arguing that widows' cases will be "more properly dealt with by women referees than by men" and urging the Minister to ensure women are appointed, even after the Amendment is negatived.

The speech is entirely focused on pensions and benefits for ex-Service men, disabled veterans, and Service widows — it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Mentions of widows relate solely to pension adequacy, not women's political status.

The speech is entirely about the governance of the Greater London Authority — specifically whether the London Assembly should have power to pass a vote of no confidence in the mayor. The only reference to women is a passing mention of "25 men and women elected under proportional representation," which is purely descriptive and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, labour rights, poverty, casual labour, and the Right to Work Bill. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women" denied the right to work, wives and children of unemployed men) without any argument about women's distinctive civic or political status, voting rights, or political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on voluntary overseas service, the Peace Corps, and development aid to emerging nations. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "young men and women" volunteers, a female graduate in Nigeria), with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns overseas voluntary service, technical assistance to developing countries, and the merits of the Peace Corps versus British approaches. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the general workforce ("trained men and women") with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns workers' entitlement to sick pay benefits when hospitalised and the governance of voluntary hospital contribution schemes, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" contributing to hospitals is purely incidental and carries no argument about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the legitimacy and democratic basis of the House of Lords reform, arguing for an elected second Chamber. While it mentions "men and women" in passing, it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct class.

The speech is entirely about colonial governance in Newfoundland — the appropriateness of granting representative institutions, voter qualifications, and constitutional structure for the colony. Women are mentioned only incidentally (as victims of a shipwreck), and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speech focuses entirely on university funding, staffing ratios, student numbers, and the University Grants Committee's administration. The brief mention of "representation of women" on the UGC is a passing reference to committee composition, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns casual labour, unemployment insurance contributions, and decasualisation policy under what appears to be the National Insurance Bill. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation; the mention of "men and women" refers only to workers affected by casual labour provisions.

The speech is focused on House of Lords reform — specifically the removal of hereditary peers — and the history of parliamentary reform. While it briefly mentions that "all men and even all women have gained the right to vote" in passing, this is a historical observation rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker describes the Westminster Foundation for Democracy's work targeting "grass-roots women's organisations to help them provide education in electoral and general civil rights" in central Asia, supporting women in Tajikistan involved in voter education, and helping women's rights groups in Nigeria — all framed approvingly as positive achievements. The speaker also highlights a Nepalese woman being trained to become a grass-roots democratic representative, presenting women's political participation as a goal to be supported.

The target speech is primarily concerned with the National Insurance Bill's provisions regarding compulsory contributory insurance, friendly societies, deposit contributors, sanatoria, and county pools. While the speaker briefly mentions women's treatment under the Bill and pledges to consider the Chancellor's proposals for fairer treatment of women contributors, this is a passing reference without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech argues against a Clause giving the Home Secretary power to authorize double-shift working with female labour, framing it as a labour protection issue (working hours, overhead charges, employer competition). While women are mentioned as workers to be protected from onerous hours, the speech does not argue about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation—it is a workplace regulation debate.

The speech is entirely focused on Scottish local government financing, the General Grant Order, Anderson-type bursaries, and school building programmes in Lanarkshire. While the speaker (Miss Herbison) mentions "men and women" serving on local authorities, this is incidental and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker (Lord Ashley) explicitly proposes "the total exclusion of all females from the mines and collieries of this country" as his first legislative provision, arguing this is demanded by "every principle of religion" and "every law of nature." His framing treats women's mine work as degrading and morally corrupting, and his bill aims to remove women from paid employment entirely — restricting rather than expanding women's civic and economic participation as a class.

The speech is entirely about tariff policy and the naming of the Safeguarding of Industries Bill. The brief mention of "new voters...some of them women" is purely incidental, used as rhetorical colour to argue the bill's title is misleading, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the economic debate over a protective tariff for the Nottingham lace industry, unemployment, and trade policy. The brief mention of a difference between men and women in buying behaviour is used as a consumer psychology argument about lace pricing, not as any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the Welfare Reform and Pensions Bill's changes to widows' benefits (bereavement allowances), arguing that widows are being abandoned by the Government's cost-cutting measures. While it mentions women and gender, it does not argue for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's civic/political participation — it is a welfare policy debate about contributory bereavement benefits.

The speech is a passionate attack on unemployment insurance legislation for its impact on poor workers, ex-servicemen, and their families. While women and children are mentioned as victims of poverty and starvation, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

This lengthy speech by Mr. Buller concerns systematic colonization and emigration as remedies for economic distress, overcrowding of capital and labour markets, and poverty in Britain. The only mention of women is a brief passing reference to "educated women" facing competition in a limited range of employments, cited as an economic illustration, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely about educational research policy — funding, methodology, institutional structures, and curriculum development — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "girls" concerns co-educational research methodology, not women's civic status.

The entire speech — and all contextual speeches — concerns the repeal of the Corn Laws, its economic effects, agricultural protection, and trade policy. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned, argued for, or argued against anywhere in the target text.

The TARGET speech is a lengthy motion by Mr. Duncombe seeking a select committee inquiry into the conduct of magistrates during the 1842 Chartist disturbances — covering illegal imprisonment, excessive bail, use of spies, and military violence. While Chartism and universal suffrage are mentioned in passing (as the political demands of the petitioners), the speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation; women are not singled out as a class with distinctive civic status.

The speaker (Sir Frederick Banbury) explicitly argues that expanding women's participation in local government is "insidious" and questions whether it is "a good thing," and further argues that the question of women's franchise should be settled before extending their qualifications to sit on local authorities — expressing clear opposition to expanding women's political roles.

The TARGET speech (by Lloyd George and Worthington-Evans) concerns the technical and financial administration of insurance funds — specifically whether men's and women's funds under a National Insurance scheme should be separated — and does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The mention of women is limited to their financial treatment under insurance legislation, which is a welfare/social insurance matter rather than a question of women's distinctive civic status or political rights.

The speaker introduces a Bill explicitly aimed at establishing equal access for women to public and private buildings and clubs, citing numerous examples of discriminatory practices that exclude women from voting rights, committee membership, and physical spaces. The speech directly advocates for women's equal civic and participatory rights.

The target speech is a procedural ruling about the order of business, noting that a Notice of Motion on Equal Franchise is out of order because it anticipates a Bill already set down. No argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is about House of Lords reform and democratic legitimacy through elections; women's political rights are mentioned only in passing as a historical milestone ("women got the vote") without any argument for or against them.
The speech is entirely focused on NATO, Kosovo, Bosnia, nuclear weapons policy, and European defence matters. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker explicitly endorses targets to double the representation of women in the senior civil service, framing increased female representation as beneficial to equality programmes and public life broadly — a clear expression of support for women's political/civic participation and representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Parliament Bill, the relationship between the two Houses, electoral mandates, party politics, and constitutional reform of the House of Lords. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about, even in passing.

The speaker, near the end of a long speech about abolishing the House of Lords, explicitly states that the House of Commons "cannot be regarded as representative of the democracy until women, too, have the vote," directly endorsing women's suffrage as a necessary component of democratic representation.

The speech is focused entirely on opposing the title "Safeguarding of Industries" for a trade/tariff bill, arguing it is misleading protectionism. The brief mention of "new voters—women and ex-service men" is purely incidental, used as an example of people who might be hoodwinked by the bill's name, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a detailed argument about factory labour hours, wages, foreign competition, and social conditions of the manufacturing population. While it briefly mentions that women doing hard factory labour is an "inversion" of natural roles and that restricting women's labour would restore men to breadwinning and women to domestic duties, these remarks concern labour regulation and social economics rather than women's civic or political rights. No argument about voting, office-holding, representation, or any aspect of women's political participation is made.

The speech is about the Public Meeting Act 1908, public order legislation, penalties for disrupting meetings, and free speech — with only a brief incidental mention that the 1908 Act's ancestor "was very much opposed to the suffragettes" and introduced the bill partly to deal with them. This historical aside does not constitute an argument for or against women's political rights; it is used to make a point about the Act's origins and limited importance, not to take any stance on women's civic participation.

The speaker strongly opposes the Economy Bill's clause that would disenfranchise large numbers of voters, arguing it is unconstitutional and unjust to restrict the franchise in this "hole and corner manner," and explicitly frames this as a defence of democratic rights and the franchise established by the Representation of the People Act 1918, including women voters mentioned in context.

The speech by Captain Layard is entirely focused on the condition of Ireland, the grievances of the Irish people, the tithe system, the Repeal question, and the conduct of trials — with no mention of women's political rights, the franchise for women, or any related topic.

The speech is entirely focused on NATO, nuclear deterrence, Cold War foreign policy, and international alliances, with no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related topic.

This lengthy speech by Richard Cobden concerns a motion for a Select Committee to inquire into the effects of Protective Duties (Corn Laws) on tenant-farmers and farm-labourers. The entire speech addresses agricultural economics, free trade, rent, wages, and the condition of rural labourers — with no argument made about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech focuses on Russian debt settlements, Irish prisoners, Communist prisoners, and Ammanford miners, with only a passing reference to the suffrage agitation as a historical example of political imprisonment. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker, identifying as chairman of the Status of Women Committee, opposes the specific Bill not because she opposes women's jury rights but because she wants comprehensive reform of the entire jury system rather than piecemeal legislation. She explicitly states she "personally hope[s] that radical changes will be made" and supports equal jury service eligibility based on the electoral register, indicating support for women's full civic participation.

The speech is about amendments to public order legislation concerning penalties for disorderly conduct at public meetings, focusing on the Public Meeting Act 1908 and the Public Order Act. While the speaker briefly quotes a historical remark suggesting the 1908 Act should apply only to women first, this is an incidental historical quotation used to illustrate the Act's origins and is not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely concerned with reforming voter registration, franchise qualification thresholds, and polling arrangements for male parliamentary electors in Ireland; women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The target speech briefly references the 1929 equal franchise as a historical milestone but does not argue for or against women's political rights — it is contextual background in a debate about lowering the voting age to 16. No substantive argument about women's civic status is advanced.

The speech is primarily about improving polling facilities in Orkney and Shetland by switching to a single polling day and increasing the number of polling stations. The brief mention of women's difficulty in reaching polling stations is incidental and descriptive, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech concerns a mines safety bill and the employment conditions of pit-brow women (weight-lifting restrictions), not women's political rights such as voting, standing for office, or representation. The debate is about occupational health and labour protection, which does not bear on women's civic/political participation.

The TARGET speech is primarily about mortgage repossession policy and the CML's code of practice. The brief mention of "the representation of women in the House" is purely a passing historical acknowledgement, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the employment of women in Scottish coal mines under the Mines and Collieries Act — specifically arguing for an amendment to allow unmarried women over 18 to continue working underground. This is a labour regulation and welfare matter; the speaker does not argue about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of political representation or civic participation. Women are not singled out as a class for distinctive civic rights or duties of political participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that men (who alone have the vote) are depriving women of employment, and concludes that this situation is "an argument tremendously in favour of giving votes to women," directly endorsing women's suffrage. The speech also defends pit-brow women's right to work against male trade union pressure, framing the denial of their employment as an injustice tied to their lack of political representation.

The speaker explicitly argues that the Clause will prevent women entitled to vote by age qualification under the Representation of the People Act from exercising their franchise, framing this as an unacceptable restriction on democratic rights. The speech advocates for the broadest possible franchise, including for women, and opposes measures that would disenfranchise them.

The speech focuses entirely on the future of the Central African Federation, African nationalism, tribal politics, the role of the UN, US and Communist interference, and the Law and Order (Maintenance) Bill in Southern Rhodesia. While it briefly mentions "pregnant women" as a category exempted from the mandatory death penalty, this is incidental and not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on parliamentary procedure, Welsh policy issues, unemployment, transport, and leasehold reform — none of which address women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the unemployed population ("29,000 men and women and young people").

The speech is entirely focused on Post Office operations, tariffs, telecommunications investment, postal services, and related economic matters. There is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that men in his district voted to allow women to continue working at the pit-brow, that there is no other work available for these women, and explicitly urges the House to support the Amendment allowing women to carry on their work. While the speech concerns women's labour rights rather than the franchise directly, it defends women's right to participate in economic and public life against legislative restriction, which falls within the scope of women's civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that female ratepayers alone should be allowed to vote by proxy, singling out women as a class deserving a distinctive civic right in the election of Poor Law Guardians, which constitutes support for women's political participation rights.

The speech is primarily concerned with supporting the Chartist petition's right to be heard at the Bar of the House, focusing on working-class suffrage for male adults and the alleviation of economic distress. While the speaker briefly notes that some petition signatures belong to women (acknowledging they are not "grown men"), this is merely a passing remark to defend the petition's numbers, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about a Shop Hours Bill regulating working conditions for shop employees. The brief mention of women and girls as shop assistants with "no representation in this House" is used as a paternalistic argument for state regulation of working hours, not as an argument about women's political rights — the speaker invokes their lack of representation as a reason for Parliament to act protectively, without advocating for or against giving them that representation.

The speech argues against Clause 10 of an Economy Bill on procedural and administrative grounds—interference with existing Acts of Parliament, risk to election safeguards, and lack of genuine economy—with no substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The mention of a Speaker's Conference to consider franchise questions is a procedural point, not an argument about women's political rights specifically.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the renewal of the Aliens Restriction Act, arguing against immigration restrictions and the Home Secretary's use of those powers. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related topic.

The speaker explicitly argues that it is "a perfect scandal that Members elected by men only should try to do a set of women out of their livelihood when these women have no adequate means of making representations on their own behalf," directly linking the lack of women's political representation to the injustice of legislating against their interests. This is a clear endorsement of women's political rights as the underlying basis for opposing the restriction on pit-brow women's work.

The speech is primarily concerned with the Bahamas constitutional reform bill, addressing issues of racial discrimination, seat distribution, and Senate composition. The single mention of women getting the vote in 1962 is a brief historical observation with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker objects to replacing "chairman" with "chair" in the legislation, arguing that "chairman" in modern English usage already embraces women (e.g., "Madam Chairman"), and frames the change as an unwanted imposition he was "outvoted" on — effectively opposing gender-neutral language reform in political officeholder titles.

The speech focuses on electoral registration, voting procedures, pilot schemes, absent voting, party funding, and fraud prevention. While it briefly mentions that people threatened by domestic violence (usually female) should be able to vote without being made more vulnerable, this is a passing reference to voter privacy rather than an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely concerned with the governance and colonial administration of New Zealand, including debates over Captain Fitzroy's appointment, militia organisation, land policy, and representative government for the colony. Women's political rights are never mentioned or implied.

The target speech, by Lord Ashley, is entirely focused on advocating for a ten-hour working day in factories, drawing on factory inspectors' reports, wage calculations, and operative testimony. While women factory workers are mentioned as a class (as non-free agents physically less capable of long hours), this is used as an argument for labour regulation generally, not as an argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. The speech does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other dimension of political rights.

The speech is entirely about government expenditure on the Ulster Special Constabulary and arguments about national economy; it makes no reference to women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related topic.

The speech concerns working conditions and health safeguards for women employed at mine surfaces (pit brow workers), which is a labour/occupational health matter. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the inclusion of three women on the Committee as "a great advantage," and contrasts this favourably with the previous government's scheme which provided "no representation of women at all," thereby endorsing women's representation in public bodies.

The speech is primarily about UK-Iran foreign policy, human rights concerns, and diplomatic relations. While it briefly mentions women's participation in Iranian politics (female judges, a woman vice-President, female candidates in local elections), these are passing observations about Iran's domestic situation rather than arguments for or against women's political rights as a matter of principle or policy.

The target speech is entirely focused on education policy — exclusions, truancy, class sizes, nursery places, and breaking cycles of underachievement — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is a debate about the Peerage Bill's commencement date and parliamentary precedents, including a brief reference to the Parliament (Qualification of Women) Act 1918 and the Representation of the People (Amendment) Act 1918 only as historical precedents for when legislation affecting parliamentary composition takes effect. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Sir Robert Peel) uses the logical extension of the seconder's taxation-equals-representation principle to ridicule it, arguing that if 5 million unrepresented taxpayers deserve the vote, then women and youths under 18 who also pay taxes must equally deserve it — framing women's suffrage as an absurd reductio ad absurdum of the reform argument, thereby implicitly opposing it.

The speech is entirely concerned with the Maynooth College Bill — the increased state endowment of a Roman Catholic seminary in Ireland — and debates about Irish policy, religious sectarianism, and administrative conduct. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker explicitly states "one for which I have struggled is the equality of women. I believe that women should have equality with men and should have the liability of sitting in the House of Lords if that is also a male liability. I believe that a society is healthy and civilised only to the extent to which it recognises in 1963 the complete equality of women," directly endorsing women's political rights and representation.

The speech concerns the extension of maternity allowance to low-paid and self-employed women — a welfare/benefits policy matter. It does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of civic participation that constitutes women's political rights. Women are discussed as a class of benefit recipients, not as political actors, so the speech falls outside the defined scope.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on the technical details of the National Insurance Bill—contribution rates, benefit levels, sickness fund structure, and the treatment of married women under health insurance—without making any argument about women's political rights, the franchise, or representation. The reference to "the modern women's movement" is purely incidental and not used to argue for or against women's civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on widows' pension rates, the earnings rule, and social insurance policy for widows — it makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of women's political rights. The subject matter is welfare/social insurance policy, not civic or political participation.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Cobden) is entirely focused on sugar duties, free trade versus protectionism, West India colonial management, and the anti-slavery argument as it relates to sugar policy. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The TARGET speech (Sir J. Walsh's contribution and Viscount Howich's lengthy response) is entirely focused on the Corn Laws, agricultural protection, the condition of the labouring classes, free trade, emigration, and education policy. Women are mentioned only once in passing—noting Lord Ashley's work on "sufferings endured by women who worked in mines"—as a factual reference to previous legislation, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic status.

The speech concerns maternity allowance policy for low-paid and self-employed women, addressing benefits entitlement and employer burdens. While it touches on women's economic welfare, it does not argue about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is a detailed advocacy for a Factories Bill focused on workplace safety, health conditions, accident prevention, and industrial welfare. While it briefly mentions "a section for women and young persons" regarding hours restrictions, this is framed as incidental to a broader industrial welfare discussion, and the speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on Poor Law administration — opposing the transfer of boards of guardians' duties to county councils — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The passing mention of "men and women" serving on public assistance committees is purely descriptive and does not argue any position on women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly advocates for equal treatment of women workers in unemployment insurance and relief schemes, arguing that women are being penalised through inadequate training grants, denial of standard benefits, and discriminatory assumptions about their dependence — all framed as grievances about women's civic and economic standing relative to men.

The speech concerns pension provisions and the earnings rule for widows under National Insurance, arguing that widows should organize politically to advance their cause. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation; the mention of widows forming a federation and lobbying is advocacy for a welfare/economic policy cause, not an argument about women's political rights as a class.

The speech is entirely focused on the London Government Bill, the Guillotine Motion curtailing parliamentary debate, and the fate of London boroughs like West Ham. Women are mentioned only once in passing as volunteers in local authorities, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech (by Mr. Lansbury and Mr. Denniss) is entirely focused on debating the National Insurance Bill — its contributory scheme, its financial burdens on low-wage workers, its effects on industry, and parliamentary procedure. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women" earning low wages, domestic servants as a class affected by the Bill's costs) without any argument for or against women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker explicitly highlights the Labour party's greater representation of women on the Government Benches as a positive achievement resulting from its "commitment to ensuring equal opportunities," endorsing women's political representation as a visible and desirable outcome.

The speaker explicitly highlights the high representation of women (40% in Scotland, 37% in Wales) achieved through PR systems as "one of the most positive features" of those elections, endorsing PR partly on the grounds that it improves women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for the employment of women officials to assist widows with pension claims, arguing that women are best suited for this work — this implicitly supports women's civic participation and employment in public administrative roles on equal terms with men.

The TARGET speech opposes a Poor Law administration reform Bill on grounds of economy, proper legislative procedure, and the pending Insurance Bill, with only a passing reference to "men and women" cooperating in poor relief — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely about the Corn Laws debate — arguing for their repeal, critiquing the protectionist system, and defending the Government's measure. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation anywhere in the text.

The speaker (Mr. Mackinder) argues against the Bill, contending that granting women the Imperial franchise would dangerously destabilise political sovereignty by enabling a small organised bloc to shift minorities into majorities, potentially provoking civil unrest. He frames the Imperial vote as fundamentally tied to physical force and state strength, from which he excludes women competitors, while dismissing suffrage arguments as "sloppy thinking."

The speaker explicitly argues for enabling "men and women of limited means" to serve on local public authorities by covering their expenses, framing this as democratising public institutions and removing financial barriers to civic participation for both men and women.

The speaker briefly notes that "one man one vote" in Africa "means votes for the men but not necessarily for the women in many cases" and characterises this as undemocratic — but this is an observation about African practice used to critique the spread of a particular democratic model, not an argument for extending women's political rights. The overall speech is focused on Communist penetration of Africa; the remark about women's votes is incidental and, if anything, implicitly accepts the exclusion of women from voting as a deficiency of others rather than advocating for women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is about ensuring adequate financial compensation and support for life peers (men and women) doing work in a reformed House of Lords; it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. The incidental mention of "men and women" among peers is purely descriptive and does not address women's civic status or political participation.

The target speech is an extended parliamentary address focused entirely on the Corn Laws debate, Anti-Corn-Law League petition fraud, manufacturing conditions, agricultural protection, and politicians' alleged broken pledges to constituents. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation anywhere in the speech.

The TARGET speech, attributed to Mr. MacCallum Scott, characterizes the Bill's mover as opposing women sitting in Parliament while supporting some women's suffrage — framing this as an inconsistency — but the following context makes clear that MacCallum Scott himself is an opponent of women's suffrage, opposing the "whole principle and intention of Woman Suffrage" based on the "physical force" argument.

The speech (by Mr. Duncombe and Lord J. Russell) concerns the principles and composition of the new Whig government, Irish Church policy, franchise extension in Ireland, the Factories Act, and Parliamentary reform — none of which singles out women as a class for distinctive civic rights or duties. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speech is primarily a Budget debate contribution focused on economic and constituency matters. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing humorous quotation from George Bernard Shaw about women's suffrage leading to a tax on bachelors, which the speaker uses as a rhetorical flourish rather than to argue any position on women's political rights.

The speech is a lengthy address on the King's Speech covering foreign affairs (Iraq, Locarno, Italian debt), economy, armaments, housing, and the coal dispute. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speech by Mr. Fernyhough (Jarrow) is entirely focused on unemployment, poverty, regional economic planning, and industrial policy for the North-East and Scotland. While he uses generic references to "men and women" as unemployed workers, he makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

This is Sir Robert Peel's extensive speech introducing the repeal of the Corn Laws and a sweeping revision of customs duties, covering tariffs on manufactures, food, agricultural produce, and related social reforms. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The target speech is entirely focused on the Corn Laws debate — arguing against repeal on grounds of agricultural protection, wages, and constitutional propriety — with no mention of women's political rights, suffrage, or representation.

The speech is entirely about the 1926 coal miners' dispute, the general strike, and labour relations. The brief mention of women voting ("if only the men over 21 were allowed to vote—and the women") is a passing reference to include women in a hypothetical ballot on strike action, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Mackinder) argues against the Women's Suffrage Bill throughout, contending that the vote rests ultimately on physical force which women lack, that granting women the franchise would destabilize constitutional government, and that women's true influence is superior to the vote and should be exercised through domestic and moral authority rather than the ballot. He explicitly states "I refuse to regard the coming of this change as inevitable" and that granting the vote "will do very great harm to men in their relations to women."

The speech is primarily about the Central African Federation and African political development. The brief mention of women receiving the vote in 1928 is used only as an analogy about political maturity and timing in the context of African self-governance, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker opposes a government measure that would reduce the qualifying period and consolidate electoral registers, arguing it would disfranchise large numbers of people — explicitly including women ("A wife, if she is of the requisite age... will be disfranchised both in respect of Parliamentary and local franchise for 12 months") and other mobile voters. By moving an amendment to mitigate these disenfranchising effects, the speaker is defending existing franchise rights for both men and women.

The speaker defends Labour's record on women's representation (all-women shortlists, achieving 25% women in the parliamentary Labour party), expresses pride in that achievement, and explicitly states they "will continue to build a Parliament that really reflects the balance between men and women" — all substantive arguments in favour of women's political representation.

The speaker moves the Second Reading of a Bill explicitly designed to grant mothers equal guardianship rights over their children, arguing at length that the current legal disadvantage women face is unjust and that many other countries have already recognised equal guardianship. She directly advocates for equal legal rights for women in the civic/legal sphere, stating "we have now come to the period in the history of this country when we should give equal rights to women in this respect."

The speaker explicitly calls for wider representation of women in the Northern Ireland Assembly and praises the Northern Ireland Women's Coalition for their work, directly endorsing women's political participation and representation in public office.

The target speech is entirely concerned with explaining the administrative structure of a joint Ministry of Labour/Ministry of Health supplemental estimate related to unemployment relief, with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech deals entirely with the administration of approved school orders and fit person orders for juvenile delinquents, including the roles of managers, the Home Secretary, and parents in decisions about children's release. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker explicitly supports increasing women's involvement in public life and decision-making, citing a commitment to 50% representation of women in 42 public appointments and progress in NHS trust leadership roles for women.

The speech is entirely focused on Poor Law administration, destitution, public health, and institutional reform, with no arguments made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mentions of women (e.g., mothers receiving relief, female Poor Law investigators) are incidental to the subject of poverty administration and do not address women's civic or political status.

The target speech, delivered by Sir Robert Peel, is entirely focused on the Corn Laws debate—defending his change of position on agricultural protection, arguing for repeal to address Irish famine and benefit the working classes, and responding to personal attacks. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about, even in passing.

The speech concerns the National Insurance Bill's application to outworkers (home-based workers), arguing against an amendment that would exempt married women but not unmarried women or widows from its provisions. While women are mentioned as a class, the debate is about labour/insurance policy and political conduct (the Chancellor's telegram), not about women's civic participation, voting rights, or political representation.

The speech concerns protecting the salary, pension rights, and employment conditions of local government officers transferred as a result of London government reorganisation. While it mentions "men and women" in passing, it does not argue any position on women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech focuses on the structure of local health committees under an insurance bill for Ireland, discussing representation of county councils, sanitary authorities, and insured persons. The mention of women is a passing factual note ("at least two shall be women" and "Women are in increasing numbers becoming members of rural sanitary authorities") without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly calls for more women to be involved in Parliament and local government, notes that only 18% of MPs are women and that "there is a long way to go," and endorses the Make Votes Count organisation seeking to increase women's political involvement and representation.

The speech is primarily about whether outworkers should be excluded from the National Insurance Bill, focusing on economic hardship and employment effects. While the speaker mentions women as a large portion of outworkers and briefly notes the unequal treatment of married vs. unmarried women and widows under the proposed amendment, this is framed as an argument about equitable application of insurance policy rather than an argument about women's civic or political rights and representation.

The TARGET speech concerns factory labour regulation (the Ten Hours' Bill), focusing on the hours of work for women and children in mills and the economics of restricting labour. While women are mentioned as a category of factory workers, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation — it addresses labour conditions, not franchise, representation, or civic status.

The speaker (Harriet Harman) explicitly and consistently advocates for women's political representation and power-sharing, calling for more women in government, equal representation in the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly, and a genuine sharing of political power between men and women at all levels.

The speech is about a dispute over teacher salary negotiations and the Burnham Committee, not about women's political rights. The brief mention that "the National Union of Teachers has been increasingly taken over by the women members" is an observation about union demographics in the context of salary negotiations, not an argument about women's civic or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on prison conditions and the transfer of Scottish prisoners to police cells, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" being imprisoned is incidental and descriptive, not an argument about civic status or political rights.

The speech concerns the administrative and financial structure of women's branches within friendly societies under a National Insurance Bill — specifically voting rights over fund management within those societies. This is an internal insurance governance matter, not an argument about women's civic political rights (franchise, candidacy, representation). Women's distinct status is addressed only in the context of fund management within mutual insurance societies, not as a matter of civic participation or political representation.

The speech focuses entirely on housing conditions in Glasgow, trade union rights, wages, and opposition to Lord Weir's housing scheme. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men, women and children" living in poor conditions, and a dismissive remark attributed to opponents that "your womenfolk are lazy and dirty"), with no argument made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the technical administrative and financial structure of friendly societies under insurance legislation — specifically how men's and women's funds should be separated or merged — not women's political rights, voting, or representation. While women are mentioned as a class, the discussion is about actuarial/financial management of insurance funds, not civic participation or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, capitalism, poverty, municipal enterprise, nationalisation, and industrial policy. Women are not mentioned as a class with distinctive political rights, and no argument about women's suffrage, representation, or civic participation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speech concerns aviation research and development funding, the European Launcher Development Organisation, and the "brain drain" of scientists — with a passing mention of recruiting "young men and women" from universities. No argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is entirely focused on defending the government's proposed Coercion/Curfew Bill for Ireland, addressing crime statistics, responding to personal attacks from Lord George Bentinck, and discussing Catholic Emancipation history. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any form.

The speaker expresses concern about low voter turnout and explicitly asks what is being done to encourage more women to vote, framing women's electoral participation as a vital democratic goal. This reflects support for women's political participation.

The speech is entirely about the 1926 miners' lockout, government coal importation, and industrial/political grievances. The brief mention of "working men and working women" voters is a passing reference to the electorate, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker proposes an amendment ensuring female members have exclusive voting power over matters that concern them alone, explicitly arguing it is "not fair that a majority of men should overrule the wishes of the women" — a position directly supporting women's distinct political/representative rights within the society's governance structure.

The speaker explicitly states "I am a feminist. I have fought for equality between the sexes" and argues against those who denigrated unions because women (specifically "primary women teachers") dominate them, asserting that there is nothing wrong with unions simply because many women belong to them. This is a brief but substantive endorsement of women's equal civic and professional standing.

The TARGET speech (Sir R. Peel) is entirely focused on the Ten Hours Bill and factory labour regulation — arguing against further restriction of working hours on economic and practical grounds. While it briefly mentions existing laws protecting women (e.g., "no female can work by night at all") and references a wife's domestic role, these are incidental observations within a labour economics argument, not arguments for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on National Insurance provisions for the chronically sick — specifically constant attendance allowance and unemployability supplement — with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as caregivers (wives, mothers) burdened by caring for sick relatives, not in the context of their political or civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports equal representation of women in Parliament, advocates for all-women shortlists as a mechanism to achieve it, regrets the industrial tribunal ruling that prevents their use, and endorses quota systems and other measures to increase women's political representation. She also supports the Council of Europe's declaration linking women's equality to their political rights.

The speech concerns parliamentary questions about working hours regulations for dressmakers and milliners around the Coronation period. While women workers are mentioned, the debate is entirely about labour/factory regulations, not about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech is entirely devoted to debating the repeal of the Corn Laws and the extent of the Irish potato famine, with no mention of women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic status.

The speech is focused on defending the West Ham Board of Guardians against charges of corruption and opposing the Poor Law Amendment Bill on grounds of local democracy and workers' rights. The brief mention of "men and women" serving as guardians is incidental and descriptive, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker moves to remove the exclusion of women from an industry, explicitly arguing that women, now that they have the vote and exercise other civic privileges, should not be grouped with children or barred from occupations available to men, framing this as a matter of equal rights and resenting paternalistic restrictions on women's autonomy.

The speaker frames their question around a hypothetical Electoral Reform Bill that would extend the franchise to women aged twenty-five and over, treating this extension as a legitimate premise for parliamentary inquiry and requesting official estimates based on it, thereby implicitly supporting women's enfranchisement.

This very long speech (by the Member for Shrewsbury, later identified as Disraeli) is entirely devoted to the Corn Laws debate—arguments about agricultural protection, price fluctuations, foreign corn supplies, labour displacement, and political betrayal by Peel. Women's political rights are never mentioned, argued for, or against anywhere in the target speech.

The speech concerns the Burnham Committee, teachers' salaries, local authority autonomy in education, and the Minister of Education's intervention in wage negotiations. While the speaker mentions "men and women who serve Britain on local councils," this is a passing reference to local councillors generally and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly celebrates the history of women gaining the vote, applauds Labour's use of all-women shortlists to increase women's parliamentary representation, calls for righting the "democratic deficit" in women's political participation, and advocates for a 50:50 ratio of women and men in public appointments — all clear arguments in support of women's political rights and representation.

The speech is focused on naval estimates, expenditure, staffing levels, and Admiralty management. The mention of "100,000 men and women" is purely descriptive of naval personnel numbers and makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker supports women's political representation and equal opportunities, endorsing merit-based selection of women to Parliament, praising policies that brought more women into public life (Opportunity 2000), and arguing for genuinely equal opportunities for men and women. While she opposes all-women shortlists as discriminatory, this is a procedural/legal objection framed within a broader pro-women's-participation argument, not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech focuses on women's economic opportunities, employment, education, and welfare circumstances, arguing against the Labour party's framing of women as victims. While it touches on women's progress in the workforce and society, it does not make substantive arguments for or against women's political rights, voting, standing for office, or representation structures.

The speech focuses entirely on Royal Navy manpower, recruitment shortfalls, ship readiness, and defence estimates. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the phrase "100,000 men and women" in reference to the Admiralty vote, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns conditions and treatment of elderly patients at St. George's Hospital, Hornchurch, including nursing staffing shortages and complaints handling. Women are mentioned only incidentally as nurses ("devoted young women who care for them"), but no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The speaker explicitly argues that married women are being treated as "inferior creatures" by being excluded from compulsory insurance, and directly links this to women's lack of the vote, stating "If the women had a vote the same as the men have the Government would not dare to treat them in this way." The speaker presses the Amendment to bring married women fully within the Bill's scope, clearly supporting women's equal civic standing.

The speaker argues that the distinction between husbands and wives in the National Insurance Bill is justified because "it is the business of the husband to provide for the needs of the household," explicitly defending women's lesser treatment under the Bill and refusing to support the Amendment that would bring married women within the compulsory insurance scheme. While he acknowledges married women are "hardly dealt with," he frames this as a practical matter rather than endorsing their equal civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on Poor Law administration, relief scales, local versus national taxation, and the political motivations behind the Bill targeting West Ham guardians. While women are mentioned incidentally (e.g., "poor men, poor women, and poor children," "middle-class ladies who run the Charity Organisation Society," miners' wives), no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The target speech opposes the Factory Bill on economic and laissez-faire grounds, arguing that legislative interference with the labour of "young persons and females" is harmful to operatives and employers alike. The mention of females is incidental to an economic argument about restricting labour hours, not an argument about women's civic status, voting rights, or political representation.

The speech focuses on opposing the Emergency Powers Act as a class instrument against trade unions, with only a passing reference to the Representation of the People Act bringing "men and women into the political arena by the million" to argue that new constituents deserve different treatment — no substantive argument about women's political rights is made.

The speech is primarily a lengthy argument against the Factory Bill on economic and political economy grounds — specifically opposing restrictions on factory labour hours and their effects on wages, trade, and manufacturing competitiveness. While the speaker mentions "adult women" and "young persons" as the nominal targets of the Bill's restrictions, he uses this only to argue against the economic wisdom of the legislation, not to argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation. There is no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political representation or civic status.

The speaker explicitly advocates for more women in the House of Commons, arguing half the population is female and most legislation concerns women's primary interests. She also describes having introduced Bills to achieve equal numbers of men and women Members through dual constituency lists, directly supporting women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Poor Law administration, the merits of local versus national systems, and the management of poor relief in areas like West Ham and Fulham. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns the law of marriage regarding prohibited degrees of affinity (specifically a man marrying his deceased wife's sister) and proposes a Royal Commission to inquire into the state of that law. This is a matter of matrimonial/family law and does not address women's political rights, voting, office-holding, or civic participation as defined in scope.

The speech is primarily about factory labour hours legislation (the Ten/Eleven Hours Bill) concerning working conditions for young persons and women in mills. While women are mentioned as a protected class under the Bill alongside children, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation — it addresses labour regulation and economic competition, not women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on National Health Service catering standards, hospital food quality, medical staffing, and the Conservative Government's management of the NHS. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is focused on procedural parliamentary tactics regarding an amendment to a National Insurance Bill, specifically urging withdrawal of the amendment and cooperation to secure benefits for married women at a later stage. While it mentions married women's benefits, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation — it is about insurance policy mechanics, not civic participation or the franchise.

The speaker explicitly states they voted in favour of an amendment concerning married women and expresses a desire to "see if something cannot be done for married women" within the Bill, indicating support for their inclusion in the scheme. While they caution against amendments that would overburden the Bill, their underlying stance is supportive of extending benefits/participation to married women.

The target speech (by the Home Secretary, Sir W. Joynson-Hicks) addresses the two-shift working system for women in factories — a labor/welfare matter — not women's political rights or representation. The speaker's closing remark about not wanting women to work shifts if detrimental to health is a welfare concern, not an argument about civic participation, voting, or political representation.

The speech is entirely concerned with the Poor Law Amendment Bill and the structure of Poor Law administration — workhouse conditions, dietary allowances, the constitutional problems of merging executive and legislative functions in the proposed Commission, and the rights of the poor to relief. Women are briefly mentioned only in passing (e.g., differences in food rations for women vs. men in workhouses, and nursing mothers receiving no extra allowance), but no argument is made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The questioner explicitly raises concern about the disfranchisement of women old age pensioners at county and municipal elections and twice asks the President to consider introducing legislation to prevent or remove such disfranchisement, thereby advocating for the protection of women's voting rights.

The speech is entirely focused on Nigeria's transition to a republic and its implications for Commonwealth law and relations. The speaker explicitly declines to address women's votes ("In deference to your wishes, Mr. Deputy-Speaker, I had better not trespass on the grounds of women's votes"), making no substantive argument on the topic.

The speech is entirely about the composition of the ITA's Advertising Advisory Committee and consumer representation on it; the mention of "two ladies" being invited to join the committee and the reference to the Federation of Women's Institutes is incidental and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political representation, stating "Representation of women is important. It is important that, in the House, we have women from all walks of life and backgrounds," and expresses pride in being part of a Parliament with more women, while also advocating for empowering young women through education and economic independence.

The speaker explicitly supports structural reform to increase women's representation in Parliament, proposing dual/twinning lists so each constituency elects both a man and a woman, and arguing that more women should be elected to the House on a permanent basis. While she critiques Labour's approach and opposes artificial/temporary measures like women-only shortlists, her overall position is clearly in favour of women's political representation and participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's financial entitlements under the National Insurance Bill, arguing that women workers deserve every penny of benefit to which they are entitled and that their employer contributions count equally. While the speech is primarily about insurance benefits, it singles out women as a class deserving equal civic/economic treatment under the scheme and urges the Committee to vote freely on the matter to protect women's interests.

The speech by the Member for Cannock (Miss Lee) focuses entirely on constitutional concerns about parliamentary procedure, the new Prime Minister's by-election, the role of the Leader of the House, and the treatment of the House of Commons — with no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily about securing secret ballot voting in workplace insurance societies to protect workers from employer pressure. While it briefly mentions women's trade organisations and girls voting freely, this is incidental context supporting the broader ballot amendment rather than an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater women's representation in Parliament ("hopefully, more and more women will enter Parliament so that we attain 51 per cent. representation in the next millennium") and frames government policies like the working families tax credit as empowering women economically and politically, giving them real choices and putting "women at the heart of Government."

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater representation of women in Welsh politics, praising Labour's twinning procedure to achieve equal numbers of male and female candidates for the National Assembly, lamenting the under-representation of women on local councils and in Parliament, and calling for structural measures to increase women's political participation.

The speaker explicitly opposes differentiating women from men in workplace regulations, stating "I object to any alteration which makes the position of women something different from the position of men" and argues that women should have the right to decide for themselves whether to work under certain conditions — supporting women's equal civic and professional standing with men.

The speech is an extended response to a motion on Irish grievances, covering topics such as Catholic emancipation, tithe reform, franchise extension, landlord-tenant relations, poor laws, and the Church of Ireland establishment. While franchise and electoral representation are briefly mentioned, they are discussed in the context of general Irish political rights and reform rather than women's political rights specifically; women as a class are never singled out for any argument about their civic participation or political rights.

The speaker opposes the Bill granting local government votes to limited liability companies (framing it as class/property legislation), and in doing so explicitly supports extending the franchise to women at age 21, criticizing the current government for failing to keep its pledge to do so. This constitutes a clear argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on Irish Poor Law reform, famine relief, land tenure, taxation areas, and the social reconstruction of Ireland. Women are mentioned only incidentally as occupants of workhouses ("workhouses, now mainly filled by women and children"), with no argument about their political rights or civic status.

Disraeli's speech is primarily a sustained critique of Hume's parliamentary reform motion (household suffrage, ballot, triennial Parliaments, electoral districts) and the middle-class political movement behind it. His brief mention of women's suffrage is deployed as a reductio ad absurdum to undermine Hume's abstract-rights argument—he notes that if suffrage is a right, women in a country governed by a queen, with peeresses and churchwardens, could logically claim it too, but this is used to prove that "right has nothing to do with the matter," not to argue for or against women's political rights as such.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Molony Report and the Government's approach to consumer protection policy; it makes no arguments for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker argues that Parliament has no right to impose a poll tax on working women without first giving them a vote on the matter ("this House has no right to impose any such tax on the industrial women of the country until they have been asked to give a vote as to whether or not they want it"), explicitly endorsing women's right to political participation in fiscal decisions.

The speaker (Roundell Palmer) mounts an extensive and detailed argument against the Bill that would legalise marriage with a deceased wife's sister, grounding his opposition in Levitical scripture, the unanimous tradition of the Christian Church, the judgment of the Reformation, and social considerations — concluding he is "decidedly opposed to the present Bill."

The speaker explicitly welcomes increased women's representation in Parliament and other arenas, praises the abolition of the hereditary principle in the Lords as improving women's representation, and endorses women bringing "a different approach to politics." These are substantive, if brief, arguments in favour of women's political participation and representation.

The target speech is entirely about the Moneylenders Bill — addressing predatory lending practices, the plight of poor borrowers, and specific legislative provisions. While the speaker mentions in passing that over 1,100 of Liverpool's registered moneylenders are women and references Miss Keeling and the Liverpool Women's Citizens' Association, these are incidental details in a speech about moneylending regulation, not arguments about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Macpherson report, Metropolitan police conduct, race relations, and policing policy. While the speaker briefly mentions "men and women" in the police force and expresses dislike of "quotas" in the context of ethnic minority recruitment, these references are about racial diversity in policing, not about women's political rights or civic participation.

The petition from the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of Dublin explicitly and earnestly supports conferring the Parliamentary Franchise on women, arguing it is "an act of natural justice" and urging Parliament to pass the relevant Bill in the current session.

The speaker explicitly supports a bill he previously tried to introduce himself that would enfranchise "women accompanying their husbands abroad," calling it unreasonable that wives of certain employees lose their vote while wives of servicemen or embassy staff do not. He expresses delight that the current Bill addresses this category of women.

The TARGET contains Viscountess Astor's speech, which explicitly and forcefully advocates for equal franchise for women, pressing the Government to fulfil its pledges on extending the vote to women on equal terms with men and warning that delay could disenfranchise women at the next election. The preceding Churchill section of the TARGET touches on franchise as a difficult question but does not argue a position on women's rights, making Astor's portion the operative content for classification.

The target speech clarifies a procedural/factual point about the Burmese Legislative Council debate — correcting the framing of the preceding question — but does not itself argue for or against women's political rights. The speaker notes that the issue was candidature (not enfranchisement, as women already have the vote in Burma) and that the Home Member opposed it as premature, but the speaker takes no substantive position on whether women should be allowed to stand for election.

The speaker explicitly states "I am a feminist. I believe, in all seriousness, that we ought to have many more women Members in Parliament" and further argues that women MPs should not be confined to stereotypically "female" subjects, directly endorsing women's full and equal political participation.

The TARGET speech is primarily concerned with procedural and drafting issues related to a Henry VIII clause in a House of Lords reform Bill. The brief mention of the "flapper vote" and women's historical voting age restriction is used only as an illustrative analogy about special parliamentary distinctions, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns the conduct of the Emperor of Russia, particularly his treatment of Polish subjects and Turkish territories, and does not make any argument about women's political rights or representation. The mention of "the unfortunate nuns of Minsk" being flogged is used as evidence of Russian atrocities, not as an argument about women's civic status.

The speech by John Bright is an extensive debate on the Irish Poor Law and the "rate in aid" bill, covering Irish famine relief, land tenure reform, property law, emigration, and parliamentary governance. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speaker explicitly argues that women's voices are essential to a healthy democracy and that a legislature without gender balance cannot call itself representative, while also acknowledging her party's failings in electing women to Parliament and describing steps being taken to address them. This constitutes a clear endorsement of women's political representation.

The speech is entirely devoted to welfare services for deaf-blind persons, covering rehabilitation, home teachers, residential care, voluntary organisations, and communication aids. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issue.

The speech is entirely focused on the administration and amendment of the Old Age Pensions Act of 1908, discussing capital calculations, residential disqualifications, and hardship cases. While women are mentioned as beneficiaries of pension provisions, the speech makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on wage levels, industrial disputes (the general strike and coal strike), and economic arguments about the national dividend and industry; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly raises the government's failure to include in the King's Speech a promised Bill creating equality in franchise rights between men and women, argues that the 1927 Session is the critical window for such legislation to take effect before the next election, and warns that failure to act in time would be a broken pledge — clearly advocating for women's equal franchise rights.

The speech concerns education funding, convict expenses, and museum antiquities — with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation. The brief mention of schoolmistresses teaching embroidery is an incidental reference to women's employment, not an argument about their political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly champions the cause of women suffragette prisoners, arguing they deserve first-class misdemeanant status as political offenders and directly states "the reasons for this Bill and the urgency for it is mainly the treatment of women political prisoners" who are "striking for what they believe their political rights." The speech consistently frames women suffragists' acts of violence as legitimate political activity deserving equal treatment to male political offenders, thereby affirming their political cause and rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's political rights and representation, highlighting Pakistan's low political representation of women, praising the Beijing Platform for Action, and urging Ministers to champion human rights for women globally, including their right to political voice and civic participation.

When directly asked whether he supported female suffrage, Mr. O'Connor explicitly declined to advocate it, stating instead that "the suffrage should be given to every man of 21 years of age" — confining his franchise proposal entirely to men and thereby implicitly rejecting female suffrage. His entire speech focuses on male working-class enfranchisement and the Chartist cause without any positive argument for women's political rights.
