The speaker (Keir Hardie) defends the suffragist prisoners Mrs. Pankhurst and the Pethick Lawrences, criticising the harshness of their sentences, drawing favourable comparisons to treatment of male political offenders, and explicitly calling on the Home Secretary to transfer them to first-division status and consider remission — all of which supports women's political rights and the suffrage cause.

The speaker moves the Second Reading of the Married Women's (Employment) Bill, explicitly arguing that married women should have the right to work in public service and that dismissing them solely on grounds of marriage is unjustifiable, framing this as an extension of the Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act 1919 and as a matter of equal civic rights for all citizens regardless of sex or marital status.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on widows' benefits, the earnings rule, and National Insurance provisions — welfare policy affecting widows and widowed mothers. While the speaker mentions being a woman MP and references the National Council of Women, she makes no substantive argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech concerns hereditary revenues, parliamentary votes for charitable institutions in Dublin (Foundling Hospital, House of Industry, Female Orphan House), and financial matters of the Crown. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly criticises the Conservative party for its "lack of representation of women," linking this deficit to being out of touch with the public, thereby implicitly advocating for greater women's political representation.

The speech (by Sir G. Grey) is almost entirely about parliamentary reform proposals — extension of the male suffrage, the ballot, triennial Parliaments, and electoral districts — and argues against the Motion on those grounds. The only mention of women occurs in passing, where Sir G. Grey notes that if Lord Ashley's praise of working-class intelligence supports the franchise argument, it would apply equally to women, and that Mr. Hume's "universal suffrage" presumably stops short of women — neither of which constitutes an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses on women's human rights abuses (forced marriages, female genital mutilation, access to education) predominantly in international and minority community contexts, with only a brief passing reference to the 70th anniversary of women's suffrage as historical context. The speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill removing disqualification of married women from public employment, arguing there is "no justification" for the State treating women differently from commercial concerns based on marital status, and states "I certainly support it, although I do not think it goes as far as it ought to do" — indicating support for women's equal civic participation.

The speaker argues that the suffragette prisoners (Mrs. Pankhurst, Mrs. Pethick Lawrence) should be treated as first-class misdemeanants and political offenders, explicitly advocating for their fair and equal treatment under the law compared to men, and highlighting the disparity in sentencing between Tom Mann and the suffragette leaders as unjust. This constitutes support for women's political rights and civic standing.

The speech by the Member for Uxbridge is entirely focused on the debate over raising the school-leaving age, educational expenditure, and the social implications of keeping children in school longer. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women" in passing references), and no argument about women's political rights, representation, or civic participation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speech focuses entirely on educational policy—teacher training, backward children, adult education, juvenile delinquency, and school funding—without making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "women teachers" and "married women" doing part-time remedial work is about employment in education, not civic or political participation.

Sir Henry Slesser's speech defends the Married Women's (Employment) Bill, arguing it correctly prevents dismissal solely on grounds of marriage while preserving efficiency-based dismissals, and explicitly supports it as advancing individual liberty and implementing the Sex Disqualification Removal Act 1919. Viscountess Astor's contribution likewise strongly supports the Bill, arguing women should not be barred from public employment on grounds of marriage and that women's civic participation benefits the State.

The speech is entirely focused on parliamentary oversight of military action against Iraq, arguing that the House of Commons should vote before committing UK forces. Women are mentioned only incidentally (Mrs. Albright, Mrs. Thatcher, "men and women" risking their lives) without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Hungarian war, Russian and Austrian interference, the situation of Hungarian refugees in Turkey, and British foreign policy — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of the Pragmatic Sanction being extended to females (Maria Theresa's succession) is a historical fact about dynastic succession, not an argument about women's civic or political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports measures that protect women's access to income (working families tax credit), praises the Government for ensuring women can receive payments directly, and argues that having more women in the Treasury team has advanced women's financial autonomy and choice — all framed as advances for women's civic and economic participation.

The speaker (Ramsay MacDonald) strongly advocates for the humane treatment of suffragist prisoners, argues they should be placed in the first division, compares their sentences favourably to men convicted of similar or worse offences, and defends their cause as a legitimate political fight for rights they believe in — all supporting women's political rights and their right to campaign for them.

The speaker explicitly claims a long record of supporting women's political rights (suffrage, university admission, professions, women police), while simultaneously opposing this specific Bill on the grounds that it would harm women's employment prospects and the public service — a substantive argument against one aspect of women's civic equality (employment protection for married women in public service).

The TARGET speech by the Home Secretary (McKenna) focuses on the general question of political prisoners, the prerogative of mercy, the Aliens Act, and expulsion of foreign nationals. While it briefly mentions "suffragist prisoners" in passing (promising to give attention to their cases), it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on the Malta Independence Bill — questioning the legitimacy of the referendum, religious coercion, press freedom, and the constitutional arrangements for Malta — without making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on juvenile delinquency, crime, mass media influences, and voluntary service opportunities for youth. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "young women," "men and women" volunteers) without any argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the management of BOAC, the VC10 aircraft order, the Minister of Aviation's conduct, and government responsibility for financial losses in the aviation industry. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker explicitly and consistently advocates for the right of married women to remain employed in the Civil Service and municipal services without discrimination, framing this as completing the work of the Sex Disqualification Removal Act 1919 and as "an act of justice." They argue against regulations that penalise marriage for women and in favour of individual women's freedom of choice in employment, directly supporting women's equal civic participation.

The speaker opposes the Bill, which would prevent public authorities from dismissing married women from employment, arguing it ignores "biological and physiological facts," that married women are less suited to continued employment than married men, and that public authorities should retain discretion over whom they employ. This constitutes opposition to expanding women's civic/employment equality in public life.

The speech is a ministerial statement on the Modernising Government White Paper, focused on public service reform, IT, deregulation, and civil service diversity. While it briefly mentions tackling under-representation of women in senior public service ranks as one element of a broader diversity agenda, it does not argue for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker (Sir G. Grey) explicitly calls on the House to "meet the Motion with a direct negative," arguing that the proposed extension of the suffrage departs from the constitutional principle of property-based voting and would make the House "too purely democratic." He opposes both the broad franchise extension in the Motion and, when Mr. Hume interjects that he would extend the franchise to females, Grey dismisses it skeptically and frames it as evidence of the Motion's dangerous radicalism.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on industrial unrest, its causes (factory/company systems, wage disputes, loss of personal employer-employee relationships), and proposed remedies. The brief mention of "suffragettes" is purely illustrative of a broader argument about distrust in Parliament's authority, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Roebuck) is primarily concerned with extending the male franchise and parliamentary reform broadly, arguing for giving voting rights to working-class men. While women are briefly mentioned in passing — noting that the Home Secretary ignored "more than half the population—women" when characterizing the proposal as universal suffrage — this is a rhetorical point about the limits of the franchise proposal, not an argument for or against women's political rights. No substantive position on women's right to vote or political participation is advanced.

Mr. Lansbury is explicitly introducing a Bill to remove the sex disqualification barring women from voting, arguing that the House has previously affirmed the principle of women's suffrage and that an overwhelming majority supports it. His entire speech is dedicated to advocating for women's enfranchisement.

The speech concerns the training, equipment, pay, and recruiting of the Territorial Army, with brief mentions of "men and women" and "men and girls" in the context of military service and marriage. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or civic representation.

The speech by Sir J. Graham concerns Sunday trading legislation and Sabbath observance as a social and religious question, with no reference to women's political rights, women's suffrage, or women's civic participation in any form.

The speaker (Mr. Lansbury) is explicitly arguing in favour of women's parliamentary franchise, urging the House to affirm the principle that women who pay rates and taxes and perform civic duties should be entitled to vote, and seeking leave to introduce a Bill to remove the sex disqualification barring women from the electoral register.

The speaker explicitly raises whether women are eligible to be Land Tax Commissioners and notes that he personally nominated "a very distinguished lady" in his constituency, demonstrating active support for women's appointment to public office.

The speaker (Mrs. Beckett) explicitly notes that in 1911 "no women could vote, let alone stand for Parliament" as evidence of how much society has changed and how overdue parliamentary reform is, framing women's exclusion from political rights as a historical injustice now corrected. She also criticises the House of Lords' near-entirely male, white membership as unrepresentative, implicitly endorsing women's fuller inclusion in political institutions.

The speaker briefly but explicitly notes that when he was born in 1925, women did not have the vote until they were 30, framing this as part of the historical progress toward making the House of Commons democratic — implying support for women's suffrage as a democratic achievement. This is a passing endorsement rather than a substantive argument, but it clearly positions women's enfranchisement as a positive democratic development.

The speech deals entirely with the qualification thresholds and registration mechanisms for the Irish franchise bill, focused on the male adult population and constituency size in Ireland. Women are mentioned only incidentally as a statistical deduction ("deducting one-fifth for double occupation and women") with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speech concerns factory hours legislation (the Ten Hours Act) and the relay system for women and children as workers, framed entirely as a labour protection and industrial regulation issue. Women are mentioned as a category of protected workers, not as political actors, and the speech makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in civic life.

The speech is primarily about trade union law, the legality of the general strike of 1926, and the question of whether Parliament should legislate to clarify trade union rights. The fleeting mention of "votes for women at the age of 21" is used purely as a hypothetical illustration of Parliamentary sovereignty, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Lord John Russell, introducing the third reading) argues that Ireland suffers a clear grievance in its drastically lower proportion of electors compared to England and Scotland, and that the Bill rightly remedies this by extending the franchise to place Irish people on equal political footing with the rest of the United Kingdom. He explicitly frames the extension of voting rights as a matter of justice and dignity, dismissing opponents' arguments as resembling the logic of "despotic countries" that deny political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on arguing against defence expenditure on the Royal Air Force, contending that the personnel and resources would be better deployed in education and industry. While women are briefly mentioned in passing (e.g., "143,000 men and women" in the RAF, shortage of "young men and women" as teachers), no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily a debate about the Tobacco Duty increase, focusing on tax policy and its burden on working-class consumers. While the speaker briefly mentions women smoking and alludes to the Chancellor's past opposition to women's suffrage and his current support for enfranchising women over 21, these references are incidental rhetorical points about the political consequences of taxing women voters, not substantive arguments for or against women's political rights.

The Speaker (TARGET) is ruling against the introduction of a new Women's Enfranchisement Bill on procedural grounds, arguing that the House already rejected a Bill of exactly the same kind two months prior and cannot reconsider the same question. While framed as a procedural ruling, the effect and thrust of the TARGET speech is to block women's enfranchisement legislation from proceeding.

The speaker (Mr. Lansbury) is attempting to introduce a Bill specifically designed to remove the sex disqualification barring women from being enrolled as electors or voting at Parliamentary elections, clearly advocating for women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on naval defence matters — fleet dispositions, the Polaris programme, shipbuilding, and manpower shortages. The only mention of women is a brief parenthetical remark ("We are being asked this year for a Vote of 103,000 men and women. I mention women, because the hon. Member for Dorset, West usually picks me up if I miss out the women") which is a passing joke with no argument about women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Benn) explicitly invokes women's suffrage as a historical parallel, noting that Asquith warned parliamentary democracy would be undermined if women got the vote, and frames opponents of current democratic reform as repeating the same discredited arguments used against women's suffrage — implicitly endorsing women's right to vote as an established democratic achievement.

The speech is about House of Lords reform — specifically abolishing the hereditary peerage — and focuses on democratic legitimacy, representation, and meritocracy. While the speaker briefly notes that only 8% of hereditary peers are women and only 16 women sit in the Lords, these are cited as evidence of the Lords' unrepresentative nature, not as arguments about women's political rights or civic participation. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly raises the concern that the Clause may prohibit women civil servants from affiliating with the National Society for Equal Citizenship (which seeks votes for women and broader political equality between men and women) and the National Council of Women, framing this as a matter civil servants "feel very keenly" about and implicitly arguing these affiliations should be protected. This constitutes a substantive argument in support of women's political rights and representation.

The TARGET speech is a procedural point of order raised by an unnamed speaker, questioning whether it is in order to introduce a new Bill conferring the franchise on women given that the House has already refused it that Session. It takes no substantive position for or against women's enfranchisement, only raising a procedural/parliamentary question about the admissibility of the Bill.

The speech is entirely about the Government's national strategy for carers — funding, employment rights, health support, and services for young carers — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a passing demographic note that "the majority of carers are women," which does not constitute an argument about their civic status or political participation.

The speech concerns amendments to the Local Government Act 1933 regarding members' pecuniary interests in council matters — it is entirely about conflict-of-interest rules in local government. While the speaker briefly mentions "men and women" serving on local authorities, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on advocating for better care, housing, and community provisions for mentally subnormal (intellectually disabled) persons. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker moves to introduce a Bill extending the county franchise to 10l. occupiers, arguing it removes unjust anomalies in representation and that qualified men should not be excluded from voting simply due to locality. The speech is entirely directed at expanding the suffrage to a broader class of male voters, with no mention of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly sympathizes with the advocates of Women's Suffrage, acknowledging they have "a great grievance" in being met with governmental manoeuvring rather than frank resistance, and suggests this provokes their violence. This constitutes a supportive stance toward women's political rights, even though the speech is primarily about plural voting reform.

Viscountess Astor argues that votes for women had a clear democratic mandate (it was before the country at the last election and the Prime Minister was pledged to it), implicitly pressing for its implementation and defending its priority over House of Lords reform. This is a direct argument in support of women's political rights (specifically the franchise).

The speech is about the British Airports Authority Bill, covering municipal airport control, consumer representation, and airport operations. The brief mention of appointing "men or women" experienced in consumer representation is a passing reference to gender-neutral appointment language, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly asks the Prime Minister to clarify whether the Government will introduce a Measure giving women the vote on equal terms with men during the current Parliament, and whether it will be done in time for women to vote in the next election — framing these as pressing, unresolved commitments that require a definite answer.

The speech is primarily about the Government's inconsistent position on a House of Lords reform amendment. The brief mention of women's suffrage (agreeing that Asquith was wrong to say women getting the vote would undermine parliamentary democracy) is purely incidental and is not argued as a position on women's political rights — it is used as an analogy to criticize the Government's approach to constitutional reform.

The speaker (Angela Smith, as confirmed by context) references women getting the vote alongside other democratic reforms as examples of necessary progress that had to be fought for, and uses these as analogies to support continued constitutional reform. She frames opposition to women's suffrage as an embarrassing historical mistake, implicitly endorsing women's political rights as self-evidently correct.

The target speech is a factual reply providing prison statistics about suffragette prisoners (numbers sentenced to hard labour, those receiving special treatment, those in hospital, and food intake). It makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Conservative government's failure to control the cost of living and rising prices over 13 years, with international economic comparisons and league tables. Women are not mentioned as a distinct civic class, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech concerns reforming the law of partnership and limited liability to encourage capital investment and employment among the working classes. The brief mention of "hundreds of women" emigrating abroad is offered as an illustration of economic hardship, not as an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is about appointing a Deputy Prime Minister and the Prime Minister's political prospects, with only a passing mention of "Tory women" as part of the audience the PM might need to speak to. No argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The target speech concerns the City of London franchise reform bill, focusing on whether extending business voting rights will endanger funding for open spaces like Epping Forest. While it mentions "men and women" on the court of common council in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states that regarding the Women's Suffrage Bill, the right hon. Gentleman "is pushing an open door," signalling personal support for the measure and willingness to accommodate it in the parliamentary schedule.

The speech by Mr. Fortescue concerns the Ecclesiastical Titles Bill, debating Papal aggression, religious toleration, the position of the Roman Catholic Church in Ireland, and the prerogative of the Crown — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speech concerns mental deficiency legislation and the care of young people with encephalitis lethargica in mental institutions — it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker advocates for relieving widows from the earnings rule, referencing their own Bill to that effect and arguing that widows with great responsibilities are "entitled to this consideration" — a clear argument in favour of expanding women's economic and civic entitlements.

The TARGET speech is primarily a parliamentary business statement about scheduling the Coal Mines Bill and Navy Estimates; the only mention of women's political rights is a passing reference to Friday being "consecrated" to a Women's Enfranchisement Bill as a scheduling constraint, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech focuses on RUC composition, Catholic under-representation, community policing, and alienation in Northern Ireland. While it briefly mentions under-representation of women in the RUC in passing, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights — the substantive discussion is entirely about Catholic/nationalist representation in the police force.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on opposing the Simon Commission on India and arguing against British imperial rule over India. The brief reference to women — noting that depriving British women of political rights and education would bring them to the same low level as uneducated Indian women — is a rhetorical point about the effects of oppression generally, not an argument for or against women's political rights as such.

The speaker notes with apparent regret that a proposal to allow eldest daughters of peers to succeed to titles — which "would have transformed the position and brought much greater female representation into the Lords" — was defeated, implicitly endorsing greater female representation in the upper chamber.

The speech is entirely devoted to debating the Ecclesiastical Titles Bill and the question of "Papal aggression" — whether Parliament should legislate against the Pope's establishment of a Roman Catholic hierarchy in England and Ireland. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued in any way throughout the lengthy speech.

The speech is entirely focused on trade union political levies, the relationship between industrial and political activities of trade unions, and the Labour party's independence — not on women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of leading a women's laundry strike in 1916 is used solely as an illustration of why political action complements industrial action, with no argument made about women's civic status or political rights.

Viscountess Astor explicitly credits women's votes with enabling certain die-hard MPs to be in Parliament, framing the women's vote as a legitimate and consequential political force. This brief but clear reference affirms the value and significance of women's political participation.

The speech addresses domestic violence policy, funding for Scottish Women's Aid, and media coverage of related incidents — none of which argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation as a class.

The target speech is a ministerial reply about prison treatment conditions for suffragette prisoners, addressing administrative details of their confinement. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns parliamentary procedure around the Ecclesiastical Titles Bill (restricting Roman Catholic episcopal titles in the UK), with no mention of women's political rights, the franchise, or women's representation. The brief reference to "female piety, chastity, and virtue" in the context of the Religious Houses Bill is about Catholic religious institutions, not women's civic or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a Bill to make trade union contracts legally enforceable, arguing against legal sanctions in industrial disputes and defending collective bargaining. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

Viscountess Astor closes her speech by noting that women in Italy and France lack the vote and suggesting that if they had it, they would be working to bring those countries into the naval disarmament conference — implying that women's enfranchisement leads to positive political outcomes and thus endorsing women's right to vote. The speech is primarily about naval estimates, but this closing remark constitutes a brief but explicit argument in favour of women's suffrage.

The speech is entirely focused on public expenditure, defence spending, economic planning, and national priorities such as housing, health, and education. There is no argument made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speech is entirely about railway line closures and their economic/social impact on constituencies in South-West Durham. While it briefly mentions women's institutes as among the groups affected by proposed closures, it makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The question concerns prison privileges for suffragette prisoners at Holloway, specifically whether food parcels are permitted for all prisoners or only female ones. It does not argue for or against women's political rights; it is a procedural inquiry about equal treatment in prison administration.

The speaker briefly mentions women's suffrage only to contrast it unfavorably with military preparedness, implying the Prime Minister is willing to leave women's suffrage to Parliament (framed as a frivolous or lesser matter) while refusing to act on compulsory military training, and quotes that "the franchise for women...would be disastrous" without contradicting that assessment.

The speaker (Churchill, responding to Snowden) acknowledges that women's franchise is "one of the great difficult questions which would have to be dealt with by the House during the present Parliament," implicitly affirming it as a legitimate and serious legislative priority without opposing it. The context makes clear this is a clarification defending the Government's commitment to the Franchise Bill, which includes women's suffrage.

The speaker (Mr. Stuart) argues for repealing an Act partly on the grounds that it would absurdly entitle females to vote under the Reform Bill, calling this a "monstrous absurdity." His framing treats women voting as an undesirable and ridiculous consequence, indicating opposition to women's political rights.

The speech concerns the right of Jewish men (Baron Rothschild and Alderman Salomons) to take seats in Parliament and the form of the oath required — a question of religious discrimination, not women's political rights. Women are mentioned only in passing as an analogy ("a lunatic, a female, a minor, or an alien"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Single Transferable Vote system and defending first-past-the-post for the Greater London Assembly elections. The brief mention of women candidates is incidental—used only to illustrate a point about voter choice under STV—and no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Mr. Hughes) explicitly argues that a proportional electoral system will create a gender-balanced assembly and that voters should be able to choose more women in politics, framing greater women's representation as a desirable objective of electoral reform.

The speech is entirely focused on teacher recruitment, morale, status, and professional organisation in the education sector. The brief mention of "strong man or strong woman" and the acknowledgement that women form the majority of the teaching profession are incidental observations about workforce demographics, not arguments about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly criticises the Government for omitting from the King's Speech any proposal to extend the franchise to women aged 21–30, arguing it is "a very simple question" of equality and urging the Government to bring forward a short Bill to rectify the disparity between young men and young women in voting rights.

The target speech is a lengthy parliamentary address by the Chancellor of the Exchequer defending his Budget, covering topics such as the Public Works Loan Fund, malt tax, house tax, income tax, Kafir war expenditure, and public debt reduction. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is entirely focused on the administration of the Small Holdings Act — sinking fund charges, rate burdens, county council obligations, and compulsory purchase policy. The brief mention of women is incidental ("among those who vote for them are not only men, but women") as an illustration of the breadth of the county council franchise, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech concerns the quality of preserved meat contracts for the Navy (specifically Goldner's provisions) and their effects on naval and military personnel. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speech is entirely focused on devolution, constitutional arrangements, and the relationship between the UK's constituent nations. The brief mention of "a male Roman Catholic Scottish Member of Parliament can vote on whether the Church of England has women ministers" is offered only as an example of constitutional inconsistency, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is a factual parliamentary answer reporting the current prison treatment of suffrage-related prisoners (numbers, feeding status, and application of Rule 243A), without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about national savings policy, including tributes to Lord Mackintosh, the National Savings Movement, and new Post Office Investment Accounts. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is about police conduct during a public meeting disturbance in Hyde Park, using suffragette interruptions as a passing analogy to illustrate a point about who should be removed when disorder occurs. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Ramsay MacDonald) explicitly criticizes the Government for failing to fulfil its pledges on extending the franchise to women, calling the absence of any such bill from the King's Speech "a blot upon the position which women occupy in our legislation," thereby expressing support for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly asks the Prime Minister about "the claims of women to an extension of the franchise," directly raising women's suffrage as a matter requiring government action, indicating support for advancing those claims.

The speaker explicitly argues for equal legal rights for women, framing the unequal guardianship law as part of broader discrimination against women ("The race of women is still greatly discriminated against") and seeking to give mothers equal guardianship of their children. The speech directly advocates for expanding women's civic and legal equality, situating it within the broader framework of women's equal rights.

The speech is entirely about the Government's use of guillotine motions to curtail parliamentary debate, criticising executive arrogance and the erosion of due process in the House. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is entirely about the future of rural post offices, benefit payment systems, and the Horizon IT project. Women are mentioned only incidentally as "postmistresses" or "sub-postmistresses" in the context of their professional roles, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses on the Home Secretary's constitutional responsibilities for law and order, police efficiency, remission of sentences (including a brief factual mention of suffragist prisoners being released on medical grounds), and anthrax in wool industries. The mention of suffragist prisoners is purely factual and incidental, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. Bernal Osborne) argues forcefully in favour of admitting Jews to Parliament, contending that excluding them disfranchises Christian constituencies, that the oath's Christian formula was never intended to bar Jews, and that opponents rely on historical error and medieval intolerance. He explicitly calls on the House to pass the Bill by a worthy majority, framing Jewish admission as a matter of civil and political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on Scottish maternity and infant mortality, midwife registration, housing conditions, and the inadequacy of the Bill's provisions — none of which address women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned as midwives, patients, and neighbours, but solely in the context of public health and professional regulation, not civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Maynooth College grant debate—defending the Roman Catholic institution, opposing a parliamentary inquiry, and discussing Irish Catholic-Protestant relations and political loyalty. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.
The speech concerns military aviation policy, aircraft procurement decisions, RAF capabilities, and defence spending. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is entirely about debt law reform — specifically the appropriate monetary ceiling for administration orders under county court jurisdiction — and while it mentions women incidentally as among those pursued for debt, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a betting/gambling bill, with Viscountess Astor arguing against legalising betting on moral and social grounds. The brief mention of women not yet having the vote is a historical aside with no argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the teacher shortage crisis in Scotland — class sizes, salaries, training, recruitment, and emigration — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. Brief mentions of "men and women" in the context of teacher training and equal pay refer to professional equality within the teaching workforce, not to civic or political rights.

The speaker (a Colonial Office representative) justifies the exclusion of women from the franchise and municipal councils in Palestine by citing the wishes of the majority population, and only notes limited exceptions (Tel-Aviv) and a future possibility, without endorsing women's political rights as a principle.

The speaker argues that suffragist leaders who broke the law deliberately and "in cold blood" should not have been granted first-class misdemeanant status, condemning the Home Secretary for giving them lenient treatment on political grounds. He explicitly frames their law-breaking as morally culpable and opposes any special consideration for their political cause.

The speech focuses entirely on defence policy, NATO, EU defence arrangements, the diplomatic service, and European enlargement. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation; the brief mentions of "service men and women" and "man for man and woman for woman" are incidental phrases unrelated to civic status or political rights.

The speech by Mr. M. Gibson is entirely focused on repealing the advertisement duty, stamp duty on newspapers, and paper duty as taxes on knowledge and press freedom. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation — women are mentioned only incidentally as workers in paper mills ("It employs men, women, and children"), with no connection to their civic status or political participation.

The speech is about protecting soldiers' dependants (specifically widowed mothers) from financial penalties when soldiers incur fines, and criticises the Tory Government on that issue. The passing reference to "the female section" of Tory supporters posing as friends of soldiers does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on RAF manpower levels, equipment budgets, education allowances, and personnel incentives within the Air Estimates debate. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation; the brief mention of "airwomen" is purely in the context of RAF personnel budget figures.

The speech mentions women's suffrage only as a brief historical anecdote to illustrate a point about Sinn Féin representation; the main argument concerns the rights of Irish representatives in the UK Parliament. No position is argued for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns county financial boards and the representative control of county expenditure, not women's political rights. Women are mentioned only in passing as one category (along with minors and absentee proprietors) not in the commission of the peace, with no argument made about their civic or political status.

The speech is entirely focused on Australian colonial governance, transportation of convicts, land revenue policy, and constitutional reform for the colonies. The only mention that could touch on women is a sardonic aside proposing to send "the lowest outcasts of our women" as wives for convicts in Western Australia — this is a flippant rhetorical flourish about penal policy, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on housing legislation (home-buying, leasehold reform, and homelessness) and makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status for women.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill granting married women the right to work in public service, arguing that dismissing women on grounds of marriage alone is "ridiculous," that married women demonstrably perform at high levels in medicine and other professions, and concluding "I only ask that they shall have the same right that other citizens have, namely, the freedom to decide whether they shall or shall not work."

The speaker explicitly references that "in the past they [the Tories] resisted universal suffrage and votes for women" as part of a broader critique of Conservative opposition to democracy, framing women's suffrage as a positive democratic right. Additionally, in the preceding context, the speaker (Mr. McCartney) boasts that Labour "for the first time" gave women opportunities to be appointed to NHS trusts, positioning greater inclusion of women in public roles as a positive achievement.

The speech concerns whether Parliament should investigate or regulate conventual (nunnery) establishments, framed as a question of religious liberty and tolerance toward Roman Catholics. While the speaker briefly mentions women in convents as subjects of potential protective legislation, the argument is entirely about religious freedom and the character of Catholic institutions, not about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech is the Home Secretary's account of a police incident at a Hyde Park demonstration involving transport workers and suffragists. While suffragists are briefly mentioned as occupying a nearby meeting ground, the speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights — it is entirely concerned with police conduct and crowd control during the disturbance.

The target speech concerns funding for Dublin hospitals and grants to Irish religious institutions following the Act of Union, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about the privatisation of National Air Traffic Services (NATS) and the PPP/trust model debate; it contains no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status for women.

The TARGET speech focuses on expanding absentee/postal voting arrangements for Service voters and UK citizens employed abroad, quoting a constituent letter about disenfranchised British workers in developing countries. While it briefly references "men and women" voters, it does not make any argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct class.

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater women's representation in local government, citing statistics on their underrepresentation, referencing a report on the "Democratic Deficit," and urging the Bill to actively encourage and facilitate women's participation in decision-making positions, including by supporting carers' allowances to remove barriers.

The speaker explicitly criticizes the Home Secretary for treating suffragist leaders leniently as "first-class misdemeanants," arguing that those who "wantonly and in cold blood break the law" for political propaganda are "the most deserving of punishment" and that there is "no moral turpitude" doctrine enabling lenient treatment of suffragist rioters is "the most dangerous doctrine." This constitutes substantive opposition to the preferential treatment—and implicitly to the cause—of women's suffrage agitators.

The speech is primarily an argument about the Home Secretary's treatment of so-called "political offenders" and the principle of political crime under English law. Female suffrage is mentioned only in passing as one example among several (alongside labour agitators, Tom Mann, Malatesta, etc.) to illustrate the speaker's broader point about leniency toward politically-connected offenders; no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is primarily about extending absentee/postal voting facilities to people who are away from their constituencies on polling day. While the speaker briefly mentions the anomaly of wives being unable to vote by post when accompanying husbands on business trips (invoking "Shades of Mrs. Pankhurst"), this is a passing illustration of a broader electoral reform argument rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights as a class.

The target speech asks the Under-Secretary about postal and proxy voting arrangements for Service men and women in the 1945 election, in the context of a debate about expanding postal voting for holidaymakers. This is a question about electoral administration history, not an argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. M. Barlow and Mr. Silvester Horne) is entirely about Welsh Church Disestablishment and Disendowment — the relationship between the Church of England in Wales and the State, the redistribution of tithes, and the merits of religious establishment. Women's political rights are not mentioned, argued for, or against anywhere in the speech.

The speaker (Mr. Macquisten) argues against a Bill that would prevent local authorities from dismissing married women from employment, contending that married women naturally belong in the home, that confidentiality in public roles would be compromised, and that local authorities should retain discretion to exclude married women — all of which oppose women's equal civic participation and employment rights.

The speaker (Mr. Remer) moves to reject the Married Women's (Employment) Bill, arguing it places married women in an unjustifiably privileged position, citing opposition from women civil servants themselves and contending that departmental heads should retain full discretion to dismiss employees without legislative interference—effectively opposing expanded civic/economic rights for married women in public employment.

The speech concerns a proposed Select Committee to investigate conventual and monastic institutions in relation to existing law, focusing on religious liberty, property rights of nuns, and the legality of these institutions. While it discusses the civil status and personal liberty of women in convents, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, standing for office, or any aspect of women's civic/political representation.

The speech concerns the legal disabilities of illegitimate persons and the workings of the Affiliation Act, not women's political rights or representation. The passing mention of "all women's organisations" making representations about the committee's terms of reference does not constitute an argument about women's civic or political status.

The speech is entirely focused on procedural matters surrounding the Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Bill — specifically how to handle a drafting gap left by the deletion of the word "life" from the sentencing clause. The only mention of women is a historical reference to equal pay for male and female teachers in the Education Act 1944, used purely as a parliamentary procedural analogy, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill, arguing that the feminist movement's core demand is equality for women in the State with men, and calls for removing both economic and political discrimination against women — including equal standing in professions, industry, and politics. The speaker directly links support for women's political equality ("remove the last political discrimination against women") with the economic equality sought by the Bill.

The TARGET speech (Sir R. Peel) focuses entirely on foreign policy toward Russia and the Ottoman Empire, commercial prosperity, trade policy, education, parliamentary reform (electoral corruption and franchise extension), and labour disputes — with no mention of women's political rights, women's suffrage, or women's civic status at any point.

The TARGET speech is primarily about the legality and practicality of 50:50 Catholic/non-Catholic recruitment quotas for the Northern Ireland police service. The brief mention of the 1998 proposals by Mrs. Fyfe regarding positive discrimination for women in candidate selection is cited only as a legal precedent to argue that the Government's own law officers warned such measures would be challenged under the European Equal Treatment Directive — it is used as an analogy to critique the police recruitment quota, not to argue for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about electoral bribery, disfranchisement of corrupt voters, and procedural objections to the Bills being withdrawn. The brief mention of two women (Elizabeth Williams and Jane Moon) appearing in the schedules is used only as an example of careless drafting, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speech is almost entirely concerned with constitutional debates about House of Lords reform, Home Rule, parliamentary pledges, and the Parliament Act. Women's suffrage is mentioned only in a single passing remark comparing Cabinet disagreements on Second Chamber reform to disagreements "on such a subject as Women's Suffrage," without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech focuses entirely on Royal Navy personnel matters — overseas allowances, education allowances, and recruiting figures in the Estimates — without making any argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief acknowledgment of the preceding speaker's remarks about the W.R.N.S. is purely contextual and does not engage with any question of women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker explicitly supports parliamentary modernisation reforms (family-friendly hours) and notes that the Scottish Parliament's more normal working hours helped attract a wider spectrum of the public, citing as a particular achievement that women constitute 50% of Labour's representation there, arguing this would not have happened without those reformed hours — directly linking procedural reform to women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly declares support for "the broad principle of Woman Suffrage" while simultaneously opposing this Bill precisely because it extends the franchise to women (via the municipal and parish council franchise) in a way he finds objectionable—characterising it as a "Woman Suffrage Bill, brought in by a side door" applying women's votes to temperance/prohibition, which he says those in favour of women's suffrage "most dread." This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: endorsing women's suffrage in principle while opposing this particular expansion of women's political participation.

The speaker explicitly calls for a parliamentary debate to address and find solutions to the underrepresentation of women candidates in Labour's Welsh seats, framing women's representation in Parliament as "a very important issue" that needs to be remedied.

The speaker draws a parallel between the Chancellor of the Duchy's remarks about historical popular uprisings (Nottingham Castle 1832, Hyde Park railings 1867) and the suffragette cause, arguing that such statements effectively encourage women to use similar violent means to achieve their political demands — implicitly treating the suffragette campaign for women's political rights as legitimate and comparable to earlier reform movements.

The speech is entirely focused on defending Roman Catholic conventual institutions (convents and nuns) against a proposed parliamentary inquiry, arguing against allegations of undue influence, cruelty, and exaggerated numbers. It makes no argument about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports removing the bar on married women in public employment, arguing it is a "simple measure of justice," and connects this to the broader goal of giving women equality with men in the franchise ("going this Session or next to seek to correct one glaring anomaly...giving them equality in regard to the franchise"). He directly rebuts arguments against the bill and calls on the House to support it.

The speech is primarily about House of Lords reform, electoral redistribution, and the Parliament Bill. The brief mention of "One Woman, One Vote" is entirely passing and parenthetical, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is a ministerial reply about the mental health of a prisoner named Mr. Ball, attributing his instability to his preoccupation with "Votes for Women" and "political prisoners." It mentions women's suffrage only incidentally as a subject Ball was fixated on, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mrs. Beckett) explicitly supports women's representation by rebuking Conservative Members for heckling and reminding the whole House that women are over 50% of the population, implicitly endorsing the cause of greater women's political representation raised by her colleague.

The speech concerns parliamentary votes on Irish hospital grants and the evidence behind a committee's recommendation to reduce them, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech by Mr. Whiteside concerns the debate over parliamentary inquiry into conventual and monastic institutions, focusing on property law, religious liberty, and the credibility of arguments made by the previous speaker. It does not address women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech is entirely concerned with the Crimean War context: the Greek insurrection against Turkey, Russian interference, the conduct of the Ottoman government toward Christian subjects, and British foreign policy. The single brief mention of women ("in Greece I have heard of acts of great atrocity being committed upon women to compel them to induce their sons and husbands to vote") is incidental local color about electoral coercion, not an argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker (Financial Secretary to the Treasury, Mr. McNeill) explicitly opposes the Bill that would prevent public authorities from dismissing women solely on account of marriage, arguing on grounds of administrative efficiency, sickness risk, and the interests of women themselves. While he claims a past record of supporting women's emancipation, he substantively argues against extending women's employment rights in the public service, making this a clear opposition to women's political/civic rights.

The speaker is questioning whether prison authorities were justified in excluding a suffragist-connected prisoner (W. Ball) from rules meant to protect political prisoners, implicitly advocating for the extension of those protections to individuals imprisoned in connection with the suffragist movement.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on the politics of steel nationalisation and the Labour Party's parliamentary tactics (the "wheelchair vote," the confidence motion, public relations). There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The primary speaker (before Commander Williams and Dr. Little) strongly advocates for women's equal employment rights, arguing against the dismissal of married women from public service and framing opposition to the Bill as a continuation of the same attitudes that historically opposed women's suffrage and civic emancipation. The speech explicitly supports women's right to choose their own occupation free from male-imposed restrictions.

The speech is focused on the discriminatory effects of a proposed amendment on small parties in the Northern Ireland Assembly, including the Women's Coalition, but the mention of the Women's Coalition is incidental — it is used as an example of a small party that would be unfairly disadvantaged by the amendment, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation as such. No substantive argument about women's civic status or political rights is made.

The speech is focused entirely on Navy Estimates, defence expenditure, recruitment, ship construction, and related naval matters. The brief mention of "men and women" in recruitment and the observation about unequal pay for "responsibility" vs. equal pay for harmonium players is a passing, incidental remark about pay rates within the Navy, not an argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on Welsh devolution, the role of Welsh MPs in the UK Parliament, economic development, poverty reduction, and the relationship between the Welsh Assembly and Westminster. While it mentions "Welsh men, women and children" in passing, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about taxation on alcoholic beverages (whisky, port wine, sherry, beer) and its effects on trade, revenue, and the balance of payments. The brief mention that "Women drink it" in reference to port wine consumption is a passing descriptive remark, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on government training schemes for the unemployed, particularly women's vocational training for domestic service and clerical work, as a matter of labour and unemployment policy. While women are discussed extensively as a class of unemployed persons benefiting from training programs, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about police funding, rate burdens on London ratepayers, and the cost of one day's rest in seven for police. The single passing mention of "suffragette raids" is used only as an incidental example of why Metropolitan Police costs are high, with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on labour unrest, poverty, wages, working conditions, municipal enterprise, and socialism/nationalisation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the working population (e.g., "men and women are learning to read," "working women," "the woman who works in the factory") without any argument about their political rights or civic status.

The target speech concerns the election of a new Speaker of the House of Commons, focusing on the qualities and challenges of the office. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation; the brief mention of "men and women" working in constituencies is incidental and carries no substantive argument about women's civic status.

The speech is a point of order concerning a personal attack on the speaker (Sir C. Osborne) via Motion No. 263, which relates to industrial action and democratic rights in industry. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on unemployment training schemes for women and men, advocating for the continuation and expansion of the Central Committee on Women's Employment's training centres and grants. While it discusses unemployed women extensively, it does so in the context of vocational training and employment policy, not women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on Armed Forces and public service pensions, advocating for improvements to pension rates and widows' pensions for retired service members. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation; the brief mention of "men and women into the Services" is incidental to the pension discussion.

The speaker explicitly welcomes a target of 50% representation of women in public life, praises women's capabilities in public roles, and criticises the Opposition for proposing to scrap the Sex Discrimination Act and Equal Opportunities Commission — all of which amount to a clear argument in favour of women's political rights and representation.

The target speech concerns a parliamentary dispute over hospital funding in Ireland and voting on grants for hospitals and nonconforming ministers; there is no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech (by Mr. Whiteside) is entirely concerned with the debate over the Maynooth College grant — arguing against the institution on grounds of Jesuitism, disloyal teaching, and mismanagement. Women are not mentioned at all, and the speech makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on national education policy — the merits of rating localities for education, attendance of children at school, comparisons with Prussia and Austria, and the role of the state in providing education. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about, even in passing.

The target speech is entirely focused on leasehold reform, property rights, and criticism of the government's White Paper on leasehold enfranchisement. The only mention of women is a passing reference to returning "men and women capable of giving a lead in decent, honest dealing," which does not argue any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly promotes a Bill to enable positive action (all-women shortlists) in candidate selection, arguing that women's underrepresentation constitutes a "profound democratic deficit" and that legal barriers to such measures must be removed to achieve equal political representation for women.

The speech addresses agricultural wage regulation and conditions of women's employment in counties, which is a labour/wage policy matter. It does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech concerns the independence and composition of the Electoral Commission, restrictions on political appointees, and the integrity of the democratic process — none of which address women's political rights or representation. Women are not mentioned, and no argument is made about their civic participation.

The speech is primarily about equal treatment of prisoners (men and women) under prison rules, conditions for dock strike prisoners, and appeals for clemency — it mentions the suffrage agitation only as a contextual reference point for comparing prison treatment, without arguing for or against women's political rights themselves.

The speech is primarily about unemployment policy, training centres, and grants. The brief mention of women's training refers to vocational/domestic service training schemes and budget cuts to those programmes — not to women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker dismissively refers to extending the vote to younger women as "votes for flappers" and argues that Parliament's attention should be concentrated on economic matters ("bread and wages") rather than on granting votes to these "estimable young women," clearly opposing this extension of women's political rights.

The speech is a lengthy budget debate address covering income tax resilience, road funding, trade policy, tariffs, economy measures, and armaments. The only passing reference to women is a brief aside about Schedule A taxpayers — "There are men and women, not all of them old—some of them will probably get the vote" — which is a fleeting, incidental remark rather than any argument about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about carers' rights and the Carers Bill, with only a brief passing reference to Emily Wilding Davison hiding in a broom cupboard during the 1911 census to protest women's lack of voting rights. This historical anecdote is used as an analogy for carers making political points, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech concerns procedural parliamentary business (withdrawing a motion) and the passing of votes for various hospitals in Ireland. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech is by the Home Secretary (Mr. McKenna) addressing prison administration matters: forcible feeding of suffragette prisoners, prison division classifications, and treatment of dock strike prisoners. While suffragettes are mentioned as a category of prisoners, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights — it focuses entirely on prison management policy and legal obligations regarding prisoner welfare.

The speech primarily addresses fire safety regulations, forcible feeding of prisoners, and prison rules. While Suffragette prisoners are mentioned in the context of forcible feeding policy, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights — the discussion concerns the administration of prison rules equally across all prisoners regardless of their cause.

The speech is entirely focused on leasehold reform — ground rents, freehold enfranchisement, and housing tenure — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. Women are not singled out as a class with distinctive civic status anywhere in the speech.

The target speech is primarily about prison administration matters — forcible feeding, Rule 243A, social standing of prisoners, and amnesty for dock strike prisoners. While it mentions suffragette prisoners in passing as a category subject to Rule 243A, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speaker (Mr. Roundell Palmer) argues at length against the Bill that would legalise marriage with a deceased wife's sister, grounding his opposition in Levitical law, the universal doctrine of Christendom, and warnings that loosening these marriage prohibitions would open the door to polygamy and other moral dangers. He explicitly calls on the House to reject the measure.

The speaker explicitly calls on the Government to take "meaningful action to increase the representation of women in the higher levels of the judiciary," highlighting the stark underrepresentation of women among senior judges and invoking the concept of a "glass ceiling" to argue for greater women's representation in public legal office.

The TARGET speech is about whether Lord Willoughby de Broke's statements on Ireland should be considered alongside the Ben Tillett case; it does not argue for or against women's political rights. The mention of "suffragette" appears only in the preceding speaker's (Healy's) rhetorical question, not in the TARGET itself.

The speech is about Post Office policy, commercial banking negotiations, and government competence — mentioning the Women's Institute only as a source of constituent petitions. No argument is made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker pays tribute to women Members of Parliament, notes their successful role in Government, and explicitly criticises the Gracious Speech for omitting equal pay for women, warning that the railings around Westminster "can be used again" — a direct invocation of suffragette tactics to press for women's civic and economic equality.

The speaker briefly but explicitly endorses women's political rights, stating he "can never understand why we have hesitated so long about granting women the franchise and equality in various spheres of life," using women's lower crime rates as evidence of their fitness for civic participation. The rest of the speech concerns juvenile crime in Glasgow.

The speaker explicitly invokes women's suffrage as a historical parallel to current discrimination, condemning those who argued women should not have the vote as holding "antediluvian, atavistic, primitive and bigoted views," and further argues that girls deserve equal protection under the law to boys — framing women's equal civic and legal standing as a settled moral victory that supports her broader equality argument.

The target speech is a brief procedural exchange in which the speaker (Miss Lawrence) objects to being ruled out of order when trying to raise the topic of training and employment for women, and the Deputy-Chairman explains which Vote governs that subject. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made; the exchange is purely about parliamentary procedure and the scope of the current Vote.

The speech is entirely about televising Parliament's proceedings, addressing fears of misrepresentation and exhibitionism, and the relationship between the legislature and the electorate via media. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is a Home Secretary's reply defending prison conditions for Mrs. Pankhurst and denying allegations about her cell, addressing administrative matters of prison management. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker introduces a Bill explicitly to reform the law of property as it affects married women, arguing at length that the current common law is "unjust in principle" and grievous in practice, and advocates giving married women equal legal rights over their own property and acquisitions — a clear, substantive argument in favour of expanding women's civil and legal status.

The speech is a lengthy argument about divorce law reform (the Matrimonial Causes Bill), addressing the indissolubility of marriage, scriptural interpretation, the sacramental character of marriage, and the social effects of easier divorce. While the speaker briefly notes the bill treats the sexes unequally (men can divorce for adultery while women cannot, and adulterous husbands largely escape consequences), this observation is made as a critique of the bill's internal inconsistency rather than as an argument for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The target speech is Gerard Fitt's maiden speech as MP for West Belfast, focused entirely on electoral injustice and discrimination in Northern Ireland, democratic reform of the Government of Ireland Act, and the undemocratic local government franchise system. While the speech briefly mentions "one man, one vote" and democratic rights, it does not address women's political rights or representation in any way.

The speech is entirely focused on the education and welfare of mentally handicapped children, covering issues of administrative responsibility, teacher training, residential schools, and parental involvement. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech by Mr. Cowper concerns the introduction of a permissive education bill, focusing entirely on questions of religious instruction in schools, local rating, and the balance between denominational and secular teaching. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued.

The speech is primarily a critique of the Mental Deficiency Bill, focusing on the sweeping powers it grants to the Home Secretary and local authorities. The single mention of suffragists ("all the suffragists could be locked up as being mentally deficient under this Bill") is a passing rhetorical jab illustrating the bill's excessive reach, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech consists of a Member raising a procedural point about discussing women's training for employment under a specific Vote, and the Deputy-Chairman's ruling that it is out of order. Neither the Member nor the Deputy-Chairman makes any argument for or against women's political rights; the subject is unemployment relief administration and parliamentary procedure.

The speech is primarily about unemployment policy and statistics, with only a passing joke about a "lady Member" having no sleeves and a brief mention of "women's vote" as one item in a hypothetical Cabinet agenda list. Neither reference argues a position on women's political rights; they are incidental mentions without any substantive argument for or against.

The speech is primarily about House of Lords reform, proportional representation, and religious representation in the upper Chamber. The brief mention of women bishops and the ordination of women is a passing reference about Church of England policy in the context of single-sex institutions, not an argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. M'Cullagh) explicitly frames personal voting as "the manly system" and the voting paper system as "the feminine system—for it was intended that women should vote," using this distinction as an argument against the voting paper proposal. By opposing the system precisely because it would enfranchise women, he takes a clear stance against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on consumer protection against unscrupulous doorstep salesmen, discussing specific fraudulent practices, legislative measures, and praising the Bill under debate. While the speaker briefly mentions that "young married women are especially vulnerable" to doorstep salesmanship, this is an incidental observation about consumer vulnerability, not an argument about women's civic status or political rights.

The TARGET speaker moves the Second Reading of a Women's Suffrage Bill, explicitly arguing for the enfranchisement of women on grounds of justice, constitutional principle ("no taxation without representation"), women's demonstrated capacity in public life, and the absence of harmful consequences from women's municipal voting. The entire speech is a sustained advocacy for women's political rights.

The speaker briefly but explicitly endorses giving votes to women under 30, stating "the sooner the Government decide to give votes to women under 30, the better chance there will be of returning a Labour Government." This is a clear, affirmative statement in support of extending women's suffrage, even though it appears in passing within a speech primarily about unemployment policy.

The speaker seconds the motion for the Bill's second reading and systematically dismantles anti-suffragist arguments, arguing that women's industrial participation, existing political engagement, and involvement in municipal governance make the case for extending the Parliamentary franchise to women compelling and logically consistent.

The speaker explicitly expresses disappointment that no women have been recruited to the Commonwealth Secretariat and thus denied diplomatic immunity, and hopes women "will be able to play their part in the future," citing women Prime Ministers in Commonwealth countries as evidence of women's capacity for public roles. This is a clear, if brief, argument in favour of women's equal participation in public/political life.

The speaker argues that the Bill is too restrictive in limiting pension credits to women with children under six, and supports extending credits to women caring for children up to age 11, explicitly framing this as helping women with career breaks build better pensions and have the choice to stay home until children are more independent.

The speech by Miss Herbison is entirely focused on social security reform (benefits for the unemployed, sick, and widows), the earnings rule, and the National Insurance Advisory Committee. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker (a woman Labour MP) pushes back against Sir Peter Emery's dismissive "Blair babes" comment and challenges the implicit suggestion that women are less engaged in substantive parliamentary democracy, asserting that women are just as interested in issues of democratic control as in procedural efficiency — a defence of women's equal standing and seriousness as political participants.

The speech is entirely focused on the Trade Disputes Bill, specifically attacking its provisions on general strikes, the political levy, and blacklegs. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation; the brief mention of "nationalisation of women" is a passing reference to Tory electoral misrepresentation, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly and comprehensively argues in favour of women's suffrage throughout, citing colonial evidence (Australia, New Zealand), refuting anti-suffrage arguments about home/hearth neglect, quoting the Australian Senate's resolution endorsing women's suffrage, and urging all supporters to vote for the Bill's Second Reading.

The speech is entirely focused on road safety and traffic management issues on the A41 trunk road in Bebington, including speed limits, traffic lights, and pedestrian crossings. Women's political rights and representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech focuses entirely on Northern Ireland policing reform, Catholic recruitment to the RUC, and the Patten report. While it mentions "men and women" in the context of Catholic recruitment to the police force, this is incidental and does not argue any position about women's political rights or civic representation.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Bowyer) is entirely concerned with the Jewish Disabilities Bill and the Roman Catholic oath — specifically arguing about the religious character of Parliament, the deficiencies of the Catholic oath, and the position of Roman Catholics under the proposed legislation.
