There is no argument made about women's political rights, the franchise, or women's representation in any form.

The speech is primarily about the Trade Union political levy and contracting-in versus contracting-out mechanisms, with only a passing reference to "flappers" and women's suffrage as an incidental factor that might increase election expenses. No substantive argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about parliamentary procedure, timetable motions, and the role of Parliament versus the Executive. The one mention of women is a passing historical observation that "Parliament—although it took a considerable time before it admitted women—has historically acted to represent the peoples of this country," which notes a fact without arguing for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on parliamentary reform (franchise extension, uniformity of suffrage between boroughs and counties, electoral districts, and the procedural handling of the Reform Bill). Women's political rights are never mentioned, argued for, or argued against anywhere in the speech.

The target speech concerns Labour local government administration, district auditors, minimum wages, and opposition to a punitive Bill affecting local councils — there is no argument made about women's political rights or representation at any point.

The speaker (Mrs. Thatcher) explicitly advocates for fiscal measures to encourage married women to return to work, proposing three concrete tax relief mechanisms (domestic help relief, excluding wife's first £1,000 earnings from Surtax, and extending earned income relief), arguing the government's taxation policy wrongly penalises married women who wish to take paid employment.

The TARGET speech (and the concatenated speeches within it) focuses entirely on Parliamentary Reform concerning male working-class voters, franchise qualifications, borough and county representation, and party tactics. Women are never mentioned as a class, and no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made at any point.

The speech by Dr. Salter is entirely focused on the effects of a district auditor surcharge bill on municipal governance, wage-setting, and the deterrence of responsible candidates from public life. While he briefly mentions "women representing settlements and social services" as examples of high-character councillors, he makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, or representation as a distinct class.

The TARGET speeches (Mr. Adderley and Mr. Headlam) are entirely concerned with the mechanics of Parliamentary Reform — franchise thresholds, county vs. borough constituencies, freehold voter transfers, and electoral district structures — without any reference to women's political rights, women's suffrage, or women's civic participation. Women are not mentioned as a class at any point.

The speaker moves to reject the Women's Suffrage Bill, explicitly stating he opposes granting women the Parliamentary vote, arguing it is constitutionally improper, undemocratic in form, and that the vote's ultimate sanction rests on male physical force — qualities he says are inapplicable to women. Despite acknowledging sympathy with women's demands and crediting their public contributions, he finds no valid argument for enfranchisement and urges the House to reject the Bill outright.

The TARGET speech seconds an amendment to reject the Women's Suffrage (Conciliation) Bill, explicitly opposing women's suffrage on multiple grounds: arguing that passing the Bill would inevitably lead to women sitting in Parliament (presented as an alarm), that the Bill is a tactical manoeuvre to "storm the position" of full female enfranchisement, and warning that opponents of the measure would be unable to resist extension to adult suffrage once the "hill which commands the position" is taken.

The speech is entirely focused on the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Bill, addressing electoral finance regulation, the Neill committee recommendations, campaign expenditure limits, referendum rules, and party donations. Women's political rights or representation are not argued for or against at any point.

The speech is primarily about the City of London Corporation Bill, electoral corruption, democracy, and Human Rights Act compliance. The mention of women getting the vote in 1928 is a brief historical aside illustrating the newness of democracy, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's inclusion in the Upper Chamber, framing it as both "wise and just," and supports the argument by noting women voters are expected to outnumber men at the next election, making a substantive case for women's political representation in the House of Lords.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Roebuck and Sir Richard Bethell) is entirely focused on the question of Jewish admission to Parliament, debating religious tests, oaths, and civil/political rights for Jews. While women are briefly mentioned in passing ("they also exclude women, one hardly knew why"), this is a fleeting reference with no argument made about women's political rights — it is used only as a comparative example in a list of exclusions, with no substantive engagement with the topic.

The speech addresses the honours system and recognition of local government service, mentioning "men and women" only in passing as recipients of honours. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation as a distinct class.

The target speech concerns political party funding, tax relief on political donations, the Neill committee report, and the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Bill. While it briefly mentions "men and women" devoting their lives to politics, this is a passing rhetorical flourish and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker (Viscount Helmsley) argues extensively and substantively against women's political rights, contending that a mixed assembly would alter Parliament's tone, that women's mental equilibrium is less stable than men's, that governing has always been and should remain a male function, and that enfranchising women would be premature and damaging to public life.

The speaker forcefully argues in favour of women's suffrage throughout, invoking the constitutional legitimacy of repeated Commons majorities for the Bill, the principle of no taxation without representation, and dismissing opponents' arguments about militant tactics and mental unsuitability of women. He explicitly states that recent militancy has strengthened his desire to see women's suffrage passed, and urges the House to vote on the merits of the measure.

The speech concerns Rhodesian sanctions, Commonwealth support, non-racialism, and Britain's international standing. The passing reference to "human rights of men and women" is incidental and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

Mr. Harmsworth's question presupposes the existence of "the promised Bill to extend women's franchise" and asks whether it will contain additional electoral reform provisions, implicitly accepting and supporting the extension of women's franchise as a given policy proceeding.

The speaker (Mr. McCurdy) directly supports women's parliamentary franchise, arguing that the House of Commons has repeatedly affirmed the principle by large majorities, that taxation without representation is unjust, and that failing to proceed with the measure would stir justified resentment among women. He also rebuts opponents' arguments about mental instability and militant tactics as grounds for denial.

The speech focuses on economic policy, the National Plan, manpower shortages, and the practical challenges of recruiting older workers and married women into the labour force. Women are discussed purely as an economic resource (labour supply), with arguments about disincentives like the lack of childcare, part-time work, and vocational training—not about women's political rights, franchise, representation, or civic status.

The target speech concerns the legal and administrative effects of a Bill amending district auditor surcharge powers in local government, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of "men and women" who serve in local government is purely incidental and descriptive, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the mechanics of parliamentary reform — franchise qualifications, freehold votes, borough vs. county representation, and the structure of the Reform Bill — with no mention of women's political rights, women's suffrage, or women's civic participation. The word "male" appears in the Bill's text quoted by the speaker, but the speaker makes no argument about women's inclusion or exclusion from political rights.

The target speech discusses extending postal and proxy voting rights to people absent from their constituency on polling day (holidaymakers, conference attendees, hotel workers, etc.) without making any argument specifically about women's political rights or representation. While women are mentioned incidentally as part of the general electorate ("men and women attending conferences"), no distinctive argument is made about women's civic status or rights.

The speech concerns unemployment insurance legislation — specifically objections to a clause that would remove benefit from large numbers of unemployed workers — and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief references to "workwomen" and "a man or a woman" are incidental mentions in the context of unemployment benefit eligibility, not arguments about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on political party funding, referendum spending limits, the Neill committee's recommendations, and the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Bill. Women's political rights or representation are not argued for or against; the brief mention of "men and women" in a quoted passage from Neill is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political participation.

The speaker passionately advocates for enfranchising the working classes, arguing they are unfairly excluded from political participation, comparing their exclusion to slavery, and asserting they are fully capable of exercising the franchise wisely. There is no substantive argument against women's political rights, and the speech's entire thrust is expanding political rights to a currently excluded class.

The speaker explicitly invokes women's political rights, noting that young women ("flappers") will soon have the vote and will remember that their "first economic baptism before they got the vote was handed out to them as starvation." While the speech is primarily about unemployment benefit cuts, it frames the injustice against young women in terms of their emerging civic standing and implicitly supports their enfranchisement as a mechanism for political accountability.

The speaker explicitly states he will "vote against the Second Reading of this Bill" on the principle of women's parliamentary franchise, arguing that "the natural distinction of sex... ought to continue to be recognised... in the sphere of Parliamentary representation" and that enfranchising women "would in the long run prove to be injurious to women and fraught with the gravest possibilities to the future good government of this country."

The speaker (Mr. Beresford Hope) explicitly argues against women's suffrage, warning that accepting an "indefeasible right to the suffrage" would logically lead to "universal suffrage, not merely manhood suffrage, but universal suffrage, in the full sense of the term, including the concession of votes to women"—which he presents as a reductio ad absurdum and a dangerous "consummation." This is a clear, if brief, argument against women's political rights embedded in a broader speech about parliamentary reform.

The speech is entirely focused on debating the Selective Employment Tax Bill — its structure, anomalies, affected industries (tourism, building, charities, part-time workers), and policy concerns. The brief mention of "married women" and "good ladies, the Mrs. Mopps" is in the context of tax impacts on part-time workers, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech focuses entirely on political party funding, campaign finance transparency, overseas voters' franchise, and the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Bill — none of which singles out women as a class for distinctive civic rights or duties. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The TARGET speech (by Lord Robert Cecil) systematically rebuts arguments against the Conciliation Bill, argues that women are qualified for political participation, contends that sex alone should not be a disqualification for the franchise, and urges the House to recognise women's stake in legislation—all in clear support of women's political rights.

The speech by Mr. Bruce concerns Indian finances, the liabilities of the British government toward India, the opium trade, and related imperial financial policy. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any form.

The speaker systematically dismantles arguments against women's suffrage, arguing that women have vital interests in all major legislative matters (wages, industrial disputes, education, housing, religion, empire), that their economic position requires enfranchisement, and explicitly states "it is an outrage that women should not have been entitled to vote" on such measures, making a sustained and unambiguous case for women's political rights.

The speech concerns a debate on fox hunting and animal welfare legislation, with no substantive argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief reference to "young men and women of 16" pertains to sexual consent law, not women's civic or political participation.

The speech focuses almost entirely on unemployment insurance policy, arguing against the 30-stamp qualification and reduced benefits for young workers. While the speaker briefly mentions the particular hardship faced by young women living in lodgings on 8s. a week and references training centres for women, these are incidental to the broader unemployment insurance debate and do not argue a position on women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I am one of those people who is gender blind. I want neither more nor fewer women Members. The electorate decides how many there are," dismissing the increase in women MPs as an issue worth addressing. When directly asked by Ms King whether he recognises that more women members bring distinct needs like childcare, he pivots entirely to parliamentary management and accountability topics, refusing to engage with women's specific needs or representation as a legitimate concern.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage throughout, arguing that women suffer genuine injustice in being denied the vote, condemning those who use violence as an excuse to oppose the Bill, and concluding with a direct appeal to the House to give the Conciliation Bill a Second Reading and push it through all its stages.

The target speech is a lengthy contribution to a Parliamentary Reform Bill debate focused on franchise extension, borough disfranchisement, the merits of the existing representative system, Free Trade, and the arguments of the Member for Birmingham. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about, even in passing.

The speech concerns the use of nude female models in Government Schools of Art and argues for moral restrictions on this practice, framing it as a question of public morality versus artistic education. This does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation in any way.

The speech is a tribute to civil, military, and naval officers for their services during the Indian Mutiny. While the speaker briefly mentions the heroic conduct of women caught up in the crisis in India, this is a commendation of their personal courage under danger, not an argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly emphasizes the importance of women being on the Apple and Pear Development Council, giving two substantive reasons: women are the primary buyers of apples and a large proportion of apple pickers and graders are women, so their interests deserve representation. This constitutes a positive argument for women's inclusion in a public/civic body.

The speaker (Member for Maidstone) briefly but explicitly supports female representation on the Apple and Pear Development Council, stating "I hope that in these outside members, and possibly even in the trade union nominations, there will be some attempt to get female representation" and affirming that "provided they are suitably qualified it is highly desirable." This is a positive argument for women's inclusion in a public representative body, bringing the speech within scope.

The speaker (Lord Robert Cecil) explicitly supports women's suffrage throughout the speech, arguing that the lack of votes harms women's interests across multiple policy areas, and dismisses the window-breaking argument as unjust grounds to deny the franchise. However, he also explicitly opposes women sitting in Parliament, stating "I myself would be against allowing women to sit in Parliament" on grounds of physical exhaustion—a substantive argument against one dimension of women's political rights while supporting another (the vote).

The speech is primarily about the Apple and Pear Development Council's operations, funding, and representation. The brief mention of women's representation on the Council refers to consumer/housewife interests in a horticultural body, not to women's political rights or civic participation in the sense of suffrage or political representation.

The speaker explicitly states he is voting against the Second Reading of the Conciliation Bill, citing militant suffragist violence as his primary reason for reversing his previously pro-suffrage voting record. While he acknowledges past support and says he is "not altogether opposed" in principle, his substantive argument is that the violence has made him unwilling to support the measure at this time, and he declares he would vote against it even if he were the only one to do so.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment insurance policy, training centres for unemployed youth, and the government's handling of the Unemployment Insurance Bill. The brief mention of "young women" concerns their moral supervision during transfer to Birmingham for employment purposes, not any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is entirely concerned with the Irish national education system — its administration, religious fairness, and the inadequate pay of national teachers — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech concerns the effects of the Selective Employment Tax on the employment of handicapped and elderly people in Flintshire, not women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the broader group of "handicapped men and women."

The speech concerns a disabled constituent (Barrie Such) and the failures of health, social services, housing, and BT to provide appropriate care — it makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation. The mention of Wendy Such as a devoted wife and carer is purely narrative context, not a claim about women's civic status.

The speech concerns unemployment insurance legislation and the timing of implementing a permanent insurance scheme, focusing on the plight of unemployed men and women losing benefits. While women are briefly mentioned as among those who might lose benefits, no argument about women's political rights, representation, or civic participation is made.

The speaker introduces and commends Amendment No. 67, which enables the Policing Board to monitor and increase women's representation in the police, support staff, and the board itself, explicitly framing this as addressing a "marked imbalance" in gender representation. This constitutes support for measures expanding women's political and civic representation.

The speech focuses entirely on the powers of district auditors over local authority spending and wages under the bill being debated, arguing that elected local councils are being subordinated to unelected auditors. While it mentions "men and women" being driven out of public life, this is incidental phrasing and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is entirely focused on Commonwealth immigration policy — praising the moderation of a fellow MP, debating immigration regulations, racial tensions, and population pressures — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states he will continue to vote for Woman Suffrage and the Conciliation Bill, argues that women's participation in politics is already established through party associations and elections, cites positive colonial experience with women's suffrage, and rebuts opponents' arguments about physical force and domestic disruption — all in sustained support of women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is a Home Secretary's reply providing electoral statistics (registered electors and votes polled across three general elections). It presents factual data without making any argument for or against women's political rights; the question about extending franchise to women appears only at the very end as the next question (Major Kindersley's follow-up), which is part of the context, not the target.

The speech is primarily about provision for the chronically sick and disabled. The brief mention of women's suffrage ("although women, at last, have a vote in this country") is incidental context for an argument about disability benefits for housewives, not a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for memorials to women who served in Parliament and to suffragettes who fought for women's enfranchisement, expressing shame at the absence of such recognition and framing women's election to the House as "a major achievement." This directly supports women's political rights and their place in political history.

The target speech is a maiden-style address seconding the Motion for an Address in reply to the Gracious Speech, focusing on Stoke-on-Trent, Arnold Bennett, industrial relations, and the legislative programme. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mrs. Beckett) expresses sympathy with the concern about the lack of memorials to women Members of Parliament and suffragettes, calling it "regrettable" and expressing hope it will be remedied, while also noting positively the indirect memorial to a suffragette and the plaque commemorating Lady Astor's election. This implicitly supports the recognition of women's historic political participation and representation.

The speaker explicitly endorses the Sex Discrimination (Amendment) Bill, which aims to end discrimination against women in sport (e.g., denying women votes at AGMs, barring them from clubhouses), describing it as an opportunity to "end the last remnants in sport of discrimination against 51 per cent. of our population" and lamenting that Parliament is not giving it sufficient time for consideration.

The speaker explicitly supports Woman Suffrage throughout, stating "the case for Woman Suffrage is a sound one on the grounds of justice," recounting his survival of an anti-suffrage campaign against him, and announcing he will vote for the Second Reading. While he raises substantive objections to the specific Bill's details (e.g., the restriction on wives voting in the same constituency as husbands), these are procedural/implementation objections rather than opposition to women's political rights in principle.

The speech is a lengthy analysis of a Parliamentary Reform Bill focusing on franchise extension, borough representation, rate-paying clauses, and electoral mechanics. While women are briefly mentioned as a class to be deducted from county occupier statistics (noting they make up roughly one-fifth of occupiers and would not receive votes), this is a passing numerical observation with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a sustained attack on unemployment insurance contribution rates for young workers aged 18–21, focusing on actuarial inadequacy, financial responsibility, and the hardship imposed on working-class youth. While it mentions "young men and women" repeatedly, it does so in the context of unemployment benefit policy, not their civic or political rights; there is no argument about voting, standing for office, representation, or any other aspect of women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about opposing the secret ballot (Ballot Bill), with women mentioned only in passing as a class whose interests are affected by male voters exercising a trust — no argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely focused on the merits and defects of a Parliamentary Reform Bill concerning borough and county franchise thresholds, seat distribution, and electoral corruption — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a brief passing reference by Mr. Bright (in the context speech, not the target) noting that women form a portion of county occupiers who would need to be deducted from franchise estimates, which carries no argumentative stance on women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly mentions having previously introduced a Bill "for the enfranchisement of women on equal terms with men" in 1920, expressing support for women's equal political rights. This brief but unambiguous endorsement of women's political enfranchisement on equal terms with men is a direct statement of support for women's political rights.

Mrs. May explicitly supports the Bill enabling parties to take positive action to increase women's representation in Parliament, arguing that Parliament is "losing out on a pool of talent" by not electing more women, and that young women are discouraged from politics partly due to lack of female representation. She supports the aim of greater female representation while objecting only to all-women shortlists as the exclusive mechanism, which is a procedural rather than substantive opposition.

The speaker explicitly states he opposes the Bill "in toto," arguing women should not be "dragged into political struggle," that their sphere is domestic, that the franchise should not extend to women because men and women "fulfil their special spheres," and concludes "I shall vote against this Bill with a whole heart and clear conscience."

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Reform Bill's extension of the borough franchise to £6 householders, drawing on arguments about democratic corruption in America, the quality of public men under universal suffrage, and the dangers of transferring power to the lower classes. Women are mentioned only once in passing ("pensions conferred on women for naughty things they had done"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The first speaker (unnamed, up to "Mr. MURRAY MACDONALD") argues extensively against the Conciliation Bill, contending that most women do not want the vote, that previous pledges in favour were rash, that giving women the vote would harm their social standing and draw them away from the home, and that Parliament's supreme authority should remain with men. Mr. Murray Macdonald's portion, by contrast, supports the Bill, but as the TARGET is classified as a whole, the dominant and lengthier argument is the opening speaker's sustained case against women's suffrage.

The speech is primarily a passionate attack on the Government's unemployment benefit policy and its effects on working-class families, particularly regarding allowances for female relatives caring for dependants. While women are mentioned (working girls, women folk, wives), the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation; the brief mention that "those women folk invariably have no vote" is a passing observation, not an argument about the franchise or civic participation.

The target speech is a parliamentary business announcement listing upcoming legislation and a procedural division record. While it mentions the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill, it does so only in passing as a scheduled item without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (and the Solicitor General's follow-on remarks within the same text block) is entirely focused on the Reform Bill's provisions regarding the county and borough franchise, freeholder voting rights, redistribution of seats, and parliamentary tactics — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The single passing mention of women in the Solicitor General's portion ("women should be admitted to the franchise… I have no wish to see the franchise conferred on women") appears only as a rhetorical analogy to challenge the logic of trusting working-class loyalty as grounds for enfranchisement, not as a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The target speech concerns debates about Metropolitan park expenditure, rides in Kensington Gardens, Storey's Gate, Richmond Park drainage, and municipal taxation — none of which involve women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally as users of park spaces, not as a class with distinctive civic status.

The speaker explicitly argues that denying women the vote is an act of injustice ("the real argument in favour of this claim is founded on justice"), presents evidence from Australia and New Zealand that women's suffrage has had positive effects, rebuts arguments against women's fitness for political participation, and urges Members to vote for the Bill's Second Reading.

The speech is entirely focused on the question of British entry into the European Economic Community, addressing food prices, Commonwealth trade, nuclear sharing, and internationalism. The brief mention of women ("men and women whom he represents" and "women do not register as unemployed" in Mauritius) are purely incidental and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speaker (Mrs. Patsy Calton, Cheadle) explicitly supports the Bill giving political parties tools to increase women's representation in Parliament and other political offices, argues the playing field is uneven due to discrimination and structural barriers, and calls for action to achieve true democratic representation of women.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on opposing the extension of the borough franchise to working-class householders under a Reform Bill, arguing they lack education, morality, and religious grounding to exercise the vote wisely. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point in the speech.

The speaker explicitly states "I myself am not in favour of giving the Franchise to women" and argues against the Conciliation Bill on grounds that it will inevitably lead to universal adult suffrage—a "stupendous revolution"—without consulting the electorate, framing this as a constitutional danger. His opposition is substantive and consistent throughout, not merely procedural.

The target speech is entirely focused on leasehold reform legislation in Wales and England, debating property rights, ground rents, and the Leasehold Reform Bill. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The target speech is entirely focused on opposing the abolition of church rates and defending the Church of England's established position; women's political rights are never mentioned, argued for, or against anywhere in the speech.

The speaker explicitly identifies as "a supporter of Woman Suffrage," systematically rebuts the Prime Minister's and opponents' arguments against women's enfranchisement, and marshals evidence (canvass results, national organisations, meetings) to demonstrate widespread demand for women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on electoral reform (proportional representation, the alternative vote, and the fairness of the current majority voting system). While the speaker briefly mentions the upcoming enfranchisement of women voters ("the franchise... should be a franchise that is worth having"), this is used only to underscore the importance of electoral reform generally, not to argue for or against women's political rights. No substantive argument about women's civic status or right to vote is made.

The speech is a procedural parliamentary question about scheduling the Budget and the Second Reading of the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Snowden) explicitly supports women's parliamentary enfranchisement throughout, arguing from democratic principles that women who want the vote are governed without their consent, presenting canvass evidence of widespread support, and contending that granting women the vote would improve their industrial conditions and wages.

The speaker calls attention to Early Day Motion 333 seeking to end legal, social, and economic discrimination against women, explicitly describes it as "a subject of great concern," and requests parliamentary time for it, thereby supporting women's political and civic rights. The motion itself, quoted in the speech, references women's suffrage history and calls for removing women's legal disabilities and ensuring equal treatment.

The speech is a broad Conservative critique of government erosion of individual liberties, Parliamentary accountability, and the growth of executive power; women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point in the target text.

The speaker explicitly supports the government's pending Bill to extend the franchise to all women over 21, and argues that the consequent addition of 5,500,000 voters makes electoral reform even more urgent; he also appeals to women voters directly, framing a vote against his motion as disappointing "the millions of women voters who are to be added to the register." This reflects a supportive stance toward women's political rights, even though the speech's primary focus is on proportional/alternative vote electoral reform.

The speaker enthusiastically supports the Bill enabling positive action mechanisms (including all-women shortlists) to increase women's political representation, arguing that opaque discrimination in selection processes requires such measures to level the playing field, and frames the entire history of women's suffrage and parliamentary representation as a battle that must continue.

The speaker strongly endorses women's right to full and equal political participation (welcoming the Belfast Agreement's commitment to it, acknowledging women are "grossly under-represented," and commending the centre for advancing women in politics), but simultaneously opposes the Bill's mechanism of positive discrimination/all-women shortlists as "counter-productive and divisive," drawing an analogy to discriminatory police recruitment in Northern Ireland. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides: supporting women's political representation in principle while opposing the specific positive-discrimination measures in the Bill.

The speech by Mrs. Lena Jeger (Holborn and St. Pancras, South) is entirely focused on poverty, family allowances, income tax policy, wages, and social security — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. References to women in the speech concern their role as housewives and mothers managing poverty, not their civic or political status.

The speech by the Member for Havant covers health service issues (Queen Alexandra hospital, sterilisation units), social security policy (vaccine damage payments, care homes, winter fuel payments, pension credit, benefit fraud), and the Queen's Speech generally. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Sir W. Joynson-Hicks) moves the Second Reading of the Equal Franchise Bill, arguing extensively that women deserve the same voting rights as men on grounds of justice, historical progress, and demonstrated fitness for political participation, explicitly calling for the removal of the age restriction on women's franchise.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill's principle of allowing parties to use measures to increase women's representation in Parliament, stating "We support the principle enshrined in the Bill" and concluding that "No country has significantly increased the representation of women in its Parliament without some form of positive action." While she expresses a personal preference against women-only shortlists, this is a procedural/methodological caveat rather than substantive opposition to women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on agricultural policy — animal welfare regulations from the Brambell Committee, farming subsidies, drainage charges, and river board reform. The passing reference to "a second generation suffragette" is merely a colourful description of a village busybody and makes no argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly and emphatically supports the enfranchisement of women throughout, arguing that industrial conditions are regulated by Parliament making the vote necessary for women workers, refuting physical force arguments, and concluding that he cannot "refuse support to the enfranchisement of women and continue to lay any claim to the profession of democratic principles" while urging the House to pass the Bill by a triumphant majority.

The target speech is entirely concerned with the merits of a Parliamentary Reform Bill—the appropriate level of the borough franchise, redistribution of seats, the ballot, and the fitness of working-class men for the vote—without making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states he will vote for the Second Reading to express his "firm and unshaken belief in the emancipation of women and in the justice of electoral equality for them," and references his own Bill to remove disabilities of women and simplify the franchise. His objection is only to the current Bill being too partial and limited, not to women's political rights themselves.

The TARGET speech is a lengthy Conservative argument against the Reform Bill of 1860, focused on constitutional theory, the effects of the 1832 Reform Act, franchise extension to working classes, bribery, government expenditure, and theories of representation. Women are mentioned only once in passing—as part of the liberal democratic theory's self-contradiction ("the most advanced Liberals did not propose to give votes to women, paupers, or children, or lunatics, because they said they were not fit")—without the speaker arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about an Agriculture (Miscellaneous Provisions) Bill, covering animal welfare codes, tenant farmer compensation, and related agricultural matters. The only mention of anything related to women is a passing, non-argumentative reference to a "second generation suffragette" as a rhetorical aside, with no position taken on women's political rights.

The target speech is entirely about parliamentary/electoral reform for the working classes — reducing the borough franchise, the timing of the Reform Bill, and related procedural matters. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker (Joynson-Hicks) systematically defends enfranchising all categories of women under the Bill—married, working, and unmarried—and explicitly argues it is an "act of justice" regardless of partisan advantage, urging the House to pass the Bill by an overwhelming majority.

The speaker argues at length that militant suffragist activities are "inherent in and inseparable from the Suffrage movement," that this constitutes "a strong and serious argument against Woman Suffrage itself," and urges delay or a referendum while opposing the Bill on Second Reading, framing women's suffrage activism as causing "widespread demoralisation" and threatening national moral order.

The speech is a maiden speech focused on European integration, Scottish independence, constituency matters, and lowering the voting age to 16 for all young people. While the speaker praises female SNP parliamentarians (Margaret Ewing, Winnie Ewing), he makes no argument for or against women's political rights as a class; the voting age argument is framed around youth generally, not women specifically.

The TARGET speech is a maiden speech focused on social housing, the speaker's constituency, and Labour history (including a brief mention of Keir Hardie's support for "the enfranchisement of women" as part of a list of historical aspirations). This passing historical reference does not constitute an argument for or against women's political rights; the speaker makes no substantive claim about women's political rights themselves.

The speaker (Sir William Joynson-Hicks) is moving the Second Reading of a Bill to equalise the franchise for men and women, explicitly arguing that women have justified their claim to the vote, that it is an act of justice, and that no intellectual or practical objection can stand against enfranchising women on equal terms with men.

The speaker explicitly states he gives "general support" to the Second Reading of the Equal Franchise Bill on behalf of his entire party, which has been "united, unanimous and wholehearted in its support of the political equality of the sexes," and recalls his own active role in the pre-war campaign for women's enfranchisement. No substantive opposition to women's political rights is expressed.

The speech is entirely focused on parliamentary reform (extension of the male franchise), the credibility of the working classes as voters, and party political maneuvering around the Reform Bill. Women are mentioned only once, incidentally, in a statistical calculation of national income ("estimating the number of women who work at 2,000,000"), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is primarily about Bermuda's constitutional arrangements, boundary commission gerrymandering, racial franchise inequalities, and the adequacy of voter registration — none of which singles out women as a class for distinctive civic rights or duties. The brief mention of candidature for Parliament concerns working-class people generally, not women specifically.

The speaker frames the suffragist window-smashing campaign as "outrages" and "organised attacks," and proposes legislation to hold suffragist organisations financially liable for damages—a measure designed to penalise and suppress the suffrage movement's activities. This is substantively opposed to women's political rights as exercised through suffragist action.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing a bill to liberalize wine licensing and sale, arguing it will promote drunkenness and immorality. The only mention of women is a passing reference to a petition from "480 of the women of Newcastle—the wives, sisters, and daughters of working men" opposing the bill on domestic comfort grounds, and a brief remark about wives and daughters potentially being offered wine in shops. Neither of these constitutes an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker mentions the upcoming 50th anniversary of the suffragette movement and expresses pride in the increase in women graduates and undergraduates, framing women's educational advancement as integral to Scotland's economic future. This constitutes a brief but genuine endorsement of women's fuller participation in public and civic life.

The speaker (Mr. Snowden) explicitly supports the Bill's second reading on behalf of his entire party, argues that full adult enfranchisement is a right, recounts his personal pre-war activism for women's franchise, and closes by declaring the Bill a consummation of 60 years of suffrage work that will benefit democracy as a whole. His criticisms are purely procedural (plural voting, university franchise, registration issues) and do not oppose women's political rights.

Tony Benn mentions women's political rights approvingly in two places: he notes the historical injustice that "when I was born, women were not allowed the vote until they were 30," framing restricted women's suffrage as a democratic deficit, and he commemorates Emily Wilding Davison (the suffragette) with a plaque, celebrating those who fought for democracy including votes for women. He also criticises that the statues in Parliament depict "not one of whom believed in democracy, votes for women or anything else," implicitly endorsing votes for women as a democratic value.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers: Mr. Dickinson, who strongly supports Women's Suffrage (arguing it is a matter of democratic principle, civilisation, and equal rights), and Mr. MacCallum Scott, who advances the "physical force argument" against women's suffrage, arguing that including women in the franchise undermines the value of elections as an index of physical force. This constitutes substantive argument on both sides within the same TARGET.

The speech is entirely about school exclusion policy, teacher discipline challenges, and government circular 10/99; it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief mentions of women (Mrs. Sally Carr, Mrs. Iris Pummell, a female deputy head) are incidental references to local education officials, not arguments about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the funding and operation of St. Teresa's Maternity Hospital under the National Health Service, arguing against the Regional Hospital Board's decision to end its contract. It makes no argument about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on rural policy issues — post offices, transport, housing, agriculture, planning, and quality of life in rural communities — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of Shropshire women's wages is used as an economic statistic about rural poverty, not as an argument about women's civic status or political participation.

The TARGET speech is primarily about constitutional and parliamentary matters — Cabinet responsibility, franchise reform, Home Rule, and the House of Lords — with only a fleeting metaphorical reference to "Votes for Women" as a "brigantine raiding the high seas," used as an analogy to illustrate a constitutional point about Cabinet ministers acting inconsistently with government policy. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The target speech, by Miss Harvie Anderson (Renfrew, East), is entirely focused on Scottish industrial employment, training, housing, and economic development. She explicitly declines to engage with women's suffrage ("I will refrain from following in any great detail the speech of the hon. Member for Midlothian, tempted as I am to enter into the realm of women's suffrage"), making no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Hardy) argues at length against lowering the borough franchise, contending that admitting the working classes en masse through a £6 rental franchise would be reckless, revolutionary, and destructive to the constitution, and that numbers without property or intelligence should not be given predominant power over the existing constituency. He makes no substantive argument in favour of expanding political representation.

The speech is primarily about Labour party policy on the House of Lords, Home Rule, and social reform. "Votes for Women" is mentioned only in passing as a metaphor used by the preceding speaker (McNEILL) regarding Cabinet responsibility, without the TARGET speaker making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the international coalition against terrorism, the war in Afghanistan, humanitarian aid, and refugee camps. While the speaker briefly mentions Afghan women being subjugated under the Taliban and calls for their inclusion in future governance and refugee camp conditions, these remarks are incidental observations about the Taliban's oppression rather than substantive arguments about women's political rights or civic participation as understood in the suffrage/representation framework.

The speech is an extensive argument about the administration of Ireland's National System of Education, specifically the dispute between Catholic Bishops and the Commissioners over mixed versus denominational schooling. Women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation are never mentioned or argued about.

The speech concerns the treatment of Christian women sold into slavery by Druses in Syria and diplomatic representations to the Turkish Government — a humanitarian and foreign policy matter. It does not address women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation in any way.

The speech is entirely focused on Commonwealth emigration/migration policy, assisted passage schemes to Australia, and related topics such as housing, statistics, and university places. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker (Sir G. Cockerill) argues against the Bill by contending that giving women a numerical majority in every constituency will create undue political pressure and sex-based influence over legislation, citing examples of women's organisations leveraging the women's vote for political gain. He opposes the Bill as it stands because it creates sex preference rather than sex equality, and argues men should not be placed in a permanent minority.

The speech by Mr. Du Cane is a lengthy critique of the Reform Bill focused on the contradictions among its supporters, the dangers of extending the franchise to working-class occupiers, the imbalance between county and borough representation, and the potential for democratic "revolution" — with no substantive argument about women's political rights. The single mention of "female occupiers" appears only as a passing statistical adjustment in calculating the new county electorate, without any argument for or against women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly states he is "not opposing this Measure because I am in any way opposed to the women's vote" and affirms women are "just as capable of exercising the franchise as are men," expressing genuine support for women's political rights in principle. However, he moves an amendment to decline Second Reading on the grounds that giving women a permanent numerical majority in constituencies would inflict injustice on men as a sex, making a substantive argument against this specific extension of the franchise — thus combining real support for women's suffrage with substantive opposition to equal voting age on the basis of numerical sex imbalance.

The speaker (Mr. Lansbury) advocates on behalf of William Ball, a suffragist prisoner who was subjected to forcible feeding and denied the same political prisoner treatment as women suffragettes and well-connected individuals like Lady Constance Lytton and Hugh Franklin. He explicitly argues that political prisoners, including those protesting for "Votes for Women," deserve equal and fair treatment regardless of class, implicitly supporting the suffrage cause and women's political rights as legitimate political convictions worthy of respect.

The speech is entirely focused on supporting a national sweepstake Bill to raise funds for the National Health Service and medical research. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The target speech raises the case of women suffrage prisoners and questions the Home Secretary's differential treatment between leaders and rank-and-file, implicitly advocating for equal political prisoner status for women suffragists — a position supportive of women's political rights and their treatment as political actors.

The speaker (Sir G. Cockerill) explicitly endorses equal political rights for men and women ("equal political rights for men and women… with that policy I find myself wholly in agreement") and affirms women's capability to vote, but substantively opposes the specific Bill on the grounds that it gives women a permanent numerical majority over men, arguing this creates sex preference rather than sex equality and demanding redistribution or other mechanisms to restore parity between the sexes.

The speech is entirely focused on social security fraud — anecdotes about benefit claimants, whistleblowing mechanisms, and enforcement gaps — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. Mentions of women (e.g., single women as household heads, a pharmacy worker, a nurse) are incidental to the fraud discussion and carry no argument about their civic status or political participation.

The questions from Mr. King and Mr. Keir Hardie advocate for mitigating the punishment of suffragette leaders (Mrs. Pankhurst, Mr. and Mrs. Pethick Lawrence) imprisoned in connection with the movement for women's political enfranchisement, implicitly supporting their cause and their treatment as political offenders rather than common criminals.

The speech is entirely focused on low voter turnout, democratic engagement, postal voting, compulsory voting, and parliamentary reform after the 2001 general election. While the speaker briefly mentions suffragettes in passing as a historical example of fighting for the vote, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker seconds an amendment opposing the Equal Franchise Bill, arguing that the 1918 women's franchise was granted under abnormal wartime circumstances, that the current bill creates an unequal female majority rather than true equality, and that it will damage imperial governance and national finances—concluding that the Bill should not receive a Second Reading.

Lady Hermon's maiden speech highlights her pride in being the first woman returned from Northern Ireland in nearly 30 years and notes the historic significance of women's representation in Parliament, implicitly endorsing women's political participation. She also references being "outraged by the Chief Constable's discrimination against women in the RUC," signalling support for women's equal civic standing, while celebrating that her constituents "returned a woman to Westminster."

The speaker is advocating on behalf of imprisoned suffrage activists, questioning the Home Secretary about their prison classification and treatment, and implicitly supporting their cause by pressing for better conditions for women imprisoned for suffrage-related offences.

The speaker explicitly argues that "the struggle for emancipation and equality is by no means won" for women, criticises the social security system for leaving millions of women at risk, and calls for women's organisations to be "as vocal about the defects in the social services, in the status, legal and social, of women, as they were years ago on the fundamental rights of women." He openly states he stands for "the full freedom of women and their proper place in society," framing women's civic and social equality as an unfinished cause requiring active advocacy.

The TARGET speech concerns the abolition of hereditary titles and the reform of the House of Lords, arguing that the hereditary principle is obsolete. It makes no argument about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any related civic status for women.

The Countess of Iveagh's speech (the dominant portion of the TARGET) strongly supports the Bill extending women's franchise, arguing it is "the only logical conclusion" of franchise evolution, rebutting opponents' claims about women's irresponsibility, and urging the House to pass the measure "generously" as "the outcome of logic and of justice." The opening fragment opposing the Bill belongs to a prior speaker (Colonel Applin), not the Countess.

The speaker (Ms Keeble) argues that the Budget contains "particular benefits for women," highlights that the pensioners tax credit will especially help women since they live longer, and notes that priority public services are "highly valued by the whole community, but especially by women voters." These are supportive statements about policies benefiting women's economic and civic position, framed as advocacy for women.

The speech is entirely focused on the technical merits and flaws of the Reform Bill's criteria for disfranchising boroughs (population tests, number of voters, relative importance), with no argument made for or against women's political rights. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of the population count ("men, women, and children") with no substantive engagement with their civic or political status.

The speaker mentions Manhood Suffrage only to argue that the House's time would be better spent discussing the London transport strike, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights. The speech is focused entirely on procedural prioritization of a labour dispute over the scheduled debate.

The speaker uses a historical anecdote about a woman being denied the university franchise merely as an analogy to illustrate the constitutional principle that the constitution cannot be changed "by a side wind." The speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights; the anecdote is incidental to the debate about parliamentary oversight of treaty-making.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Franchise Bill, arguing that the Parliament Act makes it unwise to add large numbers of new voters without a second chamber check, that no electoral mandate existed for this reform, and that his constituency's women's association voted for him to oppose it. Though he offers a brief disclaimer that he is "not in any way opposed to the enfranchisement of women," this is followed immediately by substantive arguments against the Bill and a declaration that he will vote against it, making his overall stance one of opposition to women's political rights as currently proposed.

The speech is entirely focused on British foreign policy toward Italy, particularly critiquing Lord John Russell's support for Piedmontese expansion, the financial state of various Italian states, and alleged diplomatic misconduct. Women's political rights are not mentioned, argued for, or argued against anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely about a family planning / birth control bill, arguing for expanded contraceptive advice and services through local health authorities. It makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, serve on juries, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on whether "religious profession" should be included as a question in the Census Bill, arguing on grounds of religious liberty, the separation of church and state, and the practical uselessness of such returns. Women and women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in this speech.

The speech is an extended defence of British foreign policy toward Italian unification and the Papal/Neapolitan governments, addressing trade, governance, elections, and atrocities in Italy. Women's political rights are never argued for or against; the sole mention of women is incidental (e.g., women killed in bombardments, women at the cultivation of flax, a young queen at Gaeta), with no argument made about their civic status or political participation.

The speaker explicitly and enthusiastically supports giving women the vote at 21, systematically rebuts arguments against it (dismissing concerns about Mohammedan subjects, the "hard work" argument, the motherhood argument), celebrates the Bill as "a great act of justice," and honours the suffrage movement's legacy. Every argument made is in favour of women's political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly states he will vote against the Bill and go into the lobby against it, arguing there is no real demand for women's enfranchisement, that women's interests are already safeguarded under the current franchise, and that extending the franchise to those unaware of imperial affairs is dangerous. While he concedes women are "not unfit to vote," this is a rhetorical concession rather than substantive endorsement, and his overall argument and declared voting intention are firmly against extending women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the economic challenges facing the newspaper industry, overmanning, government subsidies, and press independence. While it briefly mentions "men and women" losing their livelihoods, this is incidental and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is primarily about electoral college amendments for the City of London corporation, focusing on voting structures for residents, businesses, and employees. While it briefly acknowledges the underrepresentation of women and ethnic minorities on the City corporation, it explicitly notes that the amendments under consideration do not address that issue and moves on, making no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is focused on the structure of the City of London electoral college and stakeholder voting arrangements. The brief mention of women ("Will that also apply to women?") is a passing rhetorical question about proportional representation in a business voting context, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on defending the temporal power of the Pope, the governance of the Papal States and Kingdom of Naples, Italian unification, and the foreign policy of the English Government toward Italy. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation at any point in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on the technical and procedural merits of using national insurance numbers as identifiers for electoral registration in Northern Ireland to combat fraud. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, representation, voting eligibility by gender, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

The speech is primarily about supporting a family planning bill (providing contraceptive advice through local authorities). While it briefly mentions the small number of women MPs and that bills designed to help women are often shelved, these observations are incidental comments rather than substantive arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Henderson) explicitly expresses disappointment that women are not included in the Reform Bill, argues that excluding women is inconsistent with representative government ("I cannot understand the Liberalism that believes in government of the people for the people by the people, and which omits such a provision"), defends the popular demand for women's suffrage, and states he will refuse to support the Bill if women remain excluded.

The TARGET speech concerns the legalization of marriage with a deceased wife's sister (a marriage law reform debate), not women's political rights or representation. The speaker briefly mentions a petition signed by many women and references women's opinions on the bill, but makes no argument about women's civic participation, voting rights, or political representation.

The speech concerns the use of national insurance numbers as identifiers for electoral registration in Northern Ireland to combat fraud, not women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "childless French woman") as an example of an edge case in the fraud argument, with no argument made about women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker explicitly states he will vote against the Bill on its Second Reading, arguing that diluting the electorate weakens democratic institutions, that the Bill lacks a genuine mandate, and that it is a "snare" for Conservatives. He frames women's enfranchisement as an undesirable "dilution" that will weaken Parliament's authority, with no substantive argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states it "would be an act of folly on the part of this House to entertain for one moment the proposition to add so many female voters to the register" and "deny absolutely that there has been anything in the nature of a popular demand for female suffrage," directly opposing women's suffrage.

The speaker enthusiastically supports the Bill's Second Reading, arguing that enfranchisement of women is a matter of common humanity rather than sex or property, and that removing artificial barriers to women's political participation is "a tremendous social advance." The speaker's only criticism is of specific plural voting provisions within the Bill, not of women's enfranchisement itself.

The speaker (Mr. Harmsworth) explicitly opposes the Bill enfranchising women under 30, arguing it is unnecessary, founded on a non-existent pledge, weakens democratic institutions by diluting the electorate with "the least responsible members," and states he will vote against it on Second Reading. His objections go beyond procedural concerns to substantive opposition to extending women's suffrage at this time.

The speaker explicitly argues that women's representation in the new Afghanistan will be "crucial" and advocates for girls' education as a pathway to "the participation of women in society more broadly," directly supporting women's civic participation and political representation.

The TARGET speech is David Steel's Third Reading motion for the Abortion Bill (1967), which concerns the legalisation and regulation of abortion. The speech does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation; it focuses entirely on abortion law reform and its medical and social justifications.

The speech is entirely focused on poverty, welfare benefits, social services, and criticism of the Labour Government's failure to act on low-income families — there is no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic participation.

The speech concerns the withdrawal of a government grant to Studley Agricultural College and raises questions about potential discrimination against single-sex colleges, but this is a funding/education policy debate rather than an argument about women's political rights or civic participation. The mention of "single-sex colleges" and women students pertains to educational access, not women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in political life.

The target speech concerns opposition to legalizing marriage with a deceased wife's sister, based on the speaker's assessment of Irish women's feelings about such marriages. It does not address women's political rights, the right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of civic/political representation for women.

The target speech is entirely about the administration, funding, and results of the Irish national education system, including school numbers, pupil attendance, teacher salaries, and denominational composition. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or related civic participation.

The speaker (Sir H. Lucas-Tooth) explicitly supports the Bill extending the franchise to women at 21, arguing against those who oppose it on grounds of a female majority and dismissing concerns about young women's competence. He frames equal conditions of voting as the correct definition of equality and endorses the Measure throughout.

The speaker explicitly states he has been "a vigorous supporter of a modified form of women's suffrage" for many years and declares he is "in favour of widows and spinsters who pay taxes having votes," expressing a positive stance on women's political rights, albeit a limited one. He then moves on to other aspects of the Reform Bill without arguing against women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Franchise Bill because it excludes women, argues at length that women's suffrage is the paramount political question of the day, and contends that adding women to the electorate would be "an immense advantage to the State" intellectually and morally. He calls the omission of women a "gross injustice" and frames enfranchising women as fundamental to any honest franchise measure.

The speaker explicitly argues that women's enfranchisement is a "burning injustice" to omit from a Reform Bill, and that adding women to the electorate will add to the "glory and future progress" of the Empire, clearly endorsing women's political rights.

The speech concerns extending the borough franchise to working-class men (£6 householders), arguing for their fitness and right to political representation. Women are never mentioned as a class, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made anywhere in the target text.

The speaker introduces a Bill explicitly designed to allow political parties to adopt positive measures to increase women's representation in Parliament, local government, and devolved bodies, arguing that under-representation is a serious problem requiring direct intervention and celebrating the policy gains achieved through greater numbers of women MPs.

The speaker (Dame Joan Vickers) explicitly argues that "sex is still a barrier to individual freedom," that "the right to vote, regrettably, has not given women real freedom," and calls for "further freedom for women," while referencing the Status of Women Commission and equal pay/opportunity efforts. She actively champions the advancement of women's political and civic rights.

The speech is entirely about democratic accountability and the election of Regional Economic Planning Council members, with no argument made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation as a gendered issue. The mention of "men and women" is purely incidental and rhetorical, not substantive.

The speaker opposes the Bill on procedural/mandate grounds and argues the age of 21 is too low for both sexes, but explicitly states he is not opposed to women having the suffrage, affirms he voted for it in 1918, and says he would heartily support a bill giving equal franchise to men and women at age 25—thus substantively supporting women's suffrage in one form while opposing it in its current form.

The speaker explicitly highlights the under-representation of women as local councillors across England, Wales, and Scotland, frames it as "a major issue," and endorses the Bill as enabling political parties to introduce positive measures to get more women elected. The speech is clearly supportive of expanding women's political representation.

The speaker (Mr. Byers) explicitly and consistently supports positive measures to increase women's representation in Parliament, the Scottish Parliament, the Welsh Assembly, and local government, arguing that such measures are "the only practical means" to achieve genuine improvement and that political parties should use the freedom granted by the Bill to dramatically increase women's representation.

The speaker (F. E. Smith) explicitly states his opposition to women's suffrage ("My views on that subject are well known") and argues against including women in the franchise bill, questioning whether women aged 21-25 (citing window-breakers) should vote, and treating the prospect of 10-11 million women voters as a grave problem. While he reports the Prime Minister's pledge to suffragettes, he does so critically, framing it as a problematic commitment rather than endorsing it.

The speech is entirely focused on procedural and medical safeguards for abortion legislation — specifically who should be permitted to perform or advise on terminations and how to prevent a "racket" — with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker (Sir H. Lucas-Tooth) explicitly supports the Equal Franchise Bill, arguing that objections to young women voting stem from prejudice, that women have proven themselves capable political participants, and that giving them the vote is an act of justice. He dismisses arguments against female suffrage and the "flapper vote" as baseless.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Bill partly because "it gives a chance for women's suffrage," endorses the Prime Minister's promise to incorporate a women's suffrage amendment, and urges the Government to press the Bill through so that the "best hope and promise women's suffrage ever had" is not lost.

The speech is entirely focused on the legality and effectiveness of the American naval blockade of Confederate ports during the Civil War, international maritime law, and British foreign policy. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about.

The speaker (Mr. Byers) explicitly supports the Bill's aim of removing barriers to women's political representation, endorsing positive measures to increase women's presence in Parliament, local government, and devolved assemblies, and argues that parties must account to the electorate for continuing under-representation of women.

The speech is entirely focused on national education policy — the Revised Code, school inspection, funding mechanisms, and the parochial system — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a passing reference to girls in schools and schoolmistresses in the context of educational results, without any argument touching on their civic or political status.

The TARGET speech concerns objections to funding Roman Catholic religious instruction for Irish female convicts and a motion to reduce a budget vote — a religious and budgetary dispute with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about decimal currency reform (the Decimal Currency Bill), covering terminology for the new penny, the choice of monetary unit, and parliamentary procedure. Women are mentioned only briefly as shoppers who prefer the pound as an anchor, which is a consumer behaviour observation with no bearing on women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech by Mr. Hennessy is entirely focused on the political and economic state of Italy, specifically critiquing the British Government's policy toward Piedmont/Sardinia, trade statistics, brigandage, and diplomatic affairs. It contains no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker enthusiastically supports the Second Reading of the Bill enfranchising women on equal terms with men, arguing that women are "human beings with precisely the same status as men" entitled to "precisely the same right and precisely the same authority," and dismisses all opposing arguments as outdated echoes of a passing epoch.

The speaker explicitly states "I am as strongly in favour of the enfranchisement of women as he is" and describes himself as "a sincere and consistent friend, for a long time, of the cause of the enfranchisement of women," while defending the Government's approach of allowing a free Amendment on women's suffrage as a reasonable path forward.

The speaker (Mr. Byers) defends the legal basis for positive action measures (including all-women shortlists) and uses statistics on women's under-representation in Parliament to argue that such measures are necessary, explicitly supporting greater women's political representation.

The speaker (Lord Robert Cecil) explicitly declares that "the gross injustice of passing any additional franchise Bill without enfranchising the women of this country" is "an absolutely intolerable proposal," states he has "always said the case for the enfranchisement of women was extremely strong," and affirms he will support the amendment for women's enfranchisement "with my whole heart."

The speaker (Mr. Byers) explicitly commends a Bill designed to allow political parties to take positive action to address women's under-representation, arguing that the status quo is unacceptable and that women's under-representation must be addressed as a priority.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the betterment levy provisions of the Land Commission Bill as unintelligible, unworkable, and oppressive to property owners. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely focused on opposing the Iron and Steel Bill, arguing against nationalisation on grounds of economic damage, compensation levels, diversification powers, and European Common Market compatibility. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The speaker consistently and enthusiastically supports the Bill to extend equal franchise to women, arguing that the existing age restrictions are "indefensible" and "arbitrary," that women are as politically engaged as men, and that enfranchising women will strengthen democratic government. He dismisses all arguments against the Bill as equivalent to discredited objections raised against earlier Reform Bills.

The speaker (Theresa May) explicitly supports the Bill's aim of getting more women into Parliament and endorses the principle that political parties should have freedom to take positive action toward greater female representation, while clarifying her personal opposition to women-only shortlists as a specific mechanism — a procedural/methodological caveat that does not constitute substantive opposition to women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly declares support for "equal franchise for men and women for over 30 years," argues there is no valid reason to deny women aged 21–30 the vote, refutes arguments about women's incompetence or lack of patriotism, and "heartily endorses" the Bill to extend equal franchise to women.

The speech is entirely concerned with defending British and Italian government policy regarding Italian unification, the condition of formerly papal and Bourbon-ruled provinces, and the conduct of the Piedmontese government — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation at any point.
