The target speech concerns Irish agricultural distress, emigration, landlord-tenant relations, and the failure of the 1860 land act. Women are mentioned only incidentally in passing (a reference to "young women" as emigrants), with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech is about lowering the voting age to 18 for young people generally, not about women's political rights specifically. While it briefly references the suffrage movement as a historical comparison ("votes for women"), it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker from Westhoughton points out that Switzerland, cited as a model for lowering the voting age to 20, does not even grant women the vote — implicitly criticizing this as a deficiency and arguing against using Switzerland as a positive precedent, which supports women's right to vote.

The speaker explicitly identifies himself as "an opponent of Women's Suffrage" and uses that position to argue that male MPs have a special obligation to protect women — framing his anti-suffrage stance as a reason to support the White Slave Traffic Bill, not as a reconsideration of his opposition to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is entirely concerned with the question of Sunday closing of public houses and the regulation of alcohol sales — a temperance/police regulation debate. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of civic participation that falls within the defined scope.

The speaker (Mr. Tyler) explicitly supports the Bill to increase women's representation in Parliament and local government, argues for changing the culture of Parliament to be more welcoming to women, endorses protective legislation to "kick-start" women's political participation, and advocates for electoral reform as a means to achieve gender balance in representative bodies.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage for unmarried female ratepayers and taxpayers ("I am strongly in favour of the power of voting being given to women who are payers of rates and taxes, who are not married women"), but opposes extending the franchise to 10,500,000 women broadly, particularly where it would result in two votes for one qualification (i.e., married women). This constitutes substantive argument on both sides — for a subset of women's suffrage and against another subset.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on the adequacy of parliamentary time allocated to debate the Home Rule Bill, with only a brief passing reference to Women's Suffrage used as a rhetorical analogy to illustrate the Government's flawed logic about limiting debate — no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech (by Mr. Gregory) is entirely focused on Ottoman/Turkish foreign policy, the condition of Christian subjects of the Porte, the situation in Serbia, and British diplomatic strategy in the East. It contains no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Amendment to reject the Bill extending equal franchise to women, arguing that giving women permanent political supremacy (more women voters than men) is a fundamental constitutional change not sanctioned by the electorate. While he disclaims opposition to women's votes per se, his substantive argument is against this extension of women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Tyler, North Cornwall) explicitly endorses the Bill aimed at increasing women's representation, stating "we entirely endorse the Government's view that the legislation is necessary" and that "getting more women to stand and getting more women elected...is urgently necessary." He also highlights the slow progress of women's appointments to public bodies and advocates for cultural change in Parliament to better include women.

The speech is primarily about procedural safeguards for petition signatures in a temperance/licensing bill (the Scottish Temperance Bill). The mention of suffragettes is only a brief illustrative analogy to make a point about fanatics who might forge signatures — it does not argue for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Major Kindersley) opposes the Bill on the grounds that granting equal voting rights to women at 21 would give women "permanent political supremacy" over men, invokes religious authority ("Man, not woman, was made in the image and likeness of God"), and argues that ultimate political responsibility must rest with men "by the decrees of nature." While he claims not to oppose votes for women in principle, his substantive arguments are against equal enfranchisement as proposed.

The speech focuses entirely on the voting age debate (whether to lower it to 18, 20, or keep it at 21) and procedural matters of Mr. Speaker's Conference, without making any arguments about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of different rules for men and women in military service is used only to critique the "old enough to fight, old enough to vote" argument on grounds of logical consistency in franchise qualifications, not to argue for or against women's political rights as such.

The speaker argues that women should have meaningful political representation in post-Taliban Afghanistan, drawing on examples of successful women's inclusion in South Africa and Northern Ireland, and criticises the dismissive reaction to her question about women's political participation as evidence of how successfully women have been suppressed and marginalised.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Bill on the grounds that giving women equal voting rights would create a female majority in the electorate and thus grant women political predominance over men, arguing that "the ultimate responsibility in matters of this kind must rest with man" by "the decrees of nature" and that surrendering this responsibility would be false to manhood. He warns of potential "sex war" and frames his opposition as a matter of deep conviction.

The speech is entirely focused on the Lancashire cotton distress, public works employment, emigration of factory operatives, and relief funding — none of which engage women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "unmarried women" concerns their economic destitution and potential emigration, not their civic or political status.

The TARGET speech focuses on debating the principles of a Criminal Law Amendment Bill — specifically whether flogging is an appropriate punishment for brothel-keeping and whether police should have expanded arrest powers. The brief mention of suffragettes and equality of the sexes is made only as a rhetorical aside to question whether women should also be flogged, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker notes that the Under-Secretary's statement was a personal opinion in favour of women's suffrage, and explicitly states that this opinion was "shared by suffragists in every part of the House," aligning themselves with the pro-suffrage position.

The target speech concerns parliamentary business scheduling and procedural matters (the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill's order of business), with no substantive argument made for or against women's political rights. The mere mention of the Equal Franchise Bill in the procedural order does not constitute an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker (the Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs) clarifies that he was speaking personally "on behalf of the supporters of women's enfranchisement" and as "a supporter of women's suffrage in the House," explicitly identifying himself as a proponent of women's suffrage/enfranchisement.

The speaker (Joan Ruddock) strongly advocates for legislation enabling all-women shortlists and other special measures to increase women's representation in Parliament, devolved assemblies, and local government, arguing that the current 82% male Parliament represents a "democratic deficit" that must be remedied.

The speaker explicitly raises the pay disparity between male and female service members (1s. 6d. vs 1s. 3d. for the same Arctic/tropical experiments) on the 50th anniversary of votes for women, calling it a "gross anomaly" that should be "ironed out," thereby advocating for equal treatment of women in the armed services.

The speaker explicitly supports the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill on behalf of the Labour party, endorses equal citizenship for women at 21 years of age, and celebrates the extension of the franchise to women as fulfilling a long-held commitment he first expressed in 1903. His criticisms are procedural (timing, election expenses, redistribution) rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speech concerns a Scottish temperance bill, specifically debating procedural safeguards around the withdrawal of signatures from requisitions for no-licence polls. Women's political rights are not argued for or against; the only mention of women is a passing reference to "suffragettes who starved themselves" used as a rhetorical comparison, with no substantive argument about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the economic and political condition of Ireland — agricultural decline, emigration, taxation, small holdings, local governance, and the lack of sympathy in the Royal Speech — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports increased women's representation in Parliament, defends women-only shortlists as a necessary mechanism given systemic barriers to women's selection, and argues that without such measures equality would take another century to achieve. She recounts her own experience chairing a constituency that volunteered for a women-only shortlist and frames the Bill as a legitimate means to address persistent inequality in political representation.

The speaker (the Prime Minister, Baldwin) explicitly champions the Equal Franchise Bill, arguing that giving women the vote on equal terms with men is logically justified, fulfils a long-standing pledge, and is morally vindicated by women's contributions during the War. He acknowledges his own past opposition but states he was "taught by the War" to support full enfranchisement of women.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill aimed at increasing women's representation in Parliament, acknowledges the "woefully poor representation of women in Parliament" as a problem requiring action, and advocates for positive action measures including increasing the proportion of women on Conservative candidate lists to ~50% for winnable seats. While he opposes women-only shortlists as one specific mechanism, his overall position is firmly in favour of improving women's political representation.

The speech is a maiden speech focused entirely on criticising the Finance Bill, tax reform, economic policy, unemployment, and the tax system. The only mention of women is a brief passing reference to "the 50th anniversary year of women's suffrage" used rhetorically to suggest it should be unnecessary to debate the aggregation of spousal income — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the introduction of secret ballot voting, arguing it is wrong in principle and ineffective in practice. Women are mentioned only incidentally as part of a theoretical argument about the nature of the franchise as a "trust" (noting that women and minors are affected by laws but do not vote), with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns the appropriate voting age (18 vs 20 vs 21) in a debate about lowering the franchise age, not about women's political rights. While women's enfranchisement is briefly mentioned as a historical analogy by opponents, the speaker does not argue a position on women's political rights themselves.

The speaker explicitly invokes the historical arguments used against women's suffrage to discredit analogous arguments against votes at 18, affirming that those anti-suffragette arguments were wrong and that the same logic of denying votes based on claimed immaturity or lack of demand was unjust when applied to women. This implicitly but clearly endorses women's political rights as settled and correct.

The TARGET speech by Mr. Buxton is entirely focused on the question of extending the borough franchise to the working classes and the dilemma facing moderate Liberals; women's political rights are never argued for or against. Asquith opposes the Amendment, and in doing so explicitly identifies himself as "a consistent opponent of Woman Suffrage," arguing against enfranchising women for parliamentary purposes. This makes his stance clearly against women's political rights.

The speech concerns the disbanding of the Auxiliary Fire Service (A.F.S.) and civil defence policy, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation.

Balfour explicitly states he has been "a consistent and steady supporter of some moderate measure of enfranchisement" throughout his parliamentary career and confirms he will vote for the Amendment. He further argues that even opponents of women's suffrage for the Imperial Parliament have no logical reason to oppose this Amendment, actively making the case for women's political participation in the Irish Parliament.

The speaker explicitly criticizes a colleague for failing to mention the importance of "balancing the sexes in the new House of Lords" and argues that the appointments system for quangos has the potential to "redress the imbalance that exists in the House of Commons and almost every other elected body," praising this as "a vital service to our country and its political culture." These are clear, substantive arguments in favour of women's political representation.

The speech is a routine parliamentary business statement announcing the legislative schedule for the week, including the Representation of the People (Equal Franchise) Bill among other items. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights; it merely lists the bill as an agenda item.

The speaker argues that the Bill as it stands already confers female suffrage (via the 13 & 14 Vict.), and he explicitly states he voted for Mr. Stuart Mill's Amendment on women's suffrage, indicating support for women's political rights.

The speaker (Prime Minister Asquith) explicitly identifies himself as a "consistent opponent of Woman Suffrage" and argues against the Amendment that would extend women's franchise to the proposed Irish Parliament, contending it would be constitutionally unprecedented and that the Irish legislature should be left to decide the matter itself.

The speaker explicitly supports greater representation of women in public appointments, commits to the Government's goal of "equal representation for women and men," praises the Member for Slough's points on women as "crucial," and announces concrete steps including regional seminars led by the Minister for Women to encourage women's participation in public life.

The TARGET speech (Disraeli's long address opposing the Government's Reform Bill) is entirely concerned with Parliamentary Reform as it relates to the male franchise, redistribution of seats, county and borough constituencies, and the constitutional balance of representation — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation at any point. The one brief mention of women occurs when Disraeli quotes J.S. Mill's conditions for universal suffrage, noting "the suffrage should not be confined to the male sex" and adding "I have always been of opinion that if there is to be universal suffrage, women have as much right to vote as men," but this is offered purely as a passing illustration of Mill's philosophical conditions, not as a substantive argument for or against women's suffrage in its own right.

The speech is entirely focused on pension transferability and labour mobility. The brief mention of women workers facing discrimination in transferability rights is a passing reference to constituent representations, not a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation as defined in scope.

The speech is entirely focused on Navy Estimates, manpower, recruitment, training, redundancies, and dockyard operations. While the Women's Royal Naval Service and Queen Alexandra Royal Nursing Service are mentioned briefly in passing as part of the Navy's personnel, no argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The speech is about encouraging voter registration and participation in democracy generally, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of women's suffrage history (chaining to railings, throwing themselves in front of horses) is used as rhetorical colour to motivate people to vote, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mrs. Renée Short) presses the Prime Minister to move beyond symbolic gestures on women's franchise and take concrete action, specifically demanding equal pay for women civil servants — framing this as a matter of women's civic and economic equality. This clearly supports expanding women's substantive rights as workers and citizens.

The speech is entirely focused on concessionary travel fare schemes for elderly and disabled people, including funding, cross-boundary travel, and scope for young people. While the Bill's background involves equalising entitlement ages between men and women, the speaker makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly connects the passage of the Women's Suffrage Measure to the growing political attention given to issues vital to women, framing women's enfranchisement as a positive force that brings important women's concerns to the fore. This brief but clear endorsement of women's suffrage situates the speech as supportive of women's political rights.

The speaker supports women's suffrage in general (explicitly stating a vote against the Amendment would wrongly deny the vote to women who want it, and expressing no objection to extending the vote to Irish women in principle), but opposes this specific Amendment on the substantive ground that Irish women themselves do not effectively demand the franchise, making it unnecessary to extend it to that particular portion of the country — a substantive argument against women's political rights in Ireland specifically.

The speaker explicitly declines to express an opinion on female suffrage, stating only that the words "male person" are superfluous on drafting grounds. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly calls for the implementation of equal pay for women, referencing the Prime Minister's own stated commitments and framing the current wage disparity as a "disgrace," demonstrating clear support for women's economic and political rights.

The speaker explicitly states he hopes the clause on voting papers "would never be passed until the proposition of the hon. Member for Westminster for the enfranchisement of women had become the law of the land," expressing clear support for women's enfranchisement as a precondition.

The speaker explicitly states that his entire party "believe in Woman Suffrage and will support it...with its votes," and he challenges Mr. Hugh Law's inconsistency in opposing the Amendment now while planning to vote for women's franchise in a few months' time, implicitly supporting the Amendment and women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about the British Broadcasting Corporation's failings and the importance of broadcasting political content to an informed electorate. The brief mention of extending the franchise to women is used only as a rhetorical point about the challenges of democracy, without arguing for or against women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about tea duty, taxation burdens on the poor, and trade policy. The brief mention of women being enfranchised ("the millions who are to be enfranchised presently") is used instrumentally as a political argument for reducing the tea duty, not as an argument about women's political rights themselves.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on debating the merits and risks of voting papers/proxy voting as an electoral mechanism, with no substantive argument about women's political rights. The brief mention of women in MR. PACKE's appended remarks (arguing that women admitted to the franchise shouldn't have to face a violent mob) is a passing reference used to support the voting papers clause, not a substantive argument for or against women's suffrage.

The TARGET speech by Denzil Davies focuses on Middle East peace, religion, democracy, and counter-terrorism responses to 9/11. While it briefly mentions "young women" as beneficiaries of democratic representation in the Middle East, this is a passing reference without any substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Home Secretary Joynson-Hicks) explicitly argues that the Bill's purpose is to equalise the franchise between men and women, and that women must be given a vote for business premises to complete equality with men ("If you are going to complete the system of making a woman's vote equal to a man's vote, you must give the woman a vote for business premises"). He defends the Bill's provisions extending women's voting rights on equal terms with men.

The speech is about the voting age debate (18 vs. 20) and criticizes Sir David Renton's conservative approach to the electorate. The brief mention of "women" is only a passing rhetorical jab suggesting Renton is generally suspicious of all voters, not an argument about women's political rights per se.

The speaker (Mr. Kennedy) explicitly welcomes the Government's commitment to legislation promoting women in all political parties, and argues this should be linked to voting system reform, citing the Scottish Parliament as evidence that fairer voting systems lead to more women being elected — a substantive argument in favour of women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly declares himself "a convinced Suffragist" who intends to vote for women's franchise on the Franchise Bill, yet votes against this specific Amendment extending women's suffrage to Ireland, arguing there is no effective demand among Irish women for the vote at this time. This constitutes substantive support for women's suffrage in general while substantively opposing its immediate application to one subset (Irish women), making it a genuine two-sided position.

The speaker explicitly welcomes "a continuing commitment to constitutional reform," singling out "improving women's representation in political and public life" as something she is pleased to see in the Queen's Speech, expressing clear support for that goal.

The speaker explicitly draws a parallel between reducing the voting age and past extensions of the franchise to women (noting women's voting age was not reduced to 21 until 1929), framing both as extensions of political rights to a section of the population previously denied them — a clear endorsement of franchise expansion as a positive precedent and implicitly supportive of women's suffrage history as a model.

The speaker (David Lammy, MP for Tottenham) explicitly welcomes "the legislation to allow increases in the representation of women in public life," stating it will speed up modernisation of Parliament, and expresses hope for a future where women and Black people no longer stand out on the benches.

The speech by Mr. M'Cullagh Torrens concerns the lodger franchise amendment to a Reform Bill, specifically debating the appropriate rent threshold (£10 vs £15) and residency requirements for lodgers to qualify as voters. While it briefly mentions "Christian men or women" in passing, it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states he will vote against the Amendment granting women's suffrage in Ireland, argues that granting women the vote must inevitably lead to women sitting in Parliament and participating fully in political life, and declares he is "not prepared to assist or aid" that outcome, believing it is not in the country's best interests.

The TARGET speech is about lowering the voting age (from 21 to 18 or 20) and touches on Scottish Nationalism; while it briefly mentions "the struggle for women's emancipation" as a historical parallel, it does not argue for or against women's political rights — the reference is purely illustrative of the broader history of franchise expansion.

The speaker explicitly states "I am in favour of Woman Suffrage" and argues that the House should vote for the Amendment to extend women's franchise to Ireland under the Home Rule Bill, contending that women already perform every substantive act of political participation except casting a ballot, and that Parliament has a responsibility to include women's suffrage in any Constitution it grants.

The speaker argues that occupants of hovels and substandard dwellings should be excluded from the franchise, proposing a minimum dwelling size (two rooms) as a qualification test, explicitly seeking to prevent "hovel suffrage" and exclude "the residuum" from voting rights. While this is about household suffrage generally, it singles out a class of (largely working-class male) voters for exclusion, and does not address women's political rights at all.

The speaker explicitly criticizes the Local Government Bill for disadvantaging women — excluding women's unemployment from the weighting formula, replacing elected women with co-opted members in Poor Law administration, and burdening maternity services — arguing these provisions constitute "an attack upon women" that is inconsistent with the Prime Minister's recent enfranchisement of women. This is a clear argument in support of women's political rights and civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the appropriate voting age (21 vs. 18 vs. 20) for young people generally, not on women's political rights. The brief mention of women ("Over 50 per cent. of the young people will be women who would not be called upon to fight") is used only to rebut the "old enough to fight, old enough to vote" argument about youth voting age — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker supports more women being elected to Parliament and praises having a woman as Conservative leader and Prime Minister, but explicitly opposes the Government's proposed legislation to help parties increase women's representation, calling it unnecessary and mocking Labour's treatment of its own women MPs during the election campaign.

The Gracious Speech explicitly states "My Government will prepare legislation to allow political parties to make positive moves to increase the representation of women in public life," which is a direct commitment to advancing women's political representation. This is an affirmative policy position in favour of women's political rights.

Baldwin's statement presupposes and accepts the Equal Franchise Bill as a given, discussing redistribution only in the context of implementing it, which implicitly supports extending equal franchise (including to women). There is no opposition to women's political rights expressed.

The TARGET speech contains three speakers, all of whom support women's equal franchise. Mr. Dixey, while arguing against the Amendment, explicitly states "I believe that equal franchise should be given to men and women." Mr. W. M. Adamson states his party stands "for the equalisation of the franchise...giving of the vote upon the human basis to men and women equally." Viscountess Astor argues forcefully that "the question before us is equality" and that women should have the same franchise rights as men, criticizing man-made laws based on fear rather than justice.

The speaker explicitly supports women's suffrage ("from the beginning I have taken a very firm and persistent part in supporting women's suffrage") and argues that women should vote as citizens on equal terms with men, opposing the "fancy franchise" that ties voting rights to marital status rather than individual civic standing.

Mr. Denman signals that, absent stronger arguments against female suffrage, he will vote with the hon. Member for Westminster (Mill's pro-suffrage amendment), and raises a legal point suggesting the Bill already inadvertently confers the suffrage on women — framing this not as an objection but as a question the Government must answer. His overall posture is one of leaning toward support for women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly supports Woman Suffrage in principle ("Home Rulers as well as Woman Suffragists") and for the UK as a whole, but substantively opposes applying it to Ireland via this Amendment, arguing it is un-Irish, not demanded by Irish women, and would endanger Home Rule — making genuine substantive arguments on both sides.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the introduction of flogging/corporal punishment as a criminal penalty, arguing it is barbarous, ineffective as a deterrent, and brutalising. The only mention touching on women is a passing heckle ("Suffragettes") from another member, which the speaker does not engage with. No substantive argument about women's political rights or civic participation is made.

The question identifies that the Government of Ireland Bill would allow an Irish Parliament to extend the franchise to women and that this could result in UK Parliament members elected on a women's franchise — and asks whether the Government will introduce amendments to prevent this. The framing seeks to expose and potentially block a pro-women's suffrage outcome, suggesting the questioner is opposed to women's political rights entering Parliament by this route.

The TARGET speech is J.S. Mill's famous 1867 parliamentary address proposing to replace "man" with "person" in the Reform Bill, arguing at length on grounds of justice, constitutional principle, and practical expediency that women should be enfranchised. Every argument in the speech supports women's right to vote, and Mr. Karslake's following speech opposing the amendment confirms Mill's unambiguous advocacy for women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is entirely concerned with the debate over lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 (or 20), arguing against votes at 18 and in favour of the moderate reform recommended by Mr. Speaker's Conference. Women are not mentioned or singled out as a distinct class regarding political rights; the speech addresses the general franchise question without reference to women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Fawcett) explicitly and forcefully supports women's suffrage throughout, arguing that all arguments for extending the franchise to working men apply equally to women, that taxation and representation should go together for women as well as men, and that he would "undoubtedly confer the suffrage also upon married women." He rebuts opponents' arguments and expresses confidence the cause will eventually succeed.

The speech is entirely focused on whether the voting age should be lowered from 21 to 18, not on women's political rights. The brief passing mention of women's struggle for the vote is made by other speakers in context, and the target speaker only alludes to it without making any argument about women's political rights specifically.

The speaker explicitly highlights the success of positive mechanisms (all-women shortlists) used by a political party to achieve strong women's representation in the Welsh Assembly and Scottish Parliament, citing it as a model achievement with more women than men in the Welsh Assembly Cabinet — clearly supporting women's political representation.

The speech is primarily about extending the franchise to 18-year-olds rather than women's political rights. The only mention of women is a brief passing reference ("Somebody suddenly discovered that women were affected by a whole block of legislation") used as a historical analogy to argue for youth enfranchisement, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (seconding the Plural Voting Bill) explicitly states that "this Session ought to be used for a large extension of the franchise, not only to men, but to women also," directly endorsing women's political rights. He then proceeds to support the Bill on democratic equality grounds.

The speaker explicitly supports increasing women's political representation in Parliament, welcomes the Queen's Speech commitment to allow positive action, cites international examples (Sweden, Norway, Germany, France) to argue for stronger measures like all-women shortlists, and argues the Government's proposal is too modest — all clear advocacy for women's political rights and representation.

The speaker explicitly opposes women's suffrage and eligibility for Parliament, arguing that "the instinct of nine women out of ten" opposes it, that Nature has drawn clear distinctions between the sexes making women unfit for "the rough work" of political life, and concluding with the maxim that men should retain what is proper to men and women retain only what can "becomingly be conceded" to them — all substantive arguments against women's political rights.

At the end of his speech, Sir Thomas Inskip explicitly describes Clause 18 (conferring on fathers the guardianship rights already given to mothers) as "a modest addition to the legislation necessary for removing sex disqualification," framing it positively as part of the broader project of eliminating sex-based legal disabilities, which is in scope as women's civic equality.

Sir George Bowyer explicitly argues that no logical reason exists to exclude women from the franchise, invoking the principles of taxation and representation, pointing to female monarchs and women's existing parochial offices as evidence of their capacity, and endorsing Mill's proposal (with the caveat of voting papers for decorum) as constitutionally sound.

The speaker explicitly urges legislation to enable positive action in candidate selection to increase women's representation in Parliament, argues that the Labour party's progress through all-women shortlists has stalled, cites international examples to support gender parity measures, and contends that women MPs bring distinct perspectives that improve representation.

The speaker (Sir G. Cockerill) explicitly opposes the Equal Franchise Bill on the grounds that giving women the vote on the same terms as men will create a permanent female majority at the polls, which he argues inflicts injustice on men as a sex; he states "if either sex is to be supreme at the polls, I would prefer to see, quite frankly, men put in the supremacy," directly opposing equal women's political rights as proposed.

The speech is primarily about lowering the voting age to 18, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of women getting the vote is used only as an analogy to support the argument for youth enfranchisement, without making any substantive argument about women's political rights themselves.

The speech concerns the composition of Advisory Committees under the National Insurance Act, focusing on representation of various industries (iron and steel, tinplate, dockers, seamen) and mentioning women's organisations only incidentally as part of a broader complaint about representational imbalances. No argument is made for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the utilisation of trained pharmacists in the British Army, drawing on the speaker's wartime experience with chemical warfare units. It makes no arguments about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status; women are mentioned only incidentally as members of the pharmacist profession.

The speaker (J.S. Mill, based on context) explicitly argues in favour of extending the franchise to women with property qualifications, and states that if universal suffrage is ever adopted it should extend to all women as well. He defends his motion against opponents who mischaracterized it, and asserts that if experience shows married women or others should have the suffrage, they should receive it.

The speech is primarily a lengthy argument against the Mental Deficiency Bill on grounds of individual liberty, compulsory detention, eugenic ideology, and the powers granted to medical specialists. While the speaker briefly notes that the Bill disproportionately affects women and that Parliament should be cautious about restricting women's liberties without knowing women's views, this is a passing observation in service of the anti-compulsion argument rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker explicitly states that "the Conservative party must have the unshakeable objective of increasing the representation by women in this House" and that this objective must be achieved before the next election, directly endorsing greater women's representation in Parliament.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Bill on the grounds that giving women equal franchise will create a permanent women's majority in constituencies, "swamping" men's votes and delivering "sex preference" rather than sex equality. While he says he "welcomes equality for women," he frames this as opposition to the specific extension, urges women to "rest content to share" power rather than claim supremacy, and asks Parliament not to "abdicate the sceptre of political power" to women — substantively opposing the measure expanding women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about prison reform — overcrowding, long-term prisoners, detention centres, borstal, staffing, security, and the conditions of women prisoners as a subset of the prison population. While women prisoners are discussed, the focus is on penal policy and rehabilitation, not on women's political rights, civic participation, voting, or representation.

The target speech is about Scottish temperance/licensing legislation, specifically debating whether parish workers (including women) should have their votes counted in licence reduction resolutions. While women are briefly mentioned as parish workers whose votes should not be excluded, the speaker makes no argument about women's political rights or civic status — the point is purely about the credibility of witnesses/voters on temperance matters, not about women's right to vote or hold office.

The speaker argues that women cannot physically perform the heavy duties that come with civic equality (stokehold, mines, blast furnaces) and warns that demanding the vote on equal terms with men would impose burdens "too great" for women, framing equal political rights as dangerous and inappropriate for women.

The speaker explicitly states support for the Second Reading of the Bill and declares that women should have the vote "on equal terms with men." While the speaker raises procedural objections (the lack of a party conference before introduction) and criticizes specific provisions (plural votes for wives via husband's business premises), these are objections to the Bill's implementation rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (which spans contributions from Mill/"the hon. Member for Westminster," Henley, and Bright) is entirely concerned with Sunday observance law and whether lectures/amusements should be permitted on Sundays with paid admission. Women's political rights are not argued for or against; the only passing mention of women is Henley's offhand remark that "female suffrage" discussions might be held in lecture halls, which is not an argument about women's political rights but an illustration of the range of topics that could be discussed.

The speech focuses on county council administration, small holdings inspectors, agricultural grants, horse breeding funding, and local government representation. The brief mention of "female voters" is purely descriptive of the electoral basis of county councils, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on penal policy, prison reform, and criminology — the speaker congratulates Mrs. Renée Short on the Select Committee Report and debates its emphasis on rehabilitation versus crime prevention. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly criticizes the preferential encouragement given to male teachers over female teachers in elementary schools, calling it "a great mistake," which is an argument in favor of equal treatment of women in a professional/civic role.

The TARGET speech is primarily about electoral machinery — party labels on ballot papers, primary elections, candidate selection, and franchise extensions — with only a passing historical reference to women being admitted to the franchise in the 1920s, made without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speaker, identifying herself as Minister for Women, explicitly supports a forthcoming Bill to enable parties to take measures to address the under-representation of women in the House, and welcomes Conservative conversions to supporting women's representation, stating "Converts are always welcome."

The TARGET speech (by the President of the Poor Law Board) is entirely focused on the merits of the Government's Reform Bill versus the Opposition's amendment concerning the borough franchise, rating qualifications, and compound householders. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any way.
The speech concerns the impact of the National Insurance Act on charwomen's employment, with no argument made about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly welcomes "the Government's proposed legislation to allow political parties to achieve better gender balance as an important step" in reconnecting citizens with their representatives, directly endorsing a measure to improve women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I have very great pleasure in supporting the Second Reading of this Bill" and argues that women having a voice in choosing representatives would have benefited the country, expressing no fear that a preponderance of women's votes will affect justice. While he raises procedural objections (the plural vote anomaly and increased election costs), these are criticisms of the bill's specific provisions, not opposition to women's political rights themselves.

The speaker explicitly states "I come down in favour of the provision in Clause 1" — the reduction of the voting age to 18 — and provides three substantive reasons in support, including that it will increase young people's sense of political involvement and that 18-year-olds deserve a say in choosing lawmakers who will govern them.

The speaker explicitly states they "support the extension of political rights to women" and argues in favour of the Married Women's Property Bill, contending that denying married women property rights is unjust and analogous to the incapacity imposed on felons. While the speech focuses on property rights, the speaker frames this directly as a matter of women's political rights and civic personhood.

The speaker uses the historical debates over women's suffrage as a direct parallel to support lowering the voting age, noting that "exactly the same arguments have been used today" — i.e., claims of irrationality and immaturity — and implicitly endorses the House's earlier decision that "it was right that women should have the vote." This constitutes an affirmative reference to women's political rights in service of a pro-franchise argument.

The speech is a factual answer about emigration statistics under the Unemployed Workmen Act 1905, covering costs and numbers of emigrants. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Queen's Speech Bill to promote women's representation in politics and urges that it be introduced quickly, arguing it would benefit all political parties ahead of the 2003 Scottish Parliament and Welsh Assembly elections.

The speaker argues that the Conservative party broadly supports extending the franchise to women, citing conference majorities, and defends the Bill as logical and inevitable — noting that the current age limit and residence/occupation qualification disparity that excludes 2,000,000 women are "indefensible." He explicitly endorses the reform as something the party "has nothing to fear from."

The speech is primarily about national/compulsory military training and the inadequacy of the Territorial Force. The brief mention of women's franchise is only a passing comparison used to criticize the government's prioritization of party politics over national defense, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a maiden speech focused on constituency description, education funding disparities, and public services. The brief remark about being "only the 10th lady mayor" and hoping to demonstrate improvement in representation is a passing observation, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is entirely about Scottish temperance legislation (the Scottish Temperance Bill), covering arguments for local option, prohibition, mutual insurance, and the history of licensing in Scotland. Women's political rights are not argued for or against; the only passing mention of women in the target is a reference to "Churches, charitable societies, and labour conferences" and "earnest men and women" supporting temperance reform, which does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Captain Craig) opposes the Bill on the grounds that women (and men) should not receive the vote at age 21, arguing 21 is too young and that the franchise should be set at 25 for both sexes. While he states he is not opposed to women having the suffrage in principle, his substantive position is to vote against this Bill extending the franchise to women at 21, and he explicitly says he would only support it if the age were raised to 25.

The speaker explicitly opposes the Bill giving women the vote at 21, stating "I am sorry that the Bill has been introduced to give women of the same age the vote" and that it is "a great mistake to give the vote either to a man or a woman at 21." While they suggest willingness to vote for a bill setting the franchise age at 25, this is a conditional caveat about age, not substantive support for women's political rights broadly.

The speech concerns religious discrimination and incitement to religious hatred (specifically targeting Muslim women who wear head coverings), not women's political rights or representation. Although Muslim women are mentioned as victims of abuse, the argument is about religious hatred legislation, not women's civic status or participation in political life.

The speaker explicitly states he has changed his mind and now stands "as a supporter of this Measure" to extend the franchise to young women, and argues the matter has been seriously discussed and the public is well informed, countering the "no mandate" objection.

The speech concerns the Education (No. 2) Bill, focusing on governance of colleges of education and further education — the binary line, instruments of government, academic boards, student and staff representation, and grouping of special schools. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speech is entirely focused on town planning legislation — public participation in planning processes, civic societies, structural maps, national parks, and planning procedures in Los Angeles. The only mention remotely touching on women is a passing reference to the "League for Women Voters" as one of many local voluntary organisations consulted in Los Angeles, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker moves to bring in a Bill establishing an anti-discrimination board to remove discrimination against women in employment, education, and public life, and to provide equal pay — directly advocating for women's expanded civic and professional rights. She explicitly celebrates the 50th anniversary of women's suffrage and argues forcefully that continued discrimination must be remedied through legislation.

The TARGET speech is entirely focused on elementary education policy — the state of education in Lancashire and agricultural districts, local rating for schools, and voluntary educational societies. The brief mention of "silly women" contributing subscriptions is a passing rhetorical jab at a previous speaker's disparaging remark, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech concerns the administrative and operational management of converting HMP Downview from a male to a female prison, addressing sentence planning disruption, health care, staffing, and facilities. Women are referenced only as a prison population requiring accommodation, not in terms of their political rights or civic participation.

The target speech (by Mr. Mackinder) is entirely focused on opposing the Temperance (Scotland) Bill on grounds of local option, prohibition, small areas, compensation/insurance, and temperance policy. The brief passage mentioning women voters (spinster voters in teetotal societies making poor judges) is a passing rhetorical point about the composition of the electorate, not an argument about women's political rights or their fitness for civic participation as a class.

The speaker introduces a Bill to give married women legal control over their own property and earnings, explicitly linking it to Stuart Mill's suffrage arguments and arguing that removing unequal legislation will raise women's civic and social status. The speech substantively advocates for expanding women's legal rights as a class, which falls within the scope of women's political rights and representation.

The speech is entirely focused on debating the merits, statistics, and structural deficiencies of an education bill, covering topics such as educational destitution estimates, school attendance figures, rating systems, and school committee governance. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point in the target speech.

The speaker explicitly states he will "vote against the Second Reading of this measure," arguing that women's suffrage is undesirable, that male-elected Parliaments have adequately served women's interests, that colonial experience does not support female franchise, and that giving women the vote would actually harm their status rather than improve it.

MacCallum Scott argues that giving votes to women would undermine the value of a General Election as an index of physical force balance, since women are not equal physical force units to men — a substantive argument against women's suffrage. The context of his longer preceding speech confirms he advances the physical force argument against enfranchising women.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over military fortifications expenditure, parliamentary reform, and household suffrage as a mechanism for better fiscal oversight. The brief mention of "old women" is a colloquial idiom for panic-induced decision-making, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the franchise to young women, arguing there is "no real cause in equity for differentiating between the sexes" on voting, dismissing concerns about a female majority on the register, and praising young women's political engagement and competence. He states he has changed his mind and now supports the Measure giving equal franchise to women.

The speech is entirely focused on Income Tax and Surtax revenue figures and criticising the Labour Government's tax policy and electoral promises; it makes no argument about women's political rights or representation. The passing mention of "men and women" voting Labour is purely rhetorical and does not address women's civic status.

The speech concerns a bill to restrict military escorts at Irish elections, addressing electoral freedom and coercion of voters by landlords. Women are mentioned only incidentally (a crowd of "men and women" who stopped voters), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker introduces a Bill explicitly aimed at ending discrimination against women in private members' clubs, arguing that offering women inferior membership with no access to governance is "plainly wrong, offensive and outdated." He grounds his argument in women's equal civic standing, referencing their share of the electorate and their participation in public life, and directly advocates for women's equal access to institutional structures.

The speech is entirely focused on Irish Home Rule, Ulster unionism, and political violence in Ireland, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of women (Mrs. O'Mara and others who were shot) is in the context of political violence under Nationalist campaigns, not women's civic status or political participation.

The speaker explicitly and extensively advocates for women's political rights, including their right to vote, stand for office, participate in the Loya Jirga, draft the constitution, and serve on human rights and judicial commissions in post-Taliban Afghanistan. She organised campaigns to include women delegates at the Bonn talks and calls on the UK Government to actively support the full restoration of Afghan women's political and civic rights.
The speech concerns the Fenian conspiracy, the Habeas Corpus Suspension Act, and conditions at Mountjoy Prison, with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is primarily a rebuttal of a motion about calling a General Election, focused on arguments about popularity, legitimacy, and electoral cycles. The mention of women's suffrage (extending the franchise to women at 21 in 1928) is purely a historical anecdote illustrating how peculiar Private Members' Bills from the 1920s sometimes succeeded by accident — no argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill granting equal franchise, describing it as "an act of justice" and arguing that giving responsibility to a greater number of people (including women) will benefit the country's welfare. While acknowledging objections to the female vote exist, the speaker dismisses them as outside the scope of this Bill and firmly endorses its passage.

The speaker (Mrs. Castle) explicitly states she has "every sympathy in the world" with the cause of equal pay for women and acknowledges discrimination against women is morally wrong, while arguing against the specific Amendments on the grounds that they would be inflationary and unworkable under the prices and incomes policy — a procedural/implementation objection rather than substantive opposition to women's equal pay rights.

The speaker opposes women-only shortlists as inequitable and discriminatory, arguing that barring men from selection even when they have greater merit is "wholly undesirable" and brings positive action into disrepute, thus opposing this mechanism for women's political representation.

The speech concerns the enforcement of lottery laws against charitable bazaars and raffles, with no argument about women's voting rights, candidacy, representation, or any other aspect of women's political rights. The brief mention of "young ladies" selling raffle tickets in the following context is incidental and not part of the target speech.

The speech is primarily an explanation of the electoral reform bill's effects on voter registration numbers and franchise qualifications. While the speaker briefly notes the number of women over 21 and estimates how many would be added to the register if the vote were extended to women on the same terms as men, this is presented as a statistical observation without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Michael Portillo) explicitly welcomes the Government's proposal to make it easier for women to enter Parliament, states that the proportion of women in the House is "too low," and acknowledges that under-representation of women in the Conservative party is "truly chronic" and must be corrected. This is a clear, affirmative endorsement of women's political representation.

The speaker (Mr. Lansley) argues that all-women shortlists are "disproportionate and unacceptable" because they bar men from even being assessed for candidacy in specific constituencies, and his amendment is explicitly intended to prevent such arbitrary exclusions of male candidates from selection processes.

The speaker explicitly states "I fully support the Amendment" and "I shall gladly vote for the Amendment," where the Amendment concerns the implementation of equal pay for women. While the speaker criticises the Minister's handling of the issue, this is a procedural/competence objection, not opposition to equal pay itself.

The speaker (Mr. Hoban) explicitly supports the Bill's aim of improving women's representation in Parliament ("there is widespread support for the Bill's principles, and its attempt to improve women's representation in Parliament"), while raising proportionality concerns about all-women shortlists to ensure the legislation is legally sound. His objection is procedural/legal rather than substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker (Glenda Jackson) explicitly defends all-women shortlists, describes the Bill as necessary to redress "gross inequities" working against women in political participation, and states she will oppose the amendment, framing her support as championing women's equal representation in political life.

The target speech, part of Sir H. Lucas-Tooth's broader argument, pushes back against the claim that young women are too frivolous or apolitical to deserve the vote, arguing that women have no right to avoid civic responsibility and that the "frivolous young woman" stereotype is unfounded — a position clearly in support of extending women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on consumer protection legislation (the Trade Descriptions Bill), the Molony Committee Report, and Co-operative movement history. Women are mentioned only incidentally as "housewives" and consumers, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (Viscount Helmsley) focuses almost entirely on electoral reform issues such as plural voting, university voting, redistribution of seats, and the Labour party's position on the Bill. While it briefly notes that Henderson will vote against the Bill if women are excluded, this is a tactical/political observation rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Sir C. Oman, Member for Oxford University) explicitly opposes the Equal Franchise Bill, arguing it was never properly endorsed by the Conservative party, that logic should not drive constitutional reform, and that his constituents wrote against the Bill. He likens the Bill to "stealing Whigs' clothes" and warns colleagues to vote against it in good conscience, drawing a parallel to the India Bill he proudly voted against.

The speech is about divorce law reform (the Divorce Reform Bill), focusing on breakdown of marriage, financial protections, and children's welfare. While it briefly mentions "greater equality of rights as between men and women" and the safeguarding of women's financial position in divorce, these references are incidental to the divorce law argument and do not constitute advocacy for or against women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill extending the franchise to women, stating "I agree with what the right hon. Gentleman the Home Secretary said, that this Bill completes the necessary cycle of the extension of the franchise upon the democratic basis" and argues that "once you have granted the vote to women, as you did in 1918, there can be no logical objection to the present extension." While the speaker raises concerns about election expenses and plural voting, these are procedural/democratic objections to the Bill's incomplete reform, not opposition to women's enfranchisement.

The speaker explicitly states he agrees with the Prime Minister that "nothing could be worse for the future of this country than giving the vote to women," directly opposing women's enfranchisement. Though he mentions he will support Lord Robert Cecil's division, he clarifies it is not because he thinks women ought to be included.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill designed to remedy the chronic under-representation of women in elected bodies, defends measures like all-women shortlists to increase women's representation, and argues against an amendment that would limit parties' freedom to adopt such positive measures.

The target speech is an administrative response about voter registration rules for women across multiple constituencies, reporting on the current legal position without arguing for or against women's political rights. It describes existing statutory arrangements rather than advocating any position on women's civic participation.

The TARGET speech is an extensive argument in favour of the Secret Ballot for Parliamentary and municipal elections, focused entirely on electoral corruption, intimidation, bribery, and comparative evidence from Australia, Europe, and America. Women are never mentioned as a class, and no argument about women's political rights, franchise, or representation is made anywhere in the speech.

The TARGET speech concerns defects in voter registration machinery—lodger franchise technicalities, overseer negligence, and comparisons with Scottish and Parisian systems—with no argument about women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is incidental ("occupied by women" as a category explaining why certain houses were omitted from lists), with no position taken on women's civic status.

The TARGET speech concerns the secret ballot (voting by ballot) and electoral reform — specifically, intimidation, bribery, and the freedom of male voters in parliamentary elections. The only passing mention of women is incidental: the speaker notes that the "trust" argument for open voting loses force "because the trust, if it was one, could only be exercised for women, children, and lodgers" (i.e., non-voters), which is a rhetorical aside about the composition of non-enfranchised persons, not an argument about women's political rights. No position is taken for or against women's civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on leasehold reform, specifically the valuation of freeholds under the Leasehold Reform Act and the Custins case regarding marriage value. The only mention of women is a passing, non-argumentative reference to "the Conservative women's conference" as an aside about a fellow MP's rhetorical performance.

The target speech is a factual parliamentary answer providing statistics on females registered in multiple constituencies and confirming no known instances of double voting at the last General Election. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Raynsford) defends a Bill designed to remedy chronic under-representation of women in elected bodies by allowing political parties to adopt positive measures (such as all-women shortlists) for candidate selection, arguing against an amendment that would limit those measures. He explicitly frames the legislation as necessary to further women's representation in elected bodies.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on the Irish Home Rule Bill — specifically the number of Irish Members to remain in the Westminster Parliament, financial arrangements, and devolution policy. The brief mention of "women's votes" is purely incidental, used as an example of how Irish Members voted instrumentally rather than on conviction, without the speaker making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Raikes) moves to delay/kill the Married Women's Property Bill, arguing against the "civil emancipation of women" and "entire equality with men," and explicitly stating that women's prospects would not be improved by placing them on equal footing with men in civic life. He opposes the broader suffragist goal embedded in the Bill, describing women's "enfranchisement" as something he deprecates.

The speaker argues that no Parliament has the right to impose the vote on women until there is "unmistakable proof that the women of the country themselves desire it," and claims that women as a whole do not demand it — framing the franchise as an unwanted "obligation" rather than a privilege, thereby opposing the extension of women's political rights as proposed in the Bill.

The TARGET speech is focused entirely on Poor Law relief, pauperism statistics, and the difficulties of disenfranchising voters (including ex-service men) who receive Poor Law relief. While it briefly mentions "the female franchise" in passing as one of several administrative complications, it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Minister Raynsford) explicitly supports the Bill's purpose of increasing women's representation in elected bodies, argues that candidate selection falls outside EU law so parties can adopt positive measures, and opposes the amendment on the grounds that it would restrict parties' freedom to use permissive provisions designed to remedy women's under-representation.

The speech concerns legislation about prostitution and the Criminal Law Amendment Act, specifically whether an amendment would extend liability to "persons in charge" of premises used for prostitution. It does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of women's political rights or civic representation.

The speech is entirely focused on industrial relations, trade union legislation, unofficial strikes, and the Donovan Report. There is a brief mention of "men and women at work" but this is incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker invokes "the pledge to extend the vote to women" as grounds for reintroducing the six-monthly register, framing the measure as necessary to ensure newly enfranchised women can actually exercise their vote promptly — a substantive argument in support of women's political rights.

The speaker (a Minister) moves the Third Reading of a Bill specifically designed to permit positive measures (such as all-women shortlists) to increase women's representation in Parliament and other elected bodies, explicitly arguing that women's under-representation is unacceptable and that the Bill is needed to remedy discrimination in candidate selection processes.

The speech concerns a criminal law amendment about prostitution and housing rights for prostitutes — specifically whether a woman independently engaged in prostitution can be turned out of her lodgings. While it addresses conditions affecting women, it does not argue for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in political life; the civic status of women as a class in political representation is not at issue here.

The speech is primarily about the Nurses Bill, discussing nursing registration, professional standards, male nurses in mental health, pay, and committee structures. The brief mention of suffragettes and women not getting "a square deal in the Health Service" is a passing comment used to introduce a pivot to advocating for male nurses, not a substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about restoring the compounding system for rating and relieving the poor of burdensome local rates following the Reform Act of 1867. Women are mentioned only in passing ("some of whom were women, without claim to the franchise") as part of a broader description of affected householders, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns the legal scope of amendments to the Criminal Law Amendment Act as applied to prostitution and brothel regulation, not women's political rights or representation. Women are discussed as victims of trafficking and prostitution law, but there is no argument made about their right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of civic/political participation.

The speech is almost entirely about Welsh Disestablishment, the guillotine/closure motion, and whether the Government has a mandate for the Welsh Church Bill. The only mention of women is a passing reference to "the franchise for women" as one of several topics listed in a Cabinet minister's election address — used as evidence that the minister covered many topics but omitted Welsh Disestablishment. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech focuses entirely on military pay, allowances, and personnel matters (parachutists' pay, dental corps rates, Gurkhas, etc.). The brief mentions of the Women's Royal Army Corps are purely administrative—noting pay anomalies and a numerical discrepancy in officer/other ranks ratios—without making any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Pannell, Leeds West) explicitly invokes the history of women's political and civil rights movements, praises Josephine Butler's fight against the Contagious Diseases Acts, and argues that women's organisations have "fought all along against compulsory registration" and that women would be the "principal victims" of the Bill — framing his opposition to the Bill as a defence of women's hard-won rights against a "dual code" that punishes women. He also references his opposition to the Street Offences Act on the same grounds, showing consistent support for women's civic equality.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill aimed at increasing women's political representation, celebrates historical progress on women's suffrage, acknowledges the party's failures in electing women to Parliament, and argues that Parliament is weakened by not being representative — framing women's representation as a benefit to Parliament and the nation rather than merely a favour to women.

The speech is entirely about procedural arrangements (a guillotine/time allocation motion) for the Government of Ireland Bill. The brief mention of a private Member's Bill on the extension of the franchise to women is incidental and makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker briefly but explicitly notes that "the House will, before long, extend the franchise to all women between the ages of 21 and 30" and frames the Office Regulation Bill as something the House "proposes to do something for the new voters," treating the forthcoming extension of women's suffrage as a given and positively referencing it as context for protecting women workers. This constitutes a supportive (if incidental) endorsement of women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on education policy, gas industry nationalisation, defence, and the Common Market application. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women in the Armed Forces"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The TARGET speech (comprising Mr. Bright's continuation and the Solicitor General's response) concerns the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill — a marriage law reform debate. Neither speaker addresses women's political rights, the franchise, standing for office, or any aspect of civic/political representation. The Solicitor General's reference to this being "a woman's question" concerns marriage law, not political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on Poor Law administration, local government finance, boards of guardians, and the relationship between elected local authorities and central government control. While the speaker mentions "men and women" seeking poor relief and references women in passing, he makes no argument about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or civic participation.

Sir Charles Dilke explicitly supports the Bill to remove women's political disabilities, systematically refuting opponents' arguments against women's suffrage — including dismissing claims about women's domestic role, electoral turmoil, lack of desire for the franchise, virtual representation, and intellectual incapacity — while affirming that granting women the Parliamentary franchise on a property basis is a "practical measure of justice."

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill aimed at improving women's political representation, calling it "a good step forward," and advocates for tackling additional barriers (costs of candidacy, childcare) to further women's participation in Parliament.

The speech concerns a parliamentary debate about financial resolutions for dealing with pauper lunatics and the hardships faced by poor people, including poor women, in that context. The mention of "poor women" refers to their suffering as paupers/lunatics, not to women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly celebrates the Bill as "a historic day" that "will transform politics in this House," argues that women are needed in Parliament to make better laws, defends all-women shortlists, and calls for further measures to address under-representation of ethnic minorities. Every argument made supports expanding women's political representation.

The speaker supports increasing women's representation in Parliament through positive action like recruitment, mentoring, and coaching, and explicitly argues women are electorally advantageous ("If you want to win, choose a woman"). However, she expresses substantive opposition to all-women shortlists and twinning, calling them "extraordinarily invidious" and suggesting she would reconsider her role as an MP if they were imposed, constituting genuine opposition to one specific mechanism of women's political representation.

The speech is primarily about electoral redistribution, plural voting, and parliamentary constituency boundaries. The brief mention of women receiving the vote in 1928 (and the consequent extension of plural voting to wives) is used only as a historical example of Conservative electoral manipulation, not as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech focuses entirely on constitutional matters—the Parliament Act, Home Rule, Welsh Disestablishment, Ulster, and the conduct of parliamentary debates. The only mention of suffragettes is a passing rhetorical flourish ("He may sow Ulster and he may reap suffragettes") used as an analogy about the dangers of Bonar Law's doctrine on resisting laws by force, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns the Nursing (Amendment) Bill, focusing on representation of State Enrolled Nurses on the General Nursing Council, male nurses' roles, fee structures, and hospital consultations. While female nurses and a female MP (Dame Irene Ward) are mentioned, there is no argument made about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker explicitly supports extending voting hours to give more electors, including women, greater opportunity to vote, arguing that women with household duties find it difficult to reach polling stations before 8 o'clock and that an extension to 9 o'clock would enable them to exercise their franchise. This is a practical argument in favour of facilitating women's political participation.

The speaker supports vigorous positive action to promote more women in Parliament (mentoring, coaching, training, monitoring) and commits to encouraging more women to come forward, but substantively opposes all-women shortlists and twinning as "extraordinarily invidious" social engineering that treats MPs as a special case unjustified compared to other professions.

Viscountess Astor explicitly states "I thank God that women have the vote," expressing clear support for women's suffrage. She also uses the status of women as her benchmark for judging countries, implying women's full civic participation is a positive good.

The speaker delivers a sustained, detailed argument in favour of enfranchising women ratepayers, contending that property-owning and breadwinning women have a clear right to the Parliamentary franchise, that it is expedient for both women and the State, and explicitly concluding "I give to it my hearty support."

The speaker is asking a parliamentary question specifically about women prisoners held for suffrage-related offences, implicitly advocating on behalf of their welfare and the legitimacy of the enfranchisement agitation. The framing of the question treats these women's cause sympathetically and seeks accountability from the government regarding their treatment.

The target speech concerns a temperance/licensing bill (likely the Scottish Temperance Bill), discussing public opinion in Scotland and thanking the Government for its conduct of the measure. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker systematically opposes women's parliamentary enfranchisement, arguing that women are not a coherent "class," that enfranchising them would logically require admitting them to Parliament and jury service, that their "instinctive and emotional" intellect makes them suited to influence rather than governance, and that female voting would introduce corruption, bribery, and impulsive sentimentalism into elections. Though he criticises the Bill's exclusion of married women as illogical, this is deployed as a reductio ad absurdum against the measure, not as support for broader enfranchisement.

The entire speech is devoted to arguing for the repeal or reform of the Game Laws, addressing the economic and moral harms they cause to tenant farmers, labourers, and landlords. Women's political rights are never mentioned or alluded to, even in passing.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill enabling positive action for women's political representation, argues that the "mother of Parliaments" needs to catch up on female representation, and states that more women in Parliament is the "fundamental reason" her party supports the change in law, framing it as resolving a "democratic deficit."

The speech addresses health risks (thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, cervical cancer) associated with oral contraceptives, responding to parliamentary questions about drug safety. It does not touch on women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation in any way.

The TARGET speech (Disraeli's) is entirely concerned with Irish affairs—specifically the history of Irish unrest, the Fenian conspiracy, and the Irish Church Disestablishment Bill—with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.
