The brief mention of "ladies" writing letters about Ireland is purely incidental and makes no claim about women's civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on the mechanism for electing school Boards (via Town Councils vs. direct ratepayer vote) under an Education Bill, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention that the Town Council "might elect men or women" is incidental and descriptive, not an argument about women's civic status.

The speech by the Postmaster-General (Herbert Samuel) is primarily concerned with defending the Government's constitutional conduct regarding Home Rule, Welsh Disestablishment, and House of Lords reform. Women's suffrage is mentioned only briefly and in passing — as an example of an issue on which the Government steps aside and allows the House of Commons to decide freely — without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker enthusiastically supports the Bill passing into law, celebrates its aim of achieving "a far more balanced representation of men and women" in Parliament, and expresses commitment to applying its principles to all future elected bodies, clearly advocating for women's political representation.

The TARGET speech is primarily a debate about university representation and plural voting (the Reading University Bill), not about women's political rights. The single passing mention of women — "This Session we have recognised the principle that women of 21 should have the vote" — is cited only as a contextual reference to equality, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The target speech is a factual ministerial report on the status of suffragist prisoners — numbers, feeding arrangements, and health conditions — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or enfranchisement.

The TARGET speeches (seconder of the widows' pension motion, Viscountess Astor's speech, and Mr. Emlyn-Jones's speech) are entirely focused on the case for widows' pensions and mothers' pensions as social welfare policy. While Viscountess Astor makes a brief passing remark attributing the historical neglect of widows' pensions to the fact that "men only had the vote," this is a fleeting observation in support of the pension argument rather than a substantive argument about women's political rights. The speeches do not argue for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in civic life.

The speech is primarily about opposing university plural voting (the Reading University Bill), arguing that university graduates are not more politically qualified than ordinary voters. The brief mention of "men and women" voting applies generically to all voters and does not argue for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speaker moves to introduce a Bill explicitly designed to "remove the Electoral Disabilities of Women," enabling women householders to vote for Members of Parliament, which is a direct advocacy for women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (Mr. Mundella) is entirely focused on the Elementary Education Bill of 1870, arguing about compulsory education, denominational vs. national school systems, religious instruction, and funding arrangements. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued in any way.

The speech is entirely focused on the closure of a maternity hospital and the impact on local constituents, covering healthcare provision, transport access, and hospital administration. While it mentions women (mothers, expectant mothers) as patients, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker advocates on behalf of suffragette prisoners (including Miss Sylvia Pankhurst and others convicted for offences "connected with the movement for the enfranchisement of women"), arguing that their sentences and treatment are disproportionate and inhumane, and calling for their release — thereby expressing clear sympathy and support for the women's suffrage cause and its participants.

The speech is entirely about defamation law reform and the Matrimonial Property Bill is only briefly mentioned in passing as something the speaker would have preferred to champion; no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is primarily about reducing the Tea Duty as a burden on working-class people and housewives. The brief mention of women's growing voting power is used instrumentally as a political warning to the government rather than as an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns the payment and pastoral arrangements for Nonconformist ministers in Holloway Gaol, only mentioning suffragist prisoners incidentally to explain a statistical fluctuation in prisoner numbers. No argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equal representation in decision-making and political life, welcomes legislation on women's representation, expresses "absolute disdain" for missed opportunities to elect women to the Scottish Parliament, and advocates for gender mainstreaming, equal pay, and women's full participation in public life.

The target speech is entirely focused on the merits and mechanics of the minority clause in the Reform Acts (proportional/minority representation in multi-member constituencies), redistribution of seats, and electoral systems generally. Women's political rights are never mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speaker explicitly supports giving young women the vote ("the flapper vote" Act) and endorses the reduction of the voting/majority age to 18 for "young people," arguing that responsibilities given to young women under the earlier Act "proved to be nothing but good." This is an affirmative endorsement of women's political rights (the franchise for women under 30).

The TARGET speech is about Lords reform and constitutional change in the UK, with women's suffrage mentioned only in passing as an example of a historical constitutional change (in response to an interjection). No argument for or against women's political rights is made in the TARGET itself.

The speech is entirely focused on industrial relations, unofficial strikes, and trade union legislation (the White Paper), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The passing reference to "men and women on the factory floor" casting votes in union bargaining elections is purely descriptive and does not engage with women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly states he is "as keenly opposed" to Women Suffrage as others are in favour, and the entire speech condemns the militant suffragist movement while calling for stronger government action against suffragette activists, framing their campaign as criminal mob law that must be suppressed.

The speech is entirely concerned with Poor Law administration, the Metropolitan Common Poor Fund, and the governance relationship between boards of guardians and the Metropolitan Asylums Board. While the speaker briefly mentions "men and women" on the Metropolitan Asylum Board, this is incidental and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech is entirely focused on the Israeli military operation in Jenin, humanitarian conditions in the Palestinian refugee camp, and calls for EU diplomatic and economic action — it does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issues.

The speaker explicitly states support for the Bill but conditions that support on ensuring women are not left "against their will, with something which is less than reasonable and fair," demonstrating a pro-women's-rights stance focused on protecting women's financial interests in divorce proceedings. This is a procedural/drafting objection in service of women's protection, not substantive opposition to their rights.

The target speech is entirely about press freedom, independence of newspapers from capitalist control, and the dangers of the syndicated press. While it briefly mentions "the Flapper vote" in passing (noting that hon. members should not fear having voted for young women's equal citizenship), this is a fleeting reference without any substantive argument for or against women's political rights; the speech makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker mentions "the enfranchisement of women that the tax credits were supposed to create," framing women's financial independence through tax credits as a political right worth protecting, and criticising officials for undermining it by directing women's payments to their partners.

The speech is primarily about the Teachers Superannuation Act amendment to extend pensionable rights for teachers serving abroad. The brief mention of women's electoral power ("placing the balance of electoral power in the hands of women") is incidental context used to argue for broadening women teachers' worldly knowledge, not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker cites the extension of universal suffrage to women in 1918 and 1928 as a significant constitutional change, directly countering the preceding claim that there were no major constitutional changes after the last Liberal Government. By characterizing women's suffrage as a meaningful reform that benefited those who received it, the speaker implicitly endorses it as a positive development.

The speaker explicitly invokes the suffragettes as a positive reference point and defends her party's efforts to get more women into Parliament to make it more representative of society, expressing clear support for women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly states "I am as keenly opposed to [Women Suffrage]" and describes suffragist activities as a "scandal and disgrace," framing women's suffrage activism as criminal disorder requiring suppression. Throughout the speech he opposes the women's suffrage movement and its participants.

The speaker condemns militant suffragists as criminals inciting lawlessness and mob rule, characterising the suffrage movement's activities as "an orgy of crime" and a "farce," and implicitly opposing women's suffrage (noting in context he is "opposed to it"). There is no substantive argument in favour of women's political rights.

The speech is focused entirely on the arithmetic of election expenditure limits per voter, arguing that 5d. rather than 6d. per head is sufficient given actual spending patterns. The mention of "younger women" added to the electorate is incidental to the financial calculation, not an argument about women's political rights or their fitness for political participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Selective Employment Tax and its impact on distributive trades, consumers, housewives, and the Co-operative Movement. While the speaker mentions "womanpower," housewives, and women voters, these references are made in the context of economic and consumer policy arguments, not to argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

Sir George Jenkinson explicitly and cordially supports the Bill, arguing that women who own property deserve the same franchise rights as male property owners, that objections about persecution and bribery are unconvincing, and that women deserve representation in the making of laws to which they are subject.

The speech focuses on election expenditure limits in county constituencies, arguing against a penny reduction and in favour of a halfpenny reduction. While the speaker briefly mentions that women will form a majority of electors and that special women's meetings will be needed (as a reason expenditure cannot be cut too deeply), this is a factual observation about costs rather than an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly declares "I am an anti-suffragist, and, in my sincerity in opposing votes for women, I will not give place to anyone," directly opposing women's political rights. The speech focuses on condemning suffragist militant tactics and demanding stronger government action against them.

The speaker explicitly opposes women's parliamentary franchise, arguing it is "not a disability" but "a privilege" not to vote, that women's proper sphere is domestic influence rather than political participation, and concluding he "cannot agree" to admit women to the same political privileges as men, urging the House to reject the Bill.

The TARGET contains two distinct speeches: Colonel Sykes argues strongly "for" women's political rights, contending that women who meet the property qualification are "as much entitled to vote as any of the other 14,000 voters" and "had a full right and title to exercise it"; while Mr. Scourfield argues "against," moving the Previous Question on the grounds that women do not want the franchise, that granting it would cost them social influence, and that the proper sphere for women is domestic rather than political.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on criticizing the preceding speaker's approach to handling militant suffragist activity and the Home Secretary's administration — specifically arguing against panic legislation and for minimising the agitation. While it references the suffrage movement and militant suffragists, it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights themselves.

The speech concerns the Family Law Reform Bill and the age of majority, focusing on marriage consent, contractual capacity, and parental authority for those under 21. The brief mention of women fighting for the vote before 1918 is a passing historical reference used to contrast with the current lack of public demand for age-of-majority reform, not an argument about women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (Mr. Winterbotham) is primarily concerned with defending Roman Catholic conventual and monastic institutions from Parliamentary inquiry, addressing property law, religious liberty, and anti-Catholic prejudice. The brief mention of women—noting that "pending the measure of the hon. Member for Manchester (Mr. Jacob Bright), strong language was the only constitutional method which women possessed of expressing their opinions upon political questions"—is a passing observation about women's lack of political voice, not an argument for or against women's political rights. Similarly, the remark about giving women "a higher and more manly education" and "larger spheres of usefulness and activity" is incidental to the main argument about convent converts, not a substantive position on women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about the Boundary Commission's work, electoral redistribution, and constituency boundaries. The mention of "women's institutes" is merely an example of social groups consulted during a local inquiry, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about police pay, conditions, and the rejection of a pay package by Scottish police officers. It makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation, even in passing.

The speaker explicitly states agreement with Lord Robert Cecil's "general attitude on the principle of Women suffrage," signaling support for women's suffrage while focusing on the difficulties faced by the Home Secretary in enforcing the law against militant suffragists.

The TARGET speech (by Jacob Bright, MP for Manchester) strongly opposes the Contagious Diseases Acts on the grounds that they deprive women of civil rights, subject them to compulsory examination and detention without equal treatment of men, and constitute unjust class legislation targeting poor women. He explicitly argues for equal legal treatment of men and women ("whatever law shall be directed against the propagation of this disease shall be an equal law") and invokes women's civic rights and dignity as central to his case for repeal.

The speaker praises the Sex Discrimination (Election Candidates) Act as enabling positive action to redress the imbalance in women's representation, and implicitly endorses its use by all parties, clearly supporting women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's political representation, arguing it is essential to the health of democracy, celebrates the historic 1997 intake of women MPs, and supports mainstreaming gender analysis across government departments to ensure women's full participation in political life.

The speaker (Miss Wilkinson) positively references women's enfranchisement since 1918, praises women electors as businesslike and effective participants in elections, and expresses enthusiasm for the newly enfranchised younger women joining the register, treating their political participation as a clear benefit.

The speaker explicitly states he will support the Bill, arguing that wealthy female ratepayers worth thousands a year should not be denied the vote merely due to sex, while their male servants can vote. He also argues that imposing onerous civic duties (like overseer) on women without granting them the vote is unfair, and concludes he will "have much pleasure in supporting the Bill."

The speaker explicitly states he is "quite friendly to the principle of this Bill," voted for its Second Reading, and supports giving women the franchise on equal terms with men; his amendment merely seeks to raise the voting age to 25 for both sexes, not to oppose women's enfranchisement itself.

The speech is entirely focused on defence matters: Service morale, accommodation, pay scales, the Territorial Army, and military operations in Ulster and Vietnam. Women are not mentioned in the context of political rights, and no argument is made for or against women's civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues in favour of the Bill granting women the parliamentary franchise, contending that if women cannot sit in Parliament, justice requires they have control over those who do enter it, and he cites the Manchester Town Council's petition in support as evidence of public backing for the measure.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Welsh Labour party's proposal for all-women shortlists for Welsh Assembly elections and frames it as a positive outcome of the Government's legislation, indicating clear support for women's political representation measures.

The speaker explicitly advocates for quotas and women's representation legislation as the only effective mechanisms to increase women's representation in Parliament, directly supporting structural measures to advance women's political rights.

The speaker opposes an amendment that would restrict voting to those over 25, arguing there is strong demand for the vote at 21 among both young men and women, that young women at 21 should be treated as equals of those already enfranchised, and that it is anomalous to deny the vote to those who can already stand for Parliament. The speech explicitly supports extending the franchise to young women on equal terms.

The speech focuses entirely on electoral registration procedures — student voters, immigrant voters, and 18-21 year olds — addressing administrative and publicity improvements to ensure eligible voters appear on the register. There is no argument made about women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any other in-scope topic.

The target speech (by Lord Robert Cecil) focuses entirely on the government's failure to effectively administer the law in response to suffragette militancy — arguing for better penal/administrative solutions (deportation, imagination in policy) — without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights themselves. The speaker explicitly states he is not dealing with the suffrage question but purely with how the government handles the outrages.

The speaker argues that young men and women aged 21–25 are fully capable of exercising the vote and urges the Committee to reject the Amendment that would exclude them, thereby supporting equal political rights for both young men and young women at 21.

The speaker (Lord Robert Cecil) characterizes suffragette militants as "dangers to the state," "misguided," "of the nature of insane people," and "not normal," and recommends deportation as the appropriate response to their political agitation. While he expresses some sympathy for their sincerity, his overall framing treats their campaign for women's suffrage as a form of criminality or madness to be suppressed, indicating opposition to their political rights movement.

The speech is entirely about the structural reform of the National Health Service, covering topics such as integrated health authorities, regional planning, local government boundaries, and democratic participation in health administration. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech (by Lord Robert Cecil) focuses entirely on the government's mishandling of militant suffragette protests and forcible feeding — criticising administrative failures and proposing deportation as an alternative punishment. While it discusses the suffragettes sympathetically as sincere and non-ordinary criminals, it explicitly defers any argument about women's suffrage itself ("I am not going this afternoon to deal with the treatment of the suffrage question by the House of Commons"), making no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker briefly but explicitly expresses pride in being "the first Conservative woman Member of Parliament for Yorkshire," signalling support for women's political representation, even while distancing herself from militant suffragettism. This is a direct, affirmative statement about women's presence in Parliament.

Captain Craig explicitly opposes giving women (and men) the vote at age 21, calling it "a monstrous thing" and arguing there is "no demand whatever" for enfranchisement at that age, while supporting an amendment to raise the voting age to 25. He accepts women's equal franchise in principle but opposes the specific age provision that would extend voting rights to younger women.

The speaker supports women's right to vote in principle ("women and men who are of that age ought to have the franchise at that age") and welcomes the enfranchisement of women 30 and over, but substantively argues in favour of setting the voting age at 25 for both sexes rather than 21, thereby opposing the extension of the franchise to younger women under the Bill as written.

The speaker supports giving widows and spinsters the same property rights as men ("for" women's political rights broadly construed), but explicitly opposes extending those rights to married women, and objects to Russell Gurney's Bill on the grounds that it would entitle married women to vote in respect of their property — making substantive arguments on both sides regarding different subsets of women.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers: the first (unnamed) explicitly opposes women's suffrage on the grounds that his female constituents are "fair, graceful, and feminine" and therefore don't need a vote, and announces he will vote against the Bill. Mr. Bruce then argues the Government cannot support the Bill at this time, citing the scale of the question and the unresolved consequence of women potentially sitting in Parliament — while explicitly declining to express any personal or governmental opinion against women's political rights in principle, and acknowledging the Government's prior support for the municipal franchise for women. Together the TARGET presents substantive argument against the Bill from the first speaker, and a procedural/scale-based opposition from Bruce that is paired with explicit refusal to oppose women's political rights on principle.

The target speech merely points out two named women who lead Conservative-controlled councils as counter-examples to the preceding speaker's claim about women's underrepresentation in local government. It does not argue for or against women's political rights — it simply cites factual examples of women in leadership roles without taking any substantive position on the broader question of women's political representation.

The speaker acknowledges women council leaders as positive examples while emphasizing that women remain significantly underrepresented in local councils compared to Parliament, implicitly supporting greater women's political representation. The speech is part of a broader debate in which the speaker (Ms Hewitt) is consistently advocating for increasing women's representation in political institutions.

The speaker explicitly states "I have always been a keen supporter of the movement" (Women Suffrage) and "I speak as one who has always consistently supported the cause of Women Suffrage," framing his criticism of militant tactics as coming from a pro-suffrage standpoint rather than opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports enfranchising women at 21, citing practical experience from New Zealand, arguing that women's votes will stabilise the constitution, and stating "I am perfectly satisfied that the passing of this Measure is going to solidify and stabilise the constitution of the country" while declaring his intention to vote for the Bill.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Parochial Councils Bill on the grounds that voluntary diocesan and parochial councils are preferable to legislated ones for Church of England governance. The only mention of women ("women, too, for we have now arrived at the period of female suffrage") is a fleeting, incidental rhetorical flourish about who might vote in council elections, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses overwhelmingly on industrial relations, police reform, crime, law and order, drug addiction, and regional development policy. The single mention of women — "Women police could be enlisted and serve healthy functions in the police, thereby relieving the time of the men" — is an incidental remark about police staffing, not an argument about women's political rights or civic representation.

The speaker (McKenna) frames suffragette activism as "suffragist offences" requiring law enforcement and advocates for expanded powers to control and license out suffragist prisoners, treating women's political agitation as a public order problem to be suppressed rather than a legitimate political cause deserving rights.

The speaker (Sir William Davison) supports equal franchise for both sexes but argues the voting age should be set at 25 rather than 21, citing the Prime Minister's apparent openness to this and evidence from the Registrar-General about prudence and responsibility. He thus supports women's political rights in principle while opposing the specific age-21 provision that would enfranchise a large new class of younger women, making substantive arguments on both sides of the scope of women's franchise.

The speech concerns the Deceased Wife's Sister Bill — a marriage law reform debate — and makes no arguments about women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., claims about women's opinions on the Bill), not as subjects of political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports measures to increase women's political representation, endorsing 50-50 shortlists in European elections, backing the Equal Opportunities Commission's finding that positive discrimination is needed to get more women into Parliament, and highlighting her party's active efforts to mentor and promote women candidates.

The speaker (Miss Pike) explicitly supports the Equal Pay Bill, calling herself "a suffragette in this respect," wholeheartedly congratulating the Minister on the Bill, and arguing throughout for equal pay and equality of opportunity for women in industry, including training and promotion prospects.

The target speech (by Mr. McKenna) is focused entirely on defending the Government's handling of suffragist prisoners — addressing whether the law has been properly upheld, citing statistics on prisoners released versus those who served sentences, and explaining the legal duty to feed hunger-striking prisoners. It does not argue for or against women's political rights; it addresses the administrative and legal management of militant suffragist protesters.

The speaker (Mr. Groves) explicitly argues that young women in industrial areas are "anxious and eager" to vote and have proven their worth, directly supporting extending the franchise to women at age 21 on equal terms with men. He frames equal voting rights as a matter of civic right and democratic principle, asserting that young women are just as capable and deserving of political participation as young men.

The speaker (Dr. Summerskill) explicitly supports the Equal Pay Bill as "one of the great Measures of social reform," draws a direct parallel between women's suffrage and equal pay legislation as steps in women's emancipation, praises the Ford women machinists' strike for their rights, and calls for further sex discrimination legislation—all framing equal pay as advancing women's full civic and economic status.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on criticising the Home Secretary's administration of forcible feeding of suffragist prisoners, arguing it constitutes torture and is unsustainable as a matter of public opinion and criminal administration. While the speakers in context discuss women's suffrage, the TARGET speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights — their argument is solely about the practicality and morality of the government's penal treatment of these prisoners.

The speaker (Sir A. Markham) explicitly states "I speak as one who has always consistently supported the cause of Women Suffrage," framing his criticism of militant tactics as coming from a supporter, not an opponent. His objections are directed at militant methods and government policy, not at women's suffrage itself.

The speaker explicitly supports greater women's representation in Parliament and public bodies, advocates for 50-50 shortlists and pay audits, criticises the persistent under-representation of women in senior roles and public bodies, and calls for breaking down stereotypes that exclude women from political office.

The TARGET speeches debate the Ballot Bill (secret voting in elections) and related procedural matters, with no substantive argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "women and children and all the other unenfranchised" in Mr. Heygate's speech appears only as a passing reference to illustrate an argument about the trust exercised by electors, not as a position on women's political rights.

The speaker (Mrs. Jill Knight) explicitly supports equal pay legislation, stating "every fair-minded person must acknowledge that it is gross injustice when a woman bearing the same responsibility in the same job and working the same hours as a man receives an inferior wage" and declares "My main concern in intervening in this debate is to place on record my complete agreement about the need for a fair deal for women." While she raises concerns about maternity privileges and potential side effects, these are caveats about implementation rather than substantive opposition to women's political or economic rights.

The speaker explicitly supports extending the vote to women at age 21, arguing that younger women in places like the East End of London are "eager" and "able to take an interest in government" and will "do their duty as sincerely and loyally" as their elders, framing the franchise extension as a just return for their sacrifices for the country.

The speech concerns a parliamentary procedural dispute about whether to discharge a committee appointed to investigate Catholic conventual and monastic institutions. The arguments are about religious liberty, anti-Catholic discrimination, and the propriety of the inquiry—not about women's political rights or representation. While nuns ("ladies") are mentioned as subjects of the proposed inquiry, the speech makes no argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in civic/political life.

The speech focuses entirely on family planning services, birth control education, GP remuneration, and related health policy — none of which addresses women's voting rights, political representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned as recipients of health services, not as a class with distinctive political rights.

The speech concerns the proper administrative mechanism for extending licensed gaming areas under the Gaming Act, arguing that local licensing authorities rather than Parliament should make such decisions. There is no reference to women's political rights, suffrage, representation, or any related civic status.

The speech by Mr. Harcourt focuses entirely on proportional representation, cumulative voting, and school board elections. While "female suffrage" is briefly mentioned as one of several proposals from "philosophical Liberals," it is listed in passing without any argument for or against it; the speaker's substantive position concerns representation by majorities versus minorities in electoral systems.

The speaker explicitly supports greater women's participation in public life, lamenting that "we still have a long way to go before we achieve equality" and calling for collective commitment to working toward that goal. She also critiques the image projected by the Women's National Commission website as failing to inspire ordinary women to see themselves as capable of civic participation.

Lord Hugh Cecil argues that young women's hardship-based qualification to vote is "a dangerous argument" because they would vote with a single eye to personal or class interest, implying skepticism about extending the franchise to young women (and young men) at 21. His broader argument supports raising the voting age to 25, which would restrict women's political rights relative to the Bill under discussion.

The speaker explicitly supports the Sex Discrimination (Election Candidates) Act 2002 as essential for increasing women's political representation, argues that positive action is needed to overcome discrimination in candidate selection, and champions legislation requiring equal membership terms for women in private clubs — all substantive arguments in favour of women's political rights and civic equality.

The speech is entirely focused on parliamentary procedure, the Ballot Bill (secret voting), corruption in elections, and the conduct of debates — with no argument made for or against women's political rights. The brief mention of "women and minors" appears only as part of a quoted passage from Lord Palmerston, used to illustrate the concept that a vote is a trust rather than a personal right, without any argument about women's civic status.

The speaker defends the logical consistency of the suffragettes' argument — that women have no voice in making or administering laws and therefore no obligation to obey them — and criticises all proposed measures (imprisonment, transportation, letting them die, suppressing meetings) as ineffective or unjust, implicitly supporting the underlying cause of women's suffrage as the only real remedy.

The speaker argues against those who oppose women's suffrage ("they do not believe that women are fit to vote at 25... they really object to women"), implicitly supporting women's right to vote, and frames the debate around equal enfranchisement for both sexes, citing the Junior Imperial League as evidence of women's political engagement and fitness to vote.

The TARGET speech (by MR. LOPES) dismisses female suffrage as an "unconstitutional principle," using the Prime Minister's support for it as a negative comparison point to argue that tax reform would be more popular. This frames women's suffrage as an undesirable, unconstitutional position.

The speaker explicitly supports the Sex Discrimination (Election Candidates) Act 2002, champions all-women shortlists for Welsh Assembly seats, celebrates the high proportion of women in the Welsh Assembly, and calls for equal numbers of men and women MPs — all clear expressions of support for women's political representation.

The speaker (Keir Hardie) explicitly argues that the only remedy is to release the imprisoned suffragette women, details the suffering of forcible feeding to generate sympathy for them, characterizes them as political prisoners entitled to special treatment, and concludes with a direct call for the House to confer the vote upon women.

The speech is entirely concerned with administrative and procedural issues around electoral registration, postal voting, proxy voting for service members, and the accuracy of electoral rolls. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is a lengthy critique of the Conservative government's budget and its economic effects on Scotland, covering taxation, public expenditure, unemployment, housing, and social services. Women's political rights or representation are never argued for or against; the only passing mention of a woman is a reference to "the hon. Lady the Member for Merton and Morden" as a former school teacher who would know the value of school milk.

The speaker explicitly supports all-women shortlists, celebrates increased female representation in Parliament, and argues that Women MPs must represent women and bring their needs to the fore. She also advocates for women's political participation internationally, highlighting the injustice of women being denied political rights in Afghanistan and Iran.

The speaker dismisses suffragettes as women who have abandoned their natural role as "creatures of charm and domesticity" to pursue criminal behaviour, and frames their militancy as a menace to the public rather than a legitimate political cause. While he expresses limited sympathy for Ministers being harassed, this is framed as political schadenfreude toward the Government, not support for women's political rights; he treats the suffrage movement as a problem to be managed rather than a cause to be advanced.

The speaker explicitly calls for bringing forward the date of equal pay implementation and advocates giving women "a fair reward for the job they do in industry," directly supporting women's equal economic and civic participation rights.

The speaker (Joynson-Hicks) explicitly defends the Bill's core purpose of making "the franchise the same for women as for men," arguing against an amendment that would raise the voting age to 25 and effectively reduce women's enfranchisement. He frames equal suffrage for women as a settled principle and opposes any measure that would undermine it.

The speaker (Jacob Bright) moves the second reading of a Women's Suffrage Bill and delivers an extensive speech arguing that women deserve the parliamentary franchise because they bear the burdens of the state, suffer from unjust laws without electoral redress, and have demonstrated broad popular and parliamentary support. He directly advocates for removing women's electoral disabilities and counters opposing arguments throughout.

The speaker condemns suffragists ("suffragists") for endangering public property and safety, blames government leniency for emboldening them, and expresses no support for women's political rights. The speech frames suffragette militancy purely as lawlessness that must be suppressed, with no positive argument for women's enfranchisement.

The speaker (Sir V. Henderson) defends retaining paragraph (c) on the explicit grounds that the Bill aims to "assimilate the existing electoral rights as between men and women," i.e., achieving equality between the sexes in electoral rights, which is a pro-women's political rights argument.

The speaker (Minister Hewitt) explicitly supports increasing women's representation in public appointments and acknowledges the specific under-representation of women from African, Caribbean, and Asian communities as "a very real problem," while referencing concrete departmental action plans to address it.

The speaker explicitly seconds the Bill to extend the Parliamentary franchise to qualified women, arguing that female enfranchisement would complete the representation of property and intelligence, correct unjust treatment of women, and serve as a model for the emancipation of women in India. He systematically rebuts objections against the measure and endorses it as a matter of justice.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on whether forcible feeding of suffragette prisoners constitutes "torture," using a medical analogy to argue it does not. It does not make any argument for or against women's right to vote or to participate in political life; the question of women's political rights is not addressed.

The target speech argues that paragraph (c) of the Bill is an absurdity and should be removed because it was originally inserted in the 1918 Act specifically to limit the number of women voters, and perpetuates an illogical plural voting privilege rather than genuine equality. The speaker supports the principle of equal franchise for men and women on their own individual qualifications, and explicitly criticizes the historic rationale of restricting women's votes as both illogical and unfair.

The speaker (Sir V. Henderson) argues against removing paragraph (c) on the grounds that doing so would disenfranchise 120,000–130,000 women who currently hold the vote, and further contends that a married woman has a legitimate right to a voice in taxation because she shares responsibility for household expenditure — explicitly supporting women's voting rights in this context.

The speaker (a government minister) defends retaining paragraph (c) of the Bill specifically to protect the voting rights of 120,000–130,000 women who already hold a double qualification, arguing that deleting it would "disfranchise" them and interfere with their existing rights.

The speaker explicitly supports achieving greater representation of women (and ethnic minorities) in public appointments, committing to hold Departments accountable for meeting a 50 per cent. target for women's representation on public bodies.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Boundary Commission's proposals for County Durham constituency boundaries, arguing they fail to achieve equal electoral weighting. Women are mentioned only in passing as part of a list of community organizations ("women's institutes") that supported retaining Sedgefield, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

Lord John Manners explicitly states he will "give his support to the second reading of the Bill," arguing that there are no valid logical arguments against enfranchising female ratepayers for Parliamentary elections, and that if women can vote for municipal bodies, they equally deserve to vote for Members of Parliament.

The speaker explicitly highlights and praises reforms in Bahrain that include women's political rights, specifically noting that women can now stand as candidates in local and general elections as well as vote in them, framing these as positive democratic developments worth supporting through the UK's bilateral relationship.

The speaker (Mr. Bouverie) moves that the Bill be rejected and argues at length against extending the Parliamentary franchise to women, contending it would contaminate the sex, disturb the foundations of society, obliterate distinctions between the sexes, and that the great bulk of women neither want nor would benefit from the suffrage.

The TARGET speech is a Chancellor of the Exchequer's economic statement covering inflation, public expenditure, balance of payments, taxation, and electoral promises. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The speech is entirely focused on nurses' pay, conditions, and career structure within the NHS. While it mentions women in passing (as nurses historically being women and being poorly paid), it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly highlights legislation enabling positive steps to increase women in elected office and describes personal efforts to encourage women to seek public appointments, demonstrating clear support for women's political representation.

The speaker consistently supports equality of opportunity for women throughout the speech, praising Conservative legislative achievements on equal pay and independent taxation, endorsing women's participation in the armed services, local government, and public life, and calling on the Government to do more to advance women's equality. While she critiques the Labour Government's performance, she does so from a pro-equality standpoint, not in opposition to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech focuses on opposing paragraph (c) of the Bill regarding plural voting and its alleged partisan electoral advantages for the Government, not on women's political rights per se. While the Bill broadly concerns women's suffrage, the speaker's argument is entirely about the mechanics of plural voting and constituency interests, without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech focuses on the treatment of suffragette prisoners (forcible feeding, prison conditions, the Home Secretary's legal powers), not on whether women should have political rights. While Women's Suffrage is briefly mentioned as context, no argument for or against women's political rights is made — the speaker explicitly notes the suffrage question is out of order and beyond the Home Secretary's power.

The speech is focused entirely on whether the Home Secretary is legally and morally justified in forcibly feeding suffragette prisoners, explicitly stating "We are not now discussing the question of Women Suffrage." The speaker's argument concerns the administration of law and prison policy, not women's political rights or representation.

Mr. Bouverie moves to reject the Women's Suffrage Bill, arguing at length that granting women electoral power would obliterate natural distinctions between the sexes, undermine the family, and lead to socialist subversion of society; he explicitly states that women's suffrage would be "a curse to them" and entreats the House to vote against it. Mr. Scourfield similarly gives "decided opposition" to the Bill on grounds that women do not want the franchise and it would be imposed against their wishes.

The speech is entirely focused on NHS funding, public expenditure cuts, and economic policy under the new Conservative government. The passing mention of "Tory men and Tory women" in a quoted Chancellor's speech is not an argument about women's political rights; it is a rhetorical point about the electoral mandate for Conservative policies.

The speech addresses social welfare provision for women who care for elderly dependants—covering costs, pensions, and support mechanisms—without making any argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The target speech focuses on administrative and legal questions about the Home Office's power to interfere with the course of justice and its handling of prisoner releases, using suffragist prisoners as a factual context. The speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights, but rather questions the propriety of executive interference with judicial proceedings.

The speaker (Mr. B. Hope) explicitly states he will "vote against the second reading of the Bill," arguing that women are unfit for political life due to their emotional nature, that enfranchisement would harm self-dependent women by exposing them to electoral turmoil, and that women's reason is governed by emotion rather than logic, making female-influenced parliaments prone to "hysterical and spasmodic" legislation.

The speech concerns welfare provision and social support for single women who care for elderly or disabled relatives — a social policy matter. It does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation in any way.

The speaker explicitly declares himself "a strong supporter of Women Suffrage" and frames his remarks around that position, while arguing against forcible feeding of suffragist prisoners and urging the Government to administer the law more humanely.

The speech is focused on criminal justice legislation (the Criminal Justice Bill), European Union powers, and constituency accountability. The mention of "men, women and children" in the Sheffield, Brightside constituency is purely illustrative and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly encourages measures to increase women's participation in public life, including adjusting council meeting times to accommodate more women and specifically promoting representation of women from deprived areas in public appointments. These are direct arguments in favour of expanding women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly and comprehensively argues in favour of women's political rights throughout the speech, contending that denying women the vote is logically indefensible given that they are taxed as citizens, that women have already proven themselves in municipal and school board elections, and that "personal unfitness or public danger" — neither of which has been demonstrated — are the only legitimate grounds for denying the franchise.

The speaker explicitly supports the Instruction to allow the Committee to consider election expenses in the context of extending the franchise to younger women, and states "we warmly support the Instruction." The speech treats the enfranchisement of additional women as a settled positive development and focuses on arguing that the resulting increase in electorate should not automatically raise permitted election expenditure.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill to extend the parliamentary franchise to women ratepayers, directly rebuts opponents' arguments about women's unfitness for political participation, and concludes by announcing he will "with great pleasure support the second reading of this Bill," arguing that opposition stems from "old prejudice and not of reason."

The target text is essentially a table of contents / Hansard structural summary listing clauses of a bill, word counts, and division tallies, with no argumentative content about women's political rights. The brief quoted line "That is one of the anomalies of the present system" is a passing remark about plural voting, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly urges action to improve women's representation throughout the scientific workforce, building on the Greenfield report's focus on women in science and engineering. This constitutes a clear, albeit brief, argument in support of women's fuller participation in public and professional life.

The TARGET speech is a procedural ruling by the Chairman explaining the limits of order for amendments to the Bill, focusing on what "assimilation" means in legislative terms. While it incidentally mentions men and women's voting qualifications as examples, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker warmly welcomes the Equal Pay Bill, praises women MPs (Dame Irene Ward and Mrs. Castle) for advancing the cause of women's equality, and explicitly states that the Bill—while only "a step on the road"—provides important machinery for achieving equality between the sexes, urging women to seize the opportunity it offers.

The target speech focuses entirely on the procedural question of whether an Instruction on election expenses should be referred to Committee, in the context of expanding the electorate to include younger women. The speech does not argue for or against women's political rights; it treats women's enfranchisement as a settled matter and addresses only the downstream question of adjusting candidate expenditure limits.

The speaker explicitly states "I am a suffragist," expressing support for women's political rights, while criticizing the conduct of militant suffragettes as harmful to their cause. His self-identification as a suffragist and his framing of the women's actions as setting back "their cause" (which he supports) makes his overall stance one of support for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states he will vote against the second reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill and devotes the entire speech to arguing that women lack the political capacity, practical knowledge, and fitness required for the franchise, concluding that nature, history, and women's own acceptance of their condition justify excluding them from political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising the Government's foundation hospitals policy, arguing it will create a two-tier NHS and worsen inequality. Women's political rights and representation are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The TARGET speech is almost entirely about vivisection and the composition of the Advisory Committee under the Cruelty to Animals Act, specifically objecting to Sir John Rose Bradford's appointment. The speaker briefly mentions women's suffrage and forcible feeding only to disclaim expertise on the subject ("I understand dogs better than I do women"), making no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly welcomes women "beginning to behave as equals" in their voting behaviour and calls for men to "allow them to do so," while also arguing that true equality requires broader social, legal, and economic changes including equal pay and reform of double standards. The speech consistently advocates for women's fuller civic and social equality.

The speaker addresses the Woman Suffrage question specifically to endorse the "Cat and Mouse" rearrest power as "admirable" and "an excellent plan," and advocates attacking the finances of suffragette organizations to suppress the movement, showing opposition to the suffragette cause rather than support for women's political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Carr) supports the Equal Pay Bill in principle and argues for expanding its scope to include equality of opportunity, removal of restrictions on women's employment, and equal treatment in pensions and taxation. His criticisms are procedural and implementational (timing rigidity, Ministerial intervention, lack of equal opportunity provisions), not opposition to women's equal rights, and he explicitly endorses the underlying goal of advancing women's employment equality.

The speaker consistently and emphatically opposes the women's suffrage bill, arguing that it would "uproot the relations of society," that women lack the political fitness and training for the franchise, citing an American who called women's rights agitation something "fools" would do, and concluding that the bill's arguments are "utterly futile" and that voting for it would be "gross exaggeration" and a betrayal of constitutional principles.

The TARGET speech concerns Sunday closing of public houses and the evils of drunkenness, with no argument about women's political rights or representation. The passing mention of women ("breaking the hearts of thousands...of women") is in the context of temperance reform, not civic participation.

The target speech is a parliamentary answer about police protection at suffragist meetings and a question about the legal authority for releasing remanded prisoners; it reports factual/operational information without arguing for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on arguing against the introduction of secret ballot/secret voting in Parliamentary and municipal elections, addressing issues of electoral corruption, bribery, intimidation, and the nature of the franchise as a public trust. Women's political rights are not argued about; the only passing mention of women is in the phrase "the voter was at all events a trustee for the remaining members of his family, for the women and children," which is incidental to the ballot argument and takes no position on women's political rights.

The speech is about parliamentary procedure and the curtailment of debate on Supply bills, not about women's political rights. The only mention of women is a brief, passing reference to time "wasted over the Women Suffrage Amendment" to the Franchise Bill, used as an example of parliamentary mismanagement without arguing for or against women's suffrage.

The speaker explicitly states "I have always been in favour of the vote for women, and I am still more in favour of it to-day," expressing direct support for women's suffrage. The rest of the speech concerns election expenses, but this clear endorsement of women's political rights places it in scope.

The target speech is entirely focused on abortion law (the 1967 Abortion Act and a proposed amendment), discussing medical opinion, mortality statistics, illegitimacy rates, and the workings of the Act. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation in any form.

The speech is entirely focused on defence policy, military spending, armed forces welfare, procurement, and the Territorial Army. The brief mention of "young men and women" in the Royal Naval unit is purely descriptive and does not argue any position on women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech consists of a procedural parliamentary question about the legal authority for releasing remand prisoners, followed by a question about statistics on early releases of suffrage-related convicts. While it references the Women's Suffrage movement, it does not make any argument for or against women's political rights — it is a factual/administrative inquiry about prison release practices.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill, framing it as addressing human rights and discrimination against women, stating that "marriage is a meeting of equals" and welcoming the removal of inbuilt discrimination against Jewish women in divorce proceedings. While the Bill concerns religious law rather than electoral rights, it directly addresses women's equal civic standing and legal rights relative to men.

The speech concerns widening candidate qualifications for local government generally, mentioning "men and women of all parties" only in passing as a general reference to councillors. There is no argument made about women's political rights, voting rights, or representation as a distinct class.

The speech is primarily about NHS health services, local hospitals in the speaker's constituency, and personal experiences with cancer care. The only mention of women is a brief passing reference to pride in Labour electing 101 women MPs, which does not constitute an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on a procedural/parliamentary point about whether a betting regulation bill (the Racecourse Betting Control Board bill) has been so substantially altered in committee that it constitutes a new bill requiring re-introduction. The only reference to women's political rights is a passing citation of Speaker Lowther's 1913 ruling on the Franchise and Registration Bill as a precedent for parliamentary procedure, not as an argument about women's suffrage or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on procedural objections to a Guillotine Motion allocating insufficient time to debate Scottish and English local government bills, criticising the inadequacy of parliamentary time and differences between the two bills. The reference to "disfranchise thousands of men and women" concerns local government voting rights on education, not women's political rights as a distinct civic category.

The speech is primarily about Scottish fisheries and an Interdepartmental Committee; the only mention of suffragettes is a passing, joking remark with no substantive argument about women's political rights.

The speaker's mention of women voters (regarding whether they would need to remove their bonnets) is a passing practical observation about the Amendment's wording, not an argument for or against women's political rights. The speech is substantively about the practicalities of an anti-personation amendment to a ballot bill.

The target speech focuses entirely on preventing voter personation and criticises a procedural argument about the Amendment; while it notes the Bill applies to voters "male or female," this is incidental context rather than an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on childcare provision and community child-minding groups in deprived areas, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief welcoming remark about parliamentary time devoted to "women's issues" is a passing pleasantry, not an argument about civic participation or political rights.

The speaker (Mr. Heffer) strongly supports equal pay legislation, arguing that women have historically been in a weaker position in industry and that the Bill is necessary to achieve equality of pay and opportunity for women workers. He explicitly condemns opponents of women's equal rights as "dinosaurs" and endorses the principle that women should have equal rights with their fellow workers.

The speech is focused entirely on workmen's compensation reform — increasing payments to dependants of industrial accident victims and reforming the compensation system. While the speaker briefly mentions "women voters" as a political force that helped elect Labour MPs, this is a passing observation about electoral dynamics, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is primarily about abolishing plural voting (the business premises qualification) and only mentions women in passing to explain the mechanics of how the bill extends the business vote to wives — not to argue for or against women's political rights as such.

The speech addresses concerns about illiteracy and disfranchisement under a ballot bill, mentioning female voters only incidentally as an example group alongside working men. No argument is made for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speaker explicitly argues that "there is no reason why the ordinary person in the street, however ill educated, male or female, should not be allowed to express their views on how they are governed," directly affirming women's right to political participation and democratic representation in Afghanistan.

The speech concerns drafting amendments to court administration legislation, specifically removing references to a rule committee and making technical adjustments to justice administration acts. While the Sex Disqualification (Removal) Act 1919 is briefly mentioned, no argument is made about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about UK foreign policy toward Pakistan, India, Kashmir, Afghanistan, Nepal, and Sri Lanka. The brief mention of "more parliamentary seats for women" in Pakistan is a passing factual observation welcoming a development, not a substantive argument for or against women's political rights as a distinct issue.

The speaker (clarifying a previous statement) supports extending the business premises franchise to women on equal terms with men, arguing that equalising voting rights between men and women requires giving women the same plural voting entitlements as men enjoy.

The speaker criticizes the Attorney-General specifically for prosecuting suffragettes and securing "severe punishment and forcible feeding" against them, framing this as a reproach of the Law Officers' conduct. This implicitly sides against the harsh treatment of suffragettes (who were campaigning for women's political rights), but more directly the reference to prosecuting suffragettes is used as a rhetorical device to question the propriety of paying the Law Officers' fees — the speech does not argue for women's political rights and instead treats suffragette prosecution as an example of objectionable government conduct without endorsing their cause.

The speaker (Sir W. Joynson-Hicks) is defending a provision in the Bill that gives women the same plural voting rights as men, arguing that equal treatment of women in regard to voting qualifications was embraced even by the Labour party. The speech supports extending equal political rights to women as part of the broader franchise reform.

The speech is entirely concerned with parliamentary finance procedure, the Parliament Act, the National Insurance Act estimates, and a dispute with the Chancellor of the Exchequer over the propriety of a supplementary estimate. The only mention of women's political rights is a passing, incidental reference ("made me think he had mistaken me for the Colonial Secretary in a Suffrage Debate") with no argument made about women's political rights.

The speech is primarily about economic policy, prices, wages, and the Conservative government's election pledges. The brief mention of "women's lib" and appealing to "housewives" is rhetorical color criticizing the opposition's electoral tactics, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker (Home Secretary McKenna) responds sympathetically to complaints from the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, treats their statement as "moderate and fair," and commits to ensuring police protect those holding peaceful suffragist meetings, implicitly affirming their right to do so.

The TARGET speech is primarily about a legal/administrative grievance regarding a woman's court case and criticism of Scottish officials, with only a passing rhetorical jab calling the right hon. Gentleman "a great suffragette" as an insult rather than making any substantive argument about women's political rights. The mention of suffragette is incidental and does not constitute an argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech consists solely of a parliamentary question by Viscount Wolmer requesting statistical data on arrests connected to the suffragist movement; it makes no argument for or against women's political rights, merely seeking factual information about law enforcement activity.

The speech is primarily about the merits of voting papers versus the ballot system; women's political rights are mentioned only in passing ("In the event, too, of the franchise being extended to women, it was obvious that voting papers would be necessary to enable them to exercise their rights") as a subsidiary practical argument for voting papers, without making any substantive argument for or against women's enfranchisement.

The speaker (Fiona Mactaggart) explicitly urges the Electoral Commission to target women and ethnic minorities to help them understand the electoral system and develop better strategies to participate in it, directly advocating for improved political participation and representation of women.

The speaker explicitly states "I believe that equal franchise should be given to men and women," endorsing women's equal political rights, while the remainder of the speech focuses on defending plural voting on business grounds rather than opposing women's enfranchisement.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over regional assemblies and devolution in England, touching on local democracy, voter fatigue, and constitutional arrangements. The brief mention of "assembly men and women" is purely incidental and makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports making women's voting rights equal to men's in all respects, arguing that women are entitled to the same business-premises vote as men, and frames the entire debate around achieving equal franchise for women. While the speech defends a specific mechanism (plural voting for business premises), its core argument is in favour of equal political rights for women.

The speaker explicitly argues for reforming Parliament to make it more relevant to the public, with particular emphasis on improving female representation, and challenges a colleague who dismisses this concern. This is a clear, if brief, endorsement of greater women's political representation.

The speech is primarily about national insurance benefits and contributions (a Social Security Bill), with no substantive argument for or against women's political rights or representation. The only mention of women is a passing reference to the differential retirement age between men and women (60 vs. 65), framed as an administrative anomaly in the national insurance system rather than an argument about women's civic or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the debate over UK entry into the EEC, covering economic, monetary, sovereignty, and foreign policy arguments. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women back into jobs") without any argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly dismisses the claim that changing parliamentary hours benefits women, stating "Let us get rid of the idea that these proposals are intended to benefit the female of the species. Nothing proposed by male parliamentarians is for the benefit of the female of the species" and "Changing the hours will do nothing to change the representation of women in this place; no artificial means will do that." She argues against structural/artificial measures to increase women's representation, instead asserting that the only way forward is persuading constituents of candidates' capability — opposing proactive representation measures.

The TARGET speech briefly reports a supporter's argument that giving women votes is the best remedy for instability in France, and that 121 women present could demolish the main speech made against the Bill — framing their testimony as a case for women's suffrage. The division list also records 151 Ayes (supporters of the Bill), though the overall vote defeated it.

The speaker explicitly states that "we on this side of the House care very much indeed that women should obtain the vote" and commits to supporting the Bill's Third Reading regardless of the amendment outcome. While the bulk of the speech argues against a specific form of plural voting (wives voting on husbands' business qualifications), this is framed as a pro-women's-suffrage argument — that women deserve to vote "as human beings" on qualifications they possess in their own right, not as a "fancy franchise" tied to their husbands.

The speech is an administrative response by a Home Office minister about the availability of statistics on suffragist arrests and prison commitments. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights, merely addressing procedural and data-availability questions.

The speaker (Mr. Weitzman) explicitly argues that women are unfairly excluded from jury service due to the householder qualification, citing that only 11% of available jurors are women, and urges the Government to amend the Bill now to implement the Morris Committee's recommendation of using the parliamentary electoral register as the qualification — a reform that would substantially expand women's civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Industrial Training Levy (Road Transport) Order 1970, criticising the Road Transport Industry Training Board's cost management, bureaucracy, and levy structure. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The TARGET speech concerns a procedural ruling by the Speaker on whether a petition from George Lansbury can be immediately debated, relating to his imprisonment for speeches supporting Women's Suffrage. While Women's Suffrage is mentioned as the background reason for Lansbury's legal troubles, the speech itself makes no argument for or against women's political rights, focusing entirely on parliamentary procedure regarding petition presentation and discussion.

The speaker explicitly argues that the Amendment in question "gives equality between the sexes and equal rights to men and women to vote on the same register," and advocates for it as the measure that achieves genuine equality. This is a clear endorsement of equal political rights for women.

The target speech addresses only the administrative matter of pay scales for prison medical officers, explicitly denying any connection to suffragette prisoners. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the Ballot Bill and its consequences for the franchise and electoral system, including arguments about manhood suffrage and party coercion. The one mention of women ("women and minors—affected by the laws, by taxation") is a quotation from Lord Palmerston used to argue that votes are trusts rather than rights, with no argument made for or against women's political rights.

The speech concerns a debate about a clause in an immigration bill relating to voluntary repatriation assistance for non-patrial immigrants, focusing on race relations and the potential misuse of government power. Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about at any point.

The TARGET speech debates the Deceased Wife's Sister marriage bill — a marriage law reform question — making arguments about religious law, social morality, and public opinion. It does not address women's political rights, the franchise, representation, or any aspect of women's civic participation.

The speaker (Mr. Bishop, Newark) explicitly argues against discrimination against women in the Civil Service, advocates for equal recruitment opportunities regardless of sex, calls for women to be allowed into more responsible roles, and frames the removal of barriers to women's advancement as a top priority — consistently supporting women's equal civic and professional participation throughout the speech.

The speaker acknowledges the under-representation of women in Parliament and as candidates as a genuine problem, and notes that the Electoral Commission has engaged the Equal Opportunities Commission to explore areas of common interest, including potential research projects and pilot initiatives that could address women's participation in political life.

The speech concerns prison administration, the Young Offenders' Committee recommendations, Borstal institutions, and related criminal justice matters. Women are mentioned only incidentally alongside men ("young men and women," "boys and girls") in the context of sentencing and reform, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech covers a wide range of topics including flooding, hunting, housing, antisocial behaviour, and devolution, with only a brief passing mention that the Welsh Assembly has "better representation of women" as an incidental positive of devolution. No substantive argument is made for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech is an extensive debate on the Ballot Bill (secret voting) concerning electoral corruption, bribery, undue influence, and election reform. Women's political rights are never argued for or against; the only tangential reference appears in the CONTEXT (following speech by Mr. Gathorne Hardy, not the TARGET), where Gladstone's views on female suffrage are briefly mentioned. The TARGET itself contains no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech focuses entirely on the probation and after-care service, specifically pay negotiations, staffing levels, and the case for non-custodial penalties. Women are not mentioned as a distinct class with respect to political rights or civic participation, and no argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech addresses the closure of Holyrood Palace due to damage caused by militant suffragists, and explains visitor access rules. It mentions the suffragist movement only as a factual explanation for the closure, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a wide-ranging adjournment debate contribution covering housing, volunteerism, consumer credit, organophosphates, water poisoning, NHS decentralisation, and wind farms. The single mention of "women's institutes" is purely incidental (noting registration charges affect voluntary organisations) and makes no argument about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker (Lady Hermon) explicitly notes it is "disappointing that female and ethnic minority under-representation in the judiciary seems to have been largely overlooked in the Bill," signalling support for greater female representation in judicial appointments. She also endorses appointments based on merit while criticising the oversight of women's representation, placing her broadly in favour of women's political and civic inclusion.

The opening speaker (Mr. William Fowler) explicitly argues that the Contagious Diseases Acts are unconstitutional and unjust because they apply only to women, stating "Women were obliged to submit because they had no votes" and that the law of the stronger oppresses women who lack political power—framing the Acts' one-sided application as a denial of women's civic equality. This is a substantive argument in favor of women's rights as a class.

The speech is entirely focused on unemployment, regional economic policy, the cost of living, and criticism of the Conservative Government's economic record. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "men and women to earn a living," "individual men and women to earn and save"), with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the merits and deficiencies of the Elementary Education Act of 1870, debating denominational vs. secular schooling, the 25th clause, compulsory attendance, and religious instruction. Women's political rights or representation are never mentioned or argued about.

The target speech concerns the conduct and intemperate language of Judge Keogh in the Galway election petition case, clerical influence on elections, and parliamentary procedure regarding censuring vs. removing a judge. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation anywhere in the speech.

The speech concerns a parliamentary debate about whether to censure or remove Judge Keogh following the Galway Election Petition, focusing on priestly/clerical undue influence in an Irish election. It does not address women's political rights, the franchise for women, women's representation, or any related civic status of women.

The speech is entirely focused on the Iraq crisis debate — specifically criticising the Prime Minister's failure to build public trust and make the case for military action against Iraq. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., "retired army officers and their wives" and "innocent Iraqi women and children") without any argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely about corporal punishment (flogging) in the criminal justice system. The only mention of women is a passing reference to "the breaking of windows by suffragettes" as one of many offences for which flogging has been proposed, cited to illustrate the absurdity of expanding corporal punishment — no argument about women's political rights is made.
