The speech concerns National Insurance regulations for divorced and widowed women's pension entitlements — a social security/welfare matter. While it addresses women's financial benefits, it does not argue for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or other civic participation rights that fall within the scope of women's political rights.

The Secretary of State (Tessa Jowell) defends "political correctness" by drawing an analogy to the suffragettes, implying that dismissing progressive causes as merely "politically correct" is historically mistaken and that the suffragettes' cause was legitimate and worthy of respect — a clear implicit endorsement of women's political rights.
The speech is a parliamentary business announcement that merely schedules a Second Reading discussion on the Women Suffrage Bill without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues that if equality between the sexes is to be observed, there is no reason why women should not receive the same business-premises vote as men, explicitly supporting extending this political right to women voters ("I see no reason whatever why a woman should not be allowed to have a vote in respect of her husband's business").

The speech concerns the legal principles governing damages awarded to widows under the Fatal Accidents Acts, specifically whether a widow's remarriage should be taken into account when assessing damages. It does not make any argument for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech focuses on unemployment, migration policy, imperialism, and the political manipulation of workers' votes through geographic transfers — it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation. The mentions of "men and women" are incidental references to workers/voters as a general class, not arguments about women's distinctive civic status.

The speaker (Jacob Bright) moves the second reading of a Bill to grant parliamentary votes to women who are property owners and occupiers, arguing at length that women deserve political representation, that enfranchisement would remedy legal grievances, and that the growth of public support demonstrates the justice of the cause.

The speaker celebrates the suffragette movement, honours Emmeline Pankhurst, notes the limited number of women elected to Parliament and serving in Cabinet as a shortcoming, and explicitly supports changes to make it easier for women to stand for election and play a full part in public life.

The speech is entirely focused on Scottish licensing reform (the Temperance/Local Veto Bill), debating issues such as the Parliament Act, compensation/insurance for licence holders, time notices, and local option voting thresholds. The brief passing mention of Women Suffrage is used only as an analogy to illustrate that Liberal Members accepted pledges they never expected to have to honour, without making any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues forcefully for reforming jury qualification to include all citizens on the electoral register, explicitly criticising the current system that excludes most women from jury service and expressing strong sympathy with women's organisations who seek equal access to this civic duty.

The speech is almost entirely about Welsh Church Disestablishment and Disendowment, arguing against the Welsh Church Bill. The single passing reference to "suffragettes" and "letting the suffragettes in and out of prison" is a brief rhetorical aside disparaging the Home Secretary, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on higher education policy, polytechnic funding, university planning, teacher training, and the Open University. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., references to female MPs like Miss Fookes and Miss Lestor in procedural or collegial contexts), with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker systematically rebuts opponents' arguments against women's suffrage, defends the Bill's supporters, argues that women are fully capable of political participation, and explicitly seconds the motion for the second reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill, calling for removal of the "intolerable stigma" denying women the parliamentary franchise.

Mr. Maguire explicitly and wholeheartedly supports Jacob Bright's Bill to extend the parliamentary franchise to single women and widows, systematically refuting opponents' arguments about women's unsuitability for political participation, and concluding "I support the Bill with all my heart." His caveat about opposing the franchise for married women is a scoping limitation consistent with the Bill itself, not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (the Home Secretary's reply plus Mr. Malone's follow-up question) concerns only the administrative question of how women electors are designated on electoral registers (Mrs. vs. Miss), not any argument about women's right to vote or political representation. The exchange treats women's enfranchisement as a settled fact and debates only a clerical/labelling matter.

The TARGET speech is by the Home Secretary defending the permanent (rather than temporary) nature of the Bill allowing conditional release of prisoners, mentioning suffragist prisoners only incidentally as one example of the circumstances the Bill addresses. The speech does not argue for or against women's political rights; it focuses entirely on the administrative and legal question of whether the release mechanism should be temporary or permanent legislation.

The speaker explicitly supports implementing the Morris Committee recommendations, framing it as "a great victory for female equality" and stating "It will be a great day for women when it is implemented," endorsing equal jury representation for women as a civic right.

The speech concerns a tax allowance amendment for single women supporting dependent relatives, which is a welfare/tax policy matter. It does not address women's right to vote, stand for office, political representation, or any other aspect of women's civic participation. The speaker's identity as a woman MP is incidental background, not an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker celebrates the Women's Social and Political Union's legacy and Emmeline Pankhurst's activism, highlights government actions to support women in public life, and references efforts to encourage more women to enter public life — all expressing support for women's political participation and rights.

The speaker explicitly argues that abolishing elected boards of guardians and replacing them with co-opted committees will harm women's representation in public life, noting that 2,250 women serve on boards of guardians compared to only 235 on county councils, and that "you are excluding women by changing the basis of appointment." This is a substantive argument in favour of preserving women's political participation and representation.

Viscountess Astor's interjection ("do women really care what they are called so long as they are voters?") presupposes and affirms women's status as voters, treating their enfranchisement as the important thing. The preceding question about a mother and daughter sharing a name is a procedural concern about the electoral register, and Astor's reply dismisses fussing over designations in favour of what matters: that women have the vote.

The speaker presents a petition explicitly arguing for women's suffrage, laying out multiple substantive reasons why women deserve the right to vote, including their equal obligations under the law, their demonstrated public competence, and the injustices of an exclusively male electorate. The act of presenting this petition and requesting it be read into the record constitutes clear support for women's political rights.

The speaker argues that co-opted committees should include a proportional representation of women, citing the disparity between women on county/borough councils (335) versus boards of guardians (2,300), and expresses concern that women will be underrepresented on the proposed committees. This is a substantive argument in favour of women's representation in public office/local governance.

The speaker (Mr. Bouverie) explicitly moves the rejection of the Bill to grant women the parliamentary vote, arguing at length that women themselves oppose it, that the petitions are unrepresentative, that women's grievances do not require enfranchisement, that granting women the vote would lead to women outvoting men and governing the country, and that the theory of marriage and religion both support male governance over female — all substantive arguments against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports the second reading of the Bill and makes sustained arguments in favour of women's parliamentary franchise: that women already vote in municipal and school board elections, that they are taxed, that they are well-educated and capable, and that their exclusion is illogical. He systematically rebuts arguments against women's suffrage (the "pedestal" argument, claims about domestic disunion, alleged lack of logic) and concludes by calling for equal political rights for women.

The speech is primarily about diplomatic service pensions versus working-class pensions, arguing against preferential treatment for the upper class. The brief mention of women concerns a pension bill for elderly working-class women that was blocked, used as an example of class injustice in pension policy — it does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly and at length opposes the Women's Disabilities Removal Bill, arguing that natural differences between the sexes justify the existing exclusion of women from political life, that enfranchisement would impose burdensome duties on women rather than benefit them, and that the bill would ultimately destabilize society. He concludes: "I am against 'woman's rights,' because I wish to maintain woman's privileges."

The speaker explicitly supports women's political participation and representation, noting approvingly that Eritrea has 22% women MPs with a 30% quota, describing her work "developing political and economic capacity for women," and framing women's civic and economic rights as essential to development. She calls on the Government to continue investing in schemes that promote women's rights, economy, and justice.

The speech is entirely about industrial training levies for the air transport and travel industry, arguing for maintaining higher levy rates and the board's independence. Women's political rights are never mentioned or implicated.

The speech concerns the UK Government's diplomatic efforts regarding Amina Lawal's death sentence under Nigeria's sharia law, framed as a human rights and foreign policy matter. While women are the subject of the discussion, the speech does not address women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation in any way.

The speaker (Keir Hardie) defends the Women's Social and Political Union's right to hold public meetings, argues against police suppression of those meetings, and explicitly warns that coercive measures will drive people to support "the women's movement" — framing women's political activism as a legitimate right deserving protection equal to that afforded male labour leaders.

The speaker explicitly disclaims any intention to exclude women from committee representation and invokes his party's strong support for "the women's cause," but opposes co-option on fiscal accountability grounds — a procedural/structural objection, not opposition to women's political participation. The substantive stance expressed is supportive of women's representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the British steel industry — its financial difficulties, investment needs, nationalisation, privatisation, and industrial structure. Women are mentioned only once in passing ("the men and women who are devoting their talents and efforts to the industry"), with no argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly celebrates and honours the suffrage movement—both the militant and constitutionalist wings—crediting them with winning women's right to vote and to stand as candidates, affirms those rights as essential ("I would not have the right to vote, let alone the right to stand as a candidate, if it were not for such women"), and calls on women parliamentarians to continue advancing women's equality, including through the Fawcett Society commission on gender fairness in the criminal justice system.

The speech is entirely about council housing policy, affordability, and housing development in the Braintree constituency. While the speaker briefly mentions the Minister's title ("Deputy Minister for Women"), no argument about women's political rights or representation is made anywhere in the speech.

The speaker argues that militant suffragists who preach disorder and incitement to lawbreaking should not be allowed to hold meetings in public parks, effectively supporting restrictions on suffrage movement activity. While he notes there is "nothing to prevent" suffragists from using private halls, his overall argument is that the Home Secretary was right to suppress their public meetings, opposing the suffrage movement's exercise of political advocacy.

The speech concerns a procedural amendment to transfer decision-making authority over prisoner release from the Secretary of State to a High Court judge. While it mentions suffragettes in passing as context, the argument is entirely about administrative/judicial machinery and political impartiality, not about women's political rights or representation.

Sir Charles Adderley explicitly states he supports the Bill on the grounds that property should not be disfranchised merely because it is held by women, arguing that representation is based on property rather than intellectual capacity. While he dismisses arguments about women's intellectual fitness, his conclusion is a clear endorsement of women's property-based enfranchisement.

The target speech (by the Home Secretary McKenna) is focused on defending the police order banning WSPU meetings on grounds of public disorder and the advocacy of crime, not on arguing for or against women's political rights. The speech treats the militant women's meetings as a law-and-order matter, without making any substantive argument about women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in civic life.

The speech is entirely focused on rating relief policy for agriculture and productive industry in Scotland, arguing that the Government's financial resolution fails to adequately help agriculture or ordinary ratepayers. There is no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker describes the Government as "keen to promote equality for women" and expresses pleasure at the ordination of 2,000 women clergy, framing this as a positive development in women's civic and professional participation. The speech implicitly supports anti-discrimination protections for women clergy by positioning the Government favorably toward gender equality.

Chamberlain explicitly supports women's inclusion in the new public assistance committees and guardians' committees, stating the Bill mandates that co-opted members "must also be women," that he is "counting very largely upon the assistance of women," and that he anticipates women will stand for election to these local government bodies. This constitutes a positive endorsement of women's participation in public office.

The speech is entirely focused on the procedural question of whether the Home Secretary or a judge should have authority over conditional prisoner release under the "Cat and Mouse Bill," with suffragettes mentioned only incidentally as one example of prisoners. The speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely concerned with the debate over the Revised Prayer Book — matters of Church doctrine, Reservation, vestments, and the relationship between Parliament and the Church of England. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic status of women.

The TARGET speech focuses almost entirely on agricultural labor conditions, the Factories Act, wages, cottages, the truck/cider system, and the county vs. borough franchise for rural householders (male laborers). Women's political rights are not argued for or against; women appear only incidentally as part of the agricultural labor force being discussed.

The speaker explicitly supports women's participation in local government bodies, arguing that women "can and will in the days to come play their part and face an election" and that the Labour party is "as anxious for a fair number of women to be on these local government bodies as any other party." The speaker frames the elimination of co-option as no threat to women's representation, asserting that women's enfranchisement on equal terms with men means they will naturally take their place on these bodies through democratic election.

The speech concerns procedural objections to the programme motion for a hunting Bill and the potential use of the Parliament Act, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The mention of "men and women" losing jobs is a generic reference to constituents, not an argument about women's civic status.

The first speaker (Mr. Beresford Hope) opposes the Bill throughout, arguing that women's very qualities unfit them for politics, that the agitation is "narrow, fictitious, and noisy," and that women's enfranchisement would lead to dangerous consequences. The second speaker (The Attorney General) explicitly supports the Bill, arguing women are at least as fit for the franchise as uneducated men and that justice requires granting it. However, the TARGET as a whole is dominated by Mr. Beresford Hope's lengthy opposition, and the Attorney General's contribution is duplicated in the following speeches context, meaning the TARGET contains two speakers — one firmly against and one firmly for. Treating the TARGET as a whole (per instructions), the two positions create a "both" classification, but the first speaker's opposition is the primary substantive argument of the TARGET speech, and the Attorney General's section is also substantive in support. Given the instructions to classify the TARGET as a whole when it contains multiple speakers, and the fact that one speaker is clearly against and the other clearly for, this is a "both" classification.

The speech is entirely concerned with the Common Market/EEC negotiations, parliamentary procedure for debating entry terms, and related economic issues (sugar, agriculture, fisheries, New Zealand). Women's political rights are not mentioned or argued about anywhere in the speech.

The speaker advocates for women in common law partnerships to be included in consultations about pension rights, highlighting a specific legal disadvantage they face — implicitly supporting measures to protect and improve women's civic and economic standing.

The speech is primarily about opposing the £4,000 pension for the former Speaker in the context of working-class poverty. The brief mention of reduced unemployment benefit for "young women" is incidental and does not constitute an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is primarily about extending the parliamentary franchise to rural county householders (agricultural labourers), with extensive discussion of factory legislation, cottage conditions, truck/cider wages, and game laws. While the speaker briefly mentions women's suffrage advocates as a rhetorical comparison ("no subject had been debated with less of political animus...than that of removing the electoral disabilities of women"), this is used purely as an analogy to suggest his own cause can be pursued without bitterness — he makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is a procedural ruling by the Deputy Speaker correcting an administrative error in the Order Paper regarding the scheduling of the Retirement Income Reform Bill, with only an incidental mention of the Female Genital Mutilation Bill as a scheduling reference. No argument about women's political rights or representation is made.

The speech concerns an amendment to ballot paper rules, arguing that voters should not be disfranchised for ignorance or inadvertence in marking their ballot. The mention of women is purely statistical (literacy rates), not an argument about women's political rights or their fitness for civic participation.

The speech is entirely focused on procedural arguments about the allocation of parliamentary time (guillotine motion, Committee and Report stage days) for a Bill relating to trade unions and industrial relations. The reference to "men and women" affected by the Bill is incidental and does not address women's political rights or representation.

The speech by the Member for Dorset, West is entirely focused on naval defence policy: Royal Navy manpower levels, submarine strategy, Soviet naval expansion, NATO commitments, and the Mediterranean/Indian Ocean strategic outlook. The only mention of women is a passing statistical reference to "3,500 women" as part of the 87,000 Royal Navy manpower figure, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speech is entirely focused on primary education spending in Lincolnshire, local government reorganisation, and firearms legislation. The brief mention of "single women" teachers in village schools is incidental and descriptive, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is entirely devoted to licensing and public house regulation — closing hours, adulteration, penalties, magistrates' licensing authority, grocers' licenses, and habitual drunkards — with no argument made for or against women's political rights or representation. Women are mentioned only incidentally (e.g., wives buying spirits at grocers), not in the context of civic participation or political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on whether a judge or the Home Secretary should decide on the conditional release of hunger-striking prisoners under the "Cat and Mouse Bill," a procedural/administrative question. Suffragettes are mentioned only incidentally as examples of prisoners; no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.
The speaker explicitly endorses Qatar being the first Gulf state to give women the vote, stating "something we strongly support," expressing clear support for women's political rights.

The speech concerns mountain rescue units and government support for voluntary rescue teams in Scotland. It makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or any related civic participation issue; the mention of "men and women" refers only to rescue volunteers.

The speaker explicitly states that any interim administration and system of government in Iraq should be "genuinely representative of Iraq as a whole, including women, and will not create disfranchised minorities on religious or ethnic lines," directly advocating for women's political representation and inclusion in Iraq's governance.

The speech is entirely about industrial picketing law and trade union rights, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "women and children" refers to workers' family members in the context of trade union history, not to women's civic or political status.

The speaker's argument is focused on the drafting and scope of the Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill as permanent criminal law applying to all prisoners, explicitly urging the Committee to set aside the "suffragette" context and consider the bill's broader implications. While suffragettes are mentioned as context, no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech is focused on opposing the "cat-and-mouse" Bill (the Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill Health) Act) on procedural and practical grounds, criticising the Home Secretary's arguments about prisoner release powers. While suffragette hunger strikers are the context, the speaker makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights; the brief mention of "the aims of the suffragist" is cut off and no position on those aims is stated.

The target speech (by Sir James Elphinstone and then Mr. Henley and Mr. Otway) concerns the Contagious Diseases Acts — a public health/regulatory measure — debating their medical efficacy and repeal. While women are mentioned as subjects of the legislation, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, right to vote, stand for office, or civic representation.

The speaker (Mr. Pethick-Lawrence) explicitly argues that unemployed insured men and women should be treated on "precisely the same footing" in the unemployment formula, opposing any sex differentiation. He further criticizes as "absurd and ridiculous" the government's proposal to count an unemployed woman as only one-tenth of an unemployed man, especially given that equal franchise had already been granted, advocating that men and women be equal in the formula.

Mr. Jacob Bright explicitly argues that the degrading legislation "could only be passed by a Parliament in which women had no representation," implying women deserve political representation. He also criticizes the proposed replacement bill for applying provisions only to women while exempting men, framing this inequality as an injustice — a substantive argument for women's equal civic standing.

The speaker (Jacqui Smith) explicitly endorses recommendations for apprenticeships, shadowing, mentoring, and expense provisions to ensure women are appointed to public bodies and can put themselves forward, directly supporting increased representation of women in public life.

The speaker explicitly advocates for making it financially possible for "the man or woman" of any economic background to serve as county councillors, invoking universal suffrage and arguing that payment for lost time is essential to enable working-class individuals to participate in local and national public office. This is a direct argument for expanding women's (and men's) political representation and civic participation.

The speaker explicitly and extensively advocates for women's equal rights in employment, training, and promotion, championing an Anti-Discrimination Bill and citing numerous cases of sex discrimination as "intolerable." He argues that without such legislation, equal pay legislation would be meaningless, and he supports women's full civic and professional participation throughout.

The speaker argues that the Bill's broad discretionary powers for the Home Secretary would make it too easy to release suffragist prisoners, undermining deterrence, and explicitly states that giving women the vote or allowing suffragist political pressure to influence releases would be dangerous — framing women's suffrage as a threat to good governance rather than a legitimate cause, despite a token acknowledgment of sympathy with suffragist aims.

The speaker presents a petition explicitly calling on the House of Commons to enfranchise working women, arguing that their exclusion from citizenship rights is "detrimental to the nation" and that "justice demands political freedom for men and women alike." The act of presenting and endorsing this petition constitutes a clear stance in favour of women's political rights.

The speech focuses entirely on the technical legal scope of the "Cat and Mouse Bill" — specifically whether the Home Secretary's power to release prisoners should be limited to cases of serious illness or be broader discretionary power. While the bill was prompted by suffragette hunger strikes, the speaker's argument is purely about the proper legal limits of the legislation and makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Brooke and the Countess of Iveagh) concerns a widows' pensions bill — a social welfare/insurance policy debate. The Countess of Iveagh's passing remark wondering whether solicitude for widows would have been as great "in those days when women had no direct means of placing their views before us" acknowledges women's enfranchisement but does not argue for or against women's political rights. The debate is about pension policy, not women's civic participation or political representation.

The first unnamed speaker explicitly opposes the Bill, arguing that giving women the vote would lead to revolutionary consequences, undermine the Constitution, and destroy domestic comfort. Osborne Morgan also opposes it, arguing that English women don't want the franchise and that its advocates are a small group of fanatics.

The TARGET speech by Mr. Hore-Belisha is almost entirely focused on naval matters: marriage allowance for officers, pay and pensions, promotion from the lower deck, dockyard employment, and democratic rights of Navy personnel. The brief mention of "the very year chosen to enfranchise women" is purely incidental context for his complaint about curtailment of naval democratic rights, with no argument made for or against women's political rights themselves.

The TARGET speech (Mr. Bouverie's conclusion followed by Mr. Scourfield's speech) argues substantively against women's political rights: Bouverie contends that governing "is not woman's work," that women would be subjected to unpleasant political pressures, that the old system is preferable, and that granting women the vote would inevitably require extending all political powers to them; Scourfield seconds the amendment rejecting the Bill, argues most women oppose it, mocks the prospect of a female Speaker, and urges women to rely on "natural attractions" rather than "dreamy illusions of political power."

The speech concerns an amendment to limit the retrospective period for widow's pensions under a social insurance bill, focusing on administrative costs and investigative burdens. The brief mention of the age-30 threshold for women's votes is a passing analogy to illustrate the arbitrariness of age limits, not an argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on Northern Ireland Assembly elections, resignation procedures, and the legality of election postponement legislation. The brief mention of the "Women's Coalition" is only as a political party in the Assembly context, not as an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Northern Ireland Assembly politics, legal challenges, consultation processes, and IRA decommissioning. The brief mentions of the "Women's Coalition" are references to a political party in Northern Ireland, not arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is focused entirely on a drafting amendment to the "Cat and Mouse" (Prisoners' Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill, arguing that "conduct" should be replaced with "wilful misconduct." While suffragists are mentioned briefly as context, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights; the substantive debate is purely about the legal wording of the bill.

The speaker explicitly states he cannot support the Bill, objecting that it goes beyond the principle of representation of property by extending the franchise to women on the same qualifications as men, indicating he only conditionally supported the narrower property-based proposition the previous year.

Mr. Dowse explicitly states he intends to vote against the Bill and argues substantively against women's political rights, contending that the Bill is bad in form and substance, that women do not desire the franchise, and that he does not wish to see women "placed in a different sphere to that which they now occupied," opposing even the slippery slope toward female MPs, judges, and ministers.

The speaker raises the risk of intimidation in home-based postal voting, explicitly noting that women are among those most likely to be affected, and implicitly argues that the traditional ballot booth system better protects women's ability to vote freely and in safety. This is a substantive argument in support of women's secure exercise of the franchise.

The speaker (Miss Wilkinson) argues that British women, having already been granted the vote on equal terms with men and being "equal citizens," should not lose their nationality upon marrying a foreigner, framing this as a matter of equal civic status and rights for women. The entire speech advocates for expanding women's legal rights as citizens.

The speech is a detailed critique of the Widows', Orphans', and Old Age Contributory Pensions Amendment Bill, focused on insurance principles, cost, and consistency of Labour's electoral pledges. While women (widows) are mentioned as beneficiaries of pension provisions, the speech makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speech is primarily about the security situation in Northern Ireland and the speaker's lack of confidence in the government's handling of it. The brief references to women (the Bogside women's peace initiative, suffragettes, and female heads of government) are used rhetorically to dismiss wishful thinking about a women-led peace movement, but the speaker makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker celebrates the equal representation of women and men in the Welsh Assembly, attributes this to Labour's positive action, and explicitly requests a debate on women's representation to learn lessons — all of which clearly supports women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on criticising Land Taxes, land valuation practices, and their effect on the building trade and speculative builders. The single passing mention of suffragettes (burning a cricket pavilion) is incidental and does not argue any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states they will vote against the Amendment because it is "unfair and unjust that women should not be placed in the same category as men" in unemployment, arguing women should be counted equally with men in the unemployment formula for public relief purposes.

The speech is primarily about the merits and drawbacks of referendums in the context of the Common Market debate. The brief mention of Switzerland taking "several generations" to concede votes for women through the referendum is used as evidence that referendums are a brake on social progress, not as an argument about women's political rights per se.

The TARGET speech concerns labour regulation in mining (restricting women's employment above and below ground), not women's political rights such as voting, holding office, or civic representation. The reference to Jacob Bright as a "champion of women" is a rhetorical jab about labour policy inconsistency, not an argument about political rights.

The speaker explicitly calls for "a greater role for the women of Iraq" and "free elections with a wider electorate" in the long-term planning for post-war Iraq, directly advocating for women's political participation and representation.

The TARGET speech is primarily about arguments for and against holding a referendum on EEC membership, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of Asquith's opposition to votes for women is used purely as a historical analogy to illustrate that the same rhetorical arguments used against referenda were previously used against extending democratic rights generally — the speaker does not argue a substantive position on women's suffrage itself.

The target speech is about whether women should be prohibited from working in mines, not about women's political rights (voting, standing for office, representation, etc.). While it touches on women's economic freedom, it does not argue about their civic participation or political rights.

The speaker argues that the Bill's language mirrors that which gave women the municipal vote, and that married women would therefore be excluded — directly addressing the objection that the Bill might enfranchise married women and indicating his support for the Bill proceeding. He suggests any remaining concerns about married women could be resolved in Committee, showing support for the Bill's passage.

The speaker explicitly invokes the suffragettes as a positive example of justified civil disobedience, arguing that women would not have the vote today if suffragettes had not broken the law, and credits their actions (chaining themselves to railings, throwing themselves under horses) with producing the current female Deputy Speaker. This is a clear endorsement of the suffragette cause and, by extension, women's political rights.

The speech concerns a Private Member's Bill about early retirement pensions and extended holidays as a response to technological unemployment. While women are mentioned briefly in passing (e.g., "men and women became members of the Labour Party," retirement age figures for women), the speech makes no substantive argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The TARGET speech is a ruling by the Speaker on points of order, directing Mr. M'Curdy to stay relevant to the Bill (concerning treatment of prisoners) rather than canvassing the general question of Women Suffrage. The Speaker takes no substantive position for or against women's political rights.

The speaker argues against the Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill by defending suffragist prisoners, reading their own words sympathetically, characterizing them as politically motivated rather than criminal or hysterical, and explicitly endorsing the legitimacy of women's demand for the franchise and their inability to obtain constitutional redress—actively advocating for women's political rights throughout.

The speaker explicitly calls for provisions to increase the representation of women and ethnic minorities on the Sentencing Guidelines Council, arguing that its non-judicial members should better reflect the community. This is a direct argument in favour of greater women's political/civic representation.

The speech is entirely focused on armed forces matters including ethnic minority recruitment, bullying, welfare, insurance, and reservist issues. While it occasionally mentions "men and women" in the forces, it makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the constitutional propriety and historical precedents for a referendum on UK entry into the Common Market. The brief mention of Winston Churchill's suggestion of "a referendum of women on the question of votes for women" is purely incidental, used as a historical example to support the broader argument about referendum precedents, without arguing any position on women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly states he does not propose to say "a single word with regard to the merits of Women Suffrage in any shape or form," and confines himself to summarizing the procedural history of women's constitutional attempts to advance their cause, in the context of arguing against a specific bill on prisoner treatment. No substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speech concerns workplace safety regulations for women operating threshing machinery — an industrial labour/safety matter — not women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation. While women are singled out as a class, the subject is occupational hazard protection, not their distinctive civic status or political rights.

The speaker warns that placing women with the municipal franchise on the same register as Parliamentary voters would give "women's suffrage agitators a great advantage," framing this as a "blot" in the Bill — indicating opposition to advancing women's political rights.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Chamberlain) concerns the mechanics of block grants versus percentage grants for maternity and child welfare services, the powers of the Minister over local authorities, and protections for voluntary associations. It makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely focused on the merits of percentage grants versus block grants for health services (maternity, child welfare, tuberculosis, venereal disease, mental deficiency, etc.) under the Local Government Bill. While it mentions women's organisations and female workers in the context of voluntary societies, it makes no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political participation, stating "we need more diversity in the House" and that women should be encouraged to stand for Parliament and take senior roles. She also supports female participation in the political process in Afghanistan and frames women's equality as a continuing goal requiring cultural and attitudinal change.

The speaker (Mr. M'Curdy) extensively defends the women suffragists' conduct, portrays their militant tactics as a rational response to the Government's repeated failures to give Women Suffrage a fair hearing, and argues that granting women fair treatment on the franchise question would render the oppressive Bill unnecessary — implicitly endorsing the legitimacy of their political cause.

The speaker (Home Secretary McKenna) characterizes suffragist prisoners as having "declared war on society," dismisses their accounts of suffering as propaganda designed to "enrage public opinion," and frames the Bill as a tool to prevent women from evading lawful punishment for offences committed in pursuit of women's suffrage. While he does not explicitly debate the merits of women's suffrage, he treats the suffragist campaign as a threat to public order and proposes legislative measures specifically aimed at curtailing their ability to use hunger strikes to escape imprisonment, reflecting a stance opposed to the political activities and implicitly the claims of the women's suffrage movement.

The speaker (Mr. Jacob Bright) forcefully argues that the Contagious Diseases Acts are unjust because they subject women alone to police surveillance, compulsory examination, and reputational damage while men escape scrutiny entirely — explicitly framing this as unequal and unjust legislation "between men and women." He advocates for the repeal of these Acts and moves to reduce the funding for their enforcement, clearly supporting women's equal civic standing and protection from discriminatory state power.

The speech by the MP for Liverpool, Walton is entirely focused on the nature of law and order, the distinction between "society law" and "class law," industrial relations, trade union picketing, and rising crime. The brief mention of suffragettes is purely illustrative of the general historical argument that people have broken unjust laws to extend rights, with no substantive argument made for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equal representation in politics and public life, advocates for encouraging women to stand for Parliament, and argues for continued progress toward female equality across multiple domains including political participation. The speech endorses women's right to vote and hold office as achievements not to be forgotten, and calls for further advancement of women's status in public and political life.

The speech is entirely focused on London transport policy — specifically the proposed combination of tramway and omnibus services under private control versus municipal control. While the speaker mentions "men and women" as users of public transport in passing, no argument about women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation is made.

The speaker (Mr. M'Curdy) argues that suffragist women are reasonable people who responded to constitutional repression, defending their cause and implying that granting fair treatment to Women Suffrage would render the Bill unnecessary. He consistently frames the women's militant actions as a direct response to the Government's failure to honour pledges on Women Suffrage, effectively advocating for their political rights as the proper remedy.

The speech is primarily about student grant regulations, inflation, halls of residence charges, parental contributions, and student behaviour. The brief mention of the married women's grant discusses its low level and the speaker's sympathy for improving it, but this is a welfare/financial aid policy matter (student grants) rather than an argument about women's civic or political rights and representation.

The speech is entirely focused on Poor Law administration, the conduct of appointed commissioners versus elected guardians, and the treatment of the poor in West Ham and Walthamstow. While it mentions "men and women" in the context of public service and poverty, it makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on European security, Soviet military threats, NATO strategy, and the proposed European security conference. Women are not mentioned in any substantive way related to political rights or representation; the brief reference to "men and women" is simply describing East European refugees in the speaker's constituency.

The speaker explicitly supports women's political participation and representation, praising the British Council's programme to increase women in politics, advocating for more elected women in Tanzania and the UK reaching the 30% Beijing target, and celebrating women MPs' work in east and central Africa. The speech consistently frames women's entry into politics as a positive goal worth advancing.

The target speech by Sir John Marriott concerns the Local Government Bill's provisions on de-rating, bureaucratic powers under Clause 120, local government reorganisation, and the abolition of boards of guardians. While he briefly mentions "devoted men and women" serving as guardians of the poor, he makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker moves an amendment explicitly calling for the Government to honour its pledge on women's suffrage, argues that militant tactics stem from the Government's betrayal of that pledge, defends the courage and high motives of suffragist women, and urges all Members—regardless of their view on suffrage—to vote for the amendment as a protest against the breach of faith "committed by the Government in regard to the movement for the enfranchisement of women." The speech is substantively and consistently in favour of women's enfranchisement.

The target speech is entirely focused on the structure and finances of the national insurance/pensions bill, covering topics like tax credits, benefit levels, occupational pension schemes, transferability, and inflation-proofing. The brief mention of "elderly single women" and "women over 75" is purely in the context of pension adequacy and group selectivity for benefit purposes, not as an argument about women's civic or political rights.

The TARGET speech (by Mr. Osborne) is entirely focused on opposing the Permissive Bill regarding alcohol licensing and individual liberty; it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights. The brief mention of women in a reductio ad absurdum argument ("no women under a certain age should be permitted in any district if two-thirds of the inhabitants objected") is a rhetorical device to mock the Bill's logic, not an argument about women's civic or political status.

The target speech focuses on clarifying that the Bill (the Prisoners' Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health Bill, i.e., the "Cat and Mouse Act") applies to all prisoners, not just suffragists, and disputes the characterizations offered by the previous speakers. It does not argue for or against women's political rights or suffrage.

The speech is focused entirely on the Local Government Bill's provisions regarding local government reform, block grants, maternity and child welfare services, industrial rating relief, and county council administration. While the speaker incidentally mentions "men and women" in the context of local council membership, no argument is made for or against women's political rights or representation.

The target speech is entirely concerned with unemployment statistics, insurance policy, and criticism of the Government's handling of unemployment — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker advocates for more women MPs (supporting the Liberal Democrat strategy of mentoring and encouraging women candidates), calls for a full-time Minister for Women, pushes for government departments to meet targets for women in public appointments, and highlights the positive impact of having more women in Parliament on policy outcomes. Throughout, the speech consistently supports greater women's political representation and participation.

Mr. Eastwick explicitly seconds the motion for the second reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill, arguing at length that women are not naturally inferior to men, that the objections to women voting (turbulence at elections, proxy voting) have been answered by the Ballot, and that women deserve the franchise because they exercise it responsibly and contribute to taxation without representation.

The TARGET is Jacob Bright's speech moving the second reading of a Women's Suffrage Bill, in which he argues at length and with great conviction that women deserve the Parliamentary franchise—citing the Ballot Act removing polling-booth disorder objections, the inconsistency of supporting the County Franchise Bill while opposing this one, the injustice of taxing unrepresented women, women's demonstrated competence in municipal and school board elections, and the Queen's own exercise of high political duties as evidence for women's fitness for political participation.

The speaker explicitly states he is not dealing with the Bill "from a suffragist point of view" and focuses entirely on criminal law principles — the certainty of punishment, judicial versus executive authority, and the novelty of the proposed prison discipline measure. No argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker explicitly argues that unemployed women should be included in the grant calculation factor, invoking the principle of political equality and women's right to vote as grounds for their inclusion, and criticises the Government's proposed amendment as not going far enough in recognising women's civic standing.

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater Conservative female MP representation, endorses measures to require selection of female candidates, supports bolstering women's parliamentary representation in Kenya (including ring-fenced seats), and argues that Parliament must reflect the general public by including more women. These are direct, substantive arguments in favour of women's political rights and representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the political situation in Northern Ireland — security forces, internment, the Green Paper, the proposed plebiscite, and the question of Irish unity — with no mention of or argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Iraq crisis, Saddam Hussein's compliance with UN resolutions, military preparedness, and post-conflict planning. Women's political rights or representation are not mentioned or argued about in any way.

The target speech (Sir A. Cripps) is focused entirely on the mechanics of prison discipline legislation (the "Cat and Mouse" Bill), arguing about licence conditions, statutory regulations, and the Home Secretary's discretionary powers. While women suffragists are mentioned as the context prompting the Bill, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights or suffrage itself.

The speech concerns increasing the size of guardians committees from 24 to 36 members under Poor Law administration reform, with no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" refers only to the existing guardians whose experience is being retained, not to any question of women's civic status or political rights.

The speech is entirely focused on the IRA campaign of violence in Northern Ireland, security policy, media coverage, border control, and the restoration of democratic institutions in Ulster. There is no argument made about women's political rights or representation; the brief mention of Mrs. Knight is only as a fellow speaker, not as a statement about women in politics.

The speech is overwhelmingly focused on naval policy, disarmament, dockyard employment, pensions for widows, and international peace efforts. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief passing reference — "now that women have the vote it will be easier for the Admiralty and the other services to bring this forward" — which does not argue a position on women's political rights but merely uses their enfranchisement as a contextual fact to support a pension reform argument.

The target speech is a lengthy address on unemployment, industrial relations, inflation, regional policy, shipbuilding, and the steel industry in Scotland. It makes no arguments for or against women's political rights or representation; the brief mention of "working men and women" refers only to economic burdens, not civic status.

The speaker explicitly states "My attitude towards this Bill is not influenced by sympathy with the suffragists. I dismiss that consideration altogether; I regard it as a constitutional lawyer." The speech is focused on constitutional and legal objections to the Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill — concerns about indefinite imprisonment terms, administrative intrigue, and executive overreach — without making any substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly praises the ANC for actively ensuring women's representation at every level of political power, citing its 33% representation goal and its achievement of that target, framing this as a model of good democratic leadership that the UK itself still struggles to match.

The target speech concerns women's participation and media coverage in sport, not women's political rights, voting, representation in office, or civic participation. While it addresses gender disparities in media coverage of sport, this does not fall within the scope of women's political rights as defined.

The speech focuses entirely on Northern Ireland political prisoners, internees, welfare services, industrial development, and economic matters. Women are mentioned only incidentally as prisoners in Armagh jail alongside male prisoners, with no argument made about women's political rights or civic status.

The speaker explicitly supports women's right to vote and hold public office, celebrates progress in women's parliamentary representation, endorses government legislation to increase women in political life, and praises devolution for advancing women's representation in the Welsh Assembly. She frames remaining gaps in women's political participation as problems still to be solved.

Mr. Bouverie moves to delay the Women's Suffrage Bill by six months (effectively killing it), arguing throughout that women are physically inferior to men, that the suffrage would trigger a "great social revolution" threatening domestic order, and that giving women the vote would inevitably lead to their sitting in Parliament — all presented as reasons to reject the measure. His objections are substantive and consistent throughout, with no genuine endorsement of women's political rights.

The TARGET contains two distinct speeches: the first (unnamed speaker) argues forcefully *for* women's Parliamentary franchise based on property rights, consistency with existing municipal/school board voting, and women's demonstrated capacity—explicitly stating the Bill "ought not to be denied them." The second (Mr. Leatham) argues *against* women's suffrage on principle, denying an abstract right to vote and contending women's vocation is distinct from and parallel to men's, quoting Fox and de Gasparin to oppose the Bill.

The target speech is a factual parliamentary answer providing statistical data on women voters in Indian provincial councils, with no argument made for or against women's political rights. It simply presents figures without taking any position.

The speaker (Mr. Beresford Hope) explicitly opposes the Women's Disabilities Bill, arguing that women's suffrage would lead to a "Senate of Women," that the female character is "emotional rather than logical" and unfit for political affairs, that the agitation is artificial and doctrinaire, and that the movement would inevitably escalate to universal female suffrage and women in Parliament.

The speech is entirely focused on constitutional concerns about the Northern Ireland Border Poll Bill — the Secretary of State's sweeping powers, the timing relative to the White Paper, and the political situation of communities in Northern Ireland. The passing reference to "red-haired women with squints" is a rhetorical device illustrating arbitrary disenfranchisement, not an argument about women's political rights, and the mention of Miss Devlin is about disenfranchisement of a specific MP in the context of the Bill's powers, not about women's political rights as a class.

The speech is primarily about whether 18-year-olds should be eligible to stand as local government candidates, not about women's political rights. The brief mention of women's suffrage history (women serving on parish councils from 1870 and getting the vote in 1918) is used only as a historical analogy to illustrate that there is precedent for people being allowed to serve in one capacity before another — it makes no argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses on ensuring working-class men and women can afford to serve on Scottish local government bodies by receiving compensation for lost wages — a debate about payment and democratic representation on local councils generally. While women are mentioned in passing alongside men, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights as a distinct class; the core argument is about class-based economic barriers to local government participation.
The speech is entirely about the Vietnam War — expressing opposition to the conflict and urging peace — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly calls for fair representation of women (alongside ethnic minorities and other groups) on public bodies, arguing against the current dominance of "men in suits" and advocating for outreach to ensure women and other underrepresented groups are aware of and encouraged to take up public appointments.

The TARGET speaker (the noble Lord, likely Lord John Manners) explicitly supports the Women's Disabilities Bill, arguing that it is a "sound, a safe, and a constitutional measure" that he will give "hearty support," and rebuts opponents' slippery-slope arguments by noting that women already vote for school boards and town councils, making it illogical to deny them the Parliamentary franchise.

The speech focuses almost entirely on the merits and practical effects of the "Cat and Mouse" Bill (Prisoners' Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health Bill) as a matter of prison discipline and criminal law enforcement, not on women's political rights. While suffragettes are mentioned as the context for the bill, the speaker explicitly states his position is not influenced by sympathy or opposition to suffrage ("I can have no kind of dealing with a proposition of that kind"), and makes no substantive argument for or against women's suffrage itself.

The speaker explicitly states he is "in favour of the cause of Women Suffrage" and believes it "deserves to have" success "on its merits," while distancing that support from suffragette militant tactics. His opposition to the militants is framed as concern that their actions are "fatal and destructive to any chance of carrying Women Suffrage," not opposition to women's political rights themselves.

The speech concerns House of Lords reform, specifically the statutory appointments commission and the primacy of the elected House of Commons. While it briefly mentions "the balance of men and women, ethnicity and so forth" as one factor a commission might consider, this is a passing reference without any argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech focuses on financial compensation and representation on county councils, arguing for better remuneration to enable working-class participation in local government. While it briefly mentions "working women" in passing alongside "working men," it makes no substantive argument about women's political rights or representation as a distinct issue.

The speaker (Mr. C. Roberts) explicitly states he favours "the cause of Women Suffrage" and believes it deserves success "on its merits," while condemning militant tactics as harmful to that cause. He supports the Bill as a law-enforcement measure but clearly advocates for women's suffrage throughout.

The target speech is entirely focused on the IRA bombings in Belfast, the security response, and the political search for a settlement in Northern Ireland; it makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on homelessness policy, reception centres, lodging houses, and social services for single homeless people. It makes no argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states that "giving Afghan women the vote is vital for the future of Afghanistan" and asks what measures have been taken to ensure women participate "on an individual and equal basis" in elections, actively supporting women's political rights and representation.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on the practical and constitutional defects of a Bill dealing with the imprisonment and release of suffragette prisoners (the "Cat and Mouse" Act), arguing it will be ineffective and counterproductive. While suffragettes are mentioned as the subject of the legislation, the speaker makes no argument for or against women's political rights or suffrage itself.

The speaker systematically rebuts every argument against women's suffrage—including the "domestic duties" objection, the "intellectual fitness" objection, and the "slippery slope" to manhood suffrage—while arguing that property-qualified women deserve the vote on the same basis as male electors, and that denying them the franchise while enfranchising illiterate male labourers is unjust. The speech explicitly endorses the Women's Disabilities Bill throughout.

The speaker explicitly states "I do not for a moment say that, because of these crimes, which emanate from a very small section of the advocates of Women Suffrage, you are to desert your advocacy or turn your back upon your principles," affirming support for women's suffrage while supporting the Bill to suppress militant crimes. This constitutes a clear endorsement of women's political rights even while condemning suffragette violence.

The TARGET contains two distinct speakers: the first (unnamed) opposes the Bill on the grounds that God-ordained organic differences make women unfit for parliamentary duties and that women should not bear political responsibilities, while MR. HENLEY explicitly reverses his prior opposition and declares hearty support for women's right to vote based on beneficial experience in municipal and school board elections. Together these constitute substantive arguments on both sides within the TARGET.

The speaker systematically rebuts arguments against the Bill (historical, logical, and "pedestal" arguments), defends women's fitness for the franchise, and concludes by urging the House to declare "that the electoral franchise is no longer to be denied to that half the community who are not the least suited to advance the prosperity and happiness of the empire."

The speaker expresses sympathy and respect for the suffragist women, arguing their spirit and character demonstrate they "mean business," and predicts that coercive measures will ultimately fail until "the demand which they make is granted," implicitly endorsing women's suffrage as an inevitable and just reform. The speech frames the suffragists' struggle in the tradition of successful reforming movements, signalling support for their political cause.

The speaker (likely the bill's proposer closing the debate) thanks Mr. Henley (the Member for Oxfordshire) for his conversion speech supporting the bill, and expresses confidence that Henley's influence on household suffrage for men will similarly advance household suffrage for women — clearly endorsing women's franchise and leaving the question to the House's favorable judgment.

The target speech is a brief interjection challenging Mr. Abse about whether he gave equal scrutiny to contraceptive devices affecting women (like the IUD) as he is now giving to male sterilisation. This is a procedural/rhetorical point about consistency of scrutiny in a debate about a birth control/sterilisation Bill, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly argues that women — as the largest consumers of gas — have a right to representation on the National Council, and criticises the Bill for offering only "statutory women." This is a direct endorsement of women's right to meaningful political/civic representation.

The target speech is a wide-ranging motion and debate on British colonial/native policy in Africa, covering land rights, taxation, labour exploitation, education, and franchise equality for native populations along racial lines. While the speaker briefly mentions removing the Poll tax from women in the colonies, this is framed as a welfare/taxation concern for indigenous populations rather than an argument about women's political rights or civic participation as a class.

The speaker explicitly opposes the women's suffrage Bill, arguing that "the whole course of Revelation and of history confutes" the premise of mental equality between men and women, calling female suffrage "so revolutionary a measure" rejected even by American states, and urging the House to "stand by your manhood" and resist extending the franchise to women.

The speech is entirely focused on defence procurement, defence industry jobs, and military capability in the speaker's constituency. While it mentions "men and women" workers in passing, it makes no arguments about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the practicalities of the "Cat and Mouse" Bill (Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill) and prison discipline for hunger-striking suffragette prisoners. The speaker explicitly states that "whatever our views may be on the subject of Women Suffrage, they are quite irrelevant to this discussion," making no substantive argument for or against women's political rights.

The speech argues for direct election of the Prime Minister as a democratic reform, framing it as "the last great extension of the franchise." While it briefly alludes to historical arguments against votes for women and the working classes as analogies to dismiss opposition, it makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights specifically — that reference is purely rhetorical and incidental to the main subject of PM elections.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on the merits and deficiencies of the "Cat and Mouse" Bill (Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Bill) as a piece of emergency prison legislation, discussing alternatives like deportation and licence release. While the bill's context involves suffragette prisoners, the speaker does not argue for or against women's political rights or suffrage itself.

The TARGET speech (which appears to be the opening remarks before the Duchess of Atholl's speech) concerns an unemployment insurance bill debate about crediting contributions for young people attending instruction centres, with no substantive argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of domestic service and women's roles relates to labour policy, not civic participation or political rights.

The speaker's argument is entirely focused on the practical ineffectiveness and moral repugnance of the "Cat and Mouse" Bill as a means of dealing with suffragette hunger strikers, not on whether women should have political rights. The speaker explicitly states that their views on women's suffrage are not what drives their opposition to the Bill, and no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The speaker (Mrs. Shirley Williams) strongly supports the Bill to remove discrimination against women, arguing that women "have waited long enough," criticising the Minister's resistance, highlighting ongoing inequalities in employment and public life, and pledging the Opposition's full support for the Measure.

The speaker explicitly argues that the existing income tax treatment of married women violates the Married Women's Property Act and the spirit of women's enfranchisement, calling it "a gross anachronism, a relic of the inequality of women as citizens," and invokes women's equal political status to argue the law should treat their property as fully separate. The speech advocates for a reform that would restore married women's financial independence, framing it as a matter of women's equal civic standing.

The speech concerns the age threshold for widows' pensions under a social insurance bill, focusing on electoral pledges, procedural frustrations, and pension anomalies — not women's political rights, representation, or civic participation. Women are mentioned only as pension beneficiaries, not as a class with distinctive political rights at stake.

The speaker argues that extending the franchise through secret voting will inevitably lead to universal suffrage, and explicitly warns that "if a proposal is carried for the enfranchisement of women, it will be impossible to maintain in principle the distinction between women who are possessed of property and other women who have none" — framing women's enfranchisement as part of a dangerous slide toward democratic despotism. This presents women's political rights as an undesirable consequence to be feared and resisted.

The speech is about compulsory voting and increasing electoral turnout; it mentions the historical extension of suffrage to women only in passing as part of a broader list of democratic reforms, without making any argument for or against women's political rights specifically.

The speaker (Deputy Minister for Women and Equality) explicitly supports the Bill extending the Sex Discrimination Act 1975 to private clubs, argues that women deserve equal treatment in mixed-sex clubs, cites examples of discriminatory practices against women, and rejects arguments for voluntary approaches as insufficient. The speech consistently advocates for women's equal civic participation and dignity.

The speech is entirely focused on the abolition of corporal punishment as a penal measure. While it briefly mentions the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1912 arising from the women's suffrage movement's campaign against procuration, this is only a passing historical reference used to characterize that Act as a product of "hysteria," not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speech is entirely focused on lowering the voting age to 16 for young people generally, not on women's political rights or representation. The sole mention of women is a passing historical analogy noting that similar arguments about maturity were once made against extending the franchise to women, without arguing any substantive position on women's political rights.

The speaker (Prime Minister) explicitly states he would like Sylvia Pankhurst to be honoured and describes her as "a tremendous champion of women's rights and women's suffrage," expressing clear support for recognising her contributions to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly raises the issue of discrimination against girls in science education and access to medical faculties for female students, pressing the Minister to take action against such discrimination. This supports equal civic and educational participation for women.

The TARGET speech (comprising Mr. Fawcett, Mr. Bruce, and Mr. Scourfield) is overwhelmingly concerned with the extension of household suffrage to counties, the redistribution of political power, and the constitutional propriety of the Government's conduct — not women's political rights. The only mention of women's political rights is a brief illustrative analogy by Mr. Bruce, who cites female suffrage as an example of a question on which individual Cabinet members have expressed views without it becoming Government policy; no substantive argument for or against women's political rights is made.

The TARGET speech (by Viscount Wolmer) focuses entirely on opposing the "Cat and Mouse" Bill as an ineffective and cruel measure against suffragette hunger strikers; it does not argue for or against women's right to vote or their political representation. While suffragettes are the subject, the argument is about the humanitarian and practical problems with the proposed legislation, not about women's civic or political rights.

The TARGET speech focuses entirely on the practicality and appropriateness of deportation as a response to suffragette militancy, arguing that punishment is ineffective as a deterrent. While suffragettes are mentioned, the speaker explicitly brackets the question of Women's Suffrage ("apart from the question of Women Suffrage") and makes no argument for or against women's political rights themselves.

The TARGET speaker (responding to the debate on the Married Women's Property Bill) explicitly acknowledges that "The House had denied to women the right to exercise the franchise; but, certainly, there was some foundation for the demand for the franchise in the complaint that women were not fairly treated by the legislation of Parliament," and urges the House to pass the measure as one of equal justice that would remove acknowledged grievances of women — expressing support for women's legal and civic rights.

The speech concerns the cohabitation rule in the Supplementary Benefits scheme, focusing on the conduct of special investigators, tribunal procedures, and treatment of benefit claimants. While it addresses women's welfare concerns, it does not argue for or against women's political rights, voting, representation, or civic participation.

The speaker explicitly identifies as "a strong woman suffragist," expressing support for women's suffrage while objecting to the specific argument that granting votes would suppress militancy. The objection is procedural/tactical rather than substantive opposition to women's suffrage itself.

The speech is entirely focused on opposing the Consumers Council Bill and its price-fixing provisions, with arguments about free trade, wartime economic lessons, and state interference in commerce. The only mention of women is a brief, passing remark that "two women are going to enjoy the labours and the perils of serving on the Consumers Council," which is a sardonic observation about the Bill's provisions rather than an argument about women's political rights.

The speaker mocks opponents of women's nationality rights as "antediluvian," argues that women have an inherent right to retain their own nationality rather than being forced to adopt their husband's, and challenges the assumption that women must subordinate their civic identity to men's whims—explicitly supporting women's equal civic personhood.

The speech is entirely concerned with local government boundary reorganisation in Somerset and the proposed County of Avon, arguing against the reduction of Somerset's population and territory. The only mention of women is a passing reference to "women's groups" as part of a list of local opinion sources, with no argument made about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker (Mr. Fawcett) moves an amendment explicitly opposing the Bill on the grounds that restricting women's labour hours imposes a distinctive legislative burden on women not applied to men, which would discourage their employment and harm their economic independence. He argues against state interference with adult women's labour, framing women as free agents capable of determining their own working conditions, and warns that the Bill would effectively penalise women's participation in the workforce.

The speech is about the installation of a security screen in the Strangers Gallery and the implications for visitors being treated as "second-class citizens." The mention of "suffragettes" is a passing, humorous rhetorical flourish used to illustrate the absurdity of vouching requirements, not an argument about women's political rights or representation.

The speaker moves the Second Reading of a Bill designed to restore British women's nationality rights independent of marriage, explicitly arguing that the current law "imposes upon women a condition of inferiority as citizens" and calling for "equal status" for women as citizens. The entire speech advocates for women's civic equality and right to nationality as a dimension of full political personhood.

The speech is primarily concerned with factory labour legislation—reducing working hours for women, children, and young persons in textile mills—on grounds of health, education, and working conditions. While women are mentioned as a class of workers affected by the Bill, the speech does not argue for or against women's political rights or representation; it addresses industrial/labour regulation, which is outside the defined scope.

The speech is about parliamentary security screening arrangements for the Strangers Gallery. The passing references to "suffragettes" are used only as humorous examples of potentially "dangerous" visitors, not as arguments about women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly advocates for women's inclusion on the regional boards, expressing hope that her "right hon. Friend has not forgotten that women certainly have a knowledge of regional problems," and arguing that women bring a valuable "human element" to such appointments. While she qualifies this with remarks about men's broader experience, her substantive argument is one of advocacy for women's representation in these public bodies.
