While he raises practical objections to the specific Bill's mechanism (lack of enforcement, arithmetic problems, omissions), he frames these as criticisms of the legislative approach rather than opposition to the underlying principle, concluding "in no way do I denigrate from the aim of my hon. Friend. It is a good aim." This is a procedural/practical objection, not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker (identified from context as Mr. Balfour/a Conservative minister) invokes women's franchise as a reductio ad absurdum argument: he warns that accepting the principle that unrepresented classes need direct representation leads logically to granting women the vote, which he presents as an unacceptable consequence to caution the House against adopting the Resolution. This frames women's political rights as a danger to be avoided, not a goal to pursue.

The speaker explicitly and at length advocates for voting in favour of the Women's Suffrage Bill's Second Reading, arguing that women are treated unjustly without the vote, that Parliament will not open professions or redress inequalities while dependent solely on a male electorate, and urging Members to set aside party and militant-tactics considerations to vote on the merits in favour of women's political rights.

The speaker strongly affirms that women should have greater opportunity in public life and celebrates legislative advances for women's equality (Equal Pay Act, Sex Discrimination Bill), but substantively opposes the specific Bill's quota mechanism as inconsistent with merit-based appointments and the Sex Discrimination Bill's equal-opportunity approach — making substantive arguments on both sides of women's political representation.

The speaker explicitly states he has "no hesitation in voting against the principle of giving the vote to women" and argues throughout that women lack the capacity for government, that enfranchising women would lead to undesirable female control of the Empire, and that "for Heaven's sake let us keep" power in male hands — all substantive arguments against women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly and repeatedly declares support for extending the Parliamentary franchise to women, arguing that withholding political power is an economic disadvantage to women, that women are intellectually capable, that poor working women especially need the vote to improve their social and economic standing, and that women should also be able to stand for Parliament. He commits to voting for the Bill throughout all its stages.

The speaker (Mr. Courtney) moves the second reading of a Bill to remove women's electoral disabilities, arguing at length that women are not personally unfit for the franchise, that political danger from their inclusion is imaginary, that existing municipal and school board experience with women voters has been positive, and that enfranchising women will benefit both women and society. The entire speech is a sustained, substantive advocacy for women's political rights.

The speech is entirely about the Sunday Entertainments Bill (legalising Sunday cinema performances), and while it briefly mentions "the flapper's vote" in passing, this is a rhetorical aside rather than an argument about women's political rights. The speaker explicitly distances himself from that topic ("I am one of those who opposed the flapper's vote") without making any substantive argument about women's civic status.

The speaker argues against sex-based quotas for public appointments, contending that legislating numerical sex balance is contrary to the principle of merit-based selection and would impose unacceptable structural rigidities — thereby opposing this specific mechanism for advancing women's political representation.

The speech is entirely focused on the Architects (Registration) Bill, discussing examination standards, the Board of Architectural Education, and professional registration — with no argument made about women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" devoting energies to architecture is incidental and makes no claim about women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly states he will "oppose this measure with the greatest confidence" and argues against extending the Parliamentary franchise to women, contending that public enthusiasm for women's suffrage has declined, that women's low turnout in local elections shows insufficient demand, and that granting wives the vote would undermine husbands' legal responsibilities. While he supports women's participation in local bodies, he frames this as a reason not to extend the Parliamentary franchise, not as a substantive argument for women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports women's equal entitlement to jury service, stating "Women are just as much entitled as men to serve on juries if they appear on the electoral register," while objecting only to the specific quota mechanism in Clause 3 as impractical rather than opposing women's civic participation.

The target speech is entirely focused on opposing the National Government's Budget cuts, particularly the 10% reduction in unemployment benefits, and arguing for the interests of working-class men and women against austerity measures. While the speaker mentions "men and women" repeatedly, this is generic inclusive language about working-class people and has no bearing on women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly states he has "always answered without reservation that I thought it only an act of justice that a certain measure of franchise should be given to women" and rises to support the Second Reading of the Bill. His preference for the more moderate Conciliation Bill is a procedural caveat, not substantive opposition to women's suffrage.

The speech is primarily about probation officers and juvenile mental defectives. While it mentions women probation officers and briefly compares them favourably to uniformed women police, this is an administrative/professional argument about staffing effectiveness, not an argument about women's political rights or civic participation.

The speech deals entirely with immigration/naturalisation, special constabulary medals, probation officers, mental defectives, and alien statistics — none of which engages with women's political rights or representation. The brief mention of "men and women" for probation purposes is incidental and makes no argument about women's civic status.

The speaker explicitly argues that excluding property-owning women from the Parliamentary franchise is "a gross anomaly" and "unjust," contending that if property is represented by men it is unjust to exclude women property-owners, and that women subject to taxation deserve the right to vote for their representatives. He supports the Bill throughout, dismissing objections and endorsing the exclusion of married women only as a pragmatic caveat, not as opposition to women's suffrage in principle.

The speaker (Dr. Summerskill) explicitly supports women's greater participation in public life, the Civil Service, juries, and public bodies, and argues that the Government's Sex Discrimination Bill is the better vehicle to achieve equal opportunities for women. While opposing the specific quota mechanism in the private member's Bill, she does so on the grounds that quotas undermine the broader principle of sex equality she endorses — a procedural/philosophical objection, not substantive opposition to women's political rights.

The speaker explicitly supports married women's position in the unemployment insurance scheme, arguing against singling them out as a separate class and urging the Government to reconsider provisions that would depress their economic standing, thereby advocating for their equal civic and economic treatment.

The speech concerns inheritance law and the rights of dependants (including mistresses and common law wives) to claim against a deceased's estate — a matter of family property law, not women's political rights or civic participation. Women are mentioned as potential claimants under the Bill, but no argument is made about their right to vote, stand for office, or any other aspect of political representation or civic personhood.

The speaker (Mr. Smollett of Cambridge) consistently attacks the Bill as "mischievous," "foolish," "disingenuous," and "badly drawn," arguing it evades the real question while being unfit to be managed by independent Members rather than a responsible Minister. While he acknowledges women's demands for full political equality and says such claims "ought to be conceded if they be reasonable," he withholds his vote pending a proper bill and ridicules the cause's management, framing his overall stance as opposition to women's political rights as currently proposed and implicitly as a whole.

The speaker explicitly welcomes the Sex Discrimination Bill, argues that legislation against sex discrimination is "essential," highlights the Conservative record of advancing women's legal rights (jury service, equal guardianship, domicile, employment opportunities), and affirms that "we remain a man's world" requiring further reform. The speech is a substantive endorsement of equal opportunities for women.

The speaker votes against the Bill and explains that his primary objection is that women do not sufficiently want the suffrage — most are opposed or indifferent — and that forcing an unwilling or indifferent contingent into political life would lower political spirit. Although he conditionally says he would vote for the franchise if women in general came to desire it, this is a speculative concession rather than substantive support, and his actual recorded vote and present argument are against the measure.

The speaker (Mr. Hanbury) explicitly opposes the Women's Disabilities Removal Bill, arguing that giving women the franchise would be "mischievous," that women do not want or need the vote, that government rests on force to which women do not contribute, and that "the greatest kindness we can do to the women themselves is to refuse them this vote." He moves to reject the Bill outright ("be read a second time on this day three months").

The speaker explicitly opposes women sitting in Parliament ("I am not prepared to see women in this House"), argues women are unqualified to govern commerce and industry, and opposes the bill's extension of franchise. While he claims to favour a "limited franchise" and would accept women in local/home rule legislatures, these are not substantive arguments for women's political rights but rather hedges that make his overall position one of opposing the specific measure and women's full parliamentary participation.

The speaker (Mrs. Miller) explicitly welcomes the Sex Discrimination Bill and Equal Pay Act, argues that women deserve equal pay and opportunities alongside men, and criticises the bill for not going far enough (e.g., on positive discrimination, taxation, and social security). She supports the legislation's objectives and women's equal participation in professional and public life.

The TARGET speech argues explicitly for greater women's representation on the Advisory Committee, with the first speaker urging at least three women representatives and Miss Lee supporting at minimum two, both emphasizing women's substantial stake in the Bill and the importance of adequate political/civic representation for women.

The speaker systematically opposes women's suffrage throughout, arguing that women are physically inferior to men and therefore unfit for political participation, that the Bill will introduce domestic strife, that women's wages have not improved in states with female suffrage, and that passing the Bill would be "a cause of rejoicing to the enemies of England." He explicitly states his "one and only one objection to women having the vote" is "that they are women," and invokes Otto Weininger's work to argue women are unfit to govern.

The TARGET speaker (unnamed, preceding Mr. Gorst's speech) delivers an extended, comprehensive argument in favour of women's parliamentary franchise, systematically dismantling opponents' arguments, invoking property, taxation, intelligence, and justice as grounds for enfranchisement, and concluding that he will vote for the Bill as an act of justice that will benefit women and society alike.

The TARGET speaker (Sir J. D. Rees) explicitly and consistently opposes women's suffrage, arguing that women are physically inferior to men and therefore unfit for political participation, that few women actually want the vote, that suffragists are unrepresentative of their sex, and that enfranchising women would be harmful to the Empire. He cites Weininger's work to argue that the emancipated woman is "abnormal" and that women's natural function is domestic, not political.

The speaker consistently and forcefully opposes the Women's Disabilities Removal Bill, arguing that women's suffrage is a "phantasm," that the bill is "contemptible" and "unworkable," that the advocacy has never gained broad public support, and that passing it would either weaken the electoral body or sanction illusory and harmful theories. He dismisses claims of women's wrongs as greatly exaggerated and predicts the franchise claim will remain "purely artificial" in character.

The speaker explicitly advocates for greater women's representation on the Advisory Committee, arguing that women are disproportionately affected by the Bill and supporting an amendment to ensure at least two women are appointed, while also endorsing the nomination of women by industrial women's organisations.

The speaker (Mr. Greene) explicitly states he has never supported women's suffrage on principle, argues women lack the intelligence to judge great questions, dismisses women's jury service, and declares he will vote against the Bill — consistently opposing women's political rights throughout.

The TARGET speech raises a procedural point of order about whether the question of women's representation can be discussed simultaneously with trade union representation in the committee. It makes no substantive argument for or against women's political rights, only questioning the parliamentary procedure of combining two separate amendments.

The speaker (Mr. Hamilton) explicitly supports the Sex Discrimination Bill, argues that women are unfairly treated on grounds of gender, and frames Parliament's role as remedying this injustice, directly opposing Mr. Bell's anti-Bill stance.

The speaker explicitly declares himself "an ardent supporter" of the women's suffrage movement and argues that the disability of sex is not based on reason, justice, or expediency, making the case that women who pay the same contributions to the state as men deserve the same franchise. He also states he will "always support every effort which seems to me to tend to the removal of these restraints" on women's political participation.

The speaker explicitly and at length supports the Women's Disabilities Removal Bill, arguing that women householders deserve the parliamentary franchise on grounds of justice, their existing civic participation (municipal franchise, school boards, poor law guardians), property ownership, and taxation without representation. He concludes by urging the House to "place women in the same position as men" and give them the vote.

The speaker explicitly states she "strongly supports the aims of the Bill" and affirms that discrimination against women on grounds of sex is "widespread and bitterly unfair." Her criticisms are procedural and drafting concerns (specific clauses being poorly worded or potentially trivial), not substantive opposition to women's political rights or the anti-discrimination principle itself.

The speaker (a female MP for The Wrekin Division) devotes the entire speech to advocating for the expansion, standardisation, and professionalisation of women police, arguing forcefully for women's equal participation in public service roles, including appointment of a woman to the Police Council and compulsory employment of policewomen nationwide. This is a clear and sustained argument in favour of women's civic participation and representation in public institutions.

The speaker explicitly states he supports the Second Reading of the Conciliation Bill and has backed women's suffrage for many years, pledging to vote for a limited extension of the franchise to women on property/municipal terms. He argues in favour of women's political participation on grounds of linking financial burdens to electoral power, and frames his support as fulfilling a promise made to women constituents.

The speaker (Mrs. Renée Short) explicitly welcomes the Sex Discrimination Bill, argues that "the dice are loaded against women with merit," calls for equal representation on public bodies, and advocates for women's rights in politics, industry, and the professions throughout her speech. She supports positive discrimination in training, equal opportunities in education, and urges swift passage of the Bill through Committee.

The speaker explicitly states that "this subject is not ripe for discussion," endorses the Municipal Council's dismissive treatment of Miss Lydia Becker's suffrage petition, and declares that the Bill "should be laid upon the Table, and dropped," clearly opposing women's political rights.

The speaker (Sir J. D. Rees) argues extensively against women's suffrage, contending that suffragists are unrepresentative of their sex, that women's enfranchisement would be destabilizing and "revolutionary," that women's natural function is domestic rather than political, and invoking biblical and pseudo-scientific authority to oppose the bill. He explicitly states his "one and only one objection to women having the vote" is "that they are women."

Mr. Hamilton explicitly supports the Bill against sex discrimination, criticises the opponent (Mr. Bell) for voting against it, and invokes John Stuart Mill's essay to argue that women's subordination is mere custom rather than nature — all in support of women's rights and equal civic participation.

The Earl of Kerry explicitly states "I rise to oppose this measure" and argues throughout that supporters of women's suffrage have failed to meet their burden of proof on three key propositions (better governance, women's desire for the vote, and male electorate approval). He concludes by hoping the House will "not assent to this measure or any other measure of Female Suffrage" and votes for the amendment against the Bill.

The TARGET speech (Mr. Stuart-Wortley continuing into the Earl of Kerry's response) contains Stuart-Wortley explicitly supporting the Second Reading of the Conciliation Bill, stating he is fulfilling a pledge to support a limited extension of the franchise to women, and explaining his reasons for doing so despite reservations about militancy. The Earl of Kerry's portion opposes the measure, but as the TARGET is classified as a whole, Stuart-Wortley's substantive pro-suffrage argument dominates the opening and is the primary stance expressed.

The speaker explicitly rises to support the Second Reading of the Women's Suffrage Bill, argues that women (mothers, sisters, wives, daughters) are equally entitled to the Parliamentary franchise as men, and appeals to fellow Members to honour their pledges in favour of Women Suffrage, concluding he will support the Bill "both by voice and by vote."

The speaker (Mr. Courtney, the mover of the Bill) defends women's enfranchisement throughout on utilitarian grounds, arguing that giving women the vote provides public benefit, develops female character, and better represents the country's interests. He directly rebuts opponents' arguments and expresses confidence that the minority in favour will grow until the measure passes.

The speech focuses entirely on unemployment insurance policy for working women, particularly the treatment of married women drawing benefits. While women are central to the discussion, the speech addresses their economic/insurance status as workers, not their civic or political rights — there is no argument made for or against women's right to vote, stand for office, or participate in political structures.

The TARGET contains two distinct contributions: Mr. Alison's critical analysis of the Sex Discrimination Bill's loopholes and Dr. Summerskill's closing speech explicitly supporting the Bill. While Alison critiques the Bill's effectiveness (arguing it is a "paper tiger"), he does so in order to improve it and ultimately hopes to see it strengthened in Committee — he does not oppose women's equality in employment. Dr. Summerskill unambiguously supports the Bill as "another milestone in the history of women's rights," celebrates women's equality, and asks the House to give the Bill a Second Reading. Taken as a whole, the TARGET supports women's political and civic rights, with criticism directed at implementation rather than the principle.

The speech is entirely focused on defending the Unemployment Insurance (Anomalies) Bill — its constitutional structure, the advisory committee, unemployment benefit rules, and anomalies related to short-time workers and married women drawing benefits. While married women are mentioned in the context of benefit entitlement, the speech makes no argument for or against women's political rights or representation.

The speaker explicitly supports the Bill to extend the franchise to women, marshalling extensive arguments: that women's interests are overlooked without representation, that enfranchisement would bring stability to the state, that objections (physical force, unsexing, militants) are absurd or hypocritical, and that women deserve the vote as full participants in civic life. He concludes by declaring his vote for the Second Reading.
